- Nuclear transcription factors/chromatin regulators: acidic/Ser‑rich low‑complexity activation domains and flexible tails.
- Protein kinases and phosphatases: Ser/Thr‑rich regulatory termini and disordered linkers.
- Testis‑biased and cancer/testis antigens: prion‑like, low‑complexity IDRs.
- Bacterial/archaeal proteins: shorter polar low‑complexity segments/linkers within otherwise structured proteins.
- Cluster examples: plant gametophyte development protein—long disordered C‑terminal tail; secreted kininogen family—N‑terminal low‑complexity region after signal peptide.

Summary: Short linear motifs in intrinsically disordered/low-complexity regions, often S/T/P/G- and aromatic-rich, that include proteolytic-processing/PTM hotspots and flexible linkers adjacent to transmembrane segments; the feature favors flexible coils or short amphipathic helices and systematically avoids hydrophobic transmembrane cores
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks scattered across low-pLDDT/disordered segments; enrichment at N- or C-terminal regions, within or adjacent to cleavage and modification sites (e.g., dibasic Arg/Lys, sulfotyrosine, amidated peptide ends), and in short helices preceding/connecting to transmembrane anchors; depletion in well-structured transmembrane helices and globular cores
Exemplars: - Viral single-pass membrane immunomodulators (e.g., BNLF2a): activation in the pre-transmembrane linker/short helix and disordered N-terminus; no activation within the transmembrane helix.
- Bacteriocins/antimicrobial peptides (e.g., enterocins): activation across unstructured segments and short C-terminal helical stretches characteristic of flexible, bioactive peptides.
- Peptide hormone precursors (e.g., cholecystokinin proprotein): peaks at processing/PTM hotspots—dibasic cleavage arginine, sulfated tyrosine at the bioactive N-terminus, and the amidated C-terminal Phe within the mature peptide region.
- Herpesvirus cytoplasmic envelopment proteins: sparse peaks distributed across intrinsically disordered regions with very low structural confidence, independent of stable domain annotations.

Summary: Residue-level detector for the N‑terminal extracellular segments of secreted preproproteins, especially immediately downstream of signal peptide/processing cleavages and within small cysteine‑rich bioactive peptides (toxins/antimicrobial peptides); it favors disordered, low‑confidence regions and frequently targets cysteines that form disulfide bonds or adjacent residues
Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks; enriched near the start of the mature chain (just after signal peptide cleavage) and on/adjacent to cysteines in disulfide‑bonded secreted peptides; predominantly in low‑pLDDT, flexible coils/loops; little to no activation in the helical core of signal peptides or well‑structured domains
Exemplars: - Kininogen/bradykinin precursors: scattered peaks in disordered regions of the secreted proprotein, including near processed peptide boundaries but not confined to the peptide itself
- Venom peptide toxins (e.g., scoloptoxins): a peak at the signal peptide C‑terminus (cleavage site) and additional sparse sites within the mature toxin in low‑confidence regions
- Crustacean antimicrobial peptides (penaeidins): strong peaks on disulfide‑bonded cysteines and immediately adjacent residues, with occasional weak activation within the signal peptide
- Secreted fungal cell wall proteins: peaks confined to the N‑terminal portion of the mature secreted region with very low structural confidence; absent over the signal peptide and structured C‑terminus
- Secreted lectins: peaks near the N‑terminus of the mature chain and within unstructured extracellular loops, including sites proximal to N‑glycosylation motifs

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity N‑terminal regions enriched in serine/proline/glycine with scattered basic (Lys/Arg) and aromatic residues, used as transactivation/interaction or propeptide processing segments across diverse proteins (TFs, NF‑Y, small secreted peptide precursors, viral proteins, glycine‑rich proteins)
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short-to-extended stretches, typically starting near the extreme N‑terminus; local peaks may occur at short linear motifs (e.g., SP/TP phosphorylation motifs, dibasic Lys/Arg processing sites, and aromatic hotspots) but the signal broadly follows the low‑complexity IDR
Exemplars: - Homeobox and forkhead transcription factors: serine/proline‑rich N‑terminal transactivation domains and low‑complexity tails upstream of the DNA‑binding domain
- NF‑Y subunits (A/B/C): disordered terminal regions flanking the histone‑fold that mediate transcriptional activation and partner recruitment
- Neuropeptide and small secreted peptide precursors (including plant signaling peptides): propeptide segments with dibasic Lys/Arg cleavage motifs and C‑terminal glycine for amidation within low‑complexity stretches
- Viral regulatory/structural proteins: N‑terminal low‑complexity regions rich in Ser/Pro/Gly and basic residues that engage host factors
- Glycine‑rich proteins/peptides: glycine‑rich low‑complexity segments, often at N‑termini
- Enzymes, transporters, and other membrane proteins: flexible N‑terminal cytosolic tails or linkers enriched in S/P/G/K/R functioning as regulatory IDRs

Summary: Acidic surface patches and DE-rich sequence motifs (e.g., DxD/DxE/OPCA-like) that create negatively charged interfaces for binding partners or cations/metal cofactors; realized both in ordered domains (such as the PB1 acidic interface) and in acidic low‑complexity segments across diverse proteins
Activation pattern: Residual-level peaks concentrated on Asp/Glu (with nearby S/T/N), often forming short clustered stretches on solvent-exposed strands/loops; multiple peaks per local segment are common. Occasional single dominant peaks occur within structured domains (e.g., a specific Asp in a PB1 β‑strand). Activation is disfavored on basic or strongly hydrophobic residues.
Exemplars: - Plant Aux/IAA transcriptional regulators (PB1 domain): activation on the OPCA-like acidic triad/patch in the PB1 interface (e.g., a key Asp in a β‑strand).
- Chromatin/transcription regulators: acidic activation/repression segments and acidic patches at protein–protein interaction surfaces.
- WW domain/HECT E3 ubiquitin ligase/Hippo pathway proteins: acidic Ca2+-coordinating loops in C2 domains and acidic low‑complexity regulatory regions adjacent to interaction modules.
- Bacterial cell wall biosynthesis/remodeling enzymes (e.g., glycosyltransferases): DxD/DxE metal-binding loops at catalytic sites.
- Two‑component signaling proteins (hybrid histidine kinases/response regulators) and oxygen sensors: acidic Asp-centered active sites/patches in receiver-like domains.
- Secreted/extracellular enzymes: calcium/metal-binding acidic loops (DxD/DxE) and acidic surface patches on hydrolases/adhesion modules.
- Fungal FAD-linked oxidoreductases/secondary metabolism enzymes: conserved acidic residues and nearby acidic loops around FAD/active sites that form interaction or catalytic patches.
- Centromere/kinetochore and spindle/centrosome proteins: acidic repeats/patches used in macromolecular assembly interfaces.
- Mitochondrial ribosomal proteins and complex I assembly factors: surface acidic stretches mediating assembly contacts.
- Viral proteins: acidic low‑complexity segments that mediate host-factor interactions.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity repeat/linker tracts enriched for polar/charged residues (Q/N/E/D/H/P/R); common in secreted/extracellular or luminal segments and also in cytosolic/nuclear scaffolds; includes His-rich metal-binding patches, Q/N-rich prion-like/repeat modules, and low-complexity propeptides/linkers in secreted enzymes.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous low-complexity/repetitive segments; strongest in extracellular/luminal stretches (often following signal peptides) and in flexible linkers or flanking tails of repeat-domain proteins; little or no isolated peaks within structured catalytic cores.
Exemplars:
- Plant hydroxyproline-rich glycoproteins (extensins/PRPs): activation across Tyr/His/Pro-rich repetitive cell-wall regions.
- Histidine-rich secreted proteins and metal-binding patches: activation on His/Gln/Asp/Glu-rich tracts that chelate metals.
- Multi-C2H2 zinc-finger and other His/Cys metal-coordinating proteins: activation on low-complexity His/Gln-rich linkers or repeat arrays adjacent to the fingers rather than the core motifs.
- TALE-like repeat effectors (bacterial): activation along RVD-bearing repeat arrays enriched in polar/acidic residues.
- Plasmodium low-complexity proteins: activation on long Asn/Gln-rich prion-like segments.
- Neuropeptide/peptide-hormone precursors (basal metazoans): activation across Q/R/P-rich low-complexity propeptide regions between cleavage sites.
- Membrane receptors/adhesins and multispan transporters (e.g., MS4A, MFS/FLVCR): activation on luminal/extracellular low-complexity loops.
- Golgi/vesicle-tethering coiled-coil scaffolds (e.g., COG subunits): activation on acidic/Q-rich low-complexity linkers.
- WD-repeat RNA processing/cleavage factors (e.g., WDR33): activation on low-complexity N/C-terminal tails flanking WD propellers.
- Secreted enzymes (e.g., metalloproteinases, acetylcholinesterase): activation on signal-proximal propeptides, glycosylated insertions, or flexible linkers, not the catalytic cores.
- Testis/germline-associated low-complexity proteins: activation on prion-like Q/H/P-rich regions.
- Elastic/repetitive structural proteins (elastin-/resilin-like or repeat-rich linkers): activation on polar/charged, low-complexity repeats.

Summary: Short, glycine/alanine-rich hydrophobic alpha-helices that insert into or span membranes—most often single-pass tail anchors at the C-terminus, but also fusion peptides and pore/translocation helices—frequently containing GxxxG/glycine‑zipper motifs used for helix packing.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 15–25-residue hydrophobic segments, with residue-level peaks on small residues (especially glycine) within the helix (e.g., GxxxG). Activations typically coincide with annotated/predicted transmembrane helices or membrane-inserting amphipathic helices, are often concentrated near the extreme C-terminus (tail anchors), and can appear as multiple short activated segments in multi-pass or multi-helical proteins; N-terminal signal peptides are generally not favored relative to internal/tail-anchor helices.
Exemplars: Viral envelope/fusion glycoproteins (paramyxovirus F, coronavirus spike, retroviral Env): strong activation on the C-terminal transmembrane anchor; paramyxovirus F also activates on the N-terminal fusion peptide; Baculovirus per os infectivity factor 5: activation on the C-terminal single-pass TM helix; Toxoplasma dense granule proteins: activation on the C-terminal tail-anchor TM helix; Magnetospirillum magnetosome proteins (e.g., Mms6): activation across the single transmembrane helix and immediate lumenal flank; Bacteriocins/pyocins/colicins: activation within the hydrophobic membrane-inserting/translocation or pore-forming helix; Big defensin antimicrobial peptides: activation on the N-terminal amphipathic membrane-active helix; Human interferon-inducible small membrane proteins and ApoL family: activation on short TM or membrane-inserting helices; Bacteriophage tail structural proteins: activation on short hydrophobic helical segments within tail/tip assemblies.

Summary: Generic detector of intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments in short proteins and peptide precursors, most often marking flexible C‑terminal tails or short loops around the 50–120 aa region; common in secreted/regulatory proproteins but also present in small housekeeping, membrane, mitochondrial and viral proteins
Activation pattern: Residue-level single peaks (occasionally adjacent pairs) with no strong amino-acid preference; peaks lie within low‑pLDDT/IDR or compositionally biased stretches, frequently near C-termini and around positions 50–120 typical of many short proteins, but also at flexible termini/loops inside longer proteins
Exemplars: - Plant small secreted signaling peptides (e.g., PAMP-induced/PIP family): single peak near the C-terminus of the mature peptide within a disordered tail.
- Salivary proline-rich secreted proteins (androgen-regulated/SMR family): weak peak at the penultimate C‑terminal residue inside a long proline‑rich disordered region.
- EGF-family growth factor precursors (e.g., TGF‑alpha/EGF): peaks in disordered propeptide or juxtamembrane/cytosolic tail regions rather than in the folded EGF domain.
- Antimicrobial and reproductive basic peptides (AMPs, seminal/exocrine peptides): activation on flexible termini of propeptides or mature peptides within low‑complexity segments.
- RiPP and small peptide natural product precursors: peaks in disordered leader/core regions near processing sites in multi‑peptide precursors.
- Bacterial toxin–antitoxin small proteins and other small regulators: activation on disordered N/C‑terminal tails of compact helical proteins.
- Small ribosomal proteins: peaks on Lys/Arg‑rich disordered tails that contact rRNA.
- Membrane and secretion system components: activation on short extramembrane/periplasmic loops or terminal tails that are unstructured.
- Mitochondrial small proteins (e.g., ATP synthase subunit 8; IMS chaperones): peaks on short flexible terminal segments or loops flanking transmembrane helices.
- Viral small proteins (phage and poxvirus): activation on low‑complexity, disordered termini.

Summary: Surface-exposed β-strand edges and flanking loops (β-edge patches) that serve as interaction interfaces—commonly on secreted/virion proteins and multi-subunit assemblies—used for receptor/partner binding, assembly, adhesion, or substrate recognition; enriched in hydrophobic/aromatic and Ser/Thr residues with frequent Gly/Pro in turns and occasional Cys in extracellular contexts.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks at non-contiguous sites on solvent-exposed β-strands and adjacent coils/loops; occurs in both well-ordered (high pLDDT) β-elements and flexible, low-confidence loops; can expand to regional, extended activation across long, Ser/Thr-rich extracellular repeats; generally avoids N-terminal signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Filovirus matrix proteins (e.g., VP40): peaks on flexible loops and select β-strands on the surface implicated in membrane/host-factor interactions, not on canonical L-domain motifs.
- Staphylococcal superantigen enterotoxins: activation on β-strands flanking Zn2+ and MHC II binding residues, highlighting receptor/metal-binding interface patches.
- Viral envelope and dsRNA capsid proteins: exterior β-strands and loops used for receptor engagement and capsid assembly.
- Bacterial surface adhesins/adsorption proteins (e.g., MSCRAMM-like, repeat-rich extracellular adhesins): broad activation across Ser/Thr-rich repeats and β-sheet modules mediating host adhesion.
- Secreted proteases and hydrolytic enzymes: β-edge/loop residues lining substrate-binding clefts and inhibitor-contact surfaces.
- CRISPR effector complexes and other bacterial interaction machineries: subunit–subunit contact surfaces formed by exposed β-strands and loops.

Summary: Recognition of one face of beta-strands—an alternating side‑chain pattern enriched in hydrophobic/small residues—across beta-sheet/beta-barrel architectures, commonly forming lipid-interacting surfaces in membrane, lipoprotein, and pore-forming proteins
Activation pattern: Residue-level alternating peaks on every other position within beta-strands (DSSP class E), often extending across many strands within a domain; minimal in helices and signal peptides, with occasional spillover to adjacent coils; strong preference for hydrophobic/small residues and long beta-sheet–rich stretches
Exemplars: - BPI/LBP fold lipid-binding proteins: activation along beta-strand faces that line hydrophobic lipid-binding grooves (beta-sandwich strands with alternating pattern).
- Lipoprotein/glycolipid transporter LprF: alternating activation on one face of beta-strands essential for glycolipid binding (mutation at an activated Ala disrupts binding).
- Outer membrane beta-barrel proteins (porins/VDAC, usher PapC): strong alternating activation on barrel strands, consistent with the membrane-exposed hydrophobic face.
- Pore-forming/toxic proteins (trialysin): activation across amphipathic beta-strands implicated in membrane permeabilization.
- Photosystem II oxygen-evolving enhancer (PsbO): selective activation on specific C‑terminal beta-strands of the beta-sandwich.
- Lipid-transport precursors (vitellogenin/lipovitellin) and apolipoprotein B: activation within beta-strand–rich regions of their lipid-binding domains, showing long stretches of alternating peaks.
Summary: Generic feature, meaning not known

Summary: Secreted/luminal cysteine- and crosslink-motif detector: activates on the local sequence context around cysteines (often Cys–Cys pairs) that form intramolecular disulfide bonds or other thiol-derived crosslinks (e.g., lanthionine in lantibiotics) within secreted precursors and extracellular domains, frequently near the N-terminus; also shows weaker, non-specific activation in N-terminal signal peptide/propeptide regions of secreted peptide/hormone precursors (including cysteine-poor families); broadly covers peptide hormones, toxins/venoms, antimicrobial peptides, bacteriocins (including lantibiotics), plant small secreted peptides, and viral envelope glycoproteins
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks at or immediately adjacent to cysteines involved in disulfide or other thiol crosslinks (including CC motifs), with short clusters across cysteine-rich segments; additional shallow/occasional peaks in N-terminal signal peptide/propeptide regions that can occur even in cysteine-poor precursors; typically few peaks per protein, with many peaks only in highly crosslink/cysteine-rich secreted proteins
Exemplars: - AB5 pertussis toxin binding subunit (S2): strong peaks at residues flanking cysteines annotated to form disulfide bonds.
- Herpesvirus gL envelope glycoproteins: activation at conserved luminal cysteines forming disulfide bonds in the N-terminal domain.
- Neuropeptide prohormone precursors (including cysteine-poor families such as SCP A/B): weak hits in the signal peptide/propeptide and around any present cysteine motifs.
- Venom cystine-knot and related secreted toxins (conotoxins, scorpion/spider toxins): peaks across Cys–Cys pairs and their flanks stabilizing multiple disulfides.
- Defensins and other cysteine-rich antimicrobial/host-defense peptides: activation on canonical disulfide-forming cysteines.
- Bacteriocins and secreted bacterial peptide toxins, including lantibiotics (e.g., lacticin 3147 A1): peaks at cysteines and adjacent residues involved in lanthionine/thiol crosslinks.
- Plant small secreted signaling peptides (e.g., SCOOP, RALF/CLE/PSK): activation at conserved motifs and in the N-terminal propeptide/signal regions within secreted precursors.

Summary: Broad, structure-driven detector of short, well-ordered beta-strand segments within folded domains, often at sheet cores/edges and sometimes overlapping substrate/ligand-binding residues; not tied to a specific function or compartment.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous 6–20-residue stretches corresponding to beta-strands (often with an adjacent short loop), with sharp residue-level peaks at hydrophobic/aromatic positions in an alternating hydrophobic–polar pattern; frequently multi-segment within a protein; little activation on signal peptides or disordered regions.
Exemplars: - Metalloprotease zymogens (ADAM/ADAMTS, snake venom metalloproteinases): activation on structured beta-strand regions within the propeptide; not on the signal peptide or catalytic peptidase domain.
- Red chlorophyll catabolite reductase: activation on an N-terminal beta-strand that includes a substrate-binding glutamate, with a weaker signal on the adjacent N-terminal strand/coil.
- Nucleic-acid enzymes (e.g., RNase H family, primase/capping/polymerase components): activation on beta-strand elements of their alpha/beta cores, often near active-site strands.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes: activation along beta-strands within barrel or sandwich cores.

Summary: Residue-level detector for hydrophobic residues embedded in beta-strands of well-ordered beta-sheets, occasionally including disulfide-forming cysteines when they occur in strand context; a generic structural signal rather than a pathway- or taxon-specific function
Activation pattern: Sparse, isolated single-residue peaks (typically 1–8 per protein), confined to high-confidence beta-strands; peaks may lie within strand interiors or at strand boundaries and are sometimes adjacent to ligand-binding or catalytic loops but without a consistent functional annotation
Exemplars: - tRNA(Ile)-lysidine synthase (TilS): single Leu within a beta-strand; minor strand peaks elsewhere
- KEOPS complex (LAGE3): isolated Leu in a beta-strand
- Anthranilate/chorismate-pathway enzymes (anthranilate synthase component I): Ala/Ile in beta-strands, including sites adjacent to chorismate-binding loops
- Salicylate/isochorismate synthase: multiple Thr/Val/Ile/Leu positions in beta-strands near substrate-binding residues
- Alpha-KTx potassium channel toxin: disulfide-bonded Cys in a short beta-strand adjacent to the pore-blocking Lys
- PP2C/PPM-type phosphatases: hydrophobic residues in beta-strands near the Mn2+-binding loop
- Alkaline phosphatase: Trp within a high-confidence beta-strand; minor Val/Leu at strand boundaries
- Small heat shock proteins/alpha-crystallins: Tyr/Leu within beta-strands of the alpha-crystallin domain
- Kinesin motor proteins: Ile/Val in beta-strands of the motor domain
- DNA polymerase III beta clamp: multiple Leu/Met/Ile peaks across beta-strands in the ring

Summary: Generic low‑polarity alpha‑helical segments—long hydrophobic helices and helical cores (including transmembrane anchors and signal peptides), enriched in aliphatic/aromatic residues and often encompassing helical regions that host catalytic or oligomerization sites; tolerant of cysteine-rich stretches in secreted/extracellular proteins
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation across extended hydrophobic helices, frequently spanning many consecutive positions, with local residue-level peaks at especially hydrophobic positions and near catalytic residues within helical domains
Exemplars: - CRISPR-Cas13a HEPN endoribonucleases: activation on the helical segments carrying the catalytic R/H dyads in each HEPN-like fold
- Viral envelope glycoprotein precursors: activation on N-terminal signal peptides and C-terminal transmembrane anchors; cysteine-rich ectodomain segments also activated
- RNA virus nucleoproteins: activation across long alpha-helical oligomerization/packing regions
- Eukaryotic serine/threonine kinases: activation on the αC-helix and hydrophobic helical core elements of the kinase domain
- Structural proteins (capsid/envelope/matrix): activation on coiled-coils and other hydrophobic helical bundles
- Organellar (mitochondrial/chloroplast) proteins: activation on transit peptides and membrane-spanning helices where present

Summary: Compositionally biased, intrinsically disordered low‑complexity regions enriched in proline and serine (often with glycine), such as flexible linkers, activation domains, propeptides/transit peptides, and cytosolic tails of small membrane and viral proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation across low‑complexity/IDR stretches, often in N‑ or C‑terminal tails or cytosolic loops; residue‑level peaks on clustered S/P and glycine‑rich tracts; span and intensity scale with length of the disordered segment
Exemplars: - Homeobox/paired-box transcription factors: activation on proline/serine‑rich activation domains and low‑complexity terminal regions.
- Viral accessory/regulatory and small structural/envelope proteins: activation on disordered, compositionally biased segments and cytosolic tails flanking transmembrane helices.
- Neuropeptide/toxin/secreted peptide precursors: activation on low‑complexity propeptide regions between signal peptide and mature peptide, including gly/pro‑rich stretches near cleavage sites.
- Small eukaryotic transmembrane proteins: activation on cytosolic low‑complexity loops/tails adjacent to TM domains.
- smORFs/microproteins: activation across largely disordered, low‑complexity sequences.
- Organelle-targeted proteins (mitochondrial/chloroplastic): activation on N‑terminal transit peptides (Ser/Thr‑rich, low complexity).
- Glycine‑rich proteins: activation on glycine‑rich low‑complexity repeats and flexible linkers.

Summary: Recognition of periodically patterned hydrophobic/aromatic “hotspot” residues that form packing/interaction faces in regular secondary-structure scaffolds (especially coiled‑coil/leucine‑zipper α‑helices and WD40 β‑propeller blades) and in short terminal hydrophobic motifs of bioactive peptides
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks that repeat with secondary-structure periodicity: i,i+4 along α‑helices (amphipathic faces), heptad a/d positions in coiled‑coils/leucine zippers, and one prominent site per blade/β‑strand in WD repeats; clustered across repeat-rich domains; generally absent from disordered regions except for short peaks at hydrophobic C‑terminal peptide motifs (often amidated)
Exemplars:

Summary: Generic low-complexity segments that are intrinsically disordered, proline‑rich and/or Lys/Arg‑biased (often also enriched in Ser/Thr) with intermittent hydrophobic residues, together with short hydrophobic helices in small membrane proteins; these include propeptide/processing regions of secreted precursors, basic disordered segments in viral proteins, mucin‑like S/T‑rich patches in glycoproteins, surface loops in enzymes, and single‑pass transmembrane microproteins (e.g., organellar gene products) rather than a specific folded domain.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate tracts with residue‑level spikes on Pro clusters and polybasic runs; also activates on signal peptides and short transmembrane helices; occurs anywhere in the sequence, often including N‑terminal targeting/secretory segments and internal disordered linkers; small proteins/peptides can show activation across most of their length.
Exemplars:
- Secreted peptide hormone/neuropeptide and toxin precursors: activation on dibasic processing regions (KR/RR), adjacent Pro‑rich segments, and on cationic/cysteine‑stabilized mature peptides; mucin‑like S/T‑rich patches in glycoproteins.
- Viral proteins (including herpesvirus nuclear egress/glycoproteins and basic nucleic acid–binding proteins): activation on polybasic/proline‑rich disordered stretches, signal peptides, and amphipathic or short transmembrane helices.
- Testis/sperm/fertilization proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑rich low‑complexity tails and Pro‑rich repeats that are disordered and interaction‑prone.
- Plant/algal organellar proteins: activation on transit peptide–like segments where present and on short hydrophobic transmembrane helices in mitochondrial/chloroplast microproteins (e.g., ATP synthase subunits).
- Bacterial primary‑metabolism enzymes: activation on surface‑exposed loops/linkers enriched in P, S/T, and occasional basic/hydrophobic residues rather than on catalytic cores.
- sORF/lncRNA‑derived microproteins and uncharacterized small proteins: activation across much of the sequence due to global low complexity (Pro/Arg/Lys and Ser/Thr bias) or short hydrophobic helices.

Summary: Intrinsic disorder/low-structure terminal segments—most commonly short, flexible N‑terminal regions (including signal/transit peptides and propeptides) and other low‑complexity coils—with no strict residue preference
Activation pattern: Residue-level, sparse low-amplitude peaks concentrated in predicted disordered/coil regions (low pLDDT), frequently beginning at Met1 and extending over a short N‑terminal stretch; additional isolated peaks in internal or C‑terminal disordered patches; occasional short hydrophobic runs (e.g., signal-peptide h-regions) as well as Pro/Gly-rich and polar segments
Exemplars: - Small human regulatory/disordered proteins (e.g., ST20/tumor suppressor): isolated residues within low-confidence coils across the sequence
- Human IGF2 antisense protein: a Pro-centered peak within an annotated intrinsically disordered C‑terminal segment
- Secreted peptide/toxin and hormone precursors: activation on N‑terminal signal peptides and adjacent propeptides (hydrophobic h-region plus flexible flanks)
- Organelle-targeted enzymes (mitochondrial/plastid): activation on N‑terminal transit peptides (flexible, low-complexity, amphipathic segments)
- Viral proteins from diverse families: activation on flexible N‑ or C‑terminal low-complexity regions
- Kinases and RNA-related enzymes: activation on disordered N‑terminal tails/linkers adjacent to structured catalytic cores

Summary: Short linear interaction motif–like sites in intrinsically disordered regions of transcription factors, often corresponding to activation/cofactor-binding segments (e.g., the Hox Antp-type hexapeptide/YPWM-containing region), with occasional weaker hits in structured DNA-binding domains
Activation pattern: Sparse, low-magnitude, residue-level peaks (typically 1–5 per protein), predominantly in low-pLDDT coils or low-confidence helices outside DNA-binding domains; sporadic minor peaks within structured folds (homeobox, paired, forkhead, GATA zinc finger, T-box, ETS). Marked residues are often aromatic or proline/glycine but not restricted to a single residue class.
Exemplars: Homeobox/Hox: disordered N-terminal/linker regions and the Antp-type hexapeptide; NKX: disordered segment with rare within-homeobox helix hits; Paired (PAX): C-terminal IDR outside the paired domain; Forkhead (FOX): C-terminal IDR outside the forkhead domain; GATA: N-terminal IDR with weaker sites in zinc-finger strands; T-box (TBX5): multiple residues in disordered C-terminal activation region with minor peaks in the T-box core; ETS: strongest in disordered regions with small peaks in the ETS domain; C2H2 zinc finger TFs (e.g., rotund): disordered regions outside zinc-finger arrays.

Summary: Structural motif: hydrophobic residues within well‑ordered secondary‑structure cores—primarily beta‑strands of beta‑sheets/barrels, but also tightly packed alpha‑helical segments (coiled‑coils and transmembrane helices)—reflecting core packing rather than specific catalytic sites, across diverse folds and taxa.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks, often single positions or short runs, localized to regular secondary structure (beta‑strands most frequent; also helical segments in coiled‑coils/TM bundles); enriched for Val/Ile/Leu and aromatics; distributed wherever these elements occur; strongest in high‑confidence structured regions; generally not coincident with annotated active/binding sites.
Exemplars:
- Glycosidases (e.g., beta‑galactosidase/TIM‑barrel): activation on isolated Val/Ile/Leu within barrel beta‑strands.
- Ras‑like small GTPases: activation on a single hydrophobic residue in a beta‑strand adjacent to the effector/switch region.
- ABC transporters: activation on hydrophobic residues in NBD central beta‑sheets and, in full transporters (e.g., ABCH), in TM helix cores.
- TonB‑dependent outer‑membrane receptors: activation along beta‑barrel strands.
- TonB/ExbD inner‑membrane complex: activation on hydrophobic residues within the TM helix and periplasmic coiled‑coil.
- Thioredoxin‑like/selenoprotein redox enzymes: activation on hydrophobics in the core mixed beta‑sheet.
- Ubiquitin‑like sulfur‑carrier/modifier proteins (ThiS/MoaD/Ubl): activation on hydrophobics in the beta‑grasp sheet.
- D‑amino‑acid metabolism enzymes (TIM‑barrel/Rossmann‑like): activation on hydrophobic beta‑strand residues in core sheets.
- Ion‑motive decarboxylase membrane subunits (e.g., methylmalonyl‑CoA decarboxylase gamma): activation within TM helices.

Summary: Intrinsic low-complexity repeat tracts in disordered regions, enriched in small/polar residues (Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly/Ala, often Asn/Gln/Glu), typical of mucin-like/adhesive extracellular domains and long unstructured cytosolic tails (including His/acidic metal-binding tails); activation centers on tandem-repeat cores such as GSX, GANP-like, and PTS/PG motifs and is largely absent from well-folded domains
Activation pattern: Regional activation spanning long, intrinsically disordered segments (often entire repeat blocks or C‑terminal tails), with periodic sharp residue-level peaks at repeat core positions (e.g., the N/P in GANP-like repeats or the S in GSX); minimal to no activation over structured catalytic domains, transmembranes, or compact folds; occasionally marks short segments within small secreted effectors
Exemplars: Enamel matrix proteins (Enamelin): strong activation across the disordered C‑terminal tandem repeats (GANP-like), with peaks on Asn/Pro and scattered Thr/Pro motifs; Fungal flocculins/agglutinins (FLO/Flo11-like): activation throughout central Ser/Thr-rich repeat arrays with periodic GSX peaks, but not in the structured Flo11 domain; FHA-domain scaffolds: no activation in the folded FHA domain, strong activation over long disordered C‑terminal extensions; P1B-type heavy-metal ATPases (HMA4): activation confined to the long unstructured cytosolic C‑terminal metal-binding/regulatory tail; Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on short regions within the secreted effector, often adjacent to signal peptide/glycosylation sites, while the RxLR motif itself is weakly marked

Summary: Intrinsic disorder/low-complexity signal: the feature marks compositionally biased, non-globular regions enriched in polar/charged and small residues (S/T/E/D/R/K/G/P; often A/L), typically flexible N- or C‑terminal tails, linkers, and propeptides that host short linear motifs or processing sites, while avoiding structured domains.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks scattered within long IDRs/low-complexity segments; sometimes clustered across terminal disordered tails. Minimal to no activation inside well-folded domains. Peaks coincide with low-confidence, coil-rich regions (low pLDDT).
Exemplars: - Homeobox/developmental transcription factors: activation on long low-complexity, disordered regions flanking the DNA-binding homeobox; little to none within the folded domain.
- Neuropeptide/secreted peptide precursors (e.g., kisspeptin/Metastin precursor): activation on disordered propeptide and the processed peptide region.
- Bacterial single-stranded DNA-binding protein (SSB): strong activation on the C-terminal disordered, acidic/glycine-rich tail that mediates partner interactions; negligible activation on the structured N-terminal SSB (OB-fold) domain.
- p53-regulated apoptosis-related intrinsically disordered protein: sparse peaks across the wholly disordered sequence without association to a folded domain.

Summary: Short, well-ordered strand–loop elements centered on a β-strand within folded domains, enriched for acidic residues (D/E), glycine and/or proline in the flanking loop, and often containing/adjacent to aromatic residues (Y/F/W) with occasional His–acidic pairings; these mark conserved β-sheet segments commonly used in binding/catalytic domains across diverse protein families rather than a family‑specific active-site motif.
Activation pattern: Regional activation in short contiguous windows (~8–20 aa) with residue-level peaks on a β-strand and spillover into the adjacent loop; strongest in confidently structured regions (high pLDDT); large multidomain proteins often show multiple dispersed β-strand–centered peaks; little activation in long disordered termini or signal peptides, with only occasional weak helical signals.
Exemplars: - Rap/Ral GTPase-activating proteins (Rap-GAP domain): sharp peak on a C-terminal β-strand with an upstream coil within the GAP domain.
- Tubulin-tyrosine ligase-like enzymes (TTL/TTLL domain): strong signals on conserved β-strands in the catalytic fold, including a primary strand and a secondary strand elsewhere in the domain.
- SufE/CsdE sulfur-transfer helpers: a single β-strand in the core sheet (away from the catalytic cysteine loop) showing a focused peak.
- PARP family (WGR DNA-binding domain): a short coil→β segment within the WGR domain, consistent with the WGR β-strand region enriched in aromatic/glycine residues.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered/low‑complexity terminal segments and short unstructured peptides; occasional firing near N‑terminal leader/signal sequences and basic targeting motifs (e.g., NLS) when these occur in low-confidence/disordered context; broadly residue‑tolerant with bias toward hydrophobic, Gly/Pro, and basic residues; enriched among viral accessory proteins, microproteins, and secreted precursors but not ubiquitous, and often absent from well‑folded enzyme cores and stable transmembrane helices.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks confined to low-pLDDT coil/low-complexity tracts; typically N‑terminally biased but can occur internally or at the C‑terminus; largely silent over structured domains (e.g., enzyme cores, polymerase subunits) and within long, confidently helical transmembrane segments.
Exemplars: - Antisense/alt-ORF microprotein from the thymidylate synthase locus: peaks at the initiator Met and scattered Gly/Arg/Pro within annotated disordered regions.
- Adenovirus early regulatory protein E4 ORF6: sparse peaks across low-confidence segments, with strong activation over a basic C-terminal nuclear localization signal when disordered.
- Viral capsid-interacting accessory protein (small capsomere-interacting protein): peaks confined to very low-pLDDT coil loops lacking defined structure.
- Conotoxin precursor (alpha-conotoxin): strongest activation on the N-terminal signal peptide when low-confidence, with weaker peaks in low-confidence regions of the mature secreted toxin.

Summary: Serine/threonine‑rich low‑complexity intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)—polar, acidic/Q/N- and P/G-enriched stretches such as mucin‑like repeats, flexible linkers, and disordered tails that act as PTM‑dense segments across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended runs of S/T and other polar residues; many contiguous positions per region and multiple regions per protein; frequently includes N‑terminal low‑complexity tracts; broad, low‑amplitude activation rather than sharp single‑residue peaks
Exemplars: - Secreted mucins and cell‑surface glycoproteins: activation on S/T‑rich mucin‑like O‑glycosylation domains.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins and surface antigens (e.g., filovirus GP, coronavirus spike, influenza HA): activation on S/T‑rich hypervariable disordered loops.
- Viral capsid/structural and replication proteins: activation on long disordered linkers and acidic S/T‑rich tails.
- Eukaryotic transcription factors and chromatin‑associated regulators: activation on acidic/serine‑rich activation domains and other low‑complexity, phosphorylation‑prone regions.
- Ser/Thr kinases and signaling scaffolds: activation on regulatory S/T‑clustered disordered N/C‑terminal extensions and inter‑domain linkers.
- Bacterial type III/IV secretion effectors: activation on N‑terminal low‑complexity secretion signals and internal disordered linkers.
- CRISPR‑associated proteins (Cas families): activation on flexible low‑complexity insertions and inter‑domain IDRs.

Summary: Generic structural motif: short beta-strand segments enriched in hydrophobic and small polar residues, often at or initiating a domain (frequently very N-terminal), consistent with edge/first strands of beta-sheets rather than specific catalytic sites.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous 4-10 residue stretches forming a beta-strand, typically with a single strong peak within the strand; frequently involves very N-terminal residues and occasionally other isolated beta-strands elsewhere in the protein; largely independent of function and not centered on annotated active-site or binding residues.
Exemplars: - Carbohydrate esterase (4-O-methyl-glucuronoyl methylesterase): activation on a beta-strand within the catalytic domain; weaker activation on a beta-strand of the CBM1 module.
- Trigger factor chaperone: strong activation on the extreme N-terminal beta-strand; additional weaker hits on beta-strands within the FKBP-type PPIase domain.
- Protein tyrosine phosphatase-like protein: localized activation on a beta-strand inside the PTP domain.
- STAS-domain anti-sigma factor antagonist: first beta-strand at the start of the STAS domain.
- 4'-phosphopantetheinyl transferase: activation on a C-terminal coil-to-beta transition leading into a terminal beta-strand; minor N-terminal beta-strand signal.

Summary: Short glycine–aromatic motifs—especially GW/WG and the proline-capped variant PGW—and adjacent glycine‑rich, flexible loops that form exposed interface elements for binding or insertion (membranes, carbohydrates, nucleic acids, or protein partners). The feature primarily detects the local sequence pattern of an aromatic residue (W>Y≈F) flanked by one or more glycines within short low‑complexity stretches, a motif that recurs across extracellular/secreted proteins, viral/lytic peptides, trafficking and glycosylation factors, and diverse enzymes.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue‑level peaks centered on Trp/Tyr/Phe when immediately preceded/followed by Gly (GW/WG/PGW and related XGϕ or ϕGX patterns), often extending a few residues into nearby glycine runs. In glycine‑rich low‑complexity regions the activations can become regional, tiling multiple short GW/YG/FG motifs. Number of active residues per protein varies widely with motif copy number and repeat density.
Exemplars: - Gram‑positive surface adhesins with GW modules (cell wall/mucus‑binding repeats): activation on tandem GW/PGW motifs that mediate non‑covalent cell‑wall association.
- Tryptophan‑rich antimicrobial and venom peptides: activation on WG/GW and Trp‑flanked glycine segments that drive membrane binding/lysis.
- Viral/phage structural and lytic proteins (capsids, holins, endolysins): activation on glycine–aromatic turns in β‑hairpins and lytic segments.
- TRAPP trafficking complex subunits (e.g., Bet3/TRAPPC3 family): activation on conserved surface PGW/WG loops implicated in Rab/complex interactions.
- Methyl‑CpG‑binding domain proteins (MeCP2/MBD1/2/3 families): activation on short PGW/GW‑type patches within disordered linkers or near DNA‑binding loops.
- ER glycosylation machinery (GPI mannosyltransferases; oligosaccharyltransferase subunits): activation on luminal glycine‑rich loops bearing W/Y that contact substrates.
- Complement/alpha‑2‑macroglobulin family: activation on glycine‑ and aromatic‑containing segments within bait/interaction regions of large secreted proteins.
- Carbohydrate‑active enzymes (glycosidases and carbohydrate‑binding modules): activation on W/Y/F residues that stack with sugars when flanked by glycine in flexible loops.
- Nucleic‑acid enzymes (RNA/tRNA/rRNA methyltransferases; CRISPR‑associated and other nucleases): activation on FXGXG‑like SAM‑loop motifs and WG/GG turns along substrate‑binding channels.
- Dictyostelium spore coat and other large extracellular adhesion proteins: broad activation across glycine‑rich, aromatic low‑complexity repeats containing recurrent GW/YG/FG motifs.

Summary: Residue-level detector for coil residues (strongly favoring Ser/Thr, also Gly/Pro) that sit immediately N‑terminal to the first residue of a secondary‑structure element—i.e., N‑cap of α‑helices and the pre‑start of β‑strands—marking boundaries between flexible segments and emerging structured elements
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks at single positions just before helix/strand starts; silent within long continuous secondary structure; multiple peaks can recur across a sequence; often enriched near protein N‑termini or domain starts but present throughout
Exemplars: - Secreted bacterial proteases (e.g., extracellular metalloproteases/gingipain-like proteases): peaks at S/T/G/P immediately before β‑strands or short helices within repeat-rich regions.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes (glycoside hydrolases, lyases, sulfatases; including GAG-degrading enzymes and marine algal polysaccharide lyases): peaks at N‑cap/pre‑strand residues at the starts of helices or β‑elements in β‑helix/β‑sandwich/repeat modules and at boundaries with S/T‑rich linkers.
- Outer-membrane proteins and autotransporter/adhesin repeats: peaks at coil residues just N‑terminal to barrel strands or repeat-element secondary structures.
- Membrane insertase YidC and other membrane proteins: peaks at helix N‑cap positions at loop-to–transmembrane-helix transitions.
- Lipoprotein biogenesis/handling components: peaks at residues capping short helices or initiating β‑strands within periplasmic/cytosolic domains.
- Viral and bacterial surface glycoproteins: peaks at S/T preceding helix/strand starts in ectodomains, often near N‑terminal regions.

Summary: Compositionally biased amphipathic helical and low-complexity segments enriched in hydrophobic (L/V/I/A), basic (K/R), and Ser/Thr/Pro residues (with underrepresented Trp). The feature preferentially marks cationic, Ser/Thr/Pro- and Pro-enriched amphipathic segments rather than generic hydrophobic leaders; it captures a subset of N-terminal targeting peptides and micropeptides with this bias, and internal polybasic/low-complexity motifs in diverse proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation at N-termini or internal segments when a ≥12–25 aa stretch shows alternating hydrophobic and basic/Ser/Thr/Pro residues and low acidic content; purely hydrophobic signal peptides or globular proteins lacking such biased segments generally do not activate.
Exemplars:
- Subset of secretory signal/transit peptides with strongly basic N-regions and S/T/Pro-rich, low-acidic content (classical purely hydrophobic leaders are weak/negative).
- Cationic amphipathic helical antimicrobial and regulatory micropeptides; cystine-knot/beta-rich peptides are not primary targets unless they include such helices.
- Viral structural/accessory proteins when they contain short cationic amphipathic helices or S/T/Pro-rich leaders; viral proteins lacking these motifs are typically negative.
- Bacterial secreted/periplasmic proteins with Sec-type leaders that also exhibit the above compositional bias.
- Mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides with Arg/Ser/Thr enrichment and low acidic content.
- Cytosolic enzymes/regulators only when they harbor internal low-complexity/polybasic Pro/Ser/Thr-rich insertions or amphipathic helices; otherwise negative.

Summary: Beta-strand–connecting loop/turn residues (beta-hairpin/strand–strand linkers) in beta-sheet–rich domains, often enriched for Gly and acidic residues; a generic structural motif rather than a function-specific signal
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks on short coil/turn segments that join adjacent beta-strands, occasionally extending to strand-edge residues near these turns; concentrated in beta-sandwich/ferrodoxin-like/barrel/propeller regions and largely absent from alpha-helical segments
Exemplars: - Small heat shock proteins/alpha-crystallins: isolated peaks on loop residues linking strands within the beta-sandwich
- ATP synthase epsilon subunit: multiple peaks in the N-terminal beta-sheet domain at strand-connecting coils (none in the C-terminal helix)
- NifU/NFU1 Fe–S scaffold proteins: sparse peaks in loops adjacent to beta-strands, not on Fe–S ligands
- Rieske-type oxygenase systems (oxygenase and ferredoxin/ISP components): peaks on strand-connecting coils within the Rieske ferredoxin-like domain, near but not at the Cys/His [2Fe–2S] ligands
- KEOPS complex subunit LAGE3: single peak in the short loop linking neighboring beta-strands
- Fatty acid-binding proteins (FABP): peaks in turns between barrel beta-strands

Summary: Intrinsic disorder/low-complexity segments—especially N-terminal tails, activation/propeptide regions, and flexible linkers—enriched for Ser/Thr/Pro and basic residues, with occasional hotspots at proteolytic processing junctions (propeptide→mature chain)
Activation pattern: Primarily sparse, residue-level peaks within predicted disordered/low-pLDDT regions; often N-terminal biased; in zymogens, a narrow, localized window centered on the cleavage junction
Exemplars: - Aspartic protease zymogens (e.g., pepsinogen/pepsin): strong, localized activation spanning the propeptide–mature-chain cleavage site
- Apoptosis-related regulatory proteins with long N-terminal IDRs (e.g., p53-regulated apoptosis-inducing protein 1): scattered single-residue peaks across the disordered N-terminus
- Uncharacterized low-complexity eukaryotic proteins: weak, distributed peaks within annotated/predicted disordered terminal segments

Summary: Polar low-complexity intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)—especially Q/N-rich (prion-like) segments and S/T- and glycine-rich tracts with simple SG/TG/PG repeats—typically located in inter-domain linkers and terminal tails of eukaryotic proteins and often harboring Ser/Thr phosphorylation sites.
Activation pattern: Strong, contiguous regional activation restricted to predicted-disordered, low-complexity stretches (low pLDDT), with little to no signal in folded domains; superimposed residue-level peaks in dense S/T clusters, poly-Q/N or poly-G runs, and short unstructured linkers embedded within otherwise structured regions.
Exemplars: - Putative lipase ROG1 — activation on the C-terminal disordered acidic/polar tail; no signal in the structured catalytic region.
- Cyclic GMP-binding protein D (Ras-GEF/GRAM-containing signaling scaffold) — activation across long low-complexity disordered linkers between domains and a Q/N/S/G-rich C-terminal tail; inactive on Ras-GEF and GRAM domains.
- TRAPP complex subunit 10 — activation on an N-terminal LCD and multiple Q/N/G/S-rich disordered segments, including poly-G and terminal poly-Asn tracts, plus a Q-rich helical patch.
- SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling subunit SWI1 — strong activation over the N-terminal prion-like domain; additional spikes at short unstructured linkers in the C-terminus; no activation in the folded ARID domain.
- Post-transcriptional regulator Mkt1 — activation on short disordered S/T-rich segments that include known phosphoserine sites; structured regions remain largely inactive.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity proline-rich tandem-repeat tracts (typically enriched in P/S/T and often Q/H) found predominantly in secreted/extracellular proteins and viral surface proteins; the feature marks conserved proline positions within repeat units that form mucin-like stalks, adhesin/cell-wall repeats, or Hyp/O-glycosylation scaffolds, and it also occurs in intracellular repeat-rich proteins such as nuclear regulators and cytoskeletal/testis-specific proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered repeat domains with sharp residue-level peaks mainly on prolines at fixed positions in each repeat unit (e.g., second P in PP; the P in DPxG, NANP/NVDP, or PAA-PEA motifs). Outside these tracts, activation is low, including in structured domains (signal peptides, transmembranes, enzyme cores, or GPI-anchor/propeptide segments); however, short P-rich low-complexity inserts/propeptides within secretory-pathway glycoproteins can also activate.
Exemplars:
- Fungal GPI-anchored adhesins/flocculins: strong activation on prolines within central Ser/Thr/Pro-rich tandem repeats that form the extracellular stalk.
- Plant arabinogalactan proteins/extensins: activation on PP motifs, biased to the second P that is hydroxylated to Hyp and O-glycosylated.
- Viral envelope proteins (e.g., herpesvirus gC; Plasmodium CSP): activation on prolines within repetitive, disordered external repeats (e.g., P-D-P-A-V-A-P, NANP/NVDP).
- Mucin-like secreted proteins: activation across disordered 10–15 aa repeat arrays (e.g., DPxG-containing repeats).
- Testis-specific/cytoskeletal repeat proteins (e.g., outer dense fiber proteins): activation on prolines anchoring short tandem repeats in disordered segments.
- Nuclear transcriptional regulators with Pro-rich low-complexity regions (e.g., REST): activation over Pro-rich tracts.
- Bacterial autotransporters/actin modulators (e.g., BimA): activation on surface-exposed Pro-rich repeats.
- Secretory/vacuolar glycoproteins with short low-complexity inserts: activation confined to Pro-rich inserts, not the folded enzyme core.

Summary: Compositionally biased, low-structure terminal segments—especially N‑terminal pre-sequences and flexible linkers/tails—that precede or follow structured domains. These regions are enriched for hydrophobic/aromatic residues with Pro/Gly and often include low‑complexity repeats (e.g., Asn‑rich tracts in Dictyostelium). The concept spans signal/transit peptides of secreted/membrane/organellar proteins and intrinsically disordered tails in soluble enzymes and viral accessory proteins.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation on short (∼10–40 aa) low‑pLDDT segments at protein termini (most often the N‑terminus), with diffuse low-to-moderate signal and occasional single‑residue peaks in coils/short helices; little to no activation inside well‑structured domains.
Exemplars: - Viral capsid-interacting/accessory proteins: scattered peaks across low-confidence, disordered segments throughout the protein.
- Tricorn-like proteases: strong activation on the disordered N‑terminal pre‑domain tail preceding the first annotated domain.
- Developmentally regulated protein kinases (Dictyostelium): activation on Asn‑rich, low‑complexity C‑terminal extensions and isolated peaks in N‑terminal disordered regions.
- Secreted/membrane proteins: activation on N‑terminal signal peptides and adjacent low‑complexity luminal/cytosolic segments enriched in Leu/Val/Ile/Phe with Pro/Gly.
- Organelle-targeted proteins (mitochondrial/plastid): activation on N‑terminal transit peptides with low structural confidence.
- Soluble bacterial enzymes: activation on flexible N‑terminal tails or linkers that precede the first folded domain.

Summary: General secretory precursor processing signal: the feature activates on short proteolytic maturation motifs and nearby residues in precursors of secretory pathway proteins (secreted/extracellular, virion-surface, outer-membrane/lipoproteins, and ER/Golgi lumenal residents)—covering signal/leader peptide cleavage, double‑glycine leader processing, and dibasic/furin convertase sites—often adjacent to cysteine‑rich mature peptide regions (toxins, defensins, bacteriocins, neuropeptides) and viral envelope glycoproteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks at short cleavage motifs (signal peptidase −1/−3 positions, lipobox for SPase II, double‑Gly leaders, and dibasic KR/RR or polybasic furin sites) and at nearby residues within N‑terminal secretory segments or internal propeptide junctions; additional peaks often over cysteines in the emerging mature extracellular peptide. Small, variable number of activated residues per protein.
Exemplars: - Venom peptide precursors (three-finger toxins, conotoxins, Kunitz inhibitors): activation at propeptide cleavage sites and conserved cysteine-rich mature toxin cores.
- Antimicrobial peptides/defensins and bacteriocins (plant/fungal defensins, hepcidins; class II bacteriocins with double‑Gly leaders; lantibiotics): activation at leader peptide cleavage motifs (GG) and cysteine-rich mature peptide segments.
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursors (POMC, proenkephalin, neuropeptide Y, insulin/IGF): activation at dibasic prohormone convertase sites and signal peptide cleavage.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins (influenza HA, coronavirus spike, retroviral Env): activation at signal peptide and polybasic/furin cleavage regions, with additional peaks in cysteine-rich ectodomains.
- Bacterial secreted toxins and secretory/outer-membrane proteins, including lipoproteins: activation at Sec signal peptide cleavage and lipobox/SPase II leader processing motifs.
- Plant/fungal pathogen effectors: activation on N‑terminal secretion signals and cysteine-rich effector cores, consistent with proteolytic maturation of secreted effectors.
- ER/Golgi lumenal secretory pathway residents (e.g., ERO1/ERO1-like): activation at signal peptide cleavage and adjacent residues; ER-retention motifs elsewhere are compatible.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments enriched in small/polar residues (serine, glycine, asparagine, proline) and often basic (lysine/arginine) tracts; the feature marks compositionally biased IDRs in N/C‑terminal tails and repeat‑rich regions while avoiding folded globular domains.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level, punctate peaks scattered across long disordered stretches (coil, low pLDDT), with little to no signal in well‑structured domains; often includes early N‑terminal residues but can occur anywhere within extended IDRs.
Exemplars: - Phosphatidylinositol 3‑kinase catalytic subunit: activation on polar low‑complexity motifs within the large disordered N‑terminus; no activation over ABD, RBD, C2, helical, or kinase domains.
- Viral accessory protein Vif (HIV‑1): peaks in the basic, disordered N‑terminal segment and other low‑confidence regions; avoids any folded elements.
- Viral capsomere‑interacting protein: sparse single‑residue peaks across a largely disordered protein lacking stable structure.
- Sperm protamine P2: dispersed activation across an arginine‑rich, fully disordered DNA‑binding protein, with peaks on Gly/Arg/Ser sites.
- Homeobox transcription factors: activation confined to extensive low‑complexity, asparagine‑rich disordered regions flanking the folded homeobox DNA‑binding domain, which is largely devoid of signal.

Summary: Detects Ser/Thr/Pro-rich low-complexity tandem-repeat tracts (PTS/EXT/SRR/EXT-type stalks), predominantly in secreted and cell-surface proteins, where these regions are typically O-glycosylated in eukaryotes; also occurs in fungal adhesins/flocculins and bacterial LPXTG-anchored surface proteins when they contain such S/T-rich repeats.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long, disordered repeat segments with periodic residue-level peaks on S/T (and weaker, phased peaks on Pro); minimal activation outside these tracts. Activation requires the presence of extended S/T-rich low-complexity repeats.
Exemplars: - Plant extensins/HRGPs: periodic peaks at the serine of each repeat (weaker at a fixed proline) across long disordered tandem-repeat regions.
- Fungal adhesins/flocculins (Rbt1/Flo11-like) and secreted enzymes with Ser/Thr-rich linker/stalks: dense activation over C-terminal S/T-rich low-complexity tails.
- Mammalian mucins (e.g., MUC7/MUC22): peaks on serines within PTS repeats that often coincide with O-glycosylation sites; no activation in structured regions.
Note: Proteins lacking extended S/T-rich repeat tracts (e.g., compact enzymes without linkers, short neuropeptide precursors, cytosolic motors) are not expected to activate.

Summary: Residue-level detector of intrinsically disordered, flexible termini and proteolytic processing junctions—especially N-termini (including the first residue of the mature chain after propeptide/leader cleavage)—with no strict amino‑acid specificity and a bias toward small/charged residues; common in small, secreted/precursor and viral proteins but also present in disordered regions of diverse proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered along sequences; enriched at N-termini (initiating Met or first residues after cleavage) and in nearby propeptides/leaders; predominantly within low-pLDDT/IDR coils, occasionally in low-confidence helices; can also appear at isolated residues in disordered stretches of longer proteins.
Exemplars: - Aspartic protease zymogen (Pepsin A): peaks in the activation (pro-)peptide and a strong peak at the mature-chain N-terminus immediately after cleavage.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursor (Microcin J25): peaks in the leader/propeptide and at the second residue of the mature core peptide near the processing/cyclization junction; minor peak in the mature strand.
- Polyomavirus agnoprotein: peaks at a di-basic N‑terminal motif in a short helix and in the disordered C-terminal tail.
- BH3-like pro-apoptotic microprotein: scattered peaks restricted to low-pLDDT/disordered regions; no preference for the annotated BH3-like motif.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunit (small complex subunit): sparse peaks in low-confidence segments with minor activation at the N-terminus.
- Splicing-regulatory microprotein: multiple peaks across basic, low-complexity disordered regions and a short low-confidence helix.

Summary: Generic cytosolic/nucleocytoplasmic N-terminal low-complexity/intrinsically disordered segments, typically enriched in basic (Lys/Arg), proline, glycine and serine, often immediately preceding or flanking cytosolic-facing targeting/linker regions (e.g., pre-transmembrane cytosolic tails). Not expected on cleaved secretory signal peptides or strongly hydrophobic leader sequences.

Activation pattern: Regional activation concentrated in the first tens of residues when such low-pLDDT, compositionally biased segments are present; strongest in coil with residue-level peaks at Lys/Arg/Pro (and Gly/Ser). Little to no activation on highly hydrophobic signal peptides or multi-pass membrane N-termini, or on well-ordered enzymatic N-termini; only occasional weak spillover into adjacent helices.

Exemplars:
- Single-pass membrane proteins with cytosolic N-termini: activation on the short N-terminal cytosolic segment immediately upstream of the first transmembrane helix; weak, scattered signal within the helix itself.
- Antisense/lncRNA-derived microproteins with basic-rich N-termini: scattered peaks across N-terminal disordered coil regions.
- Viral small proteins with basic/low-complexity N-terminal tails: activation across short N-terminal low-complexity stretches (not universal across all viral proteins).
- Mitochondrial/nuclear-targeted soluble proteins: activation on N-terminal compositionally biased targeting segments such as basic-rich presequences or NLS-like tails.
- Negative/rare cases (little/no activation expected): secreted peptide hormone precursors with signal peptides, mitochondrial-encoded strongly hydrophobic subunits (e.g., ND2), and large soluble enzymes with ordered N-termini (e.g., aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases).

Summary: Residues in intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments of regulatory proteins (especially transcription factors), often within short helix‑prone MoRF‑like stretches and enriched for S/P/G/A (with mixed polar/charged context), sometimes adjacent to aromatic “anchor” residues (e.g., the residue immediately N‑terminal to W in XW motifs). The signal largely favors disordered linkers/tails flanking DNA‑binding domains but can register isolated sites within the structured cores.
Activation pattern: Predominantly sparse, single‑residue peaks dispersed across sequences; enriched in low‑pLDDT/disordered regions, frequently near (upstream/downstream of) DNA‑binding domains; minimal contiguous activation and occasional isolated peaks inside structured domains.
Exemplars: - Homeobox transcription factors (Hox): isolated residues in the homeobox recognition helix plus additional peaks in low‑confidence helical segments of disordered regions.
- Nuclear hormone receptors: peaks in a short N‑terminal disordered helix and immediately upstream of the C4 zinc‑finger DNA‑binding domain.
- GATA zinc‑finger transcription factors: scattered residues in disordered, low‑complexity linkers; little/no activation within the GATA finger cores.
- C2H2 zinc‑finger transcription factors: a residue in a low‑confidence helical N‑terminal region with weaker peaks in the finger core and inter‑finger linker.
- ETS‑domain transcription factors: a prominent site in a disordered C‑terminal helix and weaker isolated sites within the ETS domain.
- MADS‑box transcription factors (AGL family): activation in the disordered C‑terminal tail; none in the MADS box or main coiled‑coil.
- Proline‑rich intrinsically disordered regulators (PRR‑like): consistent activation on the residue immediately preceding tryptophan (XW motif) within glycine/serine‑rich disordered regions.
- Adducin‑like cytoskeletal/regulatory proteins: very weak, scattered peaks in low‑confidence helical segments of long IDRs.

Summary: Proteins with a high burden of low-complexity, intrinsically disordered sequence enriched in S/T/G/P/A and R, requiring multiple extended tracts (each >20–30 aa) distributed across the protein and cumulatively comprising a large fraction (e.g., >80–100 aa or >20%) of the sequence.
Activation pattern: Diffuse, multi-region activation across numerous long LC coil segments; minimal or absent when only short linkers, single terminal tails, signal peptides, or isolated loops are present. Excludes hydrophobic low-complexity (e.g., signal peptides/TMs).
Exemplars: - RNA-processing and splicing factors with large IDRs (e.g., U2AF large subunit C-terminus plus additional LC regions)
- Glycoside hydrolases only when they possess unusually long disordered loops near catalytic domains (otherwise largely inactive)

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered tandem-repeat tracts enriched in small residues (Ala/Thr/Val with Pro/Gly), often alanine‑rich, found in extracellular adhesin/mucin-like regions and in flexible termini/linkers; the feature marks the periodic positions within such repeats (frequently ~12-aa cadence) and is largely absent from folded catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered low-complexity segments, with residue-level periodic peaks (strongest on Ala, moderate on Val and Thr; weaker on Pro/Gly) that recur at fixed positions within repeat units; minimal to no activation in well-structured domains.
Exemplars: - Fungal cell wall adhesins/flocculins (e.g., DAN-family mannoproteins): strong periodic peaks at the A/V that initiate each 12-aa repeat in disordered repeat blocks; weaker secondary peaks later in the unit.
- Epidermal differentiation S100-fused proteins (repetin-type): activation confined to the C-terminal disordered 12-aa tandem repeats, peaking at Ala (pos2) and Val (pos6) with consistent but lower signal on Thr/Pro/Gly at their consensus positions.
- PP2C/PPM phosphatases: no activation in the folded catalytic core; strong activation on Ala clusters within low-pLDDT N- and C-terminal disordered tails/linkers.
- Alphaherpesvirus envelope glycoproteins (gC): intense, periodic activation across a long alanine-rich disordered segment with repeating A(V/S)A/AA motifs and weaker preceding Pro residues.
- Tick receptor for OspA (TROSPA): alanine-focused activation distributed across the sequence, highest in low-confidence flexible regions (coils and termini), consistent with preference for disordered low-complexity segments.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity, compositionally biased regions/tails (IDRs), typically enriched in Ser/Gly/Pro/Ala/Thr and often occurring as acidic (Asp/Glu) or basic (Arg/Lys) tracts or Gln/Asn‑/Gln‑rich repeats; these segments are common in secreted precursors, viral proteins, micropeptides, and testis‑associated proteins, and can also occur as low‑complexity termini or surface loops appended to otherwise folded enzymes; they frequently coincide with low predicted structural confidence.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks scattered across multiple positions within low‑complexity/disordered segments, frequently at N‑ or C‑terminal regions; multiple short peaks rather than a single contiguous domain; often associated with low pLDDT/low‑confidence regions, but can also appear in flexible surface loops of structured proteins.
Exemplars: - Paramyxovirus fusion glycoproteins: activation on flexible, low‑confidence loops and cytoplasmic tail regions.
- Lentiviral Vif: activation on disordered/basic segments.
- p53‑inducible stress‑response proteins: activation on disordered coil segments and isoform‑variable regions.
- Secreted extracellular matrix/precursor proteins: activation on N‑ and C‑terminal IDRs and Ser/Pro/Thr‑rich segments.
- Plant seed storage prolamins/allergens: activation on glutamine‑rich repetitive low‑complexity blocks.
- Dictyostelium low‑complexity proteins: activation on Asn‑rich disordered tracts.
- Bacterial housekeeping enzymes (e.g., guanylate kinase) and P‑loop GTPases (Obg): activation on acidic C‑terminal tails or other low‑complexity surface loops/insertions.

Summary: Membrane-interacting helical modules: cationic, Gly/Ala-rich amphipathic α-helices and short transmembrane hairpins/fusogenic segments that mediate lipid binding, insertion, or pore formation in toxins, secretion/translocation factors, and viral/secreted proteins; typically low-confidence/disordered in isolation and become helical upon membrane contact.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous helical stretches; strongest over amphipathic or hydrophobic helices (including TM segments), with peaks on small hydrophobics (A/V/L/I/G) and frequent Lys/Arg; tends to avoid structured catalytic cores, instead marking N- or C‑terminal delivery/membrane-interaction regions; often coincides with low pLDDT and predicted helices or annotated transmembranes; in peptides, activates on the mature membrane-active helix rather than the signal peptide.
Exemplars: - Cry-family insecticidal δ-endotoxins: activation on the N‑terminal pore-forming helical bundle (domain I) of Cry13Aa.
- Cationic antimicrobial peptide (moricin): activation across the mature α‑helical AMP, not the signal peptide.
- Type VI secretion effector VasX: activation over the C‑terminal membrane-inserting module comprising multiple transmembrane helices.
- LXG polymorphic toxin (YqcG): activation on a long C‑terminal, low‑pLDDT disordered segment following the LXG export domain (a membrane/translocation-prone tail-like region).
- T6SS ADP‑ribosyltransferase (mART) effector (Tre1): activation on N‑terminal glycine‑rich, low‑confidence helical regions flanking PAAR and outside the catalytic core, consistent with delivery/membrane-targeting helices.

Summary: Short, solvent-exposed loop/turn motifs (beta-turn/hinge segments) used as binding or catalytic micro-sites across many folds; typically proline- and charge/hydrophobe-rich SLiMs rather than a family-specific signature, hence frequent in extracellular/repeat-rich proteins but present broadly in soluble enzymes and regulators
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks at scattered loop/turn positions with no positional bias along the sequence; usually 1–4 sites per protein, with dense runs only in large repeat-rich extracellular domains; activated residues span Pro and a mix of basic/acidic and hydrophobic/aromatic side chains, consistent with exposed turns and short interaction/catalytic loops
Exemplars: - TonB-dependent outer membrane receptors/transporters: TonB-box/periplasmic hairpins and extracellular loop beta-turns that mediate TonB or ligand interactions
- Carbohydrate-active glycoside hydrolases (e.g., beta-galactosidases, beta-glucuronidases, beta-mannosidases/mannanases, rhamnosidases, exo-glucosaminidases): catalytic acid/base loops and substrate-binding hairpins on TIM-barrel or beta-sandwich scaffolds
- Ubiquitin-like sulfur-carrier proteins (MoaD/ThiS/SAMP/URM1/MOCS2A/CysO): exposed beta-grasp turns, including the C-terminal diglycine–adjacent loop used for E1 docking
- Structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) ABC-like ATPases: short loops in the head/hinge regions (Walker/switch/signature-adjacent turns)
- Actin-binding profilins: polyproline-binding surface loop/turn patch
- SUMO/UBL pathway components and FHA-domain proteins: surface SLiMs in UBL/SUMO machinery (e.g., Lys-centered acidic motifs) and phosphothreonine-binding loops of FHA beta-sandwiches
- Large secreted/type I receptors with cysteine-rich EGF-like repeats: inter-repeat turns and acidic Ca2+-binding loop segments within cysteine-rich modules
- Bacteriophage tailspike/depolymerases: beta-helix interstrand turns shaping carbohydrate-binding/cleaving grooves
- HMG-CoA reductases: loops flanking the HMG-CoA/NAD(P)H active site
- RNA/rRNA modification enzymes (pseudouridine synthases): the catalytic Asp-containing loop and adjacent beta-turns that position the substrate base
- ABC/ECF transport nucleotide-binding components: P-loop/Walker A and signature/C-loop turns at the nucleotide-binding site
- Endolytic peptidoglycan transglycosylase RlpA and other cell-wall enzymes: catalytic Glu-containing loops and nearby turns in lytic transglycosylase domains
- Mycobacterium tuberculosis proteins (varied functions): multiple secreted/cell-envelope proteins showing repeated exposed loop/turn motifs consistent with the above

Summary: Residues at beta-strand starts and edge strands (loop-to–beta-strand junctions) in non‑transmembrane regions; the feature marks short stretches within beta-sheets and immediately preceding coils, consistent with generic beta-structure preferences rather than a specific function
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across proteins; peaks concentrate within beta-strands or the preceding loop/turn (coil→beta transitions), usually in well-structured, high‑confidence regions; typically absent from transmembrane helices and signal peptides; occasionally appears in short beta-like segments within otherwise disordered propeptides. Enriched for hydrophobic/aromatic and some acidic/polar residues with fewer basic residues.
Exemplars: - Membrane protein insertase YidC: multiple peaks in periplasmic/cytosolic beta-sheets and adjacent coils; none in transmembrane helices.
- Pentameric ligand-gated ion channels (proton-gated/bacterial Cys-loop homologs): peaks on beta-strands in the periplasmic/extracellular domain; not in signal peptides or TM segments.
- E3 ubiquitin ligase substrate receptor (GID complex): strongest signals at a coil→beta transition and nearby beta-strand residues.
- Glycoside hydrolases (beta-xylosidase): residues within beta-sheets and the loops immediately preceding them in the catalytic domain.
- CRISPR type III RAMP subunit (Cmr1): coil segments that transition into beta-strands and an N-terminal beta-strand.
- Integrin alpha subunits: loop-to-strand junctions within FG-GAP beta-propeller repeats of the extracellular head.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors (cathelicidin): select residues in the propeptide at a short predicted beta segment; no activation in the signal peptide or mature peptide.

Summary: Compositionally biased, low-complexity repeat tracts—often at protein N-termini—enriched in Ser/Gly with frequent Pro/Arg and recurring cysteine clusters (e.g., CCXP), typical of secreted/small peptide precursors and other disordered extracellular proteins; the feature marks residues within or just downstream of simple repeats and short secondary elements embedded in disorder.
Activation pattern: Broad regional, low-amplitude activation across extended low-complexity segments (frequently starting near the N-terminus), punctuated by modest residue-level peaks on Ser/Gly and nearby Pro/Arg/Cys; peaks often occur immediately after cysteine clusters/repeats (e.g., CCXP) or at the starts of short helices/strands within otherwise coil-rich regions.
Exemplars: - Keratin-associated proteins (CCXP-repeat, cysteine-rich hair matrix proteins): activation on cysteines and adjacent small residues within and just after CCXP blocks and in short predicted secondary elements.
- Neuropeptide/hormone precursors: activation across N-terminal signal/propeptide low-complexity stretches enriched in S/G/P/R around processing-rich regions.
- Venom peptides and other disulfide-rich toxins: activation on cysteine-rich motifs and flanking Gly/Pro-rich linkers in secreted precursors.
- Antimicrobial peptides and RiPP precursors: activation on Arg/Ser/Gly-rich low-complexity tracts near core/repeat regions.
- Plant small secreted peptides (defensin-/CRP-/RALF-like families): activation on N-terminal secretory segments and S/G/C-rich regions of the mature peptide.
- Viral small/accessory proteins: activation along Ser/Gly/Arg-rich low-complexity N-terminal stretches.

Summary: Short acidic/polar mixed-charge low-complexity motifs—DE-enriched segments with G/S/T and interspersed K/R—typically located in flexible loops or intrinsically disordered regions, forming generic acidic patches used for electrostatic interactions and found across many repeat/catalytic consensus motifs.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on short clusters (usually 2–6 residues) within loops/IDRs; occasionally extends over longer acidic low-complexity tracts in large eukaryotic proteins; occurs broadly across taxa and subcellular localizations.
Exemplars: Sm/LSM small nuclear RNP core proteins and associated RNA-binding factors: activation on acidic/mixed-charge low-complexity tails and loop patches mediating RNA/protein contacts; Ribosomal proteins uS12 and bL31: activation on short acidic/polar loop segments or mixed-charge surface patches that contact rRNA or partner proteins; Sugar/polyol dehydrogenases (SDR and related oxidoreductases): activation on acidic/polar loop motifs flanking Rossmann or catalytic regions; Peptidoglycan biosynthesis/remodeling enzymes (Mur ligases, lytic transglycosylases, amidases): activation on DE/S/T/G-rich loops near active sites (e.g., DXD/DXH-like acidic patches); Urease accessory protein UreE: activation on acidic/mixed-charge segments flanking the metal-binding region; Ataxin-2 family RNA-associated proteins: activation across long acidic low-complexity tracts and mixed-charge regions involved in RNP granule interactions; COQ8/ABC1 kinase-like proteins: activation on conserved acidic activation-loop motifs (DFG/DLG/HRD-like) and nearby gly/ser-rich segments; Axonemal/radial spoke proteins: activation on acidic low-complexity repeats used in assembly scaffolds; MORN repeat proteins: activation on repeat consensus micro-motifs enriched for D/T/G (e.g., TxG…DT…); DNA repair glycosylases: activation on HhH-GPD-like acidic/polar motifs and adjacent flexible loops.

Summary: Short small/polar–residue motifs (typically glycine-rich: GG/TG/DG) that cap or nucleate beta-strands—i.e., β-turn/strand‑edge segments—commonly repeated in extracellular β‑solenoid/β‑helix architectures (adhesins, tailspikes, many CAZy enzymes), but also occurring as isolated loop‑to‑β transitions and in short N‑terminal signal/propeptide segments across diverse proteins.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks concentrated at loop→beta transitions or at the ends of beta-strands, often centered on Gly/Thr/Asp; can appear as short regional runs in flexible/disordered segments that feed into β-structure; in large repeat-rich extracellular proteins, these peaks repeat along β‑solenoid/β‑helix repeats; frequent sharp peaks at extreme N-termini when a signal peptide or propeptide is present.
Exemplars: - Bacteriophage tail spike proteins: discrete peaks in coil/β mixed regions and low-confidence β-strands consistent with β‑solenoid turn/strand‑start motifs.
