- Capsid maturation proteases (prohead proteases): activation across the disordered N‑terminal propeptide and a glycine-centered β‑strand immediately downstream of the catalytic histidine in the mature enzyme.
- Type V autotransporter adhesins: sharp N‑terminal peak within the signal peptide; in many autotransporters, repeated activation along β‑solenoid passenger repeats.
- Soluble guanylate cyclase alpha subunits: sparse peaks at loop-to‑β transitions within the cytosolic domain.

Summary: Hydrophobic, gly/ala-rich membrane‑insertion helices/peptides used by toxins and envelope proteins—most often the proteolytically generated fusion or bacteriocin core segments and single‑pass transmembrane/pore‑lining helices; these regions are low in charge, frequently disordered until contacting membranes, and span long contiguous stretches.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across a single long hydrophobic segment. Strongest on N‑terminal fusion peptides or mature antimicrobial cores immediately after leader/furin cleavage, and on C‑terminal single‑pass transmembrane/pore‑forming helices; little to no activation on signal/leader peptides or enzymatic/toxin domains. Residue‑level peaks tend to coincide with small hydrophobics and glycine motifs (e.g., GG/GxG).
Exemplars: - Ribosomally synthesized bacteriocins (e.g., class II bacteriocins like lactacin F): activation on the mature antimicrobial core after double‑glycine leader cleavage, an amphipathic α‑helical, membrane‑disruptive segment.
- Viral class I fusion glycoproteins (e.g., paramyxovirus F): activation on the N‑terminal fusion peptide immediately following furin cleavage, a short hydrophobic helix that inserts into the host membrane.
- Type III secretion system translocon components (e.g., SctE): activation on the C‑terminal helical transmembrane segment that anchors/participates in pore formation.
- Consistent with broader set: pore‑forming toxins and CDI/Rhs systems where membrane‑inserting/translocation helices or pore‑lining segments mediate entry or delivery.

Summary: Beta-strand elements of well-folded, non-transmembrane domains—most prominently extracellular/periplasmic/lumenal ectodomains of membrane/secreted proteins (e.g., beta-sandwich/jelly-roll/propeller-like cores)—and, more generally, beta-rich cores of soluble domains
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated on beta-strands and adjacent loop termini within high-confidence structured regions; minimal/absent activation in transmembrane helices, signal peptides, disordered segments, and short cytosolic tails; residue preference consistent with beta-structure (hydrophobic/aromatic with Gly/Pro at turns); can span multiple discrete sites across a beta-rich domain
Exemplars: - Plant NDR1/HIN1-like single-pass membrane proteins: activation on the folded C-terminal ectodomain beta-strands; not on the N-terminal disordered segment or the transmembrane helix
- Proton-gated ion channels (bacterial): activation across beta-strands of the large N-terminal periplasmic domain and at the first TM boundary; little/no activation within TMs
- Integrin alpha family (metazoan): activation on beta-strand/loop regions in the distal ectodomain (thigh/calf and light-chain regions); absent from the single-pass TM and cytosolic tail
- Cys-loop ligand-gated ion channels: activation on the extracellular ligand-binding beta-sandwich domain; not in transmembrane segments
- Bacterial adhesins and phage tail/fiber apparatus: activation on beta-strand-rich extracellular/periplasmic cores (e.g., jelly-roll/beta-helix-like regions)
- Clathrin adaptor complex medium (mu) subunits: activation on the beta-sandwich mu-homology domain in the cytosol
- SecB-type chaperones: activation on the beta-strand core of the tetrameric chaperone
- Type IV secretion VirB8: activation on beta-elements within the periplasmic domain
- Chloroplast/PSII and plastid-division factors: activation on beta-strand regions of lumenal/peripheral domains

Summary: Low-complexity, compositionally biased segments (intrinsically disordered or simple-architecture helices), including propeptides and flexible loops, enriched in small/polar/charged residues and sometimes alanine-rich; commonly found at N-termini of secreted/viral proteins and often overlapping N-linked glycosylation sequons in flexible regions.
Activation pattern: Regional activation: scattered, low-amplitude residue-level peaks across long stretches with low predicted structural confidence (usually coils, occasionally simple alpha-helical low-complexity tracts); frequent near N-termini/propeptides but also internal.
Exemplars: - Viral hemagglutinin: activation in unstructured loop regions and at N-X-S/T N-glycosylation sequons.
- Conotoxin precursor proteins: activation concentrated in the disordered propeptide segment, with weaker peaks near the start of the mature toxin.
- Cancer/testis–associated small uncharacterized proteins (e.g., PBOV1-like): sparse peaks across low-confidence helical/coil regions typical of IDRs/LCRs.
- Antifreeze protein (Maxi type): isolated peaks along an alanine-rich long alpha helix (simple low-complexity helix), with little/no signal in the signal peptide.

Summary: Residue-level detector of bioactive/disordered segments in secreted/extracellular proteins and virion assembly proteins, highlighting the mature peptide core of small disulfide‑rich toxins/antimicrobial peptides and the flexible extracellular or assembly/reactive loops (including viral envelope, capsid, and scaffolding proteins), often marking key functional residues within low-structure regions
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks clustered within short stretches of the mature secreted peptide, extracellular loops, or disordered assembly regions (frequently near the N-terminus after a signal peptide); enriches for cysteine, glycine, and proline in low‑pLDDT coil or short beta‑strand segments; sparse elsewhere
Exemplars:
- Venom disulfide-rich toxin (scoloptoxin): activation confined to the cysteine‑rich mature toxin peptide, spanning coils and short beta‑strands.
- Serine protease inhibitor (trypsin inhibitor): peaks on the reactive site loop, including the P1 Lys of the inhibitory bond and adjacent flexible residues.
- Beta-defensin‑like antimicrobial protein (SPAG11 family): peaks on residues within beta‑strand elements of the secreted antimicrobial region.
- Poxvirus early/secreted envelope-like protein: sparse peaks in disordered extracellular segments, with occasional minor signal in the signal peptide and flexible luminal loops.
- Phage internal scaffolding protein: sparse peaks in disordered assembly regions involved in capsid morphogenesis.

Summary: Intrinsic-disorder/low-complexity regions: flexible coils in terminal tails, linkers, propeptides, and surface loops enriched in polar (Ser/Thr/Asn/Gln), basic (Lys/Arg), and Gly/Pro residues, often near the N-terminus and prevalent across taxa (including viral proteins, small secreted peptide precursors, and membrane-protein cytosolic loops)
Activation pattern: Diffuse, low-magnitude, residue-level peaks spread across long unstructured stretches (coil); regional activation tracking low-pLDDT/low-confidence segments; frequently near N-termini and within flexible loops rather than conserved catalytic/binding sites
Exemplars: - Viral capsid proteins (e.g., polyomavirus VP1): activation on low-pLDDT surface loops and disordered termini
- Small secreted peptide/neuropeptide/toxin precursors: activation on low-complexity propeptide regions and N-terminal signal/pro-segments
- Membrane proteins (transporters/receptors): activation on cytosolic disordered tails and flexible intracellular/extracellular loops
- Enzymes and regulatory proteins: activation on unstructured N-/C-terminal extensions and linker regions separating structured domains
- Diverse viral proteins (RNA/DNA viruses, bacteriophages): activation on intrinsically disordered, coil-rich regions used for flexible interactions

Summary: A structural detector for β-sheet–dominated domains (often extracellular/periplasmic but not limited to them), preferentially marking β-strands and their adjacent turns/strand–coil junctions (as in Ig-like, ZP-module, jellyroll/β-helix, and outer-membrane β-barrel folds) across taxa and viruses.
Exemplars (add): - Small heat shock proteins (e.g., plant class II sHSP): activation on β-sandwich strands of the α-crystallin domain.

Summary: Detector of the identity of the second residue at the extreme N-terminus of proteins, with strongest preference for small/polar residues (especially Ser or Ala; also Thr/Pro), i.e., an N-terminal position-2 signal commonly associated with generic, disordered starts and co-translational N-terminus processing
Activation pattern: Single-residue peaks confined to position 2 of the sequence; near-zero elsewhere. Activation is often very weak but widespread across taxa and functions, appearing when residue 2 is S/A/T/P and absent otherwise.
Exemplars: - Gas vesicle biogenesis protein O: weak, isolated peak at Ser-2 in a disordered N-terminus.
- Exodeoxyribonuclease VII small subunit: trace activation specifically at Pro-2; no signal elsewhere.
- Lantibiotic precursor (nisin Z): no detectable peak at position 2 or elsewhere, consistent with lack of the preferred position-2 residue.

Summary: Small-residue–biased low-complexity repeat regions—typically intrinsically disordered and enriched for Gly and/or Ser/Thr with frequent acidic (Asp/Glu) residues—serving as flexible linkers or mesh-forming domains (e.g., FG repeats in nucleoporins, PTS- or Ser/Thr-rich repeats in mucins/adhesins, glycine-biased linkers of secreted/cell-wall proteins); also includes N/Q-rich LCRs in some taxa (e.g., Apicomplexa) and occasionally captures glycine-periodic repeats such as Gly–X–Y in collagen-like sequences.
Activation pattern: Predominantly domain- or regional-level activation across long low-complexity segments with residue-level peaks centered on glycine or other small/polar residues within repetitive motifs (e.g., FG, PTS, DE-rich, N-rich tracts); minimal to no activation in structured domains or transmembranes.
Exemplars:
- FG-nucleoporins: strong periodic activation on the G of FG dipeptides across intrinsically disordered FG-repeat domains; no activation in structured regions.
- Mucins and fungal adhesins: activation across Ser/Thr-rich tandem repeat LCRs in secreted precursors.
- Secreted enzymes/proteases (e.g., xylanases, subtilisins): activation in disordered low-complexity linkers or propeptides flanking the structured catalytic cores.
- Extracellular matrix/biomineralization acidic/glycine-rich proteins: broad activation across long G/E/D- or S/T-rich LCRs; collagen-like Gly–X–Y repeats show periodic glycine-centered activation.
- Occasional activation in low-complexity transit peptides (mitochondrial/plastid) and in cytosolic/periplasmic low-complexity loops of membrane proteins, consistent with broad taxonomic spread.

Summary: Polar/charged side chains located within well‑ordered beta‑strands of beta‑rich proteins—especially extracellular/surface architectures such as outer‑membrane beta‑barrels and beta‑solenoid/amyloid repeats—often at pore‑lining, interaction, or repeat “ladder” positions; occasionally the same beta‑strand chemistry in soluble ligand‑binding sites.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks restricted to DSSP beta‑strands with high structural confidence; little/no activation in signal peptides, disordered regions, loops, or TonB plug domains. In beta‑helical passenger domains, peaks recur with the repeat periodicity (~18–20 aa). In beta‑barrels, peaks are scattered across multiple transmembrane strands and avoid extracellular loops. Activated residues are enriched for N/Q/E/D/S/T (and occasionally H/Y/K).
Exemplars: - TonB‑dependent receptors (siderophore/heme receptors): activation on discrete polar residues in the outer‑membrane beta‑barrel strands; plug and signal peptide are not activated.
- Classical porins (e.g., maltoporin): peaks on N/D/Q/H within transmembrane beta‑strands, including near sugar‑transport determinants; extracellular loops are not activated.
- Autotransporter adhesins (AIDA‑I): strongly periodic peaks on Q/N/E in beta‑strands of the beta‑helical passenger domain; glycosylated S/T‑rich loops and the C‑terminal translocator barrel are not activated.
- Functional bacterial amyloids (FapE): sparse activation on N/Q/T within cross‑beta strands of the amyloid core.
- Fungal cell‑wall adhesins (Candida AWP family): peaks on Asn within beta‑strands (often at N‑X‑T sequons) while signal peptides and disordered tails are inactive.
- Plant abscisic acid receptors (PYR/PYL): sparse activation on beta‑strand residues in the START‑like fold, including ligand‑binding site residues.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity repeat tracts—especially Ser/Thr‑ and Pro‑rich segments—forming long flexible tails or linkers (often C‑terminal); includes mucin‑like S/T‑rich extracellular regions and polar LCRs in diverse proteins.
Activation pattern: Long regional activation spanning tens to hundreds of residues within low‑pLDDT, coil-rich IDRs; punctuated peaks along tandem repeats; minimal/absent in folded domains; frequently enriched toward C‑terminal regions and often commencing after signal peptides in secreted proteins.
Exemplars: - Semenogelins (gel-forming seminal plasma proteins): strong activation across the tandem repeat–rich, disordered mature chain; inactive on the N‑terminal signal peptide.
- FHA-domain proteins with long disordered tails: activation confined to the low‑complexity C‑terminal IDR; no activation in the structured FHA domain.
- DNA ligases: activation on disordered linkers and low‑confidence coil segments, including C‑terminal flexible regions.
- Shigella invasion effector IpaA: activation on polar, compositionally biased disordered C‑terminal region and other low‑pLDDT patches.

Summary: Short strand–coil–strand connectors (beta-hairpin/turn hinges), typically single glycine- or small-residue positions that cap or link adjacent beta-strands in beta-sheet–rich domains; a structural, non-catalytic loop motif recurring across many families (e.g., Peptidase A2 aspartyl proteases, BTB/POZ and MATH, C2 domains)
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks at isolated positions (often glycine) in short coils between beta-strands, sometimes at strand–coil boundaries; a few peaks per protein; within well-structured domains and near but not on catalytic residues; minimal activation in helices, transmembranes, or disordered tails
Exemplars: - Retroviral/retrotransposon aspartyl proteases (Peptidase A2): sharp peaks at glycine-centered loop hinges connecting beta-strands within the protease domain, near but not at the catalytic Asp.
- DDI1-like aspartyl proteases: loop residues between beta-strands in the PR domain, proximal to the active site but non-catalytic.
- C2-domain proteins (ferlins; PSD2-like multi-C2 proteins): single residues in coil turns between beta-strands within C2 modules; occasional peaks near interdomain linkers/processing sites.
- BTB/POZ and related families (Kelch-like, ZBTB, BTB-MATH): glycine or small residues at strand-to-coil transitions and short loops inside BTB and MATH domains.
- Voltage-gated potassium channel alpha subunits: isolated loop residue in the cytosolic N-terminal beta-hairpin.
- Glyoxalase/hydrolase enzymes (GloC): a single residue in a coil linking adjacent beta-sheets, away from metal-binding sites.

Summary: Short, cationic, amphipathic peptide segments—typically the mature cores of secreted antimicrobial/cytolytic peptides and analogous AMP‑like helices embedded in larger proteins. These regions are Lys/Arg‑rich with interspersed hydrophobes, often form (or have propensity for) an amphipathic α‑helix, and are used for membrane interaction/disruption or other bioactive signaling; they are usually produced by proteolytic processing from precursor proteins and can include RiPP cores despite post‑translational crosslinks.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous blocks (∼15–40 aa, sometimes shorter), with sharp on/off at the boundaries of mature peptide segments; minimal activation in signal peptides and propeptides. Peaks often coincide with hydrophobic residues along an amphipathic face and clusters of Lys/Arg. Frequently at N‑ or C‑terminal helices or short internal helices with low-to-moderate pLDDT.
Exemplars: - Amphibian helical antimicrobial peptides (e.g., aureins): activation precisely on the mature AMP helix, not on signal/propeptide.
- Hymenopteran venom cytolysins (e.g., myrmeciitoxins): strong activation across the mature toxin’s amphipathic α‑helix.
- Lantibiotic RiPPs (e.g., lacticin 3147 A2): activation on the modified mature lantibiotic core despite lanthionine/beta‑methyllanthionine crosslinks.
- Phage/bacterial holins: activation on the N‑terminal amphipathic helix adjacent to the first transmembrane segment; little/no activation in TM or periplasmic domains.
- Crustacean anti‑lipopolysaccharide factors (ALFs): activation on the N‑terminal cationic LPS‑binding helix of the mature peptide.
- Plant NLR immune receptors (coiled‑coil N‑termini): activation on the N‑terminal CC helix implicated in membrane permeabilization/channel activity.
- Insect stress-response secreted proteins (Turandot family): activation on a C‑terminal amphipathic α‑helix of the mature chain.
- Outer membrane polysaccharide export proteins (CtrA family): activation on a short periplasmic C‑terminal helical tail with amphipathic character.
- Kininogen‑derived peptides (bradykinin variants): activation on the short, basic bioactive peptide released from a disordered region.

Summary: Generic detector of intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity, polar/charged segments, with a strong bias toward very N‑terminal targeting peptides (signal/transit peptide n‑/c‑regions) and flexible loops; not tied to a specific fold or function.
Activation pattern: Multiple very low‑magnitude, residue‑level peaks scattered across sequences, enriched at the first 20–80 residues and other low‑pLDDT regions; prefers S, T, G, A, P, E, D, R, K; occasional isolated peaks within structured domains; no consistent secondary‑structure preference.
Exemplars: Ribosomal proteins (e.g., bL27): basic, disordered N‑terminal tails; Spliceosomal CWC21: N‑terminal disordered segment with scattered peaks including into the folded CWF21 domain; Paramyxovirus nucleoproteins: disordered N‑terminal/loop regions with short polar motifs (e.g., NKS, SQ); Secreted precursors and plant small signaling peptides: signal peptide n‑/c‑regions and low‑complexity propeptides; Penicillin‑binding proteins (D,D‑transpeptidases): N‑terminal signal peptide flanks and disordered insertions; Organelle‑targeted proteins (mitochondrial/chloroplast): Arg/Ser/Thr‑rich transit peptides; Basic chromatin/sperm proteins and micropeptides: Lys/Arg‑rich intrinsically disordered stretches; DNA replication proteins and viral polymerases: flexible linkers and termini; Oxidoreductases (periplasmic/secreted): targeting peptides and disordered loops.

Summary: Alpha-helix capping/termination motifs at helix–coil junctions (N- and C-caps), especially at transmembrane-helix ends and signal-peptide boundaries; short adjacent dipeptides (often charged/polar or small, e.g., E–G, D–G, S/T–X, G–G) that stabilize or terminate helices
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks, typically 1–2 adjacent residues; distributed throughout sequences; enriched at predicted helix termini and juxtamembrane interfaces; often coincident with transitions into loops/disordered regions
Exemplars: - DNA-directed RNA polymerase omega: activation on the E–G dipeptide capping the C-terminal alpha-helix just before a low-confidence tail
- Twin-arginine translocase subunits (TatA/TatB/TatC and related inner-membrane proteins): activation on juxtamembrane helix-capping residues at TM-helix termini
- Viral small single-pass membrane proteins: activation on residues capping the sole transmembrane helix at the membrane–loop interface
- Secreted peptide/protein precursors with N-terminal signal peptides: activation at helix-to-coil transitions around the signal-peptide cleavage region where small/polar capping dipeptides occur
- Multi-pass inner-membrane transporters and assembly factors: multiple activations at the ends of successive TM helices
- Soluble proteins across taxa: activation at surface helix caps marking helix–loop junctions

Summary: Generic signature of intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments enriched in small/polar residues (notably Pro/Ser/Gly/Gln/Tyr), commonly found in regulatory regions such as transcriptional activation domains and cytosolic tails of membrane proteins; marks SLiM‑bearing polar/proline/glycine‑biased IDRs rather than structured domains
Activation pattern: Very weak, sparse residue‑level peaks scattered within low‑pLDDT/coil regions; strongest in polar/low‑complexity N‑ or C‑terminal stretches and at TM–cytoplasmic junctions; little to no signal in well‑packed helices, beta sheets, or transmembrane segments; overall low, ubiquitous background across many proteins
Exemplars: - Homeobox transcription factors: scattered peaks across N‑terminal disordered activation regions with polar compositional bias (e.g., DLX family).
- Neuronal BEAN family regulators: multiple weak peaks in the disordered, polar‑biased C‑terminal region (including isoform‑specific segments).
- Single‑pass C‑type lectin–like receptors: enrichment in the low‑confidence cytoplasmic tail and TM–cytosolic boundary (Ser/Tyr‑bearing disordered stretches).
- Microtubule‑associated/regulatory proteins: minor peaks in flexible coil loops within otherwise structured proteins.
- Plant glycine‑rich/cold‑regulated factors: largely disordered proteins show only minimal activation unless segments are strongly polar/Pro/Gly‑biased.
- Bacterial toxin–antitoxin antitoxins: predominantly helical/coiled‑coil cores show negligible activation, consistent with absence of low‑complexity IDRs.
- Multipass membrane proteins with long C‑terminal regions: remain inactive when the disordered tail lacks the characteristic polar/Pro/Gly bias, illustrating compositional selectivity within IDRs.

Summary: Intrinsic disorder/low‑complexity segments enriched in polar/charged and small flexible residues, typically found in N-/C‑terminal tails and inter‑domain linkers of regulatory proteins—especially transcription factors—rather than in their structured DNA/ligand‑binding cores
Activation pattern: Sparse, very low‑magnitude, residue‑level peaks that preferentially fall in predicted disordered, low‑pLDDT regions (often termini and linkers); rarely align with canonical structured domains; occasional weak peaks within helices/strands of folded domains
Exemplars: - Homeobox transcription factors (e.g., Hox/caudal): weak peaks in disordered N‑terminal regions and adjacent to the hexapeptide motif; minimal signal inside the homeobox
- ETS‑domain transcription factors: peaks in low‑confidence N‑terminal segments; only scattered, weaker signal within the ETS domain
- GATA zinc‑finger factors: activation on low‑complexity disordered regions outside the zinc‑finger domains
- bHLH‑PAS transcription factors (e.g., trachealess): signal in long disordered C‑terminal tails and linkers, not the bHLH/PAS cores
- Nuclear hormone receptors: strongest in the disordered N‑terminal AF‑1 region and C‑terminal tail; occasional weak spots within the helical LBD
- Plant MADS‑box transcription factors: weak activation in non‑MADS, low‑confidence central regions
- Autophagy‑related/scaffold proteins: isolated peaks in predicted disordered segments across mixed secondary structure context
- Disordered transcriptional co‑regulators (e.g., MN1): near‑silent overall with only tiny peaks in disordered regions, consistent with a broad, low‑specificity disorder signal

Summary: Short, low‑complexity intrinsically disordered segments (S/Q/P/G/K‑rich) that often correspond to transcriptional regulatory interaction regions flanking or linking DNA‑binding domains in many (but not all) transcription factor families; primarily outside the structured DNA‑binding fold, occasionally extending to nearby residues within the fold; presence and strength are not universal across family members.
Activation pattern: Sparse residue‑level peaks or very short runs in low‑pLDDT coil regions, typically in N‑ or C‑terminal/disordered flanks around DNA‑binding domains; rare, weaker peaks within structured domains; many proteins show only a few activated residues, and some orthologs show sub‑threshold or no detectable activation.
Exemplars: Representative families (activation observed in some members, not universally): Paired/PAX factors: activation on disordered N‑ and C‑terminal regions outside the Paired domain; Homeobox/HOX: strongest in N‑terminal disordered polar segments with minor peaks in the homeobox helix; ETS family: disordered N‑terminal region preceding the ETS domain; GATA factors: disordered region mediating partner interaction (e.g., TBX21) rather than the zinc fingers; Forkhead/FOXO: C‑terminal disordered tail with minor peaks near the Forkhead domain; T‑box (Brachyury): highly disordered C‑terminus with small peaks at the T‑box boundary; bHLH (HELT/Twist): unstructured C‑terminal or interdomain regions distal to the bHLH/Orange domain; C2H2 zinc‑finger proteins (e.g., EGR/rotund): disordered or alternatively spliced segments, not the zinc fingers; Runt domain factors (RUNX): disordered segment at the N‑terminal/edge of the Runt domain.

Summary: Generic structural motif recognizing short loop/turn segments at the entrances and edges of beta-strands (beta-strand N-caps, strand-edge residues, and loop→beta transitions), often enriched in small/polar/acidic residues (G, S, T, D, E) within well-ordered domains across diverse proteins
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on many short, discrete segments scattered through structured domains; strongest at coil-to-beta transitions and the first few residues of beta-strands, with occasional signal within short beta-strands or adjacent helices; minimal activity in signal peptides, transmembrane helices, or highly disordered/low-confidence regions; can coincide with functional sites that reside on these structural boundaries (e.g., ligand-binding strands) but is not function-specific
Exemplars: - Glycoside hydrolases (alpha-L-fucosidase): multiple peaks on loops immediately preceding beta-strands and within short beta segments in the catalytic domain; signal peptide inactive
- HECT-type E3 ubiquitin ligases (UPL7): clustered peaks in the C-terminal HECT domain on coils/strand boundaries, including near the catalytic cysteine
- RING-type E3 ligases (DTX3): several loop→beta transitions and a short beta-strand outside the RING finger
- Mono-ADP-ribosyltransferases (C3 toxin): strong peaks on NAD(+)-binding strand–loop–strand elements (beta-strands and adjacent loops) within the catalytic domain; signal peptide inactive
- Chromatin/DNA-binding SAND domain proteins (Sp100): dominant peak on a loop preceding a beta-strand within the SAND domain, plus a minor helical segment
- Thioester-containing complement-like glycoproteins (CD109/alpha-2-macroglobulin family): peaks on flexible loops and beta-strand edges in the extracellular domain; not at glycosylation or thioester sites
- Zona pellucida (ZP) extracellular matrix proteins (ZP1): focal activation at coil→beta transitions within the ZP domain; absent in signal peptide, transmembrane helix, and cytosolic tail
- Plant nuclear regulators (ASI1-interacting): activity confined to the structured C-terminal region (helices/beta), with little signal in the disordered N-terminus

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments enriched in proline/serine/threonine (often proline‑rich), which act as flexible, post‑translational‑modification–prone regions (e.g., O‑glycosylation/hydroxyproline in secreted peptides; phosphorylation in cytosolic tails) across diverse taxa
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks clustered within disordered coil regions and short low‑pLDDT stretches; sparse or patchy activation across long IDRs; minimal activation within well‑folded domains
Exemplars: - Hyp-rich systemin (HypSys) peptide precursors (plant peptide hormones): activation on disordered mature peptide segments rich in proline, centered on hydroxyproline and O‑glycosylation sites.
- Serine/threonine protein kinases (eukaryotic): activation in long, low‑complexity C‑terminal tails and linkers; absent from the structured kinase and zinc‑finger domains.
- Plant virus small/accessory proteins (e.g., potyvirus proteins): dispersed activation across largely disordered, low‑confidence coil-rich sequences.
- Secreted extracellular/cuticle-like proteins: activation on Pro/Ser/Thr‑rich low‑complexity repeats typical of O‑glycosylated regions.
- Mitochondrial import/respiratory small subunits: activation on unstructured targeting sequences and low‑complexity termini rather than transmembrane cores.

Summary: Short non-domain terminal segments: N-terminal secretory signal peptides and propeptides, and more generally intrinsically disordered/low‑complexity tails and linkers outside folded domains
Activation pattern: Predominantly low-amplitude, residue-level peaks that cluster over short stretches; enriched at N-termini (signal peptides/propeptides) and within disordered or low-complexity regions, with little sustained activation in structured domain cores; can appear anywhere along the sequence but favors non-domain segments
Exemplars: - Secreted antimicrobial/neuropeptide precursors: strong activation over the N-terminal signal peptide, minimal in the mature peptide region
- Plant damage-associated peptide precursors (PROPEP): activation on a short N-terminal propeptide preceding the processed signaling peptide
- Plant viral movement proteins: sparse peaks across extensive intrinsically disordered regions and near export/localization motifs
- ETS-family transcription factors: highest activation in C-terminal low-complexity/disordered regions, with only weak, sporadic peaks inside the folded ETS domain

Summary: Residue-level detection of β-strand-connecting loop/turn positions (β-hairpin/coil apex residues) across diverse β-sheet–rich domains, with a strong preference for Gly and Asx (Asp/Asn) and occasional His/Thr at the turn.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks: sparse, single–amino-acid spikes centered on coil residues that link adjacent β-strands; multiple such peaks can appear in β-rich, multidomain eukaryotic proteins, while many bacterial proteins show only 1–2 peaks. Little activation in helices, long disordered or coiled-coil regions.
Exemplars: - E3 SUMO-protein ligase PIAS (PINIT domain): sharp peak at a coil residue between β-strands (e.g., His in PINIT; minor in RING zinc-finger loop).
- Synaptic scaffolding proteins with Fn3 and SH3 domains: peaks at Gly/Asp in Fn3 and SH3 β-hairpin loops.
- BTB/POZ domain zinc-finger regulators: single peak at a BTB loop residue between neighboring β-strands.
- Thioredoxin reductase-like selenoprotein T homologs: Asp at a loop connecting β-strands.
- TonB-dependent outer membrane receptors (plug and barrel): strong Gly at a plug-domain loop linking β-strands; weaker Gly/Asn in barrel loops.
- Signal peptidase I (periplasmic domain): Asp-centered peak in a β-strand-connecting loop.
- 2Fe-2S ferredoxin-type subunits: Gly in the short loop between β-strands flanked by Fe–S–ligating Cys residues.
- Diacylglycerol kinase delta: Gly/Cys in loops of PH and C1 (zinc-finger) domains that connect β-strands; additional weak peaks in other β-loop positions.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments enriched in small/polar residues (notably S, P, G, Q), corresponding to activation/modulatory regions and flexible linkers; common in transcription factors but present across many protein classes
Activation pattern: Diffuse, low‑amplitude activation spanning extended IDRs with low pLDDT and coil propensity; highest at scattered S/P/G/Q residues; strongly reduced over well‑structured domains (helices/sheets, zinc fingers, ligand‑binding cores); often localized to N‑ or C‑terminal disordered regions outside catalytic or DNA‑binding cores
Exemplars: - Forkhead transcription factors (e.g., FOX family): activation on Pro/Gly‑rich disordered tails flanking the forkhead DNA‑binding domain; little to no signal in the folded forkhead core.
- Nuclear receptors (e.g., Ecdysone receptor): activation on the N‑terminal AF‑1/modulating region that is disordered and polar‑biased; minimal in the C4 zinc‑finger DBD and helical LBD.
- NF‑YB (CCAAT‑binding factor subunit): activation on low‑complexity acidic/polar termini outside the histone‑fold core.
- RNA‑binding/splicing factors: activation on gly/ser/glutamine‑rich low‑complexity regions and linkers rather than RNA‑recognition or other structured domains.
- Membrane proteins/channels: activation on long cytosolic low‑complexity loops and termini, not within transmembrane helices.
- Enzymes and bacterial proteins: activation on flexible low‑complexity linkers/tails adjacent to structured catalytic cores.
- Secreted peptide/protamine precursors: activation on disordered, low‑complexity propeptide regions.

Summary: Short, aromatic- and cysteine-enriched interfacial helices/patches that mediate contacts at lipid membranes or protein/protein/nucleic-acid interfaces; typified by Trp/Phe clusters and/or palmitoylation‑prone Cys pairs/clusters; these segments act as interfacial anchors or contact elements rather than core transmembrane helices
Activation pattern: Regional activation in short (≈5–15 aa) patches with residue-level peaks; strongest on Trp (often consecutive), Phe/Leu/Ile/Val, and clustered Cys, frequently with flanking/interspersed Gly; enriched adjacent to transmembrane helices (juxtamembrane tails) and in aromatic helical modules of secreted proteins, and also present in soluble coiled-coils/interaction helices; low/absent across transmembrane cores and generic signal peptides; often helical but can occur in flexible tails
Exemplars: - GPCRs: activation on the cytosolic C‑terminal juxtamembrane segment containing Cys pairs/triples immediately after TM7, silent on the seven TM helices
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on Trp‑rich helical patches in the effector domain (WY‑like), minimal on the N‑terminal signal peptide and modest at the RxLR motif
- Viral structural/membrane proteins: activation on membrane‑proximal aromatic clusters and nearby cysteines acting as interfacial anchors
- Type III/IV secretion effectors: activation on short amphipathic/aromatic patches or cysteine clusters used for host‑membrane association
- Apicomplexan secretory organelle proteins: activation on Trp‑rich helical segments or juxtamembrane aromatic patches implicated in membrane/host interaction
- Small mitochondrial intermembrane proteins: activation on glycine‑interrupted hydrophobic/aromatic stretches consistent with membrane‑interface helices rather than full TM spans
- Soluble interaction modules (e.g., U‑box E3 ligases, KH/coiled‑coil scaffolds): activation on short Leu/Phe/Trp‑bearing helices that mediate partner binding or subcellular targeting

Summary: Short, structured coil/loop segments at alpha-helix boundaries (helix-capping and helix–helix linker loops), often immediately preceding the start of a helix (N-caps); a generic structural signal enriched in polar/charged and Gly/Pro residues and largely absent from long, stable helices or long disordered tails.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks dispersed across sequences, concentrated in short coil/turn regions that cap or connect alpha-helices (frequently just before a helix or between helices); minimal activation in extended helical segments, signal peptides, or long disordered regions; occasional emphasis on functional motifs when they occur in such loop-to-helix contexts (e.g., CXXC).
Exemplars: - Plant pectinesterase inhibitor: activation in loops linking helices within the mature domain; inactive on the N-terminal signal peptide helix.
- Ras GTPase-activating protein (Ras-GAP domain): sparse peaks in unstructured loops within/adjacent to the domain, especially at helix-connecting segments; not on the arginine finger or stable helices.
- Mini-RNase III: a single strong peak at an Asp in a structured loop within the nuclease domain; no activation at the catalytic Asp or disordered tail.
- ERO1-like disulfide oxidase: strong peak at the redox CXXC motif positioned in a loop-to-helix transition (helix-capping context).
- FeoB Fe2+ transporter: peaks in coil segments immediately preceding transmembrane helices and in loops between helices.
- Alpha-catulin (cytoskeletal adaptor): peaks in short coil linkers that precede or connect long alpha-helical/coiled-coil segments.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments enriched in Ser/Pro/Gly/Ala and basic residues (Arg) — frequently short peptides or N‑terminal tails/propeptides of diverse proteins — rather than a specific folded domain
Activation pattern: Regional activation over continuous low‑complexity tracts; strongest across Ser/Pro/Gly‑rich runs and Arg‑containing patches; often biased to N‑terminal regions but can recur at multiple disordered segments throughout long proteins; in very small proteins/micropeptides, activation spans most of the sequence
Exemplars: Herpesviridae small/tegument/regulatory proteins — activation on Ser/Pro‑rich disordered regions and basic low‑complexity tails; Plant small secreted peptides and pathogen effectors (proline‑rich/low‑complexity prepropeptides and repeats) — activation on flexible propeptides and mature low‑complexity segments; Bacterial ATP synthase epsilon subunit — activation on flexible Gly/Ser‑rich terminal tails/linkers; Bacterial lipoylation octanoyltransferase (LipB family) — activation on Gly/Ser‑rich loops/N‑terminal disordered extensions; Human testis/spermatogenesis‑associated proteins and lncRNA‑encoded micropeptides — activation across Arg/Ser/Pro‑rich low‑complexity sequences; Secreted precursors including antimicrobial/toxin peptides — activation on propeptides and adjacent low‑complexity regions; RNA‑binding/regulatory proteins — activation on RS/Arg‑ and Ser‑rich intrinsically disordered regions

Summary: Mature extracytoplasmic/luminal segments of secretory‑pathway proteins—either the cleavage‑released bioactive core of secreted precursors (toxins, neuropeptides/hormones, bacteriocins, fungal effectors) or exposed extracytoplasmic/luminal domains of membrane/envelope and surface-assembly proteins (including viral envelope glycoproteins and bacterial Type IV pilins), as well as ER‑lumenal secretory enzymes (e.g., ERO1); often small, disulfide‑stabilized modules located downstream of the signal/leader
Activation pattern: Regional activation with sharp residue‑level peaks confined to short stretches corresponding to the mature/extracytoplasmic core; commonly near the N‑terminus after the signal/leader, but in larger proteins may occur in more distal luminal/extracytoplasmic domains; few activated sites per protein, heterogeneous residue preferences rather than a single motif; multiple regions possible in multi‑peptide proproteins
Exemplars: - Conotoxin precursors: activation confined to the mature toxin peptide; signal and propeptide segments show little/no activation
- Neuropeptide/hormone proproteins: activation on the individual processed hormone/neuropeptide segments rather than the signal peptide
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: activation on cleaved N‑terminal extracellular subunits/fusion‑active or receptor‑binding segments
- Bacterial leader‑bearing bacteriocins/toxins: activation on the core toxin immediately following the leader sequence
- Bacterial Type IV pilins and related secretion/adhesion components: activation on exposed extracytoplasmic modules of the pilus subunit
- Fungal secreted small effectors and other cysteine‑rich secreted peptides: activation on the disulfide‑stabilized effector/toxin domain
- ER‑lumenal oxidoreductases (e.g., ERO1): activation on accessible luminal segments within the catalytic/disulfide relay region

Summary: Short linear proline/tyrosine/threonine–rich motifs used for host-factor recruitment and membrane trafficking/assembly (viral “late domains” PPxY/PTAP and tyrosine-based sorting/binding signals YxxΦ/YPxL/NPxY and related P/Y/T‑centered SLiMs), typically embedded in disordered loops or TM-adjacent amphipathic segments; the feature highlights the core P–T–Y and neighboring hydrophobic/aromatic residues that mediate adaptor (WW, SH3, AP, PTB/SH2) binding across viral, bacterial, archaeal, and eukaryotic proteins.
Activation pattern: Short regional activation with sharp residue-level peaks centered on the SLiM core (2–6 residues), often within cytosolic tails, flexible loops, or membrane-interfacial helices; activations concentrate on Pro and aromatic/hydrophobic residues with frequent Tyr and Thr.
Exemplars: - Retroviral Gag p6 late-domain segments – activation on PPxY and/or PTAP motifs that recruit NEDD4/ESCRT.
- Filovirus/arenavirus matrix proteins – activation on PPxY/PTAP L-domains.
- Paramyxo/orthomyxo/coronavirus envelope cytosolic tails – activation on tyrosine-based endocytic/trafficking signals (YxxΦ, YPxL).
- Adenoviral vertex/capsid-associated proteins (e.g., protein VI/IIIa/IX) – activation on short proline/tyrosine-rich motifs in membrane-lytic/trafficking segments.
- Viroporins (e.g., influenza M2, coronavirus E/ORF3a) – activation on interfacial Tyr/Pro within short TM amphipathic helices carrying YxxΦ-like signals.
- Type III/IV bacterial effectors (e.g., CagA, Tir, EspF/Tarp families) – activation on SH2/PTB-binding tyrosine phosphorylation motifs (EPIYA variants, NPxY/YPxD/YPxxP).
- Bacteriocins/colicins and antibacterial peptides – activation on short aromatic/proline-rich amphipathic stretches used for receptor engagement or pore formation.
- Gram-negative autotransporter/adhesin β-helix passengers – activation on conserved tyrosine–turn motifs (e.g., YxD/φPG turns) within repeat stacks.
- Archaeal S-layer repeats – activation on P/Y-enriched solvent-exposed loops implicated in lattice assembly.
- Eukaryotic chromatin proteins (histone H3 tails) – activation on the Y41-containing KPHRYRPGT segment (P/Y/T-rich reader/kinase target site).
- CRISPR-Cas13a endoribonucleases – activation on exposed P/Y/T-rich linker/loop segments between HEPN domains.

Summary: Short, aromatic- and glycine-rich surface loops/edge β-strands on solvent-exposed regions (extracellular, luminal, or cytosolic) that mediate membrane, carbohydrate, or protein engagement; this includes fusion peptides/loops, WSXWS-like aromatic segments in FNIII/Ig-like domains, aromatic sugar-binding patches of carbohydrate-interacting modules, and analogous active-site or binding-groove lining loops in soluble enzymes.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks forming short 10–20 aa stretches, often multiple per large domains; in membrane proteins, peaks localize to extracellular/luminal regions; in soluble enzymes/adaptors, peaks line active sites or protein-interaction surfaces.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/fusion glycoproteins (class I/II; e.g., flavivirus E/prM): activation on the aromatic, glycine-rich fusion peptide/loop used for membrane insertion.
- HAP2/GCS1 gamete fusion proteins: activation on the conserved aromatic fusion loop at the tip of the ectodomain.
- Type I cytokine/hematopoietic receptors: activation on the short WSXWS-containing aromatic segment within the extracellular FNIII domain important for folding/ligand binding.
- Plexins and MET/HGF receptor tyrosine kinases: activation on exposed loops/edge β-strands within IPT/TIG (Ig-like) ectodomains enriched in aromatics.
- Complement/alpha-2-macroglobulin/TEP family: activation on short aromatic/glycine-rich loops near thioester/bait or ligand-interaction regions.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes (glycosidases, glucan-active transferases; CBMs): activation on aromatic sugar-stacking patches/loops at carbohydrate-binding surfaces or adjacent to catalytic grooves.
- Cytosolic carbohydrate-active enzymes (e.g., glycogen debranching enzyme): activation on aromatic loops lining glucan-binding/catalytic grooves.
- Phosphoinositide 5-phosphatases (e.g., INPP5K): activation on short aromatic loops near the catalytic pocket mediating substrate binding.
- Multi-pass transporters/regulators (e.g., CNNM family): activation on short aromatic-rich extracellular/periplasmic loops.
- ER luminal protein glycosyltransferases (e.g., POGLUT2): activation on aromatic loops shaping donor/acceptor-binding sites.
- Cytosolic adaptors/scaffolds (e.g., TAX1BP1): activation on exposed loops within interaction domains that contact partners or ubiquitin.

Summary: Glycine‑centered tight β‑turn/hairpin loop motif at sheet–sheet or coil‑to‑β transitions, typically an Asx/Ser/Thr–Gly sequence (often D–G, sometimes P/S/T preceding and Lys nearby), marking short, well‑ordered loops that link adjacent β‑strands across diverse folds
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks focused on the glycine within 2–4 residue coil segments that connect two β‑strands; occasional spillover to the preceding Asx/Ser/Thr or the first residue of the following strand; multiple discrete occurrences per protein; strong in structured loops near β‑sheets, weak/absent in helices and extended disordered regions
Exemplars: - Flavin‑dependent monooxygenases and other flavoprotein oxidoreductases: activation on short DG/GxG β‑turns at the edges of the central β‑sheet of the FAD/Rossmann‑like core
- Bacterial antibiotic‑modifying monooxygenases and ubiquinone hydroxylases: glycine‑rich β‑hairpin turns linking neighboring β‑strands
- Plant chloroplastic/mitochondrial oxidoreductases (carotenoid/quinone and amine metabolism): the same DG/SG turns in sheet‑connecting loops
- FAD‑dependent histone demethylases (amine oxidase fold): glycine‑centered β‑turns adjacent to the FAD‑binding β‑sheet
- UBX‑domain proteins: a PSG loop connecting two β‑strands within the UBX β‑sandwich (sharp peak on the loop glycine)
- Cilia/flagella‑associated scaffolds and band 4.1/FERM/PH/MORN‑repeat proteins: recurrent sheet‑edge turns in β‑rich domains highlighted, with minimal signal in long low‑complexity regions
- Other quinone/redox‑chain enzymes: repeated short DG/GxG turns at β‑strand junctions across the fold

Summary: Short, exposed beta‑strand/loop patches in secreted or surface proteins that constitute carbohydrate‑recognition/adhesive interfaces (aromatic platform residues on S/T/G/A‑rich strands), typically positioned just after signal peptides at N‑terminal domain edges; in non‑carbohydrate secreted proteins the same pattern appears on N‑terminal edge strands (e.g., flanking BRICHOS domains).
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks in short local clusters (≈4–10 residues), often near N‑termini; centered on beta‑strands followed by brief loops; strong enrichment for Ser/Thr/Gly/Ala with Tyr/Trp/Phe; does not span whole domains and is inactive over signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Glycosidases (GH families): activation on aromatic-lined loops of the substrate‑binding cleft that contact sugars.
- Polysaccharide lyases (e.g., pectate/alginate lyases; beta‑helix/solenoid folds): activation on exposed rungs/ridges and aromatic platforms of the receptor‑binding surface.
- Lectins and carbohydrate‑binding modules (C‑type lectins, galectins, CBM14/CBM18/LysM): activation on sugar‑binding loops and aromatic stacking residues.
- Phage tailspike/tail fiber receptor‑binding proteins: activation on beta‑solenoid receptor‑binding faces that engage LPS/O‑antigen or capsular polysaccharides.
- Fungal chitinases and cell‑wall proteins: activation on chitin‑binding modules (e.g., LysM/CBM) and adjacent loops.
- Bacterial adhesins and pilus tip lectins: activation on glycan‑binding adhesive tips/domains involved in host attachment.
- Mammalian secreted/ECM lectin‑like proteins: activation on carbohydrate‑recognition surfaces of beta‑sandwich folds.
- BRICHOS‑domain secreted proteins (e.g., gastrokines): activation on N‑terminal beta‑strands immediately adjacent to the BRICHOS core, consistent with preference for exposed edge strands in secreted domains.

Summary: Intrinsic disorder/low-complexity segments enriched in polar/small residues (often Ser/Thr- and Pro-rich), typically in N-terminal tails and propeptides; can extend into short, flexible helices in small proteins; avoided in well-structured domains
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across low-confidence, disordered regions, usually multiple per sequence; strongest in early/N-terminal stretches and around proteolytic processing sites; little to no activation inside stable, repeat- or domain-structured cores; may include short helices when overall structure is flexible/poorly ordered
Exemplars: - p53-regulated apoptosis-inducing protein: peaks in the N-terminal intrinsically disordered region
- Plant elicitor peptide precursor (PROPEP family): activation across a disordered prodomain; absent in the short structured mature peptide
- Antimicrobial peptide precursor (Ixosin): peaks throughout the unstructured propeptide with a strong peak at the cleavage junction, plus additional sites within the short cationic helical mature peptide
- Type II restriction–modification DNA methyltransferase: activation confined to low-complexity, unstructured N-terminal regions; not in the folded C-terminal TPR repeats
- F1 ATP synthase epsilon subunit: activation along low-confidence helical segments in a small, largely flexible protein

Summary: Polar low-complexity intrinsically disordered regions enriched in Ser/Thr and small residues (often with Pro/Gly), including mucin-like extracellular repeats, RS/RG- or S/Q-rich nuclear IDRs of RNA-binding/viral proteins, and short S/T/Gly-rich tails/loops in diverse proteins.

Activation pattern: Strong activation requires windows ≥25 aa with high Ser/Thr density (≈≥40–50% S/T) and few hydrophobic/charged interruptions; scattered S/T in structured contexts yields weak/absent activation, with only brief peaks on flexible loops/termini.

Exemplars:
- Mucin-like extracellular glycoproteins: long, uninterrupted S/T/P-rich repeats strongly activate; membrane mucins with short or highly interspersed repeats (e.g., MUC1/MUC21-type) may fall below threshold and appear negative.
- Viral and host RNA-binding proteins (e.g., nucleoprotein tails, ICP27-like factors): activation only when RS/RG- or S/T-rich disordered tracts are present; fragments or variants lacking such tracts are negative.
- Dictyostelium extracellular/adhesion proteins: extended Ser/Thr-rich repeats.
- Fungal cell-wall mannoproteins/adhesins: Ser/Thr-rich repeats.
- Plant cell-wall glycoproteins (AGP/extensin-like, Ser/Pro-rich): activation on S/T/Pro-rich segments.
- Prokaryotic and organellar enzymes: largely negative; occasional brief activation on short S/T/Gly-rich insertions or termini.
- Organelle targeting peptides: only the subset with S/T/A-rich low complexity shows modest activation; Arg-rich amphipathic presequences do not.

Summary: Compositionally biased regions (IDRs or short low-complexity segments) that are explicitly Ser/Pro-biased or enriched for simple dipeptide repeats (SS/PP, RS/SR, RG/RGG) and basic residues; these tracts occur in viral accessory proteins and micropeptides and as Ser/Pro-rich linkers/termini in diverse proteins. Generic hydrophobic signal peptides without such polarity/repeat bias are not targets.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over Ser/Pro-biased low-complexity segments, especially N- or C-terminal tails and prosegments immediately adjacent to signal peptides; residue-level peaks require clustered S/P or RS/RG/SP motifs. Purely hydrophobic signal peptides and structured cores without such biased tracts are not activated.
Exemplars:
- Viral accessory and nucleocapsid proteins: SR-rich disordered regions and SP/TP clusters mediating host interactions (not all small viral proteins qualify).
- Pro/Arg-rich antimicrobial or venom peptides and small secreted/toxin precursors: activation across basic, Ser/Pro-biased low-complexity segments.
- Secreted enzymes (e.g., beta-lactamases; plant RIPs): activation on Ser/Pro/basic-biased propeptides adjacent to signal peptides; no activation on typical hydrophobic signal peptides alone.
- Eukaryotic RNA-binding/splicing and transcription regulators: RS/SR and RG/RGG repeats and SP-rich regulatory IDRs.
- Cytosolic enzymes/transporters: only when bearing S/P- or repeat-enriched insertions or termini; many lack these and are not activated.
- Multi-pass membrane proteins: only if cytosolic loops/termini are Ser/Pro-biased; many are not.

Summary: Short aromatic-centered micro-motifs—2–3 residue patches enriched in Phe/Tyr/Trp often adjacent to Gly—that create small hydrophobic/π-stacking surfaces used for ligand or macromolecular recognition; most prominently the aromatic “platforms” of carbohydrate-active enzymes and polysaccharide-binding modules, but more generally occurring as generic interfacial hydrophobic motifs across diverse proteins (outer-membrane receptors, membrane enzymes, coiled-coil/hinge interfaces, and extracellular globular domains).
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on very short di/tri-peptides (e.g., ΦΦ, ΦG/GΦ with Φ = F/Y/W), typically isolated; in some glycan-degrading enzymes the activation extends to short runs/clusters (aromatic ladders) along β-helix/CBM surfaces.
Exemplars: - Carbohydrate-active enzymes (glycosidases, lyases, phage depolymerases; including C-glycoside deglycosidase β subunits): activates on aromatic stacking residues in the substrate-binding cleft or CBMs and on β-helix aromatic ladders that contact sugars.
- TonB-dependent outer-membrane transporters/receptors: activates on Tyr/Trp-rich patches in extracellular loops/plug domains and at the aromatic belt near the membrane interface that mediates ligand/interfacial contacts.
- Signal peptidase I (LepB family): activates on short hydrophobic/aromatic motifs in the N-terminal TM anchor and adjacent interfacial segments.
- Diacylglycerol kinases: activates on GxxxG/ΦΦ-type motifs in TM helices and interfacial loops involved in lipid binding.
- SMC-family hinge/RecN: activates on compact Gly–hydrophobic/ aromatic micro-motifs at hinge/coiled-coil break interfaces used for dimerization/packing.
- SUMO E3 ligases (PIAS/SIZ/PIAL): activates on short aromatic/hydrophobic patches within SAP/SP-RING-containing regions implicated in protein–protein interactions.
- Plant TIFY/JAZ proteins: activates on the TIFY core (I–F/Y) and nearby short hydrophobic dipeptides within Jas/TIFY regions mediating partner binding.
- C1q/TNF-like proteins and extracellular matrix components: activates on aromatic clusters in the globular C1q domain and other small hydrophobic patches in extracellular folds.
- Chalcone isomerase-like (CHI/CHIL) and AtFAP proteins: activates on aromatic “clamp” residues that form the flavonoid-binding pocket.
- Diverse enzymes (deaminases, racemases, oxidoreductases, tautomerases): activates on small aromatic dipeptides/glycine-adjacent hydrophobic motifs at substrate-binding or oligomerization interfaces.

Summary: Intrinsic disorder/low-complexity detector: activates on flexible, polar/charged, Q/N/S/T/E/D/K/R- and G/P-enriched segments—often N‑terminal tails—typical of intrinsically disordered regions in small secreted peptides/toxins and viral or eukaryotic regulatory proteins, including Q/N‑rich tracts; signals low-confidence coils or labile helices rather than folded domains.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks and short runs within extended disordered/low‑complexity regions; occasional contiguous regional activation on predicted but low‑confidence helices; frequently biased toward N‑terminal segments; minimal activation in well-structured cores.
Exemplars: HIV‑1 Tat (viral transcriptional transactivator): peaks confined to disordered coil segments, including regions missing in a shorter isoform; PID‑1 (piRNA biogenesis factor): scattered activation across a disordered C‑terminal tail and other low‑pLDDT coils, adjacent to but not centered on annotated interaction sites; Wasp venom peptide/toxin (vespin): regional activation along a long, low-confidence alpha‑helix in the mature toxin, with weak activation in the N‑terminal signal peptide; Antisense-encoded micropeptide (RUSC1‑AS1): activation throughout highly disordered, low‑pLDDT regions lacking annotated domains.

Summary: Residue-level detector for small/flexible residues—especially glycine—in short, low-structure linkers and proteolytic processing signals of peptide precursors, with a strong preference for the C‑terminal amidation context in which a glycine (amide donor) immediately precedes mono/di‑basic residues (G‑K/R); outside precursors it gives sparse hits on similar small-residue sites in intrinsically disordered regions and occasionally within structured domains across diverse taxa.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks, often isolated or in short bursts. Highest peaks occur at glycine positioned immediately after mature peptide segments and before K/R (amidation/convertase sites) in unstructured linkers; additional scattered, lower peaks appear in other low‑pLDDT regions and, more weakly, within structured helices/loops.
Exemplars: - Neuropeptide hormone precursors (e.g., CAPA family, luqin): strong peaks at the glycine amide donor in G‑K/R motifs directly following mature peptides; additional peaks at adjacent linker/cleavage regions.
- Secreted plant signaling peptides (SCOOP family): peaks within disordered SCOOP motifs and linkers (including glycine in the motif) rather than in the signal peptide.
- Viral nucleoproteins (Paramyxoviridae N): sparse peaks concentrated in intrinsically disordered N‑terminal segments.
- Homeobox transcription factors: low, scattered peaks within the homeobox helix‑turn‑helix and nearby low‑complexity N‑terminal regions.

Summary: Surface-exposed charge patches in extracellular/virion surface proteins—preferentially basic residues (Lys/Arg, with contributions from Glu/Asp and polar His/Gln/Asn)—located in long low-complexity or repetitive segments, flexible loops, propeptides, and linkers, with little activation in compact catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level, sparse single–amino-acid peaks concentrated on charged/polar residues distributed across extended regions; strongest in disordered/low‑pLDDT linkers, propeptides, C‑terminal tails and repeat tracts, but also recurring periodically on exposed residues of structured repeat domains (e.g., Ig-like BIG repeats); minimal on enzymatic active sites and well-packed catalytic domains.
Exemplars: - Bacteriophage capsule depolymerase/tailspike: scattered peaks on Lys/Arg (plus some acidic/polar) across low-complexity/disordered stretches rather than a specific fold element.
- Viral spike protein: strong peaks on K/R/E/H in flexible, low-pLDDT loops; charged residues in short charged runs are favored over adjacent hydrophobics.
- GH18 chitinase: negligible in catalytic GH18 domains and chitin-binding sites; strong in long C-terminal repeat/linker regions and a CNA-B–like segment.
- Subtilisin-like serine protease (Peptidase S8): activation in the unstructured propeptide and disordered C-terminal tail; absent over the catalytic core/triad.
- S-layer surface protein: scattered K/R (and some E) peaks across both structured elements and disordered tails, including disulfide-bonded loops.
- Microsporidian spore wall protein: peaks on basic and acidic residues, including an acidic, disordered C-terminal region.
- Viral capsid protein: basic-residue peaks concentrated in low-confidence helical regions.
- Ice-binding adhesin with BIG (Ig-like) repeats: periodic single-residue peaks on charged/polar residues within multiple BIG2 domains; absent in signal peptide and nonrepeat tail.
- Cellulosomal scaffoldin: strongest on K/R/H in Pro/Thr-rich disordered linkers; weaker, loop-focused peaks in cohesin domains; minimal in CBM and dockerin modules.

Summary: N-terminal non-cleavable signal-anchor helices (Type II/III) that initiate ER targeting/insertion via a basic n-region followed by a long hydrophobic helix; cleavable signal peptides are generally not captured unless unusually hydrophobic/basic; mitochondrial transit peptides are excluded.
Activation pattern: Regional activation at the extreme N-terminus (first 10–30 residues): Lys/Arg-enriched n-region immediately preceding a sustained hydrophobic TM; lack of a canonical -3/−1 small-residue signal peptidase motif; requires an intact native N-terminus (fragments lacking the first TM/n-region are negative).
Exemplars: - Viral single-pass membrane/accessory proteins: activation on the N-terminal signal anchor.
- Type II/III and multipass membrane proteins (e.g., vesicular transporters, DHHC palmitoyltransferases): activation on the first signal-anchor helix with positive-inside bias.
- Excluded/weak: soluble secreted zymogens and peptide-hormone precursors with cleavable signal peptides (e.g., chymosin, laccases, neuropeptide precursors), cytosolic enzymes (e.g., RNase HII, PrmC/TrmB), mitochondrial precursors, and C-terminal tail-anchored proteins (e.g., PUMA).

Summary: Secondary-structure transition/turn motif: residues at the ends of beta-strands or alpha-helices and the first few positions of the ensuing loop/coil (short turns/hinges), often flexible and solvent-exposed, enriched for Gly/Thr/Ser/Pro and sometimes flanking cysteines in disulfide-stabilized peptides
Activation pattern: Short, residue-level peaks over 2–8 aa centered on strand→coil or helix→coil junctions; strongest at or just after the terminal residue of the structured element and into the adjacent loop. Frequently coincides with low-to-moderate pLDDT (flexible turns) but can also mark well-ordered turns; little activation across long continuous helices or extended intrinsically disordered regions. Common sequence signatures include GG, GT/TG, and TP, and enrichment for small/polar/charged residues.
Exemplars: - Phage capsule depolymerase (K63-specific polysaccharide depolymerase): multiple short activations in loops connecting beta-strands and immediately before an unstructured tail.
- Scorpion potassium channel toxins (alpha-KTx): C-terminal end of a beta-strand and the following coil, including the amidated terminal residue.
- LCN-type scorpion neurotoxins (CS-alpha/beta fold): end of a beta-strand followed by a short loop near the C-terminus; minor isolated turn residues elsewhere.
- Cleavage and polyadenylation factor Clp1 (RNA 5′ kinase): beta-strand to coil junction within a flexible loop.
- tRNA(Ile)-lysidine synthase (TilS): a strand→loop transition in a low-confidence loop, with a minor peak at a helix terminus.

Summary: Serine/proline–rich low-complexity intrinsically disordered segments, especially terminal tails, linkers, and N‑terminal signal-peptide regions of small or secreted proteins; structured catalytic cores are largely ignored.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over disordered, low-pLDDT tracts (often at N- or C-termini) and along repetitive Ser/Pro-rich sequences; sparse residue-level peaks appear in flexible loops within otherwise ordered domains; can extend across signal peptides in precursors.
Exemplars: - Human regulatory protein ST20: weak, sparse peaks in an N‑terminal low-confidence helix within a largely disordered protein.
- Lipoyl synthase (Radical SAM enzyme): strong activation on disordered N‑ and C‑terminal tails; central Radical SAM core remains inactive.
- Conotoxin precursor (secreted peptide toxin): activation across the N‑terminal signal peptide helix and additional low-confidence regions of the mature toxin.
- WTUN1-like small eukaryotic protein: peaks at Ser/Pro residues within an annotated disordered C‑terminal region and additional low-confidence N‑terminal segments.
- Bacterial DNA ligase: activation in an annotated disordered insertion and flexible, low-confidence loops inside the ligase domain.

Summary: Detector for intrinsically disordered, low-structure N‑terminal pre-sequences (signal peptides’ N/C regions, organellar transit peptides, and propeptides) and, more generally, flexible coil/low‑pLDDT segments; strongest bias for the first 10–70 residues but can also mark internal loops in large enzymes and short low‑complexity micropeptides.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation at the extreme N-terminus (often including the initiator methionine), enriched in small/polar/basic residues and near cleavage/processing sites; additionally shows sparse residue-level peaks within internal disordered coils/low‑confidence loops; occasionally extends into short helices of small secreted peptides or across entire low‑complexity short proteins.
Exemplars: - Secreted peptide/toxin/antimicrobial precursors: activation on the N-terminal signal/propeptide region and sometimes into the helical segment of the mature peptide (e.g., Ixosin-like anticoagulant/AMP precursors).
- Viral envelope/secreted proteins: activation over the N-terminal signal peptide and adjacent propeptide-like segments.
- Plant mitochondrial/chloroplast-targeted proteins: activation on basic/polar N-terminal transit/presequences.
- Secreted/membrane transporters and receptors: activation on their N-terminal signal peptides and luminal leaders.
- Large DNA ligases and other nucleotidyltransferases: sparse peaks on disordered N-terminal extensions and flexible loops within catalytic domains.
- Uncharacterized short open reading frame products/micropeptides: activation across N-terminal low-complexity segments or the entire disordered sequence.

Summary: Disulfide-bonded cysteine motifs in exported proteins—i.e., cysteine‑rich mature peptides and extracellular or organelle-lumen segments (defensin/knottin/venom-toxin–like and other cystine-stabilized domains) commonly produced as multi-peptide precursors across taxa
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on conserved cysteines (with supporting peaks on nearby Gly/Pro in loop/turn regions), forming regional clusters over the mature disulfide‑rich segment(s); in multi-peptide precursors, multiple activated regions correspond to each cysteine‑rich peptide; in larger extracellular proteins, activation concentrates on disulfide‑bonded ectodomain loops/repeats; occasional single strong peak at the lipobox Cys of bacterial lipoprotein precursors; in organelle-targeted precursors (e.g., chloroplast/thylakoid lumen), activation concentrates on lumen-exposed cysteine clusters/disulfide pairs within the mature region
Exemplars: - Animal venom peptides (conotoxins, scorpion/spider ICK knottins, snake three-finger toxins): activation on the conserved Cys frameworks forming the disulfide-stabilized folds.
- Antimicrobial/defensin families (alpha/beta-defensins, insect/plant defensins): activation on the canonical defensin Cys motifs of the CSαβ fold.
- Endocrine/neuropeptide precursors (insulin/relaxin, oxytocin/vasopressin, calcitonin family): activation on the Cys residues forming inter/intra-chain disulfides within the mature hormone regions.
- Plant cystine-rich peptides (knottins, trypsin-inhibitor CRPs): activation on the inhibitory cystine-knot Cys pattern.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins (e.g., influenza HA, coronavirus/spike-like, other secreted viral glycoproteins): activation on cysteine clusters in ectodomain loops that form disulfide bonds.
- Bacterial secreted toxins and lipoproteins: activation on disulfide-bonded Cys within toxin domains and at the conserved lipobox N‑terminal Cys of lipoprotein precursors.
- Large extracellular/membrane proteins with Cys-rich repeats (EGF-like, LDLR modules, TSP/CR domains): activation over the paired/triplet Cys motifs that define these extracellular repeats.
- Plant organelle-lumen proteins (e.g., thylakoid lumen/stress- or light-regulated chloroplastic proteins): activation on lumenal Cys pairs/disulfide loops within the mature domain.

Summary: Generic structural motif: short Gly/Pro-enriched turns and capping sites at secondary-structure boundaries (beta-turns/hinges and helix/strand caps), often with GP/PG dipeptides flanked by charged residues; a broad, structure-level signal rather than a specific function.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks at isolated positions; enriched in coils/turns linking beta-strands and alpha-helices, at helix N/C-caps, edge strands, and coils immediately preceding transmembrane helices; sparse, low-amplitude signals distributed across large proteins, with few sites in small peptides; sequence preference for Gly/Pro (often GP/PG) with neighboring acidic/basic residues.
Exemplars: - Trigger factor (FKBP-type PPIase/chaperone): peaks on a beta-strand at the domain edge and in connecting coils/low-structure regions.
- tRNA pseudouridine synthase (TruA family): a short helix near (but not at) the active site and small peaks in coils following beta-strands and within a strand.
- Elongation factor 2 (GTPase): linkers at beta-to-alpha transitions and a turn near the GTP-binding region.
- Translation initiation factor IF-3: dominant peak in a C-terminal coil immediately after a beta-strand; minor sites in a domain-linker and helices.
- Phenylalanyl-tRNA synthetase beta subunit: loops connecting secondary elements across the core and C-terminal domain, plus one edge-strand site.
- Kinesin motor domain (KIF7): a beta-strand site and adjacent loop within the motor domain; none in the disordered/coiled-coil tail.
- Pentameric ligand-gated ion channel (5-HT3A receptor): sites in the extracellular beta-sandwich and the coil just before TM1, including a ligand-binding aromatic.
- RNase P protein subunit (p20): N-cap of a short helix and nearby beta-strands in the structured C-terminus; absent from the disordered N-terminus.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity cationic segments (polybasic Lys/Arg/His‑rich patches often interspersed with Ser/Pro/Gly), frequently near the N‑terminus, encompassing targeting/trafficking and interaction-prone regions such as signal peptide N‑regions, transit peptides, NLS‑bearing IDRs, and effector low‑complexity tails
Activation pattern: Regional activation across flexible/low‑pLDDT segments with sharp peaks on clusters of basic residues (including His) and simple repeats; commonly concentrated in N‑terminal stretches but also in disordered C‑terminal tails; minimal preference for structured cores
Exemplars: - Herpesvirus nuclear egress proteins: activation on basic, disordered regions (e.g., C‑terminal/IDR basic clusters in UL31/UL34).
- Secreted toxins/allergens/AMP precursors: activation on the positively charged N‑region of signal peptides and adjacent low‑complexity propeptides.
- Nuclear transcription/chromatin regulators: activation on polybasic NLSs and neighboring disordered low‑complexity segments.
- Organelle-targeted proteins (mitochondrial/chloroplast/apicoplast): activation on Arg/Ser‑rich N‑terminal transit peptides.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on Arg‑rich, low‑complexity N‑termini containing/near the RxLR motif.
- Bacterial metabolic and tRNA/RNA‑related enzymes: activation on disordered basic tails/linkers and RNA‑contacting polybasic patches.
- Short human micropeptides/lncRNA‑derived proteins: activation across entire cationic, low‑complexity sequences.
- Bacillus subtilis proteins: activation on N‑terminal basic segments of secreted proteins or disordered low‑complexity tails in cytosolic proteins.

Summary: Generic detection of short hydrophobic β-strand segments and adjacent strand–loop junctions (often edge strands), frequently appearing at N-termini or disorder-to-order/domain boundaries, independent of protein function.
Activation pattern: Short contiguous runs (≈3–6 residues) with peaks on hydrophobic/aromatic residues (V/I/L/F/Y/W) and occasional K/R; map to β-strands and immediately flanking coil positions; multiple sparse clusters per protein (often including an early N-terminal strand); not targeted to catalytic or metal-ligating sites; total activated residues scale with protein length.
Exemplars: - Small heat shock proteins (HSP20/α‑crystallin domain): activation on a C‑terminal β‑strand and at the disordered tail boundary.
- ERI1 3′–5′ exoribonuclease: activation on a β‑strand within the exonuclease (DEDDh) domain.
- Y‑family DNA polymerase REV1/UmuC: activation on a β‑strand that contributes to the DNA‑interacting surface of the catalytic domain.
- CRISPR nuclease Cas12f1: activation on the N‑terminal β‑strand of the zinc‑finger subdomain (not on the Zn‑coordinating residues).
- Ribosomal protein eL20: activation on a short extended β segment marking the transition from disordered N‑terminus to the structured core.
- Molybdopterin synthase sulfur carrier (MoaD-like): activation on an early β‑strand and the following loop.
- Nicotinamide‑nucleotide amidohydrolase PncC: activation at the end of a β‑strand and the ensuing coil near the C‑terminus.

Summary: Generic β-strand hydrophobic packing signal: the feature marks single aliphatic residues (V/I/L/A/M; occasionally aromatic) embedded in well-formed β-strands of diverse folds, often in early N‑terminal strands; it is structural rather than catalytic, though it can lie adjacent to functional motifs in some proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks (typically 1–3 per protein), overwhelmingly on DSSP ‘E’ segments with high structural confidence; peaks are isolated rather than contiguous, frequently in N‑terminal strands, sometimes neighboring ATPase/P-loop regions, and only rarely appear in α-helices (including occasional weak hits in transmembrane helices).
Exemplars: - SMC/Rad50 ATPase: peaks on β-strands in both ATPase head lobes adjacent to Walker/ATP-binding regions.
- AAA+ membrane metalloprotease FtsH: β-strand peaks in periplasmic and cytosolic domains; not on TM helices or the Zn/catalytic site.
- D-xylonate dehydratase (IlvD/EDD family): a single strong peak on a core β-sheet residue.
- RidA/TdcF reactive-intermediate deaminase family: peaks confined to one β-strand, away from annotated catalytic residues.
- Molybdopterin biosynthesis cPMP synthase: isolated I/V within core β-strands.
- Flotillin/SPFH family scaffold: a single A within a short β-strand; no activation in the long coiled-coil.
- Ion-translocating oxidoreductase complex subunit G: A/V in β-strands of the soluble domain, with a weaker peak in a transmembrane helix.
- DNA utilization/competence protein HofN: an isolated I within a β-strand with minor nearby strand/coil peaks.

Summary: Short beta-strand element of the conserved SAM-dependent methyltransferase core (Rossmann-like fold), most often the terminal C‑terminal strand of the central beta-sheet, shared across diverse methyltransferase families; also present in MTase-like accessory subunits and, at lower specificity, in unrelated enzymes with similar short beta-strand geometry.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on very short, contiguous stretches (4–6 aa) that form beta-strands; frequently at or near the extreme C-terminus of the methyltransferase domain but also within the central sheet; does not coincide with catalytic motifs; enriched in hydrophobic/aromatic residues and often capped by Lys/Arg; multiple such hotspots can appear across large proteins; because the signal is largely structural, weak activation can occur in non-methyltransferase proteins.
Exemplars:
- tRNA (guanine-N7) methyltransferases (TrmB/TrmG): activation on the final C-terminal beta-strand of the MTase core.
- tRNA (guanine(10)-N2) methyltransferase TRMT11: activation on a short beta-strand within the central sheet of the MTase fold.
- METTL21 family protein-lysine methyltransferases: activation on a C-terminal beta-strand in the SAM-dependent MTase domain.
- DOT1-like H3K79 histone methyltransferases: activation on a beta-strand near the C-terminus within the DOT1/AdoMet-MTase core sheet.
- Type II DNA methyltransferases (e.g., M.HhaII): activation focused on a residue within a central beta-sheet strand of the canonical MTase fold.
- Small RNA 2'-O-methyltransferases (HEN1-like/cap 2'-O MTases): activation on a beta-strand segment in the MTase core.
- Non-MT example: dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) can show weak activation on a short terminal beta-strand, reflecting motif promiscuity.

Summary: Detector of intrinsically disordered regions, especially transient/low-confidence alpha-helical propensity segments and coil–helix junctions that often serve as short linear interaction elements in eukaryotic regulatory and viral proteins.
Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks scattered across low-pLDDT coils and weak helices, sometimes forming short adjacent clusters; frequently at termini and inter-domain linkers; tolerant to many residue types (with S/T/Y and proline common) and not confined to annotated structured domains; occasionally overlaps known interaction segments within IDRs.
Exemplars: - Autophagy cargo receptor NCOA4: multiple hits in the central disordered region enriched in weak helices, including the ferritin heavy-chain interaction segment.
- Viral phosphoprotein: scattered activations in annotated disordered/basic–acidic biased regions across the long phosphoprotein.
- Homeobox transcription factor (Hox/labial): peaks in a weakly structured helical segment outside the homeobox, with minimal signal inside the well-folded DNA-binding domain.
- G1-specific transcriptional activator (MSA1): isolated residues within intrinsically disordered coil regions.
- Meiosis-inducing protein: a proline at a coil-to-helix boundary in a low-confidence N-terminal segment.
- CK2-interacting scaffold protein: dispersed hits in disordered/proline-rich coils with one in a weak helix, consistent with SLiM-bearing IDRs.

Summary: Selective for proline/serine–rich intrinsically disordered segments in cytosolic/nuclear regulatory regions, with occasional activation on glycine/proline motifs in certain small secreted neuropeptides; suppressed in well-folded domains, transmembrane helices/outer-membrane beta-barrels, and repetitive extracellular glycoproteins (e.g., AGPs, cuticle proteins)
Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks in coil/low-pLDDT IDRs that show clear proline-rich/compositional-bias tracts; little to no activation in structured catalytic or DNA-binding domains, coiled-coil/solenoid repeats, or membrane-embedded regions
Exemplars:
- Neuropeptide precursors: activation in a subset with glycine-rich motifs within the mature peptide; no activation in signal peptides/processing flanks; generally inactive on AGP-like Hyp-rich repeats.
- Ser/Thr kinases (e.g., PAK): activation when N- and/or C-terminal regulatory tails are proline-rich; inactive across the folded kinase domain.
- Homeobox transcription factors: activation when N-terminal regions contain low-complexity proline/serine-rich tracts; absent in the structured homeodomain.
- Cytosolic signaling enzymes/regulators (e.g., Ras/Rho GEFs/GAPs) that harbor proline-rich IDRs show activation; generally inactive on viral small membrane proteins, bacterial outer-membrane proteins, mitochondrial complex I subunits, and extracellular structural glycoproteins such as cuticle proteins and AGPs.
