Summary: Extended non-catalytic scaffold regions that mediate assembly and binding in large macromolecular machines—typically alpha-helical (coiled-coil/alpha-solenoid) but also including basic low-complexity RNA/DNA-binding segments—especially in viral structural/packaging and other secreted/virulence proteins; these provide interaction surfaces rather than catalytic active sites.
Activation pattern: Broad regional activation across long, contiguous helical or basic low-complexity regions (hundreds to thousands of residues), with many activated positions and occasional peaks over nucleic-acid– or partner-binding patches; minimal activation at catalytic motifs (e.g., HEPN active sites in Cas13a).
Exemplars: - CRISPR-Cas13a endoribonucleases: strong activation on Helical-1/Helical-2/linker scaffold and crRNA-binding segments; low on HEPN catalytic residues
- Negative-sense RNA virus nucleoproteins: activation on basic, alpha-helical oligomerization arms and RNA-binding grooves that scaffold nucleocapsids
- Reoviridae core/outer capsid proteins: activation on extended helical bundles/coiled-coils for capsid assembly/stabilization
- Adenovirus packaging/vertex proteins: activation on helical assembly/packaging stalks and coiled-coil interfaces
- Herpesviridae terminase/portal proteins: activation on long helical barrel/coiled-coil scaffolds for DNA translocation portals
- Herpesvirus mRNA export regulators (ICP27/UL54 homologs): activation on basic, low-complexity RNA-binding/export segments and dimerization regions
- Apicomplexan invasion/secretory proteins: activation on secreted helical repeats/coiled-coil stalks mediating host interaction and complex assembly
- Bacterial type III secretion effectors and GEF mimics: activation on all-helical bundle scaffolds forming host-binding/activation interfaces
- Eukaryotic ER oxidoreductase ERO1: activation on non-catalytic helical scaffolding surrounding the FAD/disulfide catalytic core

Summary: Compositionally biased, intrinsically disordered/low‑complexity regions enriched for serine, proline and threonine (with frequent glycine and Q/N content), including simple tandem repeats; the feature primarily marks flexible, coil-like segments flanking or linking structured domains, with occasional isolated peaks in compositionally uniform helices (including transmembrane)
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks scattered across long disordered/low‑pLDDT coil segments and periodically recurring across repeat units; little or no signal within well‑folded domains; rare isolated peaks occur within helices (including transmembrane) as exceptions
Exemplars: - Rho GTPase‑activating proteins (Dictyostelium): activation on long S/T‑rich, polar low‑complexity disordered regions surrounding the catalytic GAP domain.
- Homeobox transcription factors: scattered peaks across proline/serine‑rich disordered segments; no activation within the structured homeobox or EF‑hand domains.
- Meiosis‑inducing protein: low‑level, sparse peaks confined to low‑confidence coil regions.
- Microsporidian polar tube protein 1: periodic activation at Gly‑Thr motifs and Q‑rich positions across tandem low‑complexity repeats.
- Cytochrome c oxidase small membrane subunit (COX8): minor activation in the disordered N‑terminal matrix tail and an isolated peak within the transmembrane helix.

Summary: Enriched—but not universal—in intrinsically disordered, low-complexity, polar-rich regulatory segments (typically N- or C-terminal tails) of eukaryotic transcription factors; folded DNA-binding domains are largely inactive.
Activation pattern: Regional activation concentrated in low-pLDDT coil regions, often appearing as short clusters or runs with residue-level peaks; enrichment for small/polar residues (S, P, Q, N, G, A) or acidic tracts. Activation requires the presence of such low-complexity polar runs and sufficient local disorder; proteins lacking these sequence/structural features may show no activation.
Exemplars:
- Homeobox proteins (e.g., CDX-type): frequent activation in disordered N-terminal regions preceding the homeobox; only weak, occasional peaks inside the homeobox helix; other homeobox proteins may show none if tails lack low-complexity polar runs.
- Paired box (PAX) factors: activation often in C-terminal unstructured tails; the structured RED subdomain is largely inactive.
- T-box transcription factors: a subset shows clusters in C-terminal disordered/low-complexity regions, but many members (e.g., TBR1) show little to no activation when such segments are absent or minimal.
- ETS transcription factors: a subset activates in disordered N- and C-terminal segments (including low-complexity tracts); many (e.g., pointed) show no activation if tails lack low-complexity polar content.
- POU-class homeodomain factors: often show peaks in N-terminal disordered regions outside the POU-specific and homeobox domains; many members show no activation without suitable low-complexity polar runs.
- Runt-related (RUNX) factors: some exhibit localized peaks in polar-biased, low-confidence disordered segments near the N-terminus; others (e.g., Drosophila lozenge) may show none.
- By contrast, many bHLH/HLH, forkhead (FOX), EGR zinc-finger, and additional TFs show no activation when their tails lack these low-complexity polar runs; non-TF/viral proteins are typically inactive.

Summary: Extracellular secreted precursors and ectodomains with disulfide-bonded cysteine-rich loops/domains (cystine-stabilized scaffolds), and a subset of secreted neuropeptide precursors whose activation concentrates on flexible, processing-rich segments even without dense cysteine content. Common in proteins with signal peptides, glycosylation, and proteolytic processing.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on cysteines and adjacent positions (often Gly/Pro and basic Lys/Arg) within extracellular regions; regional activation over cysteine-rich loops or repeats; also highlights Gly/Pro and Lys/Arg flanking propeptide cleavage motifs in cysteine-poor neuropeptide precursors; absent in transmembrane helices and cytosolic tails; strongest in low-to-moderate order ectodomain segments, sometimes near N-glycosylation and cleavage sites.
Exemplars:
- Chemokines (especially CXC): activation on conserved disulfide-forming cysteine motifs.
- Defensins/plant CRPs and knottin-like/trypsin inhibitor peptides (CSαβ/ICK scaffolds): activation across disulfide-bonded loops.
- WFDC, Kunitz, and Kazal protease inhibitors: activation on disulfide-stabilized inhibitor domains.
- Venom toxins (e.g., Kunitz-type, ShK, disintegrins): activation on clustered cysteines defining the scaffold.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins (class I/II/III): activation in cysteine-rich ectodomains near disulfide networks and glycosylation sites.
- Extracellular receptor/adhesion and metalloprotease proteins: activation on EGF-like, disintegrin, and other cysteine-rich modules.
- DEG/ENaC family channels: activation in the extracellular cysteine-rich loop.
- Neuropeptide hormone precursors (e.g., small cardioactive peptides): activation around flexible, dibasic cleavage-rich segments even with low cysteine content.
- Apicomplexan AMA1 invasion protein: activation confined to ectodomain cysteine-rich segments, absent from TM/cytosolic regions.

Summary: A generic structural signal for beta-strand entry/edge sites: the feature activates on residues at coil-to-beta transitions and early positions within beta-strands in well-folded domains, often with acidic and/or glycine residues immediately preceding the strand and aromatic/hydrophobic residues (e.g., Phe/Tyr) at the strand start. It is not tied to specific active sites but recurs across many enzyme and non-enzyme folds.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks distributed across multiple regions per protein (typically 5–15 residues), primarily in structured beta-sheet elements rather than helices or disordered segments. Peaks commonly sit at loop-to-beta boundaries (strand N-termini) or within short beta-strands; activated residues are enriched for D/E and G, with frequent neighboring K/R/H and aromatic Y/F. In histidine kinases, activations localize to the cytosolic HATPase_c module; in FR-type flavoproteins, peaks lie near but not on FAD-binding residues.
Exemplars: - Ferric reductases (FR-type FAD-binding domain): loop-to-beta transitions adjacent to the FAD-binding region (e.g., D–D loop followed by F/E or hydrophobic residues entering the strand).
- NADH–cytochrome b5 reductase (flavoprotein FR-type fold): beta-sheet residues in the FAD-binding domain, near but not overlapping cofactor-binding motifs.
- Two-component sensor histidine kinases (HATPase_c domain): glycine-bearing beta-strands within the cytosolic kinase module, away from the phosphohistidine site.
- tRNA pseudouridine synthase A (TruA family): a single loop-to-beta junction centered on a Tyr at the strand start; not at the catalytic Asp.
- Phenylalanyl-tRNA synthetase beta subunit: strongest peak on a beta-strand in the B5 subdomain with additional scattered sheet-associated peaks across the enzyme.
- Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase: N-termini of beta-strands in the beta-sandwich scaffold.
- Gas vesicle protein O: a single Gly at the start of a beta-strand in the ordered region, with minimal signal in disordered N-termini.
- Adenylate cyclase/RTX hemolysin toxin: a short beta-strand near an Asp/Gly-rich segment at the C-terminus of the hemolysin domain.

Summary: Residue-level detector of beta-propeller blades: it fires on a conserved, core-facing position within a beta-strand of each repeat (blade) in WD40/NHL and related Gβ-like propellers, largely independent of biological function and extending to propeller-like, beta-rich enzymes in bacteria.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks that recur periodically—typically one prominent peak per repeat/blade—concentrated within well-structured beta-strands of WD/NHL domains; little to no signal in non-propeller modules (e.g., EF-hands), linkers, or disordered tails. Peaks favor hydrophobic and Cys/Pro residues, often near the C-terminal end of individual repeats, and accumulate to many sites per propeller-containing protein.
Exemplars: - SCF/CRL substrate receptors (F-box/WD adaptors, e.g., Cdc4/FBXW family): single-residue peaks within beta-strands across the C-terminal WD40 blades.
- WD-repeat scaffolds (Periodic tryptophan protein/WDR family): periodic peaks in beta-strands of successive WD repeats; absent in disordered regions.
- Cilia/flagella-associated WD proteins (CFAP/centrosomal WD proteins): sparse peaks confined to beta-strands within WD repeats; no activation in EF-hand or disordered segments.
- NACHT–WD (NLR-like) regulators: multiple isolated peaks across beta-strands of the C-terminal WD domain.
- Translation initiation factor WD subunit (eIF3i): strong single-residue peaks in beta-strands of early WD repeats.
- THO/TREX WD subunit: one prominent peak per WD repeat in beta-strand regions.
- PHIP/WD scaffolds and related DCAFs: peaks in beta-strands near the C-termini of several WD repeats, minimal signal outside the WD region.
- NHL-repeat beta-propellers (NHL domains in amidation-related proteins): peaks on beta-strands within NHL blades of the propeller.
- Bacterial periplasmic oxidoreductases/outer-membrane beta-propeller factors (e.g., polyvinyl alcohol dehydrogenase, Bam-like): sparse peaks on beta-strands in their propeller-like beta-rich domains.

Summary: Generic intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments enriched for polar/acidic and small residues (especially P, S, Q, E, D, N, G), typically found in flexible N/C‑terminal tails, linkers, and propeptides; the feature avoids well‑folded domains and transmembrane helices and occasionally touches short helices embedded within otherwise flexible regions
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across sequences, with a bias toward early N‑terminal and other low‑pLDDT/disordered regions; peaks are usually isolated rather than forming long contiguous blocks; weak or absent within signal peptides and transmembrane segments; variable number of peaks per protein
Exemplars: - Homeobox transcription factors (e.g., DLX family): sparse peaks in N‑terminal intrinsically disordered regions with low pLDDT.
- MEF2 transcription factors: strongest activation in the C‑terminal low‑complexity, polar‑biased activation domain; minimal in the structured MADS DNA‑binding domain.
- Neuropeptide/peptide‑hormone precursors (e.g., pancreatic polypeptide proprotein): peaks in disordered propeptides and near processing sites; negligible in the signal peptide; occasional weak peaks within short helices of the mature peptide.
- Small bacterial inner‑membrane proteins: little to no activation across transmembrane helices; at most very weak, isolated peaks in short cytosolic/luminal segments.
- High light‑inducible membrane proteins: very weak, sparse peaks in low‑confidence cytosolic tails and only minimal signal within the transmembrane helix.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity repeat tracts enriched in Pro/Ser/Thr (often with Gln/Glu), typical of mucin‑like O‑glycosylated regions and other proline‑rich linkers in eukaryotic proteins; with a secondary sensitivity to residues immediately N‑terminal to dibasic (KR/RR) proprotein convertase cleavage sites in secretory precursors.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation across long low‑complexity segments (PTS- and/or Q/E‑rich) in disordered coils; superimposed residue‑level peaks at one or a few residues directly N‑terminal to dibasic KR/RR processing motifs within propeptides.
Exemplars: - Mucins and mucin‑like secreted/adhesive glycoproteins: strong activation across PTS O‑glycosylated repeats.
- Extracellular matrix/adhesion glycoproteins and proline‑rich structural proteins: activation on extended proline‑biased low‑complexity segments.
- Plant cell‑wall hydroxyproline‑rich glycoproteins (extensins/AGPs): activation on secreted P/S/T‑ and Pro‑rich repeats.
- Nuclear transcriptional regulators/cofactors: activation on Q/E‑rich and S/T‑rich low‑complexity activation domains and linkers.
- Reproductive proteins and cancer/testis antigens: activation on repeat‑rich disordered regions.
- Parasite/pathogen surface and secreted repeat proteins: activation on low‑complexity, repeat‑containing tracts.
- Neuropeptide/growth factor precursors (e.g., neuregulins): sharp peaks immediately N‑terminal to KR/RR cleavage sites that delimit mature peptides, with weaker activation in adjacent disordered propeptide regions.

Summary: A structural signal for short, hydrophobic β‑strand segments that form β‑sheets in β‑rich/all‑β domains (e.g., lipocalin/BPI barrels, OB‑folds, Tudor barrels, WD‑repeat propellers), often highlighting core strands or strand–coil junctions rather than loops; broadly function‑agnostic and seen across taxa.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks confined to short (≈5–10 aa) contiguous stretches that align with DSSP β‑strands; multiple peaks can occur across different strands within the same protein. Minimal activation in disordered regions, signal peptides, or helices. Strong residue bias for V/L/I with supporting T/S/K/E, consistent with amphipathic β‑sheet patterns. Peaks can occur anywhere along the sequence, including strand–coil transitions.
Exemplars: - Lipocalin/BPI‑fold lipid‑binding proteins: strong activation on defined β‑strands of the barrel and at strand–coil junctions (e.g., Lazarillo lipocalin; BPI/LBP family member).
- OB‑fold nucleic‑acid‑binding proteins (Replication Protein A RPA70/RPA1): multiple peaks on β‑strands within the OB folds; absent in adjacent disordered linkers.
- Tudor‑domain RNA‑binding proteins: repeated peaks on β‑strands within canonical and non‑canonical Tudor barrels.
- WD‑repeat/IFT β‑propeller proteins: localized activation on a propeller blade β‑strand beyond annotated repeats.
- NifU‑like Fe‑S assembly scaffolds: peaks on conserved β‑strands in the core fold.

Summary: Compositionally biased, intrinsically disordered low‑complexity segments enriched in polar/proline residues (Q/N/H/P with frequent S/G), typically outside conserved structured domains and often in C‑terminal tails of transcription factors and other proteins
Activation pattern: Absent or near-zero over folded, high‑confidence domains; appears as scattered residue‑level peaks clustered across mid‑confidence (pLDDT ~40–60) coil and short low‑confidence helices/β within long IDRs; strongest in low‑complexity, polar-rich stretches, frequently in C‑terminal regions
Exemplars: - Plant TCP transcription factors: silent on the TCP DNA‑binding domain; activates on C‑terminal low‑confidence coils/short helices (IDR tail)
- LOB/AS2-like transcription factors: no signal in the LOB core; multiple peaks immediately C‑terminal in low‑complexity helical/coil regions
- Metazoan homeobox proteins: homeodomain inactive; activation on disordered, Asn/polar‑rich low‑complexity regions
- Plant MADS-box (AGL) proteins: MADS domain and structured N‑terminus inactive; activation confined to a low‑confidence C‑terminal region
- MYB transcription factors: two HTH repeats inactive; peaks in C‑terminal disordered/low‑complexity segment
- NF‑YA subunits: structured subunit‑association/DNA‑binding regions inactive; strong cluster in C‑terminal disordered low‑complexity tail

Summary: Short, low‑complexity, Pro/Ser/Thr/Gly‑rich segments in the mature regions of secreted, periplasmic, and surface‑exposed proteins across taxa—typically flexible/disordered extracellular loops or linkers used in secretion/assembly, adhesion fibers, toxins/virulence factors, and secreted signaling peptides (often glycosylation- or protease‑accessible), rather than signal peptides
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous stretches (~10–25 aa) within the mature extracellular/periplasmic portion; multiple peaks per protein; avoids N‑terminal signal peptides
Exemplars: - Gram‑negative periplasmic assembly/chaperone proteins (e.g., PapD‑like chaperones, HdeA/HdeB, secretion adaptors): activation on Pro/Ser/Gly‑rich flexible loops and linkers exposed to the periplasm.
- Chaperone‑usher fimbrial/pilus subunits, curli components, and autotransporter passengers: activation on low‑complexity Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro stretches within repetitive regions and linkers between beta‑strand repeats in extracellular fibers/adhesins.
- RTX toxins and large secreted adhesins/virulence factors: activation on Gly‑rich low‑complexity segments (including and flanking repeat blocks) in the secreted mature region.
- Small cysteine‑rich secreted venom peptides (conotoxins and related disulfide‑rich toxins): activation on short flexible loops between cysteines in the mature peptide.
- Secreted eukaryotic cytokines and peptide hormones/growth factors: activation on short solvent‑exposed loops or Ser/Thr‑rich segments within the mature domain (often near proteolytic processing regions).
- Components of secretion systems (type II/IV/V and related periplasmic/extracellular parts): activation on short polar/proline‑rich linkers and loops that mediate assembly or surface exposure.

Summary: Acidic/proline-rich low-complexity IDRs (PEST-like, PRR/S-rich), most often at cytosolic N-termini; excludes amphipathic helical targeting leaders (signal peptides, mitochondrial transit peptides) and compact helical microproteins; a composition/IDR signal present only when clear acidic/PRR low complexity is evident.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over acidic/PRR low-complexity stretches with enrichment for P/E/S/T/Q and proline clusters; multiple patches possible; weak/absent on amphipathic helical leaders and short compact helical peptides.
Exemplars:
- Eukaryotic transcriptional coactivators/regulators: activation on N-terminal acidic/PRR activation domains.
- Membrane proteins: activation on cytosolic PRR/S-rich disordered tails; not on signal peptides.
- Enzymes: activation only on flexible acidic/PRR linkers or termini, not catalytic cores.
- Viral proteins: subset bearing prominent PRR/serine-rich low-complexity tracts; excludes small helical suppressors (e.g., ICP47, B2) lacking such regions.
- Secreted peptide/toxin precursors: activation on acidic/PRR propeptides; not on signal peptides or canonical bacteriocin double-glycine leaders.
- Small human microproteins/lncRNA peptides: only when compositionally acidic/PRR low complexity is present; not compact amphipathic helices.

Summary: Short capping micro-motif at the N-terminus of alpha-helices (β→α junction/N-cap), recognizing the coil/β-to-helix boundary and the first helical residue, with preference for polar and basic capping residues (e.g., Ser, Asn, Tyr, Arg/Lys, Gly)
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks over 1–3 residues; maxima at the last coil/β-strand residue immediately before an α-helix and/or the first helical residue. Often appears in short loop tri-peptides (including basic/aromatic combinations) that initiate helices; rarely extends beyond this boundary.
Exemplars: - Methyl-CpG-binding proteins (MBD domain): activation at a Ser→Arg coil-to-helix transition within the MBD core (helix N-cap/first turn).
- INO80 chromatin-remodeling subunits: activation on a short RRW loop motif consistent with a helix-start/capping context in a flexible region.
- Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors: activation on an N-centered triad in the loop linking a β-strand to the following α-helix (helix N-cap in the Kazal domain).
- JAZ/TIFY repressors (ZIM domain): activation on a Tyr located at the N-terminus of a predicted α-helix (helix N-cap).
- Aux/IAA transcriptional regulators (PB1 domain): activation within the β→α loop and at the first helical turn of the PB1 domain.
- Broadly across other families noted (e.g., secreted chemokines, ribosomal L31-like proteins, bacterial RlpA enzymes, respiratory complex I subunits, plant viral TGB2): hits recur at β→α junctions or helix N-caps, matching the same short boundary motif.

Summary: Residue-level detector for small side chains (primarily Gly and Ala, occasionally Ser/Thr) at beta-strand positions, with a strong propensity for the repeating strand sites of right-handed parallel beta-helix (PbH1) solenoids common in carbohydrate-active, surface/secreted proteins; the same preference also appears in beta-sheets of diverse soluble enzyme folds, indicating a structural rather than catalytic motif.
Activation pattern: Discrete single-residue peaks, chiefly within beta-strands or immediately adjacent coil; often one peak per repeat in parallel beta-helix/PbH1 architectures. Peaks can occur near the N-terminus or deep in the sequence; count scales with the number of strand/repeat units and is largely independent of annotated catalytic sites.
Exemplars: - Phage tailspike/capsular depolymerases (parallel beta-helix): repeated peaks on Gly/Ala located in the strand rungs of the pβ-helix scaffold.
- Alginate C5-epimerases (PbH1 repeat proteins): one peak per PbH1 repeat on small residues within the repeat’s beta-strand.
- Short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) enzymes: peaks on Gly/Ala in central beta-sheet strands of the Rossmann-like core, away from NAD(P) and catalytic motifs.
- FAD-dependent amine/monoamine oxidase-like enzymes: a strong peak on an N-terminal strand Gly in the first beta-strand.
- Lipopolysaccharide heptosyltransferase II (glycosyltransferase): a prominent Gly within a beta-strand of the core.
- Large adhesion/coiled-coil surface proteins: sparse peaks on Gly/Ala in predicted beta-strands with occasional weak hits at helix ends, consistent with the same small-residue-in-strand preference outside of classical enzymatic folds.

Summary: Extended beta-sheet lipid-handling architectures—especially TULIP/SMP/LLTP- and ATG2-like beta-groove/tunnel folds and related outer-membrane beta domains—used for phospholipid/LPS binding and transfer at membrane contact sites and in extracellular/periplasmic or intermembrane-space environments.
Activation pattern: Regional/domain-level activation concentrated on well-structured beta strands and adjacent loops, often spanning long continuous stretches (tens to hundreds of residues). Residue-level peaks occur at hydrophobic positions (L, I, V, F) within the beta sheets; signal is minimal in helices, low-complexity/disordered tails, targeting peptides, and transmembrane helices.
Exemplars: - ERMES SMP lipid-transfer proteins (e.g., Mdm12/Mmm1/Mdm34): activation on beta strands within the SMP-LTD that form the lipid-binding tunnel.
- Mitochondrial morphology proteins Mdm31/Mdm32: activation across beta-rich intermembrane-space domains while ignoring transmembrane helices.
- ATG2/ATG2-like bulk lipid transfer proteins: activation along extended beta-groove segments lining the hydrophobic conduit used for lipid shuttling at membrane contact sites.
- Gram-negative outer-membrane assembly/transport systems (e.g., Lpt/Lol/Bam/Omp85/OMPs): activation on long beta-strand domains that handle lipids/LPS in the periplasm and outer membrane.
- Secreted BPI/LBP/PLUNC/surfactant proteins: activation over beta-sheets forming TULIP-like lipid-binding cavities for LPS/phospholipids/surfactants.
- Vitellogenins and other large lipid transfer proteins (LLTP family): activation on the N-terminal lipid-transfer beta domain that packages and transports lipids.

Summary: A generic structural signal for ordered secondary structure: the feature marks well-formed alpha helices and beta strands (and their immediate coil-to-helix/strand junctions) across diverse proteins, highlighting stable domain cores rather than catalytic or ligand-contact residues.
Activation pattern: Broad, multi-site activation across structured domains; strong on high-confidence helices and beta strands with local peaks at helix/strand starts and short preceding turns; enriched on hydrophobic/basic residues with frequent glycines; depleted in low-confidence/disordered loops and signal peptides; typically avoids annotated catalytic/metal-binding positions.
Exemplars: - Glycosyltransferases (e.g., GT-A/GT-B chondroitin synthase): activation on structured helices/strands within A1 and A2 catalytic domains, sparing annotated catalytic and metal-binding residues.
- ECF sigma factors (HTH DNA-binding regulators): activation on the HTH helices and adjacent polymerase-core–binding helix; minimal in the central disordered segment.
- Outer membrane beta-barrel porins: activation along transmembrane beta strands and short coil-to-strand junctions; silent in the N-terminal signal peptide and flexible loops.

Summary: Serine/threonine-rich low-complexity intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)—typically long S/T-biased stretches, often containing TP/PT dipeptides—found as mucin-like/adhesin repeats, flexible terminal tails, and propeptides. These segments act as modification-prone, spacer/linker regions (phosphorylation in cytoskeletal proteins; O-glycosylation in secreted/extracellular proteins) and are largely absent from well-folded catalytic or structural cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous low-complexity segments with low-to-moderate pLDDT; strongest signals often at S/T residues (frequently in TP/PT motifs) within dense S/T runs, but can extend to neighboring residues (including small branched V/I). Predominantly localized to N- or C-terminal tails, internal repeat blocks of extracellular adhesins, or N-terminal propeptides; minimal activation in compact, structured domains.
Exemplars: - Fungal cell-surface adhesins/flocculins (e.g., Dfi1): strong activation over extracellular low-complex, S/T-rich repeat blocks consistent with O-glycosylated/mucin-like regions.
- ECM multi-domain proteins with Sushi/nidogen/EGF-like domains: activation confined to a disordered, alternatively spliced C-terminal tail absent from some isoforms.
- Keratin (intermediate filament) proteins: activation on disordered head and tail regions enriched in S/T and known phosphosites; no activation in the helical rod domain.
- Subtilisin-like serine proteases: activation on the disordered N-terminal propeptide preceding the catalytic S8 domain.
- Filamentous/structural and membrane-skeleton associated proteins: activation on flexible, low-complexity terminal segments rather than structured repeats.
- Fibrinogen alpha chains: activation in the disordered alphaC region containing low-complexity runs.
- Phage/viral surface proteins (e.g., M13 minor coat protein G3P): activation on polar, disordered C-terminal segments enriched for S/T.

Summary: Residues marking helix boundaries in flexible regions—helix caps/breakers and adjacent coil positions—most often at extreme N-termini (including signal peptides/signal anchors/transit peptides and newly formed N-termini of processed chains) but also at the start/stop of the first helix in soluble enzymes and small structural/viral proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks, typically near the N-terminus; sparse, non-contiguous activations at coil↔helix boundaries in low-pLDDT regions (including predicted helices of low confidence) with occasional scattered peaks across small largely disordered proteins.
Exemplars: - Secreted toxins, antimicrobial peptides, hormone/allergen/peptide precursors: residues around N-terminal signal peptides and helix caps; often near propeptide processing sites.
- Membrane proteins (e.g., Fluoride channel FluC; organelle-encoded ND subunits): residues flanking the first transmembrane signal anchor.
- Viral accessory/structural proteins: residues in N-terminal amphipathic helices or flexible caps.
- Soluble enzymes (e.g., bacterial PPGK, tRNA m7G methyltransferase; human TP53-target gene 3): helix-cap/breaker residues at the boundary of the first N-terminal helix or adjacent coil.

Summary: Short, isolated positions in well‑ordered beta‑strands (and immediately adjacent turns) that are enriched for bulky hydrophobic/aromatic residues—i.e., beta‑sheet hydrophobic‑packing “hotspots”—often appearing in beta‑rich, disulfide‑stabilized/extracellular domains or aromatic/Cys‑rich patches but not tied to specific catalytic sites.
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks clustered on single residues within beta-strands (DSSP E) or the short coils linking them; high-confidence structured regions; little/no signal in transmembrane helices, long disordered segments, or annotated catalytic motifs.
Exemplars: - Profilins: peak on a Tyr within a beta‑strand of the beta‑rich core (e.g., Y in a high‑confidence strand).
- DHHC-type palmitoyltransferases: N‑terminal beta‑strand patch of aromatic/Cys‑rich residues upstream of the first transmembrane helix and DHHC motif.
- Vitellogenins (VWFD domain): Tyr within the disulfide‑bonded VWFD beta‑sandwich region.
- Beta-galactosidases (GH2): non‑catalytic core beta‑strands (and an adjacent short coil) away from the active Glu residues.
- Endo‑1,4‑beta‑xylanases (GH11): Tyr in a central beta‑strand of the GH11 fold.
- Flagellar hook-associated protein 2 (FliD/HAP2): isolated Leu/Phe residues in beta‑strands of the cap domain.
- Ribosomal pseudouridine synthase B (RluB/RluF family): hydrophobic residues in the N‑terminal S4 RNA‑binding beta‑strand and neighboring coil.
- Cytochrome c biogenesis protein CcsB: aromatic/branched residues in luminal beta‑strands; no activation in transmembrane segments.

Summary: Residue-level detector for tryptophan (W) side chains, often firing on multiple W positions within a sequence and with a mild bias toward N‑terminal Ws; broadly applicable across taxa and protein classes, with frequent occurrences in short membrane/secreted proteins but also in diverse enzymes (e.g., ATP synthase ε, proteases) and mitochondrial proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on W; multiple independent peaks per protein; modest enrichment near N‑termini; occasional weak spillover to neighboring residues (C/E/Q/G/K/R) in W‑rich contexts.
Exemplars: - Viral small/accessory membrane proteins (e.g., viroporin-like): activation on Trp residues in short helices/interfacial segments.
- Bacteriocins and peptide toxins: activation on Trp-rich motifs that mediate membrane interaction/disruption.
- ATP synthase subunit ε (F1 epsilon): activation on conserved Trp residue(s) across bacteria/mitochondria.
- Proteases (serine, cysteine, metalloproteases): activation on Trp positions within the enzyme sequence.
- Secreted and transmembrane protein precursors: activation on interfacial/N‑terminal Trp residues around TM regions or signal-proximal segments.
- Mitochondrial proteins: activation on Trp residues, including in membrane-associated components.
- Eukaryotic micropeptides/antisense-encoded small proteins: activation on any Trp present, often near the N‑terminus due to short length.

Summary: Intrinsic-disorder/low-complexity peptide segments enriched for small residues (notably glycine/proline/alanine/serine with scattered basic residues), commonly found in small bioactive peptide precursors (hormones, antimicrobial/toxin peptides) and regulatory microproteins; the feature marks flexible propeptide or mature-peptide regions and sparsely tags similar IDRs in larger proteins across taxa.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered within long coil/IDR stretches; sometimes periodic in glycine-rich peptides (~4–5 residue spacing); often includes N-terminal positions in precursors; typically weaker or absent in structured helical signal peptides; in larger proteins, multiple weak peaks rather than a single motif.
Exemplars: - Proapoptotic nucleolar microproteins: sparse peaks across low-confidence disordered regions (including Pro/Arg-rich stretches).
- Kisspeptin (KiSS-1) peptide precursor: scattered activation within the disordered precursor, including residues inside the metastin bioactive segment.
- Glycine-rich antimicrobial peptides (e.g., acanthoscurrin): strong periodic activation across the gly/lys-rich mature peptide; little/no activation in the N-terminal signal peptide.
- Plant elicitor peptide precursors (PROPEP): activation localized to the N-terminal propeptide region (predicted beta strands), with minimal signal on the short C-terminal bioactive peptide.

Summary: Short, flexible coil/linker elements and helix-boundary hinge sites characteristic of intrinsically disordered or low-complexity regions, enriched in Gly/Pro and polar residues and often located at inter-domain junctions or between helices (low predicted structural confidence); the feature reflects local flexibility rather than a specific function.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks that cluster over short stretches; strongest in coils/turns, helix caps and junctions, and glycine-containing kinks; scattered across sequences with many peaks in low-pLDDT segments and inter-domain linkers, with occasional activation inside helices at glycine-induced flexibility points.
Exemplars: - ER oxidoreductase Ero1: peaks in a flexible loop just upstream of the FAD-binding site and at helix termini/loops with low confidence.
- Herpesvirus tegument protein VP16: multiple G/P-rich unstructured coil segments with low pLDDT.
- Mammarenavirus nucleoprotein: short coil linkers between helices (Gly/Asn) and helix termini in low-confidence regions.
- Positive-strand RNA virus replicase polyprotein: glycine-rich inter-domain linkers between the methyltransferase and Fe2OG dioxygenase modules.
- CRISPR Cas13a endoribonuclease: scattered low-confidence loops/turns across NTD, helical domains, and HEPN-like regions, including linkers.
- Plasmodium merozoite surface protein 9: disordered segments and coil linkers between helical elements within annotated disordered regions.
- Viral major capsid protein: helix-capping coils and glycine pairs marking hinge points preceding glycine-rich unstructured stretches.

Summary: Residue-level recognition of well-ordered beta-strand positions that form the cores of beta-sheet–rich folds across diverse proteins (Ig-like beta-sandwiches, beta-propellers, arrestin-like, F-box associated/FBA, ML/MD-2, and beta-strand enzymes); in secreted/Ig-like contexts the peaks often lie next to disulfide-bonded cysteines and frequently coincide with or flank N-glycosylation sequons.
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks concentrated on DSSP ‘E’ positions with high structural confidence; multiple peaks distributed across different strands of the same beta-rich domain; little to no activation in signal peptides, transmembranes, or low-confidence/disordered regions; occasional proximity to catalytic or ligand-binding residues located in beta-sheets.
Exemplars: Integrin alpha subunits: beta-propeller FG-GAP strand residues, including sites adjacent to disulfide bonds; Ig superfamily receptors (e.g., CD33, paired Ig-like receptors, IgSF8): beta-strand positions within V/C2 domains, often next to disulfide cysteines and N-linked glycosylation Asn; Arrestin/ARRDC proteins: residues in the well-packed beta-sheet core; COPI/coatomer subunits: beta-strands in the structured C-terminal domain; MD-2/ML lipid-recognition proteins: beta-sheet residues within disulfide-stabilized folds; F-box proteins with FBA domains (including PP2/Nictaba-like): beta-strand positions within the FBA beta-sandwich; QueD/CPH4 synthase (folate/queuosine pathway): conserved beta-strands near catalytic/metal-binding elements; Calreticulin: beta-strand residues in the structured N-domain.

Summary: Absolute N-terminal positional cue centered near the fourth residue (N+3), independent of amino-acid identity; most often within signal/transit peptides of precursors but also present in non-secreted proteins; the effect is weak and often does not produce a discrete detected site.

Activation pattern: Very weak absolute N-terminus bias centered on residue 4 (±1); frequently sub-threshold so no discrete peak or active_feature is reported; when detected, a single narrow peak at position 4 (occasionally 5); rare, much weaker secondary bumps near the start of a following propeptide; no extended regional activation.

Exemplars:
- Secreted neuropeptide precursors (e.g., tachykinins): usually sub-threshold; when detected, a faint peak near residue 4 within the signal peptide
- Antimicrobial granule proteins (e.g., granulysin): same pattern
- Venom toxin peptide precursors (e.g., actitoxins): same pattern; occasionally a faint bump at the propeptide start
- Cytosolic proteins (e.g., SulA, metallothionein): weak N-terminal bias near residue 4 despite absence of a signal peptide
- Generic peptide/toxin/antimicrobial precursors: weak bias near residue 4, with occasional faint signal at the propeptide boundary

Summary: A general secondary-structure signal for short beta-strands and their flanking turns/coil in non-transmembrane regions (extracellular or cytosolic), with a preference for small/flexible or polar/charged residues; strongly depleted in alpha-helices, especially membrane-spanning helices.
Activation pattern: Residue-level scattered peaks concentrated within short beta-strands and immediately adjacent coil/turn residues; frequent at N-termini and internal strands; minimal to absent across long helices and all transmembrane segments; enrichment for G, S, T, P, K, E at activated sites.
Exemplars: - V/A-type ATPase membrane subunits: activates on non-transmembrane N-terminal/central beta-strands and nearby coils; silent on transmembrane helices.
- Pentameric ligand-gated ion channels: activates on the extracellular beta-sandwich domain, not on the helical pore.
- Mechanosensitive channels (e.g., MscS-like): activates on cytosolic beta-sheet domains rather than TM helices.
- ClC/pH-sensitive chloride channels: activates on cytosolic CBS/alpha-beta domains, not on TM helices.
- Clathrin/adaptor/WD40 machinery: highlights strands/turns of beta-propeller and beta-sandwich scaffolds.
- Aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetases (e.g., PheRS β) and ribosomal/translation factors: marks beta-sheet elements within mixed alpha/beta cores.
- DNA replication/repair proteins (e.g., PriA helicase and related factors): activates on beta-strands and adjacent loops of RecA-like/alpha-beta domains.
- Ribonuclease P protein components: highlights beta/turn elements in RNA-binding or accessory domains.
- Trigger factor and cyclophilin-type PPIases: activates on beta-sandwich strands/turns; weak in helical regions.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes (glycosidases/xylanases/cellulases): marks beta-strands and bordering loops of TIM barrels and beta-sandwich folds.
- Phage tail and head–tail joining proteins: activates on beta-rich structural segments common in virion assembly proteins.

Summary: Short, intrinsically disordered low‑complexity segments—especially near protein N‑termini and around short linear motifs for processing/regulation (e.g., signal/propeptide regions and PTM‑adjacent sites)—with a bias toward small (Gly/Pro/Ser/Ala) and basic (Lys/Arg) residues
Activation pattern: Sparse, low-amplitude residue-level peaks clustered in N‑terminal and other low‑pLDDT/disordered stretches; preferentially on small/basic residues; occasional weak signal within the first N‑terminal helix/signal‑anchor; little signal over well‑ordered core domains
Exemplars: - Secreted neuropeptide/hormone precursors (kisspeptin/KiSS-1 family): activations on disordered, low‑complexity propeptide/metastin segments and early N‑terminal residues; avoids short structured helices and compact C‑terminal peptides
- Bacterial inner‑membrane transporters (NiaX-like): activations at the initiator methionine and nearby residues within the first N‑terminal helix/signal‑anchor
- Neuronal regeneration-related disordered regulators (NREP-like): activations across an N‑terminal disordered stretch including residues flanking a phosphoserine site and glycine‑rich patches

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments used as extracellular stalks/linkers and nuclear/regulatory IDRs. These segments are typically either polyampholyte tracts enriched in acidic and basic residues (E/D with K/R/H; often E–x–K repeats) or mucin-/extensin-like Pro/Thr/Ser-rich O-glycosylation tracts; they are common in secreted/adhesive proteins, peptide/venom/neuropeptide precursors, viral/apicomplexan low-complexity proteins, and some germ cell/testis antigens.

Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered low-complexity tracts; frequent periodic residue-level peaks on charged residues (E/D and K/R/H) when present. In S/T/P-rich mucin/extensin-like segments, activation is broad/regional and may highlight nearby acidic residues; little or no activation in folded domains, signal peptides, or short structured modules, though low-complexity propeptides of precursors can activate.

Exemplars:
- Fungal cell-wall adhesins and signaling mucins: central low-complexity stalks (K/E-rich or Ser/Thr/Pro-rich glycostalks) are activated; signal peptides and structured domains are not.
- Plant extensins (hydroxyproline/proline-rich glycoproteins): activation along long S/T/P-rich repeats with acidic patches in disordered tails.
- Germ cell/testis antigens and chromatin remodeler subunits: EK-repeat polyampholyte IDRs with sharp peaks on E/K and suppression on intervening spacers.
- Viral regulatory proteins (e.g., EBNA-LP) and apicomplexan exported proteins (e.g., RESA): long acidic/basic low-complexity repeats with periodic peaks on charged residues.
- Secreted matrix/adhesion glycoproteins (e.g., MAdCAM-1 mucin-like stalk, ovocleidin-116): disordered low-complexity extracellular regions (acidic and/or S/T/P-rich) show regional activation.
- Peptide/venom/neuropeptide precursors: low-complexity, often acidic/basic-rich propeptide segments can activate.

Summary: Short, isolated positions within intrinsically disordered regulatory regions of eukaryotic proteins—especially transcription factors and nuclear co-regulators—often in Ser/Pro- and acidic-enriched low‑complexity linkers or tails just outside structured DNA-binding/oligomerization domains, consistent with generic short linear motifs used for transient interactions or regulation
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks sparsely distributed in low‑pLDDT coils or low-confidence predicted helices; multiple small peaks can occur across long IDRs and domain linkers; occasional weak peaks appear inside folded domains; overall low, tightly clustered activation scores
Exemplars: Homeobox transcription factors (HOX): peaks in short low-confidence coils flanking the homeobox and rare residues within the domain; Forkhead transcription factors: isolated peaks in the C‑terminal disordered tail beyond the forkhead domain; BTB–C2H2 zinc-finger repressors (e.g., ZBTB7 family): multiple small peaks in the long disordered linker between BTB and zinc-finger arrays, including near annotated interaction regions; Plant MADS‑box transcription factors (AGL/AGAMOUS-like): isolated peaks in the disordered C‑terminal region outside the MADS box; PRMT5 cofactors/adaptors: very weak, isolated peaks within globally disordered segments; Centrosomal/chromosomal scaffold proteins: rare peaks in low-confidence disordered regions; Testis-expressed low‑complexity proteins: sparse peaks across unstructured regions

Summary: Long terminal segments—predominantly C‑terminal tails—characterized by extended, compositionally biased tracts (low‑complexity Gly/Pro/Ser/Thr- and charge‑rich) or the final structural element of a fold (terminal helix/last beta strand) including C‑terminal transmembrane anchors; occasionally the feature also flags extended internal stretches with similar composition/continuity. These regions often function as flexible tails, linker/interaction segments, isoform‑variable extensions, or pre/post‑membrane cassettes, and the concept is taxon‑agnostic.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long contiguous segments, most often starting near the C terminus and running to the chain end; frequently spans pre‑TM loop plus the terminal TM helix, or the last strand/helix with the adjacent tail. Structured domain cores are typically silent. Weaker activation can occur at N‑terminal disordered segments, and rare internal extended stretches with similar bias are captured.
Exemplars: - Mediator of RNA polymerase II subunit 31: strong activation on a disordered, compositionally biased C‑terminal tail; weaker on a short disordered N‑terminal segment; structured central core off.
- Phospholipid scramblase 1: activation across the C‑terminal pre‑TM cytosolic region, the single C‑terminal transmembrane helix, and the short extracellular tail.
- Poly(ribitol‑phosphate) alpha‑N‑acetylglucosaminyltransferase (wall teichoic acid glycosyltransferase): an internal, extended mixed α/β/loop segment (∼183–290) is captured as a long, continuous region (example of a non‑terminal stretch).
- Oxysterol‑binding/OSBP‑related protein 11: C‑terminal portion of the OSBP domain, especially a long helix with basic/acidic compositional bias.
- King tubby family protein: strongest signal on the extreme C‑terminal alpha‑helix; diffuse signal over the disordered N‑terminal portion; structured Tub domain interior off.
- MORN repeat‑containing protein 3: isoform‑specific, disordered C‑terminal tail (TP53‑interacting region) strongly marked; MORN repeat core off.
- MTERF family (MTERF9): activation restricted to the structured C‑terminal helical domain; disordered N‑terminus off.
- Chloroplast outer envelope porin OEP37: final intermembrane loop plus last beta‑strand and cytosolic C‑tail (isoform‑variable segment) activated.
- Formylmethanofuran dehydrogenase subunit C: unstructured, low‑confidence C‑terminal tail following repeats activated.
- Microtubule‑associated/axonemal proteins (e.g., tau/MAPT): long, low‑complexity, repeat‑rich C‑terminal tails are strongly activated.

Summary: Polar/charged low-complexity regions in secreted precursors and cytosolic/nuclear IDRs, with strongest bias toward Asp/Glu and Gly but also accommodating cysteine-rich secreted repeats (e.g., metallothioneins). The feature highlights polar/charged residues within flexible, repeat-rich segments rather than a specific folded domain.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks across long low-complexity stretches; strongest on D/E and G (often N), but can also mark Cys (and occasionally Lys) in secreted cysteine-rich repeats. Peaks are enriched in coil/low-pLDDT regions, but may also occur on acidic/polar residues within helices of soluble lumenal proteins. Activation often begins after signal/transit peptides and is minimal in tightly folded domains otherwise.
Exemplars: - Fungal adhesins (AWP family): periodic G/D/E peaks across Ser/Thr-rich disordered C-termini.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: post-signal peptide, sparse D/E peaks in disordered, compositionally biased regions; RxLR/dEER motif not emphasized.
- Mammalian mucin-like salivary/seminal proteins (e.g., semenogelins): numerous G/D (and GG/DD pairs) across long low-complexity segments.
- Kinetochore/chromatin regulators (e.g., KNL-2): activation in acidic, glycine-dotted disordered C-termini; folded domains inactive.
- Bacterial surface adhesins/enzymes: activation on acidic/gly-rich low-complexity linkers and repeats between domains.
- Secreted cysteine-rich proteins (e.g., metallothioneins): peaks on Cys and scattered acidic/gly sites within low-complexity regions.
- Plastid lumen-targeted soluble proteins (e.g., peridinin–chlorophyll a-binding proteins): occasional peaks on acidic residues within helices or adjacent low-complexity segments following targeting peptides.

Summary: A generic signature of intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regions enriched in glycine/proline and charged/polar residues, common in secreted peptide precursors and collagen-like segments as well as flexible terminal/linker regions of diverse proteins; it largely avoids well‑structured catalytic cores and transmembrane helices.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level, low‑magnitude, scattered peaks concentrated in low‑pLDDT coils and compositionally biased stretches; minimal in well‑structured domains and TM helices; occasional tiny peaks at boundaries (e.g., TM–extracellular); variable coverage and often present even in sequence fragments.
Exemplars: - Plant CLE/CLAVATA peptide precursor (FON2): weak, sparse peaks confined to the disordered C‑terminal region; no activation over the N‑terminal signal peptide helix.
- Collagen alpha chain (extracellular matrix): isolated peaks at glycine or residues adjacent to proline within disordered, Gly/Pro‑rich collagen-like stretches; no continuous activation.
- NAD-dependent DNA ligase: numerous peaks across the low‑confidence, N‑terminal tail; largely absent from the structured ligase core and BRCT domain.
- SecE membrane translocase subunit: near-zero across the transmembrane helix; tiny peak at the first periplasmic residue after the helix and a minor blip within the cytoplasmic helix.

Summary: Extended, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered tandem‑repeat tracts enriched in acidic/polar residues (E/D/Q) and Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly—i.e., mucin‑like and hydroxyproline‑rich extracellular repeats and acidic “DE” blobs in nuclear/scaffold proteins; a composition‑based marker of long, repetitive, glycosylation‑prone IDRs rather than folded catalytic domains, and also acidic/polar low‑complexity tails or loops in otherwise structured proteins (including multi‑pass membrane proteins and soluble enzymes).
Activation pattern: Regional activation spanning long contiguous segments (tens to hundreds of residues) within repeat blocks/low‑complexity regions; strongest and uniform over S/T‑/P‑rich and E/D‑rich runs (often N‑terminal or linker tracts), with little activation in structured cores but possible signal on extended disordered termini/loops in otherwise folded proteins.
Exemplars: 
- Mucins and mucin‑like extracellular domains — activation on O‑glycosylated Ser/Thr/Pro tandem repeats
- Plant hydroxyproline‑rich glycoproteins (extensins, AGPs, proline‑rich cell‑wall proteins) — activation on Ser‑Pro/Pro‑rich repeats that become Hyp‑glycosylated
- Glycine‑rich structural proteins (silk/resilin‑like and plant glycine‑rich proteins) — activation on long Gly‑rich repetitive segments
- Bacterial surface adhesins with repeat architectures (serine‑rich repeat proteins, LPXTG‑anchored adhesins; RTX‑like Asp/Gly‑rich segments) — activation on extended low‑complexity repeat tracts
- Viral tegument/nuclear proteins — activation on acidic low‑complexity repeats functioning as activation/scaffold regions
- Extracellular matrix/adhesive scaffolds — activation on acidic/polar repeat‑rich linkers between structural modules
- Coiled‑coil golgin/other long scaffolds — activation on acidic low‑complexity linkers flanking coiled‑coil rods
- Testis‑associated antigen families — activation on proline‑/acidic low‑complexity repetitive regions
- Acidic nuclear transcriptional coactivators/chaperones — activation on Asp/Glu‑rich activation domains
- Multi‑pass membrane proteins (e.g., MS4A/CD20‑like) — activation on acidic/polar low‑complexity cytosolic tails or luminal loops
- Housekeeping enzymes (e.g., bacterial phosphoglycerate kinase) — activation on acidic/disordered N/C‑terminal extensions or insertions

Summary: Generic recognition of long tandem-repeat/solenoid scaffolds—especially β-solenoids (parallel β-helix) and leucine/valine‑rich repeats (LRR, HEAT/coiled‑coil)—and allied Ser/Thr‑rich repetitive tracts that form extended, often extracellular or scaffold-like regions in enzymes, adhesins, phage tail fibers/depolymerases, and large eukaryotic complexes
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long contiguous repeats rather than discrete catalytic sites; strongest along repeat “spines” with hydrophobic-core positions (V/L/I) and frequent surface Ser/Thr; typically spans entire solenoid domains, coiled‑coil stalks, LRR arcs, or Ser/Thr‑rich low‑complexity segments
Exemplars: - Parallel β-helix/β-solenoid CAZymes: pectate/pectin lyases, alginate mannuronan C5‑epimerases (AlgE), rhamnogalacturonan lyases—activation runs along the β‑helix rungs forming the hydrophobic core and turn layers.
- Phage tailspike/fiber depolymerases: activation over the elongated β‑solenoid shafts that bind/degrade capsular or O‑antigen polysaccharides.
- Bacterial surface/secreted mega‑modules (cellulosomes, S‑layer/SLH systems, adhesins): activation on coiled‑coil stalks, repetitive linker segments, and repeat modules (e.g., cohesin/dockerin arrays).
- Leucine‑rich repeat proteins (LRR/LRR‑like receptors and ECM proteins): activation across the tandem LRR arc at conserved leucine/isoleucine core positions.
- Eukaryotic nucleoporins and Mediator subunits: activation along HEAT/ARM helical solenoids and extended coiled‑coil scaffolds within these large complexes.
- Ser/Thr‑rich mucins and fungal adhesins: activation across low‑complexity, O‑glycosylated Ser/Thr repeat tracts that form extended extracellular regions.
- Glycan‑processing enzymes and ER glycosylation pathway components: activation on repetitive β‑sandwich/CBM‑like segments or luminal repeat regions adjacent to catalytic cores.
- Ribosomal protein L24 family: activation over consecutive helical hairpins that form a compact repeat‑like helical scaffold.

Summary: Short, solvent‑exposed secondary‑structure boundary motifs—helix/strand starts and their adjacent turns/caps—enriched in small/polar and acidic residues (G/S/T/D/N) and often accompanied by an aromatic (frequently Trp); a generic structural signal marking loop‑to‑helix or loop‑to‑strand junctions that frequently occur at domain caps, inter‑repeat linkers, and surface binding interfaces.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation with narrow 8–15 residue windows centered on loop↔helix or loop↔strand transitions (including helix/strand N‑caps) and nearby flexible turns; repeated peaks across long beta‑repeat regions (e.g., phage tail fibers); little/no activation in transmembrane segments or long core helices; occasionally extends into adjacent disordered linkers at domain boundaries.
Exemplars: - Phage tail fiber/spike receptor‑binding proteins: repeated activation on beta‑strand segments and the connecting loops of the C‑terminal receptor‑binding beta‑solenoid.
- NEAT‑domain heme‑binding surface proteins (Isd family): a loop‑to‑helix boundary within the NEAT domain that includes/abuts heme‑contact residues.
- Plant LRR receptor(-like) kinases/proteins: the LRR N‑terminal cap and inter‑repeat linker turns near disulfide‑stabilized caps.
- Hotdog‑fold acyl‑CoA thioesterases/hydrolases: a short N‑terminal helix and its immediate coil (helix‑capping region).
- Polyamine aminopropyltransferases (spermidine synthase family): a beta‑strand segment directly preceding the MTA/SAM‑binding site within the PABS domain.
- CorA Mg2+ transporters: N‑terminal cytosolic domain junctions at helix→loop and strand→loop transitions; absent from the transmembrane helices.
- Plant bHLH transcription factors: a short disordered segment immediately C‑terminal to the bHLH domain (domain‑to‑tail junction enriched in polar residues).

Summary: Ordered hydrophobic segments in well-structured contexts: β-strand segments in β-sheet architectures (β-sandwich/Ig-like and other β-rich domains) and transmembrane helices in multi-pass membrane proteins; a broad structural property (not catalytic-site specific) prevalent in extracellular/surface proteins and membranes but present across compartments
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks as short consecutive runs aligning with rigid secondary structure elements—β-strands in soluble β-rich domains and TM helices in multi-pass membranes; regionally clustered (often toward C-termini of large extracellular proteins); suppressed in low-confidence/disordered regions (e.g., signal peptides/propeptides); enriched for hydrophobic/aromatic residues with frequent Ser/Thr/Gly
Exemplars: - Hyaluronate/chondroitin lyases (polysaccharide lyases): repeated activation on β-strands in well-structured regions, away from catalytic residues
- Ku70/Ku80 (DNA end-joining): discrete activation on β-strands within the Ku domain
- Lipoxygenases: activation on short β-strands in structured regions, away from metal-binding sites
- Fimbrial/pilus tip adhesins (Ig-like β-sandwich modules): activation on β-sheet segments of the mature adhesin; absent in signal peptide/propeptide
- S-layer proteins: concentrated activation on β-rich segments consistent with self-assembly scaffolds
- V/A-type ATPase subunit I (multi-pass membrane): activation on transmembrane helices

Summary: Positively charged, hydrophobic/aromatic-enriched amphipathic segments (often MoRF-like) that are typically long, contiguous N‑terminal stretches of intrinsic disorder or the first α-helix, used as generic targeting/interaction modules for membranes, nucleic acids, secretion/chaperone engagement, or partner binding
Activation pattern: Regional activation over extended, compositionally biased segments with a strong N‑terminal bias; often spans the first 20–40 residues (including an N‑terminal α-helix when present) or disordered tails adjacent to folded domains; secondary peaks can occur at internal amphipathic helices; residue-level maxima frequently coincide with Lys/Arg and aromatic (Phe/Tyr/Trp) positions; structured core β‑sheet regions are typically not activated
Exemplars: - Phage anti-defense DNA-mimic Ocr: activation on the first N‑terminal α-helix (residues ~5–25), while later helices are not highlighted.
- Poxvirus poxin phosphodiesterase toxin: strong activation on a disordered N‑terminal segment (residues ~1–26) and a moderate peak on an internal amphipathic helix containing catalytic residues.
- KCTD (BTB/POZ) family: activation on the low-complexity, disordered C‑terminal region following the BTB domain (partner/substrate-interaction segment).
- Retroviral Gag (e.g., foamy virus): activation on the N‑terminal matrix region containing a polybasic, amphipathic helix used for membrane/RNA engagement.
- HIV Vif: activation on the basic/hydrophobic, disordered N‑terminal segment that mediates partner binding.
- Type III/IV secretion effectors: activation on N‑terminal secretion/chaperone-binding regions that are disordered and amphipathic.
- Ribosome-inactivating proteins (plant/fungal toxins): activation on N‑terminal signal peptides/propeptides (basic N-region plus hydrophobic core) for secretion.
- Nucleic acid–binding/packaging proteins (viral and bacterial): activation on arginine/lysine-rich amphipathic segments that contact RNA/DNA.
- E. coli toxin–antitoxin and stress-modulator proteins: activation on basic, hydrophobic low-complexity tails/short helices used for binding and regulation.
- TIP41 family (PP2A/Tap42 interactors) and REDD stress-response proteins: activation on disordered, amphipathic interaction segments.
- Photosynthesis/carboxysome-associated small proteins: activation on short targeting/encapsulation peptides (amphipathic helices) used for microcompartment association.

Summary: Extended low‑complexity, serine/threonine‑ and proline‑enriched intrinsically disordered segments (PEST-/mucin‑like) that serve as regulatory, degradation‑prone, and glycosylation‑prone regions in eukaryotic proteins; the signal can also include contiguous β‑strand patches of β‑rich scaffolds that present polar S/T‑bearing surfaces adjacent to or within these flexible tracts
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long stretches with multiple noncontiguous clusters per protein; strongest over S/T/P‑rich low‑complexity tracts, with occasional concentrated peaks on short β‑strand blocks in β‑rich domains
Exemplars: - BTB/POZ–MATH and RING/TRAF E3 ubiquitination components: activation on long disordered regulatory tails/linkers and PEST‑like degron regions.
- Calpains: activation on PEST‑like, S/T‑ and Pro‑rich segments associated with calpain‑sensitive or autoinhibitory regions.
- Phosphoinositide/lipid‑signaling proteins (e.g., PH/PX/FYVE adaptors, PI kinases/phosphatases): activation on serine/threonine‑rich regulatory tails and proline‑rich interaction regions.
- Secreted and extracellular matrix glycoproteins (including mucins/precursors): broad activation across mucin‑like O‑glycosylated S/T‑rich low‑complexity domains and extracellular linkers.
- Plant NLR innate immunity receptors: activation on extended low‑complexity segments (e.g., N‑terminal regions and flexible inter‑repeat linkers).
- Helicases and protein translocation machinery: activation on flexible S/T‑rich termini and low‑complexity linkers used for regulation or partner binding.
- Viral structural proteins (capsid/envelope glycoproteins): activation on disordered, S/T‑rich, often glycosylated surface loops and mucin‑like regions.
- Glycosylation enzymes/pathways (glycosyltransferases, wall teichoic acid glycosylation) and their glycoprotein substrates: activation on S/T‑rich low‑complexity luminal segments in enzymes and on mucin‑like S/T‑rich stretches in substrates.
- Integrator complex subunit 7: a localized high‑amplitude cluster on a C‑terminal β‑strand block within a β‑rich domain, consistent with the feature’s inclusion of polar β‑sheet patches adjacent to flexible regions.

Summary: Short amphipathic alpha-helical segments (~10–25 aa), most often at protein N- or C-termini, that serve as generic interface helices (DNA/RNA-recognition helices, dimerization/oligomerization helices, or helical linkers) across diverse defense-, mobile-element-, and nucleic-acid–related proteins and enzymes.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on a single contiguous stretch matching an alpha helix; strongest at extreme termini; sequence shows alternating charged (K/R/E/D) and hydrophobic (L/I/V/A) residues consistent with amphipathic helices; not domain-wide.
Exemplars: - CRISPR-associated proteins (Type I/II/III subunits, e.g., Cas7/Cas8/Cse1/Cas9): activation on terminal recognition or REC-lobe helices that contact nucleic acids or mediate assembly
- Restriction–modification components (Type II endonucleases and associated HTH regulators): activation on HTH recognition helices or dimerization helices
- DNA repair/processing enzymes (MutS mismatch repair, helicases, ligases, exonucleases): activation on short terminal helices used for DNA-contact or subunit interfaces
- Antiphage/defense systems beyond CRISPR (retrons, OLD nucleases, CD-NTase/Cap effectors, defense sirtuins): activation on terminal amphipathic/oligomerization helices
- Viral and mobile-element proteins (phage capsid/tail/assembly proteins, transposases): activation on short assembly/interface helices
- Cyclic nucleotide synthases/signaling enzymes (uridylate cyclases; cGAS/DncV-like nucleotidyltransferases): activation on regulatory helices at domain edges that aid dimerization or nucleic-acid engagement
- Siderophore biosynthesis enzymes/ligases: activation on N- or C-terminal amphipathic helices linking catalytic domains or mediating dimerization

Summary: Residue-level detection of beta-strand scaffold positions, with a strong preference for the repeating right-handed parallel beta-helix (PbH1) motif and, more generally, beta-sheet elements (including beta-barrels); emphasizes hydrophobic/aromatic and small residues that support well-folded beta-rich architectures rather than catalytic sites.
Activation pattern: Sparse single-residue peaks concentrated in high-confidence beta-strands and strand-adjacent loops; periodic arrays when tandem PbH1 repeats are present; secondary peaks on short glycine-rich loop motifs preceding strands; little to no activation in signal peptides, disordered segments, or non-beta repeat modules; typically not centered on annotated catalytic residues.
Exemplars: - Alginate C5-epimerases (AlgE family): strong, periodic peaks restricted to PbH1 repeats that build the right-handed parallel beta-helix; no activation in hemolysin-type calcium-binding repeats or disordered tails.
- Phage capsular polysaccharide depolymerases/tailspikes: sparse peaks within the beta-helix host-interaction core and C-terminal beta-strands, away from catalytic annotations.
- Gram-negative outer membrane porins: isolated peaks on individual hydrophobic/aromatic residues within barrel beta-strands of the mature chain; absent in N-terminal signal peptides.
- Autotransporters (including Pmp adhesins): sharp peaks on hydrophobic/aromatic residues in beta-barrel strands of the translocator; secondary activation on glycine-glycine motifs in loops preceding strands; no activation in disordered patches.
- ABC transporter ATP-binding subunits (NBDs): scattered peaks in beta-strands and nearby loops within the ABC domain, adjacent to but not on catalytic Walker/dimerization motifs.
- SDR-family dehydrogenases/reductases: peaks in Rossmann-core beta-strands and an adjacent helix near the NAD-binding region, highlighting structural scaffold positions.
- Glycosyltransferases: isolated peaks at beta-strand termini and adjacent loops within the GT fold, excluding the catalytic Asp/Glu sites.

Summary: Beta-strand–dominated lipid-handling architectures at cellular/organellar boundaries: the feature tracks domains that create hydrophobic conduits or grooves for binding/transporting lipids or isoprenoids, encompassing outer-membrane beta-barrel pores and assembly/lipid-transport factors, soluble lipid-transfer/binding barrels (e.g., BPI, OSBP/ORD, SMP/TULIP), and bridge-like intermembrane lipid-transfer proteins (e.g., ATG2/ERMES)
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation spanning extended beta-strand/coil regions with multiple discrete residue-level peaks; enrichment on small/polar/acidic positions (G, D, E, S, T); often covers large portions of very long proteins rather than a short motif; peaks can coincide with pocket-lining or substrate-binding residues within lipid/isoprenoid-binding cavities or along beta-barrel strands and loops
Exemplars: - Autophagy lipid-transfer bridges (ATG2/VPS13-like): activation distributed along the elongated groove that ferries lipids between membranes
- ERMES/mitochondrial morphology and distribution factors (Mdm10/Mdm12/Mdm31/Mdm32): activation on the Mdm10 outer-membrane beta-barrel and on SMP/TULIP lipid-transfer domains (e.g., Mdm12) at contact sites
- Porin-like outer-membrane channels of mitochondria/chloroplasts (TOM40/VDAC; chloroplast OEPs): activation across beta-barrel strands and acidic loop regions
- Gram-negative outer-membrane assembly and lipid transport systems (e.g., LptD/E, Bam components, MCE/LetB/AsmA-like): activation along periplasmic lipid-transport barrels/rings and barrel strands involved in OM biogenesis/lipid flow
- Oxysterol-binding proteins (OSBP/ORP/Osh): activation within the ORD beta-strand–rich region forming the sterol-binding cavity
- BPI-fold lipid/LPS-binding proteins: residue-level peaks on C-terminal beta-sheets lining the lipid-binding mouth
- Aromatic prenyltransferases (LtmE/DMATS-like): activation around PT-barrel regions and active-site residues contacting tryptophan and prenyl donors

Summary: A short hydrophobic beta-strand element (often a loop-to-strand or beta-turn–beta motif) within well-folded domains. The feature highlights generic beta-sheet strands—typically enriched in V/I/L/F (often with occasional acidic or aromatic residues)—used across diverse folds, frequently in secreted/periplasmic proteins but also in cytosolic factors, and sometimes situated in regions implicated in protein–protein contacts.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous 8–15(–20)-residue segments with sharp residue-level peaks centered in the strand; usually overlaps a predicted beta-strand and may include the preceding loop/turn (coil→beta transition). Occurs once or a few times per protein, often between residues ~60–120 of mature secreted proteins, but can appear elsewhere in structured domains; does not target signal peptides or disordered tails.
Exemplars: - Chloroplast division factor ARC6: C-terminal beta-strand in the intermembrane domain at the PDV2-interaction region.
- Aromatic ring-hydroxylating dioxygenase small (beta) subunit: internal beta-strand within the well-structured core.
- NTF2-like nuclear export proteins: beta-strand inside the NTF2 fold.
- Cystatin/cystatin-like cysteine protease inhibitors: strand adjacent to the “secondary area of contact” motif within the beta-sheet.
- BPI/LBP fold lipid/ligand transfer proteins: short beta-strand segment within the lipid-binding domain.
- Photosystem II lumenal/extrinsic proteins (PsbP/PsbO/OEE): tyrosine- and hydrophobic-rich beta-strand segments in lumenal beta-sheets.
- Type IV secretion VirB8-like periplasmic components: strand in the periplasmic domain’s beta-sheet.
- Mycobacterial lipoproteins/secreted antigens: short extracellular/periplasmic beta-strand within the structured domain.
- Mitochondrial import/inner membrane–associated proteins: loop-to-strand elements in soluble intermembrane/exposed regions.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., crotalicidin precursor): structured propeptide beta-strand, not the signal peptide or mature antimicrobial segment.

Summary: Short amphipathic β‑strand/extended segments with alternating polar/hydrophobic composition (enriched for S/T/V/G and acidic residues interleaved with I/L/F/Y), including β‑edge/zipper‑like motifs that recur in β‑rich domains and S/T‑rich low‑complexity repeats across diverse proteins
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks confined to short 7–15 aa stretches predicted as extended/β (E state), often repeating many times within a protein; strongest in high‑confidence β‑strands of structured β‑rich regions, with weaker but frequent hits in disordered S/T‑rich tandem repeats that adopt extended conformations; not tied to glycosylation consensus motifs or transmembranes
Exemplars: - Fungal GPI‑anchored cell‑wall adhesins: sharp peak on a specific β‑strand within the β‑rich C‑terminal domain, with weaker recurring hits in downstream Thr‑rich tandem repeats (fits alternating S/T–hydrophobic patterns).
- Secreted toxins/effectors (lectin/β‑trefoil/β‑sandwich and pore‑forming types): multiple short activations on individual β‑strands within the β‑rich scaffold.
- Ribosomal proteins (bacterial, mitochondrial, chloroplastic): hits on short β‑strands or extended acidic segments within small β/α folds.
- Intermediate filament/lamin proteins: activations in tail/linker low‑complexity regions at short extended S/T‑rich, hydrophobic‑interleaved stretches.
- Diacylglycerol kinase family: localized activations on short β‑strand elements of the soluble/cytosolic domains.
- NAD kinase: recurrent peaks on core β‑sheet strands of the Rossmann‑like fold.
- Archaeal F420‑dependent enzymes: activations on edge β‑strands within β/α core architectures.
- Bacterial nuclease/toxin systems and diverse viral proteins: short, repeated peaks mapping to β‑strands in compact β‑rich domains.
- Carbohydrate‑active enzymes (glycosidases, glycosyltransferases, alginate/manuronan enzymes): frequent activations on β‑sandwich/β‑helix strand repeats and other short β‑sheet elements.

Summary: Short intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity coil segments enriched in acidic (D/E) and small/proline residues, with a strong preference for the extreme N‑terminus of the mature chain (often the start of tandem‑repeat or activation domains), but also occurring as similar internal flexible linkers/loops
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short stretches (≈5–20 aa) with residue‑level peaks at positions 1–10 from the N‑terminus; multiple noncontiguous activations per protein corresponding to separate disordered segments
Exemplars: - Mucin-like glycoproteins: activates on the processed N‑terminus launching a disordered tandem‑repeat tract (e.g., mucin repeat region start)
- Secreted glycosidases: activates on a short low‑confidence coil loop within the mature enzyme
- Nuclear receptors: activates within the disordered, acidic N‑terminal AF‑1 transactivation domain
- Snake venom metalloproteinases/serine proteases: activates on disordered N‑terminal segments of the mature enzyme or adjacent flexible linkers/propeptides
- Fungal secondary‑metabolism proteins (cytochrome P450s, NRPS/PKS, cluster regulators): activates on N‑terminal low‑complexity segments adjacent to targeting/anchor regions or activation domains
- Organelle‑targeted proteins: activates on disordered N‑terminal regions near/after processing of targeting peptides

Summary: Residue-identity detector for glycine (G), largely context-agnostic but with a tendency to fire on glycines in flexible/disordered, often N-terminal or membrane-proximal regions; also active on glycines within transmembrane helices; broadly taxon- and function-independent.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks confined to individual glycine positions; peaks may appear singly (e.g., an N-terminal G) or as clusters in G-rich stretches; little to no activation on other residues; occurs in coils, helices, and beta strands, frequently in low-confidence/disordered segments and sometimes within or adjacent to transmembrane helices.
Exemplars: - Viral K7-like membrane proteins: multiple glycines highlighted in disordered regions and just after/within a transmembrane helix.
- Antimicrobial bacteriocins (enterocin peptides): every glycine across the peptide, independent of local secondary structure.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factor PEX9 (peroxisomal membrane protein): glycines throughout, including inside predicted transmembrane segments and a disordered C-terminus.
- Octanoyltransferase/lipoyltransferase (LipB-like) enzymes: a single N-terminal glycine in a coil region.
- Tumor suppressor ARF (CDKN2A/p14ARF): glycines within an intrinsically disordered N-terminal interaction region and the disordered C-terminus.

Summary: Extended, compositionally biased low‑complexity polar/Lys–Gly–rich tracts and adjacent boundary/linker regions are preferentially activated, with frequent activation on β‑strand–rich structural segments when present (e.g., β‑barrels/β‑helical passengers and conserved β‑strands within catalytic domains such as kinase N‑lobe β3); long repeat-based α‑solenoids/coiled‑coils (TPR/HEAT, heptad repeats) are also commonly activated.
Activation pattern: Predominantly long regional activation across low‑complexity/disordered and repeat‑rich segments (including coiled‑coils and α‑solenoids), plus regional activation over β‑rich domains (e.g., autotransporter barrels/passengers); superimposed residue‑level peaks on specific β‑strands in compact α/β enzymes like kinases and phosphatases; elevated at boundary/linker regions abutting catalytic or transmembrane domains.
Exemplars:
- Serine/threonine protein kinases (ePK family): strong, localized peaks on the N‑lobe β‑sheet (β3 next to the ATP‑binding Lys) with minor spillover to nearby elements.
- Two‑component histidine kinases: activation in a juxtadomain stretch preceding the transmitter and within HATPase_c β‑strand regions (N/G‑box vicinity).
- Gram‑negative autotransporters (e.g., IgA protease/VacA): broad activation across the C‑terminal β‑barrel and multiple peaks within β‑helical passenger and the low‑structure segment N‑terminal to the barrel.
- Coiled‑coil/α‑solenoid scaffolds (e.g., APC6/Cdc16 TPR arrays, radial spoke proteins): extended activation over repetitive helical tracts.
- Membrane antiporters (e.g., K+/H+ antiporters): activation in long cytosolic loops enriched in acidic/polar residues.
- Metal‑dependent protein phosphatases (e.g., PP1/PP2C‑like): localized peaks on the central β‑sheet and adjacent catalytic loops; additional signal in low‑complexity linkers.
- RhoGEF modules: activation on PH‑domain β‑sandwich strands and in low‑complexity DH–PH linkers.

Summary: Intrinsic-disorder/low-complexity, polar/charged segments (often S/T- and acidic-rich) and short disorder-to-helix boundary motifs in non-catalytic terminal/linker regions; generally avoids folded catalytic cores and transmembrane helices.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation across IDRs/LCRs (density scales with protein length), enriched at N- and C-termini and inter-domain linkers; occasional sharp residue-level peaks at individual S/T or acidic residues at coil segments or disorder–helix junctions; minimal signal within structured catalytic domains or TM spans.
Exemplars: - Patatin-like triacylglycerol lipases: activation on N- and C-terminal coils (e.g., S/T near the N-terminus) and not within the patatin catalytic domain.
- Chromatin remodeling regulator (CECR2): a sharp peak at a threonine immediately after a disordered segment and before an emerging helix, with decaying signal into the helix.
- LEA/stress-response proteins (plants): broad activation across hydrophilic, low-complexity disordered regions.
- Viral/retroelements polymerases: activation on long charged linkers and termini outside the polymerase core.
- tRNA dihydrouridine synthases: signal on flexible acidic loops and disordered tails rather than the catalytic fold.
- Secreted peptide hormone precursors: activation on low-complexity propeptide segments and nearby acidic/basic clusters around processing sites, not on signal peptides/TMs.
- Membrane/transport proteins and endocytic (Rab5-pathway) factors: activation on cytosolic low-complexity loops and terminal tails flanking TM helices or domains.
- Bromodomain-containing/chromatin regulators: activation on acidic, S/T-rich IDRs flanking conserved domains.
- Organelle-targeted proteins (mitochondrial/chloroplastic): activation on polar, Ser/Thr-/Arg-rich transit peptides and adjacent disordered N-termini.
