- Lipid metabolism/handling proteins broadly: enrichment in non-catalytic acidic/polar loops and linkers outside catalytic cores.

Summary: A short, sequence-level motif marking secondary-structure junctions—especially coil/β-strand to α-helix starts, helix capping/termination sites, and β‑hairpin turns—characterized by polar/charged residues with helix-breakers (e.g., Lys/Arg/Glu/His with Pro/Gly/Thr/Ser) and frequent di‑basic Lys pairs. The motif often sits at C-termini or domain boundaries and is frequently adjacent to functional sites (ligand-binding pockets, disulfide/metal linkages), making it a broadly used structural transition/capping signal across taxa and localizations.
Activation pattern: Short contiguous segments (~6–10 aa) with strong residue-level peaks at the cap/turn residue immediately preceding or initiating an α-helix or at a β‑strand terminus; enrichment for Pro, Gly, His, acidic residues, and Lys/Lys pairs; multiple independent hits can appear within large multidomain proteins; in certain families (e.g., ribosomal L31) the activated segment occurs at a conserved positional window.
Exemplars: - Superantigen toxin (TSST-1): activation at a C-terminal coil-to-short-helix transition.
- Subtilisin inhibitor-like protein: strongest activation across a β–loop–α segment surrounding a disulfide-bonded Cys; weaker at the partner Cys loop.
- Phosphatidate phosphatase (lipin/PAH): activation in a β–hairpin loop of the N-LIP domain; weaker signal in an α-helix.
- Myotubularin (MTMR) phosphatase: activation at a coil-to-helix N-cap in the catalytic region.
- Riboflavin kinase: activation at the end of a β-strand into a loop adjacent to the FMN-binding site (strand→loop cap).
- C-C chemokine: activation at the start of the C-terminal α-helix (coil→helix transition).
- Golgi-associated RAB2 interactor (GARIL): activation spanning β-strand end → loop → helix at the C-terminus.
- Large ribosomal subunit protein L31 (bacterial and organellar; from broader set): conserved midchain short charged segment that caps/initiates a helix is repeatedly activated.

Summary: Position-driven detector of the extreme protein N-terminus—especially residues 2–5—largely independent of amino-acid identity, typically in short, unstructured signal/leader-like segments; also fires on analogous newly formed N-termini within precursors (e.g., mature peptide starts). Common across taxa, with strong representation in viral accessory proteins, secreted precursors, and micropeptides.
Activation pattern: Sharp, residue-level peaks concentrated at the first few residues after initiation (maximal at position 2), with occasional isolated secondary peaks at internal, low-structure sites that often correspond to signal/transit/leader-like segments or putative processed peptide N-termini.
Exemplars: - Coronavirus accessory protein ORF3b: peaks at the disordered N-terminus (positions 2–3) and additional isolated peaks in low-confidence regions, including a predicted targeting segment.
- Secretory membrane protein with an N-terminal signal peptide (hygromycin-B hypersensitivity protein): strongest activation at residue 2 within the signal peptide; minor scattered peaks in TM/loop regions.
- Bacteriocin (enterocin) precursor: isolated internal activation in an unstructured region consistent with the start of the mature bacteriocin peptide within the precursor.
- Testis-specific lncRNA-derived micropeptide: activation at residue 2 of a disordered N-terminus, with additional sparse peaks in low-confidence coil/helix segments.

Summary: Short acidic–hydrophobic surface loop/β‑edge motif (enriched for E/D interleaved with V/I/L/F/Y and often S/T, Y/W) that forms a negatively charged recognition or active‑site patch; recurrent at ligand/cofactor/protein‑interaction loops across many folds (e.g., SAM‑MTase active‑site/SAM‑binding loops, the switch II loop of small GTPases, metal‑coordination loops of HD/HExH hydrolases, acidic patches near Fe–S centers, and analogous loops in polymerase B‑subunits and pilin head domains).
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous segments (~6–10 aa), often multiple per protein; positions vary within proteins and are typically surface‑exposed loops/strand edges rather than termini.
Exemplars: - SAM‑dependent RNA methyltransferases (tRNA m1G37 enzymes; rRNA/tRNA C5 MTases): activation on the acidic loop flanking the SAM‑binding/catalytic region (near motif I/II).
- Protein N‑lysine methyltransferases (METTL21): acidic loop at the SAM‑binding pocket.
- Wyosine/wybutosine biosynthesis enzymes (TYW2/Taw22): short acidic–hydrophobic active‑site loop.
- Replicative DNA polymerases (Pol B/α/ε small/B‑subunits): acidic surface loop/β‑edge used for DNA or catalytic‑subunit contact.
- Small GTPases (Ras/Rho/Rab/ARF/ARL/Sar): the switch II acidic loop (DTAGQE…Y/S) and nearby guanine/Mg2+‑binding segments.
- Iron–sulfur–associated proteins (assembly scaffolds; Rieske subunits): acidic patches adjacent to cofactor‑binding motifs.
- Metal‑dependent hydrolases/phosphodiesterases and metalloproteases: HxH/HD/HExH motif‑flanking acidic loops that coordinate metal ions.
- Type II secretion minor pseudopilins and competence pilins: acidic–hydrophobic patch in the soluble head domain mediating partner interactions.
- Organelle processing/transport peptidases: acidic catalytic/processing loops.

Summary: Glycine- and small hydrophobic–rich membrane‑insertion segments that are intrinsically disordered in solution and become structured upon membrane engagement (amphipathic helices or transmembrane β‑hairpins), used for pore formation, membrane disruption/fusion, or lipid/curvature sensing in secreted and membrane‑associated proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short-to-moderate contiguous stretches, often near N‑termini or flexible loops; strong residue‑level peaks within these segments; enrichment for G/A/L/V/I/S/T with GG/GGG and GxG motifs; preferentially in low‑pLDDT regions; multiple discrete patches in large proteins.
Exemplars: - Actinoporin-like toxins: activation on a long amphipathic helix that serves as the membrane‑inserting/pore‑forming element.
- Gasdermins: activation on N‑terminal disordered loops that convert into membrane‑penetrating β‑strands in the pore.
- MACPF/perforins: activation on CH1/CH2 transmembrane β‑hairpins that insert into membranes during pore formation.
- Antimicrobial/venom peptides and small animal toxins: activation on amphipathic, glycine‑rich membrane‑disrupting helices.
- Viral entry/capsid proteins: activation on fusion/penetration peptides or lipid‑binding segments that are glycine/small‑residue rich.
- Secretory pathway and Golgi/trafficking proteins (SCAMPs, YIF/YIPF, TVP23, golgins): activation on amphipathic lipid‑binding helices or small‑residue–rich membrane‑proximal segments.
- Membrane metalloproteases (including OMA1) and other membrane enzymes: activation on small‑residue–rich insertion/TM segments implicated in membrane embedding or conformational switching.
- Bacterial outer‑membrane/secretion components and cell‑wall endolysins: activation on signal peptides or glycine‑rich membrane‑interacting loops used for export or envelope disruption.

Summary: Generic N‑terminal leader/processing signal: the feature fires on short, small‑residue–rich N‑terminal segments that function as signal/leader/transit peptides or present an N‑end compatible with methionine aminopeptidase cleavage (small P1′ residue such as Ala/Gly/Ser/Thr/Pro/Cys). This unifies Sec‑type signal peptides (including their −3/−1 small‑residue cleavage motif), bacterial leader peptides (lipobox and double‑glycine leaders), mitochondrial presequences, and simple small‑residue starts of many small proteins and enzymes across all taxa.
Activation pattern: Strong regional activation at the extreme N‑terminus, typically starting at Met1 and spanning residues 1–5, and extending to ~15–30 residues when a signal/leader/transit peptide is present; pronounced residue‑level peaks around the small residues at positions 2–4 and at the signal‑peptidase cleavage motif (−3/−1), with tolerance for cysteine.
Exemplars: - Secreted peptide/toxin precursors (chemokines, neuropeptides, disulfide‑rich animal toxins): activation on their N‑terminal Sec signal peptides, including the small‑residue −3/−1 cleavage motif.
- Bacterial secretory and lipoprotein precursors: activation on Sec/SPI signal peptides and lipoprotein “lipobox” leaders (L(A/S)(G/A)C) and on double‑glycine leader peptides of bacteriocins.
- Viral envelope/small membrane proteins: activation on N‑terminal signal peptides or signal‑anchor segments.
- Mitochondrial matrix/imported proteins (e.g., F1‑ATP synthase ε subunits): activation on the amphipathic, small‑residue–rich N‑terminal presequences.
- Housekeeping enzymes such as tRNA/rRNA modification enzymes: activation at the initiator region consistent with N‑terminal Met excision (small residue at position 2).
- Short testis‑expressed antigens and lncRNA‑derived micropeptides: activation on brief hydrophobic/low‑complexity N‑terminal segments that act as leader/signal‑like starts.

Summary: Generic extreme N-terminus detector: marks residues around position 5 (occasionally 6–7) at the very start of the polypeptide, most often within the N-region of signal/transit peptides of secreted or organelle-targeted precursors, but also in generally disordered N-termini of cytosolic/nuclear proteins; not motif- or residue-specific
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks tightly localized at the N-terminus (typically position 5), sometimes extending one or two residues; little to no activation elsewhere, with rare minor peaks nearby in signal peptides or disordered extracellular segments
Exemplars: - Adhesion G protein–coupled receptors: activation at residue ~5 within the N-terminal signal peptide; occasional faint peaks later in the signal peptide or disordered extracellular regions.
- Complement receptor–like cell-surface proteins: single low peak at residue 5 within the annotated signal peptide.
- Plant pectinesterase inhibitors (secreted cell wall proteins): localized peak at residue 5 within the helical signal peptide.
- Protamine P1 (basic sperm nuclear proteins): sharp peak at residue 5 in a fully disordered N-terminus (no signal peptide).
- Metallothioneins: single weak peak at residue 5 in a disordered N-terminal segment.

Summary: Secretory pathway export signals and precursors: the feature detects N‑terminal export leaders of proteins destined for the extracellular space/periplasm/lumen, including Sec-type signal peptides (with bacterial lipoprotein lipoboxes and thylakoid/lumenal signals) and double‑glycine/ABC‑export leaders of bacteriocins, with strong sensitivity to cysteine‑rich disulfide‑bonded secreted peptides.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation at extreme N termini (signal peptide h‑region and signal peptidase cleavage site; lipobox motif with the +1 Cys; and the basic/hydrophobic segment up to the double‑glycine motif of ABC‑export leaders), with sharp residue‑level peaks on conserved cysteines of disulfide frameworks; in long secreted proteins, additional dispersed peaks across extracellular/lumenal, cysteine‑rich segments.
Exemplars: - Antimicrobial peptides/defensins and bacteriocins (both Sec‑dependent and GG/ABC‑exported): activation on the signal/leader region and on conserved cysteines forming disulfides in the mature peptide. (Other exemplar lines unchanged.)

Summary: Tyrosine‑centered aromatic motifs in long, intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity repeat arrays—most often Y followed by Ser within Ser/Pro‑rich repeats—marking the aromatic “sticker”/crosslinking residues (with ancillary recognition of Phe/Trp and occasional His/Cys) that support adhesion, matrix assembly, or multivalent IDR interactions (e.g., CTD- and FG-type repeats).
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks that recur with the periodicity of tandem repeats, strongest on Tyr and also on other aromatics; frequent weak co‑activation on the residue immediately after Tyr (often Ser or His). Activation extends over long coil‑rich, low‑pLDDT repeat regions and is minimal in structured domains or signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Plant extensins/proline‑rich cell‑wall proteins: strong, periodic peaks on the Tyr that starts each Y–S–P/P‑rich repeat; occasional weaker signal on the following Ser/His.
- Vitelline membrane–like extracellular matrix proteins: peaks on the Tyr within each [PS][AS]YSA PA[AS] 8‑mer repeat across a disordered region.
- Fungal cell‑wall adhesins/flocculins (galactose‑binding agglutinins): one highly activated Tyr per repeat across long tandem arrays, with secondary peaks on F/H/W.
- RNA polymerase II C‑terminal domain: peaks on the Tyr in YSPTSPS heptad repeats, with modest co‑activation on adjacent Ser.
- Nuclear pore–associated disordered proteins: activation on cysteines within low‑confidence IDRs; in FG‑nucleoporins, on the Phe of FG repeats.
- Secreted peptide/toxin and fungal RiPP precursors: activation on aromatic‑rich core motifs embedded in disordered, low‑complexity segments.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity serine/threonine–rich segments (often containing SP/TP/RS repeats) that function as flexible linkers and phosphorylation‑prone regulatory tracts across diverse proteins, including viral phosphoproteins/nucleocapsid linkers and proline‑rich secreted cell‑wall proteins
Activation pattern: Broad regional activation across long disordered, low‑complexity stretches with dense residue‑level peaks on serine (and threonine), frequently flanked by proline/glycine/alanine or arginine; minimal signal in folded domain cores; signal can bleed into adjacent short helices or basic segments; often spans dozens to hundreds of residues per protein
Exemplars: - Coronavirus nucleocapsid proteins: strong activation on the central SR‑rich disordered linker between RNA‑binding and dimerization domains; structured domains largely inactive.
- Viral tegument/immediate‑early phosphoproteins (e.g., herpesviruses and similar): activation on S/T‑rich, highly phosphorylated intrinsically disordered regions.
- Viral nucleic acid–packaging proteins (nucleoproteins/phosphoproteins across families): activation on disordered linkers rich in S/T repeats connecting structured modules.
- Plant proline‑rich cell‑wall/secreted proteins (extensins, PRPs, AGP‑like): activation on repetitive Ser/Pro‑rich low‑complexity segments.
- Yeast meiosis/sporulation/recombination factors: activation on disordered regulatory regions enriched in S/T‑P motifs targeted by cell‑cycle/MAPK kinases.
- Kinases, phosphatases, and their regulators: activation on unstructured N/C‑terminal serine‑rich tails or low‑complexity regulatory inserts.
- Reproductive/spermatogenesis‑related chromatin proteins: activation on serine‑rich low‑complexity tails adjacent to basic regions.
- Small secreted peptides/toxins/micropeptides: activation on short S/T‑ and P/G/A‑rich low‑complexity tracts.

Summary: Short, surface-exposed β‑strand/loop “edge” segments at domain boundaries and coil↔β transitions, typically on non‑catalytic surfaces and often enriched in small/polar residues (G/S/T). These patches are common in extracellular/secreted proteins (glycan‑active enzymes, metalloproteases, lysosomal glycoproteins, cytokines) but also occur in intracellular nucleic‑acid proteins, where they act as recognition/hinge/linker elements and can include N‑glycosylation- or propeptide/linker regions.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue‑level peaks forming short (≈8–20 aa) segments on loops and adjacent β‑strands; multiple separated peaks per protein; strongest at coil→β or β→coil edges and at domain/linker boundaries; generally away from annotated catalytic residues; confidence ranges from well‑structured loops to flexible/low‑pLDDT linkers.
Exemplars: - Hyaluronate lyase (hyaluronidase/lyase): multiple peaks on structured coil/β elements in the C‑terminal region, upstream of a disordered tail (non‑active‑site surface loops).
- ADAM metalloproteases: strong peak in the propeptide loop just before the M12B domain, plus smaller peaks in a peptidase‑domain loop and a low‑confidence disintegrin–TM linker.
- Lysosomal membrane glycoproteins: a lumenal loop between β‑strands bearing an N‑linked glycosylation motif is highlighted.
- IL‑1 family cytokines (e.g., IL‑36β): several short peaks at coil↔β transitions and edge β‑strands within the mature β‑trefoil fold; no activation in the N‑terminal propeptide.
- Argonaute proteins: a focused peak at the L1–PAZ domain boundary on a β‑strand within a flexible linker region (hinge/interface patch).
- GH81 endo‑1,3‑β‑glucanases: a β‑strand and its following loop in a β‑sandwich subdomain show the main activation (non‑catalytic surface segment).

Summary: Short beta-strand segments that buttress and anchor functional surface loops—often the strand immediately preceding “gate/latch” or contact loops at the mouth of ligand-binding cavities or interaction interfaces—in small, beta‑rich soluble domains common in secreted/periplasmic proteins (e.g., Bet v 1/NTF2-like START receptors, lipocalin/calycin barrels, cystatin- and PsbP-like folds).
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on short contiguous patches (≈8–12 aa) within high-confidence beta-strands, frequently at the sheet→loop junction and often just N‑terminal to flexible gating/contact loops; multiple such strands may activate within a protein. Composition shows hydrophobic/aromatic residues mixed with polar/charged side chains.
Exemplars: - Photosystem II PsbP/OEE2 family: activation on a conserved beta-strand that transitions into a coil at the protein surface.
- Abscisic acid receptors (PYL/PYR; START/Bet v 1/NTF2-like): activation on beta-strands immediately preceding the Gate and Latch loops that control ligand access.
- Cystatin (cysteine protease inhibitors): activation on a beta-strand in the cystatin domain adjacent to protease-contact loops.
- Alpha/beta hydrolase esterases: activation on specific core beta-strands that precede surface loops near the active-site region.
- NTF2/NTF2-related transport and PR-10/allergen (Bet v 1-like) proteins: activation on sheet elements that brace loops forming the cavity mouth.
- Calycin superfamily (FABPs, avidin/streptavidin): activation on barrel strands that underlie loop caps at the ligand-binding entrance.
- Periplasmic/membrane biogenesis factors (e.g., YidC periplasmic domain, OM assembly factors) and TIM21 IMS domain: activation on structured beta-strands adjacent to functional surface loops.
- Chromophore-attachment/phycobiliprotein lyases: activation on beta-strands flanking substrate-binding loops in NTF2-like folds.

Summary: Generic detector of low-complexity/intrinsically disordered segments and short hydrophobic N‑terminal stretches (signal peptides/first TM anchors), with preference for S/T/P/G/A/N- and N/Q‑rich tracts; largely avoids well‑ordered helical cores
Activation pattern: Residue-level spikes spread across multiple positions, often clustered in N‑terminal regions; strongest in coil/disordered low‑complexity stretches and also along short hydrophobic N‑terminal segments; minimal signal in stable, well‑structured helical domains
Exemplars: - Nuclear transcription factor subunits (e.g., NF‑Y complex gamma): activates on Asn‑, Ser/Pro‑rich disordered linkers/tails while ignoring the structured helical core.
- Small secreted peptide/neuropeptide precursors: activates on the N‑terminal signal peptide and on Gly/Pro/Ser/Thr‑rich low‑complexity propeptide regions.
- Viral proteins (capsid/accessory/polyproteins): activates on compositionally biased disordered segments and short hydrophobic N‑terminal patches.
- Membrane transporters/channels: activates along hydrophobic transmembrane segments, especially the first N‑terminal helix.
- Dictyostelium signaling/regulatory proteins (S/Thr‑rich): activates across Ser/Thr‑rich low‑complexity regions.
- Human sORF‑encoded micropeptides/antisense peptides: activates broadly across low‑complexity, Gly/Pro‑rich sequences.
- Germline/testis‑enriched proteins: activates on repeat‑rich, compositionally biased low‑complexity regions.

Summary: Intrinsic low‑complexity tandem‑repeat regions in disordered proteins, with strongest preference for Pro/Thr/Ser‑rich (mucin/adhesin‑like) repeats and, more generally, for periodically arrayed modules in secreted precursors (e.g., polyhormone/neuropeptide repeats); the feature keys on the repeat register, often at Pro/Thr (and nearby Lys) positions and at the N‑termini of repeated peptide units.
Activation pattern: Primarily long regional activation across low‑pLDDT, repeat‑rich IDRs; strong periodic residue‑level peaks aligned to each repeat unit (commonly at Thr/Pro and adjacent basic residues). In polyprotein precursors, sharp peaks occur at the first 1–2 residues of each mature peptide immediately following dibasic (KR) cleavage sites. Activation drops in well‑structured domains but can show weaker, periodic signals across arrays of folded repeats (e.g., C2H2 zinc fingers) and is strongest in proline‑rich disordered tails.
Exemplars: - Mucins/mucin‑like cell‑surface glycoproteins: high activation across tandem Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich repeats, peaking on Thr/Pro within recurring motifs; overlaps O‑GalNAc glycosylation sites.
- Fungal flocculins/adhesins: periodic activation within 35‑aa repeat blocks, with consistent peaks at fixed Thr and mid‑repeat Ser/Thr/Gly positions in disordered segments.
- Marine/invertebrate adhesive plaque matrix proteins: activation confined to 10‑aa repeats with maxima at Lys–Pro–Thr positions; many Pro residues are hydroxylated (Hyp).
- Neuropeptide/prohormone polyproteins: repeated strong peaks at the N‑termini of each mature peptide immediately after KR cleavage, across arrays of short peptide modules in flexible precursor regions.
- C2H2 zinc‑finger transcription factors: weaker periodic signal over the ZF array but strong activation in C‑terminal proline‑rich low‑complexity tails.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regions enriched in polar/acidic and amide residues—especially Q/E/S/T/P/G—often including proline‑rich tracts and S/T clusters; these segments are flexible, cysteine‑poor, and typically lie outside structured catalytic cores (e.g., disordered tails, propeptides, and regulatory regions).
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue‑level peaks concentrated within intrinsically disordered, low‑pLDDT segments; when long low‑complexity tracts are present, activation can extend across broad regions. Little to no activation in well‑folded domains.
Exemplars: - HIV-1 Tat (viral transcriptional regulator): residues in the disordered TAR RNA‑binding/NLS region and the N‑terminal flexible segment.
- tRNA(Ile)‑lysidine synthase (bacterial enzyme): scattered residues in low‑pLDDT loops/termini, not at the ATP‑binding site or folded core.
- Amnesiac neuropeptide precursor (secreted prohormone): positions within disordered propeptide/processed peptide segments.
- Spermatogenesis‑associated protein 12 (testis‑biased IDP): sparse peaks across a globally disordered, low‑complexity protein.
- TAR1 microprotein (small/antisense‑derived protein): residues in an annotated disordered C‑terminal tail.
- DNA cross‑link repair 1 protein (interstrand cross‑link repair nuclease): dense S/T‑rich low‑complexity disordered regions (e.g., C‑terminal tract), with no activation in the structured catalytic domain.
- Dictyostelium low‑complexity proteins: extensive activation across Q/E/S/P‑rich disordered stretches typical of this lineage.
- Viral accessory/structural proteins: activation on flexible, compositionally biased regions common in small viral proteins.

Summary: Short hydrophobic α-helix segments, most often the N‑terminal signal peptide/single-pass transmembrane signal anchor (and, in soluble proteins, analogous N‑terminal amphipathic helices)
Activation pattern: Regional activation over 10–25 residue hydrophobic stretches enriched in L/I/V/F/Y/W with small/polar A/G/S/T at helix boundaries; strongest near the extreme N‑terminus (≈positions 20–40) consistent with Sec-signal peptide hydrophobic cores and signal peptidase cleavage motifs, but can also mark internal short helices (e.g., ≈200–230 in some primases)
Exemplars: - Secreted/periplasmic glycoside hydrolases (β-galactosidases, β-glucuronidases, algal polysaccharide hydrolases): activation on N‑terminal signal peptide hydrophobic cores and Ala/Ser/Thr-rich cleavage sites.
- Periplasmic PQQ-dependent dehydrogenases: activation on their export signal peptide/signal anchor.
- Peptidoglycan D,D-transpeptidases (penicillin-binding proteins): activation on the N‑terminal transmembrane anchor preceding the periplasmic catalytic domain.
- Bacterial envelope/adhesion/outer-membrane biogenesis proteins: activation on Sec signal peptides.
- Carbohydrate kinases (ROK/PfkB-like): activation on the short N‑terminal α-helix around residues 25–40 (amphipathic/dimerization helix), mimicking the same hydrophobic-helix signature.
- ER stress sensors and eIF2α kinases (e.g., PERK/IRE1-like): activation on the single-pass ER transmembrane helix/signal anchor.
- Selenoproteins (e.g., iodothyronine deiodinases and other ER/secretory selenoproteins): activation on N‑terminal signal peptides or signal anchors.
- Peroxiredoxins/thiol peroxidases (mitochondrial/chloroplast and bacterial forms): activation on N‑terminal targeting/amphipathic helices.
- DNA primases (bacterial/mycoplasma DnaG-like): activation on an internal short hydrophobic helix around 200–230.
- Eukaryotic scaffold/adaptor proteins with WD/NHL repeats and histone/other acetyltransferases: activation on short N‑terminal hydrophobic/amphipathic helices present in many members.

Summary: Short amphipathic β‑strand and strand–loop transition segments with alternating hydrophobic (V/I/L, often F/Y/W) and charged (K/R/E/D) residues—i.e., edge‑of‑sheet/hairpin-like elements that recur across many folds and functions
Activation pattern: Strong, localized peaks on short linear stretches (~9–16 aa) within structured domains; maxima typically on β‑strands or immediately at strand–loop boundaries; multiple independent hotspots can occur within one protein; not tied to termini or specific catalytic motifs, though often flanked by aromatic residues
Exemplars: - NTF2-related nuclear transport proteins: activation on an internal β‑strand within the NTF2 fold.
- dsRNA-binding/ADAR proteins: activation on a β‑strand inside the dsRBD.
- Glycosaminoglycan/chondroitin sulfate synthases (type II membrane glycosyltransferases): activation on a lumenal β‑strand segment of the catalytic/lumenal domain.
- Diphthamide biosynthesis proteins (DPH3/MB domain): activation across an N‑terminal helix→coil→β transition, peaking near an aromatic.
- tRNA pseudouridine synthase Pus10: activation on β‑strand and strand–loop segments near (but not on) catalytic residues.
- Broadly consistent with frequent activations in cystatins, PsbP-domain proteins, NAP1/histone chaperones, and diverse host-defense and mitochondrial proteins, where similar short β‑strand/turn elements are common.

Summary: N-terminal compositionally biased, intrinsically disordered segments and leader/signal-like regions: the feature prefers low-complexity, Pro/Ser/Thr- and Lys/Arg-enriched coils and also the basic N-region plus LVIA-rich hydrophobic core characteristic of signal peptides; it fires broadly across taxa in secreted/membrane proteins, small regulatory peptides, and flexible N-termini of soluble enzymes.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks scattered within long low-complexity/IDR stretches, with a strong bias to early N-terminal positions; peaks often fall on Pro, Ser/Thr, Lys/Arg, and also on hydrophobic L/V/I/A segments (e.g., the h-region of signal peptides). In disordered proteins, peaks are discrete within coils (low pLDDT); in secreted proteins, peaks can trace the N-region and hydrophobic core of the signal peptide.
Exemplars: - BH3-only apoptosis regulators (e.g., PUMA/BBC3): discrete peaks across intrinsically disordered, compositionally biased regions.
- Secreted precursors and membrane proteins with signal peptides: activation on the basic N-region and LVIA-rich hydrophobic core of the signal peptide and adjacent low-complexity propeptides.
- Viral envelope/accessory proteins: N-terminal leader/signal sequences and proline-/basic-rich low-complexity stretches.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: recognition of flexible, low-complexity N-terminal tails in an otherwise soluble enzyme.
- Bacterial metabolic enzymes: short disordered N-terminal extensions/linkers that are low-complexity and coil.
- Dictyostelium S/T-rich extracellular proteins: long serine/threonine-rich low-complexity tracts.
- Human small ORF-encoded micropeptides: short, compositionally biased N termini with Pro/Ser/Thr/basic enrichment.

Summary: Initiator methionine at the very start of the polypeptide chain (M1), i.e., the translation start residue, independent of protein family, taxonomy, membrane association, or presence of signal/leader/propeptide regions; often annotated as post-translationally removed and typically situated in a flexible, coil-like N-terminus.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peak localized almost exclusively to position 1 (M1), with low but consistent activation; occasional minor secondary peaks on immediately adjacent N-terminal residues; internal activations are rare.
Exemplars: - Gas vesicle protein O1: single-residue activation on M1 within a disordered, compositionally biased N-terminus.
- Large ribosomal subunit protein eL24: activation on M1, annotated initiator methionine that is removed post-translationally.
- Cytochrome c oxidase subunit 4B: exclusive activation at M1 at the start of the chain.
- Light-harvesting complex B-870 beta chain: activation on M1 within a propeptide preceding the mature chain.
- ESAT-6-like protein EsxB: activation on M1; initiator methionine removed with the mature chain starting at the next residue.
- Lantibiotic nisin-Z precursor: activation on M1 in the leader peptide that is cleaved to produce the mature lantibiotic.
- Nucleoid-associated protein Lsr2: activation confined to M1 in a flexible N-terminus, not on structured or DNA-binding regions.

Summary: Short, hydrophobic/aromatic-rich segments at coil-to-β transitions (β‑strand starts/N‑caps and adjacent loops) that recur across β‑sheet–containing domains; commonly enriched in Tyr with Gly/Pro kinks and sometimes Cys (for disulfides or catalytic Cys motifs). This structural motif appears repeatedly in secreted/periplasmic proteins and diverse enzymes, rather than marking a specific family.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on short contiguous windows (≈5–12 aa) that sit at or just before the N‑terminus of β‑strands, often spanning the preceding loop and into the first few strand residues; multiple occurrences per protein; strongest in well‑structured regions; absent from signal peptides/TM helices; sequence bias toward L/V/I/F/Y/W with frequent G/P and occasional Cys/CC.
Exemplars: - Thylakoid lumen PsbP/OEE2 family: Tyr‑rich β‑strand starts within the β‑sandwich core.
- Ependymin/gastrokine (secreted extracellular proteins): multiple coil→β junctions at N‑ends of β‑strands in the mature domain.
- SUMO/Sentrin/NEDD8 proteases and other DUB/cysteine proteases: hydrophobic/aromatic “Cys‑box” region around the catalytic Cys at a β‑edge/loop.
- PCAT/ABC transporters with C39 peptidase domains: catalytic Cys‑containing β‑strand start in the peptidase subdomain.
- Lipases/esterases (α/β‑hydrolase fold): nucleophile‑elbow vicinity at β‑strand/loop junctions flanked by hydrophobic residues and G/P.
- Glycosidases/α‑mannosidases: aromatic β‑strand segments forming carbohydrate‑binding platforms.
- DNA repair enzymes (alkyltransferase MGMT; DNA glycosylases): gly/pro‑rich loop→β segments (e.g., HhH‑GPD region; active‑Cys loop in MGMT).
- YidC membrane insertase: β‑like/periplasmic domain strand starts or adjacent hydrophobic loops.
- Plant NAC transcription factors: β‑strand N‑caps within the NAC DNA‑binding domain.
- Periplasmic lipoproteins/regulators: aromatic/Cys‑containing β‑edge segments in soluble domains (sometimes near the processed N‑terminus).
- Toxin–antitoxin RNases/toxins: short hydrophobic β‑strand patches in small β‑sheet cores.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity regions of eukaryotic proteins—especially the terminal tails and interdomain linkers of transcription factors—enriched in Pro/Gly/Ser and acidic residues, and generally excluded from folded DNA-binding domains.
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks scattered across long unstructured segments (low pLDDT coils/short helices), with little to no signal inside structured domains. Activation concentrates in N- and C-terminal IDRs and linkers rather than in the core DNA-binding modules; no single conserved short motif is required.
Exemplars: - Homeobox/Hox TFs (labial, CDX2, DLX, orthopedia): activation in disordered N-/C-terminal regions and linkers; minimal in the homeobox domain.
- SOX (HMG-box) TFs: activation across the disordered C-terminal tail; near-absent within the HMG box.
- Forkhead (FOX) TFs: activation in disordered N- and C-termini flanking the forkhead domain; domain itself largely inactive.
- ETS family TFs: activation across extensive disordered regions (e.g., long C-termini); not on the PNT or ETS DNA-binding domains.
- GLI/C2H2 zinc-finger TFs: activation in disordered N-terminal regions; weak or absent within structured zinc fingers.
- Pax (paired + homeobox) TFs: activation in the disordered linker between domains and the C-terminal tail; not within paired/homeobox domains.
- POU-domain TFs: activation in N-terminal glycine-rich, low-complexity regions; little to none in POU-specific and homeobox domains.

Summary: Generic beta-strand structural signal: the feature activates on individual residues embedded in well-ordered beta-sheets of soluble domains across diverse proteins, often near (but not at) catalytic, metal-binding, or selectivity motifs and largely independent of specific biochemical function.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in high-confidence beta-strands; sparse or absent in helices, disordered segments, and transmembrane regions; occasional minor signal in adjacent loops.
Exemplars: - tRNA(Ile)-lysidine synthase (TilS): single-residue peak on an Arg within a beta-strand of the catalytic domain.
- Rieske-type oxygenase ferredoxin subunit: peaks on beta-strand positions within the Rieske domain, avoiding the Cys/His [2Fe-2S] ligating residues.
- tRNA-modification factor YgfZ: peak on an Arg at the end of a beta-strand in the structured core.
- Fpg/Nei family formamidopyrimidine-DNA glycosylase: peaks on beta-strands near, but not on, the catalytic Lys and DNA-binding residues.
- CorA-family Mg2+/Co2+ transporter: peaks confined to beta-strands in the cytosolic domain; no activation in transmembrane helices or the GMN selectivity motif.
- GH32 fructan beta-fructosidase/invertase: multiple peaks on beta-strands of the beta-propeller/sandwich regions, some adjacent to substrate-binding loops.
- Pectate lyase (beta-helix fold): peak on a beta-strand away from the catalytic Lys and Ca2+-binding sites.
- Small heat shock protein (alpha-crystallin domain): dispersed peaks on beta-strands within the conserved sHSP domain; minimal signal in the disordered N-terminus.

Summary: Solvent‑exposed loop and β‑edge segments used for protein–protein assembly and interaction in the secretory/extracellular system and in coat/trafficking complexes, rather than a specific catalytic motif or fold
Activation pattern: Sparse residue‑level peaks scattered across long regions; enriched in loops, β/coil boundaries and flexible/disordered segments (often low–moderate pLDDT), with occasional peaks on helical surfaces; avoids signal peptides, transmembrane helices and short cytosolic tails; frequently enriched for G, D, E, S, T, P (with some hydrophobics); not confined to a single short motif and often spans much of the mature extracellular or interaction-mediating region
Exemplars: Zona pellucida domain proteins: activation concentrated within the ZP polymerization domain and absent from signal peptide, transmembrane helix and cytoplasmic tail; Integrin α subunits: peaks in the C‑terminal extracellular thigh/calf region and flexible linkers, with little signal in the N‑terminal FG‑GAP repeats or the TM/cytoplasmic tail; TRAPPII complex subunit (TRAPPC10): multiple short activations in low‑confidence/disordered regions, especially a long disordered C‑terminal segment and boundaries between secondary structures; COPI coatomer γ subunit: sparse peaks in the C‑terminal interaction region (e.g., ARFGAP2‑binding surface) spanning β‑strands and coils; Secreted glycohydrolase (glucoamylase): peaks in solvent‑exposed loops connecting β‑strands, away from catalytic and substrate‑binding residues

Summary: Edge beta-strand at a domain terminus (most often the C-terminus) and immediately adjacent coil—most often in secreted/extracellular or membrane-anchored proteins—frequently forming part of a ligand/cofactor/partner-binding surface (e.g., near heme axial His or host-factor epitopes). The segments are typically short (~10–20 aa), surface-exposed, and often enriched in Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly and aromatic residues. This is a broad, structural concept spanning many beta-rich and mixed alpha/beta secreted/peripheral proteins across taxa, and is also observed in PAP/fibrillin family proteins and papain-like proteases at terminal edge strands.
Activation pattern: Regional activation focused on a short window at or near a domain boundary (often at the extreme C-terminus), peaking on an edge beta-strand and spilling into the adjacent coil; residue-level peaks occur adjacent to functional sites when present. Occasional secondary peaks occur on other edge beta-strands within the same beta-rich or mixed alpha/beta domain. Minimal activation on signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Peroxynitrite isomerase/nitrobindin hemoproteins: activation on the C-terminal beta-strand harboring the heme-b axial His and adjacent residues.
- Neisserial factor H binding lipoprotein (fHbp): strongest activation on the extreme C-terminus of domain C (beta-strand → short coil) adjacent to a critical factor H-binding residue; secondary activation on a beta-strand patch in domain B linked to vaccine-epitope function.
- CD-NTase-associated accessory protein (Cap15): activation confined to the final beta-strand and short C-terminal tail, outside annotated functional regions.
- Oplophorus luciferin 2-monooxygenase catalytic subunit (shrimp luciferase): activation restricted to the last beta-strand with a short terminal coil.

Summary: Mixed‑charge, Lys/Arg‑enriched low‑complexity segments (often a short cationic amphipathic helix flanked by disordered coil) that mediate electrostatic binding to polyanionic targets—primarily nucleic acids (RNA, rRNA, ss/dsDNA) and genome packaging surfaces—and, secondarily, acidic protein clefts and anionic membranes (e.g., organelle targeting presequences); broadly conserved across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation over medium‑to‑long contiguous stretches, with peaks on clustered Lys/Arg interleaved with Asp/Glu; typically overlaps low‑pLDDT/disordered regions but can include a short alpha‑helix at one edge; occasionally spans flexible catalytic/linker loops containing acidic metal‑binding residues
Exemplars:
- PUR‑repeat nucleic acid‑binding proteins (Pur‑alpha/BpuR): activation on the PUR‑repeat helix and adjoining disordered tail that harbor residues required for ssDNA/RNA/dsDNA binding.
- SRP9/14 (signal recognition particle RNA‑binding subunits): activation on C‑terminal helix‑to‑coil segments (often isoform‑specific, low pLDDT) that engage Alu RNA.
- Class III adenylyl/adenylate cyclase: activation across a flexible, charged linker at the CA/CB junction encompassing Mg2+‑binding Asp residues near the active site.
- Bacteriophage capsid/coat and portal proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑rich N‑terminal tails and channel‑lining basic loops used for genome packaging/translocation.
- ADP‑ribosyltransferases (PARP/ARTD; phage ALT): activation on basic DNA‑binding/auto‑modification regions and adjacent low‑complexity segments.
- RNA‑targeting toxins and ribosome‑inactivating proteins; translational/ribosome‑associated proteins: activation on cationic, mixed‑charge rRNA‑binding extensions.
- Kunitz‑type protease inhibitors/related secreted inhibitors: activation on exposed cationic reactive loops/patches that contact acidic protease pockets.
- Organelle targeting peptides (mitochondrial/mitosomal presequences): activation on Arg‑rich amphipathic N‑terminal helices that engage import receptors and anionic membranes.

Summary: Aromatic (phenylalanine/tyrosine) cluster motif: short, hydrophobic low‑complexity segments enriched for F/Y that act as membrane‑interface anchors or aromatic “sticker” patches, most often at N‑termini or adjacent to transmembrane helices; recurrent in small viral/accessory proteins, secreted effectors and toxin/antimicrobial peptides, micropeptides from alt/lncRNA ORFs, and some nucleic‑acid–associated proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks on F and Y that aggregate into regional clusters (3–20 residues); strongest near the N‑terminus, within signal peptides/signal‑anchors and at TM‑helix boundaries (“aromatic belt”); can cover entire short peptides when densely FY‑rich; weak response to polar/charged residues; W/C contribute occasionally.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory/structural proteins (e.g., viroporins/small membrane proteins): activation on N‑terminal FY clusters flanking or capping a single TM helix.
- Secreted pathogen effectors (oomycete RxLR family): activation on the FY‑rich, disordered pre‑domain immediately after the signal peptide used for translocation/entry.
- Antimicrobial and toxin peptides: activation across short FY‑enriched hydrophobic segments that mediate membrane binding/disruption.
- Membrane receptors/transporters and small hydrophobic proteins: activation on aromatic belts at TM boundaries and on FY‑rich cytosolic/luminal tails.
- Alt‑ORF/lncRNA micropeptides: activation spanning the whole peptide due to dense FY content.
- Nucleic acid–associated proteins (e.g., RRM/IDR‑containing RNA‑binding proteins): activation on FY hotspots in low‑complexity regions or aromatic patches used for base stacking.
- Diverse enzymes: activation on exposed surface FY clusters or N‑terminal aromatic patches not tied to a specific fold.

Summary: Membrane‑engaging insertion elements: long hydrophobic/amphipathic segments (helical fusion/HR/MPER regions, coiled‑coil helices, or β‑hairpins) that insert into or appose lipid bilayers (or other hydrophobic interfaces) to drive membrane fusion, pore formation, or translocation; typically membrane‑proximal and often disordered until engagement
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long contiguous stretches enriched in L/I/V/A/G; frequently multiple disjoint activated segments per large protein. Peaks occur in fusion/translocation subunits, near transmembrane segments or in membrane‑proximal external/luminal regions; segments often have low pLDDT (metastable) and can be either α‑helical (including coiled‑coil/heptad repeats) or β‑strand hairpins in pore formers.
Exemplars: - Viral envelope/fusion glycoproteins (e.g., coronavirus Spike): activation on a long virion‑surface helix in the membrane‑proximal S2 region (HR/MPER‑like), with minor signals in the short intravirion tail.
- Gasdermin family: activation confined to the N‑terminal pore‑forming domain on β‑strands that form the membrane‑inserting β‑hairpins of the pore; no activation on the autoinhibitory C‑terminus.
- Gram‑negative bacteriocins/colicins and pesticidal pore‑forming toxins: activation on hydrophobic helical hairpins/helix bundles that insert into target membranes during killing.
- Type III secretion translocators/delivery proteins: activation on the hydrophobic translocator helices that form host‑membrane pores for effector passage.
- Clostridial neurotoxin systems (BoNT): activation within the translocation domain’s hydrophobic helical bundles that become membrane‑inserted under acidic conditions.
- Apolipoproteins/lipid‑binding proteins: activation on amphipathic helices that wrap and bind lipid surfaces.
- Mitofusins/Fzo and other single‑pass coiled‑coil membrane proteins: activation on extended heptad‑repeat coiled‑coils adjacent to the transmembrane anchor that mediate membrane tethering/fusion.
- Magnetosome small membrane proteins (e.g., MamD): activation starting in the C‑terminal half of the TM and extending into the adjacent lumenal, disordered MIC region that interfaces with the mineral surface.
- Filamentous phage attachment protein (G3P): activation on a flexible, low‑confidence segment in the entry/attachment region consistent with an interface‑engaging, metastable stretch that rearranges during host interaction.

Summary: Short acidic, glycine‑rich loop/turn motifs—especially DG/GD‑containing and Gly‑repeat segments—used as flexible catalytic or ligand‑recognition elements across diverse proteins (e.g., active‑site loops in enzymes and short inhibitory/recognition wedges in secreted proteins)
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks in short local patches (≈4–10 aa), often appearing multiple times per protein and without positional bias along the sequence
Exemplars: - Protein tyrosine phosphatases (receptor and non‑receptor): activation on catalytic loop regions (e.g., WPD loop vicinity and adjacent acidic/Gly-rich turns) that position the general acid/base Asp.
- Retroviral/retroelements polyproteins and proteases: activation on the aspartyl protease DTG/D(S/T)G active‑site motif and short acidic motifs in associated polymerase modules (e.g., YxDD).
- RAD50/RecF and related P‑loop NTPases: activation on the phosphate‑binding P‑loop (GxxxxGKT) and nearby acidic Walker‑B segments, i.e., short Gly‑rich/acidic loops.
- Cyclophilins/peptidyl‑prolyl cis–trans isomerases: activation on exposed substrate‑binding loops enriched in Asp/Glu and Gly (short DG/GD‑containing turns).
- Plant cystatins/cysteine‑protease inhibitors: activation on the short inhibitory wedge (QxVxG) and neighboring Gly/acidic patches that form the reversible blocking loop.
- Dirigent/phenylpropanoid‑associated proteins: activation on extracellular loop segments bearing short DG/GD and Gly‑rich turns implicated in ligand recognition.
- Nucleotide/cofactor kinases and phosphotransfer enzymes: activation on short Gly‑rich phosphate‑binding loops (e.g., P‑loops) and adjacent acidic micro‑motifs.
- Bacterial transcription elongation/anti‑cleavage factors (e.g., Gre‑like): activation on acidic tip/loop segments (DxD/E‑type short motifs, often within Gly/acidic patches) that engage RNA polymerase.

Summary: Detector for glycine‑centered tight turns/loop “hinges” at secondary‑structure junctions—typically short, well‑ordered coil segments that connect or terminate beta‑strands—with a preference for small/polar flanking residues (S/N/T/D); a broadly structural, not function‑specific, signal
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue‑level peaks on single glycines (occasionally short 2–5 aa windows including S/N/T/D around G); enriched in coils/turns and at strand termini or immediately before/between beta‑strands; can recur multiple times in long, repeat‑rich or lumenal/extracellular domains; absent from transmembrane helices and usually outside canonical ligand‑binding motifs
Exemplars: - Flavin‑dependent oxidoreductases (e.g., FMOs, AIFM1, polyamine oxidase, monodehydroascorbate reductase): sharp peaks on loop glycines that connect adjacent beta‑strands, away from FAD/NAD(P) binding motifs
- C‑type lectin receptors (CTLD): sparse peaks on loop residues within the extracellular lectin domain; none in the cytosolic tail or transmembrane helix
- Complement/thioester proteins (e.g., C4): glycine‑centered S‑G‑S/D‑G‑S motifs and nearby turns scattered across domains, often at strand edges/turns
- Nuclear pore membrane glycoprotein (GP210/Nup210): multiple loop‑localized peaks (mostly Gly/Ser) across the lumenal N‑terminal domain; no activation in the transmembrane segment or cytosolic tail
- FKBP‑type peptidyl‑prolyl isomerases: single glycine peaks in annotated turns linking beta‑strands within the PPIase domain
- MORN‑repeat proteins (radial spoke head): peaks on glycines at the C‑terminal end of MORN repeats, typically just before a beta‑strand

Summary: N-terminal leader/targeting segments: the feature activates on the extreme N-terminus (first 2–5 residues) of proteins, especially the N-region of signal peptides and organelle transit peptides, and more generally on short, disordered/low-complexity N-terminal tails; strongest at residue ~3 and largely independent of amino-acid identity, occurring across all taxa and functions.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peak at the very N-terminus (most often position 3), with occasional weaker secondary peaks at internal disordered/low-complexity sites; no strong residue preference.
Exemplars: - Secreted precursors (pro-proteins), protease inhibitors, and peptide toxins: activation on the N-region of the signal peptide.
- Single-pass membrane receptors and GPI-anchored proteins: activation on the first residues of the signal peptide.
- Organelle-targeted proteins (mitochondrial/chloroplastic small subunits): activation on the first residues of the transit peptide.
- RiPP precursor peptides: activation on the N-terminal leader region.
- Prokaryotic small regulatory/stress and specialized structural proteins (e.g., gas vesicle proteins): sharp peak at residue ~3 of an unstructured N-terminal tail, with occasional weaker peaks in internal disordered segments.
- Low-complexity structural proteins and some metallothioneins: when present, activation at the very start of the disordered chain.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity peptide-like regions (often proline/serine/threonine/glycine- and charged-residue rich) found across taxa, especially in short secreted/regulatory peptides and microproteins; captures flexible linkers, proline‑rich tracts, and IDR segments rather than a specific domain
Activation pattern: Regional activation with residue‑level peaks across low‑complexity/disordered stretches; occurs at N‑termini (including signal/propeptide regions) and internal linkers; no single conserved short motif
Exemplars: - Antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., cecropins, defensins, cathelicidins): activation on the low‑complexity, cationic mature peptide and/or propeptide segments
- Venom peptide precursors, notably proline‑rich bradykinin‑potentiating peptides: activation on proline/glycine‑rich tracts and basic processing regions
- Plant‑virus RNA silencing suppressors and other small viral regulatory/accessory proteins: activation on disordered, low‑complexity regions that mediate host interactions
- Human small‑ORF microproteins and lncRNA‑derived/testis‑expressed microproteins: activation over serine/threonine/proline‑rich IDRs
- Bacterial/archaeal small proteins and annotated fragments: activation on GS/TP/PR‑rich low‑complexity linkers and repeats

Summary: Short, surface-exposed linear segments at secondary-structure transitions and domain or protein termini—often flexible/disordered or disulfide-constrained—that act as recognition/functional loops or tails; enriched in Gly/Pro/Ser and mixed-charge patterns and common in secreted/periplasmic proteins and toxins
Activation pattern: Regional activation in short contiguous blocks (~8–20 aa) with sharp residue-level peaks; preferentially at loop/helix-cap or loop–strand junctions and C‑terminal tails (including at PDZ domain edges); can occur in low-pLDDT flexible regions or in well-defined, disulfide-stabilized loops; multiple such blocks per protein
Exemplars: - Subtilisin inhibitor-like proteins: disulfide-flanked loop and a short helical segment stabilized by a nearby disulfide.
- HtrA/Do serine proteases with PDZ: extreme C-terminal tail immediately after the PDZ domain and a catalytic/recognition loop within the protease domain (including the Asp of the charge relay).
- Type II secretion system I subunit: disordered C-terminal tail.
- L,D-transpeptidases: short helical patch within the catalytic domain (not the catalytic Cys/His itself).
- Plant expansins (EG45/CBD): loops and loop–strand junctions, including the C-terminal edge of the CBD.
- Three-finger toxins: receptor-binding Loop III and adjacent loop-transition segments.
- Magnetosome MamP (PDZ–magnetochrome protein): low-confidence segment at the C-terminal end of the PDZ domain preceding the magnetochrome motif, including a functionally important residue.
- Fungal adhesins: mixed helix–strand–coil patch within a disulfide-bonded region containing an N-glycosylation site; additional short disordered patches elsewhere.

Summary: N-terminal cationic amphipathic segment used for targeting or macromolecule association (membranes, organelles, nucleic acids, or capsids). The feature captures Lys/Arg-enriched patches often paired with a hydrophobic tract, explaining activation in secreted precursors, small viral proteins, exported proteins, microproteins, and some cytosolic binders.
Activation pattern: Regional activation concentrated in the first ~10–35 residues, often including the initiator Met. Residue-level peaks on Lys/Arg and a contiguous hydrophobic stretch (Leu/Val/Ile/Phe/Trp), with tolerance for Pro/Gly near hinge/cleavage; Cys frequently scored in secreted/toxin precursors. Also captures short basic/amphipathic patches (including NLS-like segments) even without a strong hydrophobic core when used for protein/capsid binding.
Exemplars:
- Secreted toxin/antimicrobial peptide precursors: activation on the signal peptide and adjacent cysteine-rich propeptide.
- Viral capsid/structural proteins (e.g., adenovirus protein IX): activation on N-terminal amphipathic/basic helices that bind capsid.
- Viral accessory/regulatory nuclear proteins (e.g., E4-ORF6/7): activation on basic N-termini/NLS-like regions.
- Bacterial Sec/Tat substrates and lipoproteins: activation on N-terminal signal peptides (including twin-arginine for Tat).
- Eukaryotic mitochondrial/chloroplast proteins: activation on Lys/Arg-rich targeting helices.
- Integral membrane transporters/receptors with N-terminal signal anchors: activation on the first TM and preceding basic residues.
- Small anti-CRISPR proteins: activation on N-terminal basic/amphipathic patches mediating protein–protein binding.
- Occasional cytosolic enzymes: weak activation from Lys/Arg-rich N-termini.

Summary: Short stretches within intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity N‑terminal or propeptide regions—often polar/lysine/glutamine‑rich and sometimes with transient helical propensity—common across taxa (including viral regulatory proteins and eukaryotic propeptides).
Activation pattern: Sparse residue‑level peaks clustered in predicted coil, low‑pLDDT segments, typically near the N‑terminus or within propeptides; occasional isolated peaks in flexible parts of mature chains.
Exemplars: - Viral Tat-like regulatory proteins: peaks on compositionally biased, polar N‑terminal disordered segments (e.g., T/K/Q-rich patches).
- Neurotrophin propeptides (secreted growth factors): clustered peaks within the intrinsically disordered propeptide, including a short transient helix; rare isolated peak at the start of the mature chain.
- Testis-specific basic Y (TSPY) family proteins: peaks in the N‑terminal unstructured, low‑confidence coil region of these basic, low‑complexity proteins.

Summary: A general beta‑strand register signal: the feature activates on individual residues within well‑ordered β‑strands across diverse folds, with a tendency toward hydrophobic/small positions that stabilize sheet packing and, in β‑sandwich/solenoid repeats (e.g., Ig/FN3), frequently immediately C‑terminal to an aromatic residue (often Trp). This is a structural, function‑agnostic motif that recurs in enzymes, transporters, and receptors.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks confined to E (β‑strand) segments; typically 1–3 peaks per domain (repeating across tandem β‑domain arrays), often at mid/late sequence indices; generally not coincident with catalytic motifs; occasionally adjacent to or on an aromatic residue in the strand.
Exemplars: - Ig‑like cell‑adhesion/axon‑guidance proteins (IgSF; β‑sandwich): one peak per Ig‑like domain at the strand residue immediately following a conserved Trp; weaker peaks in Fibronectin type‑III strand positions.
- ABC transporter ATP‑binding domains (NBDs): isolated Leu residues in central β‑strands of the α/β core.
- Ribosomal small‑subunit pseudouridine synthase A (RsuA; S4‑like RNA‑binding domain): Thr/Ala within N‑terminal β‑strands.
- PLP‑dependent alanine racemase (TIM‑barrel): a single Leu in a barrel β‑strand, away from active‑site residues.
- Signal peptidase I (periplasmic serine‑lysine peptidase): Thr (and weaker Met/Trp) within β‑strands of the extracellular catalytic domain, not at the catalytic dyad.

Summary: A detector of low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered, Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro/Ala‑rich segments (often N‑terminal), including proline‑rich stretches and occasional closely spaced cysteines; these regions occur in viral microproteins, secretory precursors/extracellular repeats, membrane‑proximal tails, and organelle transit peptides rather than in a specific folded domain.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks concentrated in short low‑complexity clusters; frequently enriched at N‑termini; multiple dispersed patches in long proteins; recurrent Gly runs and occasional Cys–Cys pairs included.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory/microproteins: activation spans their largely disordered, Ser/Pro/Gly‑rich sequences.
- Secreted/mucin‑like proteins and precursors: activation on Ser/Thr‑rich O‑glycosylation–prone repeats and on propeptide segments; includes cysteine‑containing stretches.
- Membrane proteins (viral and eukaryotic): activation on low‑complexity cytosolic or luminal tails with proximal cysteine pairs (palmitoylation/disulfide‑forming motifs).
- Plant organellar proteins: activation on N‑terminal chloroplast transit peptides enriched in Ser/Thr/Ala/Pro/Gly.
- Apoptosis/tumor‑related regulators and other signaling proteins: activation on disordered regulatory regions and proline‑rich motifs.
- Diverse enzymes: activation on flexible linkers and low‑complexity N‑terminal peptides within otherwise structured proteins.

Summary: Positively charged, low-complexity intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs)—enriched in Lys/Arg with frequent Pro/Ser/Gly and polybasic clusters (e.g., KR/RR)—common in short proteins and propeptides across taxa, including viral accessory proteins, neuropeptide/hormone precursors, sperm nuclear proteins, flexible enzyme tails, and microproteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation spanning extended low-pLDDT/disordered segments with numerous modest residue-level peaks (especially at Lys/Arg), occurring at N-termini or internal regions; little to no activation in well-folded domains.
Exemplars: - Retroviral integrase: strong activation in the annotated disordered central linker.
- Type II toxin–antitoxin antitoxins (TacA family): activation on the N-terminal IDR and a flexible low-confidence helix; structured C-terminus largely inactive.
- Viral tegument/accessory microproteins: diffuse activation across basic, disordered bodies.
- Neuropeptide/hormone prohormone precursors: broad activation in KR/RR-rich propeptide regions used for convertase processing.
- Sperm nuclear proteins (protamines/transition proteins): pervasive activation across Lys/Arg-rich disordered sequences.
- ATP synthase ε subunit: activation on flexible/basic tails or segments of the small subunit.
- RNA/tRNA modification enzymes: activation on low-complexity basic tails/loops implicated in RNA binding.
- Cysteine-rich venom/toxin precursors: activation concentrated in propeptide regions around dibasic processing sites rather than the folded toxin core.
- Eukaryotic microproteins/antisense-derived short proteins: widespread activation across their largely disordered, basic sequences.

Summary: Residue-level detector of intrinsically disordered/flexible regions characterized by low predicted structural confidence (low pLDDT), often in low-complexity or unstructured tails, independent of specific secondary-structure assignment
Activation pattern: Sparse, non-contiguous residue-level peaks scattered within disordered segments; enrichment where pLDDT is low (typically <~55), occurring in coils and occasionally in nominal helices/strands when confidence is low
Exemplars: Viral nucleoprotein (Measles N): peaks in low-pLDDT loops across the N protein; Peptide hormone precursor (KiSS-1/kisspeptin): residues in disordered/low-complexity regions including the Metastin/Kisspeptin segments; Tumor suppressor (Suppressor of tumorigenicity 20): widespread peaks across a highly disordered chain; TAR1 protein: residues within an annotated disordered C-terminal region; Secretory granule protein (RES18): low-pLDDT sites across the mature protein and within the N-terminal signal peptide

Summary: Membrane‑active amphipathic α‑helices enriched in small hydrophobic residues (A/V/L/I/G) that insert into, line, or associate with lipid bilayers—i.e., the pore‑forming/translocation helices of toxins and translocons and analogous lipid‑binding/stress‑sensing helices in other membrane proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous helical segments (often single helices or helical hairpins), with sparse charges and frequent Gly/Ala runs; peaks track α‑helical stretches that often fold upon membrane contact (low pLDDT in isolation). Activation typically avoids catalytic motifs and generic signal peptides/TM anchors, instead favoring amphipathic or pore‑lining helices (including lipid‑binding helices) within toxin, antimicrobial, and membrane‑associated domains.
Exemplars: - Pore-forming colicins: strong activation on the C‑terminal pore‑forming transmembrane/helical hairpin region.
- Bacillus thuringiensis Cry (δ‑endotoxins): activation on the N‑terminal pore‑forming helical bundle (domain I) with peaks in membrane‑inserting helices.
- Cationic antimicrobial peptides (e.g., Styelin‑D): activation confined to the mature amphipathic α‑helix; absent on the signal peptide and propeptide.
- Mitochondrial inner‑membrane protease OMA1: activation on amphipathic helices within the peptidase domain, including a cardiolipin‑binding/stress‑sensor region; little to no activation on the N‑terminal propeptide or the single‑pass TM anchor.

Summary: Generic short N-terminal amphipathic or hydrophobic helices: encompassing secretory signal peptides and signal‑anchor transmembrane helices (Sec/Tat), mitochondrial transit peptides, and similar amphipathic/basic N‑terminal helices found in soluble proteins; the feature can also fire on internal hydrophobic/amphipathic helices.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over a 10–30 aa helix, strongest at protein N‑termini; enriched for hydrophobic residues (L/I/V/F/W) with frequent basic residues (R/K/H) in the N‑region; tolerates amphipathic helices lacking a long continuous hydrophobic core (as in mitochondrial presequences and some cytosolic N‑termini); additional peaks may occur at later helices.
Exemplars: Viral envelope glycoproteins (signal peptides/signal anchors); Secreted peptide/toxin precursors; Plant small membrane proteins (e.g., CYSTM family) via signal‑anchor; Mitochondrial matrix/inner-membrane precursors (e.g., ATP synthase ε) via transit peptides; Cytosolic enzymes with basic N‑terminal amphipathic helices (e.g., PrmC/TrmB, RNAP Rpo6, LipB); Viral accessory proteins with basic N‑termini (e.g., Vif).

Summary: Beta-strand secondary-structure signal: the feature marks residues within ordered β-sheets (DSSP class E), often in extracellular/luminal domains but broadly across taxa and functions; enrichment for polar/charged side chains within strands rather than specific catalytic motifs
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated on individual positions inside β-strands (high-confidence pLDDT), with many peaks per sequence; minimal activation in helices, loops, transmembrane segments, or short cytosolic tails; not specifically tied to active sites, thioester motifs, or glycosylation per se (though can occur near N-glycosylation sequons)
Exemplars: - Complement/alpha-2-macroglobulin/TEP family: numerous peaks across β-strands throughout the secreted macroglobulin domains, excluding the thioester site.
- Integrin alpha subunits: extracellular β-propeller blades; activation on β-strand residues across the domain; absent from transmembrane/cytoplasmic regions; sometimes near N-linked glycosylation sequons.
- Translocon-associated protein alpha (SSR1): luminal N-terminal domain β-strands highlighted.
- MD-2/MD-2-related lipid-recognition and NPC2: β-sandwich strands within lipid-binding folds.
- Vesicle trafficking/adaptor machinery (e.g., WD40/β-propeller proteins): activation on blade β-strands.
- Bacterial trigger factor chaperone: β-strand elements within the cytosolic chaperone fold.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes (glycoside hydrolases/phosphorylases): β-strands of TIM-barrel or β-sandwich regions.
- Bacterial secretion/pilus assembly chaperones: Ig-like β-sandwich strands.
- Phage structural proteins and photosynthesis/respiratory assembly factors: β-sheet-forming strands in β-rich domains.

Summary: Generic detector of N‑terminal low-structure segments, with a strong bias toward secretory signal peptides and adjacent disordered/flexible N‑terminal stretches (often basic or hydrophobic amphipathic helices), rather than folded domains.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks; sparse, isolated activations concentrated in the first 20–100 residues (often within the first 30). Peaks occur within signal peptides and in low-pLDDT disordered coils or short helices, including at boundaries preceding annotated disordered regions; rarely form contiguous runs.
Exemplars: - Secreted serpin (antithrombin): peak in the N‑terminal signal peptide and additional peaks in a longer disordered N‑terminal segment.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursor (lumbricin): strong peaks confined to the N‑terminal signal peptide; minimal activation in the mature peptide.
- Secreted bacterial catalase–peroxidase (KatG): minor peaks in the signal peptide and immediately at the start of the mature chain.
- Poxvirus accessory protein: multiple peaks across low-confidence, disordered regions near the N‑terminus.
- Retroviral integrase homolog: peaks near the N‑terminus and at residues just before an annotated disordered linker.
- p53-induced DNA-binding protein (Killin): peaks on basic residues within a low‑pLDDT, N‑terminal DNA-binding region.

Summary: Short, mixed charged/polar active‑site loops that provide acid/base catalysis or chelate metal/phosphate cofactors—enriched in D/E/H/K/R/S/T and often adjacent to glycine—capturing canonical catalytic and metal‑binding signatures (e.g., PD-(D/E)xK/HNH/DDE, HExxH, Ser‑His‑Asp triads) and glycine‑rich phosphate/FAD‑binding loops across diverse enzymes.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks forming small clusters (typically 3–6 residues) in surface loops/turns near catalytic sites; one or a few patches per protein, with occasional multiple regions in large secreted/eukaryotic proteins; broad across all taxa and mobile elements.
Exemplars: - Restriction endonucleases and DNA repair nucleases: activation on PD-(D/E)xK and HNH catalytic metal-binding motifs (acidic/His clusters that coordinate Mg2+/Mn2+).
- Recombinases/integrases/transposases: activation on DDE/DxH metal-binding catalytic triads in the active site.
- HtrA/DegP serine proteases: activation on the Ser‑His‑Asp catalytic triad residues in the protease active-site loop.
- Site‑2 (S2P) intramembrane metalloproteases: activation on the HExxH Zn-binding motif and neighboring catalytic Asp/Glu.
- Cell wall glycan enzymes (glycosidases, lytic transglycosylases, deacetylases): activation on general acid/base (E/D) pairs in active-site loops.
- FAD-dependent monooxygenases/halogenases: activation on the glycine‑rich FAD-binding Rossmann loop (GxGxxG) and adjacent polar/charged residues contacting the cofactor.
- ATP synthase F1 ε/small subunits: activation on conserved charged patches in C‑terminal/loop regions that contact nucleotide/subunit interfaces.
- Transcription elongation/cleavage factors (GreA/GreB/TFS): activation on the acidic tip that positions/coordinates the RNAP active-site metal to stimulate cleavage.
- Phage/mobile element nucleases and accessory proteins: activation on His/acidic metal‑binding motifs (e.g., HNH-like) and short charged catalytic clusters.

Summary: Generic N-terminal initiation segments characterized by hydrophobic and/or small/turn-forming residues—often but not exclusively classical targeting leaders (signal peptides, signal-anchor TMs, mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides). The feature is compositional and also responds to non-canonical, non-secretory N-termini such as early coiled-coils, amphipathic/disordered low-complexity leaders, and short hydrophobic patches at the extreme N-terminus.

Activation pattern: Strong N-terminal bias within the first ~1–30 residues. Peaks over hydrophobic runs (signal peptide h-regions or the first TM/signal-anchor) and over low-complexity/proline/Ser/Thr-rich leaders or early coiled-coil heptads. In proteins without bona fide leaders, activation is weaker/diffuse but still preferentially maps to early hydrophobic/low-complexity segments.

Exemplars:
- Viral envelope glycoproteins and other type I membrane proteins: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide/signal-anchor segment.
- Secreted peptide hormones, chemokines, defensins, and animal/venom toxins: activation on the signal peptide and adjacent propeptide region.
- Bacterial lipoproteins and secreted enzymes: activation on Sec signal peptides, including the hydrophobic core and small-residue cleavage contexts.
- Single-pass eukaryotic receptors and viral membrane proteins: activation on the first transmembrane helix acting as a signal anchor.
- Pathogen effectors (type III/IV secretion, apoplastic fungal/oomycete effectors): activation on short, low-complexity N-terminal secretion signals.
- Mitochondrial/chloroplast-targeted proteins and microproteins: activation on N-terminal transit peptides/mitochondrial targeting sequences enriched in small/polar residues with intermittent hydrophobicity.
- Tail-anchored and SNARE family proteins (e.g., VAMPs): activation on N-terminal coiled-coil/low-complexity regions despite lacking an N-terminal targeting peptide.
- Viral and cellular cytosolic/nuclear proteins without export signals (e.g., reovirus sigma-NS, RNase P subunits): modest N-terminal activation due to short hydrophobic/low-complexity patches rather than bona fide targeting leaders.

Summary: N‑terminal start and proteolytic maturation junction detector: activates on the initiator methionine or the first residue of a newly formed mature peptide after signal peptide/propeptide cleavage, typically within low‑complexity, disordered segments enriched in Ser/Pro/Gly/Arg; most prominent in secreted and membrane precursors and small peptides, but also marking N‑termini of diverse proteins (including many viral proteins) across taxa.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks at the exact boundary (the first residue of the mature peptide and/or the immediately preceding residue), with short flanking N‑terminal stretches in low‑complexity IDRs; occasional weaker N‑terminal peaks elsewhere; broad, low‑specificity activation across taxa.
Exemplars: Plant PROPEP/Pep danger‑peptide precursors: strong peak at the N‑terminal boundary of the mature Pep within a disordered, acidic/basic‑biased prodomain; Viral envelope glycoproteins (e.g., class I fusion proteins): activation at signal peptide cleavage and/or polybasic convertase junctions, and at the extreme N‑terminus; Secreted hormone/neuropeptide and growth factor precursors: activation at propeptide removal sites that define the N‑terminus of the active peptide; Type I membrane receptors and secretory pathway glycoproteins: initiator Met and signal peptide region/cleavage site highlighted; lncRNA‑encoded micropeptides/smORFs: activation at Met1 and adjacent low‑complexity N‑terminal residues; Sperm/testis secreted or acrosomal proteins: activation on N‑terminal signal/pro‑region cleavage junctions; Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: weaker, generic N‑terminal activation at the start of disordered/low‑complexity tails; p53/apoptosis‑related proteins: N‑terminal disordered domains (e.g., transactivation/pro‑segments) show start‑proximal peaks.

Summary: Residue-level marker of intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments enriched for small/polar residues (Gly/Pro/Ser/Thr/Ala), often near N‑termini and at the starts of short, proteolytically generated peptides; broadly taxonomic and not tied to a specific fold or function
Activation pattern: Sparse, low-amplitude residue-level peaks scattered within regions of predicted disorder/low pLDDT; enriched at or just before segment starts (e.g., peptide N-termini) and at edges of structured–unstructured transitions; no strict secondary-structure preference and peaks can occur throughout long proteins
Exemplars: - HIV-1 Tat (viral regulatory protein): scattered peaks in flexible, disordered/basic N-terminal and adjacent regions, with occasional peaks in transient helix.
- Influenza A hemagglutinin (viral envelope glycoprotein fragment): very weak peaks confined to low-confidence, flexible segments across mixed secondary structures.
- Cholecystokinin prohormone (peptide hormone precursor): clear peaks at the N-termini of bioactive peptides (e.g., starts of CCK-8/CCK-5) and at a modified Tyr that serves as a peptide start, indicating sensitivity to processing boundaries within low-complexity regions.
- Inosine/xanthosine triphosphatase (housekeeping enzyme): isolated peaks in an N-terminal, low-confidence/disordered segment.
- PRCD photoreceptor disk component (small membrane-associated protein): peaks within an annotated disordered, low-pLDDT region rich in small/polar residues.
- TP53-target gene 3 (unstructured human protein): peaks on Pro/Gly/Ser in an N-terminal disordered segment and within an alternative, low-confidence region.

Summary: Short hydrophobic alpha-helical membrane-entry/anchor segments—signal peptides, signal-/tail-anchors, and fusogenic/translocation helices—often glycine-rich (frequent GxxxG “glycine-zipper” motifs) and flanked by basic residues; typically disordered/low-confidence until membrane-associated; found across viral, bacterial, and eukaryotic membrane and secretion systems
Activation pattern: Regional activation on 10–30 aa hydrophobic helices with sharp residue-level peaks within the helical core; commonly near N- or C-termini; multiple discrete peaks for multi-pass proteins; little/no activation in well-folded soluble domains; frequently coincides with predicted TM segments or low-pLDDT amphipathic helices
Exemplars: - Viral per os infectivity factor (PIF0): activation on annotated transmembrane helices and an adjacent C-terminal helical segment.
- Type VI secretion ADP-ribosyltransferase effector (PAAR–mART toxins): activation on a disordered, helical inter-domain linker, not on the structured catalytic domains.
- Bacteriocin/pyocin: activation on a short, low-pLDDT hydrophobic segment consistent with a membrane-interacting/translocation peptide.
- Botulinum-like neurotoxin: activation on C-terminal helical translocation/membrane-insertion regions outside the metalloprotease domain.
- Organelle membrane import/organization proteins (mitochondrial TOM/SAM receptors, peroxisomal peroxins, plastid OEP16/TOC components): activation on single-pass TM anchors or targeting helices, often with glycine-zipper motifs.
- Small eukaryotic membrane-associated proteins (Apolipoprotein L, ISG12/IFI6-like): activation on their solitary transmembrane helix.
- Magnetosome membrane proteins (Mam/Mms families): activation on short glycine-zipper TM helices.
- Viral fusion/envelope and phage penetration proteins: activation on fusogenic/anchor helices used for membrane insertion.
- Antimicrobial big defensins and other secreted precursors: activation on N-terminal signal peptide hydrophobic cores.
- Respiratory chain small subunits: activation on short hydrophobic TM helices (often glycine-rich) that mediate helix packing.

Summary: Extreme N-termini of proteins with methionine-enriched Sec-type signal peptides or N-terminal signal-anchor transmembrane helices; the feature highlights the initiator methionine together with nearby Met/hydrophobic residues within the h-region and does not generally mark signal peptides lacking internal Met (or sequences missing the true N-terminus).
Activation pattern: Regional activation concentrated in the first 10–20 residues (often an N-terminal alpha-helix), typically requiring one or more additional Met within the h-region: strong peaks at M1 and internal Met (with L/I/V/F also contributing); flanking polar/acidic residues (D/E/N/H) in the N- or C-regions can be included. Activation is a short N-terminal patch and drops sharply in the mature domain; generic signal peptides without internal Met are usually not activated.
Exemplars: - Phage internal scaffolding proteins: spike at the initiator Met of a disordered N-terminus when accompanied by nearby Met-rich hydrophobic patch.
- Subset of secreted bacterial enzymes (e.g., sulfatases, hydrolases, virulence factors) whose signal peptides contain internal Met: activation across the N-terminal signal peptide helix, peaking on internal Met in the h-region.
- Subset of outer-membrane/periplasmic biogenesis and transport proteins with Met-containing Sec signal peptides: activation on their N-terminal leaders.
- Two-component histidine kinases and related membrane sensors when their N-terminal signal-anchor helix includes Met: activation on the signal-anchor.
- Viral structural and membrane/accessory proteins with Met-containing N-terminal signal peptides or signal anchors.
- Small secreted peptides/micropeptides with Met-rich leader segments.

Summary: Extracellular/secretory pathway and lumenal proteins (including precursors and ectodomains) with cysteine‑constrained domains; the feature recognizes luminal cysteine patterns (disulfide frameworks or covalent cofactor‑binding cysteines) together with nearby maturation/processing signals (signal peptide cleavage and, when present, convertase/furin dibasic sites at propeptide–mature junctions)
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue‑level peaks on cysteines and adjacent residues involved in disulfide bonds or covalent attachments; spikes at dibasic Lys/Arg motifs when present; additional regional activation over signal peptides, propeptides, and extracellular/lumenal segments (including ectodomains of membrane proteins)
Exemplars: - Conotoxin and spider toxin precursors: peaks on disulfide cysteines in the mature toxin and on adjacent GKR/KR convertase sites; minor activation in the signal peptide
- Kappa‑KTx toxins and defensin‑like antimicrobial peptides: activation on the disulfide cysteine framework and propeptide/signal cleavage
