- Disulfide‑rich secreted protease inhibitors: scattered peaks on cysteines and residues near disulfide bonds across loops
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursors: regional activation on signal/propeptide; sharp peaks at KR/GKR sites when present; little on very short mature peptides
- Viral envelope and entry glycoproteins and host receptors (e.g., hemagglutinin, herpesvirus gI, receptor tyrosine kinases): activation on conserved ectodomain cysteines; peaks at furin/trypsin sites when present
- Chemokines and tick evasins: secreted disulfide‑bonded proteins with activation on cysteine motifs despite lacking convertase sites
- Lumenal organelle proteins with modified cysteines (e.g., phycoerythrin subunits): activation on chromophore‑attachment cysteines within the secretory/lumenal pathway

Summary: Compositionally biased, intrinsically disordered low‑complexity segments (often short tandem‑repeat regions) enriched in small/flexible residues and sometimes cysteine/glutamine, commonly occurring in N‑terminal/propeptide stretches of secreted precursors and small unstructured proteins; peaks can also occur in flexible terminal/loop segments within otherwise structured proteins (including enzymes); peaks can fall at residues within simple repeats or immediately flanking processed peptide segments, but the unifying concept is IDR/low‑complexity or flexibly disordered segments rather than a specific domain.
Activation pattern: Multiple residue‑level peaks scattered across extended low‑pLDDT coil/short β regions, with a frequent N‑terminal bias; little activation within stable helical cores, but occasional peaks at helix termini and adjacent loops in globular proteins; highlights specific positions within simple repeats and, in precursors, near boundaries of bioactive peptide segments.
Exemplars: Keratin‑associated proteins (hair KAP family): activation across the disordered cysteine/glutamine‑rich 5‑mer repeat block, with sharp peaks on Cys and Gln within repeats. Neuropeptide/prohormone precursors (e.g., cholecystokinin): activation on low‑complexity propeptide segments, including residues immediately preceding mature peptide start sites and in N‑terminal disordered regions. Uncharacterized intrinsically disordered proteins: activation confined to low‑confidence coil/short β segments. Globular enzymes (e.g., Mre11 nuclease, 4‑diphosphocytidyl‑2‑C‑methyl‑D‑erythritol kinase, ATP synthase ε): sparse peaks at flexible N/C‑termini or low‑complexity insertions.

Summary: Extended lipid/amphipathic–ligand handling interfaces: the feature marks long, glycine- and small–hydrophobic–rich surfaces that form tunnels, grooves, or pore‑lining segments used to bind and translocate lipids/LPS or other hydrophobic cofactors (e.g., heme) in secreted/periplasmic and outer‑membrane systems, as well as large lipid‑carrier proteins (BPI/LBP, vitellogenin, ATG2) and beta‑barrel pores (bacterial and mitochondrial).
Activation pattern: Predominantly domain‑level/regional activation over long stretches, often spanning entire lipid‑binding tunnels or beta‑barrel pore‑lining strands and flexible glycine‑rich loops; occurs at N‑terminal, internal, or C‑terminal regions rather than being terminus‑restricted; residue bias toward small/hydrophobic, glycine‑rich segments.
Exemplars: - BPI/LBP/PLUNC innate‑immunity lipid/LPS‑binding proteins: activation along the hydrophobic tunnel and adjacent glycine‑rich loops that cradle LPS/phospholipids.
- ATG2 lipid transfer proteins: activation across the elongated hydrophobic groove that ferries phospholipids between membranes at contact sites.
- Vitellogenin/large lipid‑transfer protein (LLTP) family: activation over the extensive lipid‑loading cavity and surrounding hydrophobic surfaces that carry neutral lipids.
- LptD/E outer‑membrane LPS translocon: activation on the LptD beta‑barrel interior and lateral gate that accommodates and inserts LPS.
- Type II/III secretion and type IV pilus secretins: activation on the outer‑membrane barrel wall and periplasmic vestibule/pore‑lining regions that contact LPS and membranes.
- Outer‑membrane porins and mitochondrial beta‑barrels (e.g., VDAC, Tom40/Sam50): activation along pore‑lining beta‑strands and lipid‑facing barrel surfaces.
- TonB‑dependent receptors and hemophores/heme acquisition systems: activation at hydrophobic heme/porphyrin‑binding pockets and barrel/extracellular loops that capture and transfer the cofactor.
- Additional periplasmic/secreted lipid‑binding and transfer modules beyond LPS pathways: activation on hydrophobic channels/tunnels used for phospholipid shuttling in the periplasm.

Summary: Residue-level detector for hydrophobic beta-strand positions in extracellular immunoglobulin-like domains (V-set and C2-set), with a strong preference for sites 1–2 residues from the conserved intradomain disulfide; the signal generalizes to other disulfide-stabilized, beta-sheet–rich extracellular folds (e.g., integrin FG-GAP beta-propellers and complement/alpha-2-macroglobulin–like thioester proteins).
Activation pattern: Sparse single-residue peaks confined to extracellular domains; highest in beta-strands (and occasionally at immediate strand boundaries) across repeated Ig-like domains; frequently exactly ±1–2 residues from disulfide-bond cysteines; enriched for hydrophobic residues (A, V, L, I, F, Y, W; with occasional P/G); little to no activation in signal peptides, transmembranes, or cytosolic tails.
Exemplars: - Ig-like cell-adhesion molecules (nectin/CADM and ZIG/IgCAMs): peaks in beta-strands of each Ig-like domain, typically within two residues of the conserved disulfide.
- Sialic-acid–binding Ig-like lectins (Siglecs, e.g., CD22): beta-strand residues in V-set and C2-set domains two residues from disulfide cysteines; sometimes near but not at the sugar-binding site.
- Cytokine-binding Ig-like modulators (interleukin-18–binding protein): beta-strand residues between and just after the intradomain disulfide cysteines.
- Integrin alpha subunits: beta-strand residues distributed across FG-GAP repeats of the extracellular beta-propeller.
- Complement/alpha-2-macroglobulin thioester-containing proteins: beta-strand residues, including sites adjacent to disulfide cysteines, and excluding the thioester catalytic motif.
- Neuregulin/EGF-family proteins with an Ig-like domain: beta-strand residues positioned two residues C-terminal to the intradomain disulfide cysteines.

Summary: Generic N‑terminal simple sequence motifs: short transmembrane signal‑anchor helices and short, low‑complexity Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly‑rich disordered stretches common to small membrane proteins and secreted/processing-prone peptide precursors, with occasional activation on similar IDRs in cytosolic regulators
Activation pattern: Mixed: (1) residue‑level peaks within alpha‑helical hydrophobic segments (often single‑pass TM/signal‑anchor helices, sometimes individual residues in TM bundles); (2) short regional activation across intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity patches enriched in S/T/P/G. Strong N‑terminal bias; in proline‑rich plant peptides, activation favors adjacent unmodified residues and downweights annotated hydroxyproline/glycosylated Pro sites.
Exemplars: - Mitochondrial TOM complex small subunit (Tom5): strong peak within the single transmembrane signal‑anchor helix.
- Mitochondrial microprotein PIGBOS: peak near the cytosolic border of the N‑terminal signal‑anchor helix.
- Bacterial PTS permease EIIC components: sparse, low peaks on multiple predicted transmembrane helices.
- Plant hydroxyproline‑rich systemin‑like peptide precursors (HypSys): regional activation within disordered mature peptide segments; reduced activation on hydroxyproline/glycosylated Pro residues.
- Yeast cyclin‑dependent kinase inhibitor Sic1: multiple small peaks across the N‑terminal intrinsically disordered region.

Summary: Residue-level detector of solvent-exposed, low-hydrophobicity positions—enriched for acidic and Gly/Pro/small-polar residues—typical of flexible coils/turns and coiled-coil helical surfaces; often at helix boundaries or within low-complexity segments, and in structured domains frequently marking interaction surfaces (e.g., RNA-binding) or residues adjacent to catalytic sites.
Activation pattern: Sparse, single-residue peaks (occasionally 1–3 residue micro-clusters) scattered across sequences; enriched in predicted coils and low-pLDDT regions but also appearing on selected residues within α-helices; not restricted to termini.
Exemplars: - Molybdopterin synthase catalytic subunit: residues in helix/coil near the active-site/ligand-binding region highlighted.
- Histone hairpin (RNA)–binding protein (SLBP): residues on the α-helical RNA-binding surface within the C-terminal domain.
- Coiled-coil scaffolds (Rootletin; nuclear coiled-coil components): sparse peaks within coiled-coil helices and in adjacent disordered/linker regions.
- ATP synthase peripheral/stator subunit H (mitochondrial): flexible coil residues with low structural confidence.
- Bacterial antitoxin MazE family: Gly/Pro and turn-forming positions at helix–helix connectors and C-terminal turn.
- G-patch RNA-processing factors: disordered, acidic/Gly-rich segments (including within the G-patch) carrying short linear interaction motifs.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity linker/propeptide segments enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro and acidic residues that serve as flexible spacers or prosegments between structured modules—commonly found in secreted/extracellular precursors, membrane-associated receptors, viral polyproteins, and the acidic activation regions of transcription factors
Activation pattern: Regional activation over low‑complexity stretches with local peaks (often at E/D, Pro/Gly clusters); occurs in internal linkers, propeptides, and sometimes terminal disordered regions; typically avoids signal peptides and folded domains; strongest in disordered segments with low predicted structure confidence
Exemplars: - Plant peptide hormone precursors (e.g., C‑terminally encoded peptide precursors): activation on disordered propeptide/linker regions between mature peptides, not on the signal peptide or the cysteine‑stabilized mature peptides.
- Secreted cysteine‑rich extracellular proteins (e.g., CRPs/EGF‑like/other repeat proteins): activation on Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly‑rich stalks and acidic spacers between cysteine‑rich domains.
- Transcription factors with zinc fingers or other DNA‑binding domains: activation on acidic, low‑complexity transactivation domains flanking the structured DNA‑binding regions.
- Viral polyproteins and envelope/structural precursors: activation on unstructured inter‑domain linkers and cleavage‑site–flanking segments.
- Membrane receptors and extracellular enzymes: activation on extracellular low‑complexity segments (including mucin‑like Ser/Thr‑rich stretches) and prodomain regions adjacent to structured domains.

Summary: Leucine-biased recognition of intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity hydrophobic segments—often in N‑terminal propeptides/signal-like regions or unstructured termini—while sparing well‑folded catalytic domains.
Activation pattern: Broad regional activation across long, low‑confidence/disordered stretches with residue-level peaks on Leu (and occasional weaker responses on other hydrophobics); little to no activation within structured domains.
Exemplars: - Trypsin family serine protease zymogen: activation confined to the disordered N‑terminal signal/propeptide on Leu residues; no activation in the folded peptidase domain.
- Killin (apoptosis-associated microprotein): strong activation on Leu distributed across a fully disordered chain.
- Laforin (dual-specificity phosphatase) alternative isoform: activation on Leu within annotated disordered regions across the sequence.
- Histidine kinase–like protein: activation on Leu in disordered N‑terminal half and C‑terminal tail; absent from the structured kinase core.
- Annexin-related receptor protein: activation on Leu across low‑confidence segments, including annotated disorder.
- Spermatogenesis-associated protein: activation on Leu throughout flexible/disordered regions spanning the sequence.

Summary: Prokaryotic Sec-type signal peptides and long signal-anchor helices with extended Leu/Ile/Val-rich h-regions; excludes mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides and non-secretory amphipathic leaders; often fails on short eukaryotic and many viral prepropeptide signals.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks within the first ~10–30 residues when the h-region is long/strongly hydrophobic; weak or absent on short/weakly hydrophobic signals typical of hormones/toxins/AMPs and some small viral glycoproteins; occasional peaks at internal signal anchors; absent on cytosolic/nuclear proteins and viral nucleoproteins.
Exemplars: Strong on bacterial/archaeal Sec-secreted/periplasmic proteins and some viral proteins with robust signal anchors; frequently absent on small metazoan secreted prepropeptides (toxins/AMPs, neuroendocrine peptides) and herpesvirus gN; negative on cytosolic/nuclear proteins (viral polymerases, nucleoproteins, capsid proteins) and mitochondrial precursors.

Summary: Proteolytic processing junctions in secreted/extracellular precursors, especially proprotein convertase/trypsin-like cleavage sites at dibasic Lys/Arg motifs that delimit propeptides and mature peptide chains; more generally, short disordered linker segments around cleavage sites (including viral protease sites and C-terminal GPI-anchor propeptide cleavage regions).
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks at basic residues (R/K), typically the C-terminal Arg/Lys of a prosegment just upstream of the mature peptide, often within RR/KR motifs and flanked by acidic residues; sometimes a short 8–20 aa window centered on or adjacent to the scissile bond (including peaks at nearby Gly). Activation concentrates in low-pLDDT, flexible coil/helix linkers; signal peptides and structured mature domains show little activation. Repeats across multi-peptide precursors.
Exemplars: - Amphibian antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., Maximin family): peaks at Arg marking convertase cleavage boundaries between propeptides and the Maximin peptides; additional signal at GKR processing motif.
- Spider toxin precursors (e.g., M-zodatoxin): strong activation across the propeptide culminating at a “processing quadruplet” with a peak at the terminal Arg that precedes the mature toxin.
- Fungal multi-peptide secreted effector precursors (Candida ECE1/candidalysin precursor): sharp peaks on Arg at Kex2-type dibasic cleavage sites that release the multiple peptides; mutation of these Arg residues disrupts secretion/virulence.
- Neuropeptide/hormone precursors (conopressin/neurophysin): single peak at Arg marking the end of the propeptide immediately before the active amidated peptide.
- Gamete recognition protein precursors (sea urchin bindin): strong peaks at RR motifs within the propeptide and at the propeptide C-terminus just before the mature bindin chain.
- Viral polyprotein segments (pre-core proteins): activation over a basic-rich disordered stretch spanning annotated viral protease cleavage sites, with a peak adjacent to the scissile bond.
- Fungal GPI-anchored cell wall protein precursors: peaks near the N-terminal pro-region immediately after the signal peptide and within the C-terminal GPI-anchor signal/propeptide near the ω-site that is cleaved by the transamidase.
- Insect secreted stress-response proteins (Turandot family): peak within a short disordered loop between helices in the mature chain, consistent with a protease-sensitive/processing-prone segment.

Summary: Generic alpha-helical secondary structure signal: residues located in alpha-helices across diverse proteins, encompassing both globular helices (e.g., HTH/homeodomain-like helices) and short transmembrane helices, with a slight tendency to mark well-ordered helices and helix termini rather than a specific motif or function.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks scattered across multiple helices along the chain; low to moderate amplitude; enriched in structured helical segments (often higher pLDDT), occasionally spilling into adjacent loops or disordered regions and at helix boundaries; no consistent positional bias.
Exemplars: - ECF sigma (sigma-70) transcription factors: sparse peaks on helices in domain 2 and domain 4, including within/adjacent to the helix-turn-helix DNA-binding element.
- ESAT-6-like (Esx) secretion system proteins: peaks distributed across the helical hairpin, strongest on the C-terminal helix near, but not at, the Zn2+-binding residues.
- Herpesvirus glycoprotein N: minor activation in the short intravirion alpha-helix immediately after the transmembrane helix.
- Herpesviral tegument/structural proteins (e.g., UL42-like): weak, scattered activation within helical segments, including a predicted transmembrane helix, with occasional hits in nearby disordered motifs.
- Type IV pilus minor pilins: activation within the long N-terminal alpha-helix and the N-terminal transmembrane helix/helix-termination region.
- Spo0E-family aspartyl-phosphate phosphatases: sparse peaks on residues in alpha-helices, including a helix proximal to functionally important positions.

Summary: Intrinsic disorder and flexible coil segments, with a strong bias for N‑terminal targeting presequences (chloroplast/mitochondrial transit peptides) and other low‑confidence loops/tails within soluble domains; generally avoids transmembrane helices and core catalytic motifs
Activation pattern: Mixed regional and residue-level: often strong, contiguous activation at the extreme N terminus (first ~20–40 residues) consistent with organellar transit peptides; elsewhere, scattered peaks across coil/loop regions and disordered termini or linkers within cytosolic domains; little activation within transmembrane segments; catalytic residues tend not to be highlighted
Exemplars: - Chloroplast-targeted CP12 family: strong activation across the N‑terminal chloroplast transit peptide with a sharp drop at the mature chain start.
- Two-component sensor histidine kinases: activation concentrated in the cytosolic histidine kinase catalytic domain, peaking in flexible loop/coil regions, with minimal signal over N‑terminal transmembranes/HAMP.
- Eukaryotic serine/threonine kinases: peaks on a low-confidence loop within the kinase domain and sustained activation over a disordered C‑terminal tail.
- GDP-mannose-dependent mannosyltransferases (glycosyltransferases): diffuse low-level activation over coil segments, including disordered C‑terminal regions, with little emphasis on catalytic residues.
- HEAT-repeat scaffolding proteins (MMS19/MET18 family): activation on flexible linkers between repeats and low-confidence terminal loops.

Summary: Asparagine/serine/threonine–enriched low‑complexity, disordered tracts, especially those forming N-linked glycosylation sequons (N‑X‑S/T) and S/T‑rich mucin‑like regions typical of secreted and surface proteins; more generally, polar N/S/T‑biased repeats in diverse proteins (with occasional K‑rich basic stretches in DNA‑binding regulators)
Activation pattern: Predominantly long regional activation across low‑complexity segments; strong residue‑level peaks at asparagines within N‑X‑S/T contexts; extended activation over S/T‑rich O‑glycosylated repeats and other polar low‑complexity tracts
Exemplars: - Viral envelope/membrane glycoproteins: activation on clusters of N‑X‑S/T sequons and surrounding N/S/T‑rich loops
- Secreted adhesins and mucin‑like cell‑surface proteins: activation over S/T‑rich O‑glycosylated repeats and embedded N‑glycosylation sequons
- Parasite surface/antigenic proteins (e.g., Plasmodium repeat proteins): activation across long Asn‑rich low‑complexity regions
- Dictyostelium low‑complexity proteins: activation on NST‑rich compositionally biased segments
- Neuropeptide and toxin precursors: activation on N/S/T‑rich prodomains with multiple glycosylation motifs
- Secreted carbohydrate‑active enzymes (glycosidases/lyases): activation at luminal/extracellular N‑glycosylation sequons
- Nuclear regulators (transcription factors, kinases, phosphatases; zinc‑finger proteins): activation on N/S/T‑biased low‑complexity linkers and occasional Lys‑rich basic stretches

Summary: The feature detects a subset of signal/propeptide-processing and intrinsically disordered low‑complexity segments in secreted/extracellular proteins, with preference for acidic and Ser/Pro/Gly–rich or charge-dense contexts. Peaks at signal-peptidase ends, propeptide→mature junctions, and immediate N-termini occur when these sites lie within such low-complexity/acidic neighborhoods; many compact, basic prohormones and short venom/AMP precursors lacking these contexts do not activate. Outside these contexts, only sporadic single‑residue peaks appear at functional or boundary residues in structured proteins.
Activation pattern: Mixed; (1) regional activation across acidic/Ser‑Asp repeat–rich or other low‑complexity disordered stretches; (2) sharp residue‑level peaks at cleavage sites or nascent N-termini only when embedded in low‑complexity/acidic or charge‑dense sequence; (3) rare, low‑amplitude single‑residue peaks in structured domains; absence is common in compact/basic precursors.
Exemplars: 
- Peptide hormone prohormones: detected in those with disordered acidic/Ser‑rich flanks; others (e.g., GHRH-like) may show little/no activation.
- Plant peptide hormones (CLE/GLV/RGF): conditional detection at signal and propeptide→mature junctions; not universal across family members.
- Antimicrobial/venom peptide precursors: activation mainly when an acidic/low‑complexity N‑terminal context exists; many precursors are silent.
- Extracellular acidic phosphoproteins (e.g., dentin phosphoprotein): strong, periodic activation across SD/SSD acidic repeats.
- Short regulatory micropeptides: variable activation within disordered, low‑complexity segments.
- Type II Golgi sulfotransferases: sporadic, not systematic, single‑residue peaks at functional or boundary positions.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity sequence elements enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro, with a particular sensitivity to glycine in GP/PG contexts and to S/T‑rich tracts characteristic of flexible linkers, repetitive collagen-like segments (Gly–X–Y), and regulatory tails across diverse taxa.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered within coil/disordered regions rather than continuous domain-level activation; strongest signals often on individual glycine residues adjacent to proline (GP/PG) and on selected serine/threonine positions; sparse, noncontiguous spikes distributed across long stretches, including very high sequence indices in long or repetitive proteins; both extracellular and intracellular contexts.
Exemplars: - Fibrillar collagens: peaks at glycine within Gly–X–Y repeats (frequently GP/PG) in the collagenous region.
- Serine/threonine and dual-specificity kinases, histidine kinases: S/T-rich, proline-biased disordered linkers and termini.
- RasGEFs and GAPs: low-complexity, proline- and S/T-enriched flexible linkers between domains.
- Homeobox and other transcription factors: Q/N/S/T-rich activation domains and disordered linkers.
- Ciliary/flagellar and microtubule-associated proteins: acidic and S/T-rich disordered segments involved in filament binding/regulation.
- Bacterial toxin–antitoxin antitoxins and two-component regulators: intrinsically disordered tails/linkers.
- Mycobacterial ECF sigma factors: low-complexity flexible extensions.
- Viral proteins from DNA and RNA viruses: low-complexity, disordered regions typical of regulatory tails.
- Dictyostelium signaling proteins: S/T- and Q/N-rich low-complexity regions pervasive in regulatory proteins.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered/propeptide-like segments—typically near N-termini—enriched in Gly/Pro/Ser/Ala and basic (Lys/Arg) residues, often in short repeats or polybasic clusters; the feature highlights flexible coils and secondary-structure junctions (helix/strand–coil boundaries) across very small proteins and larger proteins alike.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks that cluster in low-pLDDT coils and at transitions between secondary-structure elements; often biased toward the N-terminus and can extend over long low-complexity tracts in micropeptides; also lights up isolated flexible loops/tails within otherwise structured proteins.
Exemplars: - Neuropeptide/hormone precursors: activation on low-complexity, Lys/Arg-rich propeptide regions following signal peptides.
- Secreted peptide toxins/antimicrobial peptides: activation on pro-domains and N-terminal low-complexity stretches adjacent to signal peptides.
- Viral accessory proteins (e.g., herpesvirus, polyomavirus): activation across short, compositionally biased, largely disordered proteins or their N-terminal segments.
- Spermatogenesis/testis-associated low-complexity proteins: activation on disordered coils and helix/strand–coil boundaries (as in SPATA-family proteins).
- Keratin-associated proteins (hair/skin): activation on glycine-/cysteine-rich low-complexity repeat regions.
- lncRNA-derived micropeptides and other very small proteins: activation spanning much of the sequence due to pervasive disorder/low complexity.
- Bacterial/archaeal enzymes and transport/ATP-binding proteins: activation on flexible N-terminal tails and low-confidence loop/linker regions within structured domains.

Summary: Short beta‑strand segments (often edge or terminal strands at domain boundaries) enriched in hydrophobic/basic residues; a structural, not catalytic, signal common across diverse folds
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks: sparse, moderate-intensity activations concentrated in 3–6 residue stretches that form beta-strands; frequently positioned at or near domain junctions or terminal strands; enrichment for Val/Ile/Leu/Phe with occasional Lys/Arg/Thr; generally not coincident with catalytic or metal-binding motif residues
Exemplars: - HtrA/DegP periplasmic serine proteases (PDZ-containing): activation on a beta-strand immediately N-terminal to the second PDZ domain, plus additional peaks on a protease-domain strand and the C‑terminal terminal strand
- C-terminal processing peptidases (CtpA/Tsp, PDZ-containing): activation on the beta-strand just C-terminal to the PDZ domain, with minor peaks on a PDZ beta-strand and a peptidase-domain strand
- 2Fe–2S ferredoxin/adrenodoxin-like proteins: activation on internal beta-strands of the ferredoxin-like fold; no activation on the Fe–S–coordinating cysteines or transit peptides
- Tyrosine recombinases/integrases: activation on a short beta-strand within the catalytic domain between annotated active-site residues rather than on the catalytic residues themselves

Summary: Intrinsic structural disorder/low-complexity segments: flexible coil regions enriched in Pro/Gly/Ser/Gln/His (often in runs) found in unstructured N-/C-termini, linkers, and propeptides across diverse proteins
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks sparsely distributed across long intrinsically disordered regions; aligns with coil predictions and low-confidence structure (low pLDDT); multiple scattered peaks rather than a single contiguous motif/domain
Exemplars: - TP53TG3 family (testis-enriched regulatory proteins): activation on the disordered N-terminus and other low-confidence coil segments.
- Uncharacterized low-complexity proteins: activation on scattered residues within annotated disordered C-terminal regions and internal coils.
- Secreted extracellular matrix–associated proteins (e.g., CEMP1): activation on disordered N- and C-terminal segments and flexible/poorly resolved helices.

Summary: Serine residues within intrinsically disordered or low‑complexity segments (often N‑terminal tails), i.e., S‑rich IDRs and flexible regions rather than stable structured cores; the feature behaves as a detector of serine-rich disordered patches, with occasional spillover to nearby residues
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks almost exclusively on Ser; many peaks per protein, frequently clustered near termini and in compositionally biased/disordered regions with low pLDDT; little to no signal in well-ordered core domains; can appear in transient helices or signal peptides when those regions are low-confidence/flexible
Exemplars: Viral accessory proteins (metapneumovirus X): serines in a disordered C‑terminal tail; Herpesvirus envelope glycoprotein L: serines across the gH‑interacting segment and a disordered C‑terminus; Herpesvirus cytoplasmic envelopment proteins: numerous serines in low‑pLDDT regions; Plant ribosome‑inactivating proteins (dianthin): N‑terminal loop/coil serines; Human adaptor/regulatory protein ST20: N‑terminal serines in a low‑confidence helix/coil; Oomycete RxLR effectors: serines across the signal peptide, core, and disordered C‑terminus; Bacteriocins (enterocins): serines in flexible coil segments

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regions enriched for glutamine and histidine (often with proline/glycine runs)—flexible activation/linker segments that frequently flank structured cores (e.g., DNA‑binding or catalytic domains) in eukaryotic proteins. They are especially common in plant transcription factors, but also occur in secreted peptide precursors and in short terminal tails of enzymes (e.g., Fe(II)/2OG dioxygenases). The feature avoids folded domains and metal‑binding motifs and highlights long polar, compositionally biased coils (including poly‑Q/His patches).
Activation pattern: 
- Domain-level: Strongly off in structured DNA-binding/metal-binding/catalytic cores (POU/homeobox, TCP basic helix-loop-helix, AT-hook core, DOF zinc finger, LOB domain, TIFY and Jas/NLS motifs, MADS-box, and 2OG-dioxygenase cores); on in N-/C‑terminal or inter-domain low-confidence regions.
- Regional: Long, contiguous activation across disordered, low-pLDDT coils and low-complexity segments; occasional signal in short, low-confidence helices/extended strands; drops within well-ordered secondary structure even inside disordered tails.
- Residue-level: Enriched on Q/H (including poly‑Q/His tracts) with frequent P/G in low-complexity context; little/no signal on Zn‑coordinating Cys or Lys/Arg-rich AT‑hook motifs; avoids catalytic Hx(D/E)…H motifs of 2OG enzymes.
Exemplars:
- POU, KNOX/homeobox, and TCP transcription factors: signal on His-/Gln-/Gly-/Pro-rich disordered N/C termini and adjacent low-confidence helices; none on the DNA-binding cores.
- AT-hook/PPC proteins: silent over the AT-hook and structured PPC domain; activated on N‑terminal His/Asn patches and Gly/Pro-rich disordered C‑terminal tails.
- DOF zinc-finger and LOB-domain transcription factors: no activation on the zinc finger/LOB domain; scattered peaks across low-confidence C‑terminal coils/short helices.
- TIFY/JAZ repressors and MADS-box TFs: minimal on TIFY/Jas or MADS domains; strongest in central or terminal low-confidence coils, often Q/H-rich.
- Small secreted peptide precursors (e.g., CLE/GLV/CLEL): activation on low-complexity propeptides outside the hydrophobic signal peptide and the compact mature peptide region.
- Non-heme Fe(II)/2OG dioxygenases: off in the catalytic core; occasional activation in short disordered N-/C-terminal extensions, avoiding metal-binding motifs.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered short peptide segments enriched in small/polar/basic residues—most often at N-termini—characteristic of leader/propeptide regions of secreted prepropeptides (hormones/toxins) and of viral/microproteins; also activates on cysteine-rich secreted toxin/antimicrobial peptides and other short ORFs where compositionally biased tracts dominate
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short stretches (frequently starting near the initiator Met and extending through the low-complexity leader/propeptide); residue-level peaks on Asn/Ser/Thr/Lys/Arg/Pro/Gly and paired basic processing motifs; in longer proteins, multiple distributed low-complexity patches
Exemplars: - Peptide hormone and neuropeptide preproproteins: activation on the N-terminal propeptide/processing region (basic clusters around convertase sites) rather than the hydrophobic core
- Venom/toxin and antimicrobial peptide families (e.g., knottins/defensins/conotoxins): activation on the short cysteine-rich mature peptide and adjacent low-complexity propeptides
- Viral small/accessory proteins: activation on N-terminal basic, low-complexity segments
- Dictyostelium low-complexity proteins: activation across Asn/Ser/Thr-rich tracts
- Putative microproteins/short ORFs and annotated fragments: activation across most of the sequence due to compositional bias
- Larger enzymes/transporters/receptors with unstructured N-terminal tails or secretory prosegments: activation confined to those low-complexity regions

Summary: Solvent‑exposed residues in well‑ordered β‑strands and their adjoining turns, especially edge/terminal strands of β‑sheets in β‑sandwich or α/β enzyme cores (often in extracellular/periplasmic/ER‑lumenal domains and near β‑sheet→TM junctions), enriched for acidic/hydroxyl residues with frequent Gly/Pro and occasional aromatics.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks on DSSP E states and immediately adjacent coils/turns; short clusters (typically 2–4) scattered across structured β‑sheet cores with high confidence; largely absent from transmembrane helices, signal peptides, and long disordered/cytosolic tails; ~4–10 total activated sites per protein across diverse taxa.
Exemplars: - Pentameric ligand‑gated ion channels: extracellular/periplasmic β‑sandwich strands and strand→loop regions near the first TM helix.
- Oligosaccharyltransferase (ER glycosylation) subunits: lumenal β‑sheet core and β→TM‑proximal turns, not the TM/cytosolic tail.
- Cystatin family inhibitors: conserved β‑hairpins/edge strands (e.g., around positions ~90 and ~120) forming the inhibitory wedge.
- RNA polymerase α subunit: CTD β‑sheet surface/edge strands.
- Pterin/folate‑pathway enzymes: central β‑sheet strands in α/β folds (Rossmann‑like cores).
- Viral capsid proteins: jelly‑roll β‑sandwich edge strands.
- Translation and hydrolase/peptidase families: β‑strand segments and adjacent turns within stable β‑rich or α/β cores.

Summary: Intrinsic low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments enriched in polar/basic residues—especially Asn-rich and Ser/Thr-rich tracts (often homopolymeric runs)—serving as flexible linkers or terminal tails in signaling and membrane/secreted proteins; the feature primarily detects compositionally biased IDRs rather than folded domains.
Activation pattern: Long regional activation across disordered, low-pLDDT segments with sharp residue-level peaks on Asn and on runs of Ser/Thr; also responsive to basic homorepeats (e.g., poly-Lys); little to no activation within structured catalytic cores or transmembrane helices.
Exemplars: - Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase: strong activation on disordered linkers and N-terminus containing Asn-rich repeats and Ser/Thr runs; no signal in folded kinase domains.
- Potassium channel: activation on cytosolic disordered tails with poly-Asn and poly-Lys tracts; absent from transmembrane helices.
- ZDHHC-type palmitoyltransferase: activation on disordered N- and C-terminal regions with Asn-rich stretches (including NXS/T sequons), not in the DHHC catalytic core or TM segments.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regulatory regions of eukaryotic regulatory proteins—primarily transcription factors but also other gene‑expression and signaling regulators (e.g., RNA‑binding proteins, multidomain scaffolds)—especially acidic/Ser/Gly/Pro‑rich transactivation segments and flexible linkers/tails—while avoiding folded DNA‑binding, ligand‑binding, and other structured domains.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation across long IDRs with punctate residue‑level peaks; strongest in low‑pLDDT, coil segments enriched for E/D, S/P/G (often in acidic or compositionally biased runs); minimal to absent signal within structured domains (homeobox, forkhead, HMG, ETS, bHLH DBDs; zinc‑finger DBDs [C2H2/C4]; RRMs; PH/ANK repeats; ArfGAP catalytic domains; nuclear receptor LBDs); commonly spans N‑ and C‑terminal tails and inter‑domain linkers and often overlaps short linear motifs/PTM sites.
Exemplars:
- Homeobox transcription factors (e.g., CDX family): activation on disordered N‑ and C‑terminal low‑complexity regions; no activation in the homeobox DNA‑binding domain.
- Forkhead (FOX) transcription factors: activation confined to N‑/C‑terminal IDRs; forkhead DNA‑binding domain is inactive.
- SOX/HMG transcription factors: activation on C‑terminal low‑complexity transactivation region, including the 9aaTAD motif and a SUMO site; no activation in the HMG box.
- ETS family transcription factors: activation on N‑terminal IDRs, the linker between PNT and ETS domains, and C‑terminal tails; PNT and ETS domains are inactive.
- Nuclear receptors (e.g., SF‑1/FTZ‑F1): activation on the N‑terminal A/B (AF‑1) activation domain and disordered linkers; no activation in the zinc‑finger DBD or C‑terminal LBD.
- Plant transcription factors (various families): activation on acidic/Ser‑rich low‑complexity activation regions and disordered tails outside conserved DNA‑binding domains.
- RNA‑binding proteins (e.g., CIRP): activation on glycine‑rich low‑complexity tails and disordered segments outside RRMs.
- Multidomain ARF‑GAP/ANK/PH signaling proteins (e.g., AGAP1): activation on long disordered linkers and acidic/low‑complexity regions; no activation in PH, ANK, or ArfGAP domains.

Summary: Extended Gly/Ser/Thr–rich low‑complexity repeat segments, especially those forming or decorating extracellular polysaccharide‑directed architectures (e.g., right‑handed beta‑helix/pectate lyase–like solenoids in tail spikes/depolymerases and mucin‑like Ser/Thr‑rich stalks), i.e., a sequence‑level pattern favoring small/polar residues in long contiguous stretches across diverse taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous G/S/T‑enriched stretches (often spanning many repeats/rungs of a beta‑solenoid or mucin‑like low‑complexity segments), with occasional local boosts at short G/S/T‑rich motifs
Exemplars: - Bacteriophage tail spikes and capsule depolymerases: activation across right‑handed beta‑helix (pectate lyase–like) repeat rungs rich in small/polar residues (e.g., GGXGXD‑like hexapeptide repeats).
- Polysaccharide lyases/hyaluronidases (PL families): activation over the parallel beta‑helix core used to degrade extracellular glycosaminoglycans and pectins.
- Secreted carbohydrate‑active enzymes (glycosidases, transferases, dehydratases): activation on extended S/T/G‑rich extracellular/periplasmic segments and repeat/linker regions.
- Adhesion GPCRs/latrophilins: activation on the long N‑terminal mucin‑like Ser/Thr‑rich stalks preceding the GAIN/autoproteolysis module.
- Fungal ferric reductase family and other membrane oxidases: activation on lengthy extracytoplasmic Ser/Thr‑rich regions/loops.
- Exopolysaccharide biosynthesis and cell‑surface scaffold proteins: activation on periplasmic low‑complexity S/T/G‑rich linkers and repeats.
- Inteins (HINT‑domain splicing elements): activation across small/polar‑rich stretches within inteins and at Ser/Thr‑dependent splice junction regions.
- RNA 5′‑hydroxyl‑kinase complex proteins (NOL9/GRC3/CLP1): activation on G/S/T‑rich low‑complexity insertions and glycine/serine‑rich loops around the P‑loop/kinase core.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments—often N‑terminal tails or leader/signal regions—enriched in Ser/Pro/Gly/Arg and predicted as coils/low‑confidence structure; the feature marks flexible, poorly structured regions rather than a specific function
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered within disordered/low‑pLDDT regions, with regional enrichment in N‑terminal stretches; strongest on Pro/Ser (and other low‑complexity residues), minimal in well‑structured core domains
Exemplars: - Paramyxovirus nucleoproteins: activation across the N‑terminal intrinsically disordered tail (e.g., multiple peaks within an IDR of the measles N protein).
- Ribosomal proteins (uL13 family): peaks confined to the N‑terminal disordered extension; no activation in the structured core.
- Secreted toxin precursors (conotoxin precursors): activation in the signal/leader region and other low‑confidence segments of the precursor.
- Viral/retroelement ORF proteins with proline‑rich IDRs: strong peaks on Pro within annotated disordered regions and low‑confidence loops.
- Human regulatory/adapter‑like proteins (e.g., ST20): sparse peaks in a low‑confidence, N‑terminal helix/coil segment.
- Intrinsically disordered spermatogenesis‑associated proteins: multiple peaks across coil, low‑pLDDT regions throughout the sequence.
- Uncharacterized low‑complexity proteins (e.g., Wilms tumor upstream neighbor–like): prominent peaks in annotated disordered regions (e.g., C‑terminal IDRs), minimal in predicted helices.

Summary: Acidic, low-complexity intrinsically disordered regions (S/E/D/Q/N/P/G‑rich with scattered hydrophobic/aromatic residues), frequently at N-termini, that function as transcriptional activation domains or general acidic linear interaction regions for protein–protein binding across diverse proteins (regulators, scaffolds, and viral/effectors)
Activation pattern: Regional activation over low-complexity/acidic IDRs, often spanning long N‑terminal stretches; variable-length windows with diffuse peaks rather than sharp motif-specific spikes; can occur in multiple segments within a protein
Exemplars: - Eukaryotic transcription factors (bZIP, bHLH, zinc-finger, homeobox): N‑terminal acidic/Q/P-rich activation domains
- Transcriptional co-regulators and Mediator subunits: acidic/Q-rich IDRs that engage TFs and RNA Pol II
- Centrosomal/cytoskeletal coiled-coil scaffolds (e.g., pericentrin/CCDC/NPC components): acidic low-complexity linkers and termini flanking coiled-coils
- Viral regulatory and small membrane proteins: acidic cytosolic tails and transactivation regions
- Mycobacterial ESX/ESAT‑6 (WXG100) effectors: mixed acidic–aromatic segments (including WXG-region/acidic stretches) in small helical proteins
- Plant transcription factors (AP2/ERF, NAC, MYB): Q/N/E/P-rich N‑terminal activation regions

Summary: Serine-centered coil/turn micro-motif: the feature detects solvent‑exposed serine residues in short loops (often at secondary‑structure junctions) that frequently occur as closely spaced S/T-rich pairs or clusters in extracellular domains—sites characteristic of O‑linked glycosylation (including glycosaminoglycan attachment on proteoglycan core proteins)—and, in cytosolic proteins, as isolated loop serines with similar local chemistry (e.g., within BTB/POZ folds)
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks centered on serine with slight spillover to an adjacent residue (forming dipeptide signals); often appears as short clusters or adjacent pairs in S/T-rich segments; variable counts per protein (many in long extracellular regions, few in compact intracellular domains); examples include extremely focal activation on a KS dipeptide in a beta→alpha loop of a BTB/POZ domain and broader clusters in secreted/membrane precursors’ ectodomains
Exemplars: - Extracellular matrix proteoglycans (proteoglycan core proteins): activation on serines in SG-/S/T-rich motifs consistent with glycosaminoglycan attachment/O-linked glycosylation hotspots.
- Adhesion and matrix glycoproteins and mucin-like secreted proteins: activation across clustered S/T residues in low-complexity ectodomains (putative O-GalNAc sites).
- KCTD family BTB/POZ adaptors: isolated serine in a short loop at a beta–alpha junction near the N-terminus (e.g., KS dipeptide within the BTB core).

Summary: Generic low-complexity, intrinsically disordered sequence content enriched in small uncharged/hydrophobic residues (G, A, S, L, V, P), often at N termini of secreted precursors and pathogen effectors and in flexible loops/tails of viral and other proteins; occasionally overlaps simple secretion/targeting motifs (e.g., RxLR-dEER) but is not tied to a specific fold or function.
Activation pattern: Low-magnitude, residue-level peaks scattered across IDRs/low-pLDDT segments, sometimes forming short micro-clusters; occurs in coils, helices, or strands but consistently in low-confidence/flexible regions; frequently includes N-terminal segments and low-complexity tracts.
Exemplars: - Neuropeptide precursors (galanin): sparse peaks across the disordered N-terminal peptide and C-terminal associated peptide.
- Viral fusion glycoproteins (respiratory syncytial virus F): isolated residues in very low-pLDDT loops across mixed secondary structure.
- Integrase/recombinase-like proteins: peaks in flexible, Gly/Pro-rich disordered regions and annotated disorder segments.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation on the RxLR-dEER host-targeting region and within the N-terminal signal peptide.
- Testis-specific basic low-complexity proteins: scattered activations throughout predicted disordered regions.
- Secreted extracellular low-complexity proteins (cementoblastoma-derived protein 1): N-terminal disordered segment and helix–coil boundaries with low pLDDT.
- Viral major capsid proteins: residues within annotated disordered stretches and flexible C-terminal tails.

Summary: A structural microfeature: single small-residue hotspots (strongly Gly/Ala/Ser-biased) embedded in well-ordered beta-strands, most prominently recurring at two conserved strand positions of the GNAT (GCN5-related N‑acetyltransferase) fold, but generally marking small‑side‑chain–dependent sites in beta-sheets across diverse proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in beta-strands (DSSP E) with high structural confidence; typically 1–3 sites per protein. In GNAT/N-acetyltransferases, two recurrent peaks appear on separate strands (often in N-terminal ~50–80 and mid-sequence ~130–180 windows). Preference for Gly/Ala/Ser; occasional weaker peaks in adjacent coil.
Exemplars: - Arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase (AANAT): strongest on a glycine within a beta-strand (outside the annotated domain), with a secondary beta-strand site in the C-terminal GNAT region.
- Viral polyamine N-acetyltransferase: alanine and glycine on two beta-strands, the latter within the GNAT domain.
- NatA/NAA80 N-terminal acetyltransferase: a glycine hotspot on a GNAT beta-strand; minor secondary peak in nearby coil.
- Bacterial GNAT (AcuA): glycine on a beta-strand within the GNAT domain; weaker alanine just C-terminal to the domain.
- Aminoglycoside/streptothricin acetyltransferase (AAC): glycine and alanine on two separate GNAT beta-strands.
- tRNA(Met) cytidine acetyltransferase TmcA (GNAT module): alanine and tyrosine on GNAT beta-strands.
- Acyl-CoA thioesterase: a single alanine on a beta-strand; the same strand also contains a CoA-binding histidine.
- Lysylphosphatidylglycerol synthase component (LysX): localized to a leucine/alanine pair on a beta-strand within the lysyltransferase domain.

Summary: Low-complexity, Ser/Thr/Pro-rich intrinsically disordered segments found in N-terminal tails, propeptides, targeting presequences (signal/transit peptides), and flexible linkers—serving as mucin-like O-glycosylated stalks in secreted/viral proteins, as phosphorylation/degron-rich regulatory regions in cytosolic proteins, and as S/T-rich targeting peptides for secretion or organelle import.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous clusters, typically starting near the N-terminus and spanning disordered tails/linkers/presequences; strong preference for S/T runs and SP/TP dipeptides; D/E and Gly frequently co-occur but are not required (transit peptides can be acidic-poor); low activation in well-folded cores but may extend into the first adjacent β-strand (as seen in SecB).
Exemplars: - Viral structural/attachment proteins: activation on Ser/Thr/Pro-rich mucin-like stalks and propeptides.
- Integrin alpha subunits: activation on N-terminal prodomain/extracellular low-complexity segments.
- Cystatins (stefins/type 2 cystatins): activation on flexible N-terminal segments and PEST-/PTS-like tracts.
- Chaperones/co-chaperones (e.g., SecB, AHA1, ASF1A): activation on acidic/S/T-rich N- or C-terminal tails and adjacent first β-strand.
- BTB/POZ and MATH domain adaptors: activation on serine/proline-rich regulatory linkers/degrons tied to ubiquitination.
- DUF177A/YceD family: activation on acidic low-complexity loops/termini.
- Secreted Cu-only/Cu-Zn SOD-like proteins (fungi): activation on S/T-rich propeptides or mucin-like insertions.
- Adhesion and surface-binding proteins (including phage tailspikes/depolymerases): activation on extracellular low-complexity stalks/loops.
- RTP family membrane accessory proteins: activation on serine-rich low-complexity cytosolic regions.
- Archaeal gas vesicle protein O: activation on proline/acidic-rich disordered segments.
- Mitochondrial/chloroplast presequence-containing proteins (e.g., TIM21): activation on S/T-rich, often acidic-poor transit peptides.

Summary: Sensor of tandemly repeated, compositionally biased sequence architecture—preferentially Ser/Thr/Pro/Ala/Gln/Glu–rich low-complexity tracts (often intrinsically disordered in secreted or propeptide regions) and, more generally, the same short helical position repeated across modular domain arrays (e.g., the C‑terminal recognition helix segment of C2H2 zinc fingers).
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation across long, low-complexity repeats with strong periodic peaks on S/T/P/A/Q/E within repeat units (e.g., PAP, AQA/AQE); also residue-level periodic peaks at equivalent positions in each unit of tandem domain arrays; minimal activation in signal peptides, transmembrane helices, and structured catalytic cores.
Exemplars: Fungal cell-wall flocculins/adhesins: strong activation across central Ser/Thr-rich disordered tandem repeats, with peaks on Pro at repeat starts and on specific Ser (including PAP motif starts); Cathelicidin antimicrobial peptide precursors: activation confined to the disordered N‑terminal propeptide, absent in the signal peptide and mature peptide; Retrotransposon-like polyproteins: activation in the disordered N‑terminal low-complexity region with AQA/AQE repeats, peaking on Ala and Glu and avoiding transmembranes; C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factors: periodic 1–4 residue peaks in the C‑terminal portion of the alpha-helix within each finger across the array.

Summary: Polar/charged alpha-helical tracts (often low-complexity): E/D/K/R/S/T/N/Q-rich, low-aromatic segments occurring both in intrinsically disordered regions and as solvent-exposed helices within folded domains; these amphipathic/coiled-coil–like helices mediate oligomerization, nucleic-acid/protein binding, and assembly, especially in viral proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional—either long tracts in IDRs or multiple discrete peaks aligning to predicted alpha helices within charged segments of folded proteins; weak in hydrophobic/aromatic-dense cores.
Exemplars:
- Poxvirus morphogenesis/scaffold proteins: extended charged helical segments.
- Mononegavirus P and N/NP: charged coiled-coils and basic helix-prone RNA-binding tracts.
- Herpesvirus tegument/capsid/envelope (incl. gH/gL complexes): luminal charged helices for assembly.
- CRISPR Cas13a: polar/charged helical linkers and helix-rich surfaces flanking HEPN modules.
- Adenovirus DNA-binding/terminal/packaging proteins (incl. IIIa, terminal proteins): long charged helical segments.
- Bacterial type III secretion effectors: N-terminal charged, helix-prone secretion/chaperone-binding regions.
- Apicomplexan surface proteins: acidic/serine/asparagine repeat-rich helical stalks.
- Reoviridae/Bluetongue virus VP6 helicase: polar helices/linkers around the P-loop core.
- Plant ribosome-inactivating proteins (e.g., pokeweed antiviral protein): solvent-exposed acidic/basic helical surfaces.

Summary: A detector of tandemly repeated sequence units and domain arrays (“repeat-register” signal). It marks equivalent positions within each repeat across long tracts, activating strongly on disordered Ser/Thr/Pro-rich short repeats common in secreted glycoproteins and also on structured repeat modules such as EGF-like domains and C2H2 zinc fingers.
Activation pattern: Long regional activation across the entire repeat array with sharp, periodic residue-level peaks at a fixed offset within each repeat unit; minimal signal outside the repeats (e.g., signal peptides, transmembranes, unrelated domains). In EGF-like domains, peaks center on the loop/beta region between Cys2–Cys3, with secondary peaks on Pro immediately before a conserved Cys and near the domain C-terminus. In C2H2 zinc fingers, peaks occur at recognition-helix positions and selected beta-sheet residues, plus the Pro in the TGEKP linker; the coordinating Cys/His are not activated. In low-complexity mucin/HRGP/AGP tracts, peaks recur on specific Ser/Thr/Pro positions within 5–10 aa motifs; in neuropeptide precursors, they localize to core residues of each repeated mature peptide, avoiding basic processing linkers.
Exemplars: - Mucins (e.g., large extracellular mucins): periodic peaks across long disordered 10-aa repeat blocks; no activation in signal peptide, TM, or cytosolic tail.
- Neuropeptide precursors (e.g., Buccalin family): peaks on core residues within each tandem mature peptide; absent from signal/propeptide/linker segments.
- Plant hydroxyproline-rich/arabinogalactan proteins (HRGP/AGP): activation on Pro-centered motifs (e.g., PPVYP) within proline-rich, O-glycosylated repeats.
- Extracellular matrix proteins with EGF-like domain arrays (e.g., fibropellin/EGF-repeat proteins): repeated peaks at conserved intra-domain positions, especially between Cys2–Cys3 and at Pro-before-Cys; little signal in non-EGF modules.
- C2H2 zinc finger transcription factors: periodic peaks within each finger at recognition-helix and beta-sheet positions and on the TGEKP linker; no activation in KRAB domains or on coordinating Cys/His.

Summary: A general secondary-structure boundary signal: the feature marks short alpha-helical segments and helix/strand capping positions in well-folded, soluble domains—especially in regulatory HTH DNA-binding and two-component receiver (REC) domains—favoring acidic/polar (D/E/S/T) residues at caps/loops with leucines within the helix
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks localized to specific positions in helices and immediately adjacent loops (N-/C-caps) and at ends of beta-strands; enrichment for D/E/S/T with frequent leucines; domain-level bias toward structured, cytosolic regions (little/no activation in transmembranes or some catalytic effector domains); scattered, low-amplitude peaks elsewhere
Exemplars: - TetR-like HTH transcriptional repressors: activation at a coil-to-helix transition within the DNA-binding HTH motif (recognition-helix region).
- ECF sigma factors: peaks within the C-terminal HTH DNA-binding helices and a separate polymerase core–binding helix.
- Two-component response regulators (REC domains), including fusions with HD-GYP phosphodiesterases: activation on acidic residues in the REC active site (phospho-Asp and neighboring acidic loop/strand positions) and modestly in the inter-domain helical linker; no activation in the downstream HD-GYP catalytic domain.
- Antitoxin MazE family: a contiguous amphipathic helix in the helical bundle/dimerization region, strongest on an acidic residue within the helix.
- Short-chain dehydrogenase/reductases (SDR): isolated peaks at beta-strands and helix termini, including residues adjacent to the Rossmann-like fold and occasional NAD(P)-binding acidic/polar positions.
- Glycosyltransferases (GT folds): peaks at the C-terminus of beta-strands and adjacent coil in the cytosolic catalytic domain; absent from transmembrane segments.

Summary: Short, acidic/polar N-cap/turn motifs at the starts of alpha helices—most often near the protein N-terminus—enriched for D/E and S/T/G/A with a hydrophobic anchor (often L) and occasional Cys; recurrent sequence patterns include LCDT-like and W–G–T/P clusters; a general structural signal rather than a function-specific signature
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks in short clusters (2–8 aa) located at helix starts (N-cap/turn), frequently within the first ~70 residues; compositionally enriched for D/E and S/T/G/A with some L/I/V and occasional C; observed across diverse taxa and protein classes
Exemplars: BTB/POZ-domain proteins (ZBTB, KLHL/KBTBD/gigaxonin, KCTD): activation on an LCDT-like motif at the start of the first BTB helix; Rieske iron–sulfur proteins and Rieske-type oxygenases: activation on an N-terminal W–G–T/P cluster marking the first helix/turn; Purple acid phosphatases (PAPs): activation on short acidic S/T–D/E motifs immediately after signal peptides at the N-cap of the first helix; Phosphodiesterases: activation on D/E–S/T-rich clusters at the start of N-terminal helices in regulatory/catalytic regions; Epoxide hydrolases and other alpha/beta-hydrolases: activation on Gly/Thr/Asp-rich N-cap motifs at the first helix; RNA methyltransferases and tRNA-modifying enzymes: activation on acidic S/T clusters capping the initial helix of Rossmann-like cores; Small GTPases (ARF/ARL/Ras-like): activation around residues ~50–70 at the N-cap of helix α2 (Switch II), enriched in D/E and S/T; VPS29/retromer components: activation on short acidic/polar clusters capping an N-terminal helix

Summary: Residues at the loop-to–beta-strand transition (beta-strand N-cap), repeatedly arrayed across beta-rich architectures—especially beta-solenoids/beta-helices (including hexapeptide‑repeat left-handed beta-helices)—common in acyl/sugar‑lipid modification enzymes and extracellular adhesion/fiber proteins
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks at single positions immediately preceding beta-strands (occasionally the first strand residue); peaks often tile across long regions with ~6-residue periodic spacing in solenoid/helical repeats; strongest in well-structured domains but can also appear in low-confidence loops of long extracellular/fiber proteins; enriched for small residues (A, V, T, S, G, with frequent C)
Exemplars: - Hexapeptide-repeat acyltransferases (e.g., UDP-3-O-acylglucosamine N-acyltransferase/LpxA): repeated peaks at N-cap positions before successive beta-strands of the left-handed beta-helix core.
- Colanic acid exopolysaccharide acetyltransferases (WcaB-like): loop residues immediately N-terminal to beta-strands throughout the structured domain.
- Gamma-carbonic anhydrase: multiple N-cap peaks preceding beta-strands, including those adjacent to metal/substrate-binding strands.
- Nucleotide-sugar pyrophosphorylase/guanylyltransferase (Fucose-1-phosphate guanylyltransferase): clustered peaks in the C-terminal beta-sheet at coil-to-strand junctions and occasional first beta-strand residues.
- Phage receptor-binding/tail fiber proteins: sparser activation on C-terminal loop segments within beta-rich fiber regions.

Summary: Extended interaction-bearing regions that mediate binding to partners or small molecules—either intrinsically disordered, low-complexity acidic/S/T/P/G-rich tracts used as regulatory/scaffolding tails, or structured segments (often specific beta-strands/helix surfaces) that line effector or substrate-binding pockets
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional, long continuous activation. Strong on low-pLDDT coils enriched for Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly and acidic residues, frequently in C-terminal or inter-domain tails with PTM sites; also shows pronounced peaks across defined secondary-structure elements that form ligand/effector-binding surfaces (selected beta-strands and adjacent helices), while other structured domains (e.g., J domains, HTH DNA-binding modules) are comparatively weak.
Exemplars: - Hsp40/DnaJ cochaperones: inactive on the N-terminal J domain but strong across the central low-complexity G/F-like region and the C-terminal client-binding beta-sandwich, including residues important for activity.
- DNA polymerase delta subunit 3 (replication accessory factor): intense activation on the disordered C-terminal half containing the PCNA-interacting PIP-box and multiple phosphorylation/sumoylation sites.
- GntR/NagR transcriptional repressors: high activation throughout the structured C-terminal effector-binding domain (helices and strands) including ligand-contacting residues; little on the N-terminal HTH DNA-binding domain.
- Chorismate pyruvate-lyase (UbiC): selected beta-strands and an adjacent helix near the substrate-binding region are highlighted; other catalytic-site residues may be unmarked.
- Fatty acid-binding proteins: specific C-terminal beta-strands lining the hydrophobic ligand cavity (including some annotated binding residues) are activated, whereas non-cavity helices/loops are weak.

Summary: Serine/threonine–rich, low‑complexity intrinsically disordered segments (often N‑terminal), frequently containing proline/glycine, occurring in a subset of viral accessory/immune‑evasion proteins and secreted/extracellular or regulatory tails; these tracts act as flexible linkers and common modification hotspots (e.g., O‑glycosylation in secreted regions or phosphorylation in cytosolic tails). Presence depends on local S/T enrichment and disorder, not on protein class per se.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across short-to-long low‑complexity stretches with residue‑level peaks on S/T (often adjacent to P/G); strong N‑terminal bias; suppressed in well‑folded domains, cysteine‑rich defensins, and transmembrane helices; appears only when S/T‑rich LCRs are present and may be absent elsewhere in the same protein.
Exemplars: - Viral accessory/immune‑evasion proteins with cytosolic tails: activation on S/T/P‑rich disordered segments (e.g., EBV BNLF2a); many viral polyprotein/membrane regions without such tracts show no activation.
- Secreted mucin‑like/extracellular proteins and propeptides that are S/T‑rich: activation along low‑complexity repeats; cysteine‑stabilized peptides (e.g., defensins) typically do not activate.
- Testis/spermatogenesis‑associated proteins that carry S/T/P‑rich disordered N‑terminal tails: activated; those lacking such tracts are not.
- lncRNA‑derived micropeptides: activation only in S/T/G‑rich disordered sequences; those without S/T enrichment may not activate.
- Host immune/stress-response factors: activation on S/T‑rich regulatory IDRs; structured kinases without S/T‑rich tails show little to no activation.
- Bacterial/archaeal surface or secreted proteins: activation on S/T‑rich low‑complexity linkers between domains; absent otherwise.
- Core metabolic enzymes: rare activation, confined to S/T‑rich unstructured loops or termini; many enzymes show none.

Summary: Long, intrinsically disordered low‑complexity tandem‑repeat regions enriched in serine/threonine/proline and other small/polar/acidic residues (e.g., S/T/P/E/D/Q/G/A), including mucin‑like repeats, Q/P‑rich tracts, and acidic arrays; these segments act as flexible, repeat-based linkers or PTM‑rich scaffolds rather than folded domains.
Activation pattern: Extended regional activation across long disordered segments with periodic, residue‑level peaks that align to repeat units; highest peaks often occur on S/T/P within short motifs; little/no activation in structured catalytic domains.
Exemplars: - DExH-box RNA helicases: activation confined to long disordered C‑terminal tails with compositional bias and motifs (e.g., NLS), not the helicase core.
- Actin cytoskeletal scaffold/regulator (TRIO and F‑actin‑binding protein): strong, periodic activation across a central S/T‑rich low‑complexity repeat array with peaks every ~11–14 residues.
- Cancer/testis antigen–like low‑complexity proteins (Sarcoma antigen 1): multiple spaced peaks within Q/P‑rich motifs (e.g., SQPTP, GQPQ, QPQP) across unstructured regions.
- Inositol‑trisphosphate 3‑kinase C: activation in the N‑terminal intrinsically disordered regulatory segment with polar/charged low‑complexity tracts and phosphoserines; absent from the folded kinase domain.
- P‑selectin glycoprotein ligand‑1 (selectin ligand/mucin‑like glycoprotein): concentrated activation over extracellular decapeptide tandem repeats with periodic peaks (often at P/A) in the mucin‑like region.

Summary: Mature cores of small secreted peptide/protein domains—predominantly cysteine-stabilized folds (cystine-knot/chemokine/defensin/Kunitz-like), but also disulfide-poor secreted neuropeptides and compact secreted ecto/periplasmic domains—highlighting hydrophobic β-core and conserved turn motifs within the mature region.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks within the mature peptide segment (typically ~20–100 aa into the precursor), sparse per sequence; strongest on nonpolar/aromatic residues in β-strands and nearby turns of compact secreted domains; avoids signal peptides/propeptides; cysteines may or may not be included; in disulfide-poor neuropeptides, peaks fall on conserved hydrophobic/Pro/Gly/aromatic motifs.
Exemplars: (add to existing)
- Amidated neuropeptides (e.g., pigment-dispersing factor/PDF): activation on conserved hydrophobic/turn residues within the mature peptide.
- Viral envelope/entry proteins with compact secreted ectodomains (e.g., vaccinia OPG094): activation on β-core patches in the ectodomain.
- Bacterial pilotins/periplasmic lipoproteins (e.g., InvH): activation on β-strand hydrophobics within small periplasmic domains, whether or not disulfide-stabilized.

Summary: Exposed beta-strand and adjacent loop surfaces of beta-rich binding modules that mediate intermolecular recognition, common in secreted/extracellular and nucleic acid–binding proteins (e.g., Ig-like/discoidin-C2/CBM, jelly-roll/CUB, beta-propeller, and outer-membrane beta-barrels), including the RUNX/CSL DNA-binding cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across structured beta-domains (non-contiguous, multi-site), often on edge strands and loops; enriched for polar/charged residues (D/E/R/K/S/T) and conserved aromatics (notably tryptophan); typically one or more beta-rich domains per protein.
Exemplars: - RUNX family transcription factors: sparse peaks within the Runt DNA-binding domain on beta-strands and DNA-contacting loops.
- CSL (RBP-J) transcription factors: activation on the beta-rich DNA-binding core.
- PP1 glycogen-targeting regulatory subunits: activation over glycogen/starch-binding beta-sandwich CBMs associated with these regulators.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes: activation on carbohydrate-binding modules (discoidin/C2- and other CBMs) at strand/loop aromatics (often W) and polar residues that contact glycans.
- Secreted proteases (serine/metallo/cysteine): activation on accessory beta modules (CUB/discoidin/Ig-like) and hemopexin-like beta-propeller surfaces rather than catalytic motifs.
- Complement and thioester-containing proteins: activation on jelly-roll/CUB beta-domain surfaces involved in partner recognition.
- Notch pathway components: activation on EGF-like beta hairpins in ligands and on beta-rich DNA-binding domains in nuclear effectors.
- C2-domain and centrosomal scaffolding proteins: peaks on C2 beta-sandwich loops that coordinate Ca2+/phospholipid binding (acidic D/E clusters).
- Type III secretion pilotins: activation across outer-membrane beta-barrel strand/loop regions, including aromatic girdle residues.
- Thermophilic/archaeal secreted proteins: activation on beta-rich accessory domains associated with secreted proteases.

Summary: Intrinsic disorder/low-complexity signature: the feature marks flexible, low-confidence (low pLDDT) segments—most often terminal regions and propeptide/peptide-precursor stretches—rather than specific catalytic motifs, frequently in secreted or processing-prone proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered within predicted intrinsically disordered regions (often N-terminal), occasionally forming very short microsegments; activations are sparse and do not consistently align with annotated functional sites.
Exemplars: - Plant PROPEP/damage-peptide precursors: scattered peaks within a disordered C-terminal region that includes the bioactive peptide stretch.
- Serine protease zymogens (Peptidase S1/acrosin): multiple short peaks in low-confidence segments of the light chain and flexible strands within the catalytic domain.
- Eukaryotic regulatory proteins (e.g., ST20): weak, sparse activation across an intrinsically disordered N-terminus.
- Secreted peroxidases: multiple peaks in the N-terminal disordered segment upstream of the catalytic core, near but not on Ca2+-binding residues.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments enriched in glycine/proline and serine/threonine, often containing clusters of basic residues (Lys/Arg) and simple repeats; includes PTS- and GP-rich repeats in secreted/processed peptides and extracellular proteins, as well as basic, Ser/Arg‑rich viral and micropeptide regions. Activation requires extended low‑complexity tracts with these compositions; compact or acidic sequences lacking such tracts are typically not activated.

Exemplars:
- Subset of prohormone/neuropeptide and venom peptide precursors that have extended low‑complexity, P/S/T‑ and GP‑rich prosegments with multiple polybasic (Lys/Arg) convertase sites and Gly‑amidation motifs; compact or acidic precursors lacking such tracts (e.g., KiSS‑1) may show little activation.
- Collagens and collagen‑like proteins: strong activation over Gly–X–Y (Gly/Pro‑rich) triple‑helix repeats and adjacent propeptides.
- Mucin‑like secreted proteins: activation on PTS‑rich tandem repeats (Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich, O‑glycosylation targets).
- Cationic antimicrobial/defense peptides: activation across Lys/Arg‑rich, low‑complexity stretches.
- Subset of viral small accessory/nucleocapsid proteins with Ser/Arg‑rich, Pro/Gly‑rich disordered tails and low‑complexity regions; proteins lacking these features (e.g., acidic ICP47‑like proteins) may not activate.
- Plant glycine‑rich/proline‑rich cell‑wall proteins: activation over repetitive GP/low‑complexity segments.
- Subset of uncharacterized human microproteins/antisense ORF peptides that are globally low‑complexity and/or basic.
- Cytoskeletal/adaptor proteins with proline‑rich regions: activation on PRR/SH3‑binding low‑complexity segments and flanks.
- Bacterial secreted low‑complexity repeat proteins: activation on Gly/Pro‑rich repeats and polybasic tracts.

Summary: Basic side chains (Lys/Arg, occasionally His) embedded in alpha-helical contexts, i.e., cationic helical residues that form positive patches in DNA-recognition helices, coiled-coil rods, and transmembrane helices/adjacent cytosolic loops; the signal reflects helical positive charge rather than a specific sequence motif.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on Lys/Arg with a strong bias for alpha-helical regions; peaks cluster within DNA-binding helices (HTH/homeodomains, sigma domains 2/4), are distributed along long coiled-coils, and appear inside TM helices and at helical ends/loops on the cytosolic or matrix/IMS sides; activations on acidic residues are rare.
Exemplars: - ECF sigma factors: Arg residues in sigma domain 2 and domain 4, especially within and immediately after the DNA-binding helix–turn–helix recognition helix.
- Homeobox transcription factors: Lys/Arg within the homeodomain (including the recognition helix) and sparsely in disordered N-terminal segments.
- Myosin heavy-chain coiled-coils: numerous discrete Lys/Arg peaks spread across the rod-like S2/LMM coiled-coil.
- Mitochondrial SLC25 carriers: Lys/Arg within transmembrane helices and at matrix/intermembrane-space helical ends and loops (including modified Lys).
- Niacin/nicotinamide transporters (NiaP family): Arg/Lys in multiple transmembrane helices and connecting cytosolic loops.

Summary: Sequence contexts marking disulfide-bonded cysteines in secreted/extracellular proteins—cysteine pairs/clusters (often flanked by Gly/Pro) that form stabilizing disulfide frameworks typical of toxins, antimicrobial peptides, protease inhibitors, neuropeptide/hormone/pheromone peptides, and viral envelope ectodomains.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks at or immediately adjacent to disulfide-bonded cysteines; compact, contiguous activation across the cystine framework in short disulfide-rich peptides; multiple peaks scattered across ectodomains of large secreted glycoproteins; minimal activation in signal peptides, transmembranes, or cytosolic regions.
Exemplars: - AB toxins (pertussis toxin B subunit): peaks next to disulfide-forming cysteines within the mature chain.
- Venom disulfide-rich toxins (conotoxins; scorpion α/β-toxins; spider ω/κ-toxins): activation tracks the canonical Cys frameworks.
- Defensins and other CSαβ antimicrobial peptides: activation on the conserved disulfide pairs.
- Kunitz- and Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors: peaks around the conserved disulfide-bonded cysteines stabilizing the inhibitory fold.
- Neuropeptide hormones/pheromones with intrachain/interchain disulfides (e.g., insulin family, oxytocin/vasopressin): activation at the disulfide-forming Cys and neighboring Gly/Pro.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: multiple peaks across ectodomain cysteine clusters and Cys–Gly/Pro motifs.
- Secreted nematode extracellular/ECM-associated cysteine-rich proteins: activation over disulfide-stabilized modules.

Summary: A general marker of short, structured functional hotspots—most often alpha-helical elements within folded domains or transmembrane helices—that either contain or lie immediately adjacent to catalytic residues, DNA/ligand/metal-binding sites, protein–protein interaction/secretion motifs (e.g., ESX/WXG), or correspond to the bioactive mature segment of secreted peptides.
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks enriched in high-confidence alpha-helices (including TM helices), with occasional peaks in nearby beta-strands or loops; frequently within a few residues of annotated active/binding/interaction motifs; in secreted precursors, restricted to the mature peptide region; not specific to particular amino-acid types.
Exemplars:
- GNAT/N-acetyltransferases: peaks on a catalytic-site helix and neighboring strand adjacent to the catalytic Tyr/Glu.
- ECF sigma factors (sigma70 domain 4): peaks on the DNA-binding helix-turn-helix recognition helix.
- Tyrosine recombinases/integrases: a strong peak on the helix immediately N-terminal to the catalytic tyrosine in the recombinase domain.
- Shikimate kinase: peaks on a substrate-binding Arg and a Mg2+-binding Asp, plus nearby structured residues.
- Thymidylate kinase: peaks on internal alpha-helical elements of the kinase core outside the annotated ATP-binding loop.
- Encapsulin cargo/ferritin-like di-iron proteins: peaks on the di-iron His/Fe-binding motif and adjacent helical residues.
- Neuropeptide hormone precursors (e.g., pancreatic polypeptide): activation confined to the helical mature hormone segment, absent from signal/propeptide regions.
- Fo ATP synthase subunit c: peaks on the transmembrane helix near the essential proton-binding acidic residue.
- ESAT-6/ESX small secreted helical proteins: peaks on the helix–hairpin (WXG) secretion/interaction motif and adjacent helices.

Summary: N-terminal intrinsically disordered, low-complexity tails enriched in polar/charged (and often Pro-rich) residues—non-hydrophobic segments that act as flexible targeting/binding/secretion signals or assembly/linker arms across diverse proteins (e.g., RNA/DNA-binding tails, T3/T6SS secretion/chaperone-binding regions, and acidic linker arms)
Activation pattern: Regional activation: short contiguous blocks at the extreme N-terminus (frequently starting at Met1), sometimes with additional internal low-complexity segments
Exemplars: - Viral nucleoproteins (negative-strand RNA viruses): activation on basic, disordered N-terminal RNA-binding tails that initiate nucleic acid engagement and oligomerization
- Poxvirus OPG accessory proteins: activation on low-complexity N-terminal regions mediating host interaction/localization
- Type III secretion system effectors: activation on the non-Sec N-terminal secretion/chaperone-binding signal (short, Ser/Thr/Pro- and charge-rich IDR)
- Type VI secretion effectors: activation on disordered N-termini required for loading/targeting to the apparatus
- DNA defense proteins (restriction–modification nucleases, CRISPR-associated factors): activation on charged N-terminal tails that contact DNA or recruit partner proteins
- Anti-CRISPR proteins: activation on flexible N-termini used to bind and inhibit CRISPR effector complexes
- Second-messenger signaling enzymes (GGDEF/EAL/HD-GYP families): activation on polar N-terminal regulatory/linker segments preceding catalytic domains
- Phage replication/repair proteins (e.g., primases, helicases, SSB-like proteins): activation on basic/disordered N-terminal DNA-binding tails
- Viral capsid/assembly proteins: activation on N-terminal low-complexity arms used for assembly or host factor binding
- Cyanobacterial phycobilisome linker and light-harvesting proteins: activation on acidic N-terminal arms that mediate complex assembly

Summary: A signal for specific C-terminal beta-sheet/loop modules enriched in small/flexible residues with GP/PG/PP motifs—seen in a subset of fungal PIR C-termini that retain GP/PG/PP-rich beta-capping segments, in a subset of CNH-domain tails of RhoGEFs with similar compositional bias, and in short beta-strand capping segments in some nuclear factors—rather than a general detector of beta-sandwich/propeller folds.
Activation pattern: Long, contiguous activation with a strong C-terminal bias that often strengthens toward the extreme C-terminus; absent on long alpha-helical regions and on canonical WD-repeat beta-propellers, Smad MH2 domains, Polo-box domains, and catalytic metalloprotease domains. In single-pass membrane proteins, narrow peaks may occur only in gly/pro/ser-rich extracellular loops immediately N-terminal to the transmembrane helix and only for specific paralogs (e.g., Shisa5, but not Shisa6). PIR family members lacking the GP/PG/PP-rich C-terminal module are not expected to activate.
Exemplars: 
- Fungal PIR mannoproteins: activation on the GP/PG/PP-biased C-terminal beta-strand domain after the PIR repeat block; PIR paralogs lacking this compositional signature (e.g., some CIS3-like variants) may be inactive.
- Dbl-family RhoGEFs: activation primarily on CNH tails that display gly/pro/ser/thr–biased loops; DH and many PH-only segments remain inactive.
- Nuclear factors such as NC2/CTF-like: activation confined to short C-terminal beta-sheet caps; other clamp-loader partners (e.g., DCC1) may be inactive without the compositional signature.
- Exclusions: WD40 beta-propellers (e.g., CFAP57), Smad MH2 beta-sandwiches (e.g., SMAD4), Polo-box domains/kinase cores (e.g., PLK1), and secreted catalytic metalloproteases (e.g., MMPs) are not expected to activate.

Summary: Detector of β-strand residues in well-ordered β-sheet regions across diverse protein folds (β-barrels, β-sandwiches, and mixed α/β cores), largely independent of specific function
