Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks restricted to DSSP E segments within structured domains; sparse signals distributed across multiple β-strands per protein; minimal to absent in helices, disordered/low-confidence regions, and transmembrane helices
Exemplars: - DNA polymerase III β sliding clamp: discrete residues on several β-strands across the clamp; no signal on helices
- RNA polymerase-associated LEO1: activation only in the C-terminal β-sheet block; silent across the long disordered N-terminus and adjacent helices
- Fatty acid-binding proteins (FABPs): subset of residues on β-barrel strands; not on helices or loops and not aligned with the ligand-binding pocket
- Type II secretion system GspC: periplasmic β-strand residues highlighted; no activation in the cytosolic segment or the single transmembrane helix
- Type IV pilin major subunit: central β-sheet residues marked; silent on the long N-terminal helical/TM region and modified sites
- Small heat shock proteins/alpha-crystallins: β-sandwich (alpha-crystallin domain) strands
- MBT/Polycomb Royal family chromatin proteins: β-strands within the MBT/Tudor-like β-sandwich
- TATA-binding protein (TBP/TBP-like): β-sheet residues in the saddle-shaped core
- Autophagy E2 (UBC) enzymes: positions on the central β-sheet of the UBC fold
- NifU/NFU iron–sulfur scaffold proteins and Rieske proteins: β-strand elements in their soluble domains
- Gram-negative envelope/secretion components: β-strand-rich periplasmic domains (as in GspC)

Summary: Short hydrophobic transmembrane-like helices used for membrane targeting/insertion (signal peptides, signal-anchors, and tail-anchors), enriched for I/V/M/F runs and often marking the initiator methionine when N-terminal. While strongest at the N-terminus (SRP-recognized h-regions), the feature also flags analogous hydrophobic segments elsewhere, including C-terminal tail-anchors and early TMs following organelle-targeting sequences, across diverse proteins (viral membrane/accessory proteins, secreted peptide/toxin precursors, small human sORFs/microproteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous hydrophobic runs (~10–25 aa), strongest near termini (especially starting at M1) and in low-pLDDT coil/helix; residue-level peaks on I, V, M, F (occasional T), comparatively weaker on Leu; rare on charged/polar residues.
Exemplars: - Secreted serpins and peptide/toxin precursors: activation on N-terminal signal peptide h-regions.
- Viral small membrane/accessory proteins: activation on N-terminal TM-like segments or signal-anchors.
- Tail-anchored apoptosis proteins (e.g., PUMA): activation on C-terminal tail-anchor.
- Mitochondrial inner-membrane proteins (e.g., YME1-like): activation on the first hydrophobic TM after an N-terminal targeting segment.
Note: Occasional weak activation can occur on short hydrophobic patches in otherwise soluble proteins.

Summary: Secretory-pathway extracellular proteins and peptide precursors enriched for disulfide-bonded cysteines and/or secretory maturation motifs (dibasic Lys/Arg convertase sites, double-glycine leaders, prepilin class III signals); includes secreted toxins/venoms and hormones, OBPs, viral envelope glycoproteins, bacteriocins/lantibiotics, mucins, GPI-anchored proteins, pilins, ER luminal disulfide-folding factors, and some glycine-rich antimicrobial peptides.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks on cysteines (and nearby Pro/Gly in turns) and on maturation/processing motifs (KR/RR cleavage sites, GG leaders, prepilin signals) within secreted regions, with broader regional activation across cysteine-rich ectodomains or mature peptide segments; minimal activation in cytosolic regions; low-Cys glycine-rich peptides can activate via leader/processing signals and Pro/Gly-rich turns.
Exemplars:
- Disulfide-rich animal venom peptides (knottins, Kunitz, three-finger toxins): activation on conserved cysteine arrays and KR/RR propeptide cleavage sites.
- Insect odorant-/pheromone-binding proteins: activation on the canonical six-cysteine OBP motif and around the signal peptide/cleavage region.
- Viral envelope/entry glycoproteins (e.g., hemagglutinins, class I fusion proteins): activation on ectodomain cysteine pairs and polybasic furin sites at activation cleavages.
- ER oxidative folding enzymes (protein disulfide-isomerases, Ero1/Prx4): activation on signal peptides and catalytic CXXC/adjacent cysteine-rich motifs in luminal domains.
- Neuropeptide/hormone preproproteins (insulin-like peptides, POMC/other prohormones): activation on multiple dibasic convertase sites and the disulfide-bonded mature peptide region.
- Bacteriocin/lantibiotic precursors: activation on double-glycine leader peptides and cysteines that form lanthionine/disulfide linkages in the core.
- Secreted protease inhibitors and cysteine-rich peptides (cystatins, Kunitz-type inhibitors, plant defensins/trypsin inhibitors): activation on signal peptides and canonical disulfide motifs.
- GPI-anchored extracellular proteins (uPAR/LY6/three-finger and related): activation on cysteine-rich domains and the C-terminal GPI-attachment signal region.
- Mucin and mucin-like secreted glycoproteins: activation on cysteine-rich N-/C-terminal domains (CysD/EGF/SEA) and nearby basic processing segments; Pro/Gly-rich repeats show weaker broad signal.
- Bacterial type IV pilins and AB-type toxins: activation on prepilin class III signal peptides with basic N-regions and hydrophobic cores, and on inter-chain disulfides/Sec signal peptides plus RR/KR-like activation sites in A–B toxins.
- Plant glycine-rich antimicrobial peptides: activation on signal peptides and basic/leader processing segments; mature cores may be low in cysteine.

Summary: Intrinsic-disorder/low-complexity detector: recognizes long, compositionally biased segments—often arranged as tandem repeats—enriched in Ser/Thr/Asn and/or charged residues; frequently found in mucin-like/adhesive extracellular repeat domains and propeptide linkers of secreted precursors, as well as unstructured cytosolic tails or N‑terminal regulatory extensions of intracellular proteins; avoids well-folded domains, transmembrane helices, and signal peptides.
Activation pattern: Broad regional activation across extended IDRs with periodic, low-level banding that aligns to repeat unit spacing; occasional sharper peaks at repeat consensus positions or peptide boundaries; little to no activation in structured domains, TM segments, signal peptides, or disulfide-bonded modules.
Exemplars: - Mucin family extracellular VNTR domains: strong activation across O-/N-glycosylated tandem repeats, none in SEA domain, TM helix, or cytoplasmic tail.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., maximin/AMP proproteins): activation on low-complexity propeptide linkers and at starts of mature peptides within largely disordered precursors.
- Agglutination/adhesion repeat proteins: periodic activation over long arrays of ~35-aa repeats, highlighting conserved positions (e.g., Lys/Ile/Thr) in flexible beta/coil regions.
- Eggshell matrix proteins (ovocleidin-like): activation in disordered, compositionally biased C-terminal segments (basic/acidic, Ser/Thr/Asn-rich), absent at structured/disulfide sites.
- Metal ion transporters (vacuolar zinc transporter): strong activation in disordered cytosolic N-termini and C-terminal tails; no activation in transmembrane helices or structured cytosolic domains.
- Histone acetyltransferases (HATs): activation confined to N-terminal low-complexity repeat blocks of regulatory regions, not in the catalytic core.

Summary: Disordered, low-complexity tails and leader-like regions, typically enriched in Ser/Thr and often Lys/Arg. These are most often N-terminal signal/transit peptides and immediately downstream segments (propeptides, mucin-like repeats), but can also be short basic/disordered tails at protein termini or internal low-complexity linkers of soluble proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation frequently begins at or near the initiator Met with long continuous stretches and residue-level peaks around signal-peptide cleavage sites and within S/Thr-rich runs; activation also occurs on other disordered terminal tails or linkers (not contingent on secretion), and tapers as structured domains begin; strongest in low pLDDT segments.
Exemplars:
- Secreted subtilisin-like proteases: activation over the signal peptide and peaking just after the cleavage site into the disordered propeptide.
- Apicomplexan mucin-like/repeat-rich surface antigens and adhesins: activation on S/Thr-rich, low-complexity N-termini following signal peptides.
- Viral envelope, capsid, and small regulatory proteins: activation on N-terminal signal peptides and/or basic, disordered N-terminal tails.
- Channels/transporters and small integral membrane proteins: activation on disordered S/Thr-rich N-terminal cytosolic or luminal tails, including signal anchors.
- Plastid-associated proteins (e.g., plastid RNA polymerase subunits in green algae): activation on low-complexity Ser/Thr- and/or Lys/Arg-rich N-terminal extensions.
- tRNA/rRNA modification/processing enzymes: activation on low-complexity, basic and S/Thr-rich N-terminal extensions used for targeting or nucleic-acid-interacting tails.
- Cytosolic metabolic/regulatory and nucleic-acid enzymes (e.g., NadR, topoisomerase I, octanoyltransferase): activation on short Lys/Arg-rich disordered terminal tails or internal low-complexity linkers.
- Antimicrobial/toxin peptides and bacteriocins: activation on N-terminal leader/signal peptides (including Sec-type or double-glycine leaders) preceding the mature toxin.

Summary: Short intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments—often terminal tails or propeptide-like stretches—enriched in small/polar residues (S/T/G/A) and Pro, frequently containing charged patches (Lys/Arg clusters) and occasional Cys; these regions occur in small/viral proteins and in secreted or membrane-associated proteins, while structured domains and transmembrane helices remain largely unactivated.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short (∼10–40 aa) low‑complexity stretches, typically at N- or C-termini but also in internal flexible segments; residue-level peaks on Gly/Pro/Ser/Thr and neighboring charged residues in coil/low-confidence regions; little to no activation within folded domains or transmembrane helices.
Exemplars: - Peroxisome biogenesis factor PEX10 family: activation confined to the disordered cytosolic C‑terminal tail; no activation on transmembrane helices or the RING Zn‑finger domain.
- Cysteine-rich secreted toxins/effectors (e.g., defensin-like and cystine-knot toxins): activation on low-complexity N‑terminal signal/propeptide regions with basic clusters, not on the compact disulfide-bonded core.
- Viral small accessory proteins and micropeptides: activation on Ser/Pro/Gly‑rich, low‑complexity termini and internal stretches.
- Eukaryotic peptide hormone/defensin/toxin precursors and other secreted protein precursors: activation on low‑complexity prosegments harboring dibasic processing motifs.
- Type I membrane proteins and transporters/receptors: activation on unstructured cytosolic or luminal tails; transmembrane segments remain silent.
- Uncharacterized micropeptides and annotated fragments: activation across remaining low‑complexity/disordered regions.

Summary: Generic hydrophobic/packing signal: selects small/apolar residues in well-ordered secondary structure (alpha-helices, beta-strands, and transmembrane segments) that stabilize folds and line or flank ligand-binding pockets across many protein families, rather than targeting catalytic residues themselves.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks dispersed across structured domains; enriched on helices/strands and transmembrane segments; sparse in disordered tails; broad, multi-peak coverage rather than a single motif.
Exemplars: - Ser/Thr protein kinases (Hanks family, bacterial eSTKs): scattered peaks across the kinase domain on hydrophobic positions within helices/strands; avoids the catalytic Lys/Asp; little to none in disordered C-termini.
- Two-component histidine kinases: numerous peaks across the cytosolic HATPase_c/HisKA region (helices, sheets, coils); minimal in N-terminal TM/HAMP; does not emphasize the phospho-His.
- Rab-family small GTPases: peaks at small/hydrophobic residues flanking the P-loop, Switch I/II, and NKxD regions, reflecting packing around the nucleotide pocket rather than the catalytic switch residues.
- Membrane channels/transporters (e.g., fluoride channels): continuous activation over hydrophobic transmembrane helices.
- Helical repeat scaffolds (ankyrin repeats, plant PPR proteins): recurrent activation at hydrophobic core positions along the stacked helices that stabilize the repeats.
- Serine proteases (trypsin-like): activation on hydrophobic residues in the beta-barrel core and helical segments, not on the catalytic triad.
- Nonribosomal peptide synthetases/siderophore synthetases: widespread peaks across modules corresponding to hydrophobic cores of their alpha/beta subdomains.
- Bacterial HTH repressors: activation on hydrophobic residues within the DNA-binding helix and dimerization/interface helices.

Summary: Tryptophan‑anchored aromatic micro‑motifs—especially GxW/GW and closely spaced W–aromatic pairs (WY/WF)—most often found near the N‑terminus of secreted/extracellular proteins; includes the canonical lipocalin/plastoglobulin GxW signature and GW‑repeat modules on bacterial cell surfaces, but generally fires on short W‑rich motif patches across diverse proteins
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks on short (≈5–25 aa) segments, often multiple per protein; strongly enriched for W with preceding glycine (GxW/GW) and neighboring aromatics (WY/FY/WF); frequently located just after the signal peptide in secreted proteins, but also in internal loops/repeats
Exemplars: - Lipocalin superfamily: activates on the conserved N‑terminal GxW signature motif
- Plant plastid‑lipid‑associated proteins (fibrillins/plastoglobulins): activates on their conserved GxW motif
- Nitrobindin/peroxynitrite isomerase–like proteins (lipocalin‑like fold): activates on the lipocalin‑type GxW region
- Gram‑positive cell‑surface proteins with GW repeats/LTA‑binding modules and iron/heme acquisition factors: activates on repeated GW/GxW motifs in exported cell‑wall regions
- Secreted proteases and protease inhibitors: activates on W‑rich patches near the mature N‑terminus or exposed loops
- Autophagy‑related protein 2 (ATG2) family: activates on scattered GW/WxW/WY motifs within long disordered segments
- F‑box/WD40 E3 ubiquitin pathway proteins: activates on short W‑centered motifs within WD‑repeat/propeller blades (e.g., WD with adjacent WY/WF/GxW)

Summary: Glycine hotspots within β-strands of MORN repeat arrays (ALS2C-like, junctophilins) and some ciliary radial-spoke proteins with MORN-like repeats, yielding one sharp peak per repeat; other families show at most weak/occasional signal.
Activation pattern: Periodic residue-level peaks at a single conserved Gly in each MORN unit; negligible activation in non-MORN regions and in unrelated domains (e.g., kinase cores, SET domains, LPS assembly components, generic cysteine-rich/EGF modules).
Exemplars:
- MORN-repeat proteins (ALS2C-like, junctophilins): strong glycine peak per MORN unit.
- Ciliary/flagellar radial spoke head proteins with MORN/MORN-like repeats: similar periodic glycine peaks.
- Other families (EGF-like repeats, PE-PGRS, kinases, LPS assembly) are not defining and typically show weak activation in held-outs.

Summary: Membrane‑inserting effector segments that mediate pore formation, membrane fusion, or transient membrane insertion for toxin translocation—short to mid‑length hydrophobic/amphipathic helices or β‑hairpins that become membrane‑embedded upon activation (often after proteolytic cleavage or oligomerization) across pore‑forming toxins, MACPF/gasdermins, viral fusogens, and related membrane‑active peptides
Activation pattern: Regional activation with sharp residue‑level peaks: contiguous (~20–60 aa) low‑pLDDT segments enriched in small hydrophobics/glycine; frequently at N‑terminal effector regions or immediately downstream of activation/cleavage sites; maps to α‑helical fusion/pore‑forming modules, β‑hairpin transmembrane elements, or translocation helices; can appear as two separate peaks corresponding to twin β‑hairpins in MACPF proteins
Exemplars (edits):
- Bacteriocins and circular antimicrobial peptides — amphipathic insertion helices/loops used for membrane permeabilization or translocation (includes large colicins).
- Colicin nuclease bacteriocins — N‑terminal translocation helix/loop that transiently inserts into membranes to enable import (e.g., Colicin D).

Summary: A broadly tuned “polar low‑complexity/structure‑edge” signature: the feature detects Ser/Thr/Asn/Gln–rich, Gly/Pro–tolerant segments and secondary‑structure boundary motifs (helix caps and helix↔β transitions). It is common in large, repeat‑rich extracellular/surface proteins but also marks solvent‑exposed helices and strand edges in diverse proteins, while sparing strongly hydrophobic core transmembrane stretches.
Activation pattern: Diffuse, low‑amplitude regional activation across long S/T‑ and Q/N‑enriched low‑complexity tracts and simple repeats, punctuated by residue‑level peaks at helix‑capping sites and helix→β transitions; broadly distributed along sequences rather than termini; weak or absent within pore‑lining or highly hydrophobic TM cores.
Exemplars: - Two‑pore potassium channels (K2 family): activation on specific solvent‑exposed helices and a helix‑to‑β‑strand transition; absent on the pore‑forming transmembrane helix and other hydrophobic TM cores.
- Secreted or surface‑anchored mucin‑like/extracellular glycoproteins: activation along extended S/T‑rich, Q/N‑rich low‑complexity O‑glycosylation tracts and simple repeats.
- Large repeat‑rich surface or ECM/cell‑wall–like proteins from diverse taxa: activation spread across polar low‑complexity segments interspersed with glycine/proline‑containing turns.

Summary: Beta-sheet ligand-binding and adhesion/scaffold domains, with strongest activation on calycin family barrels (lipocalins, fatty-acid–binding proteins, avidin/streptavidin, nitrophorins) and, more broadly, on structurally related secreted beta-sandwich modules (lectins, NEAT heme/iron binders, thrombospondin type-1/CUB repeat regions in ECM and ADAM/ADAMTS/snake venom metalloproteinases, and fungal/bacterial adhesins). Similar activation also occurs in select intracellular beta-rich ligand-binding scaffolds (e.g., frataxin-like iron binders; some F-box adaptors with WD/Kelch repeats or Ser/Thr-rich low-complexity segments). The feature favors aromatic-lined binding surfaces and Ser/Thr/Gly-rich repeat segments typical of these domains.
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation across long contiguous regions corresponding to beta-barrel/sandwich folds or arrays of extracellular repeats; local peaks often coincide with Trp/Tyr motifs (e.g., WxxW) and Ser/Thr/Gly-rich stretches in binding/adhesive loops, and in some intracellular cases on acidic/beta-rich surfaces for metal binding or S/T-rich low-complexity segments.
Exemplars: • Lipocalins and nitrophorins (odorant/retinol/pheromone binders; NO/heme lipocalins): activation over the beta-barrel forming the ligand pocket
• Fatty acid–binding proteins (FABPs): activation across the 10-stranded calycin barrel
• Avidin/streptavidin biotin binders: activation across the beta-barrel that creates the high-affinity biotin site
• Plant chloroplastic lipocalins (TIL/CHL) and plastid-lipid–associated fibrillins: activation on the lipocalin-like lipid-binding core
• Bacterial lipocalin-like and lysozyme-inhibitor proteins (e.g., Blc, MliC/PliC): activation on the small beta-barrel/sandwich inhibitory/binding domain
• Heme/iron/NO extracellular binders (nitrophorins; NEAT-domain hemophores): activation on the aromatic-rich beta-sandwich regions that coordinate porphyrin/NO
• Lectins (legume/jelly-roll, galectin/PA14-like): activation on carbohydrate-binding beta-sandwich domains with aromatic stacking residues
• ADAM/ADAMTS and snake venom metalloproteinases: activation on ancillary thrombospondin type-1 (and CUB) repeat regions mediating ECM binding, not the metalloprotease active site
• Protease inhibitors (e.g., Kunitz/cystatin/WAP families): activation across the beta-sheet inhibitory folds that present aromatic/Ser/Thr-rich contact loops
• Extracellular matrix/adhesion and EGF/TSR-repeat proteins; fungal/yeast cell-wall adhesins: activation across Ser/Thr/Gly-rich, Trp/Tyr-studded repeat arrays that mediate adhesion/glycan interactions
• Frataxin-like iron-binding proteins: activation on the acidic beta-sheet surface that mediates iron handling
• F-box E3 adaptor subfamilies with WD/Kelch beta-propellers or Ser/Thr-rich low-complexity regions: activation on beta-rich blades or S/T/G-enriched segments

Summary: Basic polycationic patches enriched in arginine (often with lysine) within low-complexity/disordered regions, frequently N-terminal. These include classical monopartite NLSs, nucleic acid–binding basic tails, signal peptide n-regions and cytosolic juxtamembrane segments (positive-inside rule), and basic clusters in secreted precursors; typically depleted of acidic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation with strong residue-level peaks across contiguous basic runs; N-terminal bias; minimal Asp/Glu, Arg>Lys preference; predominantly in low-pLDDT segments and outside/adjacent to transmembranes on the cytosolic side; observed across viruses, bacteria, plants, and humans.
Exemplars:
- Viral regulators and capsid/accessory proteins: arginine-rich NLSs and nucleic acid–binding basic tails.
- Human regulators (e.g., ARF/Killin): arginine-rich disordered N-termini for targeting/interactions.
- Secreted zymogens and peptides (e.g., trypsinogen/PROPEPs): basic n-regions/dibasic clusters in pre/pro-sequences.
- Membrane proteins (transporters, respiratory chain subunits like ND2, ECF S-components): cytosolic basic patches consistent with the positive-inside rule.

Summary: Surface‑exposed coil/turn segments at β‑strand junctions on protein surfaces, enriched in (but not limited to) extracytoplasmic domains; includes ectodomain loops of Ig/FnIII and GOLD β‑sandwiches, extracellular loops of single‑ and multi‑pass membrane proteins, and surface loops of secreted and cytosolic enzymes; avoids transmembrane helices and buried catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks on solvent‑exposed loops adjacent to β‑strands, enriched for S, T, D, E, G, P; scattered across long ectodomains of single‑pass receptors and present on exposed loops of multi‑pass channels and soluble enzymes; low in transmembrane helices, signal peptides, and interior catalytic motifs; prefers structured loop/junction regions over long low‑complexity/disordered stretches.
Exemplars: Receptor‑type PTPRs—FnIII loop segments; Cytokine receptors and RTKs—ectodomain loops in Ig/FnIII/stalk regions; p24/TMED—luminal GOLD loop/β‑junctions; Lysyl‑oxidase family—short surface coils near cofactor sites; Ig/FnIII adhesion proteins—turns on β‑sandwich surfaces; ECM enzymes/modifiers—surface loops near but not at catalytic motifs; Viral/phage structural proteins—exposed capsid loops; Bacterial surface/periplasmic proteins—extracytoplasmic loop segments; Cytosolic enzymes (e.g., calpains, β‑glucosidases)—solvent‑exposed loops away from catalytic residues.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity regulatory segments enriched in acidic/serine/proline/glutamine/glycine residues in eukaryotic proteins—most prominently in transcription factors and in regulatory tails/linkers of signaling/scaffold proteins—corresponding to transactivation/repression or partner-interaction regions adjacent to but outside structured DNA-binding or catalytic domains.
Activation pattern: Sparse, low-magnitude, residue-level peaks scattered across intrinsically disordered coil regions (low pLDDT), often at N- or C-terminal tails, linkers, and helix–coil boundaries; minimal signal within folded domains (homeobox, ETS, POU, kinase cores) with only occasional isolated residues activating.
Exemplars: - Homeobox/HOX transcription factors: primary peaks in N-terminal disordered segments; occasional isolated residues at the start or within the homeobox helices.
- bHLH transcription factors: short, two-residue peaks in N-terminal disordered regions.
- BTB/POZ plus C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factors: peaks in disordered linker/C-terminal regions, including interaction-rich acidic segments just before the first zinc finger.
- ETS transcription factors: mostly weak, isolated peaks in disordered loops; rare isolated residues within the ETS domain.
- POU transcription factors: multiple small peaks across large N-terminal disordered regions; little to none in POU-specific or homeobox domains.
- Ser/Thr kinase (e.g., LMTK-like): dominant activation in long C-terminal disordered, compositionally biased tails (proline-/acidic-/glycine-rich); only minor peaks in the kinase domain.
- Large disordered scaffolds (e.g., JCAD): isolated peaks dispersed throughout extensive intrinsically disordered regions.
- Ciliary/centrosomal scaffolds: peaks in low-confidence coils and at helix N-caps within otherwise flexible segments.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity serine/threonine‑rich repeat tracts (PTS‑rich repeats, often including Pro and sometimes Tyr), serving as mucin‑like O‑glycosylated spacers in secreted/extracellular proteins and as phosphorylation‑heavy regulatory tails (e.g., Pol II CTD‑like YSPTSPS repeats) in nuclear transcription/replication factors, and in other cytosolic scaffolds/signaling proteins (e.g., intraflagellar transport components) that harbor S/T‑rich low‑complexity segments.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, repetitive low‑complexity stretches rather than single sites; strongest over extended P/T/S repeats (including YSPTSPS‑like motifs) but can also occur on shorter clustered S/T segments within low‑complexity regions; typically in non‑catalytic N‑ or C‑terminal tails, linkers, and extracellular domains; minimal activation inside structured catalytic cores.
Exemplars: - Gram‑positive serine‑rich repeat adhesins (SRRPs): very long S/T‑rich PTS repeats in extracellular stalks that are densely O‑glycosylated
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: mucin‑like S/T‑rich external loops/domains
- Mucins and mucin‑like regions of ECM/adhesion proteins: O‑GalNAc‑modified S/T‑rich linkers in extracellular domains
- Secreted metalloproteases and serine proteases: S/T‑rich propeptides or stalk/linker segments outside catalytic cores
- Peritrophins/chitin‑binding matrix proteins: S/T‑rich, glycosylated spacers between chitin‑binding domains
- Carbohydrate‑active enzymes (e.g., glycoside hydrolases, polysaccharide lyases): S/T‑rich O‑glycosylated linkers between catalytic modules and CBMs
- RNA polymerase II and transcription elongation machinery: CTD heptad YSPTSPS repeats and other S/T‑rich regulatory tails
- DNA damage/checkpoint and replication scaffolds: extended S/T‑rich intrinsically disordered regions that carry dense phosphorylation
- Glycan‑rich secretions and allergens: long mucin‑like S/T‑rich low‑complexity segments
- Ciliary/intraflagellar transport scaffolds: S/T‑rich low‑complexity linkers/tails in large TPR/coiled‑coil proteins
- Secreted signaling proteins (e.g., Wnt family) when they present S/T‑clustered low‑complexity loops or prosegments

Summary: Hydrophobic beta-strand positions: the feature detects isolated aliphatic residues (primarily Ile/Leu/Val, sometimes Ala/Thr) embedded in well-ordered beta-strands, typically reflecting sheet core/packing sites rather than catalytic or motif residues, across diverse protein families and cellular locales.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks, usually 1–3 isolated sites or very short 1–2 residue clusters confined to beta-strands with high structural confidence; often includes an early (N-terminal) strand of a domain; rarely in signal peptides or transmembrane helices; not aligned with known active sites.
Exemplars: - Isopentenyl-diphosphate isomerase: isolated Leu residues on beta-strands within the structured core
- Nudix hydrolases: Ile/Val on N-terminal and internal beta-strands of the Nudix domain
- Peptidoglycan D,D-transpeptidases (penicillin-binding proteins): Ile/Val (sometimes adjacent pair) on periplasmic beta-strands, away from the catalytic Ser
- Glutathione peroxidase: Ala/Leu on distinct beta-strands, not at the Sec active site
- Peroxiredoxins/thioredoxin-like proteins: Leu/Val on beta-strands within the thioredoxin fold
- Voltage-gated calcium channel alpha-2/delta subunit: Ala/Leu on beta-strands in extracellular Cache/VWA domains
- SCO copper chaperones (thioredoxin-like): Leu on beta-strands within the thioredoxin-like domain
- DNA primase: single Ile on a structured beta-strand outside annotated catalytic domains
- Beta-galactosidase: Ile residues on core beta-strands distant from catalytic Glu residues

Summary: Aromatic/hydrophobic β-strand junction motif of β-rich domains—predominant in extracellular ectodomains (Ig-like, FNIII, IPT/PSI, thioester/α2-macroglobulin, S-layer) but also present in periplasmic cell-envelope enzymes and intracellular β-sandwich modules (e.g., C2/PH/WW); typically centered on Trp or β-branched hydrophobes at β-strand ends or strand–loop junctions; repeats across domain arrays and is taxon-agnostic.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks in short segments mapping to β-strands or adjacent coil; strong preference for Trp with supporting hydrophobes (V/I/F/L) and small residues (A/G/S/T). Often early in mature secreted regions (~positions 40–70) and recurrent across repeated extracellular domains; little/no activation in signal peptides, transmembranes, or poorly structured stretches. Can also occur in cytosolic/peripheral-membrane proteins when a β-sandwich or W-rich module is present.
Exemplars:
- Class I cytokine receptor alpha subunits: Trp-centered peaks within ectodomain β-strands and FNIII modules.
- Receptor tyrosine kinase ectodomains (e.g., Torso): multiple IW/Trp-centered strand–loop junctions.
- Plexins: multiple extracellular β-strand segments in PSI/IPT regions plus nearby flexible coils.
- CD109/α2-macroglobulin-like thioester proteins: several short, well-structured β-strands across the mature chain.
- S-layer surface proteins: activation on loops flanked by β-strands and distinct β-strands; absent from coiled-coil and TM regions.
- Periplasmic penicillin-binding proteins: β-strand segments within transglycosylase/transpeptidase catalytic domains.
- Cytosolic inositol 5-phosphatases (INPP5 family): peaks in C2/β-sandwich or adjacent β-strands within the catalytic region.

Summary: Short linear motifs centered on Gly/Pro in flexible linkers and helix caps, with a strong preference for residues immediately preceding or flanking Pro (e.g., G–X–P–G in collagens and the C2H2 inter-finger linker TGEKP); signals concentrate on S/T/E/D/K/G in coil or helix‑boundary contexts while avoiding transmembrane cores and metal‑binding residues.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks rather than broad domains; repeated peaks across tandem repeat arrays; strongest in coil/linker segments and at helix–coil boundaries (including just after signal/TM segments), weak or absent in transmembrane helices and signal peptides; within C2H2 fingers, avoids the Cys/His ligands and highlights linker/loop residues.
Exemplars: - C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factors: activation on the conserved TGEKP inter-finger linkers (especially the Pro and adjacent T/E/K) and on coil Ser within finger loops; little/no signal on the Zn-coordinating Cys/His.
- Fibrillar collagens (collagen alpha chains): activation on the Gly–X–Y repeat, especially the X position when Y is Pro (G–X–P–G), with additional signal on Gly immediately before Pro and sometimes the Pro itself.
- Tat system small single-pass membrane subunits (TatE/TatA-like): discrete peaks in the cytosolic helical region just after the transmembrane segment, consistent with helix-capping/helix-adjacent sites; no signal in the TM helix.
- Mitochondrial ATP synthase epsilon subunit: scattered peaks within helices and at helix–coil boundaries in the mature domain; absent across the N-terminal transit peptide.

Summary: Solvent‑exposed loop/turn tips at the surfaces of repeat/solenoid architectures—most prominently right‑handed parallel β‑helix/β‑solenoids of secreted polysaccharide‑active enzymes and phage tailspikes, but also β‑propellers, LRR solenoids, and coiled‑coil solenoids—favoring Asn/Ser/Thr/Cys and generally avoiding catalytic/metal‑binding residues and N‑glycosylation sequon asparagines.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks recur across ordered module arrays (e.g., PbH1 repeats, LRRs, propeller blades, coiled‑coil heptad interruptions), concentrated in coils immediately preceding or linking secondary‑structure elements and at β‑edge strand positions; low in signal peptides, transmembrane helices, and long disordered tails; minimal within continuous helices and β‑cores except at solvent‑exposed termini or loop interruptions; typically adjacent to, but not on, catalytic/metal‑binding residues and not centered on glycosylated Asn.
Exemplars:
- Pectate lyases and endopolygalacturonases (parallel β‑helix): repeated peaks on coil/turn and β‑edge sites while avoiding catalytic acids and glycosylated Asn
- Pectin methylesterase: strong signal on coils immediately N‑terminal to β‑strands, including disulfide‑bonded cysteines, with no activation at active/binding residues
- Phage capsule depolymerase/tailspike: loop tips bridging adjacent β‑strands in the central β‑rich region (mid‑chain activation band)
- Alginate mannuronan C5‑epimerase (β‑helix): regularly spaced single‑site peaks across successive repeats; inactive in the disordered C‑terminal tail
- Non‑β‑helix glycosidases (e.g., isopullulanase): peaks at blade/edge strands or loop–strand junctions in β‑propellers or mixed α/β folds
- F‑box/LRR proteins: scattered peaks along the concave β‑sheet/loop edges of LRR solenoids
- Coiled‑coil regulatory proteins (e.g., SHCBP1): peaks at heptad interruptions and solvent‑exposed helix termini/loops
- Class C GPCR extracellular domain: cysteines and polar residues in extracellular loops and edge strands highlighted; transmembranes and disordered cytosolic tails remain off
Summary: Generic feature, meaning not known

Summary: Residue-level detector for well-ordered beta-strand scaffold positions, most strongly in the conserved beta-strands of ABC transporter nucleotide-binding domains (NBDs); it highlights structural (non-catalytic) strands rather than the Walker A/P-loop, and can also fire on beta-strands in other proteins, including TonB-dependent receptors and soluble beta-strand–rich enzymes (e.g., glyoxalase II, aldose 1-epimerase).
Activation pattern: Sparse, isolated residue-level peaks on beta-strands within annotated ABC transporter domains; often near positions ~60–80 and mid-sequence around the signature region (LSGGQ neighborhood), with little activation in disordered termini or transit peptides; outside ABCs, occasional peaks on beta-strands of outer-membrane beta-barrel/plug domains and of soluble beta-sandwich/jelly-roll enzymes.
Exemplars: ABC importer ATP-binding subunits (MalK, PotG, FbpC) — isolated peaks on internal beta-strands of the NBD, not at the ATP-binding P-loop; Energy-coupling factor (ECF) transporter A components — peaks on beta-strands within the ABC domain; Chloroplast/organellar ABC ATPases — beta-strand peaks within the NBD near the mid-sequence signature region; TonB-dependent outer-membrane receptors (e.g., FhuA) — single peaks on beta-strands in the periplasmic plug and the beta-barrel; Glyoxalase II and aldose 1-epimerase — isolated peaks on internal beta-strands of their beta-sandwich/jelly-roll scaffolds.

Summary: Alpha-helical hydrophobic membrane-insertion segments—N-terminal signal peptides/signal anchors and transmembrane helices (single- and multi-pass) across viruses, bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes; often featuring small-residue TM motifs (e.g., GxxxG) and serving as C-terminal membrane anchors in type I proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous hydrophobic blocks (~10–25 residues) that form alpha-helices; strongest at extreme N-termini for signal peptides/signal anchors and at C-terminal anchors of type I proteins; multiple activated blocks in polytopic membrane proteins; minimal activation outside these helices.
Exemplars: - Viral entry/fusion complex proteins: activation on the N-terminal signal-anchor helix.
- Membrane-anchored serine/threonine kinases: activation on the single C-terminal transmembrane anchor.
- Trans-prenyltransferases and other membrane enzymes: activation on an N-terminal transmembrane helix.
- Multi-pass membrane proteins (e.g., Wtf element membrane proteins): activation across each annotated transmembrane helix.
- Viral per os infectivity factors: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide.

Summary: Hydrophobic residues positioned within well‑ordered β‑strands of β‑sheet architectures (e.g., β‑propellers, β‑sandwich/Ig‑like, and other β‑rich domains), especially in extracellular/periplasmic or lumenal portions of secreted and membrane‑associated proteins; the signal avoids helices, transmembrane segments, glycosylation/metal‑binding sites, and most disulfide‑anchored positions.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks concentrated in short runs within DSSP/UniProt‑annotated β‑strands (high confidence), enriched for Leu/Ile/Val/Phe and other hydrophobics; sparse to moderate density depending on β‑sheet content; little to no activation in α‑helices, transmembrane helices, disordered loops, glycosylation sequons, or catalytic/metal‑binding motifs.
Exemplars: - Integrin α subunits: hydrophobic positions in extracellular β‑propeller strands; absent from the single‑pass TM helix and cytoplasmic tail.
- Arrestin‑domain proteins: core strands of the two β‑sandwich domains rather than loops or linker helices.
- Complement/alpha‑2‑macroglobulin/TEP family: hydrophobic strand positions within MG/Ig‑like and thioester‑containing β‑rich domains of large secreted glycoproteins.
- Pentameric ligand‑gated ion channels and related receptors: β‑strand cores in the extracellular ligand‑binding β‑sandwich; little activation in the helical pore.
- ML/NPC2 lipid‑recognition proteins: interior β‑sandwich strands forming the hydrophobic binding cavity.
- YidC/Oxa1 insertases: periplasmic/lumenal β‑strand elements of the large extracytoplasmic domain, not the multi‑pass helical core.
- COX11 copper‑assembly factors: β‑strand positions in the periplasmic/lumenal domain rather than metal‑ligating motifs.
- Oligosaccharyltransferase subunit 1 (Ribophorin I/OST1): luminal β‑sheet segments within the soluble domain, not TM helices.
- RNA polymerase subunit α: hydrophobic residues in N‑terminal β‑sheet regions of the α‑NTD.
- Chloroplast lumen FKBPs (immunophilins): conserved hydrophobic cores of the FKBP β‑sheet fold.
- Carbohydrate‑active enzymes (glycoside hydrolases/transferases): β‑strands of TIM‑barrels and β‑sandwich carbohydrate‑binding modules, avoiding catalytic acidic residues.
- M1 aminopeptidases and related metallopeptidases: non‑catalytic β‑strand elements in auxiliary domains rather than the metal‑binding helix/loop.
- Vesicle trafficking/adaptor/coat proteins: β‑propeller (WD‑repeat) and other β‑sheet scaffolds within coat/adaptor subunits.
- Bacterial envelope/secretion system components: extracellular/periplasmic β‑strand segments of β‑rich domains in secretion/assembly factors.

Summary: Low-complexity or membrane-interfacial segments used for flexible interactions; typically compositionally biased—often gly/pro-rich with embedded aromatics (W/Y/F), but also including cationic amphipathic helices and single-pass transmembrane anchors; additionally, exposed basic/aromatic patches within compact extracellular domains (e.g., GAG- or protease-interaction loops). Common in secreted/extracellular and membrane-associated eukaryotic proteins, scaffold proteins (e.g., kinetochore), some CAZymes, and cytosolic membrane binders (e.g., Tubby/TULP, Atg3). In precursors, activation generally maps to mature regions rather than signal peptides/propeptides.
Activation pattern: Regional/domain-level activation over contiguous segments; strongest on C-terminal TM anchors with juxtamembrane helices, extended gly/pro-rich low-complexity tracts in mature extracellular or scaffold regions, short cationic amphipathic helices or basic N-termini, and occasionally short exposed loops/patches within globular extracellular domains (e.g., heparan-sulfate–binding clusters); not confined to single residues.
Exemplars:
- Phospholipid scramblases: activation on the C-terminal transmembrane helix and preceding juxtamembrane segment
- Fungal GPI-anchored cell-wall adhesins/mannoproteins: activation over mature extracellular gly/pro- and aromatic-rich repeats
- Plant defense and lectin-like carbohydrate-binding proteins: activation on proline-rich/extensin-like segments or gly/pro-rich linkers adjoining carbohydrate-binding domains
- Kinetochore/centromere scaffolds (e.g., KNL1/Spc7-, Ndc80-complex proteins): activation across long low-complexity/coiled-coil–adjacent tracts used for multivalent binding
- RNA-binding/gene-expression regulators with prion-like/RGG- or low-complexity regions: activation on Y/F/G-rich or basic disordered segments that mediate interactions
- Bacterial/archaeal carbohydrate-active enzymes: activation on gly/pro-rich, often aromatic-bearing linkers between catalytic modules and carbohydrate-binding domains
- Cytosolic membrane-binding adaptors (Tubby/TULP, Atg3): activation on N-terminal low-complexity segments and amphipathic helices that bind acidic lipids
- Secreted cytokines and pore-forming toxins (e.g., IL-1 family/IL-33, echotoxins): activation on basic/disordered regions or membrane-inserting amphipathic helices in mature proteins
- Secreted growth factors (e.g., FGFs): activation on heparan sulfate–binding basic/aromatic surface patches within the mature beta-trefoil domain
- Disulfide-rich protease inhibitors/toxins (e.g., Kunitz/Bowman–Birk): activation on short basic/aromatic loops that contact proteases

Summary: Short linear sequence elements within intrinsically disordered, low-complexity coil regions (enriched in Gly/Pro and charged/polar residues), including proteolytic-processing–adjacent motifs in secreted peptide precursors and flexible termini/linkers of soluble or membrane proteins; with occasional sparse hits on exposed residues within folded domains
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks scattered through disordered/low-pLDDT coils; minimal or absent in stable secondary structure such as transmembrane helices; occasional isolated, low-intensity peaks on solvent-exposed residues inside structured domains
Exemplars: Insect neuropeptide/peptide-toxin precursors: peaks within the mature peptide and at adjacent dibasic convertase cleavage (e.g., KR/GKR) and glycine-amidation contexts in unstructured propeptide regions; Type II toxin–antitoxin VapB antitoxins: single weak peak in a flexible C-terminal tail; Single-pass membrane proteins (e.g., BEAN1-like): activation confined to low-complexity, disordered N/C termini with no signal in the transmembrane helix; Homeobox transcription factors: peaks in proline-rich disordered regulatory regions and sparse residues on the surface of the homeobox DNA-binding domain

Summary: Edge beta-strands of extracellular beta-sandwich domains—especially immunoglobulin-like (V-set/C2-set) and fibronectin type III folds—and equivalent strands in macroglobulin/thioester “MG” domains. The feature often targets the terminal beta-strand of these modules (frequently the C-terminal strand), includes the WSXWS segment of type I cytokine receptors, and tends to occur near N-glycosylation sites; overall it reflects a common extracellular beta-sheet signature in secreted/cell-surface proteins.
Activation pattern: Multiple residue-level peaks confined to extracellular regions, with selective enrichment on DSSP E (beta-strand) segments and adjacent loops; repeated peaks across successive Ig/FnIII-like domains; little/no activation in signal peptides, transmembranes, or cytosolic tails; frequent proximity to N-linked glycosylation sites and Ser/Thr-rich stretches.
Exemplars: - Type I cytokine receptors (e.g., Oncostatin-M receptor): strong peaks on beta-strands within the fibronectin type III-like cytokine-binding module, including the WSXWS motif, plus additional beta-strand peaks across FnIII domains near N-glycosylation sites.
- IgSF adhesion receptors (e.g., VSIG/CEACAM-like proteins): peaks on the C-terminal edge strands of Ig-like C2 domains and adjacent loops, sometimes overlapping an N-glycosylation site.
- Multidomain Ig-containing receptors (e.g., PDGFR-like extracellular regions): activation on the final beta-strand of Ig-like domains and inter-domain beta-strands.
- Alpha-2-macroglobulin/thioester-containing macroglobulins: multiple discrete peaks mapping to selected beta-strands of MG beta-sandwich domains.

Summary: Long, low-complexity, tandem-repeat intrinsically disordered regions (especially Ser/Thr/Pro-rich, mucin-like PTS tracts and other compositionally biased repeats), including secreted propeptide/linker segments with clustered dibasic cleavage sites, viral repeat LCRs, and nuclear repeat modules such as the RNA polymerase II CTD; the feature tracks repeat/low-complexity composition rather than a specific folded motif.
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation across very long, contiguous disordered stretches (hundreds of residues), with non-uniform peaks that often recur at repeat boundaries and in linker segments; in secreted precursors, peaks frequently align with Lys/Arg-rich (dibasic) processing sites. Minimal activation in signal peptides or structured domains; activated regions are coil-like with low pLDDT.
Exemplars: - Mucins (e.g., integumentary/secreted mucins): strong activation across central tandem PTS repeats and proline-rich unstructured linkers.
- Kininogen/kinin and other peptide prohormone/venom polyprotein precursors: activation over disordered repetitive propeptide regions, peaking in linkers between peptide repeats and near dibasic cleavage pairs.
- Proline-rich salivary proteins: activation spanning long PRP low-complexity tracts.
- RNA polymerase II largest subunit CTD: activation across the YSPTSPS heptad repeat array.
- Viral proteins with low-complexity repeat segments: activation on repetitive LCR tracts.
- Plant chromatin/nuclear repeat proteins: activation along extended simple-repeat, compositionally biased regions.
- Extracellular adhesive/structural repeat-rich proteins: activation over low-complexity spacer and repeat regions.

Summary: Acidic/polar residues in short coil/turn loops that connect beta-strands within repeat-based beta-sheet scaffolds—most prominently the surface loops of WD40 beta-propeller blades and MORN repeats; the feature flags periodic Asp/Glu/Asn/Ser/Thr positions in these inter-strand loops, with occasional weaker hits to analogous loops in unrelated enzymes.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks, typically on single Asp (and occasionally Glu/Asn/Ser/Thr) in coil/turn segments between beta-strands; periodic across successive repeats in WD40/MORN domains; distributed over long spans in large repeat scaffolds; sparse in small enzymes; occurs in both well-structured loops (high pLDDT) and flexible loops near beta elements; not tied to catalytic sites.
Exemplars: - WD40 beta-propeller scaffolds (e.g., Gemin5-like RNA-binding WD proteins; mTOR subunit Raptor): recurrent peaks at Asp/Asn in the loops linking the beta-strands of each WD blade.
- MORN repeat proteins: peaks at Asp within the coil loops of individual MORN repeats that connect their beta-strands.
- Telomerase-associated complex proteins (p50-like): localized activation on an acidic loop bridging adjacent beta-strands in a flexible region.
- FAD-dependent monooxygenases: very sparse peaks at Asp in structured loops between beta elements (not at FAD-binding or active-site residues).

Summary: Extended amphipathic, helix‑rich lipid‑handling scaffolds: the feature activates on giant membrane‑associated lipid transfer/assembly proteins that present long hydrophobic grooves or amphipathic helical surfaces—most prominently bridge/tunnel lipid transporters (ATG2/VPS13‑like, AsmA/TamB) and LLTP/BPI/TULIP lipid‑binding proteins (e.g., PLTP/CETP/vitellogenin)—and more generally on very large secreted/periplasmic or scaffold proteins whose long low‑complexity alpha‑solenoid/coiled‑coil segments interface with membranes.
Activation pattern: Broad regional/domain‑level activation spanning long stretches, often N‑terminal to central portions of very large proteins. Strongest on runs enriched in small/flexible hydrophobic and polar residues (G, A, L, V, S, T, P), consistent with amphipathic helices, alpha‑solenoids, and low‑complexity linkers that line lipid‑binding grooves or contact membranes; frequently covers most of the periplasmic/extracellular or cytosolic rod‑like region between terminal anchors/signal peptides.
Exemplars: - Autophagy protein 2 (ATG2) homologs (eukaryotes): activation across the elongated chorein‑like lipid‑transfer groove used to bridge ER–phagophore membranes.
- AsmA/TamB family (Gram‑negative intermembrane lipid transport and outer‑membrane assembly): activation along the long periplasmic rod that ferries lipids to the OM.
- LLTP/BPI/TULIP family lipid carriers (e.g., phospholipid transfer protein PLTP, CETP, LBP/BPI): activation on the BPI‑like tubular lipid‑binding domains that cradle acyl chains.
- Vitellogenins (yolk lipid transporters): activation over the N‑terminal LLTP lipid‑binding region and adjacent low‑complexity segments.
- Gram‑negative OM assembly/export scaffolds and large secreted effectors/toxins: activation on extended periplasmic/extracellular amphipathic and low‑complexity regions used in secretion/assembly.
- Nuclear pore complex scaffold nucleoporins (HEAT/ARM alpha‑solenoids): activation on extended solenoids and ALPS‑like amphipathic segments that contact the nuclear envelope.
- Peritrophin/chitin‑binding secreted proteins: activation primarily in Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich mucin‑like linkers flanking chitin‑binding modules rather than in the cysteine‑rich cores.
- Ciliary transport/coiled‑coil scaffolds and ER stress sensors (PERK/IRE1): activation in long coiled‑coil/solenoid or luminal sensing regions adjacent to membranes.

Summary: Residues at secondary-structure transition points—especially the ends of transmembrane helices and signal peptides—i.e., helix–coil caps and membrane topology boundaries, with a bias toward small/polar/basic residues in flexible or low‑complexity contexts
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks. Enriched at C- or N-terminal ends of transmembrane helices and immediately adjacent loops (including signal peptide cleavage junctions) and in nearby disordered/low-confidence segments; occasional scattered peaks within helices/strands consistent with helix-capping or turn residues rather than active sites
Exemplars: - Plant secreted peptide precursors: peaks at the signal peptide terminus and within the disordered, charge-biased C-terminal tail.
- DD-transpeptidases/penicillin-binding proteins: scattered peaks in the periplasmic catalytic domain at helix/turn/strand positions, consistent with capping/transition residues rather than catalytic motifs.
- Sedolisin (peptidase S53) proteases: isolated peaks within helical segments of the catalytic domain, not at active sites, consistent with helix capping/packing positions.
- NIPA3 magnesium transporter: strongest at the C-terminal end of TM helices where they exit to cytosolic/extracellular loops; minor intra-helix peaks.
- UDP-sugar (NST-like) transporters: peaks at the end of the final TM helix and in adjacent loops and C-terminal disordered tail.
- Respiratory complex I small membrane subunit (ND3/NuoA-like): peaks in the loop linking TM helices and at helix termini.
- Heme A synthase (CtaA/Cox15): repeated peaks at the C-terminal ends of multiple TM helices just before extracellular loops, with weaker intra-helix signals.

Summary: Membrane‑insertion modules used to breach or fuse lipid bilayers: the conformationally labile, hydrophobic, small‑residue–rich segments (β‑hairpins or amphipathic α‑helices) that refold to become pore‑lining transmembrane elements or fusion peptides/stems in pore‑forming toxins, immune pores, secretion translocons, and viral fusion glycoproteins.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation over one or two contiguous hydrophobic stretches (often 15–35 aa) with low predicted structure/confidence, frequently annotated as “transmembrane β‑strands/helix” or “pre‑stem/insertion” elements; strong across the core insertion segment with spill‑over into immediate flanks; minimal in well‑folded scaffold domains, enzymatic/catalytic sites, or signal peptides despite their hydrophobicity; commonly spans long, low‑complexity, small‑residue–rich regions and can cover large portions of precursor toxins.
Exemplars: - MACPF/CDC immune and bacterial pores (perforin, complement C6–C9, cholesterol‑dependent cytolysins): activation on the paired transmembrane hairpins (CH1/CH2 or TMH1/TMH2) that unfurl to form the β‑barrel pore.
- Bacillus thuringiensis Cry/δ‑endotoxins: activation on domain I’s hydrophobic helical hairpin that reorients to insert into the membrane during pore formation.
- Aerolysin‑like β‑pore‑forming toxins and lectin–pore hybrids: activation on the pre‑stem loop/β‑hairpin that becomes the pore‑lining β‑strand(s) after oligomerization; low or absent on attached lectin/receptor‑binding domains.
- Cnidarian and fish α‑pore‑forming venoms (actinoporins and related): activation on the N‑terminal amphipathic α‑helix that inserts into membranes.
- Colicin‑like bacteriocins and hemolysins: activation on the membrane‑inserting amphipathic helices/hairpins of the pore‑forming domain.
- Type III secretion system translocon proteins (e.g., YopB/IpaB/IpaC families): activation on the paired hydrophobic helices that insert into host membranes to form the translocon pore.
- Type VI secretion membrane‑lytic effectors: activation on the amphipathic insertion helices/loops that damage target membranes.
- Viral class I/II/III fusion glycoproteins (e.g., HA/F/S2, flavivirus E, alphavirus E1): activation on the fusion peptide/internal fusion loop and adjacent stem segments that engage and insert into host membranes.

Summary: A generic beta-sheet turn/junction motif: residues in short loops or turns that connect adjacent beta-strands or lie at beta-strand termini across diverse beta-rich folds (barrels, sandwiches, jellyrolls, propellers), often immediately flanking functional sites but not limited to them.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks in short, closely spaced clusters; concentrated in coil/turn segments bridging beta-strands and at strand ends within well-structured regions; frequently includes glycine, threonine/serine, acidic or aromatic residues; occurs broadly across taxa and protein classes.
Exemplars: - Pentraxin family (PTX domain): peaks in loop/turns linking beta-strands within the jellyroll domain.
- FHA domain proteins: activation at the coil between adjacent beta-strands inside the beta-sandwich, with occasional strand-edge residues.
- Two-partner secretion outer-membrane transporters (FhaC/TpsB): sparse peaks in short loops connecting transmembrane beta-barrel strands and at domain junctions (POTRA–barrel).
- Sugar-phosphate mutases (phosphomannomutase): loop segments near Mg2+-binding catalytic residues between beta elements.
- Ribosome hibernation/quality-control factor (RaiA/YfiA): turn between consecutive beta-strands and strand termini.
- tRNA threonylcarbamoyltransferase (t6A synthase, Kae1/Qri7 family): loop connecting beta-strands adjacent to catalytic acidic residues; occasional strand-end site in substrate-binding region.
- Frataxin: loop/turns between beta-strands in the mature C-terminal domain.
- Sialidase/neuraminidase (beta-propeller): two-residue strand-to-coil transition at a blade edge, with scattered weaker strand/loop edge sites.

Summary: An almost-null, non-specific background feature that weakly reflects generic protein context rather than any particular function or motif; when present, it shows slight, diffuse activation across ordered secondary structures in diverse proteins but is not enriched at catalytic, metal-binding, or ligand-interaction sites.
Activation pattern: Predominantly near-zero baseline with sparse, single-residue micropeaks scattered along the full sequence; weak, context-agnostic signals appear in helices, beta-strands, and loops (occasionally including transmembrane helices), with no consistent terminal bias and inconsistent relation to disorder.
Exemplars: - PP2C/PPM-type protein phosphatases: weak, scattered peaks within the structured catalytic domain; no signal at Mn2+-binding residues.
- ENaC/degenerin family ion channels: low-level peaks in extracellular beta strands/loops and mild clustering in TM2 and a C-terminal helix; minimal in disordered tails.
- Ser/Thr protein kinases (e.g., AGC family/Warts): essentially off across kinase and AGC-CTD regions, with only isolated micropeaks in disordered segments.
- YidC membrane protein insertase: virtually no activation across transmembrane and loop regions; only tiny sporadic peaks without structural correlation.
- Metacaspase proteases: very low, scattered activation in loops between catalytic residues; no enrichment at the active site.
- 6-pyruvoyl tetrahydrobiopterin synthase: sparse micropeaks across coils/strands/helices; absent at catalytic, zinc-binding, and phosphorylation sites.
- Peptide deformylase: diffuse, low activation across secondary structures; no signal at the catalytic glutamate or Fe-binding residues.

Summary: Universal eukaryotic N-terminal targeting presequences: the feature detects short, cleavable leader regions at the extreme N-terminus that direct proteins to organelles or the secretory pathway—especially chloroplast/apicoplast transit peptides and thylakoid lumen signals, but also mitochondrial targeting peptides and classical signal peptides. These segments are Ser/Thr- and small/hydrophobic–rich, enriched in Lys/Arg and depleted of acidic residues, typically low-structure/low-confidence and ending at the maturation cleavage site.
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to a short, contiguous block at the extreme N-terminus (≈10–80 aa), peaking near the start and dropping sharply at the annotated cleavage site; common bipartite N‑terminal activation for plastid→thylakoid or apicoplast SP+TP signals; rare secondary internal peaks correspond to additional signal-anchor–like hydrophobic segments.
Exemplars: - Plastid enzymes (e.g., carotenoid biosynthesis): activation on the chloroplast transit peptide that is cleaved before the mature enzyme.
- Thylakoid lumen extrinsic PSII subunits (PsbO/PsbP/PsbQ): activation on the bipartite chloroplast transit peptide followed by a thylakoid lumen signal (often Tat twin‑arginine).
- Apicomplexan apicoplast proteins: activation on the bipartite secretory signal peptide plus apicoplast transit peptide.
- Mitochondrial matrix and inner-membrane proteins: activation on the amphipathic, basic mitochondrial targeting presequence.
- Secreted animal/fungal proteins (hormones, ECM proteins, hydrolases, defensins): activation on the classical N‑terminal signal peptide.
- Viral envelope/secreted glycoproteins: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide used for entry into the host secretory pathway.

Summary: Alpha-helical structural elements (including coiled-coils), with a bias toward helix boundary/capping positions and key interface residues; the feature highlights short amphipathic helices and oligomerization helices rather than beta sheets or disordered segments.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks that are punctate within helices, enriched at N-cap/N1 and C-cap positions (favoring E, D, S, T, G, P) and at periodic hydrophobic sites (A, L) along amphipathic faces; frequent inclusion of very N‑terminal residues; little or no signal in beta-rich domains or compositionally biased/disordered regions; clusters can appear within helical dimerization/oligomerization segments.
Exemplars: - SMN/Gemin-1: activation on the N-terminal short helix and the C-terminal helical homodimerization segment; minimal in the beta-rich Tudor domain.
- Homeobox/HOX transcription factors: signal on the three-helix homeodomain (especially helix starts and the DNA-binding helix), not on low-complexity activation tails.
- APC/C subunits and other coiled-coil scaffolds: activation along coiled-coil heptad helices at interface positions and helix junctions.
- SLBP family (histone RNA hairpin-binding): activation on alpha-helical elements within/adjacent to the RRM rather than on beta strands.
- MazE antitoxin family: activation on the long central dimerization helix.
- Cytoskeletal/ciliary proteins (e.g., centrosomal, axonemal): activation along extended coiled-coil stalks and short amphipathic helices.
- Mitochondrial ribosomal proteins: activation on helical stretches and N-terminal helices within the protein body.
- SAM-dependent methyltransferases: activation on the alpha-helices of the Rossmann-like core (N-terminal helix and interleaved helices).
- Proteasome/ubiquitin-system auxiliaries: activation on TPR/coiled-coil helical repeats and oligomerization helices.
- Respiratory chain subunits and other membrane-associated proteins: activation on exposed amphipathic helices outside the membrane core.

Summary: Short hydrophobic/aromatic-rich β-strand segments that constitute the β-sheet cores of β-sandwich/β-barrel folds, especially in lipid-binding and membrane-targeting domains (PH/GRAM/C2/VASt) and lipid-carrier barrels (FABP/lipocalin/nitrobindin); often features Lys–Leu–Tyr/Tyr-containing stretches and reflects a structural β-strand signature rather than specific catalytic/ligand-contact residues.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks forming 3–5-residue runs within individual β-strands; multiple separate peaks can appear per protein; little to no activation in helices, loops, or disordered regions; occasionally overlaps conserved β-strand motifs (e.g., lipocalin GXW).
Exemplars: - Pleckstrin homology (PH) domain proteins (e.g., oxysterol-binding protein-related, PH-like domain family members, protein kinase D): strong peaks on short β-strands within the PH domain; sometimes adjacent to basic residues known to influence phosphoinositide-dependent membrane targeting.
- GRAM/VASt/C2 multidomain lipid adaptors (e.g., BAG-associated GRAM proteins): primary peaks on β-strands of the GRAM (PH-like) domain; secondary peaks on a short β-strand in the VASt domain; occasional weak hits in β-strands/loops of the C2 domain.
- Fatty acid-binding proteins (iLBP family): multiple peaks on interior β-strands of the β-barrel; not focused on annotated fatty-acid contact residues.
- Nitrobindin/lipocalin peroxynitrite isomerases: peaks across several β-strands, including within the conserved GXWXGXG lipocalin motif; no activation at heme-binding sites.

Summary: Hydrophobic/aromatic hotspots within intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regions (IDRs)—especially long linkers and terminal tails—marking short linear interaction–prone elements (MoRF/SLiM-like) rather than folded domains.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on L/I/V/F/Y/M (often interspersed with P), sparse and non‑contiguous, concentrated in predicted‑disordered, low pLDDT, low‑complexity segments; little to no signal in annotated structured domains; clusters can occur across extended IDRs and C‑terminal regions.
Exemplars: - Paramyxovirus phosphoproteins: peaks on hydrophobic residues in C‑terminal disordered/low‑complexity regions; absent from structured NLS/NES.
- Viral packaging/assembly proteins: sparse L/F/Y peaks across extensively disordered interaction regions involved in assembly.
- Two‑component hybrid histidine kinases: multiple clusters of L/I/F/Y in long low‑complexity linkers and C‑tails; minimal activation in PAS, histidine kinase, and response regulator domains.
- Ras GEF/Rho GAP scaffolds (amoebozoan signaling proteins): L/I/V/F peaks throughout large disordered N‑terminal regions; no activation within Ras‑GEF, Rho‑GAP, or F‑actin–binding domains.
- Multidomain cytoskeletal regulators (e.g., WD/PH/gelsolin architectures): strongest peaks confined to disordered linkers between domains.
- Bacterial type III effector/adhesin (IpaA): L/I/V/Y peaks in a C‑terminal disordered segment that forms binding helices upon partner engagement.
- Yeast regulatory proteins (e.g., stress/transport suppressors): scattered hydrophobic residues highlighted within disordered segments across the sequence.

Summary: Hydrophobic/aromatic beta‑strand positions that recur at structurally equivalent sites within the blades of beta‑propeller domains (e.g., WD40, Kelch, NHL, YWTD/LDLR‑B and catalytic propellers of quinoprotein/redox enzymes), marking the blade core rather than specific active sites
Activation pattern: Residue‑level sharp peaks enriched for W/Y/F/L/I/V (with occasional small/polar residues) restricted to beta‑strands, repeating periodically (~40–50 aa) across propeller blades; activations span the entire propeller domain while non‑propeller regions (signal peptides, TM segments, unrelated domains) show little/no signal
Exemplars: - NHL repeat propellers (e.g., PAL/NHL domain of peptidylglycine alpha‑amidating monooxygenase; NHL‑repeat proteins): one peak per NHL blade on beta‑strands.
- Kelch propellers: periodic single‑residue peaks at an equivalent beta‑strand position in each Kelch repeat.
- WD40 propellers (e.g., IFT/flagellar and ribosome/processome WD proteins): peaks on aromatic/hydrophobic residues within the beta‑strands of successive WD blades.
- YWTD/LDLR‑B propellers in extracellular matrix/receptor proteins (e.g., nidogen, LDLR/LRP family): peaks within beta‑strands across successive YWTD repeats.
- Named bacterial beta‑propeller scaffolds (e.g., seven‑bladed propellers): strongly periodic peaks spaced by blade length.
- Quinoprotein/quinocofactor and related redox enzymes with catalytic propellers (e.g., aralkylamine dehydrogenase heavy chain; dihydro‑heme d1 dehydrogenase D1‑binding domain): peaks on beta‑strand hydrophobic/aromatic residues throughout the propeller fold.
- Insect Yellow/MRJP secreted proteins: multiple peaks on beta‑strand aromatics/hydrophobics consistent with a propeller‑like beta‑sheet architecture.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regions (IDRs) enriched in small/polar and acidic residues with frequent proline (including proline‑rich segments), marking protein–protein interaction modules that contain short linear motifs and transient alpha‑helical MoRFs, typically found in large scaffolds and regulatory tails across diverse taxa
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation across long disordered segments (low pLDDT/coil), with superimposed single‑residue or short (2–3 aa) peaks that highlight candidate SLiMs/MoRFs; minimal to no activation within well‑folded domains
Exemplars: - Junctional cadherin 5–associated protein (cell junction scaffold): sparse peaks within disordered, compositionally biased (proline/polar‑rich) regions
- Dynein axonemal assembly factor 1 (ciliary assembly factor): broad activation over the C‑terminal IDR; no activation in the structured N‑terminal LRR domain
- AMER3/WTX family (Wnt pathway scaffold): scattered peaks throughout low‑confidence disordered regions, including predicted helical patches
- Ser/Thr protein kinase with long regulatory tails: activation confined to disordered N‑ and C‑terminal tails; absent from the catalytic kinase core
- Factor interacting with REF2 (nuclear/regulatory protein): numerous peaks across disordered coils lacking a defined fold
- Vac17 (vacuolar transport adaptor): strong activation in disordered PPI regions (MYO2‑ and VAC8‑binding segments), including predicted alpha‑helical elements within these binding modules

Summary: Residues that cap or initiate secondary‑structure elements—especially helix N‑caps/first helical turns and β‑strand termini/adjacent turns—across many folds; frequently realized in structured propeptides and extracellular/periplasmic domains, but not tied to catalytic sites.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks at discrete positions near starts/ends of α‑helices and β‑strands and in short coils/turns that bridge them; often absent from signal peptides; in secreted serine‑protease precursors the strongest signal concentrates in the helical inhibitory propeptide rather than the catalytic domain; number of peaks per protein varies widely.
Exemplars: - Subtilisin-like serine protease precursors (peptidase S8): peaks on helices within the I9 inhibitory propeptide; catalytic triad and Ca2+-binding sites largely unmarked.
- Trypsin-like, transmembrane serine proteases, and coagulation/complement/plasminogen proteases: residues at propeptide/activation segments and helix/strand capping sites in extracellular domains.
- Protease inhibitors (Kunitz/Kazal/serpins): helix N‑cap and β‑turn positions that stabilize the small β+α scaffolds.
- Periplasmic ABC substrate‑binding proteins (e.g., YejA/PBP-like): residues at helix starts and β‑strand boundaries within the periplasmic solute‑binding domain.
- Ribosomal protein L23 family: helix‑turn‑helix capping residues in the small helical bundle.
- Riboflavin kinase (archaea/bacteria): β→α loop positions and helix starts in the core fold.
- Cell division protein FtsX and other membrane/transport proteins: capping residues in periplasmic/extracellular loops and short helices.
- Nucleotide‑metabolism enzymes (dCTP deaminase, dUTPase): β‑strand edges and helix‑start residues around active‑site loops (not the catalytic residues themselves).
- SbcCD nuclease subunit D: helix‑turn transition sites within the DNA‑processing domain.
- Viral/phage proteins and chloroplast/photosynthetic proteins: generic β‑α transition/capping sites in soluble domains.
- Adhesion GPCR ectodomains and chromobox/chromodomain proteins: secondary‑structure capping residues in extracellular or chromatin‑binding domains.

Summary: N-terminal cationic leader/targeting segments used for protein routing and processing — including secretory signal-peptide n-/c-regions, mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides, and related short basic host-/organelle-targeting motifs
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation at or near N-termini, with residue-level peaks over Lys/Arg clusters and small residues (Ala/Ser/Gly) around processing/cleavage positions; in very short proteins the activation can span most of the sequence; occasional internal activation at signal-anchor segments adjoining basic n-regions
Exemplars: - Secreted hormone/neuropeptide precursors: activation over the N-terminal signal peptide (basic n-region and small-residue c-region around the signal peptidase site) and sometimes at dibasic KR/RR processing sites in the propeptide.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide or signal-anchor with a positively charged n-region; can also highlight proximal basic proprotein-convertase motifs.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins: activation on short Lys/Arg-rich N-terminal leaders/NLS-like basic clusters used for host targeting.
- ATP synthase epsilon (mitochondrial forms): activation on the N-terminal mitochondrial targeting presequence.
- tRNA/rRNA m7G methyltransferases and TilS: activation on N-terminal organellar transit peptides in eukaryotes (mitochondria/plastids) or on basic RNA-binding N-terminal tails in prokaryotes.
- Lipoate biosynthesis/lipoylation enzymes: activation on mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides directing enzymes to the organelle where lipoylation occurs.
- Membrane transporters and other membrane-associated proteins: activation on N-terminal signal anchors with positively charged n-regions.
- Plant proteins and plant-pathogen effectors: activation on secretory signal peptides and basic host-targeting motifs (e.g., RxLR-like) located just after the signal peptide.
- Proteases and protease-related secreted proteins: activation on the secretory signal peptide and basic propeptide processing motifs.
- Ribosome-related proteins/modifiers: activation on short basic N-terminal segments (often nucleic acid-binding/NLS-like).
- Uncharacterized micropeptides/lncRNA-encoded peptides: broad activation across short, basic N-terminal regions consistent with leader/targeting-like segments.

Summary: Intrinsic disorder/low‑complexity segments—especially Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich (often basic) tails and linkers that host phosphorylation sites and short linear motifs used for regulation and protein–protein interactions; common in signaling/regulatory proteins and many viral or secreted/testis proteins
Activation pattern: Residue-level scattered peaks across long and short intrinsically disordered regions with low structural confidence; often includes the extreme N‑terminus (including the initiator Met) and other flexible segments; enriched on S/T/P but not limited to them; little or no preference for well‑formed secondary structure and typically avoids compact folded domains
Exemplars: - Viral non-structural proteins (NSs): sparse peaks on S/T and nearby residues within low‑confidence, flexible regions (including N‑terminal segments), consistent with SLiM/PTM‑rich IDRs.
- DNA damage response adaptors/scaffolds: strongest activation within UniProt-annotated disordered regions containing key S/T residues required for interactions and function (phospho‑regulated sites).
- Testis/sperm basic proteins (e.g., protamines/TSPY-like): scattered activation across Arg/Lys‑rich, highly disordered tails; minimal activation in transient helical segments.
- Transcription factors, kinases, and signaling scaffolds: activation on low‑complexity regulatory termini and linkers enriched in S/T/P and proline‑rich motifs that mediate partner binding and phosphorylation.
- Viral envelope/secreted glycoproteins: activation on mucin-like Ser/Thr‑rich low‑complexity stretches typical of unstructured luminal regions.

Summary: Residue-level detector of intrinsically disordered terminal segments (low-pLDDT tails), often containing transient helical propensity and short linear elements used for regulation/processing/localization; avoids structured catalytic cores
Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks concentrated in N- (and sometimes C-) terminal IDRs; little to no signal in folded domains; peaks frequently fall on charged (R/K/E/D) or aromatic residues and can coincide with short, low-confidence helices
Exemplars: - tRNA (pseudouridine(54)-N1)-methyltransferase: activation restricted to the disordered N-terminal extension (e.g., a peak in a short transient helix), absent from the SAM-dependent catalytic domain
- Secreted bacterial protease: strong activation in disordered N- and C-terminal tails, none across the structured protease core
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursor (Amnesiac): isolated peaks within disordered propeptide/neuropeptide regions
- Antisense-encoded microprotein (TAR1): few peaks in low-confidence helical segments within an annotated disordered region
- Proapoptotic nucleolar protein: peaks within a broad C-terminal IDR, including near a nucleolar localization segment

Summary: A sequence-level detector of short linear motifs: 2–3-residue clusters enriched in small/polar residues (Ser, Asn, Gly) and Arg–Ser (RS) pairs, typically in flexible loops or intrinsically disordered segments and conserved at corresponding positions across orthologs, rather than tied to a specific domain or localization.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks forming very short adjacent clusters (dipeptides/tripeptides), recurring at comparable positions across orthologous proteins; observed in both secreted and intracellular proteins.
Exemplars: - Pre‑mRNA splicing factors (U4/U6.U5 tri‑snRNP, SR‑family): activation on RS/SR dipeptide clusters within RS‑rich low‑complexity regions.
- Chromatin/epigenetic regulators (methyl‑CpG‑binding proteins, histone methyltransferases, INO80 subunit Ies6): short S/N/G micro‑motifs in disordered linkers or tails.
- DNA polymerase delta subunit 3: conserved short polar clusters in flexible regions.
- Mitochondrial ribosomal proteins and respiratory Complex I assembly/structural subunits: S/G/N‑rich micro‑motifs in exposed loop segments.
- Secreted protease inhibitors with Kazal domains and extracellular matrix/matricellular proteins: short S/G/N motifs in disulfide‑bonded loops/turns; in chemokines, peaks often coincide with or neighbor the conserved cysteine motif region.
- Fungal VAO/BBE‑like FAD oxidoreductases: glycine/serine‑rich short motifs in active‑site/FAD‑proximal loops.
- Bacterial RlpA (peptidoglycan transglycosylase/SPOR‑domain proteins): conserved SG/GS motifs in SPOR‑domain loops.
- Plant hormone‑related transcription factors (auxin/jasmonate/TIFY/WOX): S/N/G‑rich short motifs within intrinsically disordered regions.

Summary: Hydrophobic alpha‑helical segments, especially N‑terminal targeting/anchoring helices (signal peptides and single‑pass transmembrane anchors) and amphipathic docking/coiled‑coil helices, characterized by hydrophobic/aromatic residues often juxtaposed with acidic residues (D/E next to Φ)
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation on helical stretches, most often near the N‑terminus; residue‑level peaks on hydrophobic/aromatic positions and on acidic–hydrophobic juxtapositions; extended continuous activation in proteins with long signal/anchor helices or helical linkers; occasional single‑site hits where a short acidic–Φ motif occurs
Exemplars: - Secreted proteases, large bacterial toxins, and class A/B penicillin‑binding proteins: activation on N‑terminal signal peptide hydrophobic cores or single‑pass membrane anchors
- TonB proteins: activation on the N‑terminal transmembrane helix
- bHLH‑PAS transcription factors (circadian/hypoxia regulators): activation across the basic helix‑loop‑helix and adjacent PAS helices, often including a conserved histidine within the helical segment
- Peroxiredoxins and glutathione peroxidases: activation on N‑terminal/surface helices flanking the active site
- Isopentenyl‑diphosphate isomerases: activation on the conserved N‑terminal helix
- Nudix hydrolases: activation on the short N‑terminal helix preceding the Nudix box
- Nonribosomal peptide synthetases and related megasynthases: activation on N‑terminal docking helices and inter‑domain helical linkers
- Coatomer/AP adaptor subunits and Ragulator: activation on N‑terminal amphipathic/coiled‑coil helices used for membrane recruitment or partner binding, often showing acidic–hydrophobic (D/E‑Φ) patterns
