Summary: Core beta-strand residues in small-molecule sensory/regulatory alpha/beta domains (GAF, PAS/PAC, Cache) and analogous beta-sheet elements in alpha/beta enzyme cores (e.g., GNAT N-acetyltransferases), i.e., conserved positions within central beta-sheets that scaffold ligand-binding/allosteric modules across diverse signaling proteins.
Activation pattern: Sharp residue-level peaks (often single residues or short 2–3 residue runs) enriched for hydrophobic/aromatic positions within beta-strands in well-structured regions; multiple noncontiguous peaks can occur within one protein, frequently across tandem sensory domains.
Exemplars: - Two-component histidine/sensor kinases (e.g., FilI): peaks on beta-strands in the PAC/PAS-adjacent sensory region and nearby interdomain beta-strands.
- cAMP/cGMP phosphodiesterases (e.g., PDE10A): peaks on beta-strands in tandem GAF domains.
- Methyl-accepting chemotaxis receptors: single-residue peak on a beta-strand within the periplasmic Cache ligand-binding domain.
- GNAT-family arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase-like enzymes: peak on a beta-strand in the GNAT catalytic core.

Summary: Flexible coil/linker segments and helix–coil junctions enriched in charged and small residues (E/D/K/R, G/P, S/T), often intrinsically disordered; in secreted proteins frequently corresponding to cysteine‑rich, disulfide‑stabilized loop modules or N‑terminal propeptide‑like regions, and in cytosolic/helical scaffolds to short loops connecting alpha‑helices (including CR‑type zinc‑finger loops)
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation over contiguous coil/IDR stretches (10–100+ residues), with sharper peaks on short loops at helix–helix boundaries; commonly near the N‑terminus immediately after signal peptides in secreted precursors; generally avoids compact catalytic cores
Exemplars: - Extracellular matrix EGF‑like/EMI/multimerin repeat proteins: activation on cysteine‑rich N‑terminal segments and disulfide‑bonded loop modules after the signal peptide.
- DnaJ/Hsp40 CR‑type zinc‑finger chaperones: activation within the cysteine‑rich Zn‑binding region, especially loops between CXXCXGXG motifs.
- Sorting nexins/retromer (BAR‑domain scaffolds): activation on short coil loops at helix–coil–helix transitions within the BAR domain.
- Ubiquitin‑conjugation factor E4 (UFD family): activation on well‑structured coil linkers connecting helical elements, not in the U‑box domain.
- Flagellar/ciliary/axonemal proteins (e.g., hook‑associated proteins): activation on intrinsically disordered coil segments.
- Bacteriophage tail/fiber/tape‑measure proteins: activation on flexible linkers/hinges within long coiled‑coil assemblies.
- Bacterial autotransporters and secreted adhesins/proteases: activation on charged, low‑complexity passenger‑region linkers immediately following signal peptides.
- Peroxisomal membrane/peroxin proteins: activation on cytosolic low‑complexity loops.
- Type IV secretion/conjugation system components: activation on periplasmic loops/linkers rich in charged residues.
- Nucleic‑acid–related enzymes and translation/scaffolding factors; plant DUF724 proteins: activation on solvent‑exposed loops/IDRs connecting secondary‑structure elements.

Summary: Generic “edge-of-domain/loop–turn” microfeature: isolated, solvent‑exposed residues (enriched for Gly/Pro/Ser/Thr and polar/charged side chains) in coils, turns, and at the ends of secondary structures, often near domain boundaries or terminal tails and not tied to catalytic or cofactor‑binding sites
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks; sparse, low-to-moderate amplitude signals at noncontiguous positions, frequently in coils/turns or at helix/strand termini and near domain borders or C-/N‑terminal extensions; count per protein varies widely
Exemplars: - HtrA/DegP-like serine protease with PDZ domain (Protease Do-like 1): isolated peaks in the PDZ domain, immediately C‑terminal to PDZ, within the protease fold, and in a flexible C‑terminal tail; avoids the catalytic triad.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursor (cathelicidin/protegrin precursor): a single peak on a disulfide‑bonded cysteine within the propeptide loop region, with minimal signal elsewhere.
- WRKY transcription factor: scattered peaks within the WRKY DNA‑binding domain concentrated near its C‑terminal edge and into a disordered tail.
- Inward-rectifier potassium channel (Kir/KirBac): few peaks confined to the cytosolic C‑terminal domain on strands/turns; includes a site whose mutation modulates conductance.
- mRNA-capping enzyme (RNA guanylyltransferase complex, beta subunit): peaks at a helix position and at the end of a long beta strand in a well-structured region.
- 2Fe–2S ferredoxin/adrenodoxin-like proteins: a main peak in a disordered C‑terminal tail just outside the ferredoxin domain and minor peaks in loops/helices within the core, away from metal‑binding cysteines.
- p24/emp24 cargo receptor (GOLD domain protein): discrete peaks within the lumenal GOLD beta‑sandwich and immediately C‑terminal coil following the domain.

Summary: N-terminal functional modules and adjacent low-complexity/disordered segments of proteins—typically signal peptides in secreted/processed precursors, but also other leader/targeting/anchor helices (e.g., RxLR-dEER, viral tegument/nonstructural tails, organelle transmembrane leaders)—and, in short precursors, the disordered bioactive peptide region.
Activation pattern: Predominantly sparse residue-level peaks near N-termini; frequent within the N-proximal helix (signal/transmembrane/leader) and the immediately downstream intrinsically disordered, low-complexity stretch; additional scattered peaks within disordered peptide segments; largely absent from well-ordered globular cores.
Exemplars: as before (KISS1, RxLR effectors, secreted serpins, peptide hormone/antimicrobial/venom and plant SSP precursors, viral envelope proteins), plus viral tegument/RNA-binding nonstructural proteins (low-complexity N-termini), organelle-encoded membrane proteins (first TM/leader helix), and nuclear regulators with acidic/basic low-complexity N-termini (e.g., zinc-finger proteins).

Summary: Secondary-structure boundary/capping motif: short turns and N-cap positions at α-helix starts and inter‑helical turns that delineate helical repeat units (especially ankyrin, PPR, ARM; often T/P/H/L‑rich), with analogous β→α junctions in α/β enzymes.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks in 1–4 aa stretches; recur periodically at repeat boundaries; concentrated in coil/turn segments just before or between helices or at the end of β‑strands entering β→α loops; occasional signal on the first helical turns adjacent to the cap.
Exemplars: TRP ion channels with N‑terminal ankyrin repeats: inter‑helical turns in ANK repeats and a specific cytoplasmic helix segment; Two‑component systems (sensor kinases/response regulators): β‑strand→helix junctions and helix N‑caps within the RR domain; Pentatricopeptide repeat proteins: repeat boundaries at coil→helix transitions of the two‑helix PPR motif; Ankyrin/armadillo repeat scaffolds: turns between the two helices of ANK repeats; ZDHHC palmitoyltransferases (ANK‑containing): multiple discrete loop/turn sites across the N‑terminal ANK array; Processive diacylglycerol β‑glycosyltransferases: coils just before β‑strands or α‑helices and occasional early helical residues; PP2C/PPM phosphatases: end of a β‑strand into the adjacent loop within the catalytic core.

Summary: Non-transmembrane, interaction-prone segments in cytosolic or luminal domains, typically alpha-helical/coiled-coil and, where present, low-complexity repeat-rich tracts (e.g., FG, Ser/Thr/Pro- and charged repeats) that scaffold protein–protein interactions or position catalytic motifs; avoids integral transmembrane helices and signal peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across continuous helical or repeat-rich segments with occasional residue-level peaks at catalytic/interaction residues; minimal in transmembrane helices and signal peptides; not restricted to high pLDDT and can occur in functional low-complexity repeats.
Exemplars:
- TRP/vacuolar calcium channels: activation on cytoplasmic regulatory helices flanking the transmembrane core, not on TM helices
- FAD-dependent ER oxidoreductases (ERO1): activation on helices surrounding the redox-active CxxC motif
- Kinesin motors: activation on C-terminal coiled-coil stalk helices
- Rab effectors/exophilins: activation across N-terminal Rab-binding helical regions
- Nuclear pore basket nucleoporins: activation across FG-repeat-rich segments
- Peptide hormone/neuropeptide precursors: activation on a structured helix in the propeptide; not on the signal peptide or disordered mature peptides
- Bacteriocins and viral tail/fiber proteins: activation on long helical or repeat-fiber segments rather than embedded membrane-spanning helices

Summary: Short, intrinsically disordered, low-complexity terminal segments (N-terminus biased) and short internal low-confidence stretches, including classical leaders (signal peptides, transit peptides, and propeptides) and analogous disordered tails in cytosolic, nuclear, viral, and organelle proteins (including mitochondrially encoded membrane subunits).
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered within low-pLDDT, low-complexity regions, strongly biased to the N-terminus but also occurring at C-termini or short internal loops; enriched for small/polar and basic residues; not a continuous domain and not tied to a specific secondary structure; number of peaks per protein varies widely.
Exemplars:
- Poxvirus accessory proteins: scattered peaks over disordered segments, especially at the extreme N-terminus of unstructured regions.
- Prohormone precursors (e.g., cholecystokinin): sparse peaks within the N-terminal propeptide/leader region of the secreted hormone precursor.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: activation on N-terminal signal/leader sequences and adjacent luminal, disordered stretches.
- Viral tegument and early regulatory proteins (e.g., herpesvirus UL46, adenovirus E4-ORF4): peaks on short disordered N-terminal regions lacking secretory leaders.
- Oomycete RxLR effector precursors: peaks on the N-terminal secretory signal and RxLR-containing presequence.
- Organelle-targeted proteins (mitochondrial/plastid): activation across positively charged, Ser/Thr-rich N-terminal transit peptides; and for mitochondrially encoded inner-membrane subunits (e.g., ND2), occasional peaks at short matrix-exposed loops or termini without transit peptides.
- Secreted toxins/defense peptides and allergens: activation on N-terminal signal peptides and short propeptides of secreted proteins.
- Small ORF peptides from non-canonical transcripts: activation across short, low-complexity N-terminal regions consistent with disordered leaders.
- Housekeeping enzymes and RNP/ubiquitin–proteasome/mitotic complex subunits (e.g., Plasmodium DHFR-TS, human RNase P p40, APC5): activation on short low-complexity N-terminal tails or internal low-pLDDT segments.

Summary: Extended assembly/interaction regions that build large supramolecular complexes—especially membrane-active systems (pore formers, ESCRT adaptors, nuclear pore scaffolds)—together with adjacent regulatory linkers; the feature highlights structured cores (α/β or helical) that mediate oligomerization/partner binding and, in some cases, nearby disordered, acidic, PTM-rich segments used for recruitment and activation.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional/domain-level activation over long contiguous stretches within large proteins; strongest in middle or C‑terminal subdomains that scaffold assembly. Frequently includes adjacent flexible linkers or protease-cleavage segments as local peaks; rarely limited to short catalytic motifs. Can cover both well-structured α/β cores and interaction‑prone low‑complexity patches when they govern complex formation.
Exemplars: - Cholesterol-dependent cytolysins (e.g., Streptolysin O): central oligomerization/pore-forming subdomain, not the small cholesterol-binding motif.
- Gasdermins (e.g., GSDMD): N‑terminal pore-forming core plus the caspase‑cleavable linker that regulates activation.
- ATG2 autophagy tethers: extensive C‑terminal interaction platform including the WIPI‑binding region and acidic, low‑complexity, phospho‑modified segments that recruit partners at membrane contact sites.
- ESCRT Bro1-domain adaptors: N‑terminal portion of the Bro1 domain implicated in ESCRT‑III binding/membrane engagement.
- Nuclear pore complex scaffolds (e.g., Nup82): C‑terminal α‑helical solenoid region used in NPC assembly.
- Aromatic prenyltransferases (ABBA/PT‑barrel enzymes): central structured core elements of the fold highlighted across helix–coil–β segments.
- STAT transcription factors: the structured linker between the DNA‑binding and SH2 domains that tunes dimer arrangement/DNA engagement.
- Mre11 (MRN complex): a localized loop position within the nuclease core, consistent with an assembly/hinge-contact hotspot.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity repeat segments enriched in small/polar residues (S/T/A/G/P) and/or acidic residues (E/D); often mucin-like O-glycosylation–prone regions in secreted/cell-surface and viral proteins, but also cytosolic low-complexity tails/linkers.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across disordered coil segments with multiple residue-level peaks; strongest in tandem repeats and low-complexity tracts; minimal in well-structured cores, but scattered peaks can occur at flexible termini/linkers of otherwise structured proteins.
Exemplars: - Mucin-like extracellular glycoproteins: activation on S/T-rich disordered repeats with O-glycosylation sites.
- Fungal GPI-anchored adhesins/effectors: activation across central S/T-rich low-complexity regions outside conserved cysteine-rich domains.
- Viral tegument/accessory proteins: activation on disordered S/T/P-rich tails.
- Cytosolic acidic low-complexity regions (e.g., GARP region of CNG-channel beta subunits) and short disordered linkers in enzymes.

Summary: Detector of conserved positions within tandem-repeat grammars: (a) small cysteine-centered modules (EGF-like, Ca2+-binding EGF, LDLR class A/LA, TB/8‑Cys, antistasin-like) and (b) long low-complexity repeat tracts (e.g., FG-, S/T/P/G/Y-, or E/Q-rich repeats), and also C2H2 zinc-finger arrays. It highlights the N-terminal aromatic before the first metal/disulfide-binding cysteine and other canonical residues in cysteine-rich modules, as well as periodic anchor residues within low-complexity repeat blocks.

Activation pattern: Residue-level periodic peaks recurring once per repeat unit; strong signal within disulfide/metal-stabilized modules and within repetitive low-complexity tracts; minimal in nonrepetitive linkers, transmembrane segments, cytosolic tails lacking repeats, and generic PTM motifs. Peaks often fall on: (i) an aromatic (Y/F) preceding the first conserved Cys of a module, (ii) acidic/glycine positions in Ca2+-binding EGF/LA loops, (iii) select helix residues (T/S and basic) in C2H2 fingers, and (iv) repeated anchors within low-complexity blocks (e.g., FG in nucleoporins; Tyr/Pro/Ser or Glu/Gln anchors in extensins/glue/involucrin; repeated peptide motifs in neuropeptide precursors).

Exemplars:
- Latent TGF-β binding proteins and Notch-pathway receptors/ligands: arrays of Ca2+-binding EGF-like and TB/8‑Cys domains; disordered nonrepetitive linkers are weak.
- LDL receptor family: repeated peaks in LA and EGF-like modules; β‑propeller, transmembrane, and nonrepetitive cytosolic tails are inactive.
- C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factors: periodic peaks at the conserved Y/F before the first Cys and a few residues in the recognition helix for each finger.
- Low-complexity repeat extracellular proteins: plant extensins (Pro/Ser/Tyr-rich), invertebrate salivary glue proteins, and keratinocyte envelope proteins (involucrin; Glu/Gln-rich) show long-run periodic activation within repeat blocks.
- FG-repeat nucleoporins (e.g., NUP98): peaks track the FG-based repeats.
- Secreted protease inhibitors with small cysteine-rich repeats (e.g., antistasin-like): activation on conserved positions within those repeats.
- Neuropeptide precursors: activation over repeated peptide-motif blocks within secreted precursors.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity polyampholyte segments enriched for Lys and acidic residues (E/D) with frequent KE/EK alternation (KEKE‑like motifs), plus N/Q, and depleted of hydrophobics and Arg; typically flexible N‑terminal tails and linker/tail regions in diverse eukaryotic and viral proteins, including many small/secreted proteins and membrane‑protein loops
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long charged stretches (often starting at the N‑terminus), with diffuse peaks on K/E/D/N/Q and avoidance of hydrophobic/TM segments; activates on flanking luminal/cytosolic loops and propeptide regions rather than structured cores
Exemplars: - Herpesvirus glycoprotein N: activation on KE/EK‑rich luminal ectodomain and cytosolic tail regions flanking the TM helix
- Herpesvirus nuclear egress proteins (e.g., pUL31/pUL34): activation on acidic/lysine‑mixed disordered segments implicated in electrostatic interactions
- Retroviral Vif and Tat: activation on low‑complexity K/E‑rich regions outside the canonical Arg‑rich core, consistent with polyampholyte IDRs
- ATP synthase ε subunits (eukaryotic/mitochondrial): activation on charged N‑ or C‑terminal tails and flexible linkers depleted of hydrophobics
- Secreted/precursor proteins (including plant signaling peptides): activation on acidic/lysine‑mixed prodomains or mature low‑complexity regions, excluding the hydrophobic signal peptide
- sORF‑encoded micropeptides: activation across the entire peptide due to overall K/E/N/Q‑rich, hydrophobe‑poor composition
- Membrane‑associated proteins: activation on cytosolic/luminal loops and terminal tails that are K/E‑mixed polyampholytes rather than the transmembrane helix
- Diverse bacterial proteins: activation on low‑complexity charged linkers and acidic/lysine‑rich tracts connecting domains

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity segments enriched in serine/threonine/proline/glycine and often basic (lysine/arginine), typically found in flexible N- or C-terminal tails and loops; highlights IDRs that may harbor short linear motifs (e.g., basic NLS patches) rather than structured domain cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with additional sparse residue-level peaks in low-confidence loops; often N-terminal-biased in short/viral proteins; rarely within well-folded cores.
Exemplars: Retroviral accessory proteins (e.g., HTLV-1 p30): activation on central and C-terminal IDRs including a basic nuclear localization signal; p53-regulated apoptosis-inducing microprotein: widespread activation across a globally disordered protein; Bacterial DNA ligase: scattered activation in an annotated disordered linker and flexible loops within the ligase domain; Uncharacterized human microprotein: multiple peaks throughout a low-pLDDT, disordered sequence irrespective of predicted secondary structure.

Summary: Residue-level signal for tight coil/turn positions that link beta-strands, with strongest and recurring activation at the inter‑blade linker loops of beta‑propeller repeat domains (especially Kelch/WD/YWTD/olfactomedin), and analogous beta‑hairpin turns in other beta‑sheet folds; favored residues are glycine and small/polar/acidic residues (e.g., G, T, D/N/S)
Activation pattern: Predominantly isolated, single‑residue peaks in coil/turn segments adjacent to beta‑strands; in beta‑propellers the peaks recur once per blade at repeat boundaries, producing a periodic pattern across the domain; occasional weaker peaks occur on nearby small/polar residues
Exemplars: - Kelch‑repeat beta‑propeller adaptors (e.g., Rab9 effectors): single glycine residues in the linkers between successive Kelch repeats/blades
- F‑box/Kelch proteins (e.g., Adagio family): short glycine‑rich loops within each Kelch blade connecting the beta‑strands
- Kelch‑repeat accessory domains in enzymes (e.g., in wybutosine‑synthesizing proteins): repeating peaks at the C‑terminal boundary of each blade
- Carbohydrate‑active hydrolases with beta‑propeller folds (e.g., GH43 beta‑xylosidases): turns between adjacent beta‑strands shaping the propeller
- Rieske [2Fe‑2S] ferredoxin subunits: well‑defined loops/turns between beta‑strands near the cluster‑binding motif
- Small heat‑shock proteins (alpha‑crystallin domain): the loop connecting core beta‑strands within the beta‑sandwich

Summary: Hydrophobic-composition signal: enrichment for valine/isoleucine/leucine within low‑complexity, repeat‑rich segments of secreted/cell‑surface and viral proteins, often corresponding to disordered propeptides/linkers and simple helices (signal peptides, transmembrane anchors, and coiled‑coils); occasionally also fires on acidic low‑complexity tracts in the same contexts.
Activation pattern: Mixed: broad regional activation across long low‑complexity/repetitive stretches; continuous bands over hydrophobic helices (signal peptides, TM segments, coiled‑coils); plus sparse residue‑level peaks on isolated I/L/V within disordered propeptides and linkers. Not confined to a specific short motif and can span multiple regions of a protein.
Exemplars: - Bradykinin‑potentiating peptide precursors (venom propeptides): sparse peaks on I/L/V across unstructured propeptide/linker regions and within some mature peptides.
- Mucins, adhesins, and fungal GPI‑anchored cell‑wall glycoproteins: regional activation across low‑complexity repetitive ectodomains with strong activation on the C‑terminal hydrophobic GPI/TM anchor and sporadic ILV residues in repeats.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: activation on N‑terminal signal peptides and C‑terminal TM anchors, with additional signal over low‑complexity ectodomain segments.
- Multi‑pass transporters and single‑pass receptors: strong activation along multiple transmembrane helices enriched in L/I/V; occasional signal in coiled‑coil stalks/tails.
- Coiled‑coil/scaffolding and cytoskeletal proteins: activation on leucine/isoleucine at heptad core positions across extended coiled‑coil regions.
- Secreted enzymes/hydrolases and plant secreted proteins: activation in signal peptides and propeptides (including acidic low‑complexity proregions) and on scattered hydrophobic residues within disordered segments.

Summary: Hydrophobic alpha-helical membrane-spanning segments—canonical transmembrane helices (including N-terminal signal peptides)—across diverse proteins and taxa.
Activation pattern: Regional activation along long hydrophobic alpha helices; multiple moderate peaks across multi-pass proteins; minimal signal in loops, disordered regions, or non-helical segments; frequent N-terminal peak on signal peptides/anchors in secreted or single-pass proteins.
Exemplars: - Urea transporters (SLC14 family): activation on each transmembrane helix, absent in cytosolic/periplasmic loops.
- GPCRs (7TM receptors): activation across the seven membrane helices with low signal in extra-/intracellular loops.
- Respiratory chain inner-membrane subunits (Complex I/IV and ATP synthase Fo): activation on hydrophobic membrane-spanning helices.
- Aquaporins and other ion/solute channels and transporters: activation on membrane-spanning helices.
- Secreted precursors and single-pass receptors: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide and/or the single transmembrane anchor.

Summary: Residue-level signal for well-ordered, solvent-exposed loop/turn and beta-edge residues enriched in charged/polar side chains that flank or modulate functional sites (ligand/metal binding pockets, catalytic environments, disulfide linkages, or proteolytic/secretion processing) rather than the core catalytic motifs themselves.
Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks (typically 1–5 per protein), mostly on K/E/R/D/Q/N/S/T/H (occasionally C/M), concentrated in high-confidence coils/turns or at beta-strand edges; can also occur within structured C-terminal secretion propeptides; not domain-wide.
Exemplars: - Apolipoprotein N-acyltransferase (Lnt): arginines in the CN hydrolase fold near the catalytic lysine.
- Isopentenyl-diphosphate isomerase (type I): arginine/glutamate in ordered loops adjacent to Mg2+ and substrate-binding positions.
- Glycerol kinase: glutamate/arginine in coil loops proximal to the glycerol-binding site.
- Ulvan lyase (type IX–secreted polysaccharide lyase): residues within the structured C-terminal secretion propeptide processed by the T9SS.
- Thioredoxin-like disulfide isomerase (TlpA): a disulfide-bonded cysteine in a beta strand and a lysine in a periplasmic loop of the thioredoxin domain.
- EGO complex subunit (EGO2): a single asparagine in a short loop connecting beta strands.

Summary: N-terminal low-hydrophobic presequence detector: preferentially marks low-complexity, small/polar-rich leaders (e.g., chloroplast transit peptides and some mitochondrial transit peptides), but generally not classical hydrophobic signal peptides or strongly Arg-rich amphipathic leaders
Activation pattern: Regional activation at extreme N-termini (first 15–60 aa), but under-activates strongly hydrophobic H-regions and Arg-rich amphipathic helices; such proteins may show only a minimal M1 baseline
Exemplars:
- Secreted/type I membrane proteins: activation only on non-classical, low-hydrophobic leaders; classical hydrophobic signal peptides are typically not activated
- Eukaryotic mitochondrial proteins: activation biased toward Ser/Thr/Gly-rich, low-hydrophobic presequences; strongly basic amphipathic leaders may be missed
- Viral proteins: activation on low-complexity leaders; not on classical hydrophobic signal peptides

Summary: Beta-strand–enriched cores of mature, soluble protein domains (including beta-sandwich/jelly‑roll/barrel and mixed alpha/beta folds), often in secreted or lumenal enzymes and lipid/ligand-binding proteins; the feature highlights long, conserved beta-strands and adjacent loops (frequently with glycine–aromatic motifs such as GXW/GXWXGXG and occasional N‑glycosylation loops) while remaining inactive on signal peptides, transmembranes, and disordered segments. It can also pick out beta-substructures within largely alpha-helical oxidoreductases (e.g., catalase-peroxidases), with transmembrane segments remaining inactive.
Activation pattern: Predominantly domain-level/regional activation as long contiguous windows spanning multiple beta-strands and connecting loops within the canonical domain; sharp onset after signal peptides; in mixed or alpha-helical folds, activation concentrates on embedded beta segments and nearby turns; catalytic residues themselves may be weak but surrounding beta elements are strongly activated.
Exemplars: - Plant dirigent/pterocarpan synthase proteins: inactive on N-terminal signal peptides; strong activation across the all‑beta mature domain with peaks on beta-strands and glycosylation loops.
- GH11 xylanases: activation confined to the catalytic beta‑jelly‑roll domain; no activation on the signal peptide or C‑terminal CBM6 modules; strongest on beta-strands and loops near (but not at) catalytic glutamates.
- Nitrobindin/peroxynitrite isomerase (lipocalin-like): strong activation across the lipocalin beta‑barrel, including the hallmark GXWXGXG beta‑strand and strands adjacent to the heme-binding region.
- Oxysterol-binding protein–related proteins: activation across the C‑terminal OSBP-related lipid-binding domain composed of multiple beta-strands; no activation on the N‑terminal PH domain or long disordered segment.
- Natural product pericyclases/hydratases (e.g., hydroalkoxylation enzyme, acyclic carotenoid hydratase): localized activation on beta‑strand clusters within the structured catalytic core.
- Decarboxylases and chorismate pyruvate-lyase: broad activation over beta‑rich or mixed alpha/beta cores encompassing the active-site region.
- Catalase and catalase-related peroxidases: activation on beta‑sheet substructures within the fold; catalytic histidines often weak.
- Holocytochrome c-type synthase: activation in soluble regions (including beta-strands) while any membrane-anchoring segments remain inactive.

Summary: Short low-polarity hydrophobic stretches—primarily signal-peptide h-regions, terminal single-pass transmembrane anchors, and short amphipathic membrane-interface helices—enriched in Leu/Ile/Val/Phe/Ala/Pro/Gly and preferentially containing aromatics and/or cysteine; used for membrane targeting/anchoring and secretion signals.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous runs (≈8–20 aa) of hydrophobic/low-complexity composition; strongest when the tract includes Phe/Tyr/Trp and/or Cys and is membrane-proximal (signal peptide or terminal anchor). Typically weak/absent on long multi-pass TM bundles lacking aromatics and on buried hydrophobic cores of soluble proteins; occurs at N- or C-termini or at membrane-interface segments.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope glycoproteins (herpes-, adeno-, orthomyxo-, corona-, poxviruses): activation on N‑terminal signal peptides with aromatics and C‑terminal single-pass TM anchors.
- Adenovirus E3/immune-evasion single-pass membrane glycoproteins: activation on signal peptide and luminal-anchor TM helix when aromatic/Cys-enriched.
- Single-pass anchors and peripheral/amphipathic membrane helices (not generic multi-pass bundles): activation on short terminal anchors or interface helices.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides and hormones/toxins: activation on the subset of signal peptides whose h-regions include aromatics and/or nearby Cys/small-residue motifs; many signal peptides without these features do not activate.
- Viral matrix/envelope-associated or peripheral structural proteins with amphipathic membrane-binding patches (not generic inner capsid proteins): activation on hydrophobic/aromatic interface segments.

Summary: A positional/structural detector of protein chain ends, strongest at the extreme C-terminus and weakly at the extreme N-terminus. It marks short terminal tail segments (typically the last 4–8 residues), usually unstructured/low-confidence and sometimes including the final turn of a helix, with signal rising toward and peaking on the terminal residue. The concept is the presence of an exposed chain terminus rather than a specific sequence motif.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated at the very C-terminus (short contiguous runs with a monotonic ramp to the last residue); interiors largely silent even in disordered regions; occasional small N-terminal blips (often at M1–L3); frequently located immediately after the last helix.
Exemplars: - Protein phosphatase 1 regulatory subunit (PPP1R35): silent internally; activation confined to the C-terminal helix-to-coil end segment, peaking on the terminal residue.
- APC membrane recruitment protein family (AMER/APC membrane recruitment protein 3): sharp hotspot on the final unstructured hexapeptide; no activation in numerous internal disordered/structured regions.
- Enhancer of split bHLH transcriptional repressor (E(spl)-M2): activation over the last 6 residues of a C-terminal coil immediately following the final helix, maximal at the terminal cysteine.
- Photoreceptor scaffolding/low-complexity protein (PIP82): weak N-terminal start signal (M1–Q6) and a strong C-terminal run culminating at the last residue; interior (including annotated motifs and helices) remains inactive.

Summary: Detector of short linear sequence motifs (SLiMs) and immediately flanking residues—most often in low‑complexity/disordered or boundary regions (frequently near N‑termini or cytosolic tails)—and, secondarily, conserved residues within structured catalytic/substrate‑binding helices of enzyme cores; enriched for acidic (E/D), proline‑rich, hydrophobic (L/I/V/F), and serine/threonine residues in these contexts.
Activation pattern: Sparse, low‑amplitude residue‑level peaks (occasionally small local clusters); biased to coils/IDRs, domain boundaries, and early N‑terminal segments, with additional peaks inside well‑structured alpha helices adjacent to catalytic or binding residues; no extended contiguous domain‑level activation.
Exemplars: - Ser/Thr protein kinases: isolated peaks in the ATP‑binding beta‑strand and near the catalytic Asp within the kinase core, plus a peak just N‑terminal to the domain boundary.
- Shikimate kinases: residues within high‑confidence helices that also contain annotated substrate‑binding Arg residues.
- Neuropeptide precursors: the dibasic KR proprotein‑convertase cleavage site and the C‑terminal Gly that donates the amide for peptide amidation at a processing boundary.
- LDL receptor family cytosolic tails: residues immediately upstream of PPxY motifs in disordered cytoplasmic regions.
- Mitochondrial dehydrogenase (NuoF): residues in an N‑terminal disordered stretch and within the mitochondrial transit peptide.
- Disordered regulatory proteins (e.g., phosphatase inhibitor 2): scattered peaks in acidic/basic‑biased disordered helices.
- tRNA modification methyltransferases: residues on a conserved, well‑structured alpha‑helix (high confidence) despite no specific site annotation.

Summary: Residue-level detector for well-ordered beta-strand positions (DSSP class E) in beta-sheets, independent of specific function; commonly realized in beta-sandwich and beta-propeller contexts (e.g., Rieske ferredoxin domains, PH domains, alpha-crystallin/sHSPs, glycoside hydrolases) and other alpha-beta proteins.
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks (often single residues or short dipeptides) confined to beta-strands in high-confidence structured regions; rarely contiguous; frequently near but not coincident with catalytic or metal-binding residues; only weak, occasional off-target signals in helices/coils.
Exemplars: - WYL domain regulators: short beta-strand segment within the WYL domain.
- Rieske [2Fe-2S] ferredoxin-like domains in ring-hydroxylating dioxygenases and respiratory/photosynthetic Rieske subunits: isolated beta-strand residues within the Rieske domain, excluding the Cys-His metal-ligand positions.
- Pleckstrin homology (PH) domain adaptors: a two-residue beta-strand segment within the PH beta-sandwich.
- Small heat-shock proteins (alpha-crystallin family): beta-strand residues within the alpha-crystallin beta-sandwich domain.
- Glycoside hydrolases (e.g., GH32 levanase; GH43/GH3 beta-xylosidase): scattered residues on beta-propeller/sheet strands, sometimes adjacent to but not at catalytic residues.
- CorA family Mg2+/Co2+ transporters: beta-strand residues in the N-terminal cytosolic domain.
- MutL/PMS2 mismatch repair endonucleases: short beta-strand segment in the C-terminal endonuclease-containing region.

Summary: Short, ordered beta-strand–loop transition motifs (beta-turn/hairpin connectors) at the ends of beta-strands within beta-rich domains, typically enriched in acidic/polar residues and glycine/proline; a broad, structural signal rather than a function-specific motif
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks over short contiguous segments (~6–12 aa) that straddle the C-terminus of a beta-strand and the immediately following loop/turn (or lie within the strand directly adjacent to such a turn). Peaks recur multiple times within a protein, are confined to well-structured regions (high pLDDT), and are rare in helices, disordered segments, signal peptides, and transmembranes. Sequence composition is biased toward D/E/K/R/S/T with frequent G/P and few cysteines.
Exemplars: - Adhesion GPCRs (GAIN/GPS region): activation on a beta-strand segment immediately preceding the autoproteolytic GPS site within the GAIN domain.
- Periplasmic oligopeptide-binding proteins (OppA family): peaks at strand-to-loop connectors linking adjacent beta-strands in the SBP fold.
- E3 ubiquitin-ligase adaptors (RWD-domain proteins such as RNF25): a beta-strand and adjacent loop within the RWD fold.
- DM13/DOMON extracellular domains (metal-reductase–associated proteins): repeated short peaks on beta-strands and neighboring loops within each DOMON/DM13 domain.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes (neutral alpha-glucosidase AB): multiple strand–loop transition sites across the structured core, away from catalytic residues.
- Polysaccharide epimerases (AlgE4): a sharp peak on the loop connecting two beta-strands at the domain’s C-terminal region.
- General transcription factors (TFIID subunit 2): turns connecting beta-strands within the ordered core (annotated beta-turns).

Summary: Intrinsic-disorder/low-complexity, polar/charged segments enriched in Ser/Thr/Lys/Arg/Asp/Glu/Gln—typically long, solvent-exposed linkers, stalks, and propeptides in secreted/extracellular or ER-luminal proteins (often “precursors”), and basic rRNA-binding tails—rather than compact catalytic cores or transmembranes
Activation pattern: Extended regional activation across long stretches with multiple peaks on Ser/Thr and charged residues; depleted in hydrophobic/TM segments; strongest in extracellular/luminal linkers, mucin-like S/T-rich regions, propeptides (often with dibasic sites), and basic tails that contact RNA; not confined to a single site
Exemplars: Carbohydrate-active enzymes (glycosidases, polysaccharide lyases): activation on S/T-rich, O-glycosylated linkers and acidic/basic low-complexity stalks between catalytic and carbohydrate-binding modules; Multicopper oxidases/blue-copper proteins (e.g., laccases, plastocyanin-like): activation on secreted propeptides and long polar loops in luminal domains; Ig-superfamily cell-adhesion/ECM proteins: activation on mucin-like Ser/Thr-rich extracellular stalks and flexible inter-Ig linkers; ER/secretory-pathway residents (luminal chaperones/enzymes): activation on acidic low-complexity luminal regions and signal/propeptide-adjacent segments; Urease enzymes/subunits: activation on flexible polar surface loops and basic/acidic terminal extensions used in assembly; Ribosomal protein uS17: activation on Lys/Arg-rich disordered tails that bind rRNA; Cysteine protease inhibitors (cystatins and parasite CPI): activation on flexible N-terminal inhibitory segment and polar loops; Ciliary/flagellar-associated proteins: activation on S/T-rich low-complexity regions adjacent to coiled coils; Viral secreted/envelope proteins: activation on mucin-like S/T-rich regions and precursor propeptides with dibasic processing motifs

Summary: Exposed boundary/loop context: the feature marks order–disorder junctions and strand‑edge loop residues—especially in precursors and modular proteins (signal/propeptide/processing regions, flexible terminal peptides, intein junctions)—rather than catalytic cores; it prefers small/polar residues in these contexts.
Activation pattern: Primarily residue-level peaks with light regional activation. Peaks concentrate in coils and low‑pLDDT segments, at N-termini and other order–disorder boundaries, and immediately before/within beta‑strands (strand edges/turns). Occasional emphasis on conserved loop micro-motifs in structured cores. Catalytic residues are typically not highlighted. Preference for D/E/K/R/S/T/G/P; coverage varies widely across proteins.
Exemplars: - Plant CEP peptide precursors: activation on the disordered C‑terminal peptide and nearby exposed Asn within that peptide; weak in the signal helix.
- Sedolisin (peptidase S53) precursors: peaks adjacent to beta‑strands in the mature domain and in the Ca2+-binding loop; minor signals near signal/propeptide–mature boundaries.
- Secreted/proprotein families (general): activation at signal/propeptide–mature junctions and other flexible, low‑pLDDT peptide segments.
- Ribosomal proteins (bacterial, organellar, eukaryotic): activation on flexible basic extensions and solvent‑exposed loop regions, not on catalytic motifs.
- Intein/homing endonuclease–containing replication/repair proteins: activation around intein–extein junctions and adjacent low‑complexity linkers.
- Cell‑wall peptidoglycan enzymes and oxidoreductases: peaks at strand‑edge loops and surface turns within the core, and at N‑terminal signal/targeting segments when present.

Summary: Hydrophobic/aromatic beta-strand elements that line small-molecule binding cavities or substrate pockets in beta-rich folds, especially in Bet v 1/START-like and NTF2/lipocalin-type barrels, with analogous beta-sheet segments highlighted in diverse enzymes and binding proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short, contiguous beta-strands (about 5–15 residues, sometimes appearing as 10–30 residue stretches), with sharp peaks at hydrophobic/aromatic positions; often multiple peaks across adjacent strands that frame a cavity
Exemplars: - Abscisic acid receptors (PYL/RCAR; Bet v 1/PR-10/START-like): beta-strands lining the abscisate-binding pocket (activation coincides with annotated ligand-contact residues)
- Hsp90 co-chaperone Aha1: well-ordered C-terminal beta-strands of the beta-sheet core
- Nuclear transport factor 2 family (NTF2-like) and nuclear export factors: beta-strands forming hydrophobic cavities for Ran/FG-repeat binding
- Lipocalin/avidin/streptavidin and nitrobindin families: beta-barrel strands surrounding hydrophobic ligand pockets (e.g., biotin, NO/peroxynitrite)
- Lipid-binding/transfer proteins and vitellogenins; chloroplast lumen/plastoglobule proteins: beta-sheet segments bordering internal lipid-binding cavities
- Rieske oxygenase small subunits, epoxide hydrolases, and secondary-metabolite cyclases: beta-strands shaping hydrophobic substrate-binding sites
- Carbohydrate epimerases/mutarotases: beta-strands of cupin/jelly-roll barrels near sugar-binding regions
- Protein kinases: N-lobe beta-sheet strands adjacent to the ATP-binding cleft
- Photosystem/pigment-associated proteins: beta-strand elements around chromophore/pigment-binding pockets
- Mitochondrial Tim21: beta-strand elements within the soluble domain that interface with binding surfaces

Summary: Leucine-/aliphatic-rich long alpha-helical segments, often amphipathic and coiled-coil–like (heptad-repeat style), used as generic assembly/partner‑interaction helices across diverse proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended alpha-helices (sometimes multiple per protein), with residue-level peaks on hydrophobic positions (Leu/Ile/Val/Phe/Ala/Met) and sharp drop-offs at helix–coil boundaries; little to no activation in coils or highly disordered regions.
Exemplars: - Paramyxovirus phosphoprotein P: strong activation on a long C‑terminal helix consistent with an oligomerization/interaction helix; activation ends at the helix-to-coil transition.
- Nairovirus (bunyavirus) nucleoprotein: multiple activated internal helices within the helical core; non-activating around non-helical motifs (e.g., cleavage sites).
- Pseudomonas syringae type III effector HopW1: dispersed activation on predicted helices throughout the protein (enriched at leucines), absent from large disordered N- and C-terminal regions.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity coil/linker segments enriched for acidic/polar and small residues (S/T/D/E/N/G with frequent P), typically at domain boundaries and in terminal tails; these regions often precede helices and serve as flexible, phosphorylation‑prone or interaction‑prone connectors rather than structured catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on isolated residues or very short microsegments, scattered across the sequence; concentrated in low‑pLDDT coils, interdomain linkers, Ala/Gly‑rich or acidic stretches, and disordered tails; minimal activation within well‑formed secondary structure or hydrophobic cores.
Exemplars: - Coronavirus nucleocapsid (N) protein: peaks in disordered coils at the CTD boundary (e.g., T near the linker) and in the C‑terminal disordered tail on S/T sites annotated as phosphorylated.
- CRISPR Cas13a endoribonuclease: multiple peaks in low‑confidence coil loops, especially the flexible linker between the two HEPN domains and other interdomain/terminal linkers.
- Adenylate cyclase/hemolysin toxin (CyaA‑type): activation within an Ala/Gly‑rich low‑complexity hemolysin region required for partner interaction, and on loop/linker residues adjacent to catalytic segments.
- Herpesvirus ICP8 ssDNA‑binding protein: sparse peaks in flexible linkers immediately preceding α‑helices and other low‑pLDDT coils, outside defined structured motifs.

Summary: Central antiparallel beta-sheet cores of small beta-barrel/beta-sandwich binding domains—especially calycin/avidin/lipocalin-like barrels and related beta-sandwich/exclusion scaffolds—i.e., the long, contiguous beta-strand framework and adjacent hairpins that form ligand/protein-interaction surfaces across secreted/surface proteins and analogous cytosolic beta-sandwiches (e.g., CBF-beta)
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation as long continuous blocks over beta-strand–rich cores; strongest on antiparallel beta strands and beta-hairpin turns (enriched for Gly/Thr with frequent GT/TG, plus Tyr/Ser/Asn/Asp); minimal on signal peptides, transmembrane helices, catalytic residues, and disordered termini; in membrane proteins, activation is confined to soluble/loop beta segments and is therefore shorter
Exemplars: - Avidin/streptavidin family: activation across the 8-stranded calycin barrel that binds biotin
- Lipocalins/calycins and nitrobindin/peroxynitrite isomerase: central beta-barrel cores that scaffold small-molecule binding
- Neisserial outer-membrane antigens and diverse bacterial lipoproteins/cell-envelope proteins: beta-barrel/sandwich cores and exposed beta hairpins/loops on the surface
- Protease and lysozyme inhibitors (e.g., Bowman–Birk/trypsin inhibitors): beta-hairpin/strand inhibitory scaffolds
- Dipeptidyl peptidase 1 (cathepsin C): N-terminal exclusion-domain beta strands/turns (while catalytic regions remain unactivated)
- Core-binding factor beta (CBF-beta/brother): central helix-plus-beta-strand block forming the beta-sandwich core and RUNX-binding surface
- CD-NTase-associated membrane proteins: internal beta-strand–rich soluble domain following N-terminal transmembrane helices
- Phycobiliprotein-related proteins/lyases: beta-strand scaffold segments that position chromophore-handling loops

Summary: Structural signal for glycine‑centered tight turns and loop→strand junctions in beta‑sheet–rich domains, especially repeated blade architectures (beta‑propellers/lectins/trefoils), with occasional hits at the first residue of a beta‑strand within a repeat; enriched for Gly and Asx (Asp/Asn) residues that accommodate tight turn geometry.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks that are sparse but recur across repeat units; strongest on Gly in short coil/turn segments connecting beta‑strands and, in some propeller repeats, at the strand N‑cap/start. Little to no activation in helices, signal peptides, or densely helical regions; peaks may cluster near functional sites but reflect structural turn/strand‑boundary positions rather than specific chemistry.
Exemplars: Peptidyl‑alpha‑hydroxyglycine alpha‑amidating lyase with NHL repeats: Gly/Asp in high‑confidence loops linking beta‑strands within NHL blades; Lysosomal sialidase/neuraminidase (beta‑propeller enzyme): Gly in short loops adjacent to catalytic/substrate‑binding residues between strands; Fibroblast growth factors (beta‑trefoil fold): Gly in turns connecting adjacent beta‑strands of the trefoil; G‑type lectin receptor‑like kinases: multiple Gly in extracellular bulb‑type lectin domain loops between strands, minor signal in a kinase loop; Tectonin/TECPR beta‑propeller repeat proteins: residues at the starts of beta‑strands marking repeat (blade) boundaries; Polysaccharide lyase family 25 (ulvan lyase): Gly/Asp in short inter‑strand turns near catalytic residues; Bacteriophage long tail fiber/tail spike proteins: Gly in flexible coil segments in the beta‑rich N‑terminal region, absent from the highly structured peptidase S74 domain.

Summary: Arginine-selective low-complexity/disordered segments—polybasic tracts and RG/RGG-type repeats—often occurring as long, repetitive stretches; includes the Arg residues embedded in repeated neuropeptide/prohormone units (e.g., RFamide-like repeats). The signal tracks local Arg identity/density with a strong preference for Arg over Lys and is largely independent of stable secondary/tertiary structure.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks on Arg that cluster over extended disordered, compositionally biased regions; broad regional activation in Arg-dense tails or repeats; minimal in well-structured domains and transmembrane helices; occasional co-activation of neighboring Gly (RG/RGG) and sometimes Trp within Arg-rich low-complexity segments; Lys generally weak.
Exemplars: - RFamide-family neuropeptide/prohormone precursors: strong peaks on the Arg within repeated peptide units (e.g., PRQFV-/XREFV-amide motifs) and nearby disordered basic-biased segments; little/no signal in the N-terminal signal peptide.
- Vacuolar zinc transporters (multi-pass membrane transporters): concentrated activation on cytosolic, disordered, Arg-rich C-terminal tails; silent across transmembrane helices and luminal loops.
- RNA-binding and chromatin-associated proteins: activation on RGG/RG boxes and poly-Arg low-complexity tracts that mediate nucleic-acid interactions/phase separation.
- Viral regulatory proteins: strong signal on Arg/Gly-rich low-complexity segments.
- Reproductive proteins (e.g., protamines, semenogelins) and long coiled-coil/golgin scaffolds, mucin-like glycoproteins, and disulfide-rich peptide toxins: activation on extended Arg-rich, repetitive low-complexity regions.

Summary: Terminal low-complexity, poorly structured segments—especially N-terminal presequences used for targeting/processing (signal peptides, mitochondrial transit peptides, removable propeptides)—and, more generally, intrinsically disordered terminal stretches regardless of secretion, including viral assembly/regulatory proteins and occasional cytosolic enzymes with flexible N-termini.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation over the first ~20–60 residues; in proteins lacking leader peptides, also appears as sparse residue-level peaks within low-pLDDT terminal coils; activation typically drops within structured cores.
Exemplars:
- Viral assembly/regulatory proteins (e.g., adenoviral E4-ORF6, phiX174 scaffolding protein B) — scattered peaks within disordered termini.
- Housekeeping enzymes with flexible N-termini (e.g., bacterial DNA ligase) — low-level terminal peaks without targeting signals.
- Secreted peptide/hormone and antimicrobial precursors — strong activation across signal peptides/propeptides; low in mature peptides.
- Mitochondrial enzymes (e.g., PanK2) — peaks on N-terminal transit peptides.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors — activation over disordered RxLR-dEER regions.
- Alternative reading frame microproteins (e.g., POLGARF) — terminal disordered activation.

Summary: Low-complexity intrinsically disordered segments (often S/T- and/or proline-rich), including targeting/secretory presequences and mucin-like regions; SP/TP motifs are common but not required
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation within low-pLDDT/disordered segments, appearing as clusters of residue-level peaks across low-complexity stretches; can occur near transmembrane flanks, in N-terminal targeting/signal peptides and secretory propeptides, and as short peaks in disordered loops of otherwise structured enzymes
Exemplars: - Viral accessory/membrane proteins (e.g., gN-type): activation on mucin-like, S/T-rich luminal loops flanking a transmembrane helix
- Viral regulatory proteins (e.g., E4-ORF6, ICP47): multiple peaks within intrinsically disordered regulatory segments (often S/T/Pro-enriched)
- Human p53-target/lncRNA-associated proteins (e.g., TP53TG3, CASC2-derived): globally disordered, low-complexity patches highlighted
- Secreted toxin precursors (e.g., conotoxin prepropeptides): activation on signal/propeptide low-complexity segments
- Bacterial metabolic enzymes/ligases (e.g., Cas6, Kdo transferase): sporadic peaks on short low-complexity/disordered surface loops

Summary: Low-complexity repeat regions of mature extracellularly deployed or surface/particle-associated proteins—often secreted—enriched in small/polar residues (Gly/Ser/Thr/Asn/Ala), typically intrinsically disordered, that frequently serve as self-assembling/adhesive modules (e.g., functional amyloids/rodlets) or as reservoirs for proteolytically cleaved bioactive peptides; includes analogous repeats in some non-secretory organellar proteins (e.g., starch-binding) and viral capsid/readthrough extensions
Activation pattern: Primarily domain-level activation: long, continuous stretches that, when a signal peptide is present, start abruptly after it and span the mature low-complexity region; activation is largely independent of local secondary structure or pLDDT and often highlights glycine-/serine-rich repeats; in non-secretory cases, analogous long activation tracts occur within disordered LCRs; signal peptides and short propeptides (when present) are typically not activated; occasional short, residue-level peaks occur within disordered coils
Exemplars:
- Functional bacterial amyloid (FapC): activation switches on at the mature chain start and remains high across all amyloid repeat modules and linkers, excluding the N-terminal signal peptide
- Fungal hydrophobin (Class I hydrophobin/EAS): localized activation on a short unstructured patch adjacent to conserved cysteines within the secreted rodlet-forming protein
- Corneodesmosin (epidermal extracellular matrix protein): strong, continuous activation across the central glycine/serine-rich, low-complexity disordered region of the mature protein, but not on the signal peptide or distal non-LC tail
- Insect seminal fluid secreted protein: broad activation over a disordered segment in the mature extracellular region immediately following the signal peptide
- Immune-induced peptide precursor: activation tracks the mature cleaved antimicrobial/immune peptides (long disordered segments), while signal peptide and removed propeptides show low activation
- Gram-negative autotransporter adhesin (Antigen 43): activation across passenger repeat/adhesive regions of the surface-exposed secreted protein
- Viral capsid readthrough protein: activation on low-complexity/disordered readthrough extensions implicated in host/vector interactions
- Plant chloroplastic ESV1: activation on low-complexity starch-granule-binding repeats
- Epidermal matrix precursor (filaggrin): activation on long low-complexity repeats that are proteolytically processed during barrier formation

Summary: Compositionally biased non‑globular segments, especially hydrophobic aliphatic‑rich helices of signal peptides and single‑pass transmembrane anchors, together with adjacent or standalone intrinsically disordered low‑complexity regions enriched in small residues and basic patches (e.g., NLS‑like)
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long contiguous stretches; strongest across hydrophobic helical segments (signal peptides/transmembrane helices), with diffuse/sparse activation across low‑pLDDT disordered coils; occasional residue‑level peaks at basic residues within short targeting motifs; frequently N‑terminal but not restricted to termini
Exemplars: - Viral envelope glycoproteins: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide, a disordered luminal segment, and the transmembrane anchor.
- Viral early/accessory proteins (e.g., adenoviral E4 ORF4): broad activation across intrinsically disordered regions with a peak at a basic residue within an NLS.
- Disordered enzymes (histone acetyltransferase with extensive IDRs): sparse activation on low‑pLDDT coils/helices lacking stable structure.
- Secreted micropeptides/uncharacterized secreted proteins: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and long disordered pro‑regions.
- Small single‑pass membrane proteins: activation centered on the predicted transmembrane helix with weaker signal in adjacent flexible segments.

Summary: Tandem‑repeat/low‑complexity and Cys‑motif detector: the feature highlights conserved, periodic intra‑repeat positions, small‑residue–rich tracts, and compact disulfide‑rich secreted microdomains. It preferentially marks G/A/S/T/P runs and characteristic Cys/His‑containing motifs, activating on structural repeat modules (e.g., C2H2 fingers, TALE/BuD repeats), extended GA/ST‑rich low‑complexity regions common in secreted or surface proteins, and conserved Cys motifs in small secreted peptides.
Activation pattern: Long, regional activation across repeat arrays with recurring residue‑level peaks aligned to each repeat unit. Within modules it favors specific landmarks: in C2H2 fingers the Y–K/T–C start, acidic core E/D residues between the Cys pair, and the C‑terminal helix basic/His sites; in TALE/BuD repeats defined helical Ile/Ala positions and Gly/Asn coil turns between helices; in GA‑rich tracts GG/GxG and GA runs in coils. Catalytic cores of globular enzymes are typically weak, but compact disulfide‑stabilized microdomains in secreted proteins can show focused activation at Cys motif positions, and low‑complexity propeptides/linkers of secreted proteases can also activate. Overall residue bias skews to small/polar and disulfide‑forming residues (G, A, S, T, P, C; His at finger ends), producing periodic spikes superimposed on extended low‑complexity stretches.
Exemplars:
- C2H2 zinc finger transcription factors: marks the conserved intra‑finger pattern (Y–K/T–C start, acidic core, helix‑end basic/His residues) across tandem finger arrays.
- Mycobacterial PE‑PGRS family: highlights central glycine/alanine low‑complexity regions, especially GG/GxG coils, while ignoring the structured N‑terminal PE domain.
- TALE/BuD repeat DNA‑binding effectors: periodic peaks at specific intra‑repeat helical Ile/Ala sites and adjacent Gly/Asn coil turns across the repeat array.
- Mucins and fungal adhesins/flocculins: strong activation across Ser/Thr‑rich O‑glycosylation‑prone repeats and other low‑complexity segments.
- Cysteine‑rich extracellular modules (EGF/VWC/SRCR) and small plant Cys‑rich antimicrobial peptides (knottin/defensin‑like): activation on conserved Cys‑patterned motifs consistent with disulfide stabilization.
- Silk/fibroin‑like and ice‑associated proteins: strong signal on GA‑ and small‑residue repeat arrays.
- Plant extensins/LEA and large bacterial surface repeat proteins: activation along proline/small‑residue LCRs and modular repeat tracts typical of secreted/surface scaffolds.
- Secreted subtilisin/furin‑like proteases: activation confined to low‑complexity propeptides/linkers and any appended Cys‑rich inserts, not the catalytic core.

Summary: Short solvent-exposed loop/turn micro-motifs enriched in small/polar/acidic residues—often triads/tetrads that end in glycine and may include histidine or cysteine—capturing generic beta-turn–like segments frequently used for binding/metal coordination and present across diverse protein families
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks forming short contiguous 3–5-residue clusters; often multiple clusters per protein; typically located in flexible loop/turn regions (including extracellular/periplasmic loops in secreted/membrane proteins) and conserved at analogous positions across orthologs
Exemplars: - CorA/ZntB metal ion transporters: acidic/histidine-containing cytosolic loop motifs (E/D/H-rich) involved in metal interaction.
- Secretins (outer-membrane secretins): short Gly/Ser/Asp-rich loop tetrapeptides in periplasmic/extracellular segments.
- Phospholipase D enzymes: small loop triads near catalytic regions (e.g., adjacent to HxK…D motifs), enriched in Gly/Asp/Ser/His with occasional aromatic caps.
- TTLL (tubulin-tyrosine ligase-like) enzymes: compact polar/acidic turns in active-site loops.
- FAM83 family: conserved small/polar triads ending in glycine around residues 230–250.
- Mitochondrial large ribosomal (mitoribosomal L) proteins: Gly/acidic loop segments at RNA-contacting surfaces.
- Secreted cysteine-rich small proteins: short Cys or Cys–Pro motifs within disulfide-stabilized loops.
- RNA polymerase III subunit RPC4: a shared short “-A/G-” centered motif at a comparable regional position.
- Nitrate reductase alpha chains (NarG): an N–C–T–G-like loop motif near the catalytic site.
- Broad enzyme classes (hydrolases, oxidoreductases, transferases/ligases): multiple discrete 3–5-residue loop motifs with small/polar/acidic residues and frequent aromatic participation.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered low-complexity regions specifically enriched for long asparagine and/or glutamine/serine/threonine runs; Pro/Gly content alone is insufficient. Activation is typically in extended linker or terminal tracts outside folded domains and is most common in organisms/proteins that harbor pronounced N/Q-rich repeats.
Activation pattern: Broad regional activation only when contiguous LCRs are long and strongly N/Q/S/T-enriched with repeat character; minimal or absent in structured catalytic domains and in IDRs lacking N/Q-enrichment.
Exemplars: 
- Serine/threonine kinases: activation on N-rich disordered inter-domain linkers; kinase domains remain inactive.
- Rho GTPase–activating proteins: N/Q-rich disordered C-terminal tails activate; GAP domains are inactive.
- Opa/mucin-like secreted proteins: activation on N/S/T-rich repetitive segments near or distal to signal peptides; signal peptides and structured regions are inactive.
- F-box/ARM-repeat proteins: activation on N-rich low-complexity N-termini; F-box and ARM repeats are inactive.
Exclusions: Compact enzymes (e.g., tRNA-modifying enzymes, deubiquitinases), membrane transporters, and viral proteins lacking long N/Q-rich tracts typically do not activate.

Summary: Short helical patches (often amphipathic and enriched in basic/aromatic residues) embedded within intrinsically disordered linkers or tails, typically positioned immediately C-terminal to signal/translocation motifs, adjacent to transmembrane segments, or at the edge of folded domains/coiled-coils. These helices mediate membrane association or adaptor docking in secretion, trafficking, and virulence contexts.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous 20–40 aa stretches with low predicted structure confidence but helix propensity; strongest residue-level peaks on hydrophobic/aromatic positions within the helix. Frequently located just downstream of motifs (e.g., RxLR-dEER), at domain termini (e.g., WD40, UBX), or proximal to transmembrane helices/coiled-coil boundaries.
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: N-terminal segment immediately after RxLR-dEER used for host entry/membrane interaction.
- Autophagy PROPPINs (Atg18/Atg21): disordered C-terminal tail with a short amphipathic helix for membrane/adaptor contacts.
- Membrane-embedded autophagy receptors (Atg39/Atg40): cytosolic amphipathic/basic helical patches adjacent to hairpin TMs for ER-phagy machinery engagement.
- UBX-domain proteins: disordered C-terminal extension after the UBX fold containing a short helix for partner interactions.
- Clathrin assembly/adaptor proteins (epsins/ENTH/ANTH/AP180/AP-2): N-terminal insertion amphipathic helices that bind acidic membranes.
- Viral coat/membrane proteins and replicase polyproteins: TM-proximal amphipathic/basic helices or basic tails that anchor or organize membranes (e.g., filamentous phage coat G8P) and amphipathic helices in replicases.
- Bacterial pathogen effectors/toxins: basic/aromatic amphipathic helices for host membrane interaction/translocation.
- LEA proteins: Lys-rich amphipathic “K-segment” helices that form upon stress and associate with membranes.
- Nuclear envelope SUN/LEM proteins: basic helical patches/linker helices near the membrane that mediate partner or membrane contacts.
- Coiled-coil scaffold proteins (e.g., TRIMs): short basic helical patches at coiled-coil termini that mediate partner docking.

Summary: Threonine‑centered tandem repeat motifs in low‑complexity domains—especially S/T/P‑rich mucin‑like and adhesion‑associated segments—and analogous Thr‑periodic positions in structured repeat scaffolds (e.g., octapeptide beta‑solenoid arrays). The core concept is the periodic placement of Thr within repeat units in surface/extracellular proteins (often mucin‑like and frequently O‑glycosylated), with similar Thr‑rich, proline‑rich low‑complexity repeats inside some viral proteins also triggering the feature.
Activation pattern: Strong regional activation confined to repeat‑rich domains; sharp, periodic residue‑level peaks on Thr at fixed offsets within each repeat unit, with weaker co‑activation on Ser and hydrophobics (I/V/M) that occupy consensus positions; minimal activation in signal peptides, transmembranes, and non‑repeat/globular regions; present in both disordered P/S/T‑rich repeats and ordered beta‑solenoid repeat architectures.
Exemplars: Mucins (e.g., MUC21): mucin tandem‑repeat domains with ~15‑aa periodicity—peaks on Thr at the repeat‑defined positions; Fungal GPI‑anchored cell‑wall adhesins (e.g., Eap1/Flo family): disordered S/T‑rich tandem repeats—periodic activation on Thr within 6–20 aa repeats; Bacterial ice nucleation proteins: octapeptide beta‑solenoid repeat arrays—peaks on Thr with co‑activation on I/V/S at consensus sites; Viral envelope glycoproteins (e.g., EBV gp350/BLLF1): mucin‑like S/T‑rich repeats—dense Thr‑centered activation across the ectodomain; Viral low‑complexity nuclear antigens (e.g., EBNA4): proline‑rich repeat segments—activation on Thr and nearby hydrophobics within repeated motifs; Amoebozoan spore/prespore coat proteins: secreted S/T‑rich repeat blocks with domain‑wide activation; Plant cell‑wall HRGP/AGP/extensin‑like proteins: S/T/P‑rich segments with clustered Thr; Bacterial secreted adhesins: extracellular Thr/Ser‑rich repeat tracts showing periodic Thr peaks.

Summary: Sequence-pattern detector for short linear motifs and compositional/periodic biases rather than a specific fold: it responds to (i) dibasic Lys/Arg convertase cleavage motifs and residues flanking amidated peptides in secreted prohormone/peptide precursors, (ii) Gly–X–Y/proline-rich collagen-like repeats (including hydroxyproline sites), (iii) hydrophobic a/d positions in coiled-coil heptads of long scaffolds, and (iv) PTM-prone Ser/Thr embedded in Lys/Arg-rich disordered tails of chromatin/DNA-binding proteins. The unifying concept is recognition of repetitive/low-complexity sequence context and short processing/PTM motifs used across diverse proteins.
Activation pattern: Predominantly sparse, residue-level peaks at motif-defining positions, distributed across long regions. Peaks occur at K/R around convertase cleavage/amidation sites; at Pro/Gly within Gly–X–Y repeats; at Leu/Ile/Met in coiled-coil heptad a/d positions; and at Ser/Thr within basic, disordered segments. Activation appears in both intrinsically disordered regions and repetitive helical scaffolds and is not strictly tied to local structure confidence.
Exemplars: - Neuropeptide/hormone precursors (urotensin-II-related; insect CAPA/PBAN/Tachykinin/FLP families): strong peaks at dibasic K/R convertase sites immediately flanking the mature amidated peptides and at nearby peptide boundaries; occasional signal peptide and intrapeptide residues.
- Antimicrobial/venom peptide precursors (e.g., amphibian AMPs): peaks across the signal peptide, acidic propeptide, and basic mature peptide segments, reflecting processing motifs and compositional biases.
- Fibrillar collagens/extracellular matrix collagens: peaks on Pro (often 4-hydroxyproline) and Gly within Gly–X–Y repeats characteristic of the collagen triple-helix.
- Golgi/centrosomal coiled-coil scaffolds (golgins and related tethers): peaks on hydrophobic residues aligned with the coiled-coil heptad repeat throughout the long alpha-helical rod.
- Chromatin proteins (linker histone H1, HMG/homeobox-associated regions): peaks on Ser/Thr within Lys/Arg-rich disordered tails (PTM hotspots) and other basic low-complexity stretches.
- Bacterial DNA-binding regulators and toxin–antitoxin antitoxins (HTH/RHH/ECF sigma-associated proteins): scattered peaks across helical bundle residues and basic/low-complexity segments consistent with repetitive or motif-like sequence patterns.

Summary: Residues on the lipid-exposed face of transmembrane beta-strands in outer-membrane beta-barrel proteins (diderm bacterial and organellar), encompassing porins, TonB-dependent receptors, autotransporter translocator barrels, ushers, Omp85/BamA/OEP barrels, TolC-like efflux channels, and outer-membrane enzymatic barrels
Activation pattern: Distributed, domain-level activation across beta-barrel/translocator regions with residue-level peaks that alternate every other position along beta-strands, favoring hydrophobic/aromatic (and some glycine) residues; little to no activation in signal peptides, periplasmic/extracellular soluble domains, or non-barrel regions; in autotransporters, concentrated in the C-terminal translocator barrel; in TonB-dependent receptors and ushers, spread across long stretches of the barrel wall
Exemplars: - TonB-dependent receptors (e.g., pesticin receptor): strong alternating peaks across the C-terminal beta-barrel, including near the TonB C-terminal box.
- Trimeric/Type V autotransporters (e.g., Neisseria adhesin A): activations confined to the C-terminal translocator beta-strands of the outer-membrane barrel.
- Omp85/BamA/TamA-family barrels (e.g., chloroplastic OEP80): peaks in the C-terminal beta-barrel after POTRA domains, showing one-face strand periodicity.
- Chloroplast outer envelope channels (e.g., OEP39): discrete peaks on beta-strands throughout the barrel domain.
- Outer-membrane efflux channels (TolC-like): clustered peaks on beta-strands within the outer-membrane barrel.
- Outer-membrane enzymatic beta-barrels (e.g., OmpLA/LpxR-like lipid/phospholipid-modifying enzymes): alternating-residue peaks on barrel strands.
- Usher proteins (e.g., FimD): multiple short activated segments on beta-strands of the usher barrel.
- General porins/OmpA-like barrels: activation on beta-strands of the outer-membrane barrel domain.

Summary: Residue-level detector of α-helical hydrophobic segments embedded in or interacting with membranes, especially within transmembrane helices of multi-pass receptors (notably class A GPCRs) and mitochondrial inner-membrane subunits, and also N-terminal signal peptides/targeting helices of secreted or organelle-targeted precursors.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on isolated positions inside predicted transmembrane α-helices or signal peptides; minimal to none in extramembrane loops, termini, or disordered regions. Typically only a few residues per protein are activated, often recurring across multiple helices in 7TM receptors (with frequent strong peaks in TM6).
Exemplars: - Cytochrome c oxidase small membrane subunit (mitochondrial respiratory chain): single-residue peak within its sole transmembrane helix.
- TIM/TOM mitochondrial import component: single-residue peak within its transmembrane helix.
- Class A GPCRs (beta-adrenergic, vasopressin V1a, adenosine A1/A2A, opsins, orphan GPCRs): sparse peaks on individual residues across TM2–TM7, consistently strongest in TM6, with negligible activation in extracellular/cytoplasmic loops and C-terminal tails.
- Small secreted peptide precursors (e.g., plant CLE/TDIF): peak(s) within the N-terminal signal peptide.

Summary: Short, solvent-exposed coil/turn segments at beta-strand boundaries—most prominently the strand-connecting hairpins and inter-blade loops of WD/kelch beta-propeller domains in eukaryotic scaffold/adaptor proteins (nuclear pore, vesicle/cilia machinery, ubiquitin-ligase and RNA-processing assemblies)—with a sequence bias toward S/T/G/D/E, frequent prolines, and occasional aromatics.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks recurring in many short segments per protein; peaks localize to loops/turns linking beta-strands or at strand–coil/strand–helix junctions. Activates both on well-ordered propeller turns (high pLDDT) and on flexible/disordered coils (low-to-moderate pLDDT). In repeat architectures (WD/kelch), peaks repeat blade-by-blade across the domain, yielding numerous activated residues, while long low-complexity stretches are often inactive.
Exemplars: WD-repeat/kelch beta-propeller scaffolds in autophagy (Atg18/WIPI family): activation on the turns/loops connecting beta-strands across multiple blades; WD-repeat cilia/cytoskeletal scaffolds (EMAP-like): inactive over long disordered N-termini but strongly active on propeller blade loops; ciliopathy-linked WD-repeat scaffolds (WDR family): activation on hairpin turns and inter-strand loops, especially in C-terminal WD-repeat regions; nucleoporins (Nup133 beta-propeller): activation on short loops/turns connecting beta-strands and other secondary elements; U3 snoRNP assembly/UTP factors: activation on flexible coil segments and strand-boundary loops; E3 ubiquitin-ligase substrate adaptors (ZIF-1-like): activation in short unstructured coil segments and beta–coil boundary regions.

Summary: A broad, low-amplitude sensor of folded, mature protein cores: it preferentially activates across well-ordered secondary-structure elements (helices and beta strands) in the mature portion of proteins, while being suppressed on N-terminal signal peptides/cleavable leaders and on flexible or poorly ordered coils; it is not specific to any residue type, function, or family.
Activation pattern: - Domain-level, contiguous activation spanning much of the sequence in structured proteins
- Elevated across helices, beta strands, and internal loops within well-packed cores; dips on disordered/low-confidence coils and terminal regions
- Strong suppression on signal peptides and immediate ramp-up at the start of the mature chain (e.g., after a lipidated Cys)
- Uniformly low, narrowly distributed scores with modest variation rather than sharp residue-level spikes
Exemplars: - Bacterial lipoprotein precursors (signal peptide + lipobox/lipidated cysteine): feature is essentially off across the signal peptide, then increases at the lipidated N-terminus of the mature chain and is strongest on well-structured C-terminal strands and helices, with dips in lower-confidence coils.
- PLP-dependent aminotransferase/decarboxylase enzymes: highest activation across the well-ordered core (notably a C-terminal helical block and several beta strands), including short inter-helix loops within that core; lower at a flexible N-terminus and not specifically tied to annotated catalytic residues.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments used for protein–protein interactions, with a strong compositional bias (polar/charged, Pro/Gly) and particular sensitivity to phenylalanine‑containing short repeats (e.g., FG/FSFG) in large eukaryotic regulatory/scaffold proteins; avoids structured catalytic or coiled‑coil cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks clustered within long IDRs: multiple short peaks across the sequence, often within regions annotated as Disordered/Low complexity and with low pLDDT; highest responses on FG/FSFG/FxFG motifs and on polar/Pro/Gly‑rich tracts (occasionally hydrophobic residues when embedded in low‑confidence helices); minimal activation in well‑folded domains (e.g., catalytic SET domains, stable coiled‑coils).
Exemplars: - Nucleoporins (FG-repeat channel proteins): activates on disordered FG/FSFG/FxFG repeat regions that form the permeability barrier.
- SET-domain histone methyltransferases: activates on long disordered linkers outside the folded RRM/SET/Post‑SET domains.
- Spindle assembly regulators: activates on low‑confidence helical/coil segments within broadly disordered regions.
- Autophagy regulators (ATG41-like): activates on short, low‑confidence helices and neighboring coils in an overall disordered protein.
- Translational regulators/scaffolds (Cup-like): activates across multiple disordered clusters throughout the protein.
- Transcriptional coactivators (PGC‑1 family): activates within disordered helical interaction regions (e.g., RNF34‑binding, LXXLL‑containing stretches).
- DNA repair scaffolds (Shieldin complex subunit 1): activates in N‑terminal low‑complexity/polar‑biased disordered segments.
- Myosin-V receptor/adaptors: activates in disordered tail regions while avoiding the central, structured coiled‑coil domain.

Summary: N-terminal leader/targeting signatures: signal peptides, transit peptides, or short, flexible N-terminal tails (with or without a subsequent transmembrane helix), with additional sensitivity to single hydrophobic signal‑anchor/transmembrane helices
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks with a strong N‑terminal bias (first ~30–100 aa) in disordered/coil regions; occasional short contiguous peaks spanning a hydrophobic signal peptide or transmembrane helix
Exemplars: Secreted fungal killer toxin precursor: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and on an internal single-pass transmembrane signal‑anchor; Viral integrase family: isolated peaks across the low‑confidence, disordered N‑terminal region; Formate/nitrite transporter (FNT family): sparse peaks in the cytosolic N‑terminal tail immediately before the first transmembrane helix

Summary: Conserved glycine-centered beta-strand/turn positions repeated across beta-sheet architectures, especially the homologous site within each leucine-rich repeat, generalizing to other beta-rich repeat/modules (CBS repeats, beta-helix and beta-barrel regions of autotransporters, and small beta-sandwich domains). The feature captures strand N-caps or hairpin bends that favor small/turn-promoting residues (G, P, S, T), with occasional non-glycine residues at the same structural register.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks that recur periodically (one per repeat) across long extracellular repeat arrays; concentrated in beta-strand or immediately adjacent turn/loop positions. Outside repeat arrays, activation is sparse at loop-to-strand boundaries within compact beta-domains, and shows low diffuse signal across many strands in large beta-barrels. Minimal or absent signal in signal peptides, transmembrane helices, and catalytic kinase domains.
Exemplars: - Plant LRR receptor(-like) kinases and receptor-like proteins: sharp, regularly spaced peaks on the concave beta-strand/turn of nearly every LRR unit.
- Gram-negative autotransporter serine proteases: sparse peaks on glycine in turns of the beta-helix passenger and low, widespread activation across beta-strands of the C-terminal beta-barrel.
- Matrix metalloproteinases: isolated peak on a glycine within the activation (pro)peptide in a tight coil/turn.
- CBS-domain proteins (AMPK gamma subunits, ClC channels): one peak per CBS repeat on a beta-strand position, often glycine.
- GYF-domain proteins: localized peaks on glycine within beta-strands of the beta-sandwich.
- DCN1/DCUN1 family: isolated residues at loop or pre-beta positions within the structured domain.
- Other repeat-rich beta-proteins (e.g., MORN-repeat proteins, ciliary radial spoke head proteins, bacterial/phage cell-wall hydrolases): activation at conserved strand/turn sites repeated across the array.
