Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low-complexity serine/threonine-rich segments (often proline-enriched) that constitute multi-site phospho-regulatory regions, typically found in termini and linkers and largely absent from folded domains.
Activation pattern: Broad regional activation across long IDRs with many residue-level peaks specifically on S/T; minimal activation inside structured domains (catalytic cores, repeats, transmembranes). Highest scores occur in low-complexity, polar/compositional-bias stretches, frequently spanning N- or C-terminal tails and inter-domain linkers.
Exemplars: - Hybrid histidine kinase (Dictyostelium): activation on numerous S/T in disordered N-/C-terminal tails and linker; no signal in the histidine-kinase or response-regulator cores.
- Cilia/flagella WD-repeat scaffold (CFAP): strong activation on S/T across a disordered, low-complexity C-terminus; absent from EF-hand and WD repeats.
- Kinetochore-associated protein (KNL2-like): activation on S/T within disordered, compositionally biased regions of the C-half; not in SANTA or Myb-like domains.
- Herpesvirus tegument phosphoprotein (VP22): widespread activation on S/T throughout disordered, low-complexity segments, including regions overlapping an NLS and partner-interaction sites.
- BAR–RhoGAP signaling scaffold: activation confined to disordered linkers and C-terminal low-complexity regions; suppressed within F-BAR and Rho-GAP domains.

Summary: N-terminal low-complexity, intrinsically disordered patches enriched in charged (Lys/Arg and Asp/Glu) and small/polar residues (Ser/Thr/Gly/Ala/Pro) — flexible motifs that commonly mediate nucleic-acid contacts or N-terminal targeting/processing features
Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks clustered within short stretches, most often in the first tens of residues after the initiator Met; conserved hotspot positions within families. Occasional mid/late-sequence peaks occur in similar charged/polar low-complexity loops.
Exemplars: - Ribosomal proteins (bacterial/archaeal/mitochondrial/chloroplastic): activation on Lys/Arg- and Gly/Ser/Pro-rich N-terminal tails that wrap and contact rRNA.
- Eukaryotic RNA splicing factors (SR proteins, hnRNPs): activation on RS/RG-rich low-complexity segments near N-termini used for RNA binding and regulation.
- Aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetases and translation fidelity/editing factors: activation on basic/polar N‑terminal loops and linkers (Gly/Ala/Ser/Thr-rich) that engage tRNA or rRNA.
- Secreted and membrane proteins (transporters, proteases): activation on the positively charged n‑region of signal peptides and nearby small residues consistent with signal peptidase −3/−1 positions; also on cytosolic charged loops flanking transmembranes.
- Small plant peptide precursors: activation on prepro regions (signal peptide n‑region and adjacent small/charged residues around processing sites).
- Viral nucleic‑acid–binding proteins: activation on short Lys/Arg-rich disordered segments used for RNA/DNA binding or genome packaging.

Summary: Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly–rich low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—most often at protein N‑termini—such as mucin‑like/propeptide regions or flexible linkers adjacent to signal/transit peptides, common in small secreted or membrane‑associated proteins and also as disordered extensions in diverse enzymes (broad taxonomic coverage, including viral and eukaryotic effectors)
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short to moderate stretches, typically near the N‑terminus; residue‑level peaks on Ser/Thr often adjacent to Pro/Gly; in longer proteins, multiple low‑complexity patches can activate; in micropeptides, activation can span much of the sequence
Exemplars: - Viral envelope/accessory microproteins: activation on N‑terminal Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich disordered segments (often mucin‑like or regulatory tails).
- Secreted eukaryotic effectors (e.g., oomycete RxLR effectors): activation on the low‑complexity region flanking the signal peptide/RxLR motif.
- Human testis‑biased and lncRNA‑derived micropeptides: activation across Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly‑rich intrinsically disordered peptides.
- Secreted precursors/propeptides: activation on N‑terminal propeptide or mucin‑like stretches following the signal peptide.
- Membrane‑associated single‑pass proteins: activation on Ser/Thr‑rich luminal or cytosolic tails adjacent to the transmembrane helix.
- Bacterial/archaeal metabolic enzymes: activation on disordered, low‑complexity N‑terminal (or other) extensions/linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro.

Summary: Short beta-strand segments enriched in hydrophobic/aromatic residues within well-folded beta-rich domains (beta-sandwich/jelly-roll/DSBH and related sheets), a structural signal common in extracellular/periplasmic proteins and also present in diverse enzyme and binding domains
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks concentrated within or immediately adjacent to beta-strands of high-confidence structured regions; biased toward hydrophobic/aromatic side chains with occasional neighboring coil/turn hits; multiple isolated sites per protein rather than contiguous domain-wide activation
Exemplars: Collagen triple-helix repeat–containing proteins: short beta-strand segments in the C‑terminal globular domain; Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate–dependent oxygenases (e.g., prolyl 3‑hydroxylase): beta-strands of the DSBH core near catalytic residues; Secreted bacterial proteases: beta-strands within the catalytic domain; Botulinum-like neurotoxins: beta-strand and adjacent coil elements in the C‑terminal receptor-binding domain; SPRY/B30.2 domain proteins (e.g., ASH2): beta-strands of the beta-sandwich fold

Summary: Short, surface-exposed loop motifs enriched in S/T, G, D/E and P with embedded aromatic residues (W/Y) that form carbohydrate-recognition and catalytic micro-sites in extracellular polysaccharide-active proteins; the same sequence grammar also matches DTG/SGG-type catalytic loops in many secreted proteases (including retroviral proteases).
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on short, contiguous patches; multiple hotspots scattered across long secreted/surface proteins, typically in loops of CBMs, catalytic clefts of glycoside hydrolases, or adhesive repeats (Ig/Sushi/TIG).
Exemplars: - Carbohydrate-binding modules (e.g., CBM20/CBM48 for starch/glycogen): activation on aromatic “clamp” loops (W/Y) flanked by S/T and acidic residues contacting glucans.
- Glycoside hydrolases (e.g., GH13 amylases, GH5/6/9 cellulases, GH16 β-glucanases): activation at short loops around catalytic E/D residues and substrate-binding subsites rich in W/Y, S/T, and G.
- Plant expansins/expansin-like (CBM63-like cellulose binders): activation on cellulose-binding groove loops with S/T-, G/P-rich segments and aromatic residues.
- Starch utilization system SusD-like outer-membrane proteins: activation on glycan-binding surface loops containing aromatic and polar/acidic residues.
- Aspartic proteases (pepsin-like A1; retroviral/retropepsin A2): activation on the DTG/DSG catalytic loop.
- Trypsin/chymotrypsin-like serine proteases (S1 family): activation on the GNSGG/GTSGG catalytic-loop region and adjacent flexible loops.
- Extracellular receptors/adhesins with Ig/IPT/Sushi/CCP/TIG repeats: activation on short surface loops mediating glycan/protein contacts enriched in S/T, G, D/E with embedded W/Y.
- Glycosylation/cell-wall glycan machinery (e.g., GT-A/GT-B glycosyltransferases, polysaccharide-modifying enzymes): activation on DxD/acidic, S/T-rich donor/acceptor-binding loops and glycan-interacting patches.

Summary: Repeat-associated, polar segments at repeat-unit boundaries in modular proteins, typically highlighting the C-terminal halves of repeat modules and adjacent linkers. In secreted/surface adhesins this maps to Ser/Thr/Pro-rich mucin-like tandem repeats, while in bacterial surface proteins it emphasizes terminal helix/strand regions of repeat domains (e.g., NEAT and helical immunoglobulin-binding B domains); the same signature also appears in cytosolic repeat assemblies (e.g., RbcS-like repeats in carboxysome proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long, contiguous stretches that recur across successive modules; peaks most often in the C-terminal portion of each repeat and in inter-domain linkers. Enriched for polar/charged and small residues, especially Ser/Thr with TP/PT and TT/TX motifs when present. Occurs in both ordered contexts (terminal helices or beta-strand/loop edges of domains) and disordered low-complexity repeats; activation is selective within repeats rather than uniform.
Exemplars: - Staphylococcal immunoglobulin-binding proteins (Sbi family): activation on well-structured helical segments within B-domain repeats and a long helix in a downstream repeat module.
- Gram-positive NEAT-domain heme-acquisition proteins (e.g., IsdB): activation at the C-termini of NEAT domains, including the heme-binding region, and a long inter-NEAT helical linker.
- Carboxysome assembly proteins with RbcS-like repeats (CcmM): activation in the C-terminal portion of each RbcS-like repeat (beta-strand/loop segments), sometimes abutting disordered regions.
- Yeast flocculins/adhesins (FLO11 family): activation within Ser/Thr-rich 32-aa tandem repeats of the mucin-like central domain, strongest in the C-terminal half of each repeat.

Summary: A short beta-turn/strand-edge loop motif at beta-sheet boundaries (coil-to-beta-strand junctions and hairpin loops), enriched in small/flexible (G, S, T, P) and often acidic residues; a generic structural element prevalent across diverse beta-rich domains in both secreted/surface and intracellular proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous blocks (~5–10 residues) with a single peak, typically spanning the end of a beta-strand and the adjacent loop or the loop connecting two beta-strands; frequently solvent-exposed and, in secreted proteins, may overlap NXS/T glycosylation sequons.
Exemplars: - Glycoside hydrolases (e.g., beta-glucosidases): coil-to-beta-strand transition within a structured beta-sheet.
- RUNX family Runt domains: loop immediately following a beta-strand in the DNA-binding beta-sandwich.
- Lamin/intermediate filament tail regions: short coil–strand junctions within the lamin tail domain.
- HAP2/GCs1 fusogens: extracellular loop connecting adjacent beta-strands, often containing N-linked glycosylation sequons.
- BBSome WD40/propeller subunits: unstructured loop that precedes a propeller blade beta-strand in the C-terminus.
- Broadly consistent with other beta-rich extracellular modules (e.g., complement/alpha-2-macroglobulin, plexin sema domains) and trafficking complexes (TRAPP), where strand-edge loops are common.

Summary: Surface-exposed loop/turn positions—especially beta-strand–connecting hairpins and helix↔sheet junctions—enriched in Asp/Glu and/or Gly (often short Gly-rich motifs), including the canonical glycine-rich AdoMet/S-adenosylmethionine binding loop; these mark interface/cofactor-recognition loops in beta-rich extracellular folds (cupredoxin/plastocyanin-like, TNF) and enzymes, rather than metal-binding sites.
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks on isolated acidic or glycine residues within well-structured loops or immediately adjacent to beta strands; frequently in the N-terminal portion of the first domain; peaks typically avoid metal-ligating residues and instead map to binding/interface loops.
Exemplars: - Cupredoxins/plastocyanin-like domains and multicopper oxidases: Asp/Glu (and occasional Ser) in strand-connecting loops across plastocyanin-like domains; not at copper ligands.
- AA9 lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases: an Asp in a loop between beta strands, with minor peaks on adjacent Gly/Gly near a strand.
- Pectate lyases: a single Ser in the loop bridging an alpha-helix to a following beta strand.
- SAM-dependent methyltransferases (Protein-L-isoaspartate O-methyltransferase, rRNA large-subunit methyltransferase E, Type II DNA methyltransferase): Gly (and nearby small/acidic residues) within or immediately flanking the glycine-rich AdoMet-binding loop; occasional additional acidic loop residue elsewhere.
- TNF homology domain ligands: acidic and glycine residues in receptor-binding loops within the THD beta-sandwich.

Summary: Extracellular/lumenal ectodomain signal focusing on beta‑strand–rich modules and carbohydrate-recognition contexts in secretory proteins—highlighting residues (often Asn, Gly, acidic/polar) within or adjacent to N‑glycosylation sequons and lectin/β‑propeller/FN3/cadherin-type domains rather than catalytic cores or transmembranes
Activation pattern: Primarily regional/domain-level activation across large extracellular/lumenal segments, with scattered single‑residue peaks in beta‑strands or nearby loops; peaks frequently occur at Asn and other polar/acidic residues and near N‑glycosylation sites or sugar-binding surfaces; little to no activation in transmembrane helices, cytosolic tails, or catalytic residues of enzymes
Exemplars: - ER lectin chaperone (Calnexin): peak in the lumenal beta‑sheet near the glycan-binding site and adjacent to an annotated N‑linked glycosylation site.
- Neuraminidase/Sialidase (β‑propeller enzyme): main peak at an Asn within a β‑strand of a propeller blade; minor signal near an Asp‑box repeat, not at catalytic residues.
- Secreted exochitinase with accessory FN3 domain: activation concentrated in the Fibronectin type‑III (β‑sandwich) module and preceding segment, absent from the GH18 catalytic site.
- Cadherin-family adhesion receptor (Calsyntenin): sparse peaks within extracellular cadherin/ectodomain β‑strands and loops; no signal in signal peptide, transmembrane, or cytosolic tail.
- Large secreted glycoprotein (Reelin): a focused peak at an Asn near the C‑terminus of the signal peptide, consistent with secretory pathway/lumenal exposure and glycoprotein context.

Summary: Residue-level detector for exposed, low-complexity/repetitive linear segments and helix-based recognition motifs, biased toward charged/polar residues. It highlights intrinsically disordered tails/loops and signal/propeptides, and also marks conserved positions in coiled-coil helices and canonical DNA-binding modules (C2H2 zinc fingers and HTH recognition helices), while largely sparing compact globular cores.
Activation pattern: Sparse, punctate single-residue peaks spread across long non-globular stretches; periodic peaks aligned to motif positions within repeats (e.g., per-finger sites in C2H2 arrays, heptad-aligned charged sites in coiled-coils). Minimal activation inside folded domain cores except at canonical recognition residues.
Exemplars: - Coiled-coil motor proteins (myosin heavy chain): peaks on E/K/R/D within the rod coiled-coil helices and adjacent disordered segments.
- Intrinsically disordered adaptors/scaffolds (NYAP2): single-residue peaks throughout low-complexity IDRs; little in more structured helices.
- C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factors (GLI/Krüppel-like): regular peaks at the start of each finger and near the second histidine within the recognition helix; additional peaks in inter-finger linkers.
- RUNX/Runt transcription factors: activation confined to disordered N- and C-terminal regulatory regions, with little to none in the folded Runt domain.
- LuxR-type HTH DNA-binding regulators (two-component response regulators like FixJ): strong peak on the recognition helix of the HTH domain; weaker in receiver-domain loops.
- Secreted toxin precursors (conotoxins): activation in the signal peptide and propeptide segments; absent across the folded cystine-rich mature toxin.
- Class A GPCRs: peaks in highly disordered cytoplasmic C-terminal tails and large intra/extracellular loops, sparing the transmembrane bundle.

Summary: Short, low‑complexity interaction segments enriched in Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly (often with nearby Lys/Arg), typically intrinsically disordered, frequently near N‑termini and harboring regulatory PTM sites; the feature also highlights analogous short cationic helices used for molecular interactions (e.g., HTH DNA‑binding helices and amphipathic antimicrobial peptides).
Activation pattern: Predominantly sparse, residue‑level peaks within disordered/low‑complexity stretches (often N‑terminal and PTM‑prone), with occasional single‑residue peaks inside short helices involved in DNA binding or membrane‑active peptides; variable extent per protein.
Exemplars: Herpesvirus ICP4–type transcription factors: peaks on Ser/Thr and basic residues within disordered, low‑complexity regions; Homeobox transcription factors (e.g., Nkx6.1): peaks in disordered regulatory tails flanking the homeodomain, including annotated PTM sites; Cancer/testis microproteins (X antigen family): N‑terminal Ser/Thr residues in disordered regions, including a phosphoserine and proximity to a SUMOylation site; ECF sigma factors (SigM): single‑residue peak within the helix‑turn‑helix recognition helix of sigma‑70 domain 4; Antimicrobial peptides (Ixosin): peaks in the mature amphipathic helical peptide, including residues at the helix start and internal S/N positions.

Summary: Residue‑level detector of high‑confidence β‑strand sites, with a strong preference for the blade‑defining strands of β‑propeller repeat domains (WD/NHL and related propellers), and sparse spillover to analogous isolated β‑strand positions in other folds (e.g., ABC ATPase, Rossmann‑like enzymes).
Activation pattern: Sharp single‑residue peaks confined to DSSP β‑strands; in propellers, most often at or just N‑terminal to annotated repeat starts (the blade’s edge/A‑strand or inter‑blade seam). Minimal/absent in disordered regions, loops, helices, signal peptides, transmembrane segments, and canonical catalytic/ligand‑binding motifs (e.g., P‑loops). Residues are often polar/charged (Ser/Thr/Lys/Glu/Asp) but not exclusively.
Exemplars: - WD‑repeat β‑propeller adaptors (SCF ubiquitin‑ligase F‑box/WD proteins such as Cdc4): discrete peaks on single residues in β‑strands immediately preceding each annotated WD blade; no signal in the N‑terminal low‑complexity/NLS region or the F‑box domain.
- NHL‑repeat β‑propeller extracellular proteins: isolated peaks on β‑strand residues across successive NHL repeats; inactive at glycosylation/disulfide sites, helices, the transmembrane helix, and the cytosolic tail.
- ABC transporter ATP‑binding subunits: sparse peaks on individual residues in β‑strands of the RecA‑like domains; no activation on Walker A/B or other ATP‑binding motifs.
- Periplasmic quinoprotein dehydrogenases (propeller enzymes): activation on blade β‑strands of the propeller scaffold.
- Other β‑sheet enzymes (e.g., nitrilase/amidase family, NAD⁺ synthetase, Ser/Thr kinases): occasional single‑residue peaks on well‑modeled β‑strands, not on catalytic loops.

Summary: Surface-exposed or flexible loop/turn and strand-edge residues in extracellular/cell-surface modules (often beta-rich and frequently large; e.g., autotransporter passengers/β-helices, phage tail fibers/spikes, lectins/CBMs, ice-binding modules, fungal adhesins, and receptor ectodomains) that scaffold ligand-recognition and processing sites. The same pattern also occurs in small metal-binding proteins (metallothioneins) and in flexible linkers adjacent to processing/cleavage sites in intracellular regulators. These positions typically flank—rather than constitute—sugar/ice/Ca2+/metal-binding motifs or N-glycosylation/cleavage sites, and are enriched for small/polar residues (G, N, T, S, D/E) with relative avoidance of Cys.

Summary: Detector of disulfide‑bonded cysteine‑rich modules in secreted/extracellular proteins, activating on the conserved Cys frameworks and β‑strand/turn cores of small extracellular repeats such as VWF C/chordin modules, EGF‑like repeats, thrombospondin type‑1 repeats (TSR), CCP/Sushi (complement control) repeats, SRCR domains, and cysteine‑rich serine protease inhibitor folds (Kunitz/Kazal/WAP/antistasin), including viral mimics of these modules
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks at conserved disulfide‑forming cysteines and immediately adjacent small/turn‑favoring or aromatic residues (Gly/Pro/Ser/Asp/Phe/Tyr) within β‑strand‑rich segments; domain‑level activation across each module, often strongest at the N‑terminal/core motifs of repeats; extended runs across tandem arrays of such domains; minimal in signal peptides, transmembranes, and low‑complexity Ser/Thr‑rich tracts; not driven by cysteine content alone but by the canonical extracellular repeat context
Exemplars: VWF C/chordin‑like and EGF‑like repeat proteins: highlights the domain entry/core and conserved disulfide cysteines aligning with β‑strands (strong in VWF C; moderate in EGF, including Ca²⁺‑binding motifs); Complement regulators/receptors with CCP/Sushi repeats and viral complement‑control homologs: peaks on the consensus Cys pairs and β‑sheet cores of SCR/CCP modules; SRCR‑domain scavenger receptors: activation on the SRCR disulfide scaffold; Thrombospondin type‑1 repeat proteins: activation on TSR Cys motifs (e.g., CSVTCG) and adjacent β‑strands; Cysteine‑rich protease inhibitors (Kunitz, Kazal, WAP, antistasin): activation on the canonical disulfide networks stabilizing the inhibitor fold; Adhesion/ECM proteins including mucin/ZP‑domain glycoproteins and fungal adhesins: activation on ZP and other disulfide‑bonded modules rather than long O‑glycosylated low‑complexity repeats; Secreted bacterial/fungal carbohydrate‑active enzymes and Dictyostelium spore/prespore proteins: activation on appended extracellular disulfide‑stabilized modules or disulfide bonds characteristic of secreted proteins

Summary: A hydrophobic membrane-anchoring feature enriched in long, contiguous, low-charge segments that mark signal-anchor helices, tail anchors, and membrane-proximal hydrophobic stretches across ER/inner nuclear membrane proteins, lipid-metabolic enzymes, viral envelope/fusion proteins, lipid droplet regulators, and Atg2 C-termini; enriched for Gly, Phe/Trp, and Pro with frequent GxxxG-like motifs and avoidance of acidic/polar clusters.
Activation pattern: Strong domain-level activation in 20–100+ residue hydrophobic windows that often overlap annotated/predicted transmembrane helices or membrane-proximal amphipathic/disordered tails; highest residue-level peaks on hydrophobic residues within these segments; frequent N-terminal (signal peptide/signal-anchor) or C-terminal (tail-anchor) windows; sharp drop in soluble/luminal/catalytic domains; consistent long C-terminal activation in Atg2 orthologs.
Exemplars: E3 ubiquitin ligases with C-terminal TM anchors (e.g., RNF217, RNF19A); glycerolipid acyltransferases (AGPAT/LPAAT) and triacylglycerol synthases (DGAT/Tgs); bacterial cell-envelope lipid-carrier enzymes (WecA/TuaA family); thyroid deiodinases (DIO1/DIO2) with N-terminal signal anchors; SUN-domain inner nuclear membrane proteins; lipid droplet proteins (seipin); ERAD/p97 adaptors (UBX proteins such as Ubx3); viral envelope/fusion proteins where activation maps to the TM/fusion region; microsomal detox enzymes with hydrophobic terminal segments.

Summary: Short beta-strand micro-motifs enriched in acidic (Asp/Glu) and hydrophobic residues (often including Tyr), occurring within diverse beta-sheet–containing domains and at strand–loop junctions; a generic structural signal rather than a family-specific active-site motif
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on short contiguous runs (few residues) within beta-strands or at strand-to-coil transitions; multiple sparse peaks per protein; typically in well-structured parts of domains with occasional peaks in adjacent flexible coils; little/no activation in signal peptides or transmembrane helices
Exemplars: Tubulin-tyrosine ligase-like enzymes (TTLL/TTL): short beta-strand segments inside the TTL domain; PARP family (WGR domain): localized beta-strand patch within the WGR sheet; Histidine acid phosphatases (e.g., prostatic acid phosphatase): E–Y–D–rich beta-strand in the catalytic domain; L-type lectin-like proteins and plant lectin receptor kinases: beta-strand residues within the extracellular lectin beta-sandwich; EGF-like repeat ligands (including viral homologs): beta-strand segment of the EGF-like domain; Nonribosomal peptide synthetases (condensation/adenylation modules): short strand segments and adjacent coil at strand boundaries; Sulfatases: C-terminal end of a beta-strand leading into a loop within the core alpha/beta fold

Summary: Short, flexible β-strand-to-coil junctions (β-turn/edge-of-sheet loop segments), especially in β-rich extracellular/repeat architectures; the feature marks residues immediately after β strands that transition into solvent-exposed loops, enriched for small/polar residues and proline
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks that start at the last 1–2 positions of a β strand and rise into the adjacent coil/loop, then decay over a few residues. Strong enrichment for S/T/G/N/D and Pro in these segments; near-zero within long α-helices and the hydrophobic core of β elements. In β-repeat domains the peaks recur repeat-wise at equivalent strand–loop positions; in long multidomain proteins they appear as multiple discrete hotspots at E→C boundaries, often in more flexible (lower-confidence) loops. In secreted precursors, activations frequently occur in early extracellular regions rather than within signal peptides or transmembrane helices.
Exemplars: - Fucose-binding lectins (e.g., six-bladed β-propellers): repeated peaks at blade strand→loop junctions; not on the canonical carbohydrate-binding aromatic residues.
- Nuclear pore complex nucleoporins (β-propeller subunits such as NUP155): discrete hotspots at β→coil boundaries and short loops; minimal signal in long helical solenoids.
- 1,3-β-glucanases/laminarinases (β-jelly roll/β-sandwich GHs): activations on loop segments flanking β strands that shape the cleft, rather than catalytic residues themselves.
- VPS10/sortilin receptors (β-propeller ectodomains): junctions between β strands and inter-blade loops.
- Bacteriophage tail fibers/receptor-binding proteins (β-helix/β-solenoid scaffolds): rung-to-rung turns and exposed sheet-edge loops.
- Small cysteine-rich secreted proteins (defensins, WAP-domain proteins, three-finger toxins; fungal hydrophobins): turns/loops connecting disulfide-stabilized β strands.
- TGF-β/BMP receptors and Shisa family extracellular domains: short β segments linked by cysteine-stabilized loops; activation on the loop/turn segments.
- Virulence enzymes with catalytic cysteines (DUBs, cysteine proteases, acetyltransferases): short flexible loops adjacent to β elements near active-site regions.
- V-ATPase accessory subunit S1 (Ac45) and lysozyme inhibitors: coil-rich luminal/extracellular loops adjoining β segments show localized peaks.

Summary: Intrinsic disorder/low-complexity segments—especially terminal or propeptide regions enriched in Pro/Ser/Thr/Gly—that serve as flexible carriers of short linear motifs; the feature avoids folded domains and highlights unstructured tails/loops across diverse proteins (including secreted precursors, viral regulators, membrane-protein tails, and micropeptides), sometimes coinciding with proteolytic processing and PTM sites
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks within annotated/predicted disordered coils (very low pLDDT), occasionally extending to short regional runs in low-complexity tracts; frequently enriched toward N-termini; minimal activation in well-folded domains or confidently predicted helices
Exemplars: - Secreted peptide hormone precursors (e.g., cholecystokinin/prohormones): peaks in unstructured propeptide segments at sulfotyrosine, amidation sites, and cleavage boundaries.
- Herpesviral nuclear egress proteins: activation on N-terminal disordered, polar-biased regions; not on the structured zinc-finger domain.
- Integrase-family proteins: scattered peaks confined to very low-pLDDT loops and annotated disordered segments, away from the catalytic core.
- Mycobacterial cell-envelope–associated proteins: single-residue/short-segment peaks within UniProt-annotated disordered coil regions.
- p53-inducible regulatory proteins: sparse peaks across N-terminal and central intrinsically disordered regions, including isoform-variable segments.
- Alternative reading frame micropeptides: activation across low-complexity, disordered coils; absent from the rare structured helix.

Summary: Membrane- and interface-active hydrophobic/amphipathic segments that mediate membrane binding, fusion, translocation, replication-organelle anchoring, or surfactant activity; the feature targets MPERs, single-pass TM anchors, short cytoplasmic tails of fusogenic/adhesive glycoproteins, and analogous amphipathic/translocation or membrane-anchoring helices in bacterial effectors and other secreted/interface-active proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional/domain-level activation over long contiguous stretches enriched in hydrophobic/aromatic residues (often cysteine-rich); frequently spans MPER–TM–cytotail junctions but can also occur as internal or N‑terminal membrane-anchoring segments within large polyproteins; in bacterial effectors, focused on low-structure N‑terminal secretion/translocation signals; may also mark C‑terminal GPI-anchor signals and amphipathic surfactant helices.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope/spike glycoproteins (RNA and DNA viruses): activation on C-terminal MPER, single-pass TM, and short cytoplasmic tail.
- HAP2/GCS1 eukaryotic gamete fusogens: activation across extracellular juxtamembrane, TM, and disordered cytotail.
- Type III secretion effectors (e.g., ExoT, SteC): activation in N-terminal disordered secretion/translocation segments, not catalytic domains.
- Type III/IV secretion translocon components: activation on hydrophobic membrane-inserting helices.
- Viral replicase/polyproteins (plant and animal RNA viruses): activation on short internal membrane-anchoring helices that scaffold replication organelles.
- Secreted interface-active proteins (e.g., ranaspumins) and small cationic toxins/bacteriocins: activation on amphipathic helices that interact with lipid interfaces or permeabilize membranes.
- Phage minor coat/attachment proteins and non-enveloped virus penetration/outer capsid proteins: activation on hydrophobic segments used for host attachment and membrane insertion.

Summary: A generic structural signal for short, solvent‑exposed coil/turn residues that cap or connect secondary‑structure elements (β‑turns, helix/strand caps, inter‑repeat/linker hinges), typically enriched in small/charged residues—especially glycine and often proline—marking flexible linkers at domain and subdomain boundaries rather than catalytic or metal‑ligating sites.
Activation pattern: Sparse residue‑level peaks scattered along sequences, preferentially in loops immediately before/after β‑strands or α‑helices and at domain/linker junctions; avoids the cores of secondary‑structure elements and known cofactor‑binding or active‑site residues; not confined to termini.
Exemplars: - 2Fe‑2S ferredoxin/adrenodoxin: signals on coil linkers flanking β‑strands/short helices and at the domain boundary; no activation on cluster‑ligating cysteines or transit peptides.
- AlkB/ALKBH Fe(II)/2‑oxoglutarate dioxygenases: activation on loops capping strands of the jelly‑roll (DSBH) fold that frame the active site, not on the metal‑binding Hx(D/E)…H motif.
- Kelch repeat/BTB proteins: inter‑blade loops of kelch β‑propellers and BTB–kelch linkers that mediate flexibility and partner binding, rather than the β‑sheet cores.
- FERM/Protein 4.1 superfamily: interdomain linkers and hinge loops between F1/F2/F3 subdomains and within surface turns of the solenoid elements.
- Plant WRKY transcription factors: coil regions around the WRKYGQK segment and loops between β‑strands of the WRKY domain; avoids Zn‑chelating Cys/His.
- CRISPR‑associated RNases/toxins (e.g., HEPN/RNase modules): solvent‑exposed loops bordering RNA‑binding grooves, not the catalytic diad.
- Ribosomal protein L27 (bacterial/organellar): flexible gly/charged loop segments within the small basic protein rather than structured cores or termini.
- Secreted/periplasmic complex components and nucleotide‑modifying enzymes: generic helix/strand caps and short linkers on the protein surface that accommodate conformational changes or partner contacts.

Summary: Generic low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments—especially at the extreme N-terminus—encompassing leader/targeting regions (signal/transit peptides or signal anchors) and flexible tails/linkers, enriched in small residues (P, G, S, A) with occasional hydrophobic runs (L, V, I); prevalent in viral proteins and secreted or membrane-associated proteins.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks within coil/low-pLDDT regions, forming short regional windows that often start at M1 and extend across N-terminal stretches; sporadic peaks can occur in predicted helices/strands when those segments are poorly structured; coverage varies widely across proteins.
Exemplars: - Adenovirus early proteins (e.g., E4-ORF6): activation on proline/glycine-rich, low-pLDDT disordered segments and short patches throughout.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins/secreted precursors: activation on N-terminal signal peptides (hydrophobic h-region) and adjacent low-complexity/cysteine-rich pro-segments.
- Fungal/plant secreted oxidoreductases and extracellular enzymes: activation on N-terminal signal peptides and propeptides.
- Single-pass membrane proteins: activation on N-terminal signal anchors and nearby unstructured cytosolic tails.
- Plant virus RNA-silencing suppressors: activation on low-complexity/disordered patches implicated in host interaction or membrane association.
- Mitochondrial proteins (e.g., ATP synthase epsilon subunits): activation on N-terminal mitochondrial transit peptides.
- Small secreted toxins/hormones: activation on signal peptides and low-complexity prepro regions.
- Viral structural proteins (capsid/portal/terminase/tegument): activation on flexible N- or C-terminal tails/linkers used for assembly and interaction.

Summary: A structural signal for short, well‑ordered β‑strand segments (often hydrophobic) within stable β‑sheets across diverse proteins; these strands frequently flank or support catalytic/ligand‑binding regions or subunit/interfaces rather than marking catalytic residues themselves.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks concentrated on short β‑strand stretches in high‑confidence structured regions; multiple sparse peaks per protein (typically 5–8), sometimes across multiple domains; occasional adjacent coil/helix hits; enrichment for hydrophobic residues.
Exemplars: - c‑di‑GMP turnover enzymes (GGDEF/EAL domains: diguanylate cyclases and phosphodiesterases): activation on β‑strands within GGDEF and EAL folds, near metal/catalytic motifs but not on them.
- CYTH superfamily enzymes (class IV adenylyl cyclase and inorganic triphosphatase): activation on the N‑terminal and internal β‑strands of the CYTH fold.
- Folate pathway dihydroneopterin aldolase (FolB): activation on a single core β‑strand of the trimeric enzyme.
- RidA/YjgF family deaminases: activation on β‑strands bordering substrate‑binding residues that shape the active‑site wall.
- MEP pathway MECDP synthase (IspF): activation on core β‑strands with nearby substrate‑binding residues.
- Fimbrial/pilin subunits (FimG): activation on the C‑terminal β‑strand of the Ig‑like fold and the N‑terminal donor‑strand region involved in subunit assembly.
- Envelope assembly proteins (e.g., CpsC): activation on short periplasmic loop β‑strands between transmembrane helices.

Summary: Detector of tandem-repeat architecture and repeat-register “anchor” residues: it activates across long arrays of short repeated modules (both structured domain repeats and low-complexity compositional repeats), with peaks at the same phase position in each unit—especially Ser/Thr-centered motifs in extracellular repeats and the canonical positions within C2H2 zinc-finger units and their conserved TGEKP linkers.
Activation pattern: Long regional activation confined to tandem-repeat regions, expressed as highly periodic residue-level peaks synchronized with the repeat unit; additional moderate activation on conserved linker motifs that separate repeats; little activation in nonrepetitive segments.
Exemplars: - C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factors: periodic peaks within each finger (sharp on a residue in the C-terminal helix, often His; moderate near the zinc-binding Cys) and on the TGEKP linker (notably Gly/Glu).
- Secreted adhesins/lectins with low-complexity repeats: strong, phased activation across tandem repeats with highest peaks on specific threonines and nearby residues (e.g., fungal galactose-specific agglutinins), predominantly disordered regions.
- Antifreeze glycoproteins: repeated activation on the A–X–Thr motif at the start of each tripeptide repeat and on short hydrophobic linkers between repeat blocks.
- Trichohyalin/cornified-envelope repeat proteins: periodic activation spanning 23–28-aa alpha-helical repeats, highlighting recurring charged (E/K/R/Q) and hydrophobic (L/V) positions that define each unit’s register.

Summary: Short amphipathic alpha-helical “recognition” segments used for binding (DNA, membranes, or protein partners), including the recognition helix of helix-turn-helix DNA-binding domains and N‑terminal targeting/signal helices
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated on alpha-helical residues (often the recognition helix of HTH domains); peaks favor basic/polar and small hydrophobic positions on amphipathic faces; regional clustering is common near N-termini when signal/targeting helices are present; weak/rare activation in coils and beta strands
Exemplars: - ECF sigma factors (Sigma70): activation on helical residues in domain 2 that contact RNAP core and on the domain 4 HTH recognition helix that binds DNA
- Two-component response regulators: activation on the HTH DNA-binding domain, especially the recognition helix
- DNA-binding zinc-finger proteins: activation on the alpha helix that reads the major groove
- Secreted antimicrobial peptides and peptide toxins: activation on cationic amphipathic helices (often N-terminal) responsible for membrane interaction
- Membrane transport/translocation machinery: activation on surface/peripheral amphipathic helices mediating partner or membrane association (not deeply hydrophobic TM segments)
- Protein targeting/import precursors and components: activation on N-terminal signal peptides/transit peptides, particularly the basic/amphipathic segments
- Viral proteins and microproteins: activation on short amphipathic helices used for nucleic acid or membrane binding

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered tandem-repeat tracts enriched in small/polar residues (Ser/Thr/Ala/Gly/Pro, often acidic), highlighting simple S/T/A/G/P-rich repeats and flexible non-catalytic tails rather than folded domains; basic and aromatic residues are disfavored.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, repetitive, low-pLDDT segments with periodic residue-level peaks on A/S/T/G (and Pro) within or immediately adjacent to repeat units (e.g., GASG motifs or residues preceding P–R repeats); little to no activation in structured globular domains or transmembrane helices and on basic/aromatic residues.
Exemplars: - Viral ICP27-like mRNA export factors: activation in disordered P–R–rich low-complexity regions, peaking on small residues that precede P–R dipeptides; arginine itself is not activated.
- Plant oleosin (tapetal) with 4-aa tandem repeats: activation across the disordered C-terminal low-complexity block, strongest on alanines within GASG repeats; the N-terminal transmembrane helix is not activated.
- ERCC4/XPF-like nuclease family proteins: activation confined to the disordered, alanine-rich C-terminal tail; the folded ERCC4 nuclease domain shows no activation.

Summary: Low-complexity, small‑hydrophobic/phenylalanine–enriched stretches that adopt extended β/coil conformations used to build elongated spikes/fibers and multivalent interaction regions—especially β‑solenoid/β‑spiral receptor‑binding/depolymerase modules of trimeric spikes and phenylalanine‑rich FG‑repeat segments of nucleoporins; also flags the phage‑derived intramolecular chaperone/autoproteolysis (ICA) module related to these fiber assemblies. While primarily capturing phage/bacterial spikes and FG nucleoporins, only some eukaryotic viral attachment fibers show strong activation.

Activation pattern: Broad regional activation across long repeat‑rich β/coil segments (often in C‑terminal halves) with many sites per large protein; strong on residues G/A/S/T/V/I/L and on Phe within FG motifs; little activation on well‑packed α‑helical/coiled‑coil regions; peaks frequently coincide with low‑pLDDT, flexible segments that become structured upon trimerization/assembly or multivalent binding; activation is reduced on highly ordered triple β‑spiral shafts (e.g., many adenovirus fibers).

Exemplars:
- Phage tail spikes/fibers/baseplates: high activation on C‑terminal β‑solenoid receptor‑binding/depolymerase domains and associated intramolecular chaperone/autoproteolytic regions
- Capsule‑depolymerase tail spikes (Klebsiella/E. coli): glycan‑binding/‑degrading right‑handed β‑helix repeats
- Type VI secretion system VgrG spikes: β‑prism/β‑helix tip regions of the trimeric puncturing spike
- Trimeric autotransporter adhesins and giant outer‑membrane adhesins: β‑rich head/adhesin repeats (not the α‑helical stalk or translocator barrel)
- Eukaryotic viral attachment fibers: some (e.g., reovirus σ1, certain coronavirus S1 subregions) show activation in β‑rich/low‑complexity regions; adenovirus fibers often show weak activation limited to flexible loops rather than the ordered triple β‑spiral shaft
- Nuclear pore complex nucleoporins: FG/FXFG/GLFG phenylalanine‑rich repeat tracts
- MYRF family: phage tailspike–like intramolecular chaperone/autoproteolysis (ICA) domain that mediates trimerization and release
- Bacterial S‑layer/large surface proteins: repetitive β‑domains and low‑complexity adhesin regions

Summary: Periodic, beta-strand–rich solenoid/repeat architecture in secreted or surface-exposed proteins (adhesins, spikes/tail fibers, ice‑nucleation proteins) and related periplasmic enzymes, with the feature marking conserved positions within long repeat tracts (rungs/turns of beta-solenoids/propellers/sandwiches) and often the flexible receptor-binding tails appended to these domains.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation across long repetitive domains, expressed as dense, sharp single‑residue peaks at fixed positions in each repeat unit; peaks frequently occur in beta‑strands or adjacent coil/turn residues and show a bias toward small/polar residues. In many spike/adhesin proteins the strongest activation concentrates in C‑terminal receptor‑interaction segments that are low‑complexity or flexible; shorter cytosolic proteins show little activation.
Exemplars: - Bacteriophage tail fibers/tips (attachment proteins): strong, localized activation in the C‑terminal host‑receptor binding region (e.g., LamB‑interacting tail tip), predominantly coil/flexible with scattered peaks.
- Type VI secretion spikes (VgrG): long, high‑density activation across the C‑terminal extension separate from catalytic sites, consistent with receptor‑interaction or effector tails.
- Ice‑nucleation/ice‑binding proteins: periodic activation across octapeptide beta‑solenoid repeats, with maximal peaks at a fixed position in each repeat (e.g., the 5th residue glycine).
- Fungal/yeast GPI‑anchored adhesins: multiple peaks in the structured N‑terminal ligand‑binding domain (beta‑strand and nearby coil), rather than the low‑complexity repeat tail.
- Gram‑negative autotransporter adhesins/serine‑protease passengers: broad activation over beta‑helix–like repeat regions that form elongated extracellular stalks.
- PQQ‑dependent ethanol/alcohol dehydrogenases (periplasmic quinoproteins): peaks on beta‑strand residues near PQQ and Ca2+ binding regions within beta‑propeller‑like folds.
- Eukaryotic extracellular receptors (e.g., EGFR): scattered single‑residue peaks within beta‑strands of the extracellular domain.
- Archaeal formylmethanofuran dehydrogenase C subunit: periodic activation confined to a 13‑residue repeat array, with maximal peaks at a fixed position in each repeat (e.g., the 4th residue methionine).

Summary: A short, compositionally biased (charged/polar, often with Ser/Thr and Pro/Gly) segment at the N‑terminal edge of a domain that marks a disorder‑to‑order transition, frequently encompassing the entry into the first secondary‑structure element (β‑strand or α‑helix) and functioning as a flexible linker or contact patch.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks over 5–10 amino acid stretches, often multiple per protein; biased toward N‑termini/early regions; enriched for Lys/Arg, Asp/Glu, Ser/Thr with common Pro/Gly; typically located at the boundary between predicted disorder (lower confidence) and the start of a structured element.
Exemplars: - TIFY/JAZ transcriptional regulators: activates at the N‑terminal edge of the TIFY domain where a coil transitions into the first β‑strand.
- Bacterial initiation factor IF‑3 and ribosomal proteins: activates on short Lys/Arg‑rich N‑terminal tails/linkers adjacent to the first structured element that engages rRNA.
- RNA modification enzymes (pseudouridine synthases): activates on charged boundary loops/N‑terminal edges leading into the catalytic fold at RNA‑binding entry points.
- Peptide deformylases: activates at the short charged N‑terminal segment immediately preceding the first α/β element of the enzyme core.
- BTB/POZ and Kelch/KCTD proteins (including viral BTB–Kelch): activates at low‑complexity N‑termini and at the transition into the BTB domain or the first strand of Kelch repeats.
- MBD/MeCP2 family: activates on short basic/acidic patches in disordered N‑terminal regions just upstream of the MBD.
- Diacylglycerol kinases: activates on Ser/Thr‑rich regulatory N‑terminal segments or linkers entering the first structured domain.
- Retroviral/retrotransposon polyproteins: activates on short charged patches in N‑terminal basic regions or inter‑domain linkers near the start of structured modules.
- Organelle‑targeted proteins (mitochondrial/chloroplastic): activates within Arg/Ser/Thr‑rich N‑terminal segments and at the transition from targeting peptides into the mature structured domain.

Summary: Generic secretory/membrane-interface signal: the feature marks proteins that enter the secretory pathway or embed in membranes, activating on N‑terminal signal peptides/signal anchors, amphipathic helices and helix-cap/loop residues at transmembrane–water interfaces, and on short disordered propeptides/peptide-hormone cores and gly/pro‑rich extracellular matrix repeats
Activation pattern: Mixed regional and residue-level: frequent N‑terminal stretches (signal peptides or signal anchors); sparse peaks at TM-helix boundaries and short interfacial helices/turns in multi-pass membrane proteins; extended activation over low-complexity extracellular repeats (e.g., Gly–X–Y in collagens); residues enriched for small/hydrophobic types (Ala/Leu/Val/Gly/Pro)
Exemplars: - Plant CLE/CLV3-like peptide hormones: strong activation over the C‑terminal mature CLE peptide within a disordered propeptide, with minor signal in the N‑terminal signal peptide.
- Aquaporins: peaks on the N‑terminal amphipathic helix preceding the first TM and at transmembrane–loop junctions (including re-entrant loops around NPA motifs), i.e., membrane–water interfaces.
- Class A GPCRs (including viral GPCR-like proteins and lipid-mediator receptors): activation on N‑terminal signal peptides/signal anchors and at helix caps/extracellular or cytosolic loops between TMs.
- Bacterial CDP‑diacylglycerol synthase and other inner-membrane lipid enzymes: activation at TM-helix boundaries and short interfacial helices near the membrane surface.
- Photosynthetic membrane complexes (e.g., photosystem/cytochrome subunits): interfacial segments between TM helices and aqueous loops highlighted.
- Collagens and extracellular matrix proteins: long activation along Gly–X–Y triple-helix repeats and proline/glycine-rich stretches, plus N‑terminal signal peptides.
- Oomycete RxLR and other secreted effectors: activation concentrated in the N‑terminal signal peptide/low-complexity secretion region.
- Membrane-associated terpenoid/carotenoid cyclases: activation on N‑terminal targeting helices and TM-adjacent interfacial segments.

Summary: Repetitive, compositionally biased segments used for assembly/scaffolding: (i) long, ordered alpha-helical repeat regions (coiled-coils, leucine zippers, and related helical repeats such as TPR/solenoids) and (ii) cysteine-dense small secreted peptides/prohormone segments and low-complexity acidic/Pro/Ser/Gly-rich tracts; the feature avoids compact globular catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Domain-level/regional activation spanning continuous helical repeats; alternatively, strong activation over contiguous low-complexity runs (acidic/Pro/Ser/Gly) or Cys clusters in secreted precursors. Low in well-folded enzyme cores; disordered tails are weak unless they contain repeat-rich/low-complexity tracts.
Exemplars: - Mediator complex subunit (MED31; helical core), - MAP kinase kinase kinase (tandem leucine-zipper coiled-coils), - NIMA-related kinase (C-terminal coiled-coil), and additionally activation on TPR-repeat outer-envelope scaffolds, microtubule-associated low-complexity repeat regions (e.g., MAP4), metallothioneins and neuropeptide/prohormone precursors via cysteine/low-complexity segments.

Summary: Residue-level recognition of conserved structural “scaffold” positions that shape functional pockets and channels—most often small or hydrophobic side chains within well‑ordered secondary structure (especially inside or at the termini of alpha/transmembrane helices, but also in beta strands) that flank or support catalytic/cofactor/ion-binding residues rather than the catalytic residue itself.
Activation pattern: Sparse, low-amplitude, residue-level peaks on a near‑zero background; peaks cluster within helices (including transmembrane segments) and at helix edges or short interhelical loops, with occasional hits in beta strands at substrate-contact positions.
Exemplars: - Orotate phosphoribosyltransferase (PyrE): highlights a single substrate-contact Phe in a beta strand while ignoring most other annotated binding residues, consistent with picking a key scaffold/contact position within the binding site.
- Na+/H+ antiporter: isolated signals within and immediately outside transmembrane helices (A/V/I/L/Y) and one loop residue, consistent with helix-core/helix-boundary packing sites that contour the ion‑translocation pathway.
- Respiratory chain NADH dehydrogenase subunit 3: peaks on a small residue in a TM helix, an interhelical loop, and a Lys at a helix terminus, again marking helix-core/edge scaffold positions rather than specific catalytic residues.
- Cytochrome P450: emphasizes residues flanking the conserved heme‑axial cysteine within the Cys‑pocket helix (not the Cys itself), consistent with recognizing the structured microenvironment that positions the cofactor.

Summary: Glycine/tyrosine- and acidic-biased, solvent-exposed loop/turn segments at the edges of β-strands—i.e., strand–coil junctions and surface loops of β-rich repeat architectures and β-barrel pores—with the same compositional signal extending to C-terminal intrinsically disordered tails of nucleoporins.
Activation pattern: Distributed/regional activation across β-rich domains with many residue-level peaks at strand–coil transitions and turns; periodic across repeat arrays. In β-barrels (VDAC/TOM40, Toc75/OEP channels) activation concentrates in C-terminal barrel regions and their loops. In nucleoporins it localizes to broad C-terminal disordered segments. Disordered low-complexity segments lacking this composition show weak activation; in β-strands, specific in-strand glycines can show local deactivation.
Exemplars: - MORN-repeat proteins (cilia/testis-associated): strong periodic activation across the β-sheet repeats and structured flanks, with dips at specific in-strand glycines.
- Nuclear pore complex proteins (e.g., Nup15-like): broad activation over C-terminal intrinsically disordered regions composed of coils and short helices.
- Mitochondrial outer-membrane porins (VDAC) and TOM40: multiple short peaks at β-strand ends and connecting loops of the β-barrel.
- Chloroplast outer envelope import pores (Toc75/Omp85-family, OEP channels): activation concentrated in the C-terminal β-barrel and its exposed loops.
- β-helix autotransporter adhesins and long repeat passengers: activation along β-helix rungs and turns and in barrel translocator loops.
- Complement system components and receptors (CCP/Sushi repeats, kelch β-propellers): activation on loops connecting β-strands within the repeats.
- Gram-positive cell-wall enzymes with β-sandwich carbohydrate-binding modules: activation on aromatic/glycine- and acidic-rich surface loops.
- Cilia/flagella structural proteins (e.g., radial spoke head families): activation across β-rich repeat segments and their inter-strand turns.

Summary: Structural motif: β-strand→coil junctions (β-strand C-terminal “capping” positions and the first loop residues), typically at sheet edges and hairpin turns, with a bias for acidic residues (Asp/Glu) and sometimes His/Lys, often followed by glycine-rich loop starts; a general feature recurring across β-rich folds (β-barrels, β-propellers, β-sandwiches, and α/β enzyme cores)
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated at one or two residues per junction—strongest at the last residue of a β-strand and/or the first residue of the ensuing coil; enrichment for Asp/Glu and occasional His/Lys at these boundary positions, with nearby Gly in the loop; proteins with many strand–loop transitions show many peaks, while others show only a few; activations typically lie away from primary catalytic/ligand sites
Exemplars: - Fatty acid-binding proteins (β-barrel): highlights glutamates at C-ends of β-strands just before glycine-containing loops (e.g., E→G transitions), not the canonical lipid-binding residues
- Small heat shock proteins/alpha-crystallin domain (β-sandwich): marks β-strand→loop boundaries within the ACD, including sheet-edge strands at oligomerization interfaces
- GH43 arabinofuranosidases and GH68 levanases/invertases (β-propellers): activates on blade edge strand termini feeding into loop segments flanking the active-site groove, often acidic-to-glycine transitions
- Two-component sensor histidine kinases: marks β-strand–loop junctions in PAS sensor domains and in the α/β ATPase (CA) domain; not the catalytic histidine in the DHp helix
- KEOPS/EKC subunits (e.g., Kae1/YgjD, Bud32): highlights β-strand C-caps leading into catalytic/ligand-binding loops in their α/β cores
- Rieske iron–sulfur proteins (β-sandwich): activates at β-strand termini adjacent to the loop carrying the [2Fe–2S]-binding motif, consistent with charged strand caps near that loop
- DNA-binding regulators (winged-helix/ribbon-helix-helix): marks the β-hairpin “wing” strand termini and adjacent turns
- Toxin–antitoxin proteins (small α/β or β-sheet folds): highlights strand–coil turns in compact β-rich scaffolds

Summary: Periodic aromatic/glycine/histidine/acidic cluster detector with a strong bias toward beta-strand repeat architectures—most notably WD40/radial-spoke beta-propellers and MORN repeats—but also recognizing similar periodically spaced motifs in flexible low-complexity repeats and structured loops of diverse proteins (including some membrane-associated carbohydrate enzymes).
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks that recur at regular intervals across repeat arrays; strongest and most regular on beta-strands at repeat starts/ends, but can also occur in low-complexity/disordered G/F/Y-rich segments and in periplasmic/loop regions; minimal outside these arrays.
Exemplars:
- MORN repeat proteins: strong peaks at the beginning of each repeat beta-strand.
- Radial spoke head WD-repeat proteins: activation at GH–W/Y–D-like positions across beta-propeller blades.
- Outer membrane porins (VDAC/TOM40): periodic but sometimes weaker activation on beta-barrel strands.
- Secreted carbohydrate-active enzymes and lectins (including chitin/cuticle/peritrophic-matrix proteins): activation across beta-rich CBMs and recurring aromatic–glycine motifs; can extend into low-complexity repeats.
- ALS2/Alsin (RCC1-like) beta-propellers: repeating beta-blade motifs within RCC1-like repeats.
- DnaJ/Hsp40 co-chaperones: recurring aromatic/glycine clusters within the disordered G/F-rich region.
- Bacterial cell-wall glycosylation enzymes (e.g., GT-C WTA GlcNAc-transferases): peaks in periplasmic loop repeats enriched for aromatic/glycine/acidic residues.
- NADH dehydrogenase I subunit N (NuoN/NDH-1 N): occasional periodic motifs in loop regions despite overall alpha-helical topology.

Summary: Short structured motifs (≈2–6 residues) in soluble domains, most often β-strand/turn elements in β-rich folds (β-sandwich/all-β) of extracellular/lumenal or periplasmic/IMS proteins, and also in adjacent loop or short-helix segments of other soluble folds; includes N-terminal edge strands of Ig-like domains and analogous short motifs in diverse folds.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on short contiguous segments, typically mapping to β-strands and immediately adjacent coils/turns, and occasionally short helices; multiple independent peaks can occur across large soluble domains; generally inactive on signal peptides, transmembrane helices, and long disordered tails.
Exemplars:
- Immunoglobulin superfamily receptors/ligands (e.g., V-set domains in B7/nectin/PVR-like proteins): strongest activation on the N-terminal edge β-strand and following turn within the extracellular Ig-like domain, with weaker peaks on other β-strands.
- MD-2/NPC2/ML lipid-recognition proteins: activation on disulfide-bonded cysteines in short loop/helix segments and minor peaks on nearby β-strands within the β-sandwich fold.
- Complement/alpha-2-macroglobulin family (e.g., C3/C5): numerous peaks that align with annotated β-strands across chains rather than with cleavage or modification sites.
- ER translocon-associated subunits (e.g., TRAP-α/SSR1): peaks on short conserved motifs in the luminal domain, often turns or short helices.
- Mitochondrial/periplasmic copper assembly protein COX11: peaks near conserved cysteine motifs within the soluble IMS/periplasmic domain, typically in short loops/turns.
- Bacterial inner-membrane insertase YidC: primary peak on a β-strand in the large periplasmic/soluble domain and into the adjacent loop.
- Arrestin-like proteins: peaks within β-sheets and neighboring flexible loops of the all-β arrestin fold.

Summary: Short loop/turn segments at connectors of secondary-structure elements within structured domains, most often in beta-rich folds (Ig-like, cupredoxin, pilin, SUN, Runt) but also in some alpha/beta enzymes (e.g., glycosidases, LPMOs). The feature primarily appears in extracellular/secreted proteins and often marks functional surface loops near ligand/metal interfaces, with a bias for small/turn-forming and polar residues and occasional histidines.
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks confined to structured domains; strongest on coil/turn regions connecting beta-strands and/or helices, sometimes spilling into adjacent strands. Little/no activation in signal peptides, transmembrane helices, or long disordered regions. Peaks frequently lie near ligand- or metal-binding residues.
Exemplars: - IgSF immune receptors (including TCR) and immunoglobulin heavy chains: short flexible loops within extracellular Ig-like V and C domains; absent from signal peptide, transmembrane, and cytoplasmic tails.
- Cupredoxin/plastocyanin-like and multicopper oxidases: strand-connecting loops bordering copper sites (near His/Met ligands) in the cupredoxin fold.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes: loops shaping substrate or metal sites, including TIM-barrel/beta-sandwich glycosidases and LPMOs (histidine-brace vicinity).
- SUN-related proteins: loops within the C-terminal nuclear-envelope SUN beta-sandwich and in fungal SUN-family beta-propeller proteins; no activation in coiled-coils or transmembranes.
- Bacterial fimbrial/pilin major subunits (FimA-like): short coils connecting beta-strands in the pilin Ig-like domain.
- Runt domain transcription factors: sparse peaks on loops within the beta-rich Runt homology domain; inactive on disordered termini.

Summary: Alpha-helical protein–protein interaction elements—coiled-coil heptad repeats and short amphipathic helices (often emerging from low‑complexity, acidic Ser/Pro/Gly‑rich segments)—that mediate oligomerization, partner docking, and scaffolding across diverse proteins and taxa.
Activation pattern: Regional activation that follows alpha‑helical segments, with residue‑level peaks on interface positions (hydrophobic a/d and charged e/g sites, helix starts/caps). Broad, near‑continuous signal across long coiled‑coils; one or a few short hotspots (often N‑terminal) in smaller proteins consistent with α‑MoRF/targeting helices. Little signal on compact beta‑rich domains.
Exemplars: - SMN complex protein: strong activation on the N‑terminal GEMIN2‑binding helix and the C‑terminal homooligomerization helix; minimal on the Tudor beta‑barrel.
- Centrosomal/cytoskeletal coiled‑coil scaffolds (CCDC/CEP, nesprins, intermediate filaments): activation spread along heptad‑repeat coiled‑coil interfaces driving assembly.
- Nuclear/chromatin and transcription regulators (HOX/homeobox factors, acidic activation‑domain proteins): activation on short α‑MoRFs within acidic, Ser/Pro/Gly‑rich regions used for cofactor docking.
- Kinases and other signaling enzymes: activation on regulatory/docking helices or accessory coiled‑coil segments that mediate complex formation.
- Phosphatase regulators/partners (PP1/PP2A modulators): activation on helical docking and scaffold‑binding motifs.
- Bacterial small regulators and toxin–antitoxin antitoxins: activation on helical dimerization and toxin‑binding elements (HTH/RHH/coiled‑coil).
- Organelle‑targeted precursors: activation on N‑terminal amphipathic helices of signal/transit peptides.
- Photosystem/light‑associated components: activation on peripheral amphipathic helices involved in complex assembly.

Summary: Flexible, membrane-facing loop/turn or short amphipathic-helix motifs that contact lipid bilayers or gate lipid-binding cavities—i.e., the local “lipid‑encounter/pocket‑rim” elements used for membrane docking or lipid transfer in diverse lipid-handling proteins and outer-membrane beta-barrels.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks confined to short segments (∼5–15 aa) in coils/turns and occasional short helices at domain surfaces; recurrently in loop tips at beta-strand–loop junctions or pocket rims; often lower structural confidence than surrounding cores; enriched for mixed acidic (Asp/Glu), Gly/Pro (flexibility) and hydrophobic residues; repeated peaks across multi-module proteins (e.g., multiple C2 domains) rather than whole-domain activation.
Exemplars: - Omp85/BamA outer-membrane assembly factors: activation on extracellular barrel loops (e.g., L1, L5) of the C-terminal beta-barrel, consistent with membrane-proximal, flexible loop elements that interface with the outer membrane/LPS.
- PRELI/UPS1 mitochondrial lipid transfer proteins: activation on a loop→short-helix segment containing residues required for phosphatidic acid binding and cardiolipin biosynthesis (membrane-contact/pocket-gating motif).
- START/StAR-related lipid transfer domains: sparse peaks on loops connecting beta elements within the START domain at the entrance to the hydrophobic cavity (lipid pocket rim).
- Ferlin superfamily C2-domain proteins: sharp peaks within multiple C2 modules on membrane-docking loop regions (often acidic/hydrophobic loop tips that engage Ca2+/acidic lipids).
- Vitellogenins (large secreted lipid carriers): localized activation on a flexible loop within the vitellogenin domain, consistent with a lipid-interacting surface element.

Summary: Residue-level detector of beta-strand structural context in well-folded domains, with a strong preference for the very start of the BTB/POZ domain (the first beta-strand or its immediate N-terminal boundary). Outside BTB proteins it similarly marks isolated beta-strand (and adjacent inter-strand loop) positions within diverse domains rather than catalytic or ligand-coordination sites.
Activation pattern: Predominantly single-residue peaks in structured regions, most often at or just inside domain starts (especially the N-terminus of BTB/POZ). Secondary, modest peaks can appear on additional beta-strands or strand-connecting loops (e.g., across Kelch repeats). Little to no signal in disordered segments, signal peptides, or propeptides.
Exemplars: - BTB/POZ zinc-finger transcription regulators (ZBTB family): sharp peak on the first beta-strand at the BTB N-terminus; occasional minor peaks in C2H2 zinc fingers.
- Kelch-like substrate adaptors (KLHL family): strong peak at the BTB domain start; weaker scattered peaks on beta-strands and connecting loops across Kelch beta-propeller blades.
- Plant NPH3/BTB proteins: narrow peak at the BTB N-terminus (residues ~29–31).
- Heterotrimeric G-protein alpha subunits: single beta-strand residue within the G domain between G2 and G3, not at GTP-binding motifs.
- Translational/small GTPases (tr-type G): isolated beta-strand residue inside the GTPase domain, away from canonical G-motifs.
- Rieske non-heme iron oxygenases: beta-strand residues within the Rieske domain (including near its N-terminus), not on Fe–S ligands.
- Aspartic protease A1 family: beta-sheet residues within the mature peptidase domain (near its start); no activation on catalytic aspartates or glycosylation sites.

Summary: Intrinsic structural disorder: long, unannotated terminal extensions and other extended segments outside annotated catalytic/structured domains (typically coil, low pLDDT), with low activation in well-folded domain cores
Activation pattern: Regional activation across contiguous intrinsically disordered stretches (often tens to hundreds of residues), frequently at N- or C-termini; sharp drop at boundaries entering folded, high-confidence domains; no specific residue-type preference
Exemplars: - Nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS megaenzyme): strong activation on the N-terminal pre-domain segment and a short C-terminal tail flanking the condensation/adenylation/carrier domains; low activation within the structured catalytic modules.
- Secreted bacterial protease (PrtH family): highest activation across a long, unannotated C-terminal extension predicted to be disordered; minimal activation in the structured N-terminal/catalytic regions.
- Aspartate–/Asparagine–tRNA ligase (aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetase): strong activation over a long N‑terminal disordered region preceding the catalytic core, with activation dropping sharply in the folded enzyme domain and rising modestly again in a flexible C‑terminal tail.

Summary: Extracellular Ig-like/FN3 β-sandwich strand-entry sites: short coil/turn residues immediately preceding or at the start of β-strands within Ig superfamily and fibronectin type-III ectodomains, frequently encompassing N-linked glycosylation sequons (N–X–S/T) and enriched in polar residues
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks that recur across successive Ig-like and FN3 modules in the ectodomain; strongest at loop/helix-to-β-strand junctions and often on the +2 Ser/Thr (and sometimes the Asn) of N–X–S/T sequons. Minimal signal in signal peptides, transmembrane segments, disordered tails, catalytic cytoplasmic domains, and on disulfide cysteines. Patterns repeat across domain arrays and are largely confined to well-structured extracellular regions.
Exemplars: - VEGF receptor family (Ig-like ectodomains on receptor tyrosine kinases): peaks at loop-to-strand transitions across C2 Ig domains, often overlapping N–X–S/T glycosylation motifs.
- Siglec/CD22 lectin receptors: discrete junction residues within Ig domains near ligand-binding loops, with activation on a nearby N-glycan sequon.
- CXADR-like IgSF cell-adhesion molecules: coil/helix-to-strand junctions in Ig C2 domains, adjacent to disulfide-stabilized regions but not on the cysteines themselves.
- GPI-anchored multi-Ig/FN3 adhesion proteins: repeated hotspots at strand onsets across Ig and FN3 repeats; silent at GPI signal and disulfide sites.
- Receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatases (Ig/FN3 ectodomains): activation on N-linked glycosylation Asn and the +2 Ser/Thr and neighboring loop/strand residues within Ig/FN3 modules.

Summary: A generic structural signal for solvent-exposed, polar alpha-helical segments (often enriched in Q/N/S/T and acidic residues), with spillover into adjacent flexible coils; these helices frequently serve as interaction-prone surfaces rather than pathway-specific motifs.
Activation pattern: Regional activation with narrow residue-level peaks centered within specific polar helices; signals recur at multiple sites across a protein and are not confined to termini; other, more hydrophobic helices tend not to activate; weaker, scattered signals appear in nearby disordered coils or short strands.
Exemplars: - Proteasome maturation factor UMP1: strong peak on a central, high-confidence polar helix; minor signals in an N-terminal polar/disordered region and a short strand.
- RNA biogenesis/processing factors (spliceosomal proteins, RNA helicases, hnRNPs): activation on solvent-exposed polar helices embedded within low-complexity S/T- and Q/N-rich regions used for assembly.
- Cell-cycle and ubiquitin–proteasome regulators (E3 ligases, APC/C subunits, deubiquitinases): acidic/polar helical patches and adjacent P/S/T-rich segments.
- Cytoskeletal/ciliary and coiled-coil scaffolds (centrosomal and dynein-adaptor proteins): polar faces of coiled-coils and other exposed helices.
- PP1-binding regulators and actin-binding adaptors: polar helical surfaces flanking short linear motifs in disordered regions.
- Ribosomal proteins (cytosolic, mitochondrial, chloroplastic): solvent-exposed polar helices and acidic loops contacting RNA or partner proteins.
- Prokaryotic enzymes and toxin–antitoxin components: polar helical surfaces within globular domains or antitoxin helices.
- Plant photosynthesis/light- and stress-associated proteins: S/T- and acidic-rich helical regions within regulatory modules.

Summary: Ala/Thr-enriched low-complexity intrinsically disordered regions, with a strong bias for N-terminal prepro/signal-peptide segments and adjacent cleavage-site neighborhoods; the feature reflects small-residue (A/T, secondarily S/P) composition in flexible, non-folded regions rather than a specific structured domain.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks on A and T that cluster within low-pLDDT, coil-rich regions—frequently in the first ~30 residues—and can extend across unstructured precursor segments; activation is largely absent from well-folded catalytic domains and concentrates at or near signal peptide C-regions/cleavage sites when present.
Exemplars: - Antimicrobial peptide precursors: strong activation within the N-terminal signal peptide, including the Thr at the signal peptidase cleavage position (-1), and nearby Ala in the nascent mature N-terminus.
- Secreted serine proteases (trypsinogens): activation confined to the unstructured prepro region (signal peptide/propeptide) with multiple Ala/Thr peaks; no activation in the folded peptidase domain.
- Apoptosis-related regulatory proteins: scattered A/T peaks across disordered, low-confidence segments with no overlap to specific functional sites.
- Transcriptional regulators (e.g., CROC-4-like): A/T-biased peaks within annotated low-complexity/disordered stretches and adjacent flexible regions.
- Telomere-associated proteins: N-terminal disordered helix/coil segments with clustered Thr peaks and additional A/T peaks in other low-confidence regions.
- Small disordered microproteins: isolated A/T peaks distributed throughout largely disordered sequences, especially in annotated disordered termini.

Summary: Cationic, low-complexity basic patches in intrinsically disordered or flexible, solvent-exposed regions—often near the N-terminus and enriched in Pro/Gln with interspersed aromatics—that bind polyanions (glycosaminoglycans, nucleic acids, acidic phospholipids, or phosphate groups) to mediate adhesion, membrane association, and host–pathogen/immune-modulatory interactions.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in short clustered stretches; typically in low-pLDDT disordered segments downstream of signal peptides in secreted proteins, but can also occur in exposed structured/basic clusters that contact polyanionic ligands (e.g., ATP/tRNA/phosphate-binding sites) in cytosolic enzymes; weak over hydrophobic signal peptides; variable number of clusters per protein.
Exemplars:
- Serpin antithrombin: activation on the N-terminal basic patch mediating heparin binding; signal peptide shows little activation.
- Viral proteins (envelope and accessory): activation on polybasic PR/QR-rich segments that bind host glycosaminoglycans or acidic membranes (e.g., GP4; ORF9c basic tails).
- Secreted precursors and micropeptides (chemokines, antimicrobial/cell-penetrating peptides, hormone propeptides; mucin-like caseins): activation on cationic, aromatic-sprinkled low-complexity stretches engaging proteoglycans or acidic membranes.
- DNA/RNA-binding microproteins and enzymes: activation on terminal/basic patches contacting nucleic acids (e.g., killin; bacterial tRNA m7G methyltransferases).
- Soluble metabolic enzymes: occasional activation at exposed basic clusters that bind phosphate-containing ligands (e.g., riboflavin kinase).
- Membrane-associated proteins/receptors: activation on luminal or cytosolic basic patches used for proteoglycan binding or membrane association (e.g., DEspR-like receptors, neuronatin).
- Reproductive/testis-associated proteins: activation on arginine/proline-rich low-complexity regions mediating polyanion-dependent interactions in the reproductive tract.

Summary: Generic short beta-strand segments (often edge strands or strand–loop junctions) defined by an alternating polar–hydrophobic composition, recurring across diverse proteins; most common in extra‑cytoplasmic/periplasmic/lumenal and lipid‑handling folds but also present in soluble enzymes.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks confined to short contiguous runs (typically ~6–10 aa), repeated at multiple positions within a protein; these runs map predominantly to predicted/annotated beta-strands (secondary structure E) or the immediate strand-to-loop cap, with high to moderate structural confidence. Activation is sparse in alpha-helices and absent from transmembrane helices. Sites are distributed across the sequence rather than termini and often display mixed Ser/Thr and Asp/Glu with hydrophobic/aromatic residues, consistent with beta-strand polarity.
Exemplars: - Ring-hydroxylating dioxygenase beta subunit: a single high-confidence beta-strand segment is highlighted.
- Vitellogenin (large lipid transfer protein, LLTP family): multiple N-terminal beta-strands within the vitellogenin/lipovitellin region are activated, while other domains are largely inactive.
- Type IV secretion system component VirB8: a periplasmic beta-strand shows strong activation; other helices and the transmembrane segment do not.
- BPI/PLUNC lipid-binding protein (BPI fold): a discrete beta-strand is activated, including a residue that can serve as an N-linked glycosylation site.
- Autophagy-related protein 2 (ATG2 lipid-transfer scaffold): several short, dispersed beta-strands along the length of the protein are activated.
- Aldose 1-epimerase (mutarotase/TIM-barrel enzyme): activation centers at the end of a beta-strand and adjacent loop just before the following helix, with a secondary peak on a distant beta-strand near the catalytic region.

Summary: Generic signature of intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity, basic‑rich segments and short cationic peptides (enriched in S/T/P/G/A/R), often at N‑termini or in basic patches, rather than structured motifs
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks sparsely distributed within low‑pLDDT regions; frequent at the starts of basic patches and in N‑terminal stretches; little to no activation on structured metal‑binding motifs (e.g., C4 zinc fingers)
Exemplars: - Viral RNA silencing suppressors: strongest peak at the start of an annotated basic region; minimal activation on the adjacent C4‑type zinc finger, highlighting preference for disordered/basic patches over structured domains.
- lncRNA‑derived microprotein (CASC2 isoform): scattered single‑residue peaks across low‑confidence coils/short helices with no mapped functional sites, consistent with IDR/low‑complexity recognition.
- Spermatogenesis‑associated proteins (testis IDPs): multiple discrete peaks in low‑pLDDT coil regions across the sequence, reflecting basic/low‑complexity disordered segments.
- Retroviral Vif proteins (from initial observations): activation on disordered/basic regions, not on the structured HCCH zinc‑binding motif.
- Short secreted cationic peptides (antimicrobial peptides, peptide toxins/hormones; from initial observations): activation over basic/polar segments of the mature peptide or precursor regions; not driven by cysteine content in cystine‑rich toxins.

Summary: General helical structural elements: the feature marks residues within helical segments across many protein classes—alpha-helices in HTH/homeodomain DNA-binding regions, coiled-coils, transmembrane helices, and signal-peptide/propeptide helices—with a characteristic periodic emphasis on Gly in the collagen triple-helix (Gly–X–Y) repeat.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation confined to predicted helices, with little signal in non-helical/disordered segments; strong peaks within key helical motifs (e.g., HTH recognition helix) and at helical caps/adjacent turns; diffuse, extended activation along long helical rods (coiled-coils, TM bundles); striking residue-level periodicity every third position in collagen triple helices, maximal on Gly of the Gly–X–Y repeat.
Exemplars: HTH-type bacterial transcription factors and ECF sigma factors: activation on the C-terminal recognition helix and nearby turn of the DNA-binding H–T–H module; toxin–antitoxin antitoxins with small helical DNA-binding domains: scattered activation across short helices; coiled-coil structural proteins (paramyosin): broad activation along the long alpha-helical rod; fibrillar collagens: dense, periodic activation across the triple-helical region, peaking on Gly in the Gly–X–Y motif; membrane transporters/sensor kinases: small peaks within transmembrane alpha-helices; neuropeptide hormone precursors (AKH/CRZ family): activation on helical signal peptides and short helical stretches in propeptides, including near processing sites.
