Summary: Hydrophobic β‑strand positions in blades of β‑propellers and related β‑sheet–rich domains (kelch-, YWTD/LDLR-, VPS10/sortilin-, Sema-, DPP4-like, PQQ‑dehydrogenase/quinoprotein, RPE65/CCO, and Yellow/MRJP), with occasional signal at disulfide‑involved cysteines; observed in soluble and luminal contexts across compartments (extracellular, periplasmic, chloroplastic, cytosolic) and in ectodomains of membrane proteins.
Activation pattern: Sparse residue‑level peaks on selected positions within high‑confidence β‑strands (often alternating along one strand face) across these β‑rich domains; little to no signal in signal peptides, helices, transmembrane segments (aside from adjacent luminal strands), disordered tails, or catalytic/metal‑binding residues; bias toward Leu/Val/Ile/Phe and occasional disulfide cysteines.
Exemplars:
- Semaphorin Sema domain: activation on β‑strand residues across the propeller; no signal in TSR repeats, TM helix, or cytosolic tail.
- Carotenoid cleavage oxygenase/RPE65‑like (seven‑bladed propeller): alternating peaks on β‑strands; metal‑binding histidines and helices inactive.
- Insect Yellow/MRJP family (secreted β‑sandwich): scattered peaks on β‑strands of the mature core; signal peptide and helices inactive.
- Dipeptidyl‑peptidase IV/S9 proteases: activation on the N‑terminal β‑propeller blades; catalytic hydrolase domain not highlighted.
- LDL receptor family (YWTD repeats): activation on luminal YWTD β‑propeller blades; little/no signal in LA repeats, EGF modules, TM/cytosolic regions.
- VPS10/sortilin receptors: activation on the N‑terminal Vps10p β‑propeller in the luminal region.
- Kelch‑repeat proteins (animals/plants/yeast/viruses; often cytosolic): activation along β‑strands forming kelch propeller blades.
- PQQ‑dependent/periplasmic dehydrogenases and related quinoproteins: activation on propeller β‑strands; cofactor‑coordinating residues and non‑β regions largely inactive.
- Channel auxiliary subunits with luminal ectodomains (e.g., CatSper auxiliaries): β‑strand peaks in luminal domain; TM helices inactive.

Summary: Solvent‑exposed strand–loop boundary residues in beta‑sheet–rich modules, most prominently the extracellular fibronectin type III (FNIII) and immunoglobulin‑like (Ig) domains of single‑pass receptors and adhesion proteins, with the same structural context also recognized in beta‑propeller WD repeats.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks scattered across multiple sites per domain; enriched in N‑terminal extracellular regions (Ig/FNIII modules and their linkers), with little/no signal in signal peptides, transmembrane helices, or intracellular catalytic tails; avoids long disordered segments; does not coincide with N‑glycosylation sequons or disulfide‑bonded cysteines; biased toward small/polar/charged residues at strand ends and nearby loops, occasionally extending to edge strands within beta‑propellers.
Exemplars: - Interferon/cytokine receptors (class II and class I/gp130 family): peaks at strand–loop transitions within the extracellular FNIII module; silent in TM and cytosolic tails.
- Receptor‑type protein tyrosine phosphatases (LAR/PTPR family): repeated peaks across Ig‑like C2 and multiple FNIII repeats of the ectodomain; off in the transmembrane segment and intracellular phosphatase domains.
- Immunoglobulin‑superfamily adhesion and axon‑guidance proteins (e.g., NCAM/L1CAM/contactins/DCC‑like): loop/edge residues of Ig‑like and FNIII beta‑sandwiches.
- Receptor tyrosine kinases with Ig‑like ectodomains (e.g., VEGFR/PDGFR): strand‑edge and loop residues within Ig‑like modules.
- Complement/alpha‑2‑macroglobulin–like extracellular proteins: loop/edge residues on large beta‑sheet modules of the thioester‑containing region.
- WD‑repeat beta‑propeller proteins (e.g., axonemal dynein intermediate chain): coil positions within WD blades and adjacent linkers near the propeller region, with occasional edge‑strand hits.

Summary: Structural signal for hydrophobic/aromatic residues that build the beta-strand cores of folded beta-sheet domains—most prominently C2 beta-sandwich and WW modules, but also other beta-rich interaction domains (SH2/SH3/PH/PTB/PDZ/GRAM) and, in some cases, alpha/beta enzyme folds with central beta-sheets (e.g., GNAT N-terminal acetyltransferases); it marks the scaffold rather than Ca2+-binding or catalytic sites.
Activation pattern: Residue-level sparse peaks confined to folded beta-sheet domains, concentrated on hydrophobic/aromatic positions within DSSP E strands (often showing an alternating pattern on one face of a sheet). Domain-level restriction to these beta-sheet regions; minimal or absent in Ca2+-binding loops, disordered linkers, transmembranes, and most helices. In multidomain proteins, the pattern repeats across each such module.
Exemplars:
- Synaptotagmins (tandem C2 Ca2+-lipid sensors): peaks on hydrophobic beta-strands of both C2 domains, not on Ca2+-binding loops.
- DOC2 family (double C2-like proteins): alternating hydrophobic residues in beta-strands across both C2 domains.
- Plant and animal C2-domain proteins: localized peaks on beta-strands within the C2 domain adjacent to Ca2+-binding motifs; no signal in transmembrane or disordered regions.
- Rab11-family interacting proteins (C2-mediated membrane targeting): sparse, high-confidence peaks on beta-strands in the N-terminal C2; negligible in the RBD and disordered tails.
- NEDD4/NEDD4L/SMURF HECT E3 ligases with C2 and WW modules: strong peaks on beta-strands in the C2 domain and on the two strands of each WW domain; only weak, scattered signal in the helical HECT region.
- N-terminal acetyltransferases (NatA/NatC; GNAT fold): sparse peaks on hydrophobic residues within the central beta-sheet core; weak/absent in surrounding helices.

Summary: Gly/Ala-rich hydrophobic membrane-inserting helices—typically 15–30 aa alpha-helical segments with glycine-zipper-like motifs (GxxxG, GG) and aromatic boundary residues—used as fusion peptides, signal/TM anchors, or pore-forming helices in single-pass and small membrane proteins across viruses, bacteria, and eukaryotes
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long contiguous hydrophobic segments (often multiple blocks per protein), corresponding to signal peptides, fusion peptides, intramembrane/TM helices; short isolated patches in otherwise soluble proteins when an amphipathic membrane-binding helix is present
Exemplars: - Retroviral envelope fusogens: activation on the fusion peptide at the N-terminus of the transmembrane subunit (e.g., Syncytin-2 fusion peptide immediately after cleavage).
- Viral envelope/fusion proteins (diverse families): activation on fusion peptides and nearby hydrophobic helices late in the sequence.
- IFITM family (interferon-inducible small membrane proteins): activation on the intramembrane amphipathic helix/C-terminal TM helix containing GxxxG motifs.
- ApoL family pore-forming proteins: activation on the membrane-insertion/TM helix used during pore formation.
- Chlamydial inclusion membrane (Inc) proteins: activation across the paired hydrophobic hairpin (two closely spaced TM-like helices).
- Magnetosome-associated small membrane proteins: activation on single-pass gly/ala-rich TM helices that embed in the magnetosome membrane.
- Bacteriocins and bacterial pore-forming toxins: activation on glycine-zipper transmembrane/pore-forming helices and, in precursors, the hydrophobic signal/leader segment (often with GG motifs).
- Phage structural proteins (tail/tape measure): activation on N-terminal signal peptides or short TM anchors used for membrane targeting/assembly.

Summary: β-strand initiation motifs: the loop/turn immediately preceding a β-strand and the first 1–2 residues of the strand (β-strand N-caps), especially repeated across multi-bladed β-propeller scaffolds (WD/YWTD/FG-GAP) and other β-sheet–rich repeat architectures; sequence bias toward Gly, Asp/Glu, Ser/Thr, Pro, with frequent Trp in WD/YWTD repeats.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks at coil/connector segments that feed into β-strands and at the strand starts; repeated periodically across domains rich in short strands (accumulating signal over entire β-propellers). Largely silent in helical cores and the interior of β-strands; strongest on flexible/edge loops and helix→coil/strand junctions, yielding long, dispersed activated residue sets.
Exemplars: - WD-repeat β-propeller scaffolds (e.g., methylosome WDR proteins): activation on inter-blade loops and the onset of blade strands.
- YWTD and FG-GAP propellers (LDL receptor, integrin α N-terminal propellers): activation around YWTD/WD- and FG-GAP–containing turns that initiate blade strands.
- Coatomer/clathrin adaptor and nucleoporin β-propellers: repeated peaks at blade edge loops and strand starts.
- Cilia/IFT WD-repeat proteins: activation on loop→strand transitions within propeller blades.
- Secreted carbohydrate-active enzymes in GH43 (xylosidase/arabinosidase; 5-bladed propellers): peaks at blade loop→strand junctions.
- Propeller hydrolases (sialidases; some lactonases): activation at blade N-caps across 6–7 bladed propellers.
- Sugar-oxidation enzymes with propeller domains (e.g., PQQ-dependent dehydrogenases): repeated loop/strand-start signals around the propeller fold.
- Non-propeller β-sheet enzymes (e.g., 6-phosphogluconolactonase): periodic coil→β-strand starts across the β-sheet.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered regions enriched in charged/polar residues (E/D/S/T/K/R) with frequent Gly/Pro, including hypervariable extracellular loops, propeptides, linkers, and disordered termini; occasionally shows weaker signal within or flanking helical segments (e.g., transmembrane or coiled-coil boundaries)
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation across long disordered/LCR stretches with many positions non-zero; residue-level peaks often at Gly/Pro/Ser/Thr and charged residues; cysteines are rarely highlighted. Secondary, weaker activation can occur in or near helices, especially at membrane-proximal or helix-capping positions.
Exemplars: - Viral envelope glycoproteins (e.g., HCV E2 HVR1 and E1 region): strong activation on the disordered, hypervariable luminal HVR1; additional moderate signal in the adjacent C-terminal transmembrane helix.
- Secreted peptide hormone precursors: activation on disordered propeptides and Lys/Arg-rich processing segments rather than the hydrophobic signal peptide.
- Actin-associated/adaptor proteins: long acidic/basic low-complexity linkers and disordered regions connecting modular domains.
- Centrosomal/ciliary coiled-coil scaffolds: charged low-complexity segments and disordered termini flanking coiled-coil repeats.
- Peroxisome biogenesis/membrane proteins: cytosolic/luminal disordered loops and low-complexity tails, with occasional signal near TM boundaries.
- RNA processing/translation regulators: polar/charged low-complexity domains (e.g., RGG/RG-rich, Ser/Thr-rich) and flexible linkers.
- Protein kinases and deubiquitinases: intrinsically disordered N/C-terminal tails and flexible low-complexity linkers between domains.

Summary: Predominantly extracellular/secreted and cell-surface proteins with exposed, flexible low-complexity segments in the mature region (often Ser/Thr/Gly-rich or proteoglycan-like), frequently cysteine-rich; with a minority of metazoan lipid-binding proteins (including FABPs) that can be cytosolic
Activation pattern: Regional activation on extended contiguous stretches of exposed/disordered segments within the mature region—Gly/Thr-enriched repeats and Ser/Thr-rich O-glycosylated linkers when present, or flexible surface loops; weak in transmembranes and compact catalytic cores
Exemplars:
- Gram-positive adhesins and sortase-anchored cell-wall proteins: activation on Ser/Thr/Gly-rich repeat stalks between the signal peptide and LPXTG anchor
- Type IV pilins and fimbrial/adhesin subunits: activation on extracellular low-complexity linker or repeat segments
- Hemophores and iron-acquisition surface proteins (HasA/Hmu/Isd/Shr): activation on exposed low-complexity patches and repeat/linker segments
- Mycobacterial exported proteins (PE/PPE families and secreted enzymes like CFP21): activation on flexible low-complexity regions or surface loops in the exported portions
- Fungal secreted allergens, agglutinins, effectors, and hydrolytic enzymes: activation on Ser/Thr/Gly-rich disordered segments or cysteine-flanked low-complexity regions
- Plant apoplastic structural/defense proteins and enzyme inhibitors (glycine-rich proteins, extensins/AGPs, BASI, PMEI): activation on glycine-/threonine-rich repeats when present or on exposed loops/low-complexity tails
- Photosystem II extrinsic protein O (PsbO/OEE1): activation on Gly/Thr-enriched flexible regions in the lumenal mature protein
- Metazoan lipid-binding/transport proteins (apolipoproteins, lipocalins, FABPs): activation on flexible loops or low-complexity insertions; secreted or cytosolic
- Viral and bacteriophage extracellular structural proteins (tail fibers/adhesins): activation on glycine/threonine-rich repeat segments in exposed regions
- Extracellular/periplasmic or membrane-tethered carbonic anhydrases (e.g., CA IX): activation on non-catalytic low-complexity loops and proteoglycan-like segments

Summary: Detector of long tandem-repeat architecture: the feature activates over extended repeat tracts (disordered VNTR/low‑complexity S/T/P-, Q/E-, G/A/V-rich repeats and structured repeat arrays such as beta‑solenoids, coiled‑coil heptads, and C2H2 zinc‑finger arrays), with residue‑level peaks at register‑defining positions that recur in each repeat unit rather than at catalytic/liganding residues.
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation across long contiguous repeat regions; within these, strong periodic residue-level peaks repeat with the unit length (e.g., ~7, ~8/16, ~10–20, ~30 aa). Peaks often fall on characteristic positions of the repeat consensus (e.g., Pro/acidic in disordered LCRs; small hydrophobics like V/I/T in beta-strand repeats; basic residues in coiled-coil heptads; non–Cys/His positions in C2H2 fingers). Little to no activation in nonrepeat modules (signal peptides, globular domains, transmembranes, catalytic cores).
Exemplars: - Epidermal structural proteins (e.g., involucrin): periodic activation across disordered tandem repeats with peaks on Pro in PE contexts and acidic residues in LE/LD positions, tracking the ~10-aa unit.
- Membrane mucins (e.g., MUC1 VNTR): strong periodic activation across the extracellular VNTR, peaking on the second Pro in PPA within each 20-aa repeat; inactive in SEA domain, TM helix, and cytoplasmic tail.
- C2H2 zinc-finger arrays (KRAB-ZFPs): repeated peaks at conserved intra-finger positions (between Cys residues, beta-turn, and helix sites) across each finger; minimal activation on the Zn-coordinating Cys/His themselves.
- Fungal/bacterial adhesins and agglutinins: long C-terminal tandem-repeat domains with alternating secondary structure; peaks on V/I in predicted beta-strands and on Pro in coil segments, repeating per unit.
- Ice-nucleation/ice-binding proteins: central beta-solenoid repeat regions with ~16-res periodic activation at the [S/N/D]-L-[T/I/V]-A motif within beta-sheets.
- Golgin coiled-coil proteins: heptad-repeat coiled-coils with ~7-res periodic peaks (e.g., recurring Arg) in the coiled-coil core, shifting distally to strong activation on Gly/Ala/Val in a low-complexity repeat tail.

Summary: A short beta-strand signature: the feature activates on compact, well-structured beta-strand segments (~8–20 aa) that often center on hydrophobic/aromatic residues (notably Tyr, Trp, Val/Leu/Ile) together with small polar residues (Gly/Thr), frequently coinciding with conserved strand motifs across diverse folds (e.g., HYTG in FKBP PPIases, WRKYGQK in WRKY domains) and sometimes adjacent to NXS/T glycosylation sites. This reflects a generic beta-sheet element rather than a family-specific function.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation on a single short, contiguous beta-strand with sharp residue-level peaks on bulky hydrophobic/aromatic positions; high structural confidence when available; minimal activation in helices or disordered regions; occasional multiple dispersed strand hits within a protein.
Exemplars: - FKBP-type peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerases (e.g., FKBP8; bacterial Mip): activation on a structured beta-strand at the N-terminus of the FKBP domain, overlapping the conserved H–Y–T–G motif.
- WRKY transcription factors: activation on the beta-strand within the WRKY DNA-binding domain that carries the WRKYGQK motif (often peaking at the Y).
- PX-domain sorting nexins (e.g., HS1BP3): activation on an early beta-strand in the PX domain around Y/E/T-containing positions.
- Hsp90 system co-chaperones (e.g., Aha1): activation on a beta-strand within the chaperone-binding domain.
- Potassium channel auxiliary beta subunits (BK channel beta-1): activation on an extracellular beta-strand adjacent to an N-linked glycosylation NXS/T site.
- Signal peptidase complex subunit 2: activation on a cytosolic beta-strand segment.
- Metabolic enzymes (e.g., mesaconyl-CoA hydratase): activation on an internal beta-strand with Tyr/hydrophobic peaks.

Summary: A residue-level detector for conformationally permissive “hinge/kink” positions—most often Gly/Pro or small hydrophobics—found in loops, strand-connecting turns, and specific sites within or at the edges of hydrophobic signal/transmembrane helices; these positions frequently lie near catalytic/metal-binding loops or proteolytic processing regions and also occur in disordered peptide segments.
Activation pattern: Sparse, single–residue peaks scattered across a domain; enriched in coils/loops, helix–coil junctions, and selected positions inside transmembrane or signal helices; occasionally coincides with annotated catalytic or metal-binding residues; typically modest numbers of peaks per protein.
Exemplars: - FAD-dependent amine oxidase (paromamine 6′-oxidase): strongest peak at a disordered-loop Pro; moderate peak at a catalytic His.
- Sedolisin/peptidase S53 proteases: peaks on Ca2+-binding Gly residues in a loop and on the catalytic Ser within the S53 domain.
- Penicillin-binding proteins/DD-transpeptidases: peak at a Gly in a loop connecting beta-strands near the active-site Lys of the transpeptidase fold.
- Catechol 1,2-dioxygenase (intradiol dioxygenase): weak peaks at non-annotated loop/strand sites, consistent with general structural sensitivity rather than the metal-binding residues.
- Small secreted plant peptide precursors (CEP family): peak at a hydroxyproline within the disordered mature peptide and minor activation near the propeptide boundary.
- IFI27-like small membrane proteins: peaks within transmembrane helices (e.g., Val, Gly) and a short linker coil between helices.

Summary: Generic hydrophobic secondary-structure signal: activates on hydrophobic/aromatic side chains that form stable α-helices and β-strands—covering transmembrane helices, coiled-coils, and the hydrophobic cores of globular domains—while avoiding catalytic/metal-binding residues and disordered segments
Activation pattern: Regional activation across ordered secondary-structure elements with residue-level peaks on Leu/Ile/Val/Phe/Tyr/Trp/Met/Ala (often Cys). Forms continuous bands along long helices (including transmembrane segments and helical bundles/coiled-coils) and discrete peaks within β-sheets. Minimal in low-confidence/disordered regions and at polar/charged active-site or metal-binding positions
Exemplars: - Peptide deformylase (metalloenzyme): peaks on hydrophobic residues in β-strands/α-helices of the catalytic core; metal-binding and catalytic residues are off
- Endoribonuclease YbeY: activated on hydrophobic positions in β-strands and select helices; Zn-binding histidines remain off
- Pyruvate dehydrogenase E2 component: hydrophobic residues in β/α core and lipoyl-binding domain are highlighted; lipoylated lysine and catalytic histidine are off; disordered linker off
- Glycine cleavage system H (lipoyl-binding protein): strongest on β-strand hydrophobics in the lipoyl domain; lipoyl-lysine site is off; helices/loops largely low
- Tol–Pal system component TolQ (multi-pass inner membrane): strong continuous activation across transmembrane helices and adjacent cytosolic helices; periplasmic loops weak
- Undecaprenyl-phosphate galactose phosphotransferase (multi-pass membrane transferase): strongest in the structured C-terminal cytosolic domain and the final TM–cytosol junction; early transmembrane helices largely weak/inactive

Summary: A generic structural motif: short segments of beta-strands and the immediately adjacent turn/loop (beta-hairpin or strand–turn junction), often capturing one face of a strand with i/i+2 periodicity; broadly distributed across proteins and not tied to catalytic residues or a specific function.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks in 2–5-residue runs within well-ordered beta-strands and the neighboring turn/loop; multiple discrete peaks scattered through structured domains; minimal activation in disordered regions and typically not on annotated active-site residues; occasional isolated weaker peaks in other secondary structures (e.g., helices).
Exemplars: - HtrA/DegP-family serine protease (with PDZ domain): peaks on PDZ beta-strands and on beta-sheets in the protease domain, avoiding the catalytic H-D-S triad.
- FMN-dependent pyridoxine/pyridoxamine 5'-phosphate oxidase: peaks on beta-strands and a loop-to-strand transition near (but not at) the FMN-binding site.
- Tetracycline dehydro reductase (oxidoreductase): main peak on an N-terminal beta-strand and the following loop; secondary peak on another strand.
- Peptide deformylase (metalloamide hydrolase): localized peak on a central beta-sheet segment and adjacent coil, not overlapping metal-binding or catalytic residues.
- Phosphoribosyl-AMP cyclohydrolase (histidine biosynthesis enzyme): peaks on an N-terminal beta-strand and subsequent turn, with additional weaker strand-centered peaks elsewhere.

Summary: Extended, non-membrane alpha-helical segments enriched in charged/polar residues (Lys/Glu/Asp/Arg/Ser/Thr), frequently forming coiled-coils or amphipathic helical bundles used for scaffolding/assembly or as helical elements flanking active sites/cofactor-binding regions; common across secreted/extracellular proteins, viral structural proteins, ER/Golgi tethers, and large cytosolic adaptors.
Activation pattern: Regional activation spanning long helix-rich blocks rather than a short motif; residue-level peaks concentrate on solvent-exposed charged/polar positions within helices and at functional helical elements (e.g., cofactor-binding helices, redox Cys-containing helices). Minimal activation over hydrophobic signal peptides/transmembrane segments; generally lower in highly disordered low-complexity regions unless they encode or transiently adopt helical/coiled-coil structure.
Exemplars: - ER disulfide-forming oxidoreductases (e.g., ERO1): strong activation across the helical catalytic core, especially FAD-binding helices and redox-active Cys pairs; low over the N-terminal signal peptide.
- A-kinase anchoring/scaffolding proteins (AKAPs): pronounced activation along long coiled-coil helices and within the PKA RII–binding helix; weaker in extended disordered linkers.
- Viral structural/tegument and packaging proteins: activation on assembly coiled-coils and helical rods mediating oligomerization.
- ER/Golgi and vesicle-trafficking tethers/adaptors (golgins and related coiled-coil scaffolds): activation along extended coiled-coil stems.
- Secreted cell-surface/cell-wall and parasite invasion proteins, including some allergens: activation across long charged Ser/Thr-rich helical/coiled-coil tracts that support adhesion/assembly.
- Bacterial defense systems (e.g., CRISPR/Cas and accessory factors): activation on helix-rich scaffolds/coiled-coil interaction regions.

Summary: Mature extracytoplasmic or otherwise solvent-exposed domains (surface or luminal) of secretory-pathway and membrane-associated proteins, with occasional capture of analogous long low-complexity linkers in soluble cytosolic proteins; favors S/T/G-rich or acidic low-complexity tracts, disulfide-bonded cysteines where applicable, glycosylation sequons in secretory proteins, and selected beta-strand/linker elements.
Activation pattern: Domain-level/regional activation that switches on at the start of the mature extracytoplasmic/luminal domain after signal peptides/propeptides and switches off in transmembrane helices and cytosolic/intravirion tails; spans long stretches with residue-level peaks in S/T/G-rich segments, N-X-S/T sequons, disulfide-forming cysteines, and certain beta/linker regions; also frequently marks long solvent-exposed low-complexity linkers in soluble cytosolic proteins.
Exemplars: - Pore-forming cytolysins (e.g., trialysin): strong activation across the mature toxin domain, absent in signal peptide/propeptide; often strongest in beta-rich C-terminal regions.
- Ig superfamily cell adhesion molecules (e.g., ICAMs): activation within extracellular Ig-like domains and juxtamembrane ectodomains; off in signal peptide, transmembrane helix, and cytosolic tail.
- Arthropod salivary secreted proteins (gSG7, Aegyptin-like): broad activation across the mature secreted chain; off in the signal peptide.
- Viral envelope and inner-envelope components: activation on virion-surface or luminal ectodomains with disulfide bonds; off in transmembrane segments and intravirion/cytosolic tails.
- Organelle luminal/membrane-associated proteins (e.g., ER/lysosomal or mitochondrial intermembrane-space–exposed regions).
- Soluble cytosolic chaperone/cofactor proteins: activation on long low-complexity, acidic/S/T/G-rich linkers (e.g., Hsp90 co-chaperone AHA1).

Summary: Membrane-penetrating hydrophobic segments—fusion‑peptide/signal‑anchor–like helices or loops positioned at proteolytic cleavage junctions or immediately N‑terminal to a transmembrane helix—that initiate or stabilize bilayer insertion for membrane fusion, pore formation, anchoring, or organelle targeting. These stretches are Gly/Ala‑rich, often dotted with interfacial Trp/Tyr and flanked by basic residues, and frequently show coil→helix propensity and low-confidence structure.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long, contiguous hydrophobic segments (typically 15–35 aa); local maxima at aromatic residues within the segment; activation often begins at/just after basic clusters and extends into the first turn of an adjacent TM helix. Multiple nonadjacent activated segments per protein are common, with secondary peaks in TM‑proximal regions (e.g., MPER) or cytoplasmic tails. Many activated regions are predicted disordered/low pLDDT but can adopt helical structure upon membrane engagement.
Exemplars: - Influenza hemagglutinin‑esterase‑fusion glycoprotein: strong activation at the HEF2 N‑terminus (canonical fusion peptide immediately post‑cleavage), plus a secondary peak near the TM start.
- HIV‑1 envelope (gp160/gp41): peak across the SU–TM cleavage and N‑terminus of the gp41 fusion peptide; minor activation in TM‑proximal/cytoplasmic segments.
- ISG12/IFI6 family (interferon‑inducible small membrane proteins): activation on the loop between TM1–TM2 extending into the N‑terminus of TM2, i.e., the membrane‑anchoring helix.
- Chlamydial inclusion membrane proteins (Inc): activation on the membrane‑anchoring helical TM region required for inclusion membrane insertion.
- Peroxisome biogenesis factor PEX3: activation across the N‑terminal peroxisomal targeting/signal‑anchor segment and the initial part of the first TM helix.
- More generally (from the broader set): bacterial pore‑forming toxins and bacteriocins show activation on their hydrophobic pore‑forming helices; Type III/VI secretion translocon components/effectors activate on hydrophobic insertion loops that penetrate host membranes.

Summary: Generic recognition of well‑ordered secondary-structure surfaces with a strong bias for β‑strand segments (β‑sheet faces) across diverse folds; in disulfide‑stabilized modules (EGF‑like), on specific cysteines embedded in the β‑strand scaffold.

Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks clustered on contiguous β‑strands within structured domains; largely silent in disordered/low‑complexity regions, signal peptides, and transmembranes. Rare, compact patches can also appear on conserved helical surfaces in all‑α folds (e.g., ribosome‑recycling factor). Activation favors hydrophobic/aromatic and selected charged strand positions; cysteine is uncommon except in EGF‑like modules.

Exemplars:
- Small heat‑shock/α‑crystallin proteins: mid‑to‑C‑terminal β‑strands of the α‑crystallin β‑sandwich.
- EGF‑like growth factors/toxins: selective disulfide‑bonded cysteines in the β‑hairpin/strand region.
- Heavy metal–associated (HMA) domains (HIPP/HPP): dominant β‑strand stretch within the HMA core; metal‑binding Cys often not highlighted.
- GH16 glycoside hydrolases (β‑jelly roll) and β‑1,3‑glucan‑binding proteins: localized patches on adjacent core β‑strands, excluding catalytic sites.
- KEOPS subunit Pcc1 and CsrA: restricted to core β‑strands.
- Galectins: β‑sandwich strands of the lectin domain.
- Plant WRKY transcription factors: Cys/His‑stabilized β‑sheet segment of the WRKY domain.
- Ribosome‑recycling factor (bacterial/mitochondrial): occasional activation on a conserved helical surface patch despite all‑α architecture.

Summary: Core-facing hydrophobic residues within β-strands of well‑ordered domains, typically selecting single Ile/Val/Leu/Ala/Phe positions that anchor β‑sheets; repeats once per WD40 blade and appears at a few β‑strand anchor sites in enzyme cores, often adjacent to (but not on) catalytic/consensus motifs
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks; a handful of sites per protein. Strongly enriched in high‑confidence β‑strand segments, frequently at coil→β transitions or mid‑strand core positions; minimal in helices and disordered tails. In WD40 proteins, one peak per blade; in enzymes, peaks cluster on central β‑sheets and near motif-bearing regions.
Exemplars: - WD40 β‑propeller scaffolds (e.g., RNA processing/chromatin WD proteins, TRM82/WDR4): one hydrophobic residue per blade within a β‑strand that packs into the propeller core; absent from disordered termini and non‑β regions.
- Nucleotidyltransferases (e.g., MntA adenylyltransferase): a single hydrophobic N‑cap at the first residue of a β‑strand immediately upstream of the catalytic GSX(10)DXD segment, highlighting the strand edge rather than the motif.
- Hydrolases (alpha/beta hydrolases such as esterases/lipases/BioH; carbohydrate‑active enzymes like glycosidases/xylanases): a few hydrophobic residues on the central β‑sheet that scaffold the active site; occasionally includes or neighbors catalytic Ser/His/Asp/Cys positions.

Summary: Functionally constrained cores in energy, signaling, and assembly domains: the feature marks conserved microenvironments in ATP/GTP-dependent enzyme cores (eukaryotic Ser/Thr kinases, histidine kinases, and P-loop NTPases) and in transmembrane energy/signal-transducing bundles (e.g., GPCRs, rotary ATPase c-rings, TonB), as well as conserved core residues in stable ribonucleoprotein assemblies.
Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks within well-structured domains, including transmembrane helices; highest near phosphate/ligand-binding loops and adjacent catalytic/switch elements in NTPases/kinases, and at conserved TM/bundle positions involved in coupling, ion/proton binding, or microswitches; minimal in long disordered/low-complexity tails and peripheral regions.
Exemplars: Ser/Thr protein kinases (eukaryotic and bacterial): peaks near the glycine-rich/ATP-binding elements and catalytic loop Asp or HATPase_c N/G1/G2 motifs, absent from non-kinase tails/TM; Small GTPases (Rab): peaks at the P-loop, Switch regions, and NKXD-flanking residues; Kinesin motors: peaks in the motor domain near the ATP-binding loop, none in long disordered/coiled regions; Two-component histidine kinases: peaks in the HATPase_c ATP-binding motifs and dimer interface; GPCRs: peaks within the 7TM bundle near conserved microswitch motifs (e.g., DRY, CWxP, NPxxY) and coupling-facing residues; ATP synthase subunit c: peaks around the conserved proton-binding residue within the TM helix; TonB: peaks near the TM helix and conserved periplasmic core residues; Ribosomal/RNAP assembly proteins: peaks on conserved core/RNA-binding residues that stabilize the complex.

Summary: Short, compositionally biased segments (typically 10–60 aa) that function as targeting/processing signals or linker/stabilization modules in both extracellular/membrane and cytosolic/nuclear proteins; includes basic, amphipathic leader/transit peptides (signal peptides, signal anchors, mitochondrial presequences), internal or terminal Pro/Gly/Ser‑rich low‑complexity linkers, Lys/Arg‑rich clusters (including NLS-like patches), and Cys‑rich clusters forming disulfides or serving as lipidation sites (e.g., palmitoylation).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous windows (10–60 aa), frequently at termini but also internal; occasional sharper peaks on short motifs (e.g., PxxP, dibasic Lys/Arg clusters, Cys clusters).
Exemplars: Fungal cytochrome P450 monooxygenases: activation on the N‑terminal signal‑anchor helix and adjacent proline‑rich hinge; Secreted toxins, lectins, and pathogen effectors: activation on signal peptides/propeptides and nearby Cys‑rich extracellular segments; Collagens/ECM: activation across Gly–X–Y collagenous repeats and proline‑rich linkers; CFEM‑domain proteins: activation over the ∼60‑aa cysteine‑rich CFEM module; Plant receptor‑like kinases/LRR receptors: activation on N‑terminal signal peptides and Pro/Gly/Ser‑rich extracellular linkers; Mitochondrial proteins: activation on N‑terminal Arg‑rich transit peptides; Histones/chromatin factors: activation on Lys/Arg‑rich tails or NLS‑like basic clusters; Cytosolic enzymes and kinases (e.g., PFK, CDK4/6): activation on internal low‑complexity P/G/S‑rich loops or basic clusters; NTF2‑like transport factors: activation on basic patches or low‑complexity tails; Viral accessory proteins (e.g., Vif): activation on proline‑rich, basic, and Cys/His motifs; Neuronal SNAREs (e.g., SNAP‑25): activation on central Cys clusters for palmitoylation and adjacent low‑complexity segments.

Summary: Short, surface-exposed loop/turn motifs at β-strand boundaries within globular domains—often enriched in Gly, Asp/Glu, and Pro (with occasional aromatics)—that flank or position functional residues for binding, ion coordination, or catalysis across diverse protein families.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in brief coil segments linking secondary structure elements, especially at strand–coil junctions or β-hairpin tips; sparse elsewhere. Typically absent from long disordered tails and transmembranes. Peaks frequently lie adjacent to acidic clusters or known catalytic/metal-binding residues. Number of peaks per protein varies from a single hot spot to several per domain.
Exemplars: - C2-domain Ca2+-binding proteins (e.g., Munc13/UNC13): loops adjacent to Ca2+-coordinating Asp-rich sites within C2 domains.
- Aspartic proteases (BACE family): turns/loops around the catalytic Asp dyad and at the entry to the peptidase A1 domain.
- β-sheeted pore-forming/venom toxins (δ-stichotoxin): short coil preceding a β-strand that forms a surface loop on the toxin scaffold.
- VHL tumor suppressor β-domain: loop connecting β-strands that contains disease-sensitive residues.
- NF-κB/Rel family (Rel Homology Domain): inter-strand loops linking β-strands/helix elements within the DNA-binding/dimerization domain.
- Complex I assembly factor CIA30/NDUFAF1: β-strand-flanking loops in the C-terminal half of the protein.

Summary: Generic early N-terminus positional signal peaking at residue ~5–7, most often within cleavable leader/targeting segments (signal peptides, transit peptides, propeptides) of precursor proteins, and more generally the disordered N-tail preceding the first structured domain; residue identity is not specific
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks highly localized to the first 10 residues, maximally at positions 5–7; usually confined to N-terminal leader/targeting or propeptide regions, with occasional weak secondary peaks in downstream low-complexity/disordered segments; little to no activation in folded domains or mature regions after cleavage
Exemplars: - Lantibiotic/bacteriocin precursors (e.g., gallidermin): peak at K5/E6 within the N-terminal leader peptide; mature antimicrobial peptide shows no activation
- Ig-superfamily cell-adhesion receptors (e.g., Nectin family): peak at G6 within the N-terminal signal peptide
- Secreted trypsin-like serine proteases (zymogens): peak at G6 in the N-terminal signal peptide, with minor peaks in adjacent disordered N-tail
- Plant secreted proteins with signal peptides: peak at S6 within the signal peptide; scattered weak sites in distal disordered regions
- Homeobox transcription factors: peak at E6 within a disordered N-terminal tail; structured DNA-binding homeobox domain lacks activation

Summary: Hydrophobic residues on conserved beta-strands that form the core of α/β folds, most characteristically the central beta-sheet of GNAT/NAT acetyltransferases lining the acetyl‑CoA/substrate-binding groove; the same signal appears at structurally analogous beta‑strand positions adjacent to catalytic or other functionally critical sites in diverse proteins, including non-enzymes such as ribosomal protein uL22.
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks on 1–3 hydrophobic positions per protein; concentrated on well-structured beta-strands (high confidence) within the catalytic core, often in the 30–150 aa region of GNAT/NAT domains and immediately flanking annotated acetyl‑CoA or substrate-binding residues; occasional hits at analogous beta‑strand core sites in non-GNAT proteins.
Exemplars:
- Thialysine Nε-acetyltransferase (GNAT family): Leu on a beta-strand just upstream of a substrate-binding Glu and adjacent to the acetyl‑CoA-binding region; minor peak on an N‑terminal beta-strand.
- Aminoglycoside 3‑N‑acetyltransferase (antibiotic resistance GNAT): Ile on a central beta-strand within the catalytic GNAT core.
- Gcn5-like acetyltransferase (mycobacterial GNAT, Rv2170-like): Leu on a beta-strand near a functionally critical acidic residue in the GNAT domain.
- Histone acetyltransferase Hpa2 (GNAT): Ile on a beta-strand immediately adjacent to the annotated acetyl‑CoA-binding segment; weaker activation on an N‑terminal beta-strand.
- Molybdenum cofactor biosynthesis protein C (MoaC): Ile on a beta-strand near the active-site Asp in the catalytic region.
- Ribosomal protein uL22: hydrophobic residue on a conserved beta-strand within the tunnel-forming region.

Summary: Sterically constrained small-residue positions within well-ordered secondary structures of folded domains, often packing the core or lining/flanking ligand/cofactor-binding and catalytic/motor pockets; a generic structural micro-environment rather than a family-specific motif.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks; sparse, isolated single-residue activations distributed across proteins, enriched in structured regions (helix/strand/ordered coil), with little or no signal in signal peptides or disordered tails; can occur just N-terminal to domain boundaries as well as within domains.
Exemplars: - Serine hydrolases/esterases: isolated low-level peaks on L/V/T within beta-strands and helices of the mature enzyme (e.g., between disulfide-bonded cysteines); signal peptides largely inactive.
- Carboxylesterase-like proteins (inactive homologs): scattered peaks on L/A/F in ordered coil/helix/strand with no specific annotated site, consistent with packing positions.
- AA9 lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases: residues immediately N-terminal to copper- and oxygen-binding residues (around His/Tyr/Gln) plus nearby helix positions; occasional weak signal in the signal peptide.
- Flavin-dependent thymidylate synthase (ThyX): a peak on the FAD-binding serine and weaker peaks in the ThyX insert/motif.
- Kinesin motor proteins: peaks within the motor domain and just N-terminal to it, consistent with residues in or adjacent to nucleotide/microtubule-interacting cores.

Summary: Intrinsic disorder/low-complexity segments, especially N-terminal tails and targeting/processing regions (transit peptides, propeptides) enriched in Lys/Arg and polar residues (Ser/Thr/Asp/Glu) with Gly/Pro, common in secreted, membrane-associated, and viral proteins, with little signal in well-folded domains.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches—frequently at the N-terminus—with additional sparse residue-level peaks in other low-pLDDT coils/loops; minimal to no activation in high-confidence structured cores or transmembrane helices.
Exemplars: - Bacterial ubiquinone monooxygenase UbiM: activation confined to a disordered N-terminal extension; no activation in the structured enzymatic/membrane region.
- Human spermatogenesis-associated/testis protein: multiple isolated peaks across predicted intrinsically disordered regions; no overlap with annotated structured domains.
- Viral accessory/envelope proteins: activation on low-complexity termini or flexible cytosolic/extracellular tails used for host interaction.
- Secreted adhesins/mucin-like proteins and toxin precursors: activation across Ser/Thr/Pro-rich extracellular low-complexity repeats and unstructured propeptides.
- Housekeeping metabolic enzymes: activation restricted to low-complexity termini or insertions; globular catalytic cores largely inactive.
- Organellar proteins (mitochondrial/chloroplast/peroxisomal): activation on N-terminal targeting peptides and other flexible, basic/polar-rich extensions.

Summary: Generic detector of short, aliphatic-rich β‑strand segments that form the cores of β‑sheets in diverse domain scaffolds and repeats (e.g., PDZ, SRCR, LysM, LRR, KH/R3H, ubiquitin/UBL β‑grasp), rather than a function-specific motif; sequence windows show alternating small/polar and hydrophobic residues, strongly enriched in V/L/I/A and often with nearby Ser/Thr, and in secreted modules may be flanked by cysteines.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks confined to contiguous 5–8 aa β‑strands (DSSP E), with sharp, localized maxima; multiple short hotspots recur along long, repeat‑rich proteins; minimal activation on helices, coils, or low‑confidence/disordered regions; can occur at inter‑domain junctions; does not track catalytic/binding loops (e.g., GTP-binding regions remain off).
Exemplars: - PDZ-domain scaffold/adaptor proteins (cell junction/synaptic polarity): activation on internal β‑strands of the PDZ β‑sandwich.
- SRCR-type secreted receptors/precursors: activation on short aliphatic β‑strands within disulfide‑rich SRCR repeats (often Cys-flanked).
- LysM-domain peptidoglycan-binding proteins (Gram‑positive cell wall enzymes): activation on the β‑strand elements of LysM repeats and other β‑rich cell-wall–associated modules.
- Leucine-rich repeat proteins: activation on leucine-packed β‑strands forming the parallel sheet on the concave LRR surface.
- Bacterial RNA-binding KhpB/EloR: activation on specific β‑strands in Jag_N, KH, and R3H domains (strong at the Jag_N–KH junction).
- Flagellar biosynthesis GTPase FlhF: activation on a single short N‑terminal β‑strand segment.
- Ubiquitin/ubiquitin-like proteins (and some ligase-associated β‑domains): activation on the β‑strands of the β‑grasp fold.

Summary: Low-complexity, Pro/Thr/Ser/Gly/Ala–rich linker/spacer regions in secreted, extracellular modular proteins—especially carbohydrate-active enzymes (glycoside hydrolases and polysaccharide lyases) and secreted proteases—characterized by repetitive TP/PT/GT motifs and glycine clusters; these intrinsically disordered segments connect catalytic domains with CBMs, dockerins/cohesins, or other modules and are often O-glycosylated to provide flexibility, extension, and protease resistance (also appearing in analogous linkers of phage tail fibers/adhesins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, low-complexity stretches (often tens to hundreds of residues) rather than catalytic residues; typically between or flanking domains in secreted proteins.
Exemplars: - Bacterial cellulases and hemicellulases (e.g., GH5/GH9/GH10/GH11): activation on Pro/Thr-rich linkers between catalytic domains and CBMs or dockerin modules.
- Pectin/pectate and other polysaccharide lyases (e.g., PL1/PL3/PL9; marine PL7 alginate lyases): activation on S/T/G-rich repetitive spacers connecting modules in secreted enzymes.
- Multi-modular cellulosome components (scaffoldins and dockerin/cohesin-bearing CAZymes): activation on extended PT/TS-rich linkers separating cohesins, dockerins, CBMs, and catalytic domains.
- Secreted proteases/peptidases (e.g., S8 subtilisin-like, M4 thermolysin-like, M23/LytM lysins): activation on low-complexity propeptides and inter-domain spacer regions.
- Marine polysaccharide-degrading systems (e.g., agarases/carrageenases GH16/GH86, alginate lyases PL7): activation on glycine/threonine-rich disordered linkers within secreted, modular enzymes.
- Phage tail fibers/adhesins: activation on glycine/serine/threonine-rich flexible linkers that separate receptor-binding or structural domains.

Summary: Composition-driven detection of intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments—especially serine/threonine–rich stretches with interspersed Pro/Gly and small hydrophobics, and often including basic (Lys/Arg) residues—commonly found in secreted/extracellular proteins and short basic accessory or micropeptides, rather than a specific motif or domain
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across long disordered/low‑complexity regions (often near the N‑terminus), with strongest signals on S/T and additional hits on P/G, A/V/I, and sometimes Lys/Arg or Cys; little preference for signal peptides, transmembranes, or catalytic motifs per se
Exemplars: - Fungal GPI-anchored cell-wall adhesins (e.g., AWA1/adhesin-like): peaks on S/T and small hydrophobics within disordered, low‑complexity O‑glycan–prone repeats; not on the signal peptide or GPI site.
- Herpesvirus envelope glycoprotein L homologs: highlights disordered, compositionally biased segments in small secreted accessory glycoproteins.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: marks the N‑terminal disordered host-targeting region around the RxLR region with S/T- and basic-residue–enriched low complexity.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunit: flags flexible/disordered tail segments in this small basic enzyme subunit.
- Human micropeptides/lncRNA‑derived and cancer/testis proteins: activates on low‑complexity, often basic S/T/P/G–rich stretches in short, largely disordered proteins.
- Cysteine‑rich keratin‑associated proteins: highlights residues within low‑complexity, cysteine‑biased disordered regions.
- Small viral accessory/regulatory proteins: emphasizes N‑terminal and internal low‑complexity/disordered segments enriched in S/T/P/G and basic residues.

Summary: Short, surface‑exposed secondary‑structure junctions/capping segments (loops/turns at helix↔coil or strand↔coil transitions), with a strong bias toward the disulfide‑constrained loops of Ly6/uPAR three‑finger folds in secreted proteins but also occurring as analogous flexible capping loops at domain edges in diverse intracellular proteins
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks confined to narrow 10–25 aa windows; strongest on coil segments that cap or connect helices/strands (helix–coil–helix, coil→β, coil/strand→helix). In secreted proteins the windows often lie 50–120 aa after the signal peptide and can include Cys‑rich/CC motifs; in soluble proteins they mark non‑catalytic, surface loops with context‑specific chemistry (e.g., Lys/Arg‑rich in mitoribosomal proteins, acidic N‑caps for helices). Catalytic cores and stable secondary‑structure interiors are typically ignored.
Exemplars: Ly6/uPAR three‑finger proteins and snake three‑finger toxins: activation on short, disulfide‑stabilized loop segments (often CC‑containing) in the post–signal peptide three‑finger domain; Fish Bouncer fertilization proteins and mammalian LY6/SLURP family: same three‑finger loop patches; Fungal small secreted cysteine‑rich/antifungal proteins: activation on Cys‑rich exposed loops; Periplasmic serine protease DegP/HtrA: activation on a PDZ2 loop‑to‑β transition segment, not on the protease active site; PWWP‑domain chromatin proteins: activation on a short helix–coil–helix segment immediately C‑terminal to the PWWP core; Type II membrane glycosyltransferases (e.g., xylosyltransferase): activation on lumenal coil/strand‑to‑helix patches away from catalytic motifs; Mitochondrial large ribosomal proteins: activation on short Lys/Arg‑rich exposed loops likely contacting rRNA; Phage tail tube/terminator proteins and replicative helicases: activation on short exposed non‑catalytic loops within structural domains; Deubiquitinases and other chromatin‑associated enzymes: activation on surface loop segments rather than catalytic residues.

Summary: Repetitive beta-strand solenoid architecture (beta-helix/beta-solenoid–like repeats) and their tight turns/edge-of-sheet positions, especially in large secreted/surface or virion spike/fiber proteins; the feature keys on the small/polar residue–rich repeating skeleton (G/S/T/N; A/V/I) that builds these extended beta-rich scaffolds, and occasionally marks similar beta-sheet oligomerization patches in other proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional-to-domain activation across long beta-solenoid segments with superimposed residue-level peaks on beta-strands and adjacent turns/coil links; preferentially beta-rich regions, sometimes extending into flexible coil segments that connect repeats; little to no signal in helices or unrelated disordered tails.
Exemplars: - Autotransporter adhesins/proteases: recurrent peaks at glycine-rich turns and edge-of-strand sites throughout the passenger beta-solenoid and within the C‑terminal outer-membrane beta-barrel loops.
- Bacteriophage baseplate wedge proteins: scattered peaks in flexible coil loops and beta-strand edges within the beta-rich wedge scaffold.
- Type VI secretion system spike proteins (VgrG): extended C‑terminal segment with multiple peaks consistent with a repeat/solenoid-like beta-rich extension rather than the structured N‑terminal core.
- Receptor tyrosine kinase extracellular domains (EGFR): discrete peaks within beta-strands of approximate-repeat L-domains (solenoid-like), absent from the transmembrane/kinase regions.
- Fungal GPI-anchored cell-wall adhesins (e.g., Candida Iff family): selected asparagines in beta-sheets and Gly/Pro in turns across the beta-rich adhesin domain.
- Ice-binding proteins: numerous peaks across beta-strands of the beta-solenoid core, not restricted to specific ice-binding motifs.
- Nucleotide-sugar pyrophosphorylases (UGPase): residues in beta-strands and adjacent coils within the C‑terminal oligomerization beta-sheet region.
- Myelin gene regulatory factor-like proteins: a short beta-strand/coil patch in an interdomain linker consistent with a small beta-sheet segment.

Summary: Short, surface-exposed loop and linker segments with low hydrophobicity and enrichment for Pro/Ser/Thr (often containing SP/TP and occasionally NXS/T motifs), typically flanking or connecting secondary-structure elements in both soluble and lumenal/extracellular proteins; these patches mark polar coil/turn regions rather than catalytic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation in short contiguous patches (about 15–50 residues), often multiple per protein; strongest at coils/turns and edges of helices or beta-strands, appearing in both flexible interdomain linkers and ordered surface loops; composition skews to P/S/T/G with charged residues and few bulky hydrophobics; generally away from active sites but sometimes adjacent to PTM-prone positions.
Exemplars: - Glucan endo-1,3-beta-D-glucosidases (GH81 laminarinases): activation on a beta-sandwich surface loop/edge region within the catalytic domain, peaking in a coil, not at catalytic residues.
- Argonaute/Piwi proteins: strong activation on the L1 interdomain linker between the N and PAZ domains, with minor activation at the L2–Mid boundary and a Mid-domain helix.
- V-ATPase accessory subunit 2 (Voa2 family): activation in lumenal N-terminal helix–loop segments and a flexible lumenal loop.
- Uronyl 2-sulfotransferase (Golgi type II membrane sulfotransferase): activation in the lumenal domain on a helix/adjacent coil containing an NXS/T glycosylation site and just N-terminal to the catalytic histidine; a second lumenal helix also activates.
- Cry pesticidal crystal proteins: activation across a helix–loop–helix surface loop within a well-structured region.

Summary: Outer-envelope beta-barrel architecture signal: the feature marks residues within the membrane-spanning beta-strands of outer-membrane/outer-envelope channels (bacterial OMPs and organellar porins), especially immediately after periplasmic loop-to-strand starts and at aromatic/hydrophobic positions; secondarily, it highlights beta-strand frameworks of outer-membrane–associated beta-rich proteins.
Activation pattern: - Domain-restricted but residue-level: strong, sparse peaks on high-confidence beta-strands (DSSP E) of the barrel; minimal on signal peptides, TonB boxes, plug/soluble domains, extracellular loops, and helices.
- Hotspots often sit just into the strand following a periplasmic turn (coil→strand), with preference for hydrophobic/aromatic residues (notably tryptophan, phenylalanine, leucine/valine) and occasional small residues at tight turns.
- Multi-residue clusters appear across multiple strands; in Type V autotransporters, activation is confined to the C‑terminal translocator barrel.
Exemplars: - TonB-dependent transporters (e.g., vitamin B12 receptor): activation on transmembrane beta-barrel strands, especially at periplasmic loop→strand onsets; plug domain, TonB box, and ligand-binding residues are inactive.
- Classical porins/outer-membrane proteins (e.g., OMP P1-like): peaks on well-predicted beta-strands and strand starts; helices and low-confidence loops are silent.
- Type V autotransporter adhesins: activation restricted to the C-terminal translocator beta-barrel; passenger/stalk regions are inactive.
- Chloroplast outer envelope porins (OEP family): sparse but strong hotspots within beta-strands and loop→strand junctions of the outer-envelope barrel.
- Outer-membrane–associated beta-rich proteins (e.g., MltA-interacting/MipA-like): isolated hotspots on the mature beta-strand framework; helical segments remain inactive.

Summary: Short, surface-exposed charged micro-motifs (E/D/K/R/H) that act as electrostatic “hotspots” for catalysis, metal coordination, and binding of anionic ligands (DNA/RNA, nucleotides/phosphate, phosphoinositides) or partner proteins; includes canonical acid/base and His/Glu metal-binding motifs and basic patches in binding loops
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on short clustered segments (typically 2–6 residues) enriched in juxtaposed acidic and basic residues; occasionally multiple distributed peaks across proteins with many such patches
Exemplars: - Zn-dependent metalloproteases (MMP/M12-like): activation on the catalytic HExxH motif and neighboring Glu/Asp metal/co-catalytic residues
- DNA ligases (ATP/NAD-dependent): activation on the KxDG Lys/Asp active-site motif and adjacent basic DNA-phosphate–binding patch
- Sliding clamp (PCNA/β clamp): activation on basic surface loops that contact the DNA backbone and acidic/basic interface patches for partner docking
- rRNA/tRNA methyltransferases and tRNA(Ile)-lysidine synthase: activation on Lys/Arg-rich RNA-binding loops and nearby Asp/Glu/His catalytic residues
- Inositol phosphate/PIP kinases: activation on basic phosphate-binding clusters and conserved Asp/Lys catalytic pairs in the active site
- Heat-shock chaperones (Hsp70/Hsp90/GroEL): activation on conserved charged submotifs in NTPase domains (e.g., HPNID-, DVxK/E-containing segments) and acidic/basic interface loops for co-chaperone binding
- Type II secretion pseudopilins/prepilins: activation on the positively charged N-terminal leader/processing region and the conserved acidic residue near the cleavage site
- Ferredoxin components of monooxygenase systems: activation on acidic/basic docking patches near cofactor/partner interaction surfaces
- PH-domain adaptors: activation on the K/R-rich β1–β2 loop that binds phosphoinositide headgroups
- Molybdenum-cofactor oxidoreductases: activation on charged residues around the Moco-binding pocket (Lys/Arg engaging the phosphate and His/Asp/Glu catalytic residues)

Summary: Generic ordered-secondary-structure signal: activates on residues embedded in well-structured elements—especially alpha-helices (including transmembrane helices) and beta-strands/adjacent loops—favoring hydrophobic or small residues that contribute to packing; often near but not on catalytic/ligand sites; depleted in disordered/low-confidence regions.
Activation pattern: Diffuse, low-magnitude residue-level peaks scattered across structured regions; enrichment in continuous helical segments, transmembrane helices, helix–coil junctions, and beta-sandwich loops/strands; minimal activation in flexible/disordered tails; no single short motif.
Exemplars: - Metal-dependent ADP-ribosylhydrolase (ARH3): peaks on Ile/Ala within helices and nearby coil surrounding the catalytic core (high pLDDT), rather than on the metal-binding residues themselves.
- Mitochondrial transcription factor: strongest on a short alpha-helix adjacent to an annotated ligand-binding residue; smaller peaks on other SSEs; little signal in the disordered C-terminal tail.
- Na+/H+ antiporter (CPA family): sparse peaks within predicted transmembrane helices and at helix boundaries.
- Major facilitator superfamily (MFS) transporter: activation on a cytoplasmic helical linker between TM helices, within TM segments, and across TM–loop junctions.
- TRIM/B30.2–SPRY domain scaffold: concentrated in the structured B30.2/SPRY beta-sandwich (loops and beta-strands), with low signal in the disordered N-terminus.
- Y-family DNA polymerase IV: long, well-structured alpha-helices within the catalytic domain show peaks; catalytic/metal-binding residues are not highlighted.
- P4-ATPase lipid flippase: peaks at the exoplasmic end and within TM helices, plus smaller peaks in structured regions of the cytoplasmic domain; disordered C-terminal region is largely inactive and ATP/Mg2+-binding residues are not specifically highlighted.

Summary: Short, surface-exposed beta-strand/turn “edge” patches of beta-sheet domains—often disulfide-stabilized in extracellular adhesion/recognition modules, but also present in cytosolic beta-sandwich/RRM-like folds—marking strand-edge/turn elements used for binding or domain interfaces; enriched in T/G/S (often C in extracellular contexts) with occasional W/Y.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks forming short contiguous bands (≈6–25 aa) that track beta-strands and tight turns; multiple independent bands per protein in repeat-rich extracellular regions. The feature is largely off in transmembranes and long low-complexity/disordered stretches (e.g., FG repeats), and centers on structured strand/turn segments at domain edges.
Exemplars: - Netrin receptors (UNC5 family): weak bands in extracellular thrombospondin type-1 (TSR/TSP-1) repeats near conserved cysteines; strong band on the C-terminal edge beta-strand of the cytoplasmic ZU5 beta-sandwich.
- Nucleoporins (Nup145/Nup98 family): sharp, isolated band within the NRM fold at a helix-to-strand transition and short turn; no activation over FG-repeat regions.
- Adhesion GPCRs (ADGR): short patches in the extracellular region (GAIN/GPS vicinity and adjacent beta-rich modules) highlighting cysteine/Trp-containing strand–turn elements.
- Lectins/selectins and other extracellular recognition modules: peaks on disulfide-stabilized beta-sheets/loops that form carbohydrate-recognition surfaces.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes (glycoside hydrolases, CBMs): strand/turn patches lining substrate-binding grooves or within beta-sandwich CBM repeats.
- Bacteriophage tail spikes and capsule depolymerases: turns and strand edges along right-handed beta-helix repeats that form receptor-binding ridges.
- Serine proteases and protease-like autotransporters: short strand–turn and disulfide-linked loops in extracellular/passenger regions or processing segments.
- Bacterial adhesins/invasins (e.g., internalins, serine-rich adhesins): multiple bands across repeat-rich extracellular beta-domains consistent with adhesion interfaces.
- Innate immunity/ECM proteins: repeated short activations in Ig-like, TSR, and related small beta-rich modules.

Summary: Composition-driven recognition of long, low-complexity, acid-poor segments enriched in small hydrophobic and small polar residues (A, V, L, I, G, S, T)—often GA/AS-rich stretches—that are typically disordered but can form amphipathic, membrane-interacting surfaces; these regions are widespread in secreted/extracellular and viral structural proteins and are used for membrane binding, translocation/export signals, assembly interfaces, and surface display.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended, contiguous low-complexity blocks (frequently N‑terminal or internal), with broad plateaus over Gly/Ala-rich runs and Ser/Thr/Ala repeats; weak activation on acidic residues; not a short, motif-specific signal but a compositional bias that can encompass amphipathic helix-forming segments.
Exemplars: - Viral capsid/entry proteins: activation on low-complexity arms/loops and membrane-binding segments used in capsid assembly and host entry.
- Antimicrobial peptides and venom toxin precursors: activation on amphipathic helix-forming mature peptide cores and adjacent low-complexity proregions.
- Plant LEA/dehydrin/cold-regulated proteins: activation on Gly/Ala/Ser/Thr-rich disordered repeats that stabilize proteins/membranes under stress.
- Fungal GPI-anchored cell-wall adhesins/mannoproteins: activation on Ser/Thr/Ala-rich, O-glycosylated low-complexity regions and signal-like low-complexity stretches.
- Lipid-droplet scaffolds (perilipins/oleosins): activation on amphipathic lipid-binding helices and adjacent GA-rich low-complexity segments.
- Bacterial virulence and secretion proteins (Type III/IV effectors, translocon-associated factors): activation on N-terminal, acid-poor, small-residue–rich export regions and membrane-interacting segments.
- Apicomplexan secretory proteins (rhoptry/dense granule/perforin-like): activation on low-complexity export/membrane-binding regions supporting secretion and membrane disruption.

Summary: Repeated scaffold domains used in trafficking and secretory/extracellular systems, primarily beta-propellers (WD40/Kelch/olfactomedin/Vps10/clathrin/neuraminidase-like) but also solenoidal tether/adaptor repeats (CATCHR/HEAT/armadillo) and select beta-helix–type CAZymes; includes some ER-lumenal beta-rich sensor domains (e.g., IRE1).
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation across repeat units (propeller blades, HEAT/armadillo hairpins, or beta-helix rungs), realized as discontinuous short segments on beta-strands or helical hairpins and adjacent loops; typically absent from coiled-coils, transmembranes, and low-confidence/unstructured regions.
Exemplars:
- Olfactomedin family extracellular proteins: activation within the C-terminal olfactomedin beta-propeller; N-terminal coiled-coils inactive.
- WD-repeat proteins in ciliary/flagellar transport (e.g., IFT WD40): activation spans WD40 blades.
- Kelch-repeat/BTB-Kelch substrate adaptors: activation across the Kelch beta-propeller domain.
- Type I Vps10/sortilin receptors: activation on the luminal N-terminal beta-propeller.
- Clathrin-related machinery and coat/sorting adaptors: activation on terminal beta-propeller domains.
- DDB1-like multipropeller scaffolds: activation across beta-propeller subdomains.
- HOPS/CORVET/CATCHR tethering subunits (e.g., Vps16) and Rho/Rab GEF subunits (e.g., Ric1): activation across solenoidal HEAT/armadillo/CATCHR repeats mediating complex assembly.
- ER stress sensors (IRE1): activation within the lumenal beta-rich sensor domain.
- Secreted bacterial/viral lectins and carbohydrate-active enzymes adopting propeller or beta-helix folds (e.g., neuraminidases; rhamnogalacturonan lyases): activation over their repeated beta-strand units.

Summary: Short, surface-exposed coil-to-β transition loops (“β-edge/capping turns”) enriched in glycine (often di‑glycine) and frequently containing an aromatic residue (especially Trp) together with charged residues; these motifs sit at the edges of β‑sheets/β‑sandwiches and act as flexible interaction patches near active/binding sites, commonly in secreted/periplasmic proteins but also across diverse cytosolic proteins
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks confined to short segments (~6–12 aa) centered on turns/coil immediately preceding or following a β‑strand; multiple discontiguous patches per protein; strongest when Gly (often GG) is present and when the loop mixes charged and aromatic residues (Trp/Tyr/Phe); frequently adjacent to disulfide-stabilized regions in secreted proteins but not restricted to any single domain
Exemplars: Photosystem II PsbP/OEE2 lumenal proteins: activation on acidic surface loops capping β‑strands that mediate PSII lumenal interactions; Outer-membrane lipoprotein BamE: activation on β‑sandwich edge loops that contact BAM components; Lysozyme inhibitor Ivy: activation on the short turn preceding a β‑strand next to the inhibitory His and a disulfide (β‑cap/loop); Secreted cysteine- and metalloproteases: activation on substrate-binding/gating loops that are coil→β transitions bordering the active-site cleft; Rieske oxygenase small subunits: activation on β‑edge loops involved in subunit/interface and channel contacts; NTF2/NXF/Ran transport factors: activation on β‑edge loops lining FG‑repeat/partner-binding surfaces enriched in aromatic/charged residues; Lipid-binding/transfer proteins (START/TULIP/OSBP-like, membrane contact-site proteins): activation on mouth loops that cap β‑strands around hydrophobic pockets; Plant ABA receptors (PYR/PYL/RCAR): activation on “gate”/“latch” loops (coil→β) over the ligand cavity; Archaeal gas vesicle protein O: activation on exposed glycine-rich β‑edge turns; Periplasmic/secreted enzymes such as urocanate reductase and Gram‑negative envelope/stress-response factors: activation on short β‑edge loops near disulfide-stabilized or interface regions

Summary: Generic local-structure boundary detector: the feature highlights isolated residues at secondary-structure junctions and peripheral linkers (turns, helix caps/kinks, strand edges, and short terminal/domain-connecting coils), without preference for residue type or protein class.
Activation pattern: Sparse, low-magnitude, residue-level peaks scattered along sequences; enriches at short coils/turns and at the ends or junctions of helices/strands and domain termini; occasionally appears within stable helices/strands at kink/edge positions; rarely aligns with annotated catalytic or binding sites and does not span whole domains.
Exemplars: - AGC/serine-threonine kinases (e.g., SCH9): strongest signals in the C-terminal AGC regulatory tail and the linker to the kinase core, with additional single residues inside the well-folded kinase domain.
- Spliceosome factor SLU7: peak at a turn connecting two beta-strands, with minor signals within a long alpha-helix and low-confidence coil.
- Anaphase-promoting complex subunit (APC16): localized peaks in a short C-terminal coil marking the transition from a helical region to an unstructured tail.
- DEG/ENaC/ASIC ion channels (e.g., MEC-4): isolated activations across the structured extracellular domain on both beta-strands and helices, with little signal in transmembrane or cytosolic segments.
- Membrane protein insertase YidC: numerous weak, isolated peaks across disparate contexts—beta-strands of the soluble/periplasmic region, transmembrane helices, and short coils—consistent with boundary/edge positions rather than a specific motif.
- Cilia- and flagella-associated protein: very weak, scattered peaks in flexible, low-confidence coil regions near the N-terminus and other short turns.

Summary: Residues that act as N-cap/strand-start positions at coil-to-secondary-structure junctions—most often immediately N-terminal to beta-strands and at the starts of folded domains—preferentially small/polar/acidic (D/E/S/T/G); a broad structural motif rather than function-specific.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks at isolated positions or very short runs directly before annotated helices/strands; repeated at repeat-blade edges and domain starts; little to no signal within secondary-structure cores or long disordered segments; widespread across proteins with variable counts per sequence.
Exemplars: - Kelch-like BTB/POZ proteins (e.g., KLHL family): coil residues just before kelch-blade beta-strands and a strong N-cap immediately preceding the BTB domain start.
- BTB/POZ family more broadly: N-terminal residues (positions ~20–60) that cap the first secondary-structure elements of the BTB fold.
- Secretins (outer-membrane secretion pores): loop residues preceding successive beta-strands of the barrel/periplasmic beta domains.
- Hydrolases (proteases, lipases/esterases, glycosidases, phosphatases): loop-to-beta junctions at the starts of core-sheet strands in alpha/beta folds.
- RhoGAP regulators: helix/beta N-cap positions at loop-to-secondary transitions in the GAP domain core.
- SMAD/TGF-beta pathway components: N-cap residues at coil-to-strand transitions within MH1/MH2 domains and at domain boundaries.
- Nucleic-acid processing complexes (RNA polymerase III subunits, exosome, DNA polymerase subunits): residues immediately preceding beta-strands within the large beta-sheets of the enzyme cores.
- Secreted/extracellular precursors: short acidic/polar clusters marking the first residues of folded domains immediately after signal/propeptide regions.

Summary: Aromatic sugar-binding surface patches on proteins that engage polysaccharides or sugar‑phosphate polymers—the carbohydrate-binding faces of CBMs and lectin‑like loops with neighboring Trp/Tyr (often Trp–Trp) supported by Ser/Thr/Asp/Gly‑rich loops—found in secreted/ER‑lumenal as well as cytosolic/plastidial contexts (e.g., glycogen/starch, cell‑wall polysaccharides, glycosaminoglycans, teichoic acids, inositol phosphates, and occasionally nucleic‑acid sugar‑phosphate backbones).
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short loop/edge β‑strand segments with sharp residue‑level peaks near Trp/Tyr; often multiple discrete segments per large multidomain protein; enriched in coil/β with low‑to‑moderate structural confidence; signal peptides and transmembranes are not activated; occurs in both extracytoplasmic and intracellular glycan/sugar‑phosphate–interacting proteins.
Exemplars:
- Glycogen-targeting PP1 regulatory subunits (CBM21): activation on the CBM carbohydrate‑binding surface
- ER oligosaccharyltransferase complex (RPN2/OST2): activation on luminal loops engaging glycan donor/acceptor
- Proteoglycan xylosyltransferases: activation at C‑terminal lumenal loop contacting substrate glycans
- Archaeal S-layer proteins: multiple aromatic, flexible loops consistent with cell‑wall polysaccharide binding
- Complement/macroglobulin and adhesion modules: extracellular GAG‑binding patches
- Plant starch‑pathway enzymes (chloroplastic and secreted): starch‑binding modules and CBM20/48/53‑like regions
- Bacterial cell‑wall enzymes and biosynthetic factors: accessory CBMs or loops contacting glycan/teichoic‑acid polymers (e.g., cyclomaltodextrinase substrate‑binding loops; Tar polymerases)
Summary: Generic feature, meaning not known

Summary: Ampiphathic alpha-helical segments that act as solvent‑exposed interaction surfaces (protein–protein, protein–RNA, or membrane‑proximal), typically well ordered and enriched in alternating hydrophobic (Leu/Ile/Val) and charged (Lys/Arg/Glu/Asp) residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous 10–30 aa stretches that coincide with alpha‑helices; strongest in the helix core and tapering into adjacent coil/turn (occasionally including a preceding short beta‑strand). Multiple long segments can activate within large proteins, with a mild bias toward central/C‑terminal helices in eukaryotic proteins.
Exemplars: - Signal recognition particle protein SRP19: activation on a defined C‑terminal alpha‑helix with spillover into adjacent coil/disordered tail.
- Bacterial secretion system–associated SPI‑2 protein C: strong activation on a long C‑terminal alpha‑helix.
- SH2‑domain adaptor proteins (e.g., STAP1): activation on the canonical C‑terminal alpha‑helix within the SH2 fold, with the adjoining short beta‑strand/turn also included.

Summary: Extended terminal (often C-terminal) membrane-interacting/assembly regions that mediate bilayer binding, insertion or translocation—spanning β-barrel/pore-forming segments, amphipathic/disordered tails, and terminal lipid-anchoring sites—common in large secreted, outer-membrane, and lipid-handling proteins (including lipid-binding/transfer families).
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation forming long, dense blocks, most frequently near protein C-termini; occurs in both structured β-rich domains and low-complexity/disordered tails. Secondary, lower-level patches can appear elsewhere in long proteins. Occasional sharp residue-level peaks at terminal anchor/modification sites (e.g., prenylation) or glycosylation.
Exemplars: - BPI/PLUNC lipid-binding proteins: strong activation across the C-terminal structured region (mixed helix/β) that contributes to the lipid-binding surface; includes peaks near an N-linked glycosylation site.
- Autophagy-related protein 2 (Atg2): intense activation on a large C-terminal membrane-binding segment and an extended disordered/low-complexity region implicated in membrane tethering and lipid transfer.
- Gram-negative autotransporters: activation centered on the C-terminal β-barrel translocator domain and adjacent C-terminal segments that mediate outer-membrane insertion/assembly.
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factor 19 (PEX19): activation on the N-terminal disordered docking region that binds PEX3/peroxisomal membrane, and a sharp peak at the extreme C-terminus at the farnesylation (CAAX) site for membrane anchoring.
- Flotillin-like inner-membrane scaffolds: activation confined to the disordered C-terminal cytoplasmic tail involved in oligomerization and association with membrane microdomains.

Summary: Hydrophobic lipid-interacting interfaces of membrane-associated proteins—especially outer/organellar-membrane beta-barrels and long bridge-like lipid-transfer/carrier proteins—highlighting beta-strands and connecting loops that contact bilayers or line lipid-transfer grooves/tunnels
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation across long proteins with many residue-level peaks; strongest on hydrophobic residues within beta-strands and the inter-strand loops/turns that face membranes or form the walls of lipid-binding grooves; in beta-barrels, peaks occur both on strands and external loops
Exemplars: - AsmA/TamB/ATG2 bridge-like lipid transfer proteins: activation tracks the extended hydrophobic groove/tunnel used to shuttle lipids between membranes.
- Gram-negative outer-membrane assembly/transport beta-barrels (e.g., BamA/Omp85, LptD): lipid-exposed beta-strands and extracellular/periplasmic loops contacting the bilayer or LPS.
- Mitochondrial outer-membrane porins (VDAC) and beta-barrel import/assembly factors (SAM/Tom components): residues within barrel strands and connecting loops at the membrane interface.
- BPI/PLUNC/CETP/PLTP lipid-binding proteins (TULIP-fold carriers): hydrophobic tunnel/cavity surfaces that bind/transport lipids.
- C2-domain membrane-trafficking proteins: Ca2+-dependent membrane-inserting loops and adjacent hydrophobic patches mediating phospholipid binding.
- Autotransporter adhesins (Neisseria and other Gram-negatives): C-terminal beta-barrel and nearby beta-solenoid segments that interface with the outer membrane.
- Vitellogenins and other large serum lipoproteins: extensive amphipathic/hydrophobic surfaces forming lipid-binding channels.
- Plant chloroplast outer-envelope beta-barrels (e.g., Toc/OEP proteins) and lipid-related envelope proteins: beta-strands and loops lining the lipid-exposed barrel surface.
- Lower-scoring phage tail/spike and Type VI secretion structural proteins: beta-rich solenoids with hydrophobic stripes mimicking lipid-interacting surfaces.

Summary: Extreme C‑terminal disordered tails of eukaryotic proteins encode short linear targeting/docking signals used for scaffold recruitment, membrane anchoring, cargo adaptor binding, or nuclear targeting. These commonly include PDZ‑binding motifs at the very end and prenylation CAAX boxes flanked by polybasic/palmitoylation clusters, but also PDZ‑independent C‑terminal SLiMs such as basic or acidic/proline‑/glutamine‑rich tracts. The feature ignores structured catalytic domains and turns on in low‑complexity, often isoform‑variable terminal segments.
Activation pattern: Regional activation concentrated in the final ~20–40 residues of long proteins; silent across internal structured domains. Peaks align with key residues of C‑terminal SLiMs (e.g., terminal hydrophobes of PDZ motifs; CAAX cysteine with nearby Lys/Arg/palmitoylation sites; basic NLS‑like patches; acidic/proline‑/Q‑rich tracts). Frequently isoform‑specific tails; occasional minor N‑terminal blips.
Exemplars:
- Phosphoinositide phosphatase SAC2/INPP5F: activation only in the extreme tail harboring a PDZ‑binding motif, not over the SAC catalytic domain.
- Paralemmin family (peripheral membrane adaptors): strong activation on the C‑terminal membrane‑anchoring cassette—polybasic patch, dual palmitoylation sites, and farnesylated CAAX box—with decay over the cleaved AAX.
- RGS12 (regulator of G‑protein signaling): activation restricted to the last disordered residues containing a class I PDZ‑binding motif; no activation on internal PDZ/RGS/RBD/GoLoco domains.
- PHLPP phosphatases (Akt/PKC regulators): activation on their C‑terminal PDZ‑binding motifs that mediate docking to PDZ scaffolds at membranes.
- Ciliary GTPase regulators (e.g., RPGR): activation on C‑terminal CAAX prenylation motifs for ciliary/membrane targeting.
- Yeast vacuolar transport/cargo adaptors (e.g., Vac17): activation on PDZ‑independent acidic/proline‑rich C‑terminal docking segments for motor/adaptor binding.
- Nuclear regulators (e.g., HAM‑1/SHOX‑like): activation on terminal basic clusters/NLS‑like or Q/acidic tracts in disordered tails.

Summary: Generic structural signal for well-ordered beta-strand positions (DSSP class E), with a bias toward aliphatic (Val/Leu/Ile) and occasional basic (Arg/Lys) residues; highlights non-catalytic strand residues across diverse enzymatic domains rather than specific active-site motifs
