Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks (typically 1–4 contiguous residues) confined to beta-strands with high structural confidence; rarely overlaps annotated catalytic residues or signature motifs; occurs across soluble, periplasmic/secreted, membrane-associated, and organellar proteins
Exemplars: - Thioredoxin-like oxidoreductases (AhpE, DsbE/CcmG): peaks on strand residues within the TRX fold, away from the Cys-based redox motif
- Glutathione peroxidases: isolated peaks on beta-strand Arg/Lys in the peroxidase domain
- SCO copper chaperones: strand-localized aliphatic residues in the thioredoxin-like domain, not metal-binding sites
- Radical SAM maturation enzymes (AlbA): single beta-strand Arg peak in a C-terminal structured segment outside the core Radical SAM region
- Apolipoprotein N-acyltransferase (Lnt; CN hydrolase domain): beta-strand Leu/Thr in the catalytic domain but not at the catalytic triad
- DNA primase (DnaG): single Val in a beta-strand outside the Zn-finger and TOPRIM motifs
- Penicillin-binding D,D-transpeptidases (PBPs): multiple aliphatic strand residues within the periplasmic transpeptidase domain, distinct from the catalytic Ser
- HtrA/Deg serine proteases: Ile/Val on beta-strands within the protease domain, not at the catalytic triad

Summary: Short, ordered coil/turn segments that flank β‑strands lining enzyme active or ligand‑binding pockets (“β‑strand‑adjacent gatekeeper loops”), typically enriched in charged/polar residues and shaping/coordinating access to cofactors or substrates rather than marking the catalytic residue itself.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue‑level peaks (often 1–5 per protein; occasional short 2–4‑residue runs) localized to well‑modeled coil/turns immediately N‑ or C‑terminal to ligand‑binding β‑strands and inter‑strand loops near pockets; avoids core helices/β‑strands and usually spares the nucleophilic/catalytic Cys/His/Sec themselves.
Exemplars: - FGGY family sugar/glycerol kinases: highlights turns directly adjacent to ATP/ADP‑ and substrate‑binding β‑strands (e.g., inter‑strand loops flanking β1 and β‑strands contacting the sugar), not the conserved binding residues themselves.
- c‑di‑GMP enzymes (GGDEF cyclases/EAL phosphodiesterases): activates on charged turns bordering the β‑strand‑embedded GGDEF/EAL and RxxD I‑site regions that shape the nucleotide pocket.
- Two‑component histidine kinases (HATPase_c/CA domain): marks β‑strand‑flanking loops around the ATP‑binding site rather than the phosphoacceptor His in the DHp domain.
- Radical SAM/RiPP‑maturation enzymes: picks loops capping β‑strands around the SAM/Fe–S pocket, adjacent to but not on the CxxxCxxC motif.
- Peroxiredoxins and glutathione peroxidases (including selenoproteins): emphasizes pocket‑lining β‑adjacent turns near the peroxidatic site, typically not on the catalytic Cys/Sec.
- Thiol–disulfide oxidoreductases (e.g., DsbA) and SCO copper chaperones: activates on β‑edge loops neighboring metal/thiol coordination sites rather than on the coordinating cysteines/histidines.
- Glutathione hydrolases/γ‑glutamyltransferases: highlights short turns at β‑strand boundaries that gate the nucleophile pocket.
- Diverse proteases: marks substrate‑cleft‑lining turns at the edges of β‑sheets in the catalytic domain.

Summary: Recognition of conserved anchor residues at repeat-unit boundaries in beta-strand–based tandem repeats, strongest for the MORN repeat consensus (Y–x–G–x–W / Y–E–G–[D/E]–W), but generalizing to analogous positions in other short beta-rich repeat domains (e.g., the C-terminal Cys4 strand of CCP/Sushi modules and hydrophobic “rungs” of beta-helices)
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks that recur periodically across arrays of repeats, mapping to a short beta-strand (often the N- or C-terminal strand of each repeat) and its adjacent loop; peaks center on an aromatic/hydrophobic residue or a disulfide-forming cysteine. Outside of repeat architectures, activation is sparse, appearing as isolated peaks.
Exemplars: - MORN-repeat proteins (MORN repeat proteins; ALS2/Alsin; radial-spoke–associated): periodic peaks at the N-terminal subsegment of each MORN repeat, centered on W/F/Y preceded by Gly (e.g., G–x–[Y/F/W], Y–E–G–[D/E]–W).
- Complement control proteins with CCP/Sushi domains (e.g., Factor H and homologs): one peak per domain at the C-terminal beta-strand/loop centered on the fourth conserved cysteine (disulfide-bonded).
- Autotransporter adhesins with beta-helix passenger domains: regularly spaced peaks on hydrophobic Val/Ile within each beta-strand rung (~18–19 residue spacing).
- Adhesion GPCR extracellular regions and other cysteine-rich repeats: localized peak on a disulfide-forming cysteine within a short beta segment.
- Cytosolic adapter/kinase-like proteins (e.g., SH3-containing): occasional isolated peak on a beta-strand hydrophobe; rare off-target single residues in other structured elements (e.g., a glycine in MutS).

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regions enriched in serine, threonine, proline and polar/charged residues—flexible regulatory linkers/tails and propeptide segments that often host short linear motifs (e.g., phosphorylation- and proline‑rich motifs) and proteolytic processing sites; signal is absent from well‑folded catalytic domains and is common across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered stretches with many sparse residue‑level peaks; avoids structured domains; peaks biased toward S/T/P, glycine, and charged/polar residues; frequently concentrated in N‑ or C‑terminal IDRs and around cleavage/processing sites; can span hundreds of residues in large eukaryotic proteins
Exemplars: - PAK family serine/threonine kinases: activation on the N‑terminal regulatory IDR preceding the kinase domain (including low‑confidence helical propensities), not in the folded kinase domain.
- Rap/Ras GTPase‑activating proteins: activation on disordered, low‑complexity linkers; absent from the structured GAP domain.
- CARMIL (actin/capping protein regulators): activation on a C‑terminal proline/basic‑rich disordered tail.
- Centrosomal/kinetochore and chromosomal scaffold proteins: multiple low‑complexity, disordered tracts with scattered peaks.
- Transcriptional/chromatin regulators: activation on N‑terminal low‑complexity/activation domains and compositionally biased regions.
- Ribonucleotide reductase large subunit‑like proteins: activation on N‑terminal disordered tails, including proline‑rich segments.
- Neuropeptide/prohormone precursors: activation in disordered propeptides and at termini of amidated peptides, often adjacent to cleavage sites.

Summary: Coil-to-β-strand transition motifs (β-strand starts/edges) and the short preceding loops that frame solvent‑exposed sheet edges and pocket rims, often adjacent to substrate/ligand-binding sites across diverse proteins
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated at the first residues of β-strands and in the immediately preceding loop (coil→β transitions); short regional clusters spanning a loop plus flanking β-strands that outline binding-pocket edges; multiple dispersed peaks across large, multidomain proteins; enrichment for polar/charged/Gly residues (D/E/K/R/S/T/G); may border but not necessarily hit catalytic residues
Exemplars: - Membrane protein insertase YidC: strongest peaks at loop-to-β transitions within the YidC core (e.g., around S326) and minor peaks in PDZ-domain loops.
- Cellobionic acid phosphorylase (carbohydrate phosphorylase): activation on the loop connecting two β-strands and on the adjacent strand residues within the α/β core.
- Tubulin polyglutamylase (TTLL/TTL domain ligase): peaks within the TTL domain at a β-strand start (P433) and a mixed β/loop region that includes an ATP-binding Lys.
- Secreted nuclease (DNase/RNase family): strong activation at two coil→β transitions (e.g., near V35 and Y188), not on the catalytic His or metal-binding residue.
- Copper/topaquinone-dependent primary amine oxidase: extended activation across β-strands and connecting loops that form the substrate-binding pocket, encompassing the topaquinone Tyr and substrate-binding residues, with a minor peak near a strand between copper-binding histidines.

Summary: Short, flexible helical or helix–coil boundary motifs (MoRF/SLiM-like) used for partner, nucleic‑acid, and targeting interactions; compositionally biased toward small hydrophobic/flexible residues (G, A, L, V, S, T, P), common in viral proteins, secretion effectors, and trafficking/assembly factors, and typically adjacent to but not coincident with catalytic residues.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered across long proteins, enriched in low‑to‑moderate confidence regions (low pLDDT) and at secondary-structure boundaries in helices and coils; broad domain coverage with punctate hotspots, often near binding/targeting sites rather than on core catalytic residues; coverage varies widely between proteins.
Exemplars: - CRISPR-associated RNases (Cas13a): peaks in the Helical-1 domain around the pre-crRNA processing site (e.g., near R438/K441/I442) and at boundaries across helical/HEPN regions, but not on the HEPN catalytic tetrads.
- Type III secretion effectors (e.g., Shigella IpaA): sparse peaks in low-confidence α-helical segments within disordered regions typical of host-interaction SLiMs.
- Paramyxovirus nucleoproteins (e.g., Nipah N): disordered helices and helix–coil transitions near RNA-binding surfaces.
- Pneumovirus phosphoproteins (RSV P): MoRF-like boundary segments in an overall disordered protein, including the onset of an NLS and flexible turns.
- Apicomplexan ookinete/surface proteins (e.g., PIMMS43): low/moderate-pLDDT ectodomain helices/coils away from signal peptide and transmembrane segments, consistent with linear epitope/interaction motifs.
- Herpesviridae tegument and DNA-packaging/capsid accessory proteins; Adenoviridae structural/replication proteins; Poxvirus proteins: many short peaks across low-complexity regions used for assembly and host interactions.
- Peroxisome biogenesis/targeting proteins: flexible tail/IDR motifs (e.g., NLS/PTS-like targeting signals) in otherwise variable contexts.
- Secreted peptide hormone/neuropeptide precursors: disordered propeptide segments carrying short processing/interaction motifs (excluding signal peptides).
- Bacterial type III/IV secretion effectors and host-manipulating enzymes (ubiquitin/ADP-ribosylation-related): SLiM-bearing disordered helices used for host targeting and binding.

Summary: Short acidic, gly/pro-rich β-turn/loop elements at β-sheet edges and active-site/ligand-binding grooves, most prominently in β-sandwich/jelly-roll and related β-strand–rich folds; the feature highlights conserved turns and carboxylate-containing motifs (often with E/D, G/S/A, P and nearby hydrophobics) that mediate peptide, cofactor, or macromolecule binding across diverse families
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks concentrated in 3–6-residue loops/turns (enriched for E/D, G/S/A, P with adjacent L/I/V); multiple peaks per domain and sometimes clustering to give regional activation across β-sandwich/jelly-roll domains; observed broadly across taxa and subcellular localizations
Exemplars: - PDZ-domain scaffolds: activation on the GLGF carboxylate-binding loop that forms the peptide C-terminus–recognition groove
- Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate (AlkB/2OG) dioxygenases: activation on the HxD…H metal/2OG-binding motif and neighboring β-turns of the jelly-roll fold
- ADP-ribosyltransferases (PARP/ARTD): activation around the HYE catalytic region and adjacent gly/acidic loops shaping the NAD+/ADPR pocket
- Bacterial MotB and other OmpA-like periplasmic domains: activation on the conserved acidic, gly/pro-containing peptidoglycan-binding loop of the β-sandwich
- Large ribosomal subunit proteins L22/L23 (bacteria/archaea/organelles): activation on exposed turn/loop segments that project into the exit tunnel and contact rRNA
- Immune/secreted Ig-like proteins (e.g., beta-2 microglobulin): activation on strand-edge β-turns within the Ig β-sandwich
- Cytochrome P450s and other oxidation enzymes: activation on the heme-binding loop (FxxGxxxCxG) and nearby ExxR/acidic turn elements forming the active-site wall
- Bacterial transport/periplasmic and outer-membrane proteins: activation on surface β-hairpins/acidic loops that mediate ligand or cell-wall interactions
- Plant oxidoreductases and scaffolds: the same conserved β-turn/acidic loop elements within β-rich domains recurring across plant proteins

Summary: Ser/Thr- and Asn-enriched, surface-exposed coil loops between beta-strands—most prominently within beta-sandwich modules such as Fibronectin type III and Ig-like/CCP domains—often coinciding with N‑X‑S/T sequons and other glycosylation-prone motifs in modular extracellular/secreted proteins (and analogous loops in related beta-rich proteins)
Activation pattern: Multiple short regional activations per sequence with sharp residue-level peaks on Ser/Thr (and neighboring Asn), concentrated in coil loops between beta-strands; repeated across successive extracellular/repeat domains; weak in structured strand/helix cores and transmembrane segments
Exemplars: - Fibronectin type III modules (e.g., in myosin-binding protein C): strong peaks on loop Ser/Thr across multiple Fn3 domains.
- Fn3-containing synaptic/scaffolding proteins (RIM-binding protein family): narrow Thr-centered peaks and broader loop-region activation within Fn3 repeats; minimal signal in SH3 cores.
- Bacteriophage baseplate/tail proteins: sparse activation in flexible N-terminal loops between beta-strands with low structural confidence.
- Cell-surface receptor ectodomains (receptor tyrosine kinases, receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatases, class I cytokine receptors): activation on Ig-like/CCP/Fn3 loop segments enriched for Ser/Thr and N‑X‑S/T motifs.
- Extracellular matrix and adhesion proteins (IgSF CAMs, fibronectin-type III repeat proteins): activation on exposed, flexible loops within modular ectodomains.
- Secreted bacterial hydrolases/proteases: activation on surface-accessible loop/linker regions enriched in Ser/Thr ± Asn.

Summary: Beta-turn initiation residues at beta-strand→coil junctions (short loops linking adjacent beta-strands), especially Asx/ST/Gly-Gly-type turns in beta-rich, repeat/barrel architectures common in secreted and surface-exposed proteins; captures the first residue of the turn where glycine and acidic/hydroxyl side chains are enriched
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks that recur periodically along beta-rich domains; sharp 3–5 residue windows with the highest signal at the first coil residue immediately following a beta-strand; the number of peaks scales with the number of strand–turn repeats
Exemplars: - Type VI secretion system toxins/effectors (e.g., Tse family): repeated peaks at each beta-strand→loop transition across the repetitive fold
- Mitochondrial outer membrane porins (VDAC/TOM40): turns connecting barrel strands on periplasmic/cytosolic loops
- Bacterial outer-membrane beta-barrel/surface proteins (porins, autotransporters, adhesins): tight hairpin turns between adjacent strands of the barrel
- Fatty acid-binding proteins (FABPs): beta-barrel strand-connecting turns throughout the 10-stranded barrel
- Lectins and lectin-like domains (beta-sandwich/propeller): short loops linking strands/blades, enriched in Gly and Asp/Ser/Thr
- Extracellular serine proteases (trypsin-like fold): beta-sheet turns in the double beta-barrel protease domain
- MORN repeat–containing proteins: recurrent tight turns that delimit repeat units
- Radial spoke head/flagellar beta-rich proteins: strand-connecting loops within beta-sandwich elements
- Nonribosomal peptide synthetase modules: glycine/Ser/Thr-rich turns at strand–loop boundaries within beta elements of Rossmann-like subdomains

Summary: Long, low-complexity intrinsically disordered regions of secretory-pathway proteins—especially extracellular/luminal tracts enriched in acidic and Ser/Thr/Pro residues that are heavily post-translationally modified (phosphorylation, glycosylation, sulfation) and often proteolytically processed; the feature also extends to expansive disordered tails outside transmembrane cores of membrane proteins.
Activation pattern: Domain-/regional-level activation across extended IDRs with low pLDDT; absent in signal peptides and transmembrane helices and largely depleted in folded domains (e.g., FN3, EGF, DSCP-N). Peaks follow compositional-bias segments (acidic clusters, polar S/T-rich, low complexity) and PTM-dense zones; not tied to a specific secondary structure and strongest in coils.
Exemplars: - Extracellular matrix acidic phosphoproteins (e.g., osteopontin/secreted phosphoprotein 1): activation spans the entire disordered, acidic mature region (including RGD), off in the signal peptide.
- Secretory granule/neuropeptide precursors (chromogranin/secretogranin family): continuous activation over long disordered proproteins rich in phosphorylation, sulfation, glycosylation sites and proteolytic peptide regions.
- Gamete adhesion/egg coat–associated glycoproteins (e.g., sperm equatorial segment protein): high activation across the disordered, glycosylated ectodomain; absent in the signal sequence.
- Fibronectin type III–containing adhesion proteins: strong activation on long C‑terminal low‑complexity disordered tails and linkers; weak/none in FN3 domains.
- Spore coat extracellular structural proteins: activation on disordered linkers and C‑terminal tails; none in structured DSCP‑N or Follistatin‑like domains.
- Single‑pass adhesion/ECM receptors with NIDO/EGF modules: activation on extended disordered segments of the ectodomain; not in the structured repeats, TM helix, or cytosolic tail.
- Secreted GPCR ligands (e.g., folded gastrulation): activation across low‑complexity, glycosylated mature regions, strongest in annotated disordered/acidic tracts.
- Multi‑pass solute carriers with very long termini (e.g., SLC38 family): activation confined to expansive disordered, PTM‑rich tails outside the transmembrane core; none within TM helices.

Summary: Glycine-centered flexibility motif: the feature recognizes glycine residues in coils/turns, linkers, and glycine-rich low‑complexity segments (e.g., G‑patch–like tracts), often marking secondary-structure boundaries (especially helix/coiled‑coil starts) or short glycine-rich loops adjacent to functional sites; it appears across both disordered regions and well-ordered hinge loops and can weakly include small/flexible neighbors such as serine or proline.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks on Gly that often cluster within G-rich stretches; enriched in intrinsically disordered, low-pLDDT segments and in short coil/turn linkers within structured domains; frequent at helix/coiled-coil N-termini and domain interfaces; occasional weaker signals on Ser/Pro in similar contexts.
Exemplars: - Cyclophilin-type peptidyl-prolyl isomerase: peaks on glycine in a disordered C-terminal tail and on glycine in loop/turn connectors within the PPIase domain.
- Calpain protease family: sharp activation on a short GGC motif in Domain III and additional glycines in coils.
- SWR1/SRCAP complex subunit VPS72 (histone chaperone): a single boundary glycine at the start of a long coiled-coil.
- Exon junction complex protein Y14: glycines in a glycine-rich disordered N-terminus and at a linker glycine immediately before the RRM domain.
- Cilia/flagella-associated protein: very weak signals limited to glycine/serine in low-confidence coils.
- Plant pentatricopeptide repeat proteins: glycine within a disordered C-terminal Type E motif and sparse sites within helical repeats.
- BAHD acyltransferase family enzyme: glycine residues in high-confidence loops connecting secondary elements, including a glycine-rich loop adjacent to the catalytic Asp.

Summary: Polybasic, lysine/arginine‑rich low‑complexity segments (polybasic patches and Lys‑containing repeats), typically intrinsically disordered and often located near protein termini; these regions commonly serve as nucleic‑acid/chromatin‑interacting or other acidic‑surface–binding tails, and the feature keys on the basic residues within them across diverse proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on Lys (and Arg) within long low‑complexity/disordered stretches; regional activation increases in dense Lys clusters or repetitive K‑containing motifs; minimal/absent in well‑folded domains and signal peptides; can still activate over locally helical segments if they are compositionally Lys‑rich.
Exemplars: Chromatin-associated nucleosome-binding protein (Dsup/HMGN-like): peaks on Lys in the disordered C‑terminal nucleosome‑binding tail; Serine/arginine‑rich splicing factor (SRRM1): sparse peaks on K/R across a disordered, basic, low‑complexity C‑terminal region with a Lys‑rich segment near the end; Nucleolar snoRNP factor (Nop56 family): selective activation on Lys in a C‑terminal basic tail annotated disordered/compositionally biased; Multidomain proteins with large IDRs: sharp K/R peaks confined to N‑terminal and C‑terminal disordered regions, absent in the structured catalytic/binding domain; Secreted salivary low‑complexity repeat proteins: strong activation on Lys within KP/KxxK and related K‑containing repeats in the mature disordered region, not in the signal peptide.

Summary: Extracellular/mature segments of secreted proteins — the bioactive peptide or ectodomain of secreted precursors — including toxins, chemokines/peptide hormones/neuropeptides, antimicrobial peptides, protease inhibitors, extracellular matrix modules, viral envelope ectodomains, bacterial toxins/lipoproteins, fungal/oomycete effectors, and secretory granule proteins. These segments are typically cationic and often cysteine‑rich/disulfide‑stabilized, but can also be disulfide‑poor (e.g., certain neuropeptides); the feature tracks mature peptides/ectodomains rather than signal peptides or cytosolic tails.

Activation pattern: Regional activation within extracellular/mature segments with residue‑level peaks, especially at basic residues (Lys/Arg; including prohormone convertase sites) and, when present, cysteines; strongest over well‑structured extracellular cores or compact mature peptides; minimal to absent in signal peptides and often lower in low‑complexity pro‑segments.

Exemplars: - Disulfide‑rich venom peptides (e.g., kappa‑/scorpion/centipede toxins, conotoxins): activation on the mature toxin’s folded core; in kappa‑scoloptoxin, strongest on the C‑terminal helical/disulfide region.
- Chemokines and peptide hormones/neuropeptides (e.g., CXCLs; natriuretic peptides, oxytocin/vasopressin‑like, insulin‑like; and disulfide‑poor peptides such as SIFamide): activation on the mature peptide/core, not on the signal/propeptide.
- Antimicrobial peptides (defensins and other cationic AMPs): activation across the extracellular peptide core.
- Protease inhibitors (Kunitz, Kazal, plant cystine‑knot/knottins): activation on the inhibitory domain.
- Extracellular matrix/serum glycoproteins with cysteine‑patterned modules (EGF/TSR/Ig‑like, albumin family): activation on extracellular repeats/domains.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: activation on luminal ectodomain loops.
- Bacterial secreted toxins and lipoproteins: activation on secreted extracellular segments (including lipobox‑proximal Cys and mature toxin domains).
- Fungal/oomycete small secreted effectors: activation on compact extracellular cores.
- Secretory pathway enzymes/chaperones (PDI/Ero1/QSOX) and granule proteins (e.g., 7B2): activation on luminal Cys motifs or basic, structured regions within the secretory lumen.

Summary: Predominantly extracellular/luminal cell-surface or secreted proteins, with preference for beta‑strand–based domains and disulfide‑stabilized motifs (e.g., Ig-like and fibronectin type III modules, Ly6/uPAR three‑finger folds, S‑layer repeats, and secreted enzymes such as purple acid phosphatases); a general marker of secreted‑like beta‑strand surface architecture, mostly extracellular but occasionally present in intracellular enzymes with similar folds (e.g., inositol phosphate 5‑phosphatases)
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks distributed across multiple segments of the extracellular region, enriched on beta-strands and strand–coil boundaries; frequent hits on aromatic and polar/charged residues and on select disulfide-bonded cysteines; occasionally extends into Ser/Thr-rich glycosylated/low-complexity stretches; multiple peaks per protein rather than a single motif
Exemplars:
- Ly6/uPAR three-finger proteins (e.g., PSCA): strong peaks on specific disulfide-bonded cysteines within beta-strands of the cystine-rich fold
- Receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatases: peaks on beta-strands within extracellular Ig-like and fibronectin type III domains
- Plant purple acid phosphatases (secreted/apoplastic): peaks on well-structured beta-strands in the catalytic domain
- Bacterial S-layer/hexagonally packed surface-layer proteins: peaks on beta-strands and at strand–coil boundaries, sometimes adjacent to disulfide bonds
- Broadly recurring extracellular enzymes and modules noted among activators (e.g., LPMOs, glycosidases, sulfatases, CUB/Sushi/LDLa, fasciclin): activation on exposed beta-sheet surfaces and Ser/Thr-rich extracellular segments
- Intracellular inositol phosphate 5-phosphatases (e.g., INPP5K): peaks on beta-strands within the catalytic domain

Summary: Residue-level detector of β-strand face positions—typically a same-face i and i+2 pair—within well-ordered β-strand segments across diverse folds (structural, not function-specific), sometimes at the start of a strand and often conserved across orthologs
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks; usually 1–3 residues per protein; frequently two residues separated by two positions (i and i+2) within a single β strand; occasional single peak at the first residue of a strand; little/no signal in helices, loops, or disordered regions; can appear near N-termini when a β strand begins there
Exemplars: - Cyclophilin-type PPIase domain: a same-strand i/i+2 pair within a β strand plus an additional single β-strand residue in another strand
- UBX domain (p97 cofactor family): a localized i/i+2 pair within a UBX β strand
- Thioredoxin-fold protein (SCO1 family): a peak at the first residue of a β strand and another peak within a separate β strand
- Across other recurring families in the set (acyl/acetyltransferases, two-component histidine kinases, BTB/POZ-Kelch/ZBTB regulators, small GTPases, ribosomal L31/mL55, plant SAUR/TIFY/HMG-box), the feature similarly highlights short i/i+2 pairs or single residues embedded in β strands of their respective domains

Summary: Residues in flexible loops and secondary-structure boundaries (coil/turn and helix/strand junctions), enriched in small/charged/proline amino acids, that frequently flank catalytic or metal/prosthetic‑group binding motifs within diverse domains but can also occur in disordered termini; a general “active‑site/ligand‑environment and boundary-loop” signal rather than the catalytic residue itself.
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks dispersed across sequences; bias toward coils and structural boundaries, with occasional peaks inside helices adjacent to functional motifs; often near N‑terminal segments but not confined to any subcellular location or fold; does not form contiguous domain-wide activation.
Exemplars: - Membrane protein insertase (YidC): isolated residues across soluble and transmembrane regions, strongest near a β segment adjacent to the C‑terminal TM helix (structure boundary).
- Sortase A transpeptidase: coil residues adjacent to the catalytic His, near the catalytic Cys and the Ca2+-binding loop.
- Peptide deformylase: loop between β‑strands and a helix containing the catalytic Glu and Fe‑binding His residues; additional peaks on C‑terminal helices.
- Copper chaperone for SOD1 (CCS): disordered C‑terminal tail and scattered positions elsewhere, not focused on the copper‑binding Cys.
- bHLH transcription factor: flexible residues at the start of the bHLH domain and in adjacent linker regions.
- High‑molecular‑weight cytochrome c: helices housing axial heme‑ligating histidines and nearby coil/transition regions around heme‑binding motifs.
- PP2C/PPM phosphatase: residues within the catalytic domain at coil regions between helix and β‑strand; excludes the Mn2+ ligands themselves.
- Archaemetzincin metalloprotease: coil preceding the active‑site helix and residues within nearby helices; minor activation on a Zn‑binding cysteine.

Summary: Short, tandemly repeated low-complexity microdomains enriched for cysteine and small residues (C/G/P/S/T)—especially Cys‑Xn‑Cys and CP/PC motifs—characteristic of secreted, disulfide‑bonded extracellular modules (EGF, CCP/Sushi, VWC/chordin, TSP1, disintegrin‑like), plus analogous repeat-rich tracts in structural/cytoskeletal scaffolds, including P/S/T/G/A‑rich, acidic SD/E‑rich, and centrin‑binding/coiled‑coil repeats.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks concentrated on cysteines and immediately flanking small residues, appearing in many short windows distributed across arrays of repeats rather than a single long region; strong in secreted precursors with multiple cysteine‑rich modules, with secondary activation on repetitive low‑complexity motifs even without cysteines (Pro/Ser/Thr/Gly/Ala‑ or Asp/Glu‑rich tracts, or conserved aromatic consensus elements in coiled‑coil/centrin‑binding repeats).
Exemplars:
- EGF‑like repeats in extracellular receptors/adhesion proteins: peaks on the conserved Cys pairs and nearby Gly/Pro within each repeat.
- CCP/Sushi (complement control) repeats: activation on the Cys‑Xn‑Cys core and CP/PC motifs in each Sushi domain across complement regulators.
- von Willebrand factor type C (VWC)/chordin‑like BMP‑binding cysteine‑rich modules (chordin/CRIM/KCP, crossveinless‑2, brorin/VWC2): peaks across the dense cystine motifs of each module.
- Thrombospondin type‑1 repeats (TSP1): activation on cysteine‑centered motifs (e.g., C…C, CSVTCG) and adjacent small residues.
- Disintegrin‑like and cysteine‑rich domains of ADAM/ADAMTS and snake‑venom metalloproteinases: peaks across disulfide‑bonded loops and CP/PC motifs.
- Insect peritrophins and peritrophic matrix proteins (peritrophin‑A/chitin‑binding repeats) and mucins: activation on cysteine arrays within chitin‑binding repeats and on P/S/T/Pro‑rich low‑complexity segments.
- Pacifastin‑like small disulfide‑rich protease inhibitors: peaks on the disulfide‑stabilized loops of inhibitory modules.
- Secreted lectins (e.g., C‑type lectin‑like domains) and serum albumin/afamin: activation on clustered disulfide motifs spread across domains.
- Ciliary/axonemal and cytoskeletal anchoring proteins: activation on proline/serine/threonine‑rich low‑complexity tracts.
- Some bacterial/mycobacterial low‑complexity proteins: activation on glycine/alanine‑rich repeat segments even with fewer cysteines.
- Nebulin/nebulette Z‑disk scaffolds: activation on SD/E‑rich nebulin repeats and adjacent low‑complexity tracts.
- Sfi1/centrin‑binding repeat scaffolds: activation on conserved repeat consensus within coiled‑coil arrays.
- GPSM/GoLoco‑motif proteins: activation on proline‑rich/disordered segments adjacent to helical repeat elements.

Summary: Acidic Ser/Thr/Pro-rich low-complexity disordered segments that often serve as glycosylated linkers/stalks around adhesion/ectodomain modules (Ig, FNIII, CCP/Sushi, TSR) in secreted and cell-surface proteins; the same composition-based signal also occurs in intracellular proteins where it forms flexible acidic tails/linkers for protein–protein interactions across taxa.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long, low-complexity stretches with multiple patches per protein; strongest over S/T- and Pro-rich, acidic segments (often with Thr–Pro runs and near NXS/T sequons), and weak/absent in the folded cores of globular domains.
Exemplars: - Receptor tyrosine kinases and receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatases: activation on extracellular glycosylated stalks and linkers between Ig/FNIII modules and the transmembrane region.
- Class I/II cytokine receptors: activation on S/T-rich, glycosylated ectodomain segments flanking the cytokine receptor homology domain.
- Ig-superfamily and FNIII-containing cell-adhesion molecules: activation on interdomain linkers and mucin-like inserts between Ig/FNIII repeats.
- Complement regulators and alpha-2-macroglobulin family: activation on CCP (Sushi) domain linkers and other flexible, acidic, glycosylated regions (including bait-region–adjacent segments).
- ECM proteins with thrombospondin type-1 repeats or CCP/Sushi modules: activation on glycosylated spacers and low-complexity stalks.
- Viral envelope and capsid proteins: activation on mucin-like ectodomains or acidic S/T/P-rich loops bearing dense glycosylation.
- Prokaryotic/archaeal surface adhesins and S-layer glycoproteins: activation on repetitive S/T/P- or Asp/Glu-rich extracellular stalks and low-complexity regions.
- Intracellular factors with acidic S/T-rich low-complexity tails/linkers (e.g., telomere-binding proteins, ciliary IFT scaffolds like WD-repeat proteins, and some E3 ubiquitin ligases): activation on disordered acidic segments outside structured domains.

Summary: Alpha-helical segments embedded in low-complexity/disordered contexts, including short amphipathic helical peptides and longer helix-prone stretches (enriched in Q/A/L/S with tolerated P/G), often near termini or proteolytic cleavage sites; the feature highlights the helix-like portions of low-complexity blocks while avoiding well-folded domains and non‑helical glycine-repeat coils.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across contiguous helix-length stretches (typically 10–30 aa, sometimes forming longer runs) that align with predicted alpha-helices even when structural confidence is low; sharp onset/offset at peptide or boundary edges; low or absent in structured globular domains (e.g., RRMs), signal peptides, and purely coil-like glycine-rich repeats; frequent bias toward terminal regions.
Exemplars: - Prohormone/prokineticin precursors: activation on a C-terminal helical stretch within the propeptide immediately before the bioactive peptide; minimal signal on the signal peptide and processed peptides.
- Vespid venom chemotactic peptides: strong activation across the entire mature amphipathic helical peptide, but not on the signal peptide or preceding prosegment.
- Yeast nuclear RNA-binding/splicing factors (RRM-containing RBPs): activation on low-complexity, helical-prone segments in disordered tails and linker regions; no activation in the folded RRM domains.
- Plant-pathogen harpin (HrpZ) effectors: activation on specific alpha-helical segments (including within peptide-binding regions) and in low-confidence flexible helices; absent on glycine-rich coil repeats.
- Viral structural proteins (capsid/nucleocapsid/readthrough proteins): activation on low-complexity helical arms or termini implicated in assembly/packaging.
- Drosophila eggshell/glue proteins and plant low-complexity/storage proteins: activation along long, low-complexity helical stretches near termini within secretion-associated proteins.

Summary: Ubiquitous “structural anchor” signal: short, ordered residues at secondary‑structure elements and their junctions—helix/strand cores or caps and loop→secondary‑structure transitions—often adjacent to functional motifs; in membrane proteins this frequently maps within or at the edges of transmembrane helices, and it avoids disordered/hydrophobic signal peptides.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks; only a few localized spikes per protein, typically clustered within a short stretch; preferentially in high‑confidence structured regions (helices, strands, tight loops). In soluble proteins there is a bias toward small/basic or glycine‑rich patches; in membrane proteins peaks occur on hydrophobic/aromatic residues within TM segments or at TM boundaries.
Exemplars: - cGAS/CD‑NTase enzymes: sharp peak on the ordered loop immediately preceding the catalytic DVD motif; occasional secondary peak on a nearby metal‑binding loop.
- P‑type ATPases (e.g., KdpB): single peak on a cytoplasmic beta‑strand/helix within the structured core of the actuator/N/P domains.
- Na+/H+ antiporters: sparse peaks within transmembrane helices and at helix termini at the membrane interface.
- FKBP‑type PPIase FkpA: peak on a long, well‑ordered alpha helix in the periplasmic domain; no activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide.
- Ribosomal proteins (uS9/uS13, uL2/uL15/L22/L27/L32, eL43; including organellar precursors): peaks on short ordered basic/glycine‑rich patches that contact rRNA.
- Uracil phosphoribosyltransferases (UPRTases): activation on the glycine‑rich PRPP‑binding/PRTase loop adjacent to catalytic residues.
- Thiamine biosynthesis/processing enzymes: peaks on gly/polar loops near phosphate‑binding active‑site segments.
- Peptidoglycan D,D‑transpeptidases (PBPs): activation on the ordered loop surrounding the SXXK catalytic motif.
- SMN/Gemin‑1 complex components and CWC21 splicing factor: peaks on low‑complexity Q/N‑ or basic‑rich N‑terminal tracts that transition into structured domains.
- Plant CEP peptide precursors and other small integral membrane/micropeptides: activation on the ordered mature/propeptide segment or within a TM helix, rather than on the signal peptide.

Summary: Extracellular interaction modules (often glycan-binding/processing) and repeat-rich adhesion regions: the feature highlights carbohydrate-binding/processing surfaces and other disulfide-stabilized loops in secreted or luminal proteins, including mucin-binding repeats (TKW/YTWD‑like motifs), lectin/CBM/SRCR-type domains, phage tailspike/depolymerase interfaces, ancillary extracellular domains on membrane proteins, and cysteine-rich growth-factor modulators; activation is enriched at aromatic (Trp/Phe) and cysteine positions that form binding grooves or stabilized loops.
Activation pattern: Mostly regional-to-domain activation across long, repetitive extracellular segments; residue-level peaks at Trp/Phe and cysteines within loop/strand motifs; strong signal in extracellular/luminal domains, minimal in transmembrane helices and cytosolic tails; in multidomain proteins, focuses on specific binding loops (e.g., coils between β-strands in disulfide-rich subdomains); small secreted peptides can show near‑global activation; rare intracellular proteins show localized, weaker activation at exposed aromatic/cysteine-rich loops while enzyme cores remain largely silent.
Exemplars:
- Gram-positive mucin-binding adhesins (MUB/MucBP-repeat proteins): activation spans TKW/YTWD-containing repeat blocks mediating mucin/teichoic-acid binding.
- MSCRAMM-type adhesins/invasins with Big/CnaB/GW modules: activation across long extracellular repeat tracts used for cell-surface adhesion.
- Bacteriophage tail spikes and capsular depolymerases: activation along β-helix/β-solenoid surfaces that bind and cleave capsular or O-antigen polysaccharides.
- Bacterial glycoside hydrolases and related CAZymes: activation in carbohydrate-binding modules (CBMs) and aromatic-lined catalytic clefts that engage sugars.
- C-type lectins and other lectin-like receptors: activation on glycan-binding loops of the extracellular domain.
- SRCR-domain scavenger receptors: activation over disulfide-rich SRCR modules that recognize polyanionic glycans/microbial ligands.
- Transmembrane serine proteases (e.g., TMPRSS/hepsin family): activation on extracellular accessory domains (SRCR/LDLRA/CUB) and aromatic/cys-lined surfaces, not TM/cytosolic regions.
- Defensins and other cysteine-stabilized antimicrobial peptides: activation across disulfide-bonded loops that contact microbial surfaces.
- Amyloid precursor-like proteins: focused activation in the E1 copper-binding subdomain loop that contributes to heparin/glycosaminoglycan/metal interaction.
- Cysteine-rich BMP/TGF-β modulators (e.g., chordin-like/KCP): activation over disulfide-stabilized CR modules mediating ligand interactions.
- Rare intracellular enzymes (e.g., deubiquitinases like USP7): weak, patchy activation on exposed aromatic/cysteine-rich surface loops.

Summary: A structural detector for short beta-strand units, with a strong preference for strand starts enriched in Tyr (often accompanied by acidic and/or Gly residues), that tile across beta-rich repeat architectures (e.g., beta-solenoids of Rhs/T6SS toxins, MORN-repeat arrays, and beta-barrels). It marks beta strands rather than a specific function, explaining broad taxonomic coverage and frequent co-localization with ligand- or substrate-binding strands in diverse proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level sharp peaks (typically 5–7 aa) aligning with predicted beta-strands, often rising from the preceding coil; periodically spaced across long repeat regions (~20–25 aa between peaks) in beta-solenoid/other beta-repeat architectures; strong bias toward aromatic (Y/F) and Gly positions; generally weak or absent on helices (occasional spillover at helix starts near active sites).
Exemplars: - Type VI secretion/Rhs toxins: repeated peaks on each beta-strand across the C-terminal beta-solenoid, producing long, periodic activation trains.
- MORN-repeat proteins: peaks at the aromatic residue that initiates each MORN repeat, coinciding with short beta-strands.
- Fatty acid-binding proteins (lipocalin-like beta-barrels): sparse peaks on beta-strands, including residues that line the ligand-binding pocket.
- Thermolysin-like zinc metalloproteases (bacillolysin): a peak on a beta-strand in the propeptide (aromatic pair) and weaker signal at the start of the catalytic helix.
- Myotubularin lipid phosphatases: a single low-amplitude peak on a Gly within an N-terminal beta-strand outside the catalytic domain, illustrating structure-driven, not function-specific, activation.

Summary: A short, surface-exposed interaction/processing loop segment used at functional sites—often a β-hairpin or flexible loop enriched in Pro/Gly and basic plus aromatic residues (frequently including a Pro–Trp, PW, motif)—that serves as an inhibitory/recognition wedge or a proteolytic processing tail adjacent to active or ligand-binding pockets across diverse proteins.
Activation pattern: Short contiguous segments (~20–40 aa) with residue-level peaks centered on exposed loops and nearby β-strands; frequently enriched for Lys/Arg, Pro/Gly, and aromatics (W/Y/F; PW common in cystatins); peaks often align with binding pockets, catalytic residues, or cleavage junctions; may occur in flexible low–pLDDT loops within otherwise structured domains; multiple discrete segments can appear in a single protein; not whole-domain activation.
Exemplars: - Cystatin family cysteine protease inhibitors: inhibitory L2 loop containing the hallmark PW motif that inserts into protease active sites.
- Fungal RNase T1-like ribonucleases: C-terminal β-strand/loop block harboring catalytic/substrate-binding residues (e.g., around catalytic His).
- Plant ribosome-inactivating proteins (e.g., gelonin): C-terminal propeptide and cleavage junction of the secreted precursor.
- SH2-domain adaptor/signaling proteins: loop spanning the phosphotyrosine-binding pocket within the SH2 domain.
- SCP/PR-1/CRISP (venom allergen 5-like) CAP-domain proteins: exposed loop elements implicated in ligand or target interactions.
- Bacterial secretion/competence/pilus components and lysozyme inhibitors: short surface loops mediating attachment or enzyme antagonism.
- Gas vesicle protein O (archaea): conserved exposed loop segment.
- Tim21 family (mitochondrial import): short interfacial loop contacting the TIM23 machinery.
- Copper amine oxidases: surface/processing loop near the active site.
- Pathogen-derived toxins/effectors: receptor-binding or processing loops on secreted toxins.

Summary: A short, solvent‑exposed beta‑strand micro‑motif common in secreted/extracellular proteins: ~10–12 residue beta‑strand segments enriched for a central Tyr/Thr step (often G–Y/T) followed by a small hydrophobic (V/L/I), frequently glycine‑bounded and flanked by acidic residues. This marks generic beta‑sheet register segments rather than catalytic sites, recurring across secreted proteases, carbohydrate‑active enzymes, and surface/scaffolding proteins in all domains of life.

Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks confined to narrow 8–15 aa windows that map to continuous beta‑strands in well‑folded regions; multiple independent windows per protein; peaks typically on Tyr/Thr and adjacent small hydrophobics, with activation tapering at glycine/acidic flanks; little/no activation in helices or coiled‑coils; avoided in alpha‑helical transmembranes, but outer‑membrane beta‑barrel strands can activate when solvent/lumen‑exposed.

Exemplars:
- Metallocarboxypeptidases (M14‑like, e.g., carboxypeptidase X): activation on a discrete C‑terminal surface beta‑strand outside the catalytic core, showing the G–Y/T–(V/L/I) pattern with acidic neighbors.
- Polysaccharide lyases (e.g., rhamnogalacturonate/pectin lyases): activation on a continuous beta‑strand within the folded core, displaying G–Y/T–(V/L/I) with nearby D/E.
- GH18 chitinases: repeated hits on short beta‑strands across the catalytic and accessory (Ig‑like/CNA‑B) domains, peaking on small hydrophobics and occasional Tyr within strands.
- Bacterial S‑layer/surface scaffold proteins: strong activation on extracellular beta‑strand segments (Y/T step followed by hydrophobics) in the mature secreted region, with minimal activation in coiled‑coil or transmembrane alpha‑helical tails.
- Outer‑membrane TonB‑dependent receptors (SusC family): activation on beta‑barrel strands or extracellular‑facing segments that present the Y/T–hydrophobic motif.

Summary: Hydrophilic extracytoplasmic domains (non-cytosolic segments) of secreted, cell-surface, or periplasmic proteins—typically internal-to-C-terminal subdomains used for adhesion, oligomerization/pore assembly, or partner/secretion-system recognition; compositionally biased toward Ser/Thr and acidic/polar residues and often including disulfide-stabilized loops; includes β-strand–rich domains and amphipathic helix–rich secreted/luminal proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional/domain-level activation across long contiguous internal or C-terminal stretches; strongest on β-strands and adjacent loops, and on amphipathic helices in secreted/luminal proteins; little to no activation on N-terminal signal peptides or transmembrane helices.
Exemplars: + Secreted amphipathic apolipoproteins: activation within long helical segments.

Summary: Short linear motifs in intrinsically disordered, often N‑terminal regions that are compositionally biased toward proline and serine/threonine with frequent S/T‑P and PR/PxxP patterns (proline‑directed phosphorylation and proline‑rich interaction motifs); in secreted disulfide‑rich proteins the feature often tags analogous short cysteine‑paired motifs (e.g., CC/CXC) due to their short, strongly biased composition.
Activation pattern: Multiple short regional windows (~10–20 residues) per protein, frequently near the N‑terminus, with residue‑level peaks centered on S/T‑P, PR/PxxP and, in extracellular proteins, Cys‑Cys or Cys‑X‑Cys motifs.
Exemplars: - Plant TIFY/JAZ transcriptional repressors: activation on Ser/Pro‑rich N‑terminal IDRs carrying SP/TP and PR motifs between conserved domains.
- BTB/POZ family (KCTD, Kelch–BTB): activation on low‑complexity linkers and N‑terminal tails enriched in S/T‑P and proline‑rich segments.
- Chromatin/DNA‑binding regulators (MBD/MeCP2, SETDB1, ARID, RYBP/YY1‑binding proteins): activation on disordered regulatory regions with clusters of S/T‑P (CDK/MAPK sites) and proline‑rich/PR motifs.
- Ribosomal proteins and translation factors (bacterial, archaeal, mitochondrial, chloroplast): activation on basic/proline‑biased low‑complexity tails (short RNA‑contacting IDRs) near termini.
- Chemokines: activation on the short N‑terminal CC/CXC disulfide motif and adjacent basic/Pro residues.
- Cysteine‑rich protease inhibitors (Kunitz/Kazal/cystatin‑like): activation on 10–20 aa disulfide‑bonded loops containing Cys pairs.
- Carbohydrate‑active enzymes (glycoside hydrolases, fungal glucanosyltransferases): activation on N‑terminal propeptides/IDRs enriched in SP/TP/PR and, in secreted forms, short cystine motifs.
- Voltage‑gated potassium channels and regulators: activation on cytosolic N‑/C‑terminal tails with clusters of S/T‑P phosphorylation sites and proline‑rich SH3/WW‑binding motifs.
- Kinetochore/centromere proteins: activation on dense S/T‑P clusters in disordered regions targeted by cell‑cycle kinases.
- Glycosphingolipid‑degrading enzymes: activation on luminal propeptides/loops with short cysteine‑containing motifs or Ser/Pro‑rich stretches.

Summary: Recognition of glycine-rich, small/hydroxylated–residue low‑complexity segments (G/S/T/A), especially GG‑enriched intrinsically disordered tracts, with secondary sensitivity to conserved glycine‑rich catalytic loops (often GGH) embedded within otherwise structured enzymes; commonly found in secreted/outer‑facing or membrane‑associated proteins and large scaffolds.
Activation pattern: Primarily long, domain‑scale activation across disordered low‑complexity regions; minimal in well‑folded β‑strands; occasional sharp, residue‑level peaks at GG/GGX (often GGH) motifs within flexible active‑site loops of enzymes.
Exemplars: - MICOS/mitochondrial morphology proteins (e.g., Mdm10/Mitofilin): strong activation over polar, low‑confidence disordered loops while structured β‑barrels/β‑strands are silent.
- Autophagy lipid‑transfer tethers (ATG2): extended activation across gly/ser‑rich disordered linkers in very large proteins.
- Type III secretion effectors (plant pathogens): long C‑terminal low‑complexity G/S/T/A‑rich stretches activated.
- Lipid‑binding/transport proteins (e.g., apolipoproteins): activation on gly/ser‑rich flexible segments and linkers.
- Gram‑negative outer‑membrane assembly/transport systems: periplasmic/extracellular low‑complexity loops and segments highlighted.
- Folate biosynthesis enzymes (HPPK/DHPS/Fol1): residue‑level peaks at the glycine‑rich catalytic loop, frequently the GGH motif (single His flagged).
- Nonribosomal peptide synthetases and related megasynthases: isolated activation at conserved His within local gly‑rich flexible loops.
- Functional amyloid systems (e.g., curli and extracellular amyloid precursors): repetitive low‑complexity segments (G/S/T/A with N/Q) activated.
- Y‑family translesion DNA polymerases (Pol IV/η/κ, REV1): activation concentrated in disordered C‑terminal tails/interactors, not the structured polymerase core.
- Plant organellar and starch/granule‑associated proteins: low‑complexity transit/linker regions and repeats activated.

Summary: Short, well‑ordered beta‑strand segments enriched in hydrophobic/aromatic residues (generic beta‑sheet elements), most often in the structural cores of carbohydrate‑active enzymes but also present in soluble regions of membrane/secreted proteins; not tied to active‑site chemistry
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks on short contiguous stretches (~6–10 aa), often multiple per protein; consistently map to DSSP ‘E’ beta‑strands with high pLDDT; occur at varied sequence positions (N‑, internal, C‑terminal) and generally do not overlap annotated catalytic/binding sites or transmembrane helices
Exemplars: - Polysaccharide lyase (ulvan lyase): strong activation on a C‑terminal beta‑strand adjacent to other sheet elements
- Alpha‑galactosidase (glycosidase, GH): distinct peaks on N‑terminal and C‑terminal beta‑strands
- 4‑alpha‑glucanotransferase (amylomaltase/GH): a single, well‑defined C‑terminal beta‑strand segment
- Beta‑hexosaminidase (GH20): a short beta‑strand immediately after the signal peptide in the mature N‑terminus
- YidC membrane insertase: short beta‑strand segments in non‑TM soluble regions (loop/domain) rather than helices
- Galactose mutarotase (aldose 1‑epimerase): a continuous internal beta‑strand segment with additional minor peaks on other strands

Summary: Amphipathic hydrophobic‑ligand (lipid/LPS and lipid‑like small molecules) binding and handoff patches: short, mixed‑polar surface segments at the mouths of hydrophobic cavities or along grooves used in extracytoplasmic/periplasmic and organellar lipid transfer, and in soluble carriers/receptors of lipid‑like small molecules; includes Gram‑negative LPS transport/outer‑membrane assembly factors and diverse soluble lipid carriers (lipocalin/BPI/LBP, START, vitellogenin, Atg2/Vps13, plastid lipid‑associated proteins)
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short mixed‑polar loops/edges and amphipathic turns adjacent to ligand‑binding pockets or membrane‑contact surfaces; multiple discrete peaks across large proteins; avoids long hydrophobic transmembrane helices
Exemplars (add):
- Avidin/streptavidin‑like biotin‑binding proteins: activation at the β‑barrel mouth that coordinates biotin via cationic/apolar patches
- Plant ABA receptors (PYR/PYL/RCAR; Bet v1‑like cavity proteins): activation around the cavity entrance that binds the hydrophobic ABA ligand

Summary: Disulfide‑rich extracellular modules and peptides: the feature encodes the cysteine/disulfide framework (often with nearby prolines) characteristic of secreted or ectodomain regions, including small cystine‑knot/toxin and antimicrobial peptides and cysteine‑rich repeat modules such as EGF‑like, LDLR class A, Kunitz/Kazal/WAP, and thrombospondin type‑1 repeats; it also fires on cysteine‑rich loops of viral envelope glycoproteins and immune chemokines.
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation across extracellular repeat modules with sharp residue-level peaks on conserved cysteines (and adjacent prolines); in small toxins/AMPs only a few core Cys/Pro positions spike, whereas in large multidomain ectoproteins many sites across N‑terminal/extracellular repeats are activated.
Exemplars: - Cysteine‑knot toxins and antimicrobial peptides (defensins, plant cyclotides/knottins, cone/snail/scorpion toxins) — peaks on the conserved cystine‑knot cysteine framework.
- Protease inhibitors (Kunitz, Kazal, WAP/four‑disulfide core) — activation on the disulfide scaffold and the reactive‑site loop (often including Pro).
- EGF‑like and LDLR class A repeats of extracellular receptors (LDLR/LRP, Notch/coagulation/selectins) — activation on the repeat’s conserved cysteines (and Ca2+‑binding loop in LDLR‑A).
- Thrombospondin type‑1 repeat (TSR/TSP1)–containing proteins (thrombospondins, ADAMTS/ECM proteins) — peaks on TSR disulfide‑bonded cysteines flanking the WxxW ladder.
- Adhesion GPCR ectodomains — activation across their long N‑terminal cysteine‑rich modules preceding the GPS/GAIN site.
- Chemokines (CC/CXC/CX3C) and other immune complement‑related extracellular proteins — peaks on the defining cysteine motifs in the N‑terminal/loop regions.
- Viral envelope/membrane glycoproteins — activation on disulfide‑stabilized cysteine‑rich loops in ectodomains.
- Secreted serine proteases — broader activation over disulfide cysteines in the catalytic domain and associated propeptides.

Summary: Generic hydrophobic segment detector: the feature marks hydrophobic secondary-structure elements (alpha-helices, beta-strands) and continuous hydrophobic segments, including transmembrane helices and signal peptides, as well as hydrophobic cores of repeat scaffolds (HEAT/ARM/TPR/LRR and WD/beta-propellers); it shows extra sensitivity near secondary-structure junctions and reflects hydrophobic packing rather than a specific function
Activation pattern: Regional activation across hydrophobic elements (helices and beta-strands), often spanning an entire segment and slightly into flanking loops; residue-level peaks at segment cores and at secondary-structure boundaries; multiple such regions dispersed along proteins
Exemplars:
- Major facilitator superfamily (MFS) transporters: strong activation on individual transmembrane helices and their cytoplasmic/extracellular boundaries
- BAM complex subunits: helical-repeat BamD segments and hydrophobic blades/loop-helix regions in the WD40-like beta-propeller BamB
- HEAT/ARM repeat karyopherins: leucine-rich alpha-helical solenoid repeats across the transport domain
- Plant LRR receptor(-like) proteins: N-terminal signal peptides and single-pass TM anchors, plus leucine-rich ectodomain repeats
- Teichoic acid export system TagG/H: TagH ABC ATPase shows activation on hydrophobic helices within the NBD (and any N-terminal anchor), while TagG permease shows strong activation on TM segments
- HTH-type transcriptional regulators: hydrophobic cores of the helix-turn-helix bundle, including the recognition helix
- GNAT acetyltransferases and dehydrogenases: hydrophobic alpha-helices and beta-strands forming enzyme cores around active/binding sites
- WD-repeat beta-propellers: hydrophobic beta-blades and adjoining loop/short-helix regions (e.g., U5-40K, BamB)
- General membrane proteins and receptor precursors: signal peptides and transmembrane helices across diverse taxa

Summary: The feature captures the hydrophobic core positions of alpha-helical coiled-coils—the ‘a’/‘d’ residues of the heptad repeat—across long coiled-coil oligomerization/stalk domains used for assembly and scaffolding in diverse cellular and viral proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level periodic peaks every 3–4 residues within extended regions annotated/predicted as coiled-coils; dense, long stretches with strong preference for L/I/V (with M/F tolerated) at heptad ‘a’/‘d’ positions; little to no activation in adjacent globular domains; continuous activation often terminates just before transmembrane anchors.
Exemplars: - Meiotic linear-element/synaptonemal complex proteins (e.g., Mug20-like): activation on the central coiled-coil heptad core positions.
- Cytolinker/spectrin–plectin–interaptin–like scaffolds: strong, continuous activation across the long C‑terminal coiled-coil stalks; CH or other globular domains are inactive.
- Ciliary/flagellar and centrosomal/centriolar coiled-coil proteins (CCDC/axonemal scaffolds): activation along oligomerization coiled-coils.
- Viral structural proteins (class I fusion glycoprotein HR1/HR2, capsid/spike coiled-coils): activation on heptad-repeat hydrophobic stripes mediating trimerization.
- Viral non-structural polyproteins with membrane association: activation on internal coiled-coil segments adjacent to transmembrane regions that scaffold replication complexes.
- Bacterial/archaeal surface and cell-envelope proteins (S-layer, adhesin stalks): activation along repetitive coiled-coil stalk domains.
- Yeast nuclear envelope/spindle pole body scaffolds (e.g., Spc/Mps coiled-coils): activation over elongated coiled-coil assemblies.
- Bacterial pore-forming/adhesin systems with coiled-coil oligomerization segments: activation on their coiled-coil cores.
- Motor and cytoskeletal assemblies (plant kinesin/dynein/myosin stalks): activation on dimerization coiled-coils; also observed in chloroplast/membrane-associated enzymes containing coiled-coil linkers.

Summary: Enzymatic toxin/effector payload domains—especially the C‑terminal catalytic modules of polymorphic toxins and Gram‑negative secretion system effectors (T3SS/T6SS, Rhs, colicins)—that act on host or bacterial targets (ADP‑ribosyltransferases, DNase/RNase/tRNase nucleases, cysteine/metallo‑proteases, and peptidoglycan hydrolases); the feature focuses on the catalytic cores and adjacent loop/β‑strand regions and occasionally fires on analogous nucleic‑acid–interacting surfaces in viral structural proteins
Activation pattern: Predominantly domain-level/regional activation concentrated on toxin/effector payload domains, often at C‑termini of large scaffolds (e.g., Rhs). Within these domains, strongest signal occurs over catalytic cores and adjacent flexible loops/short β‑strands enriched in G/S/T/D/E/K, with sharp residue-level peaks at essential catalytic or toxicity-determining residues (e.g., the toxic loop in Tse2). N‑terminal secretion/chaperone/scaffold regions show weak activation; multiple long activated stretches per protein are common.
Exemplars: - Type VI secretion toxins (Tse2/Tae/Tde families): activation across the toxic segment, peaking in catalytic loops that determine cytotoxicity (e.g., loop containing essential serine/threonine).
- Rhs polymorphic toxins: activation restricted to variable C‑terminal toxin payloads (e.g., HNH/HHH nuclease, ADP‑ribosyltransferase, protease payloads), not the RHS shell.
- ADP‑ribosyltransferase toxins (diphtheria/cholera/C3/ExoS‑like): activation at NAD+‑binding pockets and H–Y–E/R–S–E catalytic motifs and surrounding loops.
- Bacteriocins/colicins: activation on C‑terminal DNase/RNase/tRNase domains (HNH/AHH nuclease metal‑binding loops and nucleic‑acid‑contacting surfaces).
- Peptidoglycan hydrolases and phage lytic transglycosylases: activation at catalytic glutamate/DxE motifs and glycan‑binding loops that mediate cell wall cleavage.
- Cysteine and metalloprotease effectors (e.g., deubiquitinases, zincins): activation around catalytic Cys/His dyads or HExxH motifs and adjacent substrate‑binding strands.
- Type III secretion effectors modulating host signaling (e.g., ExoU‑like patatin phospholipases, SopB‑like PI phosphatases, GAP/GEF‑like modules, NEL‑type E3 ligases): activation in catalytic pockets/loops that engage lipids, GTPases, or ubiquitin.
- Viral capsid/nucleoproteins subset: activation over basic/polar nucleic‑acid‑binding surfaces that mimic toxin nuclease interaction patches.

Summary: Surface-exposed loop/edge segments in extracytoplasmic proteins (secreted, lumenal/periplasmic) — most prominently within modular β‑rich recognition domains (Ig‑like, fibronectin type‑III, LRR, complement/macroglobulin), but also in exposed loops of diverse secreted enzymes and secretion/accessory lipoproteins; these patches often include N‑linked glycosylation sequons in eukaryotes and frequently contain tryptophan
Activation pattern: Short contiguous peaks (~8–10 residues) concentrated in non-cytosolic regions and largely absent from signal peptides, transmembrane helices, and cytosolic catalytic domains; when repeats are present, peaks recur roughly once per module, whereas in non-repeat enzymes/accessory proteins they occur as isolated exposed-loop patches; many peaks in eukaryotes coincide with N‑X‑S/T sequons; mixed residue composition with frequent G/P and occasional Trp
Exemplars:
- Receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatases (e.g., VE‑PTP/PTPRB): repeated narrow peaks inside each extracellular FN3 domain, none in the TM or cytosolic phosphatase.
- Type I/II cytokine receptors (hematopoietic/cytokine receptors): activation on the cytokine-binding FN3-like modules (CHR) in their ectodomains, often overlapping N‑glycosylation sites.
- Immunoglobulin superfamily cell-adhesion/guidance proteins (e.g., NCAM/L1/contactins/DSCAM/Robo): short loop/edge β‑strand patches within Ig-like domains used for recognition.
- Receptor tyrosine kinases with Ig/FN3/LRR ectodomains (e.g., FGFR/VEGFR/Tie): activation confined to their extracellular recognition modules, not the intracellular kinase.
- Extracellular matrix proteins with FN3 repeats (e.g., fibronectin, tenascin): recurring peaks within each FN3 module along the secreted protein.
- Complement/macroglobulin families (e.g., C3/C4/C5, α2‑macroglobulin): surface loops within β‑rich extracellular domains (CCP/CUB/MG) frequently highlighted.
- LRR-containing receptors/adhesins: short segments on the solvent-exposed face/loops of the extracellular LRR region.
- Bacterial secreted adhesins/enzymes and secretion-accessory lipoproteins (e.g., subtilisin-like proteases such as Vpr, T3SS pilotin YscW): peaks on exposed β/loop segments despite lacking Ig/FN3 repeats.
- Secretory pathway glycosyltransferases (e.g., xylosyltransferase 1): short patches on lumenal loops of the catalytic domain.

Summary: Generic structural signal marking isolated hydrophobic packing positions within regular secondary structure (primarily Leu/Ile/Val/Phe/Met in alpha-helices or beta-strands), reflecting the hydrophobic face/core of secondary elements rather than a specific functional motif
Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks (typically 1–5 per protein), strongest on bulky hydrophobics in helices or sheets, occasionally appearing in coils; scattered across long polypeptides and diverse protein classes
Exemplars: - Inner nuclear membrane LEM-domain protein (Heh2): isolated Leu residues in predicted helices (and one nearby Cys in coil) within a large C-terminal region, consistent with hydrophobic positions contributing to helical packing/interfaces
- Hydroxylamine reductase (Fe–S enzyme): L139 in a long helix and F280/I193 in beta-sheets (plus a loop G21 near Fe–S-binding Cys), matching preference for hydrophobic residues in well-structured elements, often near buried cores/cofactors
- Monomethylamine methyltransferase MtmB (pyrrolysine-dependent methylamine:corrinoid methyltransferase subunit): L70 and one helix Asp (outlier) within separate helices, predominantly aligning with a helical hydrophobic packing position

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity regulatory segments enriched in Ser/Thr/Pro and charged residues (often bearing SP/TP/PP repeats and acidic activation-like stretches), frequently adjacent to or alternating with leucine/isoleucine-rich coiled‑coil scaffolds used to assemble large complexes; in structured enzymes, the feature instead fires on exposed acidic/charge‑rich loops or termini
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation on non‑globular stretches (IDRs and predicted coiled‑coil heptads), often in multiple discontiguous segments within the same protein; residue‑level peaks at SP/TP/PP clusters and runs of acidic/basic residues; commonly located in mid‑to‑C‑terminal portions of long proteins
Exemplars: - Mediator complex subunits: acidic, Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich activation regions and low‑complexity linkers
- Kinetochore/spindle‑checkpoint scaffolds (e.g., Ndc80/KNL1/Mad/Bub families): coiled‑coil rods plus S/T‑P‑rich disordered regulatory segments
- Ubiquitin‑system components (Cullin‑RING ligases and adaptors, E2s, RWD/UEV proteins): low‑complexity acidic/proline/serine‑rich linkers and phospho‑regulated degron‑like segments; occasional coiled‑coil scaffolds
- Vesicle coat/adaptor complexes (AP and COPI/II subunits): leucine/isoleucine‑rich coiled‑coils and acidic low‑complexity linkers
- Regulatory protein kinases (cell‑cycle/stress): non‑catalytic Ser/Thr‑rich tails/insertions harboring SP/TP clusters for docking/phosphoregulation
- Frataxin/CyaY: acidic, charge‑rich surface loops or termini
- RNase H/HIII enzymes: acidic/basic‑rich surface loops or low‑complexity terminal segments
- Viral regulatory/structural proteins: acidic, Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich transactivation/linker regions

Summary: Short, basic/polar N‑terminal leader/transit segment immediately after the initiator methionine (positions ~3–6) — i.e., the positively charged/polar start of signal peptides and organelle transit peptides, and more generally low‑acidic, disordered N‑terminal patches (including occasional cysteine‑rich starts) used for targeting, export, rRNA binding, or membrane topology cues
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peak at the extreme N‑terminus with a short contiguous run (typically 3–5 residues at positions 3–6; less often 1–2); occasional secondary weak sites elsewhere
Exemplars: - Secretory signal peptides (Sec pathway): activation on the basic N‑region just after Met that precedes the hydrophobic h‑region
- Mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides: activation on the Ser/Thr‑ and Arg/Lys‑rich start of the amphipathic targeting helix
- Thylakoid/photosystem and chloroplast stromal proteins: activation on the basic/polar N‑terminal transit segment
- Ribosomal proteins (bacterial, mitochondrial, chloroplastic): activation on Lys/Arg‑rich, disordered N‑terminal tails that contact rRNA
- Respiratory/energy‑conversion and translocation complexes (e.g., inner‑membrane subunits, Sec/Tat components): activation on N‑terminal positive‑inside patches or targeting presequences
- Secreted peptide precursors and RiPPs (lantibiotics, bacteriocins, lasso peptides, pheromones): activation on the basic/polar start of the leader peptide that guides modification/export
- Metallothioneins: activation on cysteine‑rich, low‑complexity N‑terminal stretches
- Stress‑response/chaperone proteins (organelle/periplasmic): activation on N‑terminal transit/signal segments or basic disordered starts

Summary: Generic alpha-helical hydrophobic packing signal: prefers small/hydrophobic residues within alpha-helices—spanning transmembrane helices, coiled-coils, and tandem helical repeat solenoids—rather than catalytic motifs
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks dispersed across many well-structured helices; often extended, low-to-moderate activation along long helices/transmembrane segments and periodic peaks across repeated helical units; minimal activation at catalytic polar motifs or in disordered loops
Exemplars: - Two-component sensor histidine kinases (including quorum-sensing kinases): activation along N-terminal transmembrane helices and helical HAMP/PAS linkers and DHp coiled-coils.
- Ankyrin/armadillo and PPR repeat proteins: activation on the hydrophobic faces of the paired helices that constitute each repeat in the solenoid.
- Glycosyltransferases and LPS/capsule biosynthesis proteins: activation on multipass inner-membrane helices and helical segments within GT folds.
- Short-chain dehydrogenase/reductases and other dehydrogenases: activation on the N-terminal Rossmann beta–alpha–beta helix and other hydrophobic helices; not on the catalytic Tyr/Lys motif.
- ECF/alternative sigma factors: activation on helix-turn-helix elements and helical linkers.
- c-di-GMP/light/cell-surface signaling proteins and membrane channels: activation along transmembrane and downstream coiled-coil helices.
- Dictyostelium repeat-rich proteins: activation across ankyrin/PPR-like helical repeats and membrane-associated helices.

Summary: Intrinsic low-complexity/disordered segments (IDRs)—especially Ser/Pro/Gly- and/or His-rich tracts in terminal regions and linkers—while avoiding folded domains (e.g., zinc‑finger cores); commonly corresponds to flexible activation/propeptide/basic stretches in regulatory, viral, and secreted small proteins across taxa.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in coil, low-confidence (low pLDDT) regions; often clustered at N-termini or within internal low-complexity runs, with minimal signal inside well-structured domains; in very small peptides, peaks can extend across most of the sequence.
Exemplars: AN1/A20 and C2H2 zinc-finger proteins: activation on disordered, compositionally biased linkers and tails while skipping the metal-binding cores; Plant TCP/LOB transcription factors: Ser/Pro/Gly-rich disordered activation regions; SR-rich splicing factors and other RNA-binding proteins (hnRNPs, DEAD-box helicases): RS/RGG- and other low-complexity IDRs; Viral accessory/regulatory proteins from diverse families: short basic, disordered segments; Secreted precursors, antimicrobial peptides, and small toxins: flexible signal/propeptide regions or cationic amphipathic low-complexity peptides; Mycobacterial regulators/enzymes: histidine-rich repeats and disordered linkers.

Summary: Residue-level marker for the onset of β-strands and adjacent loop→β junctions in well‑ordered domains, often near the N‑terminus of a protein or domain; a general structural motif that recurs across β‑rich and α/β folds
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks; strongest at the first residue(s) of a β‑strand or the immediately preceding loop, with sparse signals within the strand; little to no activation on helices or long disordered segments; proteins containing many loop–strand transitions (e.g., β‑propellers/repeats) show many peaks, whereas others show only a few
Exemplars: - Cleavage and polyadenylation factor CPSF2: peaks at an N‑terminal loop→β junction and at additional strand starts in the structured N‑terminal domain.
- Exosome complex subunit RRP46: strongest signal at the start of a β‑strand, with minor peaks within another β‑strand; no activation across disordered N‑terminal tail or helices.
- BTB/POZ–Kelch E3 ligase adaptors (KLHL/KBTBD; ZBTB transcription factors): recurrent peaks around early N‑terminal positions and numerous signals across Kelch β‑propeller blade strand starts.
- Retroviral/retropepsin-like aspartic proteases and DDI1 proteases: activation on β‑sheet elements and loop→strand entries forming the protease core.
- Metallo‑β‑lactamase superfamily nucleases and phosphodiesterases (e.g., RNase J, PDEs): signals at loop→strand transitions feeding into the central β‑sheet of the α/β core.
- Acid phosphatases (purple/alkaline) and diverse α/β hydrolases: activation at β‑strand edges and junctions within their α/β cores.
- Acetyl‑CoA carboxylase carboxyltransferase subunits (α/β): peaks at the starts of core β‑strands in Rossmann‑like/αβ architectures.

Summary: A membrane-pore/channel beta-structure motif: the feature preferentially recognizes beta-hairpin/beta-strand segments (often glycine-/small-residue–enriched) that insert into or line membrane pores and beta-barrels in pore-forming toxins and channel proteins; it also highlights related beta-hairpin motifs in secreted antimicrobial beta-sheet folds. Outside these contexts it fires sparsely on isolated small residues.
Activation pattern: Mostly regional/domain-level activation across contiguous beta-structured stretches that comprise the membrane-inserting hairpins or pore-lining beta-strands of the mature effector domain (often inactive on signal peptides/propeptides). Within these regions it shows multiple sharp peaks at small residues in beta-strands and turns. In unrelated enzymes or small disordered proteins, activation collapses to rare single-residue peaks.
Exemplars: - Gasdermins (bacterial and eukaryotic): strong activation on the N-terminal pore-forming module, especially the helix-to-beta transition immediately upstream of the membrane-inserting beta-hairpins.
- MACPF/CDC pore-formers: extended activation over the TMH1/TMH2 region that refolds into membrane-inserting beta-hairpins within the MACPF domain.
- Beta pore-forming toxins (e.g., monalysin): activation across the mature pore-forming beta-strand domain and adjacent long beta-strand.
- Insect antimicrobial proteins (Attacins): activation over the mature beta-sheet fold with peaks at beta-hairpins within the oligomerizing/antimicrobial domain.
- Porins and translocation-channel components (e.g., chloroplast outer envelope porins; TOM/TIC/Sec channel subunits): activation on beta-barrel strands and pore-lining segments.
- ERMES/TOM complex outer-membrane subunits (e.g., Mdm10): activation on beta-barrel/channel strands; peripheral ERMES partners may show weaker hits in small-residue–rich segments.
- Streptomyces rodlet (chaplin/rodlin) proteins: activation on gly/ala-rich beta-aggregating segments that assemble into surface beta-sheets.
- Polymorphic toxins and type III/VI effectors: activation on glycine-/small-residue–rich low-complexity segments implicated in membrane interaction/permeabilization.
- Non-pore housekeeping proteins (e.g., metallothioneins, GTP cyclohydrolase 1): only sparse single-residue peaks at small residues, likely incidental.

Summary: Surface-exposed flexible segments (loops, intrinsically disordered linkers, and some helix/loop interfaces), generally non-catalytic, often found in secreted/lumenal proteins, large proline-rich scaffolds, beta-rich fibers, and capsid/shell-like assemblies; these segments are frequently, but not necessarily, enriched in acidic and Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation in tens-of-residue tracts, often as multiple discrete peaks per protein. Peaks concentrate in coil/turn-rich sequences and strand–coil junctions, and can also occur in amphipathic/heptad-repeat helices proximal to proteolytic or fusion regions in viral envelope proteins. Activation frequently flanks proteolytic processing sites or glycosylation-prone regions and occurs in non-catalytic loops within stable domains.
Exemplars:
- V-ATPase accessory subunit S1 (Ac45): activation in the lumenal propeptide and a mature-domain strand, with weaker signal near the furin cleavage and a glycosylation site.
- 1,3‑beta‑glucanases (laminarinases; GH16/GH17): activation across an N‑terminal beta‑sandwich’s strands/loops, away from catalytic residues.
- Proline-rich signaling scaffold (ADAP/p140Cap-like): strong activation in disordered, proline-biased C‑terminal segments.
- PglZ alkaline phosphatase‑like phosphohydrolase: activation in a long loop linking a beta‑strand to an alpha‑helix and adjacent helices.
- Viral fusion glycoproteins (e.g., RSV F): activation in fusion‑proximal S2 helices and adjacent loops near cleavage/glycosylation.
- Bacteriophage long tail fiber proteins (Gp37-like): periodic activation across strand/coil segments of the beta‑solenoid fiber, not in the intramolecular chaperone domain.
- Argonaute/Piwi nucleases: activation in surface loops and interdomain linkers outside catalytic motifs.
- Encapsulin shell proteins: activation in exposed loops of the icosahedral shell.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments enriched in small/polar and acidic residues (A, S, T, P, G, V, E), typically found as terminal tails and flexible linkers—especially in Gram‑negative cell‑envelope/secreted proteins, but broadly present across taxa.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated within long, low‑confidence (disordered) regions—most often N‑ or C‑terminal tails or coil loops—with little to no activation in well‑structured catalytic cores; sparse peaks can span many sites across extended extracellular/passenger regions; depleted in aromatics.
Exemplars: - Peptidoglycan amidases (AmiB/autolysins): activation on C‑terminal disordered tails and internal low‑confidence loops.
- Secreted glycoside hydrolases (e.g., dextranase): activation on long C‑terminal disordered tails and N‑terminal low‑complexity regions.
- Secreted bacterial proteases (e.g., IgM/IgA protease–like): scattered peaks in flexible, low‑confidence regions outside the catalytic core.
- Gram‑negative autotransporter adhesins and pilus/secretion components: extensive activation across proline/glycine‑rich extracellular linkers and repeats.
- Periplasmic electron‑transfer/photosynthetic complex subunits: activation on acidic, low‑complexity tails.
- Magnetosome‑associated proteins: activation on compositionally biased, disordered regions.
- Bacterial Ser/Thr kinases: activation on low‑complexity termini or flexible regulatory segments.
- Viral capsid/surface and eukaryotic secreted proteins: activation on repeat‑rich, disordered extracellular segments.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity Ser/Thr/Pro–rich tracts (PTS‑rich IDRs) — including mucin‑like/O‑glycosylation‑prone regions and proline‑rich flexible linkers or terminal tails — common in secreted/viral proteins but also present as extended disordered insertions in otherwise globular enzymes and membrane‑associated factors
