Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation across long, contiguous coil segments with low pLDDT, often beginning at termini (frequently N‑terminal) or in extended C‑terminal tails; superimposed residue‑level peaks on S/T/P and short repeats (SP/TP, PP, GP); little to no activation in well‑structured secondary elements or transmembrane helices
Exemplars: - Polyomavirus agnoproteins: widespread activation across fully disordered, P/S/T‑ and proline‑rich microproteins with peaks on S/T/P residues
- Peroxisomal biogenesis factors (PEX membrane proteins): activation on low‑pLDDT cytosolic loops/tails; suppressed in the transmembrane helix
- Glycoside hydrolases (e.g., intracellular arabinofuranosidases): strong activation on long C‑terminal disordered, low‑complexity tails annotated as compositional bias
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: activation on S/T‑rich mucin‑like regions adjacent to signal peptides/propeptides
- Secreted peptide hormones/toxin precursors: activation on low‑complexity pre/propeptide stretches enriched in S/T/P
- Small proteins and micropeptides: broad activation across extended low‑complexity disordered segments

Summary: Short β-strand/loop motifs in extracellular/secreted proteins, especially within β-sandwich accessory domains (Ig-like, carbohydrate-binding modules, adhesin/hemagglutinin repeats) and stabilizing P-domains; the feature highlights surface-exposed strand edges and loop-to-β transitions that support ligand binding or Ca2+-stabilization rather than catalytic sites.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks clustered in 3–8 residue segments; concentrated in β-strands and loop→β junctions of ectodomains, CBMs, Ig-like/P-domains, adhesin repeats, and sometimes in propeptides/linkers; catalytic cores show little or no activation.
Exemplars: - Subtilisin-like extracellular serine proteases: strong peaks at the Ca2+-binding loop in the mature domain and a short β-strand in the C-terminal propeptide.
- Proprotein convertase (kexin/furin family): localized peaks at a helix→β transition within the β-sandwich P/Homo B domain that stabilizes the enzyme (Ca2+-associated region).
- Lys-gingipain (Porphyromonas gingivalis) cysteine protease: sparse peaks across the catalytic subunit and more distal β-rich adhesin/hemagglutinin repeats, not at the catalytic dyad.
- GH16 beta-porphyranase: a short β-strand segment in the C-terminal region outside the catalytic domain.
- GH81 endo-1,3-β-glucanase with CBM6/CBM56: peaks within CBM β-strands/loops and the adjacent linker, near a ligand-binding residue.
- Secreted immunoglobulin-like receptor (Ig-like C2 domain): loop-to-β transition within the Ig β-sandwich.

Summary: Short, low‑complexity polar/charged micro‑motifs in intrinsically disordered terminal tails—most often C‑terminal cytosolic tails or propeptide tails—composed of mixed E/D/K/R/S/T with small residues (A/G/P), frequently annotated as compositionally biased and outside folded domains.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks on contiguous 3–6‑residue windows, strongly biased to extreme or near‑extreme C‑terminal regions within IDRs; typically low structural confidence (disordered), though short helical propensity may appear within the disordered tail.
Exemplars: - Twin‑arginine translocase subunit TatA: mixed acidic/basic, disordered C‑terminal tail patch.
- Class A GPCRs (e.g., dopamine receptor): tiny motif in the cytoplasmic C‑terminal tail.
- Forkhead transcription factors: extreme C‑terminal disordered residues outside the DNA‑binding domain.
- Homeobox transcription factors (Hox proteins): proline‑biased disordered C‑terminal segment.
- Adrenomedullin/peptide hormone precursors: short patch within the C‑terminal portion of the propeptide (disordered context).

Summary: Alpha-helical and His/Cys-centered functional microenvironments: strongest on the C-terminal histidine(s) of Cys2His2 zinc-finger helices (and immediate linkers), also on isolated small/polar residues within transmembrane alpha-helices, and on His/Cys-rich metal/ligand-binding sites in soluble regulators and enzymes; not a general helix marker.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks at His/Cys/Ser/Thr/Gly within structured elements. In C2H2 fingers, activation concentrates on the terminal zinc-ligating histidine and spills into the following linker; little in non-finger domains (e.g., BTB, SET). In multi-pass membrane proteins, activation is sparse but restricted to transmembrane helices, favoring small/polar positions and avoiding loops. Additionally, sparse peaks occur at metal-sensing/coordination residues within soluble helical or mixed-structure proteins (e.g., HTH metalloregulators, alanyl‑tRNA editing/deacylase and Fe(II)/2‑oxoglutarate dioxygenases) and at conserved small/polar sites in viral structural/helicase-like scaffolds; generic coils without such motifs remain largely inactive.
Exemplars: - C2H2-type zinc-finger transcription factors (BTB/POZ ZBTB proteins): peaks on terminal histidines of finger helices; minimal in BTB and most disordered regions except immediately after fingers.
- PRDM family zinc-finger proteins: silent across PR/SET, strong on histidines (and flanks) in the C-terminal finger array.
- Cys2His2 regulators (e.g., lsy-2): sharp peaks at terminal histidines and first linker residues; little on the corresponding cysteines.
- Heme A synthase/COX15 (CtaA): activation exclusively within transmembrane helices at isolated small/polar positions.
- Prokaryotic HTH-type metalloregulatory repressors: peaks at His/Cys that coordinate metals within helical DNA-binding/dimer interfaces.
- Alanyl‑tRNA editing/deacylase and Fe(II)/2OG dioxygenases: signals at catalytic His/Asp/His triads or adjacent polar microenvironments.
- Viral proteins: envelope glycoproteins show TM-helix peaks; capsid/helicase-like and tail fiber proteins show sparse peaks at conserved His/Ser/Thr/Gly within helical or beta-helical repeats.

Summary: Alpha‑helical polar/charged “hotspots” used for coordination or helix–helix interfaces, with a strong bias toward histidines that act as axial ligands to b‑type heme in membrane redox proteins, and also capturing polar residues at coiled‑coil heptad positions and conserved His‑containing catalytic motifs (e.g., HRD, HxGH)
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue‑level peaks confined to selected helical positions; often isolated His peaks in transmembrane helices (frequently a four‑His pattern in cytochrome b561‑like proteins) or short runs across one to two heptads in coiled‑coils. Little to no activation in nonhelical/disordered regions or bulk hydrophobic TM core apart from the coordinating sites.
Exemplars: - Cytochrome b561 family and related membrane oxidoreductases: discrete peaks on the conserved axial heme‑ligating histidines within TM helices (four‑His pattern).
- Eukaryotic protein kinases: peaks on the catalytic HRD histidine and nearby polar residues in the catalytic loop.
- Diacylglycerol kinases: peaks on the HxGH motif histidines in the catalytic domain.
- Plant MYB/PHR1‑like transcription factors: short activated stretches in C‑terminal coiled‑coil/leucine‑zipper regions (e.g., LHEQLE motif; Q/E/H positions).
- Pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins: polar residues on helical repeat surfaces implicated in RNA recognition.
- Rho/Rac/Ras pathway regulators (GEFs, GAPs, effectors): charged/polar residues on helical dimerization or switch‑binding coiled‑coils.
- Photosynthesis/chloroplast membrane proteins: heme‑center ligands or coiled‑coil interface residues in thylakoid/inner membrane components.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments exposed to solvent; commonly Ser/Thr/Gly-rich, but also acidic (Asp/Glu-rich) or basic (Lys/Arg-rich) tracts in secreted/extracytoplasmic proteins, and short flexible linker/loop regions in intracellular proteins that often serve as modification-prone or cleavage-prone sites
Activation pattern: Regional activation over low-complexity/disordered stretches (composition may be S/T/G-, acidic-, or basic-biased) in secreted or lumenal proteins; shorter peaks on flexible linker/loop motifs within globular intracellular proteins
Exemplars: - Vitellogenins: phosvitin Ser-rich low-complexity tract
- Secreted/surface and periplasmic proteins (including bacterial lipoproteins and chaperones like LolA, and NHBA): activation on disordered LCRs that can be S/T-rich, acidic, or basic (e.g., NHBA’s basic N-terminal region)
- MTTP large subunit: lumenal flexible regions
- PsbO/OEE1: low-complexity acidic/Ser/Thr-enriched loops
- Bcl-2 family (including viral homologs): central unstructured Ser/Thr-rich regulatory loop
- Gasdermins: low-complexity interdomain linker with protease sites
- MutS/MSH: flexible interdomain linkers/loops with short S/Thr-rich or acidic motifs
- Exosome/RNase PH-like: low-complexity tails/surface loops (small/polar or acidic)
- Bacteriophage tail/tube/connector proteins: low-complexity spacer/hinge regions between structured elements
- Heterotrimeric G protein alpha subunits: activation on N-terminal tails and switch-region loops with low complexity/small-polar or charged residues

Summary: Generic detection of intrinsically disordered/low‑complexity segments and helix–coil linkers/edges, especially in acidic/Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly‑rich regions, marking flexible tails and linkers rather than catalytic cores
Activation pattern: Sparse, low‑magnitude residue‑level peaks scattered across sequences; enriched in predicted disorder (low pLDDT) and at starts/ends of helices or coil linkers; variable coverage from single sites to many peaks; only occasional weak signals inside well‑ordered helices; rarely aligns with catalytic motifs
Exemplars: - Centrosomal scaffold/adaptor (Flattop): isolated peaks in N‑terminal coil and within an annotated disordered C‑terminal region.
- PP2A regulatory subunit (TAP46): strongest signal in a compositionally biased, disordered C‑terminal segment, with additional scattered peaks including one in a stable helix.
- Protein lysine methyltransferase (eEF1A‑KMT4): peak in an N‑terminal low‑confidence helix; minor peaks near, but not on, catalytic/consensus motifs, consistent with flexible termini or helix edges.
- Toxin–antitoxin antitoxin (MazE family): peaks at the linker between alpha helices and within moderate‑confidence helical segments.
- Bacterial transcriptional repressor (NRR homolog): highest peak at the start of a long helix immediately following a disordered N‑terminus (order–disorder transition).
- Actin capping protein inhibitor (CARMIL‑like): multiple peaks confined to annotated disordered, low‑pLDDT regions; little overlap with the structured interaction module.

Summary: Short, intrinsically disordered C‑terminal tails of secreted or membrane‑associated proteins (from microproteins to larger multi‑pass enzymes) and viral accessory microproteins, typically low‑complexity and enriched in proline and basic residues, often immediately downstream of a hydrophobic signal/transmembrane segment; can include cysteine‑rich patches in secreted/toxin peptides.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 10–30 aa windows, most frequently at the extreme C‑terminus; often spans a brief helix that transitions into coil with peak signal in the disordered coil; commonly adjacent to a hydrophobic (signal/TM) segment and characterized by low pLDDT; can also occur in short cytosolic juxtamembrane loops of larger multi‑pass proteins.
Exemplars:
- Oomycete RxLR secreted effectors: activation on the C‑terminal tail immediately following a predicted hydrophobic segment, in a low‑confidence helix/coil region.
- Human ST20 (apoptosis/stress‑related microprotein): activation on a short C‑terminal helix‑to‑coil, highly disordered stretch.
- Small uncharacterized microproteins: activation confined to the last ~10–15 residues forming a disordered coil tail.
- Viral accessory/viroporin‑like proteins: activation on basic/proline‑rich cytosolic C‑tails adjacent to a single‑pass TM helix; also applies to non‑TM viral accessory proteins with disordered C‑tails (e.g., Vif).
- Small secreted cysteine‑rich toxins/defensin‑like peptides: activation on short cationic/cysteine‑biased segments within the mature or processing tail.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: activation on a conserved, short, disordered C‑terminal regulatory segment in these small mitochondrial/bacterial proteins.
- Multi‑pass membrane enzymes (e.g., phytoene dehydrogenase): activation on short cytosolic C‑terminal or juxtamembrane tails adjacent to TM helices.

Summary: Generic short beta-strand (and immediately strand-adjacent loop) segments enriched in hydrophobic/small residues, marking well-ordered sheet elements across diverse proteins and folds rather than catalytic motifs
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks in short local clusters (typically 1–5 residues per protein); most peaks fall within DSSP ‘E’ beta-strands (high pLDDT) or the short coil linking adjacent strands; avoids signal/transit peptides, transmembranes, and active-site residues; biased toward I/L/V/F/M/Y with G/A and occasional S/T
Exemplars: - Peroxiredoxin (thioredoxin-like fold): peaks on a beta-strand within the core domain and a residue just before an N-terminal strand; no activation at catalytic cysteines.
- Acyl-CoA thioesterase: peaks at G/V within high-confidence beta-strands of the enzyme core.
- D,D-transpeptidase/penicillin-binding protein: peaks on an alanine within a catalytic-domain beta-strand and a nearby loop; not on the active-site serine; recurrent highlighting of an N-terminal periplasmic R–G–I strand motif.
- Apolipoprotein N-acyltransferase (Lnt; CN hydrolase domain): peaks on beta-strands within the C-terminal CN-hydrolase fold.
- CN hydrolase/nitrilase-family amidase: peaks on a leucine in a beta-strand and a serine in the short coil between adjacent strands.
- TRAPP complex subunit: localized peak on the N-terminal beta-strand of the subunit.

Summary: Non-membrane α‑helical secondary structure—especially amphipathic/polar helices and their capping/turn residues—across diverse soluble proteins; generally avoids β‑strands and hydrophobic signal/TM segments
Activation pattern: Regional/domain-level activation along α‑helical stretches with many medium peaks across helix-rich regions; residue-level preference for charged/polar positions (E, D, K, R, S, T, N, Q) and helix caps/turns (including some G/P); sparse on β‑strands and low on hydrophobic signal peptides/transmembrane helices; can cover large fractions of helix-dense proteins
Exemplars: - ER oxidoreductases (Ero1-like FAD-dependent oxidases): strong activation on multiple soluble α‑helices of the oxidase core, including helices around the catalytic disulfide; weak on the N‑terminal signal peptide and N‑glycosylation sequons.
- Viral structural/replication proteins: activation across helical bundles and coiled-coil segments common in capsid, nucleoprotein, and polymerase subdomains.
- Type III secretion system effectors/virulence factors: activation on amphipathic, charged α‑helical regions and helical cores rather than β‑rich elements.
- CRISPR Cas13a endoribonucleases: activation on α‑helices within HEPN domains and helical linkers.
- Plant cell-wall galacturonosyltransferases: activation on luminal/catalytic α‑helices of GT domains, weaker on β‑strands.
- Eukaryotic cytoskeleton/mitotic apparatus proteins: activation on soluble coiled-coils and helical stalk/rod regions.
- Nucleic acid metabolism/binding proteins: activation on α‑helical subdomains that present charged, solvent-exposed faces for RNA/DNA or protein interactions.

Summary: Residue-level signal for functionally critical sites in structured catalytic/ligand-binding pockets, with a strong bias toward metal- and phosphate/nucleotide-interacting chemistry (acid/base catalytic residues, metal coordinators, and immediately adjacent pocket residues); in non-enzymes, it highlights conserved polar residues lining ligand/cofactor-binding microenvironments.
Activation pattern: Sharp, residue-level peaks clustered within annotated catalytic domains and their active-site loops/strands/helices; minimal in disordered regions; multiple peaks when proteins contain repeated catalytic modules; occasional scattered peaks on conserved polar residues within transmembrane helices that form ligand-binding/activation sites.
Exemplars: - Tubulin polyglutamylases (TTLL/TTL domain): peaks on ATP-binding and Mg2+-coordinating residues and the catalytically essential glutamate/glutamine positions within the TTL domain; no signal in disordered tails.
- Receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatases (PTP domain): peaks over the catalytic pocket (e.g., WPD-loop Asp and neighboring secondary structure) and substrate-trapping region; weak outside the catalytic domain.
- PP2C (PPM-type Ser/Thr phosphatases): peak on Mn2+-binding Glu and other residues across the catalytic core.
- Inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatases: focused, low-level peaks within “Catalytic 1/2” segments, including catalytic Asp.
- PLD-family phosphodiesterases/exonucleases (e.g., PLD3): peaks on HxK active-site motifs in both PLD repeats and adjacent β-strands.
- RNase II/Dis3-like 3′–5′ exonucleases: strong peaks on acidic metal-binding triad (Asp) and a nearby helix in the nuclease active site.
- Class A GPCR/Vomeronasal receptors: scattered peaks at conserved polar residues within transmembrane helices and cytosolic helix consistent with ligand/ion-binding or activation micro-switches.
- Frataxin/CyaY: peaks on a conserved β-strand/turn surface adjacent to the functional acidic ridge implicated in iron handling, marking a functional binding surface.

Summary: Short tyrosine‑centred short linear motifs in exposed loops/low‑complexity segments, typically featuring a G–x–Y pattern (often within G/P/S/T‑rich stretches) that act as recognition/ligand‑contact sites. These include PY‑like interaction motifs and GxY‑bearing loop tips used for metal or carbohydrate engagement, explaining activation across cupredoxins/CuA domains, secreted enzymes, and cytosolic trafficking/regulatory proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks that occur in small local clusters around the G–x–Y (or related PY/Y‑based) motif; mapped to solvent‑exposed loops, flexible linkers, and cytosolic tails rather than whole domains; multiple short clusters can appear per protein.
Exemplars: - Multicopper oxidases (ceruloplasmin/laccases): activation on cupredoxin‑like loop segments near copper‑ligating sites that include GxY/PY‑like turns.
- Cytochrome c oxidase/quinol oxidase subunit II (CuA domain): activation on the periplasmic CuA‑binding loop adjacent to the Cys–Cys motif, where a GxY‑rich loop supports the metal site.
- Cupredoxin family (azurin/plastocyanin/rusticyanin): activation on short loop tips abutting the metal‑binding pocket containing GxY/GPY patterns.
- Complement/alpha‑2‑macroglobulin‑like proteins (C3/C4/A2M): activation on flexible, acidic G/P/S/T‑rich loops near the thioester/bait regions that frequently harbor GxY/PY‑like motifs.
- Carbohydrate‑active enzymes (glycosidases, transferases, lyases, CBMs): activation on aromatic Tyr‑bearing surface loops that contact sugars, often arranged as GxY within low‑complexity stretches.
- HECT‑type E3 ligases and PY‑motif interactors (including viral late‑domain proteins): activation on PPxY/PY‑like motifs embedded in proline/glycine‑rich regions.
- TRAPP complex subunits and other secretory‑pathway factors: activation on short Y‑based interaction/sorting motifs within disordered linkers.
- Fungal velvet regulators: activation on gly/ser/thr‑rich linker loops within the velvet domain region containing local GxY peaks.
- Cilia/flagella‑associated scaffolds: activation on proline/glycine‑rich low‑complexity segments with Y‑centred SLiMs used for protein‑protein contacts.

Summary: Surface-exposed loop/turn motifs at beta-strand–loop junctions within extracellular Ig-like and Fibronectin type III beta-sandwich domains, which form adhesion and receptor–ligand interfaces in secreted/type I membrane proteins; enriched for Asn and Ser/Thr and other small/polar or acidic residues; recurring across tandem Ig/FnIII repeats and occasionally in analogous loops of other extracellular modules.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in short segments (typically 2–5 residues) within loops connecting beta-strands, often toward the C-terminal portion of individual Ig/FnIII domains. Frequent biphasic shape with a main peak followed by a smaller one two residues downstream. Multiple discrete peaks per protein reflecting repeated Ig/FnIII modules. Rarely activates in signal peptides, transmembranes, or cytosolic regions; may mark strand-to-coil transitions and flexible, lower-confidence regions. Not strictly tied to annotated glycosylation sites despite Asn enrichment.
Exemplars: - IgSF cell adhesion molecules (e.g., L1/NCAM/contactins/DSCAM): peaks on loop regions between beta-strands in each Ig-like domain used for cell–cell adhesion.
- Receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatases (PTPR family such as PTPRμ/δ/σ): activation across loops in extracellular Ig and FnIII repeats; limited or no signal in the MAM module itself.
- Receptor tyrosine kinases with Ig/FnIII ectodomains (VEGFR/PDGFR/FGFR): loop/turn segments in ligand-binding Ig-like modules.
- Axon guidance receptors and ligands (DCC/UNC5/ROBO/Neogenin): loop turns within Ig/FnIII repeats that mediate guidance cue recognition.
- Type I/II cytokine receptors and viral cytokine decoys: FnIII loop regions at cytokine-binding interfaces.
- Phage structural proteins with FnIII-like inserts (e.g., tail tube proteins): C-terminal strand-to-coil junctions of FnIII domains.
- Secreted bacterial enzymes with FnIII accessory modules: exposed loops on FnIII-like inserts adjoining catalytic domains.
- LRR ectodomain proteins: occasional activation on solvent-exposed loop segments that serve as interaction surfaces.

Summary: A mature extracytoplasmic/lumenal domain signature: the feature activates on structured loops and adjacent β/coil segments of secreted or periplasmic proteins (including surface-anchored enzymes), especially around catalytic and metal-binding pockets, while ignoring signal peptides, transmembranes, cytosolic tails, and low-confidence/disordered regions.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks clustered across the mature extracellular/periplasmic domain (typically 8–20 sites per protein), enriched on short loops that connect secondary-structure elements and on nearby β/coil residues; frequent hits on small/hydrophobic and Gly, with Asp/Glu and Ser/Thr common at the peaks; no activation in signal peptides/propeptides, transmembrane segments, or disordered N-terminal regions.
Exemplars: - Sortase A extracellular catalytic domains: peaks on loops immediately flanking the catalytic His–Cys–Arg machinery and neighboring β-strands; no activation in the N‑terminal TM/cytosolic region.
- Staphylococcal nuclease domains: sparse peaks within the structured mature nuclease, including a Ca2+-binding Asp in a β-strand/loop; absent from signal peptide and propeptide.
- Copper cuproproteins/cupredoxins (e.g., CopI-like): peaks in loops that border Cu-binding sites (between Cys/His ligands) and at turns linking β to α; none in signal peptide or disordered tails.
- Extracellular/periplasmic superoxide dismutases: activation on solvent-exposed loops near metal/active-site surfaces within the mature periplasmic enzyme.
- Secreted/lumenal immunophilins (FKBPs/cyclophilins): activation on structured loop regions of the PPIase domain in extracytoplasmic contexts.
- Gram-positive surface/lipoprotein and cell-wall proteins (including virulence and heme/iron-acquisition factors): activation across their exposed, β-rich extracellular domains, often near ligand/catalytic motifs.
- Plant thylakoid lumen proteins: activation confined to the lumenal mature domains following transit/signal peptide cleavage.

Summary: General detector of folded, globular domains (alpha/beta cores) that sharply distinguishes ordered functional domains from low-complexity/disordered termini and linkers, independent of specific function.
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation over long, contiguous stretches spanning both helices and strands; sharp drop at inter-domain linkers and acidic/low-complexity tails; occasional local peaks at functionally important residues (e.g., metal- or DNA-contacting), but broadly marks the entire folded core.
Exemplars: - PUR-repeat nucleic acid–binding proteins (Pur-alpha): strong activation across each PUR repeat; low in flanking disordered regions.
- E2F/DP transcription factors: activation confined to the structured DNA-binding domain; minimal in disordered N- and C-terminal regions.
- dUTPases: activation across the central catalytic domain; termini with disorder show little/no activation.
- HotDog/ACOT thioesterases: activation on both HotDog domains; suppressed in the low-confidence linker between domains.
- Acetyl-CoA decarbonylase/synthase beta subunit (metalloenzyme complex): activation on the structured core with peaks near some [Ni-Fe-S]-liganding residues; complete loss over the acidic, disordered C-terminal tail.

Summary: Short, well-ordered coil/turn elements that cap or connect secondary structure elements—especially alpha-helix to beta-strand (and vice versa) junctions—i.e., helix-capping/connector motifs common across enzyme folds rather than catalytic sites
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on single residues or very short segments in high-confidence coils/turns at alpha/beta transitions; sparse, scattered activations per protein; typically outside annotated active or ligand-binding residues, sometimes adjacent to cofactor-binding loops
Exemplars: - SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase: sharp peak on a short loop (Pro-rich) connecting an alpha-helix to a beta-sheet adjacent to the SAM-binding loop
- GT8 family glycosyltransferase: multiple peaks on coil linkers between helices and strands, largely outside the catalytic domain
- 4-hydroxy-2-oxoglutarate aldolase: peaks on turns linking an alpha-helix to a beta-strand, away from the active site
- Rieske oxygenase reductase component (FAD/2Fe-2S reductase): coil linkers between alpha-helices and beta-strands in the C-terminal region, outside cofactor-binding domains
- Alpha/beta hydrolase-like enzyme: loops connecting an alpha-helix to a beta-strand near (but not at) the catalytic histidine
- Prephenate/arogenate dehydrogenase (TyrA family): a short coil-to-helix transition within the catalytic domain and additional isolated residues in coil/helix regions

Summary: Intrinsic disorder/low-complexity segments in short proteins, especially the signal peptide and propeptide regions of secreted/toxin precursors and analogous flexible regions in small regulatory/viral microproteins, rather than the structured mature peptide cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level, multi-site peaks concentrated in low-pLDDT, N-terminal and propeptide stretches; strongest near signal-peptide C-termini and adjacent prosegments in prepropeptides; in nonsecreted microproteins, scattered across intrinsically disordered regions with no specific secondary-structure dependence.
Exemplars: - Conotoxin-like peptide precursors (venom prepropeptides): activation on the signal peptide and N-/C-terminal propeptides, peaking near cleavage boundaries, with little on the mature disulfide-rich toxin.
- cAMP-dependent protein kinase inhibitors (PKI isoforms): scattered peaks across intrinsically disordered regions of these short inhibitory microproteins.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins: activation over short, low-complexity N-termini and other disordered segments.
- Short secreted peptide/hormone/toxin precursors broadly: signal peptides and pro-sequences highlighted rather than the folded mature peptide.
- Human testis-associated or lncRNA-derived microproteins: activation across Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly–enriched disordered stretches.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments enriched in polar/charged small residues (especially S/T/Q/E/P/G/K/R, often including Q‑rich/poly‑Q tracts), used as flexible regulatory/linker regions (e.g., phosphorylation clusters and activation domains) rather than structured domains; can also include short acidic/polar low‑complexity linkers within otherwise folded proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation spanning long IDRs with multiple broad peaks and occasional residue‑level spikes over S/T clusters or Q‑runs; minimal activation within well‑folded domains (e.g., BTB, zinc fingers); also detects short low‑complexity linkers between domains (e.g., in two‑component response regulators); widespread coverage across large scaffold proteins and also present in small IDPs/propeptides.
Exemplars: - BTB‑zinc finger transcription factors (e.g., Broad‑complex): strong activation across long disordered, low‑complexity activation/linker regions; no activation in folded BTB or C2H2 domains.
- Centrosomal/Golgi coiled‑coil scaffolds (e.g., golgins, pericentrin/AKAPs): activation on S/T/Q‑rich low‑complexity tracts within and flanking coiled‑coil regions.
- Rab/vesicle‑trafficking effectors and TBC‑domain GAPs: activation on disordered linkers and serine/threonine‑rich low‑complexity segments between domains.
- Cytoskeletal motors (kinesin/dynein/myosin): activation on disordered tails and low‑complexity coiled‑coil–adjacent regions.
- Secreted neuropeptide/prohormone precursors: activation in low‑complexity propeptide/spacer regions around cleavage sites (not in hydrophobic signal peptides or cysteine‑rich mature domains).
- Nuclear/chromatin regulators and coactivators: activation on acidic/Q‑rich and S/T‑rich activation domains and flexible linkers.
- Viral regulatory proteins (transactivators/host modulators): broad activation across acidic/Q‑rich disordered regions typical of viral IDPs.
- Bacterial two‑component response regulators (e.g., FixJ): activation limited to short acidic/polar low‑complexity linkers between receiver and DNA‑binding domains.

Summary: Short, flexible N‑terminal segments of the mature chain (post–signal peptide when present), typically 15–30 residues, enriched in Gly/Pro and charged residues and often including cysteines (e.g., N‑glycosylation sequons or disulfide‑forming residues). These correspond to loop/finger elements at the start of small disulfide‑rich extracellular domains (e.g., LY6/three‑finger folds) and, more generally, to intrinsically disordered or mixed‑secondary‑structure N‑terminal tails/linkers that precede the first well‑structured domain across diverse proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on one or a few short contiguous windows near the start of the mature protein; sharp local peaks within these windows; little/no signal on signal peptides or on well‑packed catalytic cores; can recur as separate local peaks in large, multidomain proteins.
Exemplars: - LY6/uPAR domain proteins and snake three‑finger toxins: activation on an N‑terminal “finger/loop” segment within the disulfide‑rich three‑finger fold of the mature extracellular domain.
- KEOPS/EKC subunit GON7: activation on the intrinsically disordered N‑terminal tail (β–helix–coil mix; low pLDDT) spanning residues ~14–52.
- Bacterial pullulanase and other CAZy hydrolases: activation on an early N‑terminal mixed‑structure/linker region of the mature enzyme (after the signal peptide), not on the catalytic core.
- Ponticulin‑like GPI‑anchored/adhesion proteins: activation begins exactly at an N‑linked glycosylation sequon within the extracellular N‑terminal segment of the mature chain.
- Ribosomal proteins (small/large subunits): activation on basic, flexible N‑terminal tails that contact rRNA.
- Prokaryotic toxin–antitoxin/CRISPR components: activation on short, low‑complexity N‑terminal segments or interdomain linkers.
- Plant/fungal secreted defense/adhesion proteins: activation on cysteine‑rich N‑terminal stretches adjacent to secretion signals in small secreted proteins.

Summary: Aromatic-rich beta-strand edge motifs centered on tyrosine—typically YY, YxY, or YD—found in beta-rich repeat modules and compact beta-domains. The feature marks the tyrosyl (and nearby F/W/H) positions that recur across YD/Rhs repeats, chitin-binding R&R domains, WW domains, and phage tail-fiber beta-solenoids, and can occasionally register adjacent positions in analogous short beta-strands (e.g., in IMP/PAP phosphatases and the WRKY domain).
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks on aromatic residues (Y > F/W, sometimes H), often flanked by acidic D/E (e.g., YD). Peaks occur in short 3–6 aa windows within a beta-strand or at a strand-to-coil junction and repeat periodically across long repeat arrays, producing clustered activation tracts. Occasionally the peak falls on a neighboring non-aromatic residue within the same short beta-strand segment.
Exemplars: - Rhs/YD-repeat polymorphic toxins (T6SS-associated): periodic strong peaks on the Y of each YD repeat at beta-strand–to–coil edges across the repeat region.
- Arthropod cuticle proteins (chitin-binding R&R domain): sharp peaks on strand tyrosine/phenylalanine residues within the R&R motif that contact chitin.
- WW-domain proteins (e.g., PRP40 family): peaks on YY motifs embedded in beta-strands of WW modules.
- Phage long-tail fiber/receptor-binding proteins: multiple short peaks on F/Y at strand–coil transitions dispersed along the beta-solenoid fiber.
- Plant WRKY transcription factors: peaks on the WRKY-domain tyrosine (WRKYGQK region) and nearby Y/C positions within the domain.
- Inositol monophosphatase/PAP phosphatases: isolated weak activation on a short beta-strand segment not tied to annotated catalytic sites.

Summary: A glycine-biased structural micro-motif: short coil/turn residues that cap an α-helix and link it to a following β-strand (helix C-cap/helix→β linker), acting as a flexible hinge. This occurs in conserved regions across diverse proteins—especially Sm/LSm-like folds and nucleic acid machinery—but is a general structural motif rather than family-specific.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks in 1–3 residue hotspots, strongest on Gly and sometimes adjacent acidic/polar residues (Asp/Glu/Asn). The activated sites are coils/turns between defined secondary structures, most often at an α-helix C-terminus leading into a β-strand or immediately preceding a β-strand. Frequently near N-terminal segments in Sm/LSm proteins; otherwise appears as short local clusters in conserved regions.
Exemplars: - Fpg/Nei/Neil DNA glycosylases (Endonuclease 8): Gly residues in N-terminal helix→β turns (e.g., tight loops after an α-helix that feed into a β-strand).
- Trigger factor chaperone (FKBP-type PPIase domain): Gly/acidic residues in coil loops within the PPIase fold.
- DNA-directed RNA polymerase β′ subunit: a conserved glycine-centered loop bridging a short helix and adjacent elements, between Zn-binding cysteines.
- Riboflavin kinase (RibR): a Gly (± acidic neighbor) in the loop immediately preceding a β-strand.
- Sm/LSm core proteins (e.g., LSM8): N-terminal helix–β1 linker in the Sm domain.
- Decapping enhancer EDC3 (Sm-like protein): Gly in the N-terminal Sm-like region involved in DCP1A/P-body interactions.
- Ataxin-2 family (LSm/LSmAD region): Gly in the coil between the N-terminal helix and first β-strand of the Sm-like module.
- Cohesin regulator PDS5: a Gly in a helix→β turn acting as a hinge at the edge of a structured island within a disordered region.

Summary: Hydrophobic residues in alpha-helical membrane-spanning segments (transmembrane helices and signal peptide hydrophobic cores) of integral membrane proteins, with frequent emphasis on aromatic anchors at helix cores or membrane interfaces
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks concentrated within or at the boundaries of annotated/predicted alpha-helical transmembrane segments and N-terminal signal peptides; multiple peaks per protein with occasional single sharp peaks; strong bias toward hydrophobic/aromatic residues; minimal activation in loops or disordered regions
Exemplars: - Class A GPCRs (e.g., octopamine/adrenergic-like receptors): peaks on Phe/Leu within TM helices (notably TM6, plus TM2, TM5, TM7), with minor spillover into short cytoplasmic loops.
- ABC-type drug efflux permease subunits: a single prominent Ile within a TM helix of the ABC transmembrane domain, with weaker peaks on other helical residues.
- Mitochondrial TOM complex receptor subunits (TOM22): a Tyr peak near the C-terminal end of the single-pass TM anchor (membrane-interface aromatic anchor), minor activation in an N-terminal helix.
- SLC38 sodium-coupled neutral amino acid transporters: multiple peaks within and at the edges of TM helices (e.g., Gly/Phe/Leu sites), including helix starts/ends.
- Bacterial nodulation/secretion-associated proteins: peaks in helical regions including the hydrophobic core of the N-terminal signal peptide; absent from disordered C-terminal segments.

Summary: Amphipathic, membrane-inserting segments (often long helices) that bind, perturb, or fuse lipid bilayers; typically adjacent to activation cleavages or fusion peptides and distinct from canonical transmembrane helices or coiled-coil heptad repeats. Includes pre-hairpin segments of β-pore-forming toxins that form β-barrel pores upon insertion.
Activation pattern:
- Regional activation across long, contiguous amphipathic segments enriched in Leu/Ile/Val/Ala with small polar residues (Thr/Ser/Gln/Asn), frequently predicted helical but not strictly so.
- Frequently turns on immediately downstream of proteolytic cleavage or fusion-peptide regions, spanning the membrane-active stem/insertion block; drops at the onset of coiled-coil HRs and within transmembrane helices.
- Strongest in secreted or processed precursors; tolerant of scattered glycosylation within the segment; generally silent in cytosolic tails except for minor patches.
- In viral class I fusion proteins, peaks on the fusion-peptide–proximal stem/immunosuppressive region and is off on the fusion peptide proper, HR coiled-coils, and the TM helix.
Exemplars:
- Viral class I fusion glycoproteins (retroviral gp41, paramyxovirus F, influenza HA2, coronavirus S2): activation on the extracellular stem/immunosuppressive region immediately C‑terminal to the fusion peptide; not on HR coiled-coils or the TM helix.
- Bacillus thuringiensis Cry/Cyt pore-forming toxins: activation on amphipathic insertion helices of the membrane-inserting bundle (domain I).
- Type III secretion translocon components (YopB/YopD, IpaB/IpaC, PopB/PopD): activation on amphipathic insertion helices assembling the host-cell pore.
- Perforin/MACPF and cholesterol-dependent cytolysins: activation on helical TMH regions that refold into membrane-inserting β-hairpins during pore formation.
- β-pore-forming toxins (staphylococcal α-hemolysin/leukocidins, including γ-hemolysin): activation on amphipathic pre-stem/insertion segments that become β-hairpins in the pore.
- Gasdermins: activation on amphipathic, membrane-binding segments within the N‑terminal pore-forming domain.
- Antimicrobial peptides/proteins (e.g., cathelicidins, cecropins): activation along long amphipathic segments that disrupt membranes.
- Apolipoprotein L and other lipid-interacting apolipoproteins: activation on amphipathic segments that associate with lipids or form channels.
- Magnetosome-associated inner membrane proteins: activation on small amphipathic helices mediating bilayer association.
- Viral/phage penetration/lysis helpers and bacterial exotoxin translocators: activation on membrane-penetrating segments used for entry or translocation.
- Mitochondrial fusion machinery (mitofusins/OPA1): activation on juxtamembrane amphipathic helices that engage mitochondrial membranes.

Summary: Short Trp–Ser/Thr–centered turn/loop motifs at β-strand boundaries—typified by the extracellular WSXWS motif of class I cytokine receptors—and their generalization to Ser/Thr-rich, often Pro-adjacent coils at the C-terminal edge of β-sandwich domains (Ig/FnIII/C2/Velvet) and adjacent linkers
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on Ser/Thr within short coils/turns (≈3–7 aa) often flanked by Trp (W–S/T or WSXWS), frequently at the C-terminal boundary of extracellular β-sandwich modules or interdomain linkers; can appear as sharp localized peaks inside structured β-turns of other β-sandwich domains; occasionally extends over longer S/Thr-rich low-complexity stretches when multiple W–S/T pairs are present
Exemplars: - Class I interleukin/cytokine receptors: activates on the canonical WSXWS motif and neighboring membrane-proximal linker in the extracellular module
- Ig superfamily Fc receptors/Fc receptor-like proteins: peaks in the coil immediately C-terminal to Ig-like C2 domains, centered on Ser/Thr and near Trp, often preceding glycosylated regions
- Other Ig-like immune receptors: similar activation at β-strand-to-linker transitions around W–S/T patterns
- C2-domain/exocytosis machinery and ferlin family: localized activation at β-strand/loop boundaries within C2 β-sandwiches where W–S/T pairs occur
- Ubiquitin-pathway components (E3 ligases/adaptors/DUBs): short W–S/T-centered turns in flexible linkers or β-hairpins
- Secreted microbial enzymes/adhesins/toxins: activation across Ser/Thr- and Pro-rich extracellular segments when sporadic Trp creates repeated W–S/T pairs
- Fungal Velvet-domain regulators: sharp peak on a Ser in a β-turn between strands within the Velvet β-sandwich
- Lipid signaling/metabolic enzymes: isolated W–S/T motifs in surface loops

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered Gly/Pro/Thr‑rich segments (flexible linkers and repeat‑stalk regions) characterized by GG/GP motifs and clusters of charged residues; widely used in secreted/surface proteins and in nucleic‑acid–associated/enzymatic proteins, with occasional W‑rich patches in fibrinogen‑like/lectin contexts
Activation pattern: Regional activation on mid‑chain low‑complexity stretches (≈10–50 aa), peaking over runs of G, P, and T (GG, GP, poly‑T) and adjacent basic/acidic clusters; typically internal but can occur later in long precursors; W‑rich peaks appear in fibrinogen/lectin‑type regions
Exemplars: - Gram‑positive adhesins and secretion/assembly components (sortase‑anchored surface proteins, pili/fimbrial and secretion system parts): activation on Thr‑rich and Gly/Pro‑rich repeat stalks and flexible interdomain linkers
- CRISPR‑associated RAMP proteins and endoribonucleases (Cas7/Csm/Cmr/Cas13): activation on Gly/Pro‑containing, often basic low‑complexity loops adjacent to RNA‑binding surfaces
- Peptidyl‑prolyl isomerases (cyclophilins/FKBPs): activation on Pro/Gly‑rich loops and disordered N/C‑terminal tails flanking the catalytic core
- PP2C/PPM phosphatases: activation on long acidic/basic low‑complexity inserts and termini outside the metal‑dependent catalytic domain
- Cu‑Zn superoxide dismutases: activation on Gly‑rich surface loops including the copper‑binding GGH/HGGH loop and nearby flexible segments; in secreted forms, also low‑complexity pro/signal‑proximal regions
- Fibrinogen/fibrinogen‑like lectins and secreted cytokines/growth factors: activation on mucin‑like S/T‑rich stalks and W‑rich patches preceding the structured domain
- DNA repair/replication and other nucleic‑acid‑binding proteins: activation on Gly‑rich/basic disordered tails and linkers that mediate nucleic‑acid contacts
- Phage tail/structural proteins: activation on Gly‑Gly/Pro‑rich flexible linkers and threonine‑rich repeats within tail fibers and accessory modules

Summary: Residue-level detector for well-ordered beta-strand positions in beta-sheet–rich domains, most prominently in immunoglobulin-like (V- and C2-set) modules of extracellular proteins, but generalizing to other beta-sandwich/jelly-roll and related beta-sheet folds (arrestin, SPRY/B30.2, cupin, ferredoxin-like). Activated residues are often polar/charged, reflecting side chains accommodated within or along beta-strands rather than loops or helices.
Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks (a few positions per domain) concentrated on beta-strands with high structural confidence (DSSP E). In Ig-like domains, peaks commonly occur on the C-terminal strand around positions ~130–150 and sometimes on the N-terminal strand (~20–40). Minimal to no activation in signal peptides, transmembrane helices, or disordered cytosolic tails; peaks typically do not coincide with catalytic/cofactor-binding sites.
Exemplars: - Immunoglobulin-superfamily receptors/adhesion molecules (e.g., butyrophilins, TREM receptors, CAR/CTX family, myelin protein zero-like, TIM/HAVCR2): activation on beta-strands within V- or C2-type Ig-like domains, often on the C-terminal strand.
- Butyrophilin SPRY/B30.2 domain: additional peaks on a beta-strand within this beta-sandwich.
- Arrestin family scaffolds: peaks on beta-strands in the arrestin beta-sandwich domains.
- 2Fe-2S adrenodoxin/ferredoxin-like proteins: peaks on beta-strands of the ferredoxin fold, away from [2Fe-2S]-binding cysteines.
- Acireductone dioxygenase (cupin superfamily): peaks on adjacent arginines within a beta-strand of the jelly-roll barrel.

Summary: A short, surface‑exposed β‑strand/turn (β‑hairpin/edge‑strand) motif characteristic of cystatin‑like domains and widely reused in small β‑rich extracellular/periplasmic proteins; often includes the cystatin L2 Pro–Trp hairpin and basic/aromatic residues, serving as a protease‑binding/inhibitory loop in cystatins and propeptides and as an analogous interaction loop in other β‑sandwich–type folds.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on 20–40 aa windows centered on a β‑strand and its immediately flanking loop/turn (frequently a strand→coil→strand block); sharp residue‑level peaks on the strand and adjacent turn; low on long helices, intrinsically disordered segments, and transmembrane helices; commonly in secreted/periplasmic portions and near disulfide‑bonded cysteines; enriched for Pro/Trp and Lys/Arg alongside Gly/Pro motifs.
Exemplars: - Cathelicidin precursors (cathelin/cystatin‑like proregions): activation over the central β‑sheet core and flanking loops of the cathelin domain, including disulfide‑proximal residues.
- Papain‑family cysteine protease zymogens (e.g., streptopain/SpeB): a single hotspot within the ordered propeptide β‑strand/coil segment that occludes the active site; catalytic domain remains inactive.
- Cell‑wall–associated secreted/periplasmic regulators with a single transmembrane helix: selective activation on extracellular β‑strands and adjacent turns near the C‑terminus; absent in the TM and cytosolic regions.
- Gas vesicle structural proteins (GvpO): activation confined to a C‑terminal helix–strand–turn–strand block centered on an edge β‑strand, with earlier β‑strands and disordered N‑termini remaining off.

Summary: Detector of long tandem-repeat architectures and their stereotyped inter-repeat linkers in very large proteins. The feature turns on over arrays of repeated modules (e.g., C2H2 fingers, CCP/Sushi domains, cohesins, RTX/hemolysin repeats, PbH1 beta-helix blocks) and commonly their short, glycine/acidic/polar linkers, emphasizing the secondary-structure cores within each unit and the canonical linker motifs that connect them, while de-emphasizing unrelated domains, metal-binding cysteines, and transmembrane/cytosolic tails.
Activation pattern: - Domain-level: Silent in nonrepeat modules (e.g., KRAB, CBM3, signal peptides, transmembranes), then near-continuous activation across long repeat arrays; often drops after the final repeat. Peaks frequently occur at or just before repeat boundaries.
- Residue-level: Preference for positions forming repeat cores (recognition helices or beta-strands; often hydrophobic/aromatic) and hallmark linker motifs enriched in S/T/E/G/K/P (e.g., TGEKP/Y between C2H2 fingers; GGXGXD in RTX). Metal-binding/disulfide cysteines (Zn-coordinating Cys/His; CCP disulfides) are consistently downweighted.
- Regional: Disordered, compositionally biased tracts are highlighted when they serve as repeat/linker belts within the array, but generic low-complexity segments outside such architectures can be suppressed.
Exemplars: - C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factors: strong activation across each finger’s recognition helix and the TGEKP/Y inter-finger linkers; low on Zn-coordinating Cys/His; KRAB N-termini inactive.
- Complement control protein (Sushi/CCP) domain arrays in complement receptors: high on hydrophobic beta-strands within CCP modules; low on disulfide cysteines; transmembrane helix and cytosolic tail off.
- RTX/hemolysin-type calcium-binding repeat proteins (e.g., FrpC, alginate epimerases): periodic peaks at GGXGXD and conserved hydrophobic/S/T positions within each RTX unit; activation falls after the last repeat.
- Cellulosomal scaffoldins: cohesive activation across cohesin domain arrays and their boundary linkers; N-terminal CBM domains largely inactive.
- Right-handed beta-helix (PbH1) repeat enzymes (alginate C5-epimerases): strong, contiguous signal across PbH1 blocks and associated hemolysin-type repeats; polar disordered linkers between repeats also elevated.
- Secreted mucin-like glycoproteins: accentuation of long S/T/N-rich, low-complexity disordered regions and their edges that function as linker belts.
- Telomere-associated nuclear megaprotiens: preference for hydrophobic secondary-structure blocks (repeat-like modules), with suppression over isolated low-complexity tracts.

Summary: Exposed beta‑strand face motif in extracellular beta‑rich ectodomains—especially Ig-, cadherin-, FnIII/PKD/MAM, CBM, beta‑helix/propeller scaffolds—characterized by Gly–Tyr and Tyr–(small/hydrophobic) repeats that form adhesive/ligand‑binding surfaces on secreted and cell‑surface proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks that pick alternating positions along beta strands (i, i+2, i+4), creating short runs within strands and clusters repeated across multiple ectodomains in long, modular proteins; strong in secreted/extracellular regions and largely absent from transmembrane helices and cytosolic tails; enriched for Tyr/Phe, Gly, small/hydrophobic (V/I/L, S/T) and depleted in basic residues; number of hits scales with repeat content and ectodomain length.
Exemplars: - Cadherins (classical cadherin EC repeats): alternating picks along E‑strands within cadherin domains, strongest on Tyr/Gly positions; no signal in the single-pass TM helix or cytoplasmic tail.
- Ig‑superfamily CAMs and class I/II cytokine receptors: recurrent D–G–Y or Y–(small) motifs on the sheet face of Ig-like and cytokine receptor homology domains that contact ligands.
- Fibronectin type III, PKD, and MAM modules in extracellular receptors/GPI‑anchored scaffolds: repeated strand‑face activations across beta‑sandwich modules mediating cell–cell/matrix adhesion.
- Bacterial carbohydrate‑active enzymes (glycoside hydrolases/polysaccharide lyases): clusters on beta‑strands and adjacent loops of CBMs and catalytic domains where aromatic residues line carbohydrate‑binding surfaces.
- Phage tailspike/tail fiber/baseplate/decoration proteins: runs along beta‑solenoid/beta‑helix rungs enriched in G–Y or Y–(small/hydrophobic) patterns used for host surface recognition.
- Prokaryotic S‑layer and outer cell‑wall adhesins: broad activation across beta‑rich surface modules with GY/Yx repeats.
- Secreted matrix‑targeting proteases (e.g., collagenases, gingipains): signal concentrated in accessory beta‑rich domains (Ig/FnIII/PKD/hemopexin-like) rather than the catalytic protease core.

Summary: Charged, amphipathic alpha-helical segments (often coiled-coil or assembly helices) characterized by Lys/Glu-rich patterning and used as protein–protein or macromolecular interaction surfaces across diverse proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation on a single contiguous helix of ~15–40 residues with strong center-heavy peaks; prefers sequences enriched in alternating acidic/basic residues (Lys/Glu) consistent with amphipathic/coiled-coil helices; typically well structured (high pLDDT); occurs independently of overall domain or taxonomy and is common in secreted/extracellular and structural proteins
Exemplars: - Gram-positive superantigen/enterotoxin family: activation on a defined alpha-helix within the sialyl-Lewis X–binding region (assembly/interaction helix)
- HORMA family proteins (MAD2/REV7/ATG101): activation on internal helical elements of the HORMA fold implicated in protein–protein interactions
- Intermediate filaments and lamins: activation on coiled-coil rod segments mediating dimerization/assembly
- Fibrinogen/fibrinogen-like and angiopoietin(-related) proteins: activation on N-terminal coiled-coils required for oligomerization
- Viral structural proteins (bacteriophage tail and capsid components): activation on coiled-coil/assembly helices used in particle/tail formation
- Plant JAZ/TIFY and NDR1/HIN1-like proteins: activation on coiled-coil or amphipathic helices mediating dimerization/signaling
- Ribosomal proteins (cytosolic/mitochondrial/chloroplastic): activation on basic amphipathic helices that contact rRNA
- Protein translocase SecD/SecDF: activation on charged periplasmic helical linkers/hairpins within the large extracytoplasmic domains
- Cytochrome c biogenesis proteins: activation on soluble helical segments used in assembly/partner interactions

Summary: Short Gly/Thr-rich strand–loop–strand (β-hairpin/edge‑of‑sheet) motif, often centered on TG/KTG/GxG patterns and frequently flanked by aromatics, that forms a small, structured loop used as a catalytic/ligand‑binding microenvironment across many folds (e.g., the KTG loop of PBPs/β‑lactamases) and taxa.
Activation pattern: Short contiguous patches (~15–30 aa) that span a β‑strand–loop–β (or strand–helix–strand) unit; strongest residue‑level peaks at loop glycines/threonines (often in TG/KTG/GxG), with basic residues common and Y/F frequently flanking; typically high-confidence structure with the loop being the local activation maximum; occasionally multiple patches reflecting repeated units.
Exemplars: - Penicillin-binding proteins/β-lactamases: activation over the conserved KTG β‑hairpin at the transpeptidase active-site edge (PBP/PbpX family).
- Small alarmone synthetase/GTP pyrophosphokinase (YjbM): β‑strand–loop–β segment that forms the nucleotide-binding loop containing binding residues.
- Oxygen-evolving enhancer protein PsbP/OEE2: two adjacent β‑strands and the connecting loop; peak at the glycine-centered turn of the β‑hairpin.
- Serpin family (C1 inhibitor): paired β‑strands and the short connecting loop within the serpin fold (distinct from the reactive center loop).
- Profilin: compact β‑sheet region with short connecting coils forming the gly/thr‑rich loop on the binding surface.
- mRNA-capping enzyme β subunit (RNA triphosphatase): strand–helix–strand element with a glycine-centered turn in a well-ordered C‑terminal segment.
- TBP/TBP-like proteins: long loops connecting secondary elements within each repeat (β↔α/β), corresponding to the repeat’s sheet‑edge insertion loop involved in DNA interaction.

Summary: N-terminal processing/targeting junctions: the feature marks the C-terminal end of signal peptides or signal anchors and the immediate N-terminus of the downstream segment in exported proteins (secreted/periplasmic and organelle-targeted, e.g., mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides), typically within low-structure, compositionally biased regions enriched for small/hydrophobic residues with frequent Pro/Ser and basic residues; it also generalizes to IDR-rich N-terminal segments with similar composition in non-secretory proteins (including viral accessory proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation with peaks at N-terminal processing/targeting boundaries (last residues of the signal peptide/signal anchor/transit peptide and first residues of the mature domain), often extending 5–20 residues across the junction; additional moderate peaks at internal peptide starts in multi-peptide precursors; strongest in predicted coils/IDRs but can overlap short helices; pronounced N-terminal bias.
Exemplars:
- Neuropeptide/prohormone and toxin precursors: peaks at signal peptide/propeptide junction and at starts of individual processed peptides.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors: activation straddles the SP end and the N-terminus of the mature AMP.
- Bacterial periplasmic enzymes (e.g., beta-lactamases): activation at the signal peptide cleavage region.
- Organelle-targeted proteins (e.g., mitochondrial ribosomal proteins): activation at the transit peptide cleavage region.
- Proline-rich secreted salivary proteins: activation over the disordered, proline-biased N-terminus after SP cleavage.
- Intrinsically disordered and microproteins (including human antisense/lncRNA-derived): multiple short activations in IDR segments, often at the N-terminus.
- Viral accessory proteins (membrane or non-membrane): activation at N-terminal signal peptide/signal anchor when present, or over IDR-biased N-termini when not.

Summary: Amphipathic, interaction-prone secondary-structure segments (medium-length helices or beta-strand patches with alternating hydrophobic and charged residues) that form solvent-exposed protein–protein docking interfaces in large soluble assemblies and viral capsids; not transmembrane and often found in mid-to-C‑terminal regions.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous stretches of ~30–150 residues. Peaks align with structured amphipathic elements (coiled-coils or beta-strands interleaved with short helices/loops); some segments are preformed (high pLDDT) while others are flexible/low pLDDT and likely fold upon binding. In large proteins, activation frequently concentrates toward the C-terminus rather than the N-terminal signal/targeting regions.
Exemplars: - Mediator complex subunits (Med1/14/15/17/27): long amphipathic helical/coiled-coil regions used for subunit docking and transcription factor engagement.
- Kinetochore/centromere/spindle checkpoint proteins (e.g., KNL1-complex members): extended amphipathic helices/coiled-coils that scaffold complex assembly and partner recruitment.
- Ubiquitin system enzymes (E1/E2/E3 ligases): helical interface segments or amphipathic tails mediating E1–E2–E3 and substrate/adaptor interactions.
- ARP2/3 complex subunits: amphipathic helices at inter-subunit/regulator contact surfaces.
- Frataxin family: central beta-strand-rich sheet segment forming an exposed interaction face.
- Viral capsid/coats (phage and alphavirus capsid proteins): beta-strand patches (with short helices/loops) that mediate inter-subunit assembly interfaces.
- Bacterial type III/IV secretion effectors and chaperones/adapters: amphipathic, non-TM interface segments (often chaperone/adaptor-binding regions) used for secretion/complex formation.
- Ribosome-inactivating proteins (e.g., saporin): internal beta/helix/loop region forming an amphipathic surface implicated in protein–protein contacts, sometimes flexible until binding.

Summary: Preference for bulky hydrophobic residues occupying beta‑strand positions in well‑ordered beta‑sheet regions (sheet/core or strand‑edge) across diverse proteins; a structural, not function‑specific, signal that favors aliphatic/aromatic side chains in beta‑strands while avoiding helices, transmembranes, signal peptides, and disordered segments.
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue‑level peaks confined to beta‑strands (or immediately adjacent turn/strand‑edge positions) within high‑confidence structured regions; occasional short clusters along a single strand. Strong enrichment for Leu/Val/Ile/Phe/Tyr/Trp/Met; Gly/Pro only rarely. Little to no activation in alpha‑helices, transmembrane helices, signal peptides, or low‑confidence/disordered tails; sometimes near but not on annotated catalytic/binding residues.
Exemplars: - Mechanosensitive channel MscK: isolated L/I/V positions in beta‑strands of the C‑terminal cytoplasmic domain; no activation in TM helices.
- Lipid transport MCE/MlaD protein: periplasmic MCE domain beta‑strands (e.g., L84); absent from the N‑terminal TM helix and disordered tail.
- Cysteine desulfurase (SufS): single leucine within a C‑terminal beta‑strand, away from the catalytic cysteine.
- Peptide methionine sulfoxide reductase (MsrA/MsrB): scattered V/I residues in multiple beta‑strands of the catalytic domain.
- Aspartate‑semialdehyde dehydrogenase: beta‑strand residues adjacent to catalytic and NAD(P)+‑binding sites.
- Periplasmic oligopeptide/solute‑binding protein (SBP/AppA family): hydrophobic residues within beta‑strands across the beta‑sheet core; no signal on the signal peptide or helical regions.
- Ribonuclease P protein component: M/L/I in beta‑strands of the structured core.
- tRNA pseudouridine synthase B: hydrophobic residues in central beta‑strands; inactive at the catalytic Asp and the C‑terminal PUA domain.

Summary: Short amphipathic α‑helical surface micro‑motifs (often helix‑cap/face patches) enriched in mixed charged and aromatic residues, occurring as 3–6 residue stretches within folded domains rather than in β‑strands or long disordered regions
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on very short, contiguous runs inside α‑helices (often at N/C caps or exposed faces); little to no signal on adjacent β‑strands or extended disordered tails; multiple independent peaks recur across a protein as it traverses several helices; sequences frequently include basic/acidic residues with occasional Gly/Pro at helix boundaries and interspersed Tyr/Phe/Trp
Exemplars: - CRAL‑TRIO lipid‑binding proteins (e.g., SFH/PITP family): brief α‑helical stretches within the structured domain core (strongest peaks on 4–5 aa helices; absent on neighboring β‑strands).
- YTH‑domain m6A readers: short exposed α‑helical patches on the YTH domain surface containing charged/aromatic residues.
- Deubiquitinating enzymes (USPs/UBPs): repeated short α‑helical runs in catalytic/regulatory subdomains.
- RNase P protein components (archaea) and polymerase/helicase/nuclease subunits: basic/aromatic α‑helical surface patches implicated in nucleic‑acid engagement.
- Plant MORF/RIP RNA‑editing factors and NFU Fe–S assembly proteins: coiled‑coil/helix‑bundle faces with brief activated runs at helix caps.
- WRKY transcription factors: short helices flanking or outside the WRKY zinc‑binding core showing mixed‑charge helical patches.
- Periplasmic nitrate reductase electron‑transfer subunits (NapB, c‑type cytochromes): short amphipathic α‑helices near heme‑associated regions.

Summary: Charge-rich, solvent-exposed alpha-helical interaction surfaces (often including coiled-coils) that mediate electrostatic binding to nucleic acids and/or partner proteins; highlights helical scaffolds rather than catalytic cores
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long alpha-helices and helical linkers (frequently coiled-coil–like), with residue-level peaks biased to K/E/D (and some Y/F, S/T); depleted on beta-strands and enzymatic active-site residues; can span large portions of helical-rich domains
Exemplars: CRISPR-Cas13a endoribonucleases: activation tracks crRNA-binding and linker helices adjacent to HEPN domains while sparing catalytic H/R; Viral fusion/assembly and capsid-fiber families (e.g., hemagglutinin/fusion stalks, adenovirus fiber, coiled-coil capsid scaffolds): activation on long heptad-repeat helices mediating trimerization and virion exposure; Type III secretion and Legionella effectors: activation on acidic/basic helical segments and coiled-coil motifs used for secretion-chaperone binding and host-target engagement; Nucleic acid–binding replication/packaging proteins (nucleoproteins, helicase/loader and genome-packaging factors): activation on basic helical patches that contact RNA/DNA; Eukaryotic cytoskeletal/mitotic scaffolds (HEAT/ARM and coiled-coil repeat proteins): activation across extended alpha-solenoid/coiled-coil regions; Apicomplexan adhesins/secreted host-interaction proteins: activation on coiled-coil stems and charged helical repeats exposed to the extracellular milieu

Summary: Extracellular, luminal, or virion‑exposed ectodomains of exported proteins—including secretory‑pathway proteins, viral envelope glycoproteins, and non‑enveloped virion surface proteins—long post‑export/processing regions that are often (where applicable) disulfide‑ and N‑glycosylation‑rich, frequently low‑confidence/disordered, and typically mediate fusion/attachment or other extracytoplasmic functions
Activation pattern: Broad, domain‑level activation over hundreds of residues starting immediately after the signal peptide or other export/processing leader (e.g., propeptide, secretion signal); strongest across low‑pLDDT/disordered or coiled/helical ectodomain segments; frequent peaks at glycosylation sequons, disulfide‑forming cysteines, and mapped functional/interaction sites; activation drops before C‑terminal transmembranes and is absent from signal peptides, transmembranes, and cytosolic tails; in proteins lacking a classical signal peptide (e.g., T3SS translocators/effectors, bacteriocins, some bacterial toxins, non‑enveloped virion capsid proteins), activation spans the exported/virion‑exposed domains
Exemplars: Herpesvirus gH ectodomain—activation across the virion‑exposed region including the gL‑interaction site and N‑glycans, but not TM/cytosolic tail; HAP2/GCS1 fusogens—strong activation over the N‑terminal ectodomain (including disordered loops and disulfide networks) with peaks at fusion‑critical residues, ending before TM/cytoplasmic region; Viral fusion/attachment glycoproteins—activation on the cleaved, glycosylated external subunits of multi‑subunit precursors; ER luminal ERO1‑like oxidoreductases—activation over the N‑terminal luminal domain containing FAD‑binding residues, N‑glycan sites, and redox‑active disulfides, with reduced activation in ordered C‑terminal regions; Non‑enveloped virion surface proteins (e.g., reovirus outer/minor capsid proteins)—activation on virion‑exposed receptor‑binding regions; Bacterial secreted toxins and secretion/translocation components (e.g., aerolysin family, colicins, T3SS translocon proteins)—activation on exported protoxin/translocon domains and pro‑peptides; Phage attachment/maturation proteins—activation on tail fiber/spike ectodomains; Bacillus Cry protoxins—activation across extracellular protoxin regions that form pores after proteolysis

Summary: Edge/loop elements at the starts and ends of β-strands within β‑rich repeat scaffolds (β‑propellers, β‑solenoids/β‑grooves/“taco” folds, β‑barrels and related β‑sandwiches) that are common in extracellular/periplasmic/luminal domains of lipid‑transport/tethering and outer‑membrane/secretory biogenesis proteins, and also present in soluble cytosolic β‑rich complexes and some α/β barrel enzymes; the feature favors small/flexible residues in coil segments flanking β‑strands and highlights repeated strand‑capping/linker loops across these architectures.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks that recur many times across β‑repeat arrays, concentrating in coil segments immediately adjacent to β‑strands (coil→β or β→coil boundaries) and on exposed β‑edge/loop positions; largely absent in transmembrane helices, long disordered cytosolic tails, and glycosylation sequons.
Exemplars:
- AsmA/TamB family lipid-transport tethers: repeated β‑groove/“taco” folds; activation along periplasmic edge loops linking successive β‑strands that line the lipid conduit.
- ATG2/VPS13/BLTP rods (including SHIP164/BLTP3B): extended β‑groove repeats; activation across small, flexible loops capping adjacent β‑strands along the groove.
- Omp85 (BamA/Sam50/Toc75): periplasmic POTRA repeats and β‑barrel edges; activation on coil loops at β‑strand boundaries in POTRA domains and on exposed barrel loops.
- Secretins/two-partner secretion/CDI OM translocons: large β‑barrels with periplasmic β‑repeat domains; activation on repeated β‑edge loops and strand starts.
- Integrin α subunits (FG‑GAP β‑propellers): activation on extracellular coil loops within FG‑GAP repeats at coil↔strand transitions; no activation in the single-pass TM helix or cytosolic disordered tail.
- Secreted lipid/ligand-binding β‑domains (lipocalins/OBP and TULIP/BPI folds): activation on solvent-exposed loops shaping the hydrophobic tunnel.
- ERMES/SMP (TULIP) and autophagy proteins: β‑sandwich/β‑meander lipid‑binding domains; activation on loop segments shaping the hydrophobic tunnel.
- Outer-membrane biogenesis and LPS transport components beyond Bam (e.g., Lpt/auxiliary OM factors): β‑rich periplasmic scaffolds; activation at repeated β‑edge/loop sites.
- Chloroplast outer envelope pores (e.g., Toc75/OEP β‑barrels) and membrane-associated stress/immune receptors with β‑domains: activation on luminal/periplasmic β‑loops.
- OST1/Ribophorin I (oligosaccharyltransferase subunit): luminal β‑rich scaffold; activation on exposed β‑loops rather than glycosylation sequons.
- TRAPP complex subunits and other large trafficking/tethering proteins (including Trs85): activation on surface loops at β‑strand boundaries within β‑containing subdomains of these complexes.
- Exosome subunits (e.g., Rrp42/Rrp43): isolated activation at coil→β boundaries marking strand starts in the β‑core.
- Macroglobulin/complement proteins (C3/A2M/CPAMD family): activation on loops between strands in MG β‑sandwich domains.
- ABBA‑fold aromatic prenyltransferases (e.g., NotF): activation at loop/edge positions capping β‑strands of their α/β barrels.

Summary: Residue-level detector of buried hydrophobic side‑chain packing in well‑ordered secondary‑structure elements (primarily alpha‑helices but also beta‑strands) that form the structural cores of globular domains; broadly distributed across proteins (with enrichment in helical small‑GTPase regulatory domains such as RhoGAP) and not tied to a specific catalytic chemistry.
Activation pattern: Discrete, sparse residue-level peaks (most often Leu, Val, Phe, and sometimes Cys) repeated across multiple sites within structured domains; strongest in high‑confidence regions (high pLDDT), largely absent from disordered tails; peaks can appear adjacent to active or ligand‑binding motifs but reflect local packing rather than a specific active site; multiple peaks per protein, often in mid/late sequence positions of large multidomain proteins.
Exemplars: Rho family GTPase-activating proteins (RhoGAP domain): multiple peaks on Cys/Leu residues across separate alpha‑helices within the GAP fold; Metacaspases (cysteine-protease–like): aliphatic/aromatic residues across the alpha/beta catalytic core with a minor peak near the catalytic His; Kinesin motors and CH-domain cytoskeletal regulators: Leu/Val peaks in CH-domain helices and within motor-domain helices/sheets, with occasional signal in a structured loop near the ATP‑binding site; Fibroblast growth factors (FGF, beta‑trefoil): sparse peaks on Leu/Val within beta‑strands and adjacent coil segments of the trefoil core.

Summary: A short tyrosine‑centered beta‑strand micro‑motif (often Y–x–H and enriched for Y with nearby hydrophobics and/or His) that occurs on solvent‑exposed beta‑sheets, especially in secreted/surface proteins; frequently lies adjacent to metal/ligand sites (notably copper) or mediates surface interactions.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue‑level peaks over narrow 2–5 aa windows within beta‑strands, with the maximum on Tyr and smaller peaks on adjacent Val/Ile/Leu and/or His; occasionally also fires on short His–Gly–His metal‑binding motifs in loops neighboring beta‑sheets.
Exemplars: - AA9 lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases: Y–x–H beta‑strand segment proximal to the copper active site.
- Lysyl oxidase family: Y/H‑rich segments around the copper/LTQ cofactor region.
- Cu/Zn superoxide dismutases: His–Gly–His metal‑binding loop adjacent to beta‑strands.
- Transthyretin and other beta‑sandwich secreted proteins: surface‑exposed beta‑strand Tyr patches.
- Trypsin‑like and other secreted proteases: Tyr‑containing beta‑strands on the catalytic domain surface.
- Bacterial fimbrial adhesins and archaeal S‑layer glycoproteins: short Tyr‑bearing beta‑strands in surface interaction domains.
- Complement/alpha‑2‑macroglobulin/TEP proteins: Tyr/His‑containing beta‑strands within macroglobulin beta‑sheet scaffolds.
- Calpain proteases: isolated Tyr peaks in terminal beta‑strands outside the catalytic core.

Summary: Acidic, aromatic-enriched β–α/helix–loop junctions (helix N‑cap/β–α loop motifs): short surface connectors between secondary-structure elements that often contain Asp/Glu with Gly/Pro and at least one aromatic residue (frequently Trp), typically peaking in the coil/N‑cap linking a preceding strand/helix to the following helix/strand; a general structural sequence property rather than a family-specific motif
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short (≈20–60 aa) windows that straddle secondary-structure transitions; signal usually rises across a β‑strand or helix, peaks in the intervening loop/N‑cap, and tapers into the following helix/strand. Multiple windows can occur per protein. Bias toward N‑terminal regions in many proteins; loops may be moderately flexible while flanking elements are well structured.
Exemplars: - HipA serine/threonine toxin kinase: end of β‑strand → short helix → loop (peak) → next helix.
- Toluene-4-monooxygenase effector component: helix C‑terminus and following loop (peak) continuing into the next helix/β‑strand.
- XRCC4-like NHEJ factor: β‑sheet → α‑helix → coil (peak) → α‑helix within the N‑terminal head domain.
- SAICAR synthetase (AIRC; purine de novo): canonical β‑strand–coil (peak at Asp)–long α‑helix β–α loop.
- Bacteriophage tail assembly protein G: helix–acidic coil (peak at Asp)–helix hinge.
- SOCS family SH2 adaptor: paired β‑strands and the intervening loop within the SH2 core (peak at an aromatic within the β‑sheet/loop segment).
- Additional families frequently hit across taxa (consistent with the same motif): frataxin (acidic β1–α1 ridge), TGT/tRNA-guanine transglycosylase subunits (β–α loops around the base-binding pocket), Type III/VI secretion components and viral tail proteins (helix–loop–helix connectors).

Summary: Extracellular and select intracellular β-sandwich modules with Ser/Thr-enriched, small-residue motifs on solvent-exposed loops and terminal edge β-strands (Ig-like and fibronectin type-III), extending to Ser/Thr-rich mucin-like segments—i.e., surface patches on cell-surface/secreted proteins and analogous motifs on cytoskeletal scaffolds.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks in many short (≈4–6 aa) segments distributed across large extracellular regions and within cytoskeletal Ig/FN3 arrays; recurrent at the C-terminus of Ig-like and FN3 domains (FG loop/edge β-strand and adjacent coil, often at strand–coil transitions); minimal/absent in transmembrane helices and cytosolic tails of single-pass receptors; also lights up Ser/Thr runs interspersed with Gly/Ala/Val in low-complexity mucin-like stretches.
Exemplars:
- Immunoglobulin superfamily cell-adhesion molecules (neuronal guidance CAMs): peaks near the C-terminus of each Ig-like domain (FG loop/strand G), including binding-critical residues.
- Turtle/roundabout-like Ig/FN3 single-pass receptors: multiple short peaks across extracellular Ig-C2 and FN3 domains, especially on edge β-strands and terminal loops.
- Receptor tyrosine kinases with Ig/FN3 ectodomains (FGFR/VEGFR/AXL): activation on extracellular Ig/FN3 edge strands and solvent-exposed loops.
- Cadherins/protocadherins/desmogleins: activation on Ser/Thr-rich extracellular loops/interdomain linkers and mucin-like stalk segments.
- GPI-anchored adhesion proteins and mucins: strong activation on low-complexity Ser/Thr clusters (O-glycosylation-prone regions).
- Secreted microbial hydrolases/proteases: activation on exposed Ser/Thr/Ala/Gly-rich surface loops.
- Viral/phage secreted or structural proteins: activation on solvent-exposed S/Thr-rich virion-facing segments.
- Intracellular sarcomeric/cytoskeletal Ig/FN3 scaffolds (e.g., myomesin/titin-associated proteins): activation on edge β-strands and solvent-exposed loops within internal Ig/FN3 domains.
- Secreted ECM glycoproteins with TSR/EGF-like repeats (e.g., ADAMTS-like): activation on Ser/Thr-bearing loops and adjacent low-complexity linkers.

Summary: General secondary-structure propensity: the feature highlights short, well-ordered regular elements (∼10–30-residue α-helices or β-strands), often the first structured segment of a domain or immediately following targeting/signal peptides; it can also mark leucine-rich helical coiled-coils. It is agnostic to function and tends to avoid long disordered regions and catalytic/metal-binding motifs themselves.
Activation pattern: Regional activation in compact 10–30 aa blocks with sharp residue-level peaks; multiple discrete hotspots per multi-domain protein. Hotspots align with predicted H/E secondary structure (high confidence), frequently at N-termini or domain edges (e.g., right after signal/transit peptides); minimal signal in extended disordered segments or specialized small domains (e.g., zinc fingers) and away from active-site motifs.
Exemplars: - GIY-YIG structure-specific endonucleases (e.g., SLX1 homologs): activation on β-strands within the N-terminal nuclease core (including a strand near the GIY–YIG region), not on the downstream zinc-finger or disordered tails.
- c-type cytochromes (e.g., SHP): activation on the first α-helix of the mature periplasmic domain immediately after the signal peptide; not on the CXXCH/Heme-binding region.
- Metallopeptidases/peptidase-like proteins: activation on short helices/β-strands within the structured catalytic core rather than the catalytic motif itself.
- E3 ubiquitin ligases, p97/UBX cofactors, cullin/NEDD8 pathway proteins: activation on leucine-rich helical coiled-coil segments used for scaffolding/adaptor interactions.
- Mitochondrial ribosomal proteins and other organellar factors: activation on short, ordered helical/strand elements within otherwise low-complexity or basic N-terminal regions.
- Bacterial RNAP ω subunits and RNAP-interacting phage proteins: activation on compact helical/β segments forming the small structured core.

Summary: Residue-level detector of alpha-helical secondary structure, with a bias toward amphipathic/charged helices and helical bundles/repeats, independent of specific function or taxonomy.
Activation pattern: Sparse, discrete residue-level peaks concentrated within DSSP H helices across long stretches of proteins; largely absent from disordered tails; insensitive to local pLDDT (appears in both low- and high-confidence helices); occasionally touches transmembrane helices but does not uniformly mark them.
Exemplars: - CRISPR-associated endoribonuclease Cas13a: peaks in the helical linker and HEPN helical elements, including residues near crRNA-binding and catalytic helices.
- Viral capsid-associated protein (VP80): scattered single-residue peaks confined to alpha-helices across the capsid protein.
- Arenavirus nucleoprotein: sharp peaks in the helical core; little/no signal in the disordered C-terminal tail.
- Type III secretion effector (HopM1): numerous peaks across predicted alpha-helical segments spanning the effector.
