Exemplars: - Coiled-coil scaffolds (e.g., liprin-α/golgins/centrosomal coiled-coil proteins): activation scattered across the extended N-terminal coiled-coil helical region.
- Extracellular matrix collagens: strong activation along Gly–X–Y, Gly/Pro-rich triple-helix repeats.
- Bacterial lipid A galacturonosyltransferases (inner-membrane enzymes): discrete peaks within transmembrane helices and at helix starts.
- CRISPR-associated Cas13a (HEPN endoribonucleases): low-magnitude peaks in flexible loops within HEPN-like folds and occasional helical segments.

Summary: Amphipathic/hydrophobic helical signal segments and adjacent flexible N‑terminal regions that mediate secretion or membrane association (signal peptides or transmembrane signal anchors), with the feature also highlighting internal amphipathic alpha‑helices that contact membranes or line hydrophobic ligand‑binding cavities in lipid‑handling proteins.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional and N‑terminal: strong, continuous activation over 10–70 residue stretches at the extreme N‑terminus (signal peptides, TM signal anchors, and immediately downstream low‑complexity Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich segments), with little or no signal on well‑folded beta‑barrel or catalytic cores; occasional long internal helical segments are also activated when they form membrane‑interacting surfaces or the walls of hydrophobic ligand/sterol pockets; flexible C‑terminal tails may show weaker reactivation.
Exemplars: Plastid‑lipid‑associated/fibrillin (plastoglobulin) proteins: activation on long internal amphipathic helices within the mature protein that likely mediate plastoglobule membrane association; Odorant‑binding proteins (lipocalins): activation restricted to the N‑terminal secretory signal peptide, with the beta‑barrel core inactive; Nitrobindin/peroxynitrite isomerase (lipocalin‑like): activation on the short, low‑confidence N‑terminal helix/coil preceding the barrel; Avidin/streptavidin: strong activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide and immediately post‑cleavage segment, with reactivation on the flexible C‑terminus and inactivity across the avidin‑like core; Interleukin‑1 receptor antagonist (IL‑1 family): activation confined to the N‑terminal signal peptide; Fatty acid‑binding proteins: activation on the disordered N‑terminus and first helices that gate the hydrophobic cavity, with the beta‑barrel core largely inactive; OSBP/ORP sterol‑binding proteins: activation across an internal helical segment in the N‑terminal portion of the ORD containing residues essential for cholesterol/PIP binding; Phosphatidylserine decarboxylase proenzymes: activation on an early N‑terminal helical segment of the beta chain, away from the catalytic/cleavage sites and consistent with membrane engagement; CD‑NTase‑associated protein 15: activation across the N‑terminal transmembrane helix required for toxicity.

Summary: Alpha‑helix capping and helix–coil boundary motifs: short, low‑complexity polar/acidic segments (enriched in D/E/S/T with Gly/Pro and sometimes Lys/Arg) that sit at helix termini or link adjacent helices, often extending into flexible/disordered acidic linkers or tails.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue‑level peaks at coil residues immediately preceding or following alpha‑helices (N‑cap/C‑cap and helix–helix junction loops), with occasional broader regional activation across low‑complexity disordered segments; weak within transmembrane helices or catalytic cores.
Exemplars: Carbonic anhydrases: helix–loop–helix junction with peak on an acidic residue in the loop between adjacent helices; SLC6 neurotransmitter transporters: cytoplasmic segment immediately after the last transmembrane helix where a coil transitions into an alpha‑helix; Sirtuin deacetylases (SIRT1‑like): flexible linker just N‑terminal to the catalytic domain at a coil→helix transition; Type II membrane glycoproteins: short, well‑structured loop directly preceding a helix in the luminal domain (often glycine‑capped); Lipase chaperone/foldase (Lif): multiple coils that terminate at helix starts (repeated N‑cap sites), little/no signal in the transmembrane helix; Germ cell nuclear acidic proteins: acidic, low‑complexity disordered C‑terminal tails with intermittent short helices, showing broad activation with peaks in coil/incipient helix positions.

Summary: Short, exposed beta-strand–loop hairpins at the edges of beta-sheets in extracellular/periplasmic proteins (with a strong but not exclusive bias to secreted/lipoprotein contexts), typically enriched in His/Cys and nearby aromatics and often coinciding with or flanking coordination/recognition motifs (e.g., Cys–x(1–2)–His, CXXCH heme sites) or disulfide-bracketed loops; the same structural motif also appears in soluble beta-rich scaffolds such as fatty acid–binding proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous segments (~8–20 aa) that span the C-terminus of one beta-strand, the connecting loop, and into the next strand; sharp residue-level peaks frequently occur at His or Cys (and neighboring aromatic residues); multiple separated activated segments can occur within a single protein.
Exemplars: - TNF ligand superfamily (THD): activation on a loop connecting two beta-strands within the extracellular beta-sandwich.
- MliC family lysozyme inhibitors: activation on a C-terminal beta-strand and adjacent coil within the beta-sheet core, away from the annotated inhibitory residues.
- Fatty acid–binding proteins: activation at the C-terminal beta-strand that transitions into a coil at the barrel edge.
- Extracellular Cu-only superoxide dismutases: activation on a strand–loop segment that includes the copper-ligating His and may overlap glycosylation, within a disulfide-bracketed region.
- Cupredoxins (blue copper proteins): activation on short strand/loop segments bearing Cys/His copper-ligation motifs at beta-sheet edges.
- c-type cytochromes: activation overlapping the CXXCH heme-binding motif embedded in a short strand/loop context.

Summary: Detector of recurrent small/Gly–Pro–centered β-turn motifs in extracellular repeat architectures; strongest in β-propeller blade repeats (FG-GAP in integrin α, Kelch, NHL/WD, sema/VPS10, neuraminidase-like propellers), but also triggered in non-propeller extracellular enzymes and adhesins that present periodically spaced Gly/small–Pro motifs (e.g., certain polysaccharide lyases, GPI-anchored polarity proteins, Yellow/MRJP family).
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks that recur with the repeat periodicity in structured extracellular regions, typically on G–x–A/S–P triads or GG dipeptides at turn/strand junctions; largely silent in transmembrane segments, cytosolic/disordered tails, and at unrelated glycosylation/metal-binding sites.
Exemplars: - Integrin α FG-GAP, Kelch, NHL/WD, semaphorin (sema) and VPS10/sortilin propellers: one peak per blade at small/Gly–Pro-centered turns.
- Neuraminidase/sialidase propellers: periodic peaks across blades.
- Secreted polysaccharide lyases/hydrolases (e.g., ulvan lyase): repeated peaks on Gly/small–Pro loop motifs.
- GPI-anchored/polarity proteins (e.g., Rax2) and Yellow/MRJP family: clusters of peaks on recurring Gly/small–Pro motifs in extracellular repeat regions.

Summary: Generic surface-pattern signal: preference for solvent-exposed, polar/charged residues in ordered domains (alpha helices and interhelical coils), not tied to a specific catalytic motif or family and largely avoiding transmembrane segments, with occasional spillover into flexible cytosolic tails.
Activation pattern: Residue-level sparse peaks scattered across well-folded regions (helices and coils), rarely forming a contiguous motif; bias toward E/D/K/R/H/S/N/Q/T with frequent glycine; little or no signal in long disordered segments or membrane spans, except occasional activation in cytosolic C-terminal tails; uniformly low, tightly clustered scores.
Exemplars: - Heterotrimeric G-protein alpha subunits: scattered peaks in interhelical coils within the Gα domain, including near but not restricted to G1/G2 nucleotide-binding motifs.
- Regulator of G-protein signaling (RGS) proteins: dispersed peaks across the structured RGS domain; non-domain N-termini inactive.
- Na+/H+ antiporters: activation in the cytosolic, flexible C-terminal tail rather than the transmembrane core.
- PLP-dependent serine palmitoyltransferase: strongest at a noncatalytic coil residue; only weak signal in a transmembrane helix and none at the PLP-modified lysine.
- DNA methyltransferases: multiple peaks on long, high-confidence helices in the catalytic region’s vicinity but not centered on annotated catalytic residues.
- DNA helicase (RRM3 family): activation confined to the structured C-terminal region; absent from the disordered N-terminus and not on annotated ATP- or DNA-binding sites.
- La-related RNA-binding proteins: signal concentrated in the HTH La-type RNA-binding domain (minor in RRM) with disordered termini largely silent.
- bHLH transcription factor (RHD6): near-absent activation across both the bHLH domain and disordered regions, illustrating the feature’s low specificity and context dependence.

Summary: Short linear motifs in exposed loops: proline-centered di/tri-peptides flanked by charged/polar residues, and (in secreted proteins) cysteine-containing motifs (e.g., CC/CXC) associated with disulfide-bonded loops; broadly marking flexible, surface SLiMs rather than a specific domain
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on isolated adjacent dipeptides/tripeptides; scattered hotspots across sequences. In secreted/organellar precursors, peaks often occur near signal/transit peptides and around disulfide-forming cysteines; in intracellular proteins, peaks concentrate in low-complexity, charged–proline-rich linkers/loops.
Exemplars: - Bacterial and organellar ribosomal proteins: charged–Pro short motifs in basic, disordered rRNA-binding tails and surface loop turns.
- Spliceosome/snRNP and RNA-processing factors: SP/TP/DP/KP-type proline–charged di/tri-peptides in low-complexity regions mediating interactions.
- Chemokines: cysteine pairs (CC/CXC) and nearby charged residues in the mature secreted region and at the signal peptide–mature junction.
- Kazal-type serine protease inhibitors and related secreted inhibitors: disulfide-bonding cysteines and short charged/Pro motifs around the reactive/disulfide-stabilized loops.
- Plant JAZ/TIFY repressors: short SLiMs in the TIFY/Jas regions with Pro/charged residues (e.g., PY and basic clusters) in disordered segments.
- DNA polymerase delta subunit 3 orthologs: short acidic/charged–Pro motifs in flexible linkers (SLiMs mediating partner binding).
- SDHAF4 (succinate dehydrogenase assembly factor 4): N-terminal mitochondrial targeting segments and nearby charged–Pro hotspots in small disordered regions.
- Chromatin regulators (Polyhomeotic-like, RYBP/YY1-interactors, PWWP2A/B, MBDs, ARID): proline/charge-rich SLiMs (e.g., PxxP/PPxY-like and basic patches) in disordered regions used for modular interactions.
- Viral proteins (diverse lineages): proline- and charge-rich SLiMs (e.g., PPxY-like motifs) and occasional cysteine motifs in secreted/structural proteins.
- Bacterial intracellular enzymes and membrane proteins: DP/EP/KP/PK-like turns on solvent-exposed loops and short N-terminal targeting/processing segments.

Summary: Short, flexible domain-boundary/linker segments around small modular repeats—typically the N-terminal flanks and inter-repeat connectors of domains such as zinc-binding/BIR, chitin-binding type-2, and hemopexin repeats—and, in some cases, the first helix/loop just inside the domain; these regions are often low-complexity or partially disordered and are common in modular (often secreted or viral) proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation in 10–30 residue stretches that cluster just upstream of annotated domain starts or at repeat junctions, with peaks often immediately before the domain boundary and a rapid drop within the structured core; occasionally extends into the domain’s N-terminal helix/strand; repeated patterns across tandem arrays; generally low-to-moderate pLDDT/coil with short helices.
Exemplars: - Matrix metalloproteinases (hemopexin-like repeat domain): activation at the linkers between the four hemopexin repeats and at repeat boundaries.
- IAP family (BIR-domain proteins): activation within the N-terminal helix/loop segments of each BIR repeat; absent from non-BIR regions (e.g., CARD, RING).
- Papillomavirus E6 oncoproteins (Cys-rich zinc-binding domains): activation at the extreme N-terminus and on short helical/strand elements within the zinc-binding domains.
- Tandem CCCH zinc-finger RNA-binding proteins: activation in ~15–20 aa linkers immediately N-terminal to each C3H1 finger, dropping inside the finger after the first conserved Cys.
- Peritrophins/chitin-binding type-2 domain proteins: activation just N-terminal to and into the start of the chitin-binding domain, overlapping flexible segments and potential glycosylation sites.
- Axonemal microtubule stabilizers: multiple short, low-pLDDT disordered/helix segments consistent with linker or boundary regions between annotated modules.

Summary: Hydrophobic alpha-helical membrane-embedded or membrane-associated segments (signal anchors and internal TMs, and occasional interfacial amphipathic helices), enriched in Leu/Ile/Val/Phe/Tyr/Ala/Trp with occasional Gly/Ser/Thr; generally excluding soluble cores and motifs.
Activation pattern:
- Residue-level peaks and short clusters in membrane-embedded or interfacial helices, often centered mid-helix
- Frequent strongest signals in the first N-terminal signal-anchor, recurring across internal/C-terminal TMs in multi-pass proteins
- Little to no activation in cytosolic/periplasmic loops, disordered segments, beta strands, or pore-loop motifs; pore-lining helices may show signal on hydrophobic faces
Exemplars:
- Membrane insertases (YidC/Oxa1/Alb3): isolated peaks on aromatic/hydrophobic residues within TM helices, strongest in the N-terminal TM
- Potassium channels (K2P and Kir): clusters at mid-helix positions within M1/M2/TM segments; minimal signal in the pore-forming loops
- Mechanosensitive channels (MscS family): short clusters in TM1 and TM2; absent in large cytosolic domains
- Mitochondrial/thylakoid single-pass anchors (EMRE, UQCC6, FtsH, thylakoidal processing peptidase): signals on the anchor helix
- Photosystem I-associated linker CpcL: activation on an interfacial hydrophobic helix that anchors to the thylakoid membrane

Summary: Short amphipathic alpha-helical segments that mediate assembly, nucleic-acid/protein binding, or membrane association; common in intrinsically disordered regions or flexible linkers, but also present as coiled-coils or small helix-bundles within otherwise structured proteins; occasionally overlap or flank transmembrane helices. Enriched in mixed charged and hydrophobic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation with multiple discrete residue-level peaks on short helices; frequently in low-confidence/disordered helices, but also in stable amphipathic helices (coiled-coils, helix-bundle repeats) and, in some cases, within/near transmembrane segments.
Exemplars:
- Herpesvirus capsid triplex proteins (VP19C/VP23): amphipathic coiled-coil/helical segments used in capsid assembly.
- Arenavirus/Mononegavirales nucleoproteins and phosphoproteins: basic, disordered helices for RNA binding/oligomerization.
- Influenza polymerase subunits (PA, PB2): flexible helical linkers/low-confidence helices between domains.
- Legionella DrrA/SidM: N‑terminal amphipathic membrane-targeting helix and flexible helical segments.
- Chlamydia Tarp: repetitive/coiled-coil and disordered helical regions.
- Staphylococcal Protein A: small helix-bundle Ig-binding domains and C‑terminal membrane/sortase region with amphipathic/TM helices.
- CRISPR-Cas proteins (Cas13a and Cascade/Csy3/Cas7 family): flexible/linker or surface amphipathic helices within ribonucleoprotein assemblies.
- Apicomplexan rhoptry/high MW proteins (e.g., CLAG/RhopH, ROP3): scattered low-confidence helices including marginal/true TM segments in secreted precursors.
- Adenovirus structural/core proteins: basic amphipathic helices implicated in DNA binding/assembly.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors and bacterial Type III/IV effectors: MoRF-like helices within IDRs for host engagement.

Summary: A short, polar/proline- and glycine-enriched secondary-structure boundary/capping micro-motif (helix/β caps and hinge-like loops) that marks coil↔helix or coil↔β transitions, often at domain termini or adjacent to intrinsically disordered tails, and sometimes flanking active or ligand-binding sites; a structural signal present in a subset of proteins across taxa (not universal within families).
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks confined to short windows (~6–12 aa), often multiple per large proteins; strongest at helix/strand caps, short helices or loops bridging secondary structures, and at domain boundaries. Activation occurs only when the boundary segment is Pro/Gly-rich with mixed-charge residues and lacks long hydrophobic runs; many homologs lack such segments and will be inactive (especially at hydrophobic transmembrane ends). Frequently low-to-moderate pLDDT (flexible/disordered context), but can appear on short, well-formed helices adjacent to functional sites.
Exemplars: Observed in some (not all) members of the following families—BamE (cap near disordered C-terminus), FlgH (coil→β caps in flexible regions), Rieske iron–sulfur subunits (polar caps just beyond domain boundaries when present), ring-hydroxylating dioxygenase small subunits (flexible C-terminal loops), Nudix hydrolases (coil→β near active sites), isopentenyl-diphosphate isomerase type I (loop/β caps near catalytic residues), and xanthine/nicotinate dehydrogenase subunits (caps adjacent to cofactor sites).

Summary: Low-complexity, compositionally biased segments in intrinsically disordered regions, typically enriched in Gly and/or Pro and frequently punctuated by aromatic residues (Tyr/Phe/Trp). YG/YGG/GYG motifs are common but not required. These tracts are common in secreted/extracellular proteins, antimicrobial/allergen precursors, and prion-like or reproductive IDRs.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across low-pLDDT coil-rich tracts with short Gly/Pro runs and intermittent aromatics; local peaks at Gly, Pro, and aromatic residues. Strongly off in well-structured helices/strands, transmembranes, and folded domains; activation often concentrates in N-terminal low-complexity leaders or propeptides.
Exemplars:
- Peroxisomal membrane protein PEX13: N-terminal Gly/Pro- and Tyr/Phe-punctuated low-complexity coil; off in TM and SH3 domain.
- Small heat shock protein (Hsp42): N-terminal IDR with Y/F/G/P motifs; off over the alpha-crystallin domain.
- Keratin-associated proteins and other extracellular structural proteins (e.g., caseins, chorion components): activation on Gly/Pro/Tyr-rich repeats.
- Plant HIPPs: activation on Pro/Tyr/Gly-rich low-complexity segments.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., clavanin) and allergens: activation on low-complexity signal/propeptides or IDRs that can be Pro/His-rich with occasional aromatics.
- Proline-rich salivary proteins (e.g., opiorphin/PRP1 precursors): activation on basic Pro-rich low-complexity stretches.
- Reproductive proteins including protamine/protamine-like: activation on simple Arg/Lys-rich low-complexity segments or cleaved propeptides when present.

Summary: Residue-level detector for the right‑handed parallel beta‑helix/beta‑solenoid scaffold, focusing on the short coil/turn and N‑cap positions that precede or initiate beta‑strands in repeat units; prevalent in secreted/surface polysaccharide‑active proteins (autotransporters, phage tailspikes/depolymerases, pectate/pectin lyases, ice‑nucleation repeats) and, more broadly, analogous coil→beta boundaries in other beta‑rich domains; often enriched for small/polar residues (Gly/Ser/Ala/Asn/Asp) and can include acidic residues that participate in Ca2+ binding or catalysis along the solenoid groove.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks, sparse but repeated across long beta‑rich repeat domains; strongest at glycine- and small/polar residues in coil turns that link repeats or at the first residue of a beta‑strand; frequently periodic in solenoids (e.g., 8‑residue repeats); largely absent from signal peptides and outer‑membrane translocator segments; mostly in well‑structured regions (high pLDDT) but can extend into glycine/Asn/Gln‑rich low‑complexity segments of secreted effectors.
Exemplars: - Autotransporter passenger (pertactin): sharp peaks at turns linking beta‑strands within the beta‑helix; no activation in the signal peptide or C‑terminal translocator.
- Fungal cell‑wall adhesin (AWP2): glycine‑rich coil turns connecting beta‑strands across the structured N‑terminal half; occasional proximity to glycosylation motifs.
- Phage capsule depolymerase catalytic domain: peaks within the pectate‑lyase–like beta‑helix core, including an active‑site Asp; noncatalytic lectin/carbohydrate‑binding appendages largely inactive.
- Pectate lyase A: residues at beta‑strand starts and loop turns within the right‑handed beta‑helix.
- Pectin/pectate‑interacting carbohydrate‑binding domain: turns preceding beta‑strands plus acidic Ca2+‑binding residues along the binding groove.
- Type VI secretion spike (VgrG): sparse peaks across a glycine/Asn/Gln‑rich C‑terminal effector segment predicted as disordered, consistent with repeat‑like coil regions.
- Ice nucleation protein: periodic activation every eight residues on serines in the octapeptide beta‑solenoid repeat, typically at coil positions just before beta‑strands.
- Formyltransferase/hydrolase complex subunit C: internal beta‑turns and strand starts in well‑ordered beta‑sheets, reflecting the same local coil→beta geometry outside classical solenoids.

Summary: Cysteine-rich, disulfide‑stabilized extracellular repeat modules—principally EGF‑like repeats and closely related small domains (CCP/Sushi, WAP/TIL, disintegrin, LDLR class‑A, and von Willebrand–type modules)—found across secreted proteins, extracellular matrix components, proteases/inhibitors, and receptor ectodomains.
Activation pattern: Multi‑repeat, domain‑level activation across ectodomains with residue‑level peaks at the conserved cysteines that form disulfide frameworks and adjacent Gly/Pro positions; little to no activation in signal peptides, transmembranes, or cytosolic regions; occasionally highlights Ca‑binding and N‑glycosylation motifs within Ca‑binding EGF‑like repeats.
Exemplars: - Notch/lin‑12 receptors: activation confined to tandem EGF‑like repeats, not LNR/ANK/TM.
- LDL receptor/LRP family: activation on LDLR‑A (LA) repeats and EGF‑like modules of the ectodomain.
- Complement regulators (e.g., factor H, CR1, C4BP): activation across CCP/Sushi domains.
- Coagulation factors/regulators (factors VII/IX, protein C, thrombomodulin): activation on their EGF‑like domains.
- ECM/matricellular proteins (fibrillin, fibulin, tenascin, laminins): activation on EGF‑like and other cysteine‑rich modules.
- Metalloproteases and related toxins (ADAMs, snake‑venom metalloproteases): activation on disintegrin/cysteine‑rich domains.
- WFDC/WAP protease inhibitors (SLPI/elafin family): activation on the WAP four‑disulfide core.
- von Willebrand factor–containing proteins: activation on cysteine‑rich VWF‑type modules.
- Secreted fungal CAZymes: activation on cysteine‑rich carbohydrate‑binding modules (e.g., hevein‑like/CBM18 or CBM1), not on catalytic cores.

Summary: Long amphipathic alpha-helices with heptad-repeat character, especially coiled-coil–forming segments used for oligomerization and scaffolding in assembly and membrane/cytoskeleton-related proteins; the feature emphasizes hydrophobic core positions (a/d) of coiled coils and, more generally, helical protein–protein interaction surfaces
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation across extended helices, showing a periodic pattern every 3–4 residues consistent with heptad repeats and peaking on helix-favoring hydrophobics; in globular proteins, appears as sparse residue-level peaks confined to helical interface segments; activation commonly spans long contiguous runs rather than short motifs
Exemplars: - Extracellular matrix laminins: strong, periodic activation along the C-terminal trimeric coiled-coil stalk, highlighting a/d core positions
- WAVE regulatory complex subunit CYFIP1: discrete peaks on hydrophobic residues within predicted helices in RAC1-interacting regions, consistent with helical PPI surfaces
- ER oxidoreductase ERO1: high activation on stable helices (including near the FAD-binding helix), reflecting recognition of long amphipathic helices even outside canonical coiled coils
- Viral tegument/structural proteins: activation across long coiled-coil segments used for virion assembly and tethering
- Bacterial secretion system effectors/chaperones and toxin oligomerization domains: activation on coiled-coils or helical hairpins mediating secretion, dimerization, or pore assembly
- ESCRT/Bro1/Alix pathway and centrosomal/cytoskeletal scaffolds: activation on coiled-coil arms that mediate membrane remodeling and scaffold formation
- Chlamydial inclusion membrane proteins and apicomplexan invasion/surface proteins: activation on extended coiled-coil stalks implicated in host interaction
- Archaeal/bacterial repeat-rich scaffolding proteins: activation along coiled-coil repeat tracts used for higher-order assemblies

Summary: Short beta‑strand micro‑motifs in enzyme catalytic cores: the feature fires on 2–5 residue β‑strand segments that juxtapose a polar/charged residue with a nearby aromatic or small residue (e.g., H–x–Y, R–x–Y, D–x–A). These segments lie within the structured core of enzymatic domains, frequently adjacent to (but not overlapping) canonical catalytic/metal or substrate‑binding motifs.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks confined to very short, high‑pLDDT β‑strand stretches; typically a main peak on His/Asp/Tyr with weaker flanking peaks ±1–3 residues. Peaks recur as isolated patches within catalytic domains rather than covering whole domains or consensus motifs.
Exemplars: - Nudix-family hydrolases (MutT/NUDT; mRNA decapping DCP2): activation on β‑strand segments carrying His or basic→aromatic patterns (e.g., H flanked by Phe/Tyr; basic at +2 and aromatic at +4), positioned within the Nudix domain but outside the Nudix box.
- Diphosphoinositol polyphosphate phosphohydrolases (NUDT/DIPP): activation on a Tyr‑centered β‑strand segment adjacent to annotated substrate‑binding Lys/His.
- Trypsin-like serine proteases (Peptidase S1; secreted/transmembrane/venom): activation on the D–x–A β‑strand motif immediately surrounding the catalytic Asp of the charge‑relay system.
- Glyoxalase I (VOC family): activation on an acidic residue (Asp/Glu) within a core β‑strand of the VOC domain, distinct from the annotated catalytic Glu.
- SAM-dependent protein methyltransferases (e.g., EEF1A lysine methyltransferase): activation on an H/H/Y cluster at the coil→β transition in the central β‑sheet of the catalytic core.

Summary: Coil-to–α-helix initiation sites in intrinsically disordered, low-complexity, charged segments—i.e., helix N-cap/N1 motifs (MoRF-like) often at N-termini or processing/targeting junctions—typically centered on Gly/Pro and flanked by Lys/Ser/Thr, with little Cys.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on Gly or Pro immediately N-terminal to or at the first residue of a short α-helix, sometimes spilling into the first helical turn; located in low-pLDDT coil preceding helix, frequently within Lys/Ser/Thr-rich runs and near N-termini; multiple non-contiguous sites can activate in long IDPs.
Exemplars: - Dehydrins/LEA stress proteins: repeated Gly N-cap residues preceding short helices within disordered segments.
- Ribonuclease E (bacterial endoribonuclease): a Gly in the disordered C-terminal tail directly before a short α-helix.
- Sec translocase subunit SecE: N-terminal basic/disordered stretch with a Gly peak marking the onset of the first helix.
- Venom toxin precursor (e.g., spider neurotoxin): Gly at the propeptide cleavage site that is the first residue of the helical mature peptide, with minor activation across the initial helical turn.
- LXG family toxin (YqcG): disordered C-terminal tail with a Pro-centered peak consistent with a helix-capping/turn site within a low-confidence region.

Summary: Short solvent-exposed strand-capping/β-turn motif centered on an Asx–Ser/Thr pair (Asn/Asp adjacent to or near Ser/Thr, often NS/NT and frequently followed by Gly), occurring at β-strand→loop boundaries in β-rich domains (propellers, sandwiches) and β→α connections (e.g., TIM-barrels); a generic structural loop motif rather than a specific PTM site (not tied to N-glycosylation)
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks over 2–5 aa segments enriched for S/T/N/D/G (often with E/K/R nearby), repeatedly distributed across large multidomain extracellular/luminal proteins; sparse in hydrophobic cores, transmembrane helices, and long cytosolic tails; tends to occur at E→C secondary-structure transitions flanking β-strands
Exemplars: - Integrin α subunits (FG-GAP/β-propeller): activates on short coil/turns that cap β-strands within FG-GAP repeats; no activation on TM helix or cytoplasmic tail and does not coincide with annotated N-glycosylation sequons
- Secreted glycoside hydrolases (cellulases, β-glucosidases, xylosidases, β-galactosidases, sialidases): selects polar turns in β→α or loop regions around active sites featuring Asn/Ser/Thr±Gly
- Complement and α2-macroglobulin family: highlights exposed loop/turns between β-strands within macroglobulin/complement domains
- Vesicle coat/adaptor components (AP complexes, coatomer/COPI, retromer/GGA, TRAPP, TRAP/SSR): marks short turns between blades/repeats in β-propeller or β/α-solenoid segments
- MD-2/MD-1 (ML domain) and plant ML-like proteins: activates on β-sandwich loop turns enriched in Asx–Ser/Thr
- Urease components and COX11: picks out polar surface turns adjacent to β-strands in soluble/periplasmic or IMS-exposed regions

Summary: Active-site beta-strand/loop signature of hydrolases that rely on acidic residues for catalysis—predominantly divalent-metal–activated phosphoester/phosphodiester hydrolases (nucleases, phosphatases, phosphodiesterases), but also CN hydrolases—capturing segments that include or flank metal-liganding/catalytic D/E with nearby H and aromatics, often featuring a WN dipeptide.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks focused on short beta-strands and their flanking loops within well-structured catalytic domains; maxima frequently sit on the strand/loop immediately adjacent to annotated metal-binding or catalytic residues (D/E/H), often at Gly/Leu, with multiple peaks when several metal sites are present; minimal activation in disordered or transmembrane regions; occasionally broadens across an extended catalytic subregion.
Exemplars: Inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatases (Type IV): peaks on beta-strands overlapping the “Catalytic 1” segment harboring active-site acidic residues; Neutral sphingomyelinases: activation on beta-strands/loops containing an Mg2+-liganding Glu and the catalytic His, plus nearby substrate-recognition Asn; CCR4–NOT deadenylase subunits: peaks on beta-strands flanking Mg2+-liganding acidic residues in the nuclease core (DEDDh/EEP-like); Lariat debranching enzyme (DBR1): activation adjacent to divalent-metal-binding Asp/His in the metallophosphoesterase fold; MRE11 nuclease: loops next to Mn2+-binding Asp/Asn and the catalytic His; Glycerophosphodiester phosphodiesterase (metallo-β-lactamase-like PDE): activation in loops immediately preceding Fe-binding residues; CN hydrolase superfamily enzymes (Apolipoprotein N-acyltransferase/Lnt; 2-oxoglutaramate amidase/omega-amidase): strong peaks at the catalytic-loop Glu (proton acceptor) and adjacent beta-strand within the CN-hydrolase domain; PGAP2-interacting multipass membrane protein: strong signal on two beta-strands in the soluble C-terminal domain consistent with this catalytic strand/loop signature.

Summary: A composition/secondary-structure signal for short, hydrophobic, low-basic-content segments with alpha-helix propensity—most strongly the h-region of N-terminal signal peptides and other amphipathic helices (e.g., the recognition helix of HTH regulators)—and, more weakly, compositionally similar stretches within low-complexity or disordered regions.
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks in short stretches (often near the N-terminus), enriched for L/V/I/A/S/T/P/G and occasional acidic/polar residues, with few Lys/Arg; strongest when the segment is a short predicted helix, but also appearing on low-pLDDT coil in low-complexity proteins; variable number of peaks per protein.
Exemplars: - HTH-type ArsR transcriptional regulators: peaks in the DNA-binding H-T-H region, especially the recognition helix.
- Secreted venom/chemotactic peptide precursors: single weak peak within the N-terminal signal peptide helix; little to none on the mature peptide.
- Viral chemokine (IL-8) homologs: peaks in the signal peptide h-region, occasionally a weak site in a disordered tail.
- Plant CLE/CLAVATA propeptides: peaks in the signal peptide and a short helical segment of the propeptide; occasional Pro in the mature peptide region.
- Insect adipokinetic hormone precursors: strongest activation in the signal peptide; additional peaks in helical propeptide segments; absent on the mature hormone.
- Milk caseins: multiple weak peaks across low-confidence, low-complexity segments (some transient-helix predictions) within the mature chain.
- Keratin-associated proteins: sparse peaks within Ser/Thr/Gly-rich repeats of low structural confidence, with occasional short helical sites.
- Retroviral accessory proteins (e.g., HTLV p30II): discrete peaks across disordered regions, including near a short helical targeting motif at the C-terminus.

Summary: Short, cationic low‑complexity segments (Lys/Arg- and often Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly‑rich) that function as amphipathic, polyanion‑binding/targeting patches—typically terminal tails or flexible loops outside structured domains—used for binding RNA/DNA or acidic membranes (e.g., rRNA‑binding tails, organellar transit peptides, antimicrobial cationic stretches, and basic regulatory extensions).
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous windows (~15–40 aa), with residue‑level peaks on Lys/Arg clusters and nearby Ser/Thr; strongest in low‑confidence coil/turn that can taper across an adjacent short helix; generally silent across globular catalytic cores and structured domains.
Exemplars: - Ribosomal protein uL22 and orthologs: activation on Lys/Arg‑rich rRNA‑binding tails/loops lining the exit tunnel.
- Translation factors and other ribosome‑associated proteins: activation on basic, low‑complexity RNA/ribosome‑binding segments.
- Histone/chromatin, RNA/DNA, and small‑molecule methyltransferases/acetyltransferases: activation on basic terminal patches or low‑complexity tails outside the catalytic core that mediate nucleic‑acid/acidic‑surface interactions or targeting.
- Polyamine aminopropyltransferases (spermidine synthases): activation on the C‑terminal basic extension immediately beyond the PABS domain, peaking at a coil/turn and fading across a short helix.
- PP2C‑family protein phosphatases: activation on short basic regulatory tails/loops distal to the metal‑dependent catalytic fold.
- Phage structural proteins: activation on Lys/Arg‑rich DNA‑binding segments or terminal basic patches.
- Bacterial secretins: activation on basic periplasmic loops/terminal segments.
- Antimicrobial beta‑defensins/gallinacins: activation on cationic stretches within the mature peptide that contact acidic membranes.
- Organellar‑targeted proteins (mitochondrial/chloroplastic): activation on Ser/Thr‑rich, Arg‑enriched N‑terminal transit peptides.
- mRNA cap and other RNA‑modification systems: activation on RS/RG/lysine‑rich RNA‑binding regions.

Summary: Short strand-edge motifs at loop-to–beta-strand transitions and within beta-strands of extracellular beta-rich domains (especially FN3/Ig-like and cupredoxin folds) in secreted and cell-surface proteins; a generic structural signal of beta-sandwich/β-rich ectodomains used in adhesion/receptor modules and secreted enzymes, rather than catalytic or PTM sites.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks clustered on hydrophobic/aromatic and small polar residues within beta-strands and at loop-to-strand starts; multiple peaks recur across repeat-rich extracellular domains (Ig/FN3, cupredoxin, adhesin repeats), leading to many activated positions in large ectodomains; sparse activation elsewhere and typically not coincident with catalytic residues, disulfides, or glycosylation motifs.
Exemplars: - Fibronectin type III and Ig-like adhesion modules and receptor ectodomains (e.g., in receptor-type tyrosine phosphatases/kinases): localized peaks at loop-to-strand transitions within FN3/Ig beta-sandwich repeats.
- Glycoside hydrolases (e.g., beta-mannosidase): isolated peaks on beta-strands away from catalytic glutamates and annotated PTMs.
- Cupredoxin/copper-oxidase family redox proteins: peaks along beta-strands of the cupredoxin beta-sandwich.
- Bacterial/archaeal adhesins and S-layer proteins: repeated beta-rich extracellular domains with numerous strand-edge activations.
- Extracellular matrix proteins and protease inhibitors: beta-rich domains (e.g., FN3-like/Kunitz-containing ECM proteins) showing similar strand/loop-edge activation.

Summary: Heptad-repeat coiled-coil oligomerization helices embedded within low-complexity, phosphorylation-prone intracellular (non-membrane) regions, often flanked by Ser/Thr/Glu/Asp/Gln/Asn-rich IDRs, used as scaffolds in nuclear/chromatin, spindle/centrosome, viral and RNA-processing assemblies.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, continuous tracts: strongest over coiled-coil helices and adjacent acidic/serine-rich low-complexity segments, with spillover into nearby IDRs; minimal or absent in compact globular domains and transmembrane helices; for membrane proteins, restricted to cytosolic tails.
Exemplars: - EAG/ERG voltage-gated K+ channels: activation on a distal C-terminal cytosolic helix consistent with the oligomerization/coiled-coil region; silent on PAS/PAC domains, S1–S6, and pore.
- Microtubule-associated coiled-coil scaffolds (e.g., TORTIFOLIA1): strong activation precisely on the annotated coiled-coil rod; no signal on other non-coiled helices.
- Kinetochore/centrosome/spindle organizers: long coiled-coil segments mediating dimerization/assembly are highlighted.
- Nuclear DNA maintenance/chromatin factors: activation on low-complexity acidic/serine-rich tracts and coiled-coil segments that scaffold repair/replication complexes.
- Viral phosphoproteins (P proteins) and regulatory factors: central oligomerization coiled-coil with flanking phospho-rich disordered regions is targeted.
- RNA processing/decapping and transcription-coupled factors: low-complexity, phosphorylation-prone regions and coiled-coil scaffolding segments show activation.

Summary: Generic hydrophobic-segment detector: emphasizes alpha-helical transmembrane helices and their membrane-interfacial start/stop residues (helix caps and short helices flanking TMs), with secondary sensitivity to hydrophobic/aromatic residues marking the onset of other secondary structures (e.g., beta-strands) and to short hydrophobic motifs within secretory precursors/mature micropeptides.
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks scattered along sequences; strongest and most frequent in high-confidence alpha-helical regions inside or immediately adjacent to transmembrane spans, often at the first few residues of a helix entering the membrane; additional weaker peaks within helix cores; occasional peaks at the start of beta-strands in soluble proteins; can also appear on aromatic/proline/glycine residues in disordered secreted peptide regions; frequent inclusion of very N‑terminal positions.
Exemplars: - A-type ATP synthase subunit I (membrane subunit): multiple peaks within TM alpha-helices and adjacent helical segments, consistent with membrane-helix interiors and interfaces.
- FtsW peptidoglycan glycosyltransferase/translocase (multi-pass membrane protein): peaks in several TM helices and a short extracellular helix at a TM transition; little/no signal in long disordered cytosolic tails.
- Neurensin-1 (two-pass neuronal membrane protein): strongest at the start of the first TM helix with additional peaks within TM helices.
- Formate–nitrite transporter (FNT family channel): peaks at short helices flanking TMs and at the start of the final TM, marking soluble-to-membrane transitions.
- Plant C-terminally encoded peptide (CEP) precursor (small secreted peptide hormone): concentrated on aromatic/proline residues within the processed mature peptide region and weakly in the N‑terminal signal peptide helix.
- Cholesterol oxidase (soluble FAD-dependent oxidoreductase): sharp peak at the onset of a beta-strand and minor peaks at hydrophobic/aromatic residues in structured regions, matching sensitivity to hydrophobic starts of secondary structure.

Summary: Non-catalytic effector/regulatory segments: the feature highlights regions outside enzymatic catalytic cores, comprising either long, low‑complexity intrinsically disordered regulatory tracts or compact secreted effector/toxin domains (often cysteine‑rich or helical), frequently located at termini and in precursor/mature peptide regions.
Activation pattern: Regional to domain-level activation over contiguous stretches rather than isolated residues; commonly concentrated near N-termini of secreted precursors and across long disordered tracts; typically suppressed over structured catalytic domains.
Exemplars: - Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation spans the folded, alpha‑helical C‑terminal effector domain, while the N‑terminal signal peptide and RxLR‑dEER region remain inactive.
- Wee1/Swe1 family mitotic kinases: strong, widespread activation across the extensive N‑terminal low‑complexity/disordered regulatory region; minimal activation over the C‑terminal protein kinase domain.
- ATP‑dependent DNA ligases: activation on the N‑terminal intrinsically disordered extension preceding the ligase catalytic core.
- Venom toxins and antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., defensins, conotoxins, hepcidins): activation on cysteine‑dense mature peptide regions following signal/propeptide segments.
- Viral polyproteins (e.g., hepatitis C virus): activation on processed, compositionally biased segments (often basic/low‑complexity) rather than enzymatic domains.
- Core metabolic and cofactor biosynthesis enzymes (e.g., pyruvate kinase, isocitrate lyase, molybdopterin synthase MoaE/MOCS2B) and tRNA/RNA‑modification enzymes: activation confined to short contiguous stretches in non‑catalytic termini or flexible insertions, consistent with accessory/disordered patches rather than the conserved catalytic cores.

Summary: Modules that initiate DNA replication and primer synthesis—principally primase/initiator catalytic cores (DnaG/Toprim, AEP/PrimPol, HUH/relaxase) together with cognate regulatory and origin-binding/helicase-linker segments (e.g., PriL subunits and helicase OBD/primase-interaction regions, including catalytically degenerate homologs such as Twinkle).
Activation pattern: Predominantly domain-level, extended activation over 80–300 aa within the primase/initiator module; strongest signals align with conserved metal- and NTP-binding segments (acidic Asp/Glu clusters with nearby basic Lys/Arg, often glycine-rich contexts). A contiguous, strongly activated stretch is also common immediately N-terminal to the AAA+ helicase ATPase domain, in both fused polypeptides and standalone helicases.
Exemplars: - DnaG-type primase (TraC/Tra-type primases): high activation focused in the C-terminal Toprim catalytic subdomain, matching the Toprim core that coordinates divalent metal ions and catalysis.
- AEP/PrimPol-type primase–polymerase: strong, localized activation within the primase catalytic region covering residues annotated as essential for primase activity; adjacent polymerase and helicase regions show little to no activation.
- Helicase-associated origin-binding/primase-interaction segments: long, contiguous activation immediately N-terminal to the helicase ATP-binding domain in fused or standalone helicases (e.g., papillomavirus E1, Twinkle).
- Rolling-circle replication initiators (Rep/RepA, G2P/relaxase-like): extended activation across the well-structured HUH nicking–joining core.
- PriL-type regulatory subunits of AEP primase: activation in metal/acidic–basic rich regions that scaffold and regulate the PriS catalytic subunit.

Summary: Short loop/beta submotifs within extracellular cysteine-rich repeat domains—most strongly EGF-like repeats (classical, calcium‑binding, and laminin‑type) and closely related 8‑cysteine TB modules—found in long ectodomains of secreted or single‑pass proteins involved in adhesion, ECM organization, and ligand/receptor interactions.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks that recur periodically across arrays of repeats (typically 1–3 short 5–7 aa peaks per domain), concentrated in the C‑terminal half and inter‑strand loops of each repeat. Peaks align with conserved motifs adjacent to disulfide‑bonded cysteines and often center on Gly/Tyr/Pro and acidic residues characteristic of EGF/TB consensus sequences. Minimal activation in signal peptides, transmembranes, coiled‑coils, or catalytic cores; occasional weaker activation in adjacent CUB modules.
Exemplars: - Adhesion GPCR ectodomains: repeated activation across consecutive N‑terminal EGF‑like repeats.
- Notch-like EGF repeat proteins: periodic peaks in the C‑terminal segment of each EGF repeat, often maximal on conserved Gly.
- Laminin gamma chains: strong, repeated activation across laminin‑type EGF repeats; absent from N‑terminal laminin domain and C‑terminal coiled‑coil.
- Tolloid/BMP1 metalloproteases: focused activation in the C‑terminal calcium‑binding EGF domain with weaker peaks in neighboring CUB domains.
- Latent TGF‑beta–binding proteins (LTBPs): discrete peaks within TB (8‑cysteine) modules and multiple calcium‑binding EGF‑like repeats distributed along the ectodomain.

Summary: Short beta-strand elements that form the blades of beta-propeller/WD-repeat–like and other beta–sheet–rich scaffold domains used by large eukaryotic assemblies (e.g., trafficking, ciliary, nuclear pore, and ER lumenal receptors)
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on 5–7-residue beta-strands (DSSP E) that repeat across a domain, yielding periodic activation over long regions; minimal signal on alpha-helices, disordered loops, transmembranes, or catalytic kinase modules; enrichment for hydrophobic strand-core residues (L, I, V, F, A); often concentrated in N-terminal or lumenal beta-sheet scaffolds
Exemplars: - Nuclear pore scaffold (Nup133): activation on N-terminal beta-propeller strands; no activation on the alpha-helical C-terminal domain.
- ER stress sensor kinase PERK/EIF2AK3: selective activation on beta-strands in the lumenal sensor domain; none on signal peptide, transmembrane helix, or cytosolic kinase domain.
- RhoGEF regulatory scaffold (Rho1 GEF2): strong, repeating activation across beta-strands of the CNH 7-bladed beta-propeller; not on DH/PH domains.
- CRL4 substrate receptor (DCAF family): multiple peaks on beta-strands consistent with WD40-like beta-propeller blades.
- Ribosome biogenesis factor (U3 snoRNP/Utp protein): activation on beta-strands within WD repeats and adjacent propeller blades.
- WD-repeat cell cycle/kinetochore factor (Minichromosome loss protein 1): peaks on beta-strand blades across multiple WD repeats.
- ER membrane complex subunit (EMC1): numerous lumenal beta-strand motifs highlighted across the large N-terminal domain.
- Elongator complex scaffold (ELP1): periodic activation on N-terminal beta-strand–rich regions; absent from the alpha-helical, dimerizing C-terminus.

Summary: Low-complexity, intrinsically disordered segments with a bias for serine/threonine (often with proline and nearby basic/acidic residues) that encode short linear motifs for regulation or targeting (e.g., phosphosite motifs, RxLR-dEER), typically found in secreted/viral ectodomains near signal peptide–transmembrane boundaries and in flexible regulatory tails.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation across disordered, low-pLDDT stretches with many sites per segment; superimposed residue-level peaks on S/T and adjacent charged/proline residues. Strong at luminal/extracellular segments immediately before (or occasionally within) signal peptides and at TM boundaries; minimal in folded domains and transmembrane cores.
Exemplars: - Coronavirus nucleocapsid proteins: central low-complexity, disordered regions enriched in Ser/Thr with known phosphosites, plus disordered C-terminal tails.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: disordered N-terminal ectodomains just upstream of transmembrane helices, with peaks on threonines; no activation within the TM core.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: flexible N-terminal/mature regions around the RxLR-dEER host-targeting motif, with peaks on E/S/R within low-confidence structure.
- Conotoxin precursors (secreted toxins): activation on the N-terminal signal peptide helix and on flexible residues within the cysteine-rich toxin region.
- Disordered human regulatory proteins (e.g., p53-induced apoptosis factors): scattered, low-level activation across intrinsically disordered segments lacking stable structure.

- Summary: append “Rare intracellular matches occur via the same short Y/T/C beta‑strand/loop motifs (e.g., ribosomal proteins), likely reflecting convergent surface-exposed beta segments.”
- Exemplars (CAZymes): change to “activation in appended carbohydrate-binding modules (CBMs) or in catalytic beta‑strand/loop segments of glycosidases/lyases.”
- Exemplars (phages): change to “Bacteriophage tail fibers/tailspikes/capsid proteins/decorators: …”

Summary: N-terminal propeptides/leader regions of secreted preproproteins that are proteolytically removed before maturation (including RiPP leader peptides and zymogen prodomains), typically lying between the signal peptide and the mature toxin/enzyme/peptide core
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation on a single, contiguous N-terminal segment that begins immediately after (or near) the signal peptide and ends at the annotated propeptide/leader cleavage site; little to no activation in the signal peptide or mature chain. Segments range from ~20 to >150 aa, often low-to-moderately structured (coil/helix) but can be well-structured in protease prodomains. Sequence bias toward acidic residues with frequent basic (K/R) and occasional dibasic processing sites.
Exemplars: - Plant cyclotides (e.g., cycloviolacins): activation on the N-terminal propeptide; absent on signal peptide and cyclic cystine-knot core.
- RiPP precursors (linaridins/lantibiotics/thiopeptides; e.g., cypemycin): activation on the N-terminal leader peptide; absent on the modified core peptide.
- Spider venom peptides (ICK/hexatoxins, linear cytotoxins): activation on the pro-region upstream of the disulfide-rich/cationic toxin domain.
- Defensin precursors (e.g., plectasin): activation on the acidic propeptide between the signal peptide and defensin core.
- Serine protease zymogens (e.g., trypsin-like secreted proteases such as Streptogrisin-B): activation on the inhibitory activation peptide/prodomain; absent on catalytic domain.
- Papain-like cysteine proteases (e.g., Staphopain B): activation across the entire inhibitory propeptide; off in the mature enzyme.
- Secreted metalloproteases (e.g., fragilysin): activation on the N-terminal pro-region preceding the Zn-dependent catalytic domain.
- Secreted hydrolases (e.g., c-type lysozymes): activation on the N-terminal propeptide removed to yield the mature enzyme.

Summary: Hydrophobic α‑helix-in-membranes signature: the feature marks lipid‑bilayer–embedded transmembrane helices and signal‑peptide hydrophobic cores, with weak spillover to short hydrophobic helices in soluble proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation across membrane-spanning α‑helices (strongest in multi‑pass proteins), with residue‑level peaks on aliphatic hydrophobes (Leu/Ile/Val/Ala) and less frequent Phe/Trp; occasional Ser/Thr or Lys at helix ends/caps. Single‑pass or soluble proteins show few peaks, typically in N‑terminal signal peptides, targeting/anchor helices, or isolated hydrophobic helices; sporadic peaks can occur at helix–loop junctions.
Exemplars: 7TM GPCRs (e.g., rhodopsin and other class A receptors): activation across all seven transmembrane helices; ABC transporter permeases (e.g., LacG): strong peaks within the ABC transmembrane type‑1 helices, including helix–helix junctions; two‑component histidine kinases: activation on the N‑terminal sensor transmembrane segments; response regulators (CheY‑like): weak, localized activation on hydrophobic helices in the receiver domain, sometimes including the conserved Lys ~100–110 at a helix cap; metal transport/resistance systems (P‑type ATPases, RND/CDF efflux pumps): broad activation across multiple transmembrane helices; cardiolipin synthases (Cls): activation on their inner‑membrane helices; bacterial envelope/glycan biosynthesis multipass enzymes (e.g., Wzx/Wzy and related glycosyltransferases): activation throughout transmembrane segments; mitochondrial/peroxisomal β‑oxidation proteins: activation primarily in N‑terminal targeting signal peptides or membrane anchors; thioredoxin family proteins: activation mainly on secretory signal peptides in exported/periplasmic forms, minimal elsewhere; motility/chemotaxis receptors (MCPs): activation on the two transmembrane helices.

Summary: Extracellular, repeat-based ectodomains that mediate carbohydrate processing or recognition—especially beta-propeller-like and Asp-box/BNR- or FG-GAP–repeat scaffolds (e.g., neuraminidases/sialidases, polysaccharide lyases, fructansucrases/levansucrases) and related disulfide-rich receptor modules; the feature highlights the folded luminal/secreted head or mature domain rather than signal peptides or transmembranes.
Activation pattern: Primarily domain-level activation across large, well-folded extracellular catalytic or binding domains; within receptors, sparse peaks over repeat units (BNR/Asp-box, FG-GAP) and cysteine-rich segments, often near N-glycosylation sequons; occasional single-residue peaks at disulfide-forming cysteines; rare, patchy activation in non-secreted enzyme cores.
Exemplars: - Polysaccharide lyases (PL25 ulvan lyase): broad activation across the entire mature secreted domain, excluding the signal peptide/lipid anchor; covers catalytic and binding sites.
- Fructansucrases/levansucrases (GH68): peaks on beta-strands and adjacent loops framing the active site (around catalytic residues), with minor signals in flexible termini.
- Integrin alpha (FG-GAP beta-propeller): sparse activation within multiple FG-GAP repeats of the N-terminal ectodomain; no activation in TM/cytosolic parts.
- Sortilin-related/similar luminal receptors with BNR/Asp-box repeats: contiguous activation in luminal segments plus peaks within BNR repeats and cysteine-rich regions, including sites adjacent to N-linked glycosylation.
- Neuraminidases/HN (viral and bacterial): activation concentrated on the luminal head beta-propeller domain, not on transmembrane segments.
- Furin-like cysteine-rich repeats in secreted/surface proteins: isolated peak(s) at specific cysteines within the repeat module.
- Receptor tyrosine kinase ectodomain fragments (ErbB family): sporadic single-residue activation at an N-terminal cysteine.
- Aromatic prenyltransferases (PT-barrel enzymes): weaker, scattered activation across mixed secondary structure elements (likely off-target relative to the core extracellular glycan-focused concept).

Summary: Residue-level detector for acidic/polar hotspots within intrinsically disordered regions (often N‑terminal), with a strong preference for Asp, Asn, His, and Tyr; highlights acidic low‑complexity stretches and flexible loops rather than structured domains
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks scattered in IDRs (low pLDDT/low-confidence helices or coils), sometimes forming small clusters within acidic compositional-bias segments; minimal activation inside well-structured domains (e.g., zinc fingers, catalytic cores)
Exemplars: - Adenovirus E4-ORF4 regulatory protein: peaks on Tyr/His (and some Asp/Asn) in highly disordered loops outside annotated motifs
- Viral RNA-silencing suppressor with a C4-type zinc-finger: peaks on Asp and Tyr in low-confidence helical regions adjacent to, but not within, the zinc-finger
- Small viral accessory protein (RDUR-like): sparse peaks on Asn/Asp/His/Tyr across predicted disordered segments with no mapped functional sites
- Neuronal EF-hand Ca2+-binding regulator (calsenilin/DREAM/KChIP3): strong peaks on N-terminal Asp residues within an annotated disordered region
- Retrotransposon polyprotein: scattered peaks on Asp/Asn in long, acidic low-complexity, disordered regions

Summary: Signal peptide–directed secreted proteins: the feature marks the mature extracytoplasmic/periplasmic/extracellular (or thylakoid lumen) soluble domain, typically in the mid‑to‑C‑terminal portion of the protein and downstream of the signal peptide
Activation pattern: Regional activation on a single long, contiguous segment (often around positions 140–230), excluding the N‑terminal signal peptide; covers folded α/β elements or, in some families, polar/low‑complexity repeat segments; peaks can occur within short helices but the signal spans an extended domain region
Exemplars: - Periplasmic thiol:disulfide interchange proteins (DsbL/Dsb family) — activation across the C‑terminal half of the thioredoxin fold, not the signal peptide or catalytic motif.
- Secreted/periplasmic monofunctional chorismate mutases — activation on the C‑terminal helical segment distal to substrate‑binding sites.
- Flagellar L‑ring (FlgH) outer‑membrane lipoproteins — activation on the periplasmic ring‑forming domain of the mature protein.
- Pilus/fimbrial subunits and periplasmic assembly factors — activation over their exported/mature periplasmic domains.
- Outer‑membrane porins/channels and other lipoproteins — activation on large extracytoplasmic/periplasmic portions of the mature protein rather than the signal peptide.
- Secreted virulence factors and secretion‑system components — activation on exported soluble domains.
- Functional amyloid (Fap) system proteins — activation across repeat‑rich secreted segments driving fibrillation.
- Vertebrate secreted cytokines/hormones (and viral cytokine homologs) — activation on the mature secreted cytokine/hormone domain.
- Plant/algal thylakoid lumen extrinsic photosystem proteins — activation on the lumenal extrinsic domain after transit/signal peptides.

Summary: Periodic self-assembly scaffolds, with a strong preference for heptad‑repeat, amphipathic α‑helical coiled‑coil oligomerization segments (leucine‑zipper–like); in non‑helical repeat folds (e.g., WD40 β‑propellers) the feature weakly marks the recurring hydrophobic anchor positions that follow the repeat’s periodic pattern.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation over long, contiguous α‑helical stretches—most often mid‑to‑C‑terminal—overlapping annotated coiled‑coil/oligomerization domains; residue composition shows heptad‑repeat enrichment for L/A/V with interspersed E/K/R/Q. Minimal signal in disordered regions and in structured non‑coiled domains. Secondary mode: sparse, regularly spaced residue‑level peaks repeating once per structural repeat (e.g., one Y/F per WD blade) within β‑propeller scaffolds.
Exemplars: - Band‑7/SPFH (stomatin/prohibitin/flotillin/erlin/podocin, e.g., vacuolin): strong activation on C‑terminal coiled‑coil oligomerization helices.
- Plant trihelix transcription factors: activation confined to the C‑terminal coiled‑coil dimerization helix; the MADF DNA‑binding region remains off.
- WD40 β‑propeller scaffolds: weak, periodic peaks on one aromatic (Y/F) within each blade’s β‑strand, consistent with repeat‑scaffold anchor positions.
- Bacteriophage portal proteins and DNA‑packaging terminase small subunits: long coiled‑coil assembly helices highlighted.
- Phage lysis module proteins (holin/pinholin/spanin): periplasmic/membrane‑proximal coiled‑coil oligomerization segments activated.
- Type III secretion/filament needles and pilins: polymerizing helical (coiled‑coil–like) segments activated.
- Retroviral/retrotransposon Gag/Capsid/Pol regions: coiled‑coil or helical assembly modules highlighted.
- ATP synthase subunit c: oligomeric membrane helices in the c‑ring show activation despite not being classical coiled‑coils.
- Plant stress/defense coiled‑coil proteins: activation on their coiled‑coil oligomerization regions.

Summary: N-terminal “mature head” segments of proteins: the first structured or disordered region immediately following the signal peptide when present (or the extreme N-terminus otherwise), encompassing the initial 20–150 residues that initiate the main domain or interaction region rather than the hydrophobic signal peptide or catalytic core
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long, contiguous N-terminal stretches; onset is abrupt just after signal peptide cleavage (signal peptides themselves are not activated) or at Met1 in non-secreted proteins; spans the first few secondary-structure elements or low-complexity/polar segments; little to no activation in downstream catalytic cores or C‑terminal domains
Exemplars: - Fungal GPI-anchored cell-surface adhesins (e.g., alpha-agglutinin): activation on the mature N-terminal head immediately after the signal peptide, before Ig-like/repeat regions.
- Outer-membrane porins (KdgM/OMBB): activation on the first β-strand and adjacent elements of the β-barrel directly following the cleaved signal peptide.
- Aromatic/indole prenyltransferases (DMAPP transferases/DMATS family): activation on the N-terminal helix–turn–helix segment preceding the catalytic core and ligand-binding sites.
- Kinetochore complex subunits (e.g., Mcm21): activation on the N-terminal coiled-coil/low-complexity region implicated in assembly interactions; not on the structured C-terminus.
- Nucleoporins (e.g., Nup133): activation on the disordered N-terminal segment required for NPC organization, distinct from more structured downstream regions.

Summary: N-terminal regions of proteins, emphasizing targeting and processing segments when present (Sec/Tat signal peptides, signal anchors, and mitochondrial transit peptides) and, otherwise, the first disordered/low-complexity stretch of the polypeptide; frequently includes prepropeptides of secreted proteins and the initial cytosolic tails of non-secretory proteins across all taxa.
Activation pattern: Regional activation at extreme N-termini (start through ~30–100 residues), with residue-level peaks at cleavage motifs when present (signal peptidase -3/-1, polybasic convertase sites); in non-secretory proteins, enrichment over Pro/Ser/Gly/Ala/Thr-rich or basic/acidic clusters and short disordered N-tails; may also highlight the first transmembrane signal anchor or mitochondrial transit peptides.
Exemplars:
- Viral envelope and secreted precursors (herpes gL; neuropeptide precursors): activation on signal peptide and propeptide cleavage.
- Viral accessory/regulatory proteins (e.g., Vif): activation on disordered, Pro/Ser-rich N-termini lacking secretory signals.
- Polytopic and single-pass membrane proteins (e.g., VAChT, PRCD): activation on the first signal anchor/TM and adjacent cytosolic/extracellular segment or lipidation motif.
- Mitochondrial proteins (e.g., ATP synthase ε): activation on N-terminal transit peptides.
- Cytosolic housekeeping enzymes (e.g., APS kinase, DNA ligase) and nuclear factors (e.g., EID-2B, TEX19): activation on short, low-complexity/disordered N-terminal segments preceding the globular core.

Summary: General helical secondary-structure elements, with strongest activation on short DNA-binding recognition helices (HTH/homeodomain/σ-factor region 4) and on extended helical repeats including collagen Gly–X–Y triple helices; also frequently engages signal/transmembrane helices in secreted and membrane proteins
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks that map onto helices: concentrated within specific functional helices (e.g., HTH recognition/pol core-binding helices, signal peptides) and sparsely distributed along long helical repeats (collagen). Often clusters near N-termini of bacterial proteins (N-terminal HTH or signal peptides), while long eukaryotic helical proteins show peaks across broad regions.
Exemplars: - ECF/σ70 sigma factors: peaks on C-terminal domain 4 HTH recognition helix that contacts DNA (e.g., loss-of-function sites within this helix).
- HTH transcriptional regulators/repressors (bacteria/archaea): N-terminal DNA-binding helices.
- Two-component systems: response regulators’ C-terminal HTH helices; histidine kinases’ helical HAMP/coiled-coil linkers.
- Toxin–antitoxin antitoxins: DNA-binding helices (HTH/RHH-like) used for autoregulation.
- Membrane transporters/translocases: N-terminal signal peptides and transmembrane α-helices.
- Collagens: repetitive Gly–X–Y triple-helical region across the length of the chain.
- Neuropeptide precursors (e.g., RFamide family): N-terminal signal peptides and short helical segments in propeptides.
- Eukaryotic nuclear transcription factors: DNA-contacting helices in homeodomains and in C2H2 zinc-finger modules.
- Core transcription/translation subunits (e.g., RNAP ω, ribosomal proteins): compact α-helical cores.
- Metal homeostasis regulators (e.g., Fur-like): DNA-binding HTH helices sensing metal-responsive promoters.

Summary: A cross-taxa feature marking solvent-exposed loop/turn segments within ectodomains of secreted and single-pass membrane proteins involved in adhesion/immune recognition, plus analogous exposed loops in extracellular matrix glycoproteins, SUN domains, and copper-binding cupredoxin/LPMO enzymes.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated in N-terminal extracellular domains (Ig-like V/C2 domains, SUN domains, plastocyanin/cupredoxin folds, AA9 LPMO surfaces), typically in coils/turns at beta-sheet edges and inter-strand loops, often near ligand- or metal-binding motifs; little/no activation in signal peptides, transmembranes, or cytosolic tails; enrichment for acidic/polar/small residues (E, D, S, T, G, P) with rare Cys; variable number of peaks per protein.
Exemplars: 
- IgSF receptors and immune checkpoints (nectins, TLT-2/TREM-like, PD-L1/B7 family, TCR variable chains, CD8 beta, CD200R): activation on exposed loops within Ig-like ectodomains.
- Polymeric immunoglobulin receptor: activation within its multiple Ig-like ectodomains.
- SUN-domain proteins (human SUN-domain ossification factor; plant SUN4): activation on loop/coil segments inside the C-terminal SUN domain.
- Cupredoxins/phytocyanins (auracyanin/plastocyanin-like; ENODL phytocyanins): activation on loops flanking copper-binding histidines.
- Fungal AA9 LPMOs: activation on surface loops surrounding the active-site copper.
- Extracellular matrix glycoproteins (EMILIN-1): activation on exposed acidic loop regions in extracellular domains.

Summary: Low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered short segments enriched for Gly/Pro and polybasic residues (often with WG/GW, GG, KR/RR motifs) that frequently occur in leader/propeptides and at proteolytic processing sites, but also in non‑processed IDRs (terminal tails, cytosolic/nuclear loops) of diverse proteins, including membrane and enzymatic proteins—marking disordered patches rather than structured cores.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short (~10–40 aa) disordered windows, with peaks at GG, KR/RR or polybasic clusters, GP‑rich tracts, and junctions between disordered and structured regions; weak in hydrophobic transmembrane helices and well‑folded catalytic cores.
Exemplars:
- Class II bacteriocin/lantibiotic precursors: strong on N‑terminal double‑glycine leaders up to the GG cleavage motif; weak on mature toxin cores.
- Secreted peptide/toxin and prohormone precursors: activation on low‑complexity prosegments containing dibasic convertase sites and nearby GP/WG repeats.
- Sperm protamine precursors: concentrated on disordered propeptides and at propeptide–mature boundaries; minimal on highly basic mature cores.
- Viral accessory/regulatory microproteins: polybasic, GP‑rich low‑complexity patches (often NLS‑like) in short basic proteins.
- lncRNA‑encoded micropeptides and very small uncharacterized proteins: WG/GW‑ and GP‑rich disordered segments.
- Plant transcription factors with WG/GW‑ and GP‑rich low‑complexity regions: activation on those patches.
- ATP synthase epsilon subunits: signal on short GP‑rich linkers or terminal low‑complexity tails.
- Large enzymes (e.g., DDX11 helicase, acyl‑CoA synthetase): activation on disordered N/C‑terminal low‑complexity regions or basic/GP‑rich insertions.
- Small mitochondrial membrane proteins (ATP8): signal on short basic matrix‑exposed loops or termini flanking TM helices.

Summary: C-terminal end-of-chain micro-motif: the feature marks the extreme C-terminus (last 1–3 residues) of proteins, typically in a disordered/coil tail at a helix-to-coil transition, with a preference for small/aliphatic or small polar residues often mixed with acidic residues. It reflects a positional/structural tail signature rather than a specific function.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated on the final dipeptide/tripeptide at the C-terminus; largely silent across structured domains and annotated catalytic/ligand-binding sites.
Exemplars: - CRISPR-associated Cas2 endonuclease: no signal in the folded core; activation only at the terminal two residues in a low-confidence C-terminal coil.
- Two-component system sensor histidine kinase: absent in transmembranes and kinase domain; activation restricted to the last three residues at a helix-to-coil transition in the C-terminal tail.

Summary: A structural motif: the model fires on well‑ordered secondary‑structure building blocks of repeat‑based scaffolds—primarily α‑helical hairpins/solenoids (annexin/PFTA/HEAT‑like) and, when present, short β‑strands that form blade units (ABBA/propeller)—with a bias toward N‑terminal domain segments and helix/strand termini that often contain aromatic (especially Trp) and glycine‑rich motifs used at ligand or subunit‑interaction surfaces.
Activation pattern: Mixed regional and focal: dense, contiguous activation across runs of repeats in structured cores, with superimposed residue‑level peaks at helix ends, short β‑strands, and adjacent turns; prefers structured over disordered regions, is frequently stronger in the N‑terminal half of domains, and can collapse to a single hotspot in linker helices between domains.
Exemplars: - Annexins: strong activation on α‑helical segments in repeats 1–2 of the core domain.
- Protein farnesyltransferase α‑subunit (PFTA/HEAT‑like solenoid): activation along helices of repeats 1–4 and a larger helical bundle in the structured core.
- Nucleoporins (Nup84, Nup107–Nup85 subcomplex): scattered peaks at coil→helix boundaries and helix termini within the α‑solenoid/propeller junction regions.
- Aromatic/indole prenyltransferases (ABBA/DMATS family): β‑strands and adjacent turns near the DMAPP‑binding site and catalytic Trp.
- CRISPR type III small subunit Cmr5: N‑terminal α‑helical array specifically, despite a helical C‑terminus.
- V‑type ATPase subunit d: N‑terminal coil/first helix and a mid‑region turn; low activation in the C‑terminal third.
- Two‑component histidine kinases: pinpoint activation on a single residue within the helical HAMP–kinase linker.

Summary: Extracellular/cell-surface secretome signature: the feature recognizes ectodomains of secreted or surface-presented proteins, especially cysteine-rich, disulfide-stabilized peptides and repeats (e.g., toxins, EGF/disintegrin/adhesion modules, lectins), C-terminal regions surrounding GPI-anchor attachment sites, and also short exofacial loops of multi-pass membrane proteins when these loops are cysteine- and/or glycan-rich; it captures appended extracellular carbohydrate-binding modules of secreted CAZymes
Activation pattern: Primarily regional/domain-level activation over long, contiguous stretches of extracellular sequence (often at protein termini), with residue-level peaks near Cys clusters and adjacent residues (aromatics/Pro/Ser/Thr); frequently highest around the GPI omega site and drops within cleaved C-terminal propeptides; can cover complete mature secreted peptide chains or selectively highlight appended extracellular modules (e.g., CBMs) rather than catalytic cores; additionally, can mark short exofacial loops (not necessarily at termini) in multi-pass transporters when they contain Cys–Cys/Cys-x(n)–Cys or NXS/T glycosylation motifs
Exemplars: Trypanosome variant surface glycoproteins (VSGs) – strong activation across the disordered C-terminal GPI-anchor region, peaking at the omega site and disappearing in the cleaved propeptide; Ciliate mating pheromones – activation across the mature secreted cystine-rich peptide with peaks at N-terminal aromatic residues and reduced signal on disulfide-bonded cysteines; Secreted carbohydrate-active enzymes – activation on C-terminal CBM10 carbohydrate-binding modules and adjacent helices, not on the catalytic cores; Disulfide-rich venom peptides and Kunitz/other protease inhibitors – extended activation across the mature, disulfide-stabilized chains; Viral envelope/entry glycoproteins – activation on cysteine-rich ectodomain loops; EGF-like/disintegrin/adhesion modules and lectins – activation on cysteine-constrained extracellular repeats/domains; SLC/GLUT-family transporters – activation on short extracellular loops bearing conserved disulfide-bonded cysteines and glycosylation sites

Summary: Short, basic/low-complexity N‑terminal boundary segments at the transition from targeting/disordered tails (signal peptides, mitochondrial transit peptides, unstructured N‑tails) into the first folded region (domain N‑cap), often spanning proteolytic/processing sites and sometimes containing Trp-centered micro-motifs; a generic N‑terminal processing/junction element shared across diverse proteins (nuclear/chromatin factors, secreted/envelope enzymes, mitochondrial proteins).
Activation pattern: Regional activation in one or more short tracts (≈15–40 aa) concentrated near the extreme N‑terminus. Peaks frequently occur at signal/transit peptide cleavage junctions or within the first β‑strand/coil of an N‑terminal domain; segments are typically low-to-moderate confidence/disordered, though can include small structured elements. Core folded domains away from the N‑terminus show little/no activation; occasional secondary weak peaks appear in nearby loops.
Exemplars: - Methyl-CpG-binding (MBD) proteins: activation on the N‑terminal portion/N‑cap of the MBD domain.
- Kinetochore/chromatin SANTA-domain proteins (e.g., KNL2): activation on the N‑terminal β‑strand/coil cluster within the SANTA domain.
- Mitochondrial proteins (e.g., mitochondrial-processing peptidase β subunit, mitoribosomal protein mL55): activation spans the transit-peptide–mature-chain junction and peaks at the cleavage site (often including a local Trp/Gly).
- Secreted/envelope enzymes (e.g., bacterial peptidoglycan transglycosylase RlpA; GH11/GH12 xylanases and related glycosidases/esterases): activation immediately downstream of the signal peptide/propeptide.
- BTB/POZ KCTD proteins: activation on the disordered N‑terminal tail preceding the BTB domain, including sites of N‑terminal acetylation and phosphorylation.
- Plant TIFY/JAZ repressors: activation on short, basic/polar N‑terminal segments around the ZIM/TIFY region.

Summary: Hydrophobic α-helical targeting segments used for export or membrane insertion—primarily the h‑region of Sec-type N‑terminal signal peptides (including bacterial lipoprotein and chloroplast thylakoid lumen signals), with secondary activation on short transmembrane/signal‑anchor helices. The feature prefers compact, low‑charge runs of L/I/V/F/A with occasional S/G interruptions and is common in secreted, periplasmic, and outer‑membrane systems.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short (∼8–25 aa), contiguous hydrophobic α-helices, most often within residues ~5–30 at the N-terminus; multiple patches can appear if several hydrophobic helices are present. Peaks center on the signal peptide h‑region; activation drops at signal boundaries and is absent from structured catalytic cores and active sites; occasional activation on internal transmembrane helices.
Exemplars: - Secreted serine protease (SplB family): activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide h‑region; none on the protease domain/catalytic triad.
- D‑alanyl‑D‑alanine endopeptidase: activation confined to the N‑terminal signal peptide h‑region.
- Pertussis toxin subunit (secreted exotoxin component): activation on the helical core of the signal peptide.
- Periplasmic solute‑binding proteins (ABC/SBP family): activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide; no activation on ligand‑binding residues.
- Gram‑negative lipoproteins/outer‑membrane‑associated proteins: activation on the lipoprotein signal peptide hydrophobic core or N‑terminal signal anchors.
- Bacteriophage lysis/envelope proteins: activation on N‑terminal signal sequences/signal anchors.
- Chloroplast thylakoid lumen proteins: activation on the hydrophobic h‑region within the thylakoid transfer signal (after the transit peptide).
- Integral membrane proteins: activation on short transmembrane helices.

Summary: Extracellular/lumenal ectodomains of secretory‑pathway glycoproteins (viral envelope spikes and eukaryotic surface/lysosomal proteins), characterized by dense N‑linked glycosylation sequons and disulfide‑bonded cysteines; often Ser/Thr/Asn‑rich and spanning long ectodomain stretches immediately after a signal peptide
Activation pattern: Dominant domain-level activation across long extracellular/lumenal segments beginning just after the signal peptide; little to none in transmembrane helices or cytosolic tails. Broad plateaus with local peaks at/near N‑X‑S/T sites and disulfide-forming cysteines; present in both structured beta/alpha regions and low‑complexity/mucin‑like loops.
Exemplars: - Viral envelope/fusogen glycoproteins (e.g., herpesvirus gB/gH): strong activation across the glycosylated, disulfide‑rich ectodomain; minimal in TM/cytosolic tails.
- Lysosomal type I membrane glycoproteins: activation confined to the lumenal domain containing multiple N‑glycosylation sites; absent from TM segments and cytosolic sorting tails.
- ER DSC E3 ubiquitin ligase complex subunit (luminal glycoprotein): high activation over the N‑terminal lumenal region with clustered N‑glycosylation; none over transmembranes or cytosolic RING domain.
- Trypanosome transferrin receptor subunit (ESAG6): activation on the extracellular helix/loop ectodomain containing an N‑glycosylation site and a disulfide bond.
