- Gelsolin-like actin-binding/severing proteins: multiple sharp peaks on beta-strands across repeat domains in high-confidence structured regions.
- Cullin scaffolds: peaks on hydrophobic residues within alpha-helical repeat regions consistent with structured-core preference.

Summary: Beta–strand-rich extracellular modules—primarily beta-sandwich domains (Ig/C2-type and fibronectin type III, FNIII) but also related beta-strand modules (e.g., MAM, CCP/Sushi, C1q-like)—in metazoan proteins; predominantly in cell-surface/secreted ectodomains and also in intracellular Ig/FNIII scaffolds; includes occasional bacterial Fn3-like inserts.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks repeated across module arrays; strongest on beta-strands and immediately adjacent loop/coil positions at strand-to-coil transitions (often a high peak followed by a secondary peak two residues downstream). Activation tracks beta-strand-rich accessory domains (Ig/FNIII and homologs) and is absent from signal peptides, transmembrane helices, enzymatic catalytic cores, and low-complexity regions; location bias is extracellular but not exclusive. Enriched for S/T/E/D with many G/P; cysteines comparatively underrepresented.
Exemplars: - IL-1 receptor family (Ig-like C2-type ectodomains): peaks on beta-strands and nearby loops within each Ig domain; no activation in TM or TIR.
- Class I cytokine receptors (e.g., oncostatin-M receptor): peaks at strand-to-coil junctions within each FNIII repeat; cytosolic tail inactive.
- MAM/Ig/FNIII GPI-anchored adhesion proteins (e.g., Contactin/MDGA): recurring high-then-medium doublets at C-terminal strand-to-loop edges across Ig, FNIII, and MAM domains.
- IgSF CAMs, receptor-type PTPs, and RTKs with Ig/FNIII or FNIII-like ectodomains (e.g., Eph receptors): broad coverage of beta-sandwich strand/loop edges across extracellular repeats.
- ECM/cartilage proteins with non-Ig/FNIII beta-strand modules (e.g., CILP/CILP2) and metalloproteinases with accessory extracellular beta-strand domains (e.g., MMP-23): same strand-to-loop motif on their beta-rich modules.
- Intracellular cytoskeletal Ig/FNIII scaffolds (e.g., obscurin-like proteins): same motif across internal Ig/FNIII arrays.
- Viral Ig-like immunomodulators and bacterial enzymes bearing Fn3-like inserts: activation on beta-sandwich strands and adjacent loops consistent with the motif.

Summary: Short polybasic amphipathic segments (Lys/Arg- and Ser/Thr‑biased, interspersed with hydrophobics) used as generic targeting/processing and electrostatic interaction patches—frequently at extreme N termini (signal/transit/NLS-like regions) and as internal basic patches for membrane or nucleic acid binding
Activation pattern: Regional activation on multiple short (≈5–20 aa) segments per protein; strong enrichment at the very N terminus, with additional non-contiguous peaks internally; no strict consensus beyond Lys/Arg + Ser/Thr with mixed hydrophobics
Exemplars: - RAD50/SbcC DNA repair ATPases: basic patches near the N-terminal ATPase module and additional internal basic segments along the coiled‑coil/hinge regions.
- Dynamin/Obg large GTPases: short amphipathic/basic helices and loops (membrane/PIP2- or partner-binding patches) and N‑terminal basic segments.
- Secreted/metalloproteases (ADAMs, snake venom SVMPs) and other peptidases: N‑region of signal peptides (positively charged) and polybasic proprotein convertase sites in prodomains.
- Aspartic/signal peptidases: basic leader segments and polybasic processing/cleavage motifs.
- Fungal adhesins/cell‑wall glycoproteins: N‑terminal signal peptide N‑regions and Ser/Thr‑rich, basic low‑complexity segments.
- Retrotransposon/retroviral polyproteins and bacteriophage proteins: polybasic membrane-targeting patches and basic cleavage/processing sites.
- Central metabolic lyases/dehydratases (aconitase family, homoaconitase, 2‑methylcitrate dehydratase, IPMI): short surface basic patches; in organellar isoforms, N‑terminal transit‑peptide segments.
- Cell‑envelope/nucleotide‑sugar metabolism enzymes and related ligases/kinases: basic signal/leader regions for secretion/periplasmic targeting.
- Archaeal F420‑cofactor enzymes: N‑terminal or internal short basic amphipathic segments used for targeting or electrostatic interactions.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments enriched in polar/charged residues with Gly/Pro, especially when present as extended (>25–30 aa) N‑terminal propeptides/transit-like regions and flexible linkers/repeats; common but not universal across proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation in short contiguous clusters aggregated within longer low‑complexity tracts; strongest near N‑termini and in cytosolic/extracellular disordered loops/linkers; short amphipathic signal peptides/MTS or compact cysteine‑rich domains generally do not activate; residue‑level peaks over charged/polar and Gly/Pro rather than hydrophobic cores.
Exemplars:
- Mitochondrial/chloroplast ribosomal proteins: activation in a subset with extended basic/disordered tails (chloroplast transit peptides often Ser/Thr‑rich); mitochondrial MTS alone is often insufficient if short/amphipathic.
- DNA/RNA polymerase subunits: activation only when species‑specific low‑complexity insertions or flexible linkers are present; orthologs lacking such insertions may not activate.
- Secreted proteins: strong activation in large glycoproteins with mucin‑like repeats or disordered propeptides; simple cysteine‑rich inhibitors (e.g., Kazal) typically lack sufficient low‑complexity and may not activate.
- Membrane enzymes and receptors: activation in proteins with long disordered cytosolic tails or luminal loops; small hydrophobic or multi‑pass proteins with short loops (e.g., DHHC family, gas vesicle proteins) usually not activated.
- Extracellular matrix glycoproteins (mucins, proteoglycans, collagen‑like proteins): multiple Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich O‑glycosylated repeats and flexible linkers activate strongly.
- Viral polyproteins/structural proteins: activation on low‑complexity charged segments/flexible linkers when present; not universal.

Summary: Self-maturation zones of extracellular/virion spikes and adhesins: beta-strand–rich C‑terminal scaffolds (often right‑handed β‑helix or β‑barrel elements) together with adjacent propeptide/auto‑chaperone/self‑cleaving segments (including intein HINT domains), frequently immediately flanking or overlapping proteolytic processing junctions and enriched for short G/S/T/N/D‑rich repeats.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation across long C‑terminal stretches of large secreted or surface/virion structural proteins; strongest in beta‑strand/coil segments enriched for short GG/GT/TT/TG motifs and small/polar residues, sometimes extending through contiguous β‑barrel translocators or β‑helix spikes. Sharp local peaks occur at or just N‑terminal to proteolytic cleavage sites (auto‑proteolysis or virion protease processing). In intein-containing proteins, activation is confined to short patches within the intein core, with exteins largely inactive. Outside these contexts, only sparse single‑residue hits are observed. Taxonomically biased to phages of Gram‑negative bacteria and Gram‑negative surface proteins; rare elsewhere.
Exemplars: Phage tailspike/receptor‑binding proteins with intramolecular chaperones: activation across the terminal portion of the mature β‑helical scaffold immediately N‑terminal to the auto‑proteolytic release site of the chaperone. Type VI secretion system VgrG spikes: activation in the conserved C‑terminal spike/needle region. Gram‑negative autotransporter adhesins: continuous activation from the C‑terminal passenger auto‑chaperone region into the translocator β‑barrel, with additional patches in the β‑helical passenger. Adenovirus capsid‑associated protein VIII: high activation across the disordered propeptide, peaking adjacent to virion protease cleavage sites. Intein‑bearing enzymes (e.g., RFC subunits): sparse activation within the intein HINT domain motifs, absent from flanking exteins. Eukaryotic surface/secreted proteins (e.g., Warthog family): only weak, isolated residue hits, consistent with incidental sequence motifs.

Summary: A short, charged, amphipathic alpha-helix used as a generic interaction element across diverse proteins, often serving as the recognition helix in nucleic acid-binding domains or as a surface helix within compact folds (including the single helix of Kunitz-type inhibitors), rather than a family-specific motif.
Activation pattern: Localized activation on short contiguous segments (~10–15 aa) that map to an alpha-helix with strong residue-level peaks within the helical core and decay into flanking coil/cap residues; windows are enriched for E/D/K/R and can recur to produce extended activation in multi-helical regions of large proteins.
Exemplars: - Methyl-CpG-binding (MBD) proteins: activation on the core alpha-helix within the MBD DNA-binding domain.
- AP2/ERF transcription factors: activation on the alpha-helix inside the AP2 DNA-binding domain.
- Respiratory complex I 21 kDa subunit: activation on a specific C-terminal alpha-helix in the structured region.
- Ribosomal L20/eL20 proteins: activation on the basic rRNA-contacting helix.
- Phage integrases/recombinases: activation on the DNA-recognition helix of HTH-like modules.
- Nucleases/RNA-processing enzymes: activation on short basic helices forming nucleic acid–binding surfaces near active sites.
- ADP-ribosyltransferase/PARP family: activation on charged helical segments within the catalytic/DNA-binding regions.
- Kunitz-type protease inhibitors/toxins: activation on the fold’s single short helix, often adjacent to conserved cysteine pairs.

Summary: Surface-exposed beta-strand edges and their flanking turn/coil or helix-capping segments—short patches at strand entry/exit and domain-end caps that often form interaction surfaces rather than buried secondary-structure cores.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks in short clusters. Strongest signals occur in coils immediately before/after beta-strands, flexible terminal loops, and occasional solvent-exposed positions within edge beta-strands or a C-terminal helix. Little to no signal in buried helices or the interior of well-ordered sheets, and generally not across long low-complexity disordered segments.
Exemplars: - Aromatic-ring oxygenase small beta subunits (Rieske oxygenases): activation on coil segments just upstream of beta-strands and a flexible C-terminal loop.
- Chemokines (CCL/CXCL family): activation on solvent-exposed residues in core beta-strands and on the C-terminal alpha-helix that make receptor/heparin-contact patches.
- Plant WRKY transcription factors: activation on selected beta-strand positions within the WRKY DNA-binding domain and the adjacent helix-to-coil segment immediately C-terminal to the domain.

Summary: Residue-level signature for short turns and capping positions that connect secondary-structure elements—especially beta-strand–beta-strand hairpins and beta-to-alpha linkers—enriched for Pro, Gly, and acidic residues at strand edges or immediately adjacent loops, generally non-catalytic and common across diverse folds.
Activation pattern: Sparse, single-residue peaks (typically 1–5 per protein) at strand ends and in short coils/turns linking secondary structures; often on Pro/Gly/Asp/Glu, sometimes at helix N-caps; occurs in both well-ordered beta-rich cores and more flexible/low-confidence beta segments.
Exemplars: - Small heat shock proteins/alpha-crystallin: peaks on Pro/Gly/acidic residues in loops connecting beta-strands within the alpha-crystallin beta-sandwich and at an N-cap of a short helix.
- Sm/LSM/Sm-like domains (snRNP core SmE; NatC auxiliary subunit NAA38): focal activations on an acidic residue within a beta-strand and nearby loop/strand-end positions characteristic of the Sm fold.
- Type III secretion system secretins and flagellar L-ring proteins: isolated residues within or immediately adjacent to beta-strands of periplasmic beta-rich domains, including flexible, low-confidence segments.
- Protein kinase-like (TP53RK): Pro and Gly in coil linkers bridging beta-strands to alpha-helices near the ATP-binding region (turn/cap positions rather than catalytic sites).
- Bacteriophage lambda repressor cI: Proline- and acidic-enriched turns/short coils that link beta-strands in the C-terminal beta-domain.
- Diaminopimelate epimerase: discrete peaks at turns and strand edges (including a substrate-binding turn), avoiding catalytic cysteines.

Summary: Short, acidic/charged, Gly/Pro-enriched secondary‑structure junctions—especially the C‑termini of α‑helices and adjacent loop/turn (often helix–turn–β) segments—used as assembly/linker elements in phage/tube/flagellar/export apparatus proteins but occurring broadly as generic helix‑capping motifs across proteins
Activation pattern: Regional, 10–30 aa windows with residue‑level peaks; strongest at the last ~5–10 residues of an α‑helix and into the following loop/turn, sometimes extending to the first residue(s) of a β‑strand; multiple disjoint windows in multi‑repeat scaffolds; enriched for D/E/K/R and Gly/Pro
Exemplars: • Phage tail/baseplate/tube/spike proteins: conserved short windows (e.g., tube 70–110) and multiple sites in baseplate/hub, consistent with helix–loop/turn elements at assembly interfaces
• Type VI secretion system components (VgrG/Hcp): shared motif around mid‑100s mapping to helix–loop segments in spike/tube architecture
• Flagellar hook‑associated protein 2 (FliD/HAP2): N‑terminal helix around residues 50–70, covering the helix C‑end and following loop
• Omp85/TpsB family (e.g., CdiB POTRA domain): helix–turn–β junction within POTRA (α‑helix into loop and first β residue)
• Trigger factor chaperone: short α‑helix with a Pro‑centered kink at the helix–loop boundary
• Methionine aminopeptidase, GTP cyclohydrolase, sulfate adenylyltransferase: isolated helix C‑ends with adjacent loop, or a β‑strand with flanking loops
• Lon protease N‑terminal domain: multiple low‑confidence mixed helix/β/coil segments consistent with flexible helix–coil/linker regions

Summary: Parallel beta-helix/β-solenoid (PbH1-type) repeat architecture characteristic of secreted, polysaccharide-active proteins and phage capsule depolymerases; the feature detects the repeating rung starts and strand cores of the β-helix scaffold rather than catalytic motifs
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation spanning long β-helix regions; strong residue-level peaks at the first residue of each PbH1 repeat (coil-to-β-strand boundary) with secondary peaks on internal hydrophobic β-strand positions; minimal signal in flanking non-β-helix modules (e.g., intramolecular chaperones, hemolysin-type repeats). Activated residues are enriched in small/aliphatic (G, A, S, T, V, I) and appear in extended repeat arrays of large, secreted proteins.
Exemplars: - Mannuronan C5-epimerases (AlgE family): activation tracks the PbH1 repeat array with maxima at repeat starts and within β-strands (e.g., AlgE6).
- Pectate/pectin lyase-like CAZymes (across bacteria, fungi, plants): activation over the pectate lyase-like β-helix scaffold in the catalytic domain.
- Bacteriophage tail spike/capsule depolymerases specific for diverse capsular/O-antigen polysaccharides: activation across the central β-helix shaft; chaperone/autocatalytic C-termini show little activation.
- Plant pollen pectate lyase-like allergens: activation on the β-helix core that underlies the allergen fold.
- Extracellular autotransporter/adhesins with β-solenoid passengers (pertactin-like): activation along the β-solenoid repeat region.
- Additional extracellular CAZymes acting on acidic/structural polysaccharides (alginate, carrageenan, glycosaminoglycans): activation when their domains adopt β-helix/β-solenoid architecture.

Summary: Mature secreted bioactive peptide module from preproproteins—especially cysteine‑rich, disulfide‑bonded and/or cyclic toxins, antimicrobial/defense peptides, and pheromone/inhibitory peptides. The feature marks the processed functional peptide (often tens of residues; frequently cationic and crosslinked) rather than the N‑terminal signal/leader.
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation over a contiguous region that begins at or just after the signal/leader cleavage site and spans the entire mature peptide; minimal/absent on N‑terminal signal peptides and most propeptide segments. Activation is broad across secondary-structure types (helix, strand, coil) and present in both compact disulfide-stabilized folds and disordered bioactive tails; individual cysteines are not uniquely required or maximally peaked.
Exemplars: - Conotoxins (venom peptides): strong activation confined to the mature conotoxin; no activation on signal/propeptide.
- Plant cyclotides (defensin-like, head-to-tail cyclic): activation exactly across the cyclized mature peptide region.
- Fungal defensins (e.g., plectasin): activation across the mature defensin domain; absent on signal/propeptide.
- Bacterial heat-stable enterotoxin II: high activation on the mature toxin peptide; none on the signal peptide.
- Fungal/yeast killer toxins (KP4 family): activation across the mature secreted toxin chain; not on the signal peptide.
- Plant cyclopeptides (e.g., pumilarin precursor): activation restricted to the annotated cyclopeptide region.
- Gram-positive peptide pheromones/inhibitors (Rap phosphatase inhibitor propeptide): activation on the C‑terminal disordered bioactive peptide segment produced by processing.

Summary: A structural signal for the β‑strand cores of small, secreted β‑rich domains—most prominently the β‑trefoil fold—found across extracellular lectins and signaling proteins (e.g., ricin B–type lectins, IL‑1 cytokines, FGFs) and related cell‑surface adhesion modules.
Activation pattern: Regional/residue-level peaks confined to the structured β‑rich domain of precursors, with multiple short contiguous segments mapping to individual β‑strands (often centered on hydrophobic residues like Leu/Ile/Val and sometimes adjacent loops); absent from signal peptides, low‑complexity/disordered regions, and unrelated catalytic domains.
Exemplars: - Ricin B–type lectin domains appended to glycosidases: activation limited to the lectin domain, highlighting several distinct β‑strands; no activation in the catalytic glycosidase domain.
- Interleukin‑1 family cytokines (e.g., IL‑33): activation on three β‑strands within the mature β‑trefoil cytokine, including strands near receptor‑contact residues.
- Fibroblast growth factors (FGFs): activation on loop/β‑strand elements that form the β‑trefoil core, including regions flanking conserved disulfide bonds.
- Fungal cell‑wall adhesion/PIR proteins: activation restricted to β‑strands in the structured N‑terminal domain; no activation in the disordered, repeat‑rich C‑terminal region.

Summary: Exposed aromatic–hydrophobic patches (often WxxW/WSxWS-like arrangements) in short β-strand/loop segments of β-sandwich domains on protein surfaces (both extracellular and cytosolic) that create ligand-recognition or folding/trafficking hot spots across secreted proteins, cell-surface receptors/adhesins, glycan-binding modules, and cytosolic scaffolds.
Activation pattern: Short contiguous peaks (~8–12 aa) mapping to individual β-strands or loop tips on surface-exposed modular domains; many long, repeat-rich proteins show multiple such patches. Enriched for W/F/Y with V/L/I plus S/T/E/D, frequently with nearby Prolines.
Exemplars:
- Type I cytokine/growth-factor receptors: activation on the conserved WSXWS/WSXW-like segment in their extracellular FN3 region that supports folding/trafficking and ligand engagement.
- Thrombospondin type-1 repeats (TSR) and complement properdin/adhesive TSR modules: activation on WxxW/WSxW “tryptophan ladder” faces forming binding grooves.
- Immunoglobulin-superfamily adhesion receptors (e.g., ICAM/VCAM-like) and CCP/Sushi repeats of complement regulators: activation on aromatic β-strand patches that mediate protein–protein binding.
- Thioester-containing alpha-2-macroglobulin/complement C3–C5 family: activation on exposed aromatic β-strands/loops adjacent to interaction/activation surfaces within their β-rich auxiliary domains.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes and CBM20/CBM48 starch-binding modules (plant chloroplastic/amyloplastic enzymes; bacterial CAZymes; AMPK/SNF1 β-subunits): activation on aromatic platforms (Trp/Tyr clusters) that stack with sugars.
- Archaeal S-layer glycoproteins and bacterial surface anchors (SLH/pilotin/secretin-associated proteins): activation on repeated aromatic–acidic surface patches used for cell-surface anchoring or partner recognition.
- C2-domain scaffolds and synaptic SH3/β-sandwich proteins: activation on Ca2+-dependent membrane-interacting loops (C2) or aromatic pockets for proline-rich ligands (SH3) in cytosolic scaffolds (e.g., PI3K-C2α, RasGAP, RIM-BP family).
- Viral/phage host-interaction proteins: activation on Ig-like/β-propeller/TSR-like motifs providing aromatic binding patches for host receptors or glycans.

Summary: β-strand–dense domains in secreted/periplasmic systems and polymorphic toxin scaffolds, with a strong preference for β-solenoid/β-helix repeat regions (e.g., RHS/YD) but also recognizing compact β-sandwich and α/β enzyme cores that present clustered internal β-strands.
Activation pattern: When β-solenoids are present, residue-level periodic peaks spaced ~20–22 amino acids across long C-terminal segments; otherwise, broader regional activation over internal β-strand clusters (e.g., PDZ β-sandwiches, lipoprotein β-sandwich cores, α/β enzyme sheets), with minimal activation at N-terminal signal peptides.
Exemplars:
- RHS/YD-repeat polymorphic toxins: sharp, regularly spaced peaks across successive YD-repeat rungs in C-terminal β-solenoids.
- Tc/C-type toxin carriers (e.g., YenC subunits): periodic activation along β-helix-like repeat segments.
- HtrA/DegP/Do-like proteases: activation over C-terminal PDZ β-sandwich regions rather than signal peptides.
- Envelope/outer-membrane biogenesis lipoproteins (e.g., BamE) and assembly factors: activation on β-sandwich repeat segments.
- Soluble toxin/enzyme effectors (e.g., DddA cytidine deaminase), secreted proteases (glutamyl endopeptidase, gelatinase), and metabolic enzymes (urease, oxidoreductase and hydrogenase subunits): activation on internal β-sheet–rich cores.
- Autotransporter passengers and secreted β-helix enzymes (pectate lyases, deacetylases): periodic activation along β-helix rungs when present.

Summary: Amphipathic alpha-helical interaction segments—including coiled-coils and short helices at helix–coil junctions—that mediate generic macromolecular binding (protein–protein and RNA/DNA), typically enriched for leucines and charged/polar residues and found across diverse proteins/taxa.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation with sharp residue-level peaks within short helical stretches and immediately flanking helix–coil transitions; occurs both in well-formed coiled-coils and in lower-confidence/disordered regions that can form helices upon binding; distributed along sequences rather than confined to termini.
Exemplars: - APC/C subunit (APC16): helix terminus and adjacent coil in a small helical subunit, consistent with a helix–coil boundary used in complex assembly.
- Histone RNA hairpin-binding protein (SLBP): C-terminal RNA-binding helix within the annotated RNA-binding region.
- Survival motor neuron (SMN): C-terminal oligomerization helix required for self-association, with minor sites in an N-terminal helix and loop adjacent to a helical element.
- Transforming acidic coiled-coil protein (TACC3): strong activation within the C-terminal coiled-coil that targets the spindle.
- Homeobox transcription factor (Hox protein): multiple weak sites in disordered/low-complexity regions and sparse peaks within the helical homeodomain DNA-binding fold.
- Protein phosphatase inhibitor 2 (PP1 regulator): helix in the phosphatase-binding region and nearby coil-to-helix transitions.

Summary: Short, Lys/Arg‑rich cytosolic juxtamembrane segment immediately N‑terminal to (and sometimes including the first residues of) a transmembrane helix—the “positive‑inside” n‑region of signal peptides/signal‑anchors or stop‑transfer motifs; often a disordered-to-helix transition, sometimes containing Pro/Gly breaks and an interfacial Trp, used to specify membrane insertion/orientation across diverse taxa and protein families.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on 8–20 aa stretches directly preceding the start of a TM helix, with residue‑level peaks 2–5 residues before the helix or at its N‑cap; frequently near the N‑terminus (~positions 10–50); often low pLDDT coil transitioning into the TM helix; strong bias for basic residues and occasional P/G and Trp at the interface.
Exemplars: - Anti-sigma factor (RsiV family): cytosolic basic patch immediately before its single-pass TM anchor.
- Bacterial receptor Ser/Thr kinases (Pkn family): flexible, Lys/Arg‑enriched cytosolic linker directly N‑terminal to the TM anchor of the membrane-anchored kinase.
- Respiratory chain subunits (cytochrome c oxidase small subunits): matrix-side positive N‑cap just before and into the first TM helix.
- Copper-transporting P-type ATPases: cytosolic loop enriched in basic residues directly preceding the first TM helix, enforcing positive‑inside topology.
- UstYa-family oxidases: N‑terminal basic helix that transitions into the TM helix from a disordered segment.
- Tetrahydromethanopterin S‑methyltransferase membrane subunits: short helix immediately N‑terminal to the TM helix with moderate basicity.
- Viral membrane/accessory proteins (e.g., envelope/ER-resident): basic cytosolic stretch that precedes and may include the first residue of the signal‑anchor TM.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity segments enriched in Gly and acidic/Ser/Thr residues that form flexible, surface‑exposed linkers, stalks, or extended loops. These regions often occur in secreted/outer‑membrane and cell‑wall proteins (e.g., adhesins, porins, secretion translocons) and, by analogy, as lid/hinge or insert loops in soluble enzymes and viral structural proteins; they frequently follow signal peptides but are not the signal peptide itself, serving roles in adhesion, glycosylated stalk formation, interaction modulation, or substrate access.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on internal mid‑to‑C‑terminal stretches (~50–120 aa), typically diffuse across the entire low‑complexity segment; commonly surface‑exposed/disordered; rarely at extreme N‑termini despite many precursors.
Exemplars: - Bacterial autotransporter/fimbrial adhesins and functional amyloid subunits (e.g., LapA/Fap families): activation on long Ser/Thr- and Asp/Glu‑rich low‑complexity repeats/stalks mediating adhesion/aggregation.
- Type III secretion system translocon components (YopB/YopD/IpaB/IpaC/PcrV families): activation on acidic, low‑complexity coiled‑coil/loop segments exposed during pore formation.
- Outer membrane porins and TonB‑dependent receptors: activation on extended extracellular loops that are acidic and low‑complexity.
- Lipase foldases/chaperones (lipase-specific foldases such as Lif/LipH): activation on flexible acidic low‑complexity segments used for client binding.
- Iron uptake/periplasmic accessory proteins (siderophore receptors/components): activation on disordered acidic linkers connecting structured domains.
- Aromatic prenyltransferases (ABBA‑fold enzymes such as NphB/CloQ-like): activation on glycine/acidic “lid” or insert loops that gate the active site.
- Fungal/yeast cell‑wall adhesins (Flo/Als/Hyr-type): activation on Ser/Thr‑rich, O‑glycosylated low‑complexity stalk regions.
- Vertebrate apolipoproteins (ApoA/ApoE classes): activation on acidic, low‑complexity amphipathic repeat segments involved in lipid interaction.
- Plant chloroplast outer‑envelope/tetrapyrrole‑pathway proteins: activation on acidic, glycine‑rich flexible linkers or envelope‑exposed low‑complexity regions.
- Restriction endonucleases and related DNA enzymes: activation on acidic, glycine‑rich loops adjacent to catalytic or DNA‑binding surfaces.
- Viral capsid/tail/envelope proteins: activation on gly/acidic disordered hinge or linker regions between structured domains.

Summary: Buried hydrophobic-core signal for structured, non-transmembrane domains—capturing hydrophobic packing layers in beta-sandwiches, coiled-coils/alpha-solenoids, and compact enzyme/ATPase folds—rather than true transmembrane segments.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks in short runs; often regularly spaced across repeats/solenoids and extended lumenal regions, but also present as shorter, less periodic runs within compact globular cores; strong enrichment for ILVFY/W with interspersed polar/charged residues; little to no activation in signal peptides, transmembrane helices, or long disordered tails.
Exemplars:
- TMEM131 family: strong, regularly spaced peaks across the N‑terminal lumenal PapD‑like beta‑sandwich region and adjacent lumenal repeats; no activation in the TM helix or cytosolic tail.
- Cilia/flagella-associated scaffolds (CFAPs): activation along extended coiled‑coils at a/d hydrophobic positions that form the coiled‑coil core.
- ER membrane VAP tethers: activation over the MSP beta‑sandwich core and coiled‑coil stalk packing residues.
- Vesicle coat/adaptor complexes (AP complexes, COPI coatomer subunits): frequent activation across alpha‑solenoid/HEAT/ARM repeat cores; some adaptors with smaller VHS/GAT modules (e.g., GGA) show weaker or patchy signal.
- TRAPP complex subunits: represented variably; long solenoid subunits can show modest or patchy activation.
- DNA damage/checkpoint scaffolds (FHA-domain proteins): activation on the FHA beta‑sandwich hydrophobic core, with strength varying by domain context.
- RNA helicases (DEAD/H-box; RecA-like ATPase cores): activation within the hydrophobic interiors of the RecA-like domains.
- Inositol polyphosphate 5‑phosphatases: activation in the catalytic domain’s hydrophobic interior.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes (glycoside hydrolases/cellulases, mannanases, chitinases; CBMs): activation on TIM‑barrel or beta‑sandwich/CBM cores, with variable strength across families.
- Secreted proteases (subtilisin-like and others): activation across the protease fold’s buried helices/strands.
- Urease components: activation within the oligomeric enzyme subunits’ hydrophobic cores.
- Integrin β family: activation in extracellular structured domains (I‑like/β domains and cysteine‑rich repeats) where hydrophobics form internal packing.
- General secretory precursors: activation throughout mature extracellular/lumenal domains, but not in signal peptides or transmembrane helices.

Summary: Parallel β-helix/β-solenoid repeats that form elongated, surface-exposed shafts/blades used for receptor binding and (often) carbohydrate recognition/depolymerization in viral/phage spikes and bacterial adhesins; the feature captures the mature β‑solenoid architecture (including triple β‑spiral variants) rather than generic β‑strands or associated chaperone/translocator domains.
Activation pattern: Domain-level: strong, continuous activation across the mature β‑solenoid region of very long extracellular proteins; off in N‑terminal low-complexity segments, C‑terminal intramolecular chaperone/autopeptidase (Peptidase S74) modules, and outer-membrane β‑barrel translocators. Residue-level: peaks on extended β‑strands and immediately flanking turns, minimal in helices; biased toward small/polar residues (G, T, N, S, Y) with common GTN/TGT and GG motifs; activation often terminates sharply at autocleavage sites separating the β‑solenoid from chaperone domains.
Exemplars: - Bacteriophage tailspikes/tail fibers (receptor-binding and polysaccharide-depolymerase modules): activation across the trimeric parallel β‑helix core; no activation in the C‑terminal intramolecular chaperone/autopeptidase.
- Gram-negative autotransporter adhesins: activation on β‑helical/β‑solenoid passenger segments mediating adhesion; absent from the C‑terminal β‑barrel translocator.
- Type VI secretion system spikes (VgrG): activation on the gp5-like β‑helix spike region.
- Viral attachment fibers (e.g., adenovirus fiber shaft, reovirus σ1): activation along triple β‑spiral/β‑solenoid repeats forming the shaft.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes linked to adhesion (pectate lyase-like depolymerases, phage sialidases): activation over β‑solenoid blades used for glycan binding/cleavage.
- Plant lectins and animal extracellular adhesion/ECM proteins: weaker but consistent activation on β‑sheet carbohydrate-recognition modules.

Summary: Solvent-exposed, flexible loop/coil segments flanking beta-strands in beta‑rich domains (especially beta‑sandwich/jelly‑roll, cupredoxin, GOLD and related lectin/PH-like folds), most often in secreted/lumenal and viral structural proteins; the feature emphasizes gly/ser/thr/pro‑enriched, low‑complexity loops (often with extracellular disulfide cysteines) rather than catalytic residues.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long, contiguous stretches corresponding to loops and edges of beta-sheets within a domain; multiple local peaks on small/hydroxylated residues (e.g., Gly/Ser/Thr), frequently in low–moderate pLDDT segments; little/no activation on signal peptides or on catalytic dyads/triads.
Exemplars: - p24 cargo receptors (TMED family, GOLD domain): activation concentrates on a subregion of the GOLD beta‑sandwich, peaking on a surface loop in the N‑terminal half.
- Peptide-N-glycosidase F (PNGase F): activation on flexible loops connecting beta‑strands of the catalytic domain, with peaks at Gly, away from catalytic residues.
- Copper-dependent monooxygenases (DBH/PHM/MOXD): activation on cupredoxin‑like beta‑sandwich domains, especially exposed loops.
- Viral major capsid proteins (jelly‑roll fold): activation along surface loops that decorate the eight‑stranded beta‑sandwich.
- Lectins (legume-type/galectins/C-type lectin-like): activation on beta‑sandwich loop regions that contact glycans.
- ADAMTS/ADAMTS‑like ECM proteases: activation on ancillary beta‑rich, disulfide‑bonded modules (e.g., TSR/disintegrin-like/cysteine‑rich) rather than the metalloprotease active site.
- Subtilisin-like proprotein convertases (PCSKs): activation on their beta‑rich P/PA domain and adjacent surface loops, not on the catalytic triad.
- SEC14/OSBP-related lipid/sterol transfer/sensing proteins: activation on N‑terminal GOLD or PH beta‑sandwich loops, and other exposed coil segments.
- Adhesion GPCRs (latrophilins/CIRL, EVA-1 family): activation on N‑terminal extracellular lectin‑like/mucin‑like beta‑rich segments and flexible loops.
- Secretory pathway/Golgi cargo and glycosylation enzymes: activation on luminal, gly/ser/thr‑rich loops within beta‑rich catalytic or accessory domains.
- Calpains: activation on flexible loop/linker regions (including EF‑hand–adjacent coils) rather than the papain‑like catalytic core.
- Chromatin acidic chaperones/COMPASS–ASH2 components: activation on acidic, low‑complexity coil segments that resemble exposed loops in beta‑rich domains.

Summary: Hydrophobic core positions of the immunoglobulin-like beta-sandwich fold—most prominently fibronectin type III (FN3) and C2-set Ig-like domains—across proteins that carry these repeats (commonly receptor/adhesion ectodomains but also cytoskeletal/scaffold proteins)
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks focused on single hydrophobic/aromatic residues (Leu/Ile/Val/Phe/Trp, occasional Gly) within beta-strands (and immediately adjacent loops) of FN3 and Ig-like domains; multiple peaks recur across tandem modules; little to no activation in signal peptides, transmembrane helices, or non-Ig/FN3 regions
Exemplars: - IgSF cell-adhesion molecules (e.g., Nephrin): peaks on beta-strands within Ig C2-type domains and the terminal FN3 module in the ectodomain
- Class I cytokine receptors (e.g., G-CSF receptor): strongest peaks on beta-strands of multiple FN3 domains, with weaker activation in the N-terminal Ig-like domain
- Cytoskeletal kinases with Ig/FN3 modules (e.g., myosin light chain kinase): sharp peaks on hydrophobic residues in beta-strands of an FN3 (actin-binding) domain and several Ig-like domains
- E3 ubiquitin ligases containing FN3 modules (e.g., Midline-1): localized peak on a beta-strand within the FN3 domain

Summary: Beta-strand/loop–rich accessory regions of lumenal/periplasmic or secreted enzymes, predominantly carbohydrate-active hydrolases and lyases, characterized by acidic and aromatic residue–biased surfaces; the feature tracks beta-sandwich–like domains and adjacent surface loops that form substrate- or metal-binding belts (also seen in other extracellular enzymes such as copper amine oxidases), with rare isolated tryptophan hits in unrelated proteins.
Activation pattern: Broad regional activation over long beta-strand/coil segments (often tens to >100 residues), typically peripheral to the canonical catalytic nucleophile but spanning substrate- or metal-binding surfaces; enrichment for D/E/G/W; occasional sharper peaks at catalytic or copper-binding residues; rare single-residue activation on Trp.
Exemplars: Alpha-mannosidase II (GH38): strong activation on a C-terminal lumenal beta-strand/loop accessory region, away from the catalytic nucleophile; Sulfoquinovosidase (GH family): activation across an internal beta-strand/coil segment lacking annotated active-site residues; Alpha-D-galactosamine galactosaminidase (GH36): activation on an N-terminal beta-rich block preceding the GH36 catalytic domain; Copper amine oxidase: activation across the catalytic beta-strand/coil belt including the proton-acceptor Asp, the copper-binding His pair, the TPQ-forming Tyr, and nearby acidic metal-binding residues; YidC membrane insertase: activation over the mid-sequence periplasmic flexible beta/coil (P1) region; Viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (hepatitis E virus): a single activated Trp within the polymerase region.

Summary: Signature of extracytoplasmic/envelope-associated structural regions—preferentially the mature (post-cleavage) portions of virion and surface/secreted proteins and single-pass membrane anchors—with a sequence/structure bias for small/polar residues (G/S/T/D/N) flanking hydrophobics at secondary-structure edges (helix/strand caps, loop→strand transitions); avoided in signal peptides and well-folded accessory domains like BIG2
Activation pattern: Mixed: (1) regional/domain-level activation over long stretches in virion tail/capsid and other surface/extracellular regions; (2) sharp residue-level hotspots at glycine or polar residues positioned just before/after beta-strands or at helix termini and membrane interfaces; suppressed over signal peptides and certain globular domains
Exemplars: - Bacteriophage tail tube proteins: strong, continuous activation across the N-terminal assembly-prone region, dropping over the structured C‑terminal BIG2 domain
- Photosystem II OEE1/PsbO: no activation in the signal peptide; activation starts at the cleavage site and spans the mature lumenal protein, with peaks in flexible gly-rich segments
- Fungal cell wall mannoproteins (CWP family): localized peaks on beta/coil elements within the mature extracellular domain; absent on the signal peptide and C‑terminal propeptide
- Mmm1 family (ER single-pass membrane anchors): activation across the transmembrane helix and highest at the cytosolic helix-cap immediately after the TM
- Urease accessory protein UreE: single-residue hotspot at a glycine immediately preceding a beta-strand (loop-to-strand cap)
- Endoglucanase carbohydrate-binding modules (CBM2): isolated activation within a beta-strand of the extracellular binding domain

Summary: Intrinsic disorder/low‑complexity segments enriched in small, polar and charged residues (S/T/N/G/A/E/D/R/K), especially N‑terminal tails and inter‑domain linkers that contain short repeating motifs; common in nucleic‑acid–associated regulators and many viral proteins, and largely absent from structured domains
Activation pattern: Regional activation across low‑pLDDT coil regions with dense stretches and periodic residue‑level peaks (often on Ser/Asn within short repeats or in acidic/basic runs); frequent strong hotspots at extreme N‑termini and flexible C‑terminal tails; minimal activation within folded domain cores
Exemplars: - C2H2 zinc finger transcription factors: strong activation on the intrinsically disordered linkers between tandem fingers (short, repeating polar/charged linker motifs), not on the folded zinc‑finger domains.
- Meiosis regulator HED1: sharp activation on the disordered N‑terminal segment (Asn/Ser‑biased) and weaker activation in a disordered C‑terminal tail; no activation on the central helical core.
- Viral regulatory/nucleic‑acid–binding proteins: activation on low‑complexity N/C‑terminal tails and charged tracts used for RNA/DNA binding or host‑interaction.
- Small/uncharacterized human microproteins and pseudogene‑derived proteins: diffuse activation across polar/charged low‑complexity stretches characteristic of IDRs.

Summary: Activation corresponds to long, low‑complexity, non‑globular regions—often Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly‑rich—such as intrinsically disordered tails and linkers, targeting peptides, and simple helical repeats (coiled‑coils) and TM‑adjacent luminal segments; compact, well‑folded globular domains are typically not activated. This pattern is common in secretory and membrane‑associated proteins across taxa.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long continuous tracts (frequently N‑ or C‑terminal or luminal loops); strongest on low‑pLDDT disordered segments and Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly‑rich low‑complexity stretches; moderate on simple helices (coiled‑coils, signal/transit peptides) and some transmembrane segments; minimal on structured globular domains.
Exemplars: - SUN‑domain nuclear‑envelope proteins: activation on perinuclear coiled‑coil stalks and TM‑proximal regions; SUN globular domain inactive.
- Seipin ER membrane proteins: strong activation on N‑terminal low‑complexity/ID segments and highly disordered C‑terminal tails; moderate near the second TM helix.
- Bacillus thuringiensis Cry δ‑endotoxins: activation confined to long, disordered C‑terminal extensions; N‑terminal helical core inactive.
- Mitochondrial preproteins/Complex I accessory factors: activation on N‑terminal transit peptides and C‑terminal disordered tails; structured cores not activated.
- Secreted lectins (jacalin‑related, ZG16) and ECM/cell‑adhesion proteins: activation on Ser/Thr‑rich mucin‑like linkers/stalks outside carbohydrate‑recognition/adhesion domains.
- Plant virus movement/capsid/readthrough proteins: activation on extended, low‑complexity readthrough/C‑terminal regions.
- SUMO E3 ligases and secreted proteases/glycan enzymes: activation on signal/propeptides, coiled‑coil/low‑complexity regulatory regions, and inter‑domain linkers rather than catalytic cores.

Summary: Asparagine-rich low-complexity intrinsically disordered tracts, typically long and often at protein N-termini (including organelle transit peptides in protists), enriched in polar/charged residues (N with Q/K/S/T/D/E); activation is composition-driven and is excluded from folded catalytic cores and transmembrane helices.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over extended low-complexity segments (sometimes multiple per protein), with residue-level peaks on N runs/repeats; strong N-terminal bias and sharp drop at the onset of well-structured domains; no activation within transmembrane segments or conserved catalytic domains.
Exemplars: - ZDHHC-type palmitoyltransferase: activation on the disordered, low-complexity N-terminal cytosolic tail and additional unstructured low-complexity patches; absent from transmembrane helices and the DHHC catalytic core.
- Serine/threonine protein kinase: activation on an internal asparagine-rich disordered insert; no activation across the structured kinase core or ATP-binding site.
- Ribonuclease H–like enzyme: activation confined to the N-terminal low-complexity, low-confidence region (often helical propensity but disordered); absent from the C-terminal RNase H–like catalytic domain.
- Apicoplast 2Fe-2S ferredoxin: activation across the apicoplast transit peptide and adjacent disordered N-terminal stretch; terminates at the boundary of the structured ferredoxin domain.

Summary: Beta-strand elements of repeat-based all‑beta scaffolds—especially RHS/YD right‑handed beta‑helix and WD‑repeat beta‑propeller segments—that form the structural framework of Gram‑negative secretion/spike/toxin proteins and cross‑kingdom assembly scaffolds; the feature primarily marks the solenoid/propeller scaffold rather than catalytic domains, with occasional isolated hits in other secondary structures.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional, multi‑peak activation across long N‑ to mid‑segments of large repeat scaffolds, concentrated on short (3–6 residue) runs within DSSP E beta‑strands; minimal signal in C‑terminal catalytic appendages. In smaller/housekeeping proteins, the signal collapses to isolated residue‑level peaks in well‑structured helices or strands. Composition often includes acidic/polar/small residues (E, D, R, T, Y, G) typical of YD/WD repeats, though peak centers can be hydrophobic. Tends to cover long stretches in very large proteins and is sparse across the broader proteome.
Exemplars: - RHS/YD repeat toxins (e.g., Yen toxin complex subunits, Rhs-family effectors): strong, distributed peaks on beta‑strands within N‑terminal RHS repeat solenoids; little/no signal on downstream catalytic/deaminase regions.
- Type VI secretion system VgrG spike proteins: clustered activation in the conserved spike region enriched in beta‑structure.
- Bacteriophage tailspike/fiber adhesins: extended activation along beta‑helix blades of the spike/fiber scaffold.
- WD40 repeat scaffolding proteins (e.g., U3 snoRNP‑associated WD proteins): patches on beta‑propeller blade strands.
- Periplasmic outer‑membrane/anti‑sigma factor regulatory proteins: regional activation over periplasmic beta‑rich repeat segments.
- Housekeeping enzymes (beta‑galactosidase/GH2, choline oxidase): isolated residue‑level peaks in structured helix/strand segments away from active sites.
- Dynamin‑like GTPases: single‑residue peaks in the C‑terminal helical stalk.

Summary: Methionine residue identity, with a strong bias toward the N‑terminal initiator Met and early hydrophobic N‑terminal segments; generally fires on Met in diverse structural/functional contexts and is largely structure-agnostic.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on Met; often includes the initiator Met at position 1 and occasionally nearby bulky hydrophobic/aromatic residues (W, V, L, I; sometimes T, C). Typically only a few residues per protein are active, with a tendency to cluster near the N-terminus but also occurring on internal Met.
Exemplars: - cAMP-specific phosphodiesterase (PDE4A) fragment: exclusive activation on multiple internal Met residues independent of secondary structure or disorder.
- Secreted precursors (hormones, toxins, bacteriocins): activation on the initiator Met of the signal peptide/propeptide.
- Viral accessory/immune-modulatory proteins: short, N-terminally focused activation on M1 and occasional internal Met.
- Membrane-associated proteins (signal anchors/transmembrane leaders): activation on the N-terminal Met and Met within early hydrophobic segments.
- Human microproteins and testis/spermatogenesis-related proteins: sparse activation on M1 and any internal Met in short proteins.
- Glycoprotein precursors: activation on the initiator Met at the start of signal peptides.

Summary: General beta-strand recognition: the feature marks individual residues embedded in well-ordered beta-sheets within structured, beta-rich domains across diverse folds (e.g., alpha-crystallin/sHSP ACD, sliding clamp, glycoside hydrolases, CS/p23, FERM, Rieske). It prefers strand positions with typical side chains (hydrophobic/aromatic and Ser/Thr, with some Lys/Arg), often adjacent to functional sites but not the catalytic/liganding residues themselves, and avoids disordered regions and helices.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks; sparse, isolated activations confined to beta-strands with high structural confidence; concentrated within structured domains and largely absent from disordered segments and helices.
Exemplars: - Small heat shock proteins (alpha-crystallin domain): peaks on beta-strand residues within the ACD; no activation in the disordered N-terminus.
- DNA sliding clamp proteins (bacterial beta clamp/PCNA): isolated activations on beta-strands across the ring-shaped beta sheet architecture.
- Glycoside hydrolases (e.g., levanase; beta-D-galactofuranosidase): multiple peaks on aromatic/hydrophobic residues within beta-strands, often near strands that harbor catalytic Asp/Glu but not on the catalytic residues.
- Prostaglandin E synthase 3 (p23/CS domain): activations on beta-strands of the CS (p23-like) domain; absent in the C-terminal disordered region.
- FERM domain proteins: sparse peaks on beta-strand residues within the beta-sandwich subdomain.
- Rieske iron–sulfur proteins (ISP): peaks on beta-strands of the Rieske domain, including near the [2Fe-2S] cluster-binding region but not on the ligating residues.

Summary: Generic alpha-helix initiation/capping and coil-helix boundary signal, with secondary preference for residues within stable helices and coiled-coils; a structural (not functional) feature that marks helix starts (N-caps) and nearby linkers across diverse proteins
Activation pattern: Predominantly sparse, single-residue peaks at the N-termini of alpha-helices and adjacent coil segments; additional weaker peaks within helical cores, especially in long coiled-coils; enriched for small/capping and helix-forming residues (A, G, S, T; L, V, I; plus E/D/K/R at caps); generally absent from long low-confidence disordered tails or transit peptides; frequently occurs near the protein N-terminus in small bacterial proteins
Exemplars: - tRNA adenosine deaminases and CMP/dCMP-type deaminases: residues on the N-terminal alpha-helix and nearby coil, including positions adjacent to catalytic His/Glu.
- RNA polymerase omega subunit: N-terminal alpha-helix residues and an early coil segment.
- Glutamyl-tRNA(Gln) amidotransferase subunit C (GatC): isolated peaks on internal alpha-helices in the structured core.
- Golgin coiled-coil scaffolds: the first helical turn at the N-terminus and scattered leucines within the central coiled-coil; little signal in the disordered tail.
- Epsin ENTH-domain proteins: single-residue peaks within helical elements of the ENTH fold, not in the disordered C-terminus.
- RuvA branch migration factor: an N-cap at the start of a helix in domain III and residues in coil linkers connecting helices.

Summary: Short, hydrophobic/aromatic beta-strand segments (and adjacent loop-to-strand transitions) that recur across beta-rich scaffolds such as beta-propellers and beta-sandwich/jelly-roll domains; a structural signal rather than a specific function, frequently present in secreted/luminal and membrane-associated complexes as well as large cytosolic scaffolds
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks in short contiguous clusters (typically 6–12 residues) that align with predicted beta-strands or immediately preceding loops; repeated across proteins with many strands (propellers/sandwiches), yielding multiple peaks distributed throughout long scaffolds
Exemplars: - Carbohydrate-active enzymes and cellulosomal scaffoldins: activation on surface beta-strands of CBMs/cohesins that present aromatic residues for carbohydrate contacts (e.g., cellulases, xylanases, chitinases, beta-glucosidases).
- Vesicle coat/adaptor complexes (AP-1/2/3/4, COPI) and TRAPP subunits: activation on beta-strand elements within beta-propeller/sandwich subdomains used for cargo binding and complex assembly.
- Integrin alpha subunits: activation across FG-GAP beta-propeller blade strands in the extracellular region.
- Pore-forming toxins (actinoporin-like): localized peaks on loop-to-beta-strand segments within the beta-rich core.
- YidC insertases: peaks within the periplasmic beta-structured domain.
- COX11 copper chaperones: activation on soluble domain beta-strands.
- Inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatases: peaks on C-terminal beta-sheet segments (as in type I 5-phosphatase).
- RNA helicases (e.g., SDE3): a single N-terminal beta-strand shows a strong local peak.

Summary: Detects N‑terminal targeting leaders only when they are immediately followed by extended low‑complexity/repeat‑rich tracts (Gly/Ser/Pro, GD‑rich); leader presence alone is insufficient. Intein clause: inteins do not trigger activation by themselves—activation occurs only if junctions are flanked by biased, low‑complexity segments. Activation pattern: Strong regional activation over basic N‑regions plus adjacent long low‑complexity stretches; weak or absent on compact signal peptides followed directly by structured domains and on cytosolic proteins lacking such tracts.

Summary: Subset-of-secretome marker: the feature preferentially activates on mature, non‑cytosolic portions of secretory‑pathway proteins downstream of the N‑terminal targeting segment, with strongest signals on disordered/low‑complexity, glycosylation‑adjacent, or certain lipidated extracellular/periplasmic regions; it is not universal across all secreted proteins.
Activation pattern: Inactive over signal peptides and pre/pro‑segments; often an onset at/after the cleavage site (e.g., lipobox +1 Cys), followed by regional activation in the mature extracellular/periplasmic domain. Strongest coverage occurs on long low‑confidence/disordered stretches and loops near glycosylation sites; sharp single‑residue peaks can occur near functional motifs. Activation can be sparse and may not yield high sequence‑level scores; it is frequently weak/absent on compact cysteine‑rich microdomains (e.g., UPAR/Ly6, hydrophobins), many Gram‑negative periplasmic SBPs (e.g., MetQ), and some ice‑binding and tyrosinase proteins.
Exemplars:
- Vitellogenins (yolk precursors): no activation on the signal peptide; strong activation across the disordered phosvitin/low‑complexity region, including residues adjacent to N‑glycosylation sequons.
- Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein homologs: activation in the N‑terminal portion of the mature ER‑lumenal domain, including a low‑confidence helix harboring lipid‑transfer mutagenesis sites; signal peptide excluded.
- Selected bacterial lipoproteins (e.g., glycolipid transporter LprF): signal peptide inactive; onset at the lipidated +1 cysteine with sustained activation across the periplasmic domain; not universal across SBPs (e.g., MetQ may be weak).
- Secreted peptidoglycan‑binding/reductase enzymes with LysM: no activation on the signal peptide or LysM module; strong activation over an unstructured C‑terminal region of the secreted enzyme.
- Ice‑binding/antifreeze proteins: occasionally a focused peak near an ice‑binding motif within the secreted domain, but overall sequence‑level activation can be low.
- UPAR/Ly6 family (GPI‑anchored extracellular proteins): occasional short activated segments within the Ly6 domain (e.g., loops near N‑glycosylation and selected beta‑strands), often with low overall activation; no activation on signal peptide or GPI‑anchor propeptide.
- Tyrosinases (secretory/lumenal copper enzymes): possible single‑residue peaks within the luminal catalytic domain, often yielding low overall activation.
- Class I hydrophobins (secreted fungal surface proteins): may show a short activated beta‑strand adjacent to disulfide‑bonded cysteines, with generally low global activation.

Summary: Short, recurring structural edge motifs at helix starts (N-caps) and β-strand/turn loops across repeats and compact domains; often stabilized by disulfide bonds in extracellular cysteine-rich modules, but also occurring in β-rich globular proteins (e.g., FGFs) and in cytosolic helical rods/coiled-coils.
Activation pattern: Multiple discrete, residue-level peaks in 5–10 residue segments that are (i) the N-terminal portion of the first α-helix in each helical repeat or coiled-coil segment, and (ii) loop/β-edge elements adjoining conserved positions (frequently cysteines when disulfide-bonded, but not required) in extracellular domains and enzyme barrels/CBMs. Activation is confined to well-structured regions and is absent from signal peptides, transmembranes, low-complexity linkers, and unrelated cytoplasmic tails.
Exemplars:
- PUF/Pumilio RNA-binding proteins: N-terminal part of the first α-helix of each PUM repeat within the PUM-HD.
- TNF receptor CRDs and Kazal/FS/TB modules: β-strand/turn segments around conserved residues (often disulfide-bonded cysteines) in the extracellular region.
- Disulfide-rich endothelins and venom cystine-knot peptides: short disulfide-anchored loop/turn elements within the knot.
- CCCH-type zinc finger RNA-binding proteins: Cys/His-containing loop/turn that coordinates Zn2+.
- Fibroblast growth factors (FGFs): conserved β-edge/turn motifs within the β-trefoil, sometimes near the lone disulfide when present.
- Secreted bacterial CAZymes (e.g., GH/CE with CBMs): short loop/β-edge motifs at barrel edges or CBM interfaces, often Gly/Pro/Asp/His-enriched, disulfide optional.
- Cilium/centrosome/ODF-like coiled-coil proteins: helix N-cap/helix-break motifs within rod-like helical segments.

Summary: Extracellular modular ligand-binding repeats in secreted and cell-surface proteins—predominantly thrombospondin type-1 repeats (TSR/TSP1) and complement control protein modules (CCP/Sushi)—with additional coverage of other ectodomain repeat modules that present solvent-exposed beta-strand/loop surfaces (e.g., EGF-like, LDL-A, LRR/internalin, Vps10p beta-propeller), including pathogen mimicry of these modules.
Activation pattern: Strong domain-level activation across repeat modules (TSR, CCP, and other ectodomain repeats), often spanning tandem arrays; sharp residue-level peaks on beta-strands and adjacent loops, including canonical motifs (e.g., Cys pairs, W-ladder/WxxW in TSR) and glycosylation-prone segments; little/no activation on unrelated regions (e.g., FU repeats, low-complexity tails), with weaker signal on isolated small extracellular domains.
Exemplars: - Complement components and regulators (C6–C9, Factor H, C4BP, CR1/CR2): activation on CCP/Sushi domains; in terminal components that also carry TSRs, activation on both TSR and CCP modules.
- TSR/TSP1-bearing secreted and ECM proteins (R-spondins, thrombospondins, ADAMTS proteases, spondins, properdin, CCN family): activation concentrated on their TSP1/TSR domains and not on neighboring non-TSR modules.
- ECM glycoproteins with other cysteine-rich repeats (EMILINs with EMI/C1q, fibulins, spondins; BMP modulators with vWFC/EGF-like): activation over these compact extracellular modules.
- Adhesion GPCR ectodomains: activation on embedded small extracellular repeats (e.g., EGF-like) within long N-termini.
- Bacterial surface adhesins/secreted virulence factors, including LRR/internalin-type adhesins: activation over their extracellular repeat segments.
- Viral complement modulators (e.g., VCP/SPICE homologs): broad activation across tandem CCP repeats.
- Sorting receptors (VPS10/sortilin family): activation on luminal Vps10p beta-propeller repeat regions.

Summary: Generic detector of ordered, mature protein regions: the feature preferentially activates within folded domains and secondary-structure elements and is largely suppressed over long intrinsically disordered segments and N‑terminal targeting/signal peptides; within folded regions it often emphasizes residues at secondary-structure termini and domain/processing junctions rather than catalytic sites.
Activation pattern: Sparse, low-magnitude, residue-level peaks scattered across folded domains, with occasional short runs across stable helices; minimal or absent signal over signal/transit peptides and extended low‑pLDDT disordered regions; sporadic peaks at domain boundaries and proteolytic processing sites; no strong amino-acid-type specificity.
Exemplars: - Ser/Thr kinases (e.g., LATS1): numerous small peaks across the structured kinase core and AGC C‑terminal elements; little activation in the long N‑terminal intrinsically disordered region.
- Bacterial RNase P protein subunit: sparse peaks in coil/turns and structured loops, including occasional signal in lower-confidence flexible C‑terminal segments, without linkage to specific catalytic residues.
- 2Fe‑2S ferredoxins/adrenodoxins: activation throughout the folded ferredoxin domain but absent on the N‑terminal mitochondrial transit peptide.
- Chromatin-associated coiled‑coil proteins (MEAF6): peaks along a stable coiled‑coil helix and at the start of a disordered C‑terminal tail; additional sparse peaks in moderately ordered coil regions.
- Cilia/flagella-associated scaffolds (HOATZ): distinct peak near the end of a long alpha‑helix at the helix‑to‑coil transition, with minor signal nearby.
- MAGUK scaffolds (DLG family): activation within PDZ, SH3, and GK-like domains; minimal signal across large disordered N‑terminal regions.
- DEG/ENaC sodium channels: widespread activation in the structured extracellular domain and a C‑terminal cytoplasmic helix; little to none in the low‑confidence N‑terminal cytoplasmic region.
- Bacterial alkaline phosphatase: scattered peaks across the structured enzyme (beta strands, helices, loops), often near but not on catalytic/metal-binding residues.
- Cysteine proteases (metacaspase): strongest peak at the autoprocessing cleavage site and adjacent secondary structure, exemplifying emphasis at processing/junction regions.

Summary: N-terminal targeting leader peptides, primarily classical Sec-type signal peptides for secretion (including bacterial lipoprotein signal peptides) and also chloroplast transit peptides. The feature captures the positively charged n-region and hydrophobic h-region of signal sequences or the Arg-rich, low-complexity transit peptides that mediate plastid import. Additionally, weak activation can occur on non-secretory N-termini that present short basic/amphipathic helices mimicking leaders (e.g., arginine-/histidine-rich N-termini), even without a canonical cleavage motif.
Activation pattern: Strong, highly localized activation at the extreme N-terminus. For secretory signal peptides, activation peaks across residues ~2–25 within the predicted helical, hydrophobic core and drops sharply at the signal peptidase cleavage site (or at the lipobox cysteine for lipoproteins), sometimes with a small spillover into the first residues of the mature chain. For chloroplast transit peptides, activation spans a longer N-terminal stretch (~1–60), is associated with low pLDDT and coil/amphipathic helix propensity, and ceases at the transit-peptide cleavage site. Little to no activation in propeptide segments or mature functional domains. In proteins lacking bona fide leaders, only submaximal, short-span activation is observed at the extreme N-terminus and does not extend into the protein core.
Exemplars: - Spider venom peptide precursors (e.g., phi-liotoxin family): activation confined to the N-terminal signal peptide; no activation in propeptide or mature toxin.
- Insecticidal peptide precursors (cytoinsectotoxins): strong activation across the signal peptide only.
- Salivary anticoagulant proteins (anophelin): activation on the N-terminal signal peptide; mature thrombin-inhibitory domain not activated.
- ER-lumen/secretory pathway enzymes (protein disulfide-isomerase A4): activation on the N-terminal signal peptide directing entry into the secretory pathway.
- Bacterial secreted/periplasmic lipoprotein enzymes (ulvan lyase): activation over the signal peptide up to the lipobox cysteine that is lipid-modified.
- Molluscan shell matrix proteins (prismalin family): activation matches the N-terminal signal peptide for secretion.
- Plant plastid proteins (plastid transcriptionally active complex subunits): broad activation across the chloroplast transit peptide required for chloroplast targeting.
- Occasional weak matches: basic/amphipathic N-termini without cleavage sites (e.g., viral arginine-rich regulatory proteins, bacterial cytosolic proteins with basic tails).

Summary: Non-catalytic all‑alpha helical scaffold/repeat segments (alpha‑solenoids/helix–turn–helix arrays) used for cargo binding and protein–protein interactions in large multidomain proteins. The feature targets long amphipathic helical regions and their inter‑helical linkers in domains such as the vitellogenin/LLTP N‑terminal module, the PI‑kinase PIK helical domain, and PUF/Pumilio helical repeats; in secreted proteins these regions often encompass N‑glycosylated helices, while catalytic cores, beta‑rich modules, PH domains and transmembranes are largely ignored.
Activation pattern: Predominantly domain‑/regional‑level activation across tens to hundreds of residues within all‑alpha helical regions, with sub‑peaks at helix–turn connectors, repeat boundaries, and occasionally at Asn in N‑glycosylation sequons; minimal activation in catalytic domains, beta‑rich modules (e.g., VWFD), PH domains, long disordered tails, or transmembrane helices.
Exemplars: - Large lipid transfer proteins (vitellogenins, microsomal triglyceride transfer protein): strong, contiguous activation across the N‑terminal vitellogenin/LLTP helical module, including N‑glycosylation sites; little signal in the C‑terminal VWFD domain.
- Phosphatidylinositol kinases (e.g., PI4K): activation concentrated in the PIK helical domain; catalytic PI3K/PI4K kinase core and PH domain are inactive.
- PUF/Pumilio RNA‑binding proteins: activation within the PUM‑HD helical repeat array, especially at repeat boundaries and structured turn/coil linkers; disordered N/C tails are inactive.

Summary: Coiled-coil–like amphipathic alpha-helices with heptad-repeat character (hydrophobic a/d layers often L/A and charged/polar e/g positions enriched in E/Q/K/R/S/T), as found in long dimeric/oligomeric scaffolds, adaptors, and motor tails; the signal also extends to shorter amphipathic helices in peptide precursors.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks sparsely distributed along predicted alpha-helical segments, with many peaks spanning long coiled-coil regions; depleted in folded globular domains and usually low in disordered segments; occasional peaks at helix–coil junctions; no single short consensus motif.
Exemplars: CEP290 (centrosomal/ciliary scaffold): sparse peaks across the N-terminal coiled-coil essential for ciliogenesis, minimal in disordered patches; CLIP-170 (+TIP microtubule adaptor): peaks confined to the extensive C-terminal coiled-coil, absent from CAP-Gly and CCHC zinc finger domains; Myosin-7 (motor tail): scattered peaks along the coiled-coil rod/stalk and nearby coil segments; SCLT1 (sodium channel and clathrin linker/coiled-coil appendage protein): peaks within long alpha-helical coiled-coil segments and a short coil linker; RFamide neuropeptide precursor: localized peaks within short predicted helical stretches of mature peptides.

Summary: Interface-prone segments of viral and bacterial extracellular assemblies (often surface-exposed or cementing), with a strong bias for bacteriophage distal tail fibers/spikes/baseplates (including many glycan-binding/depolymerase tips) and analogous connector/surface regions in bacterial envelope proteins (flagellar hook/cap proteins, S-layer tails, secretins). These segments are typically flexible or short helical stretches enriched in small/polar/acidic residues (G/S/T/D/N) and often coincide with glycan-associated motifs (e.g., NXS/T) or low-complexity tails; occasionally similar motifs occur in flexible linkers/tails of secreted carbohydrate-active enzymes.

Activation pattern: Primarily regional: short stretches at N- or C-termini and flexible loops of virion tail/fiber/spike proteins; extended activation across intrinsically disordered, glycosylated C-terminal domains of surface-layer proteins; isolated residue-level peaks within long alpha-helices of fibrous assemblies (tail sheath, flagellar connectors/caps); and analogous patches in internal virion cementing/intermediate-layer proteins (e.g., adenovirus pVIII, rotavirus VP6). Activation tends to avoid well-ordered catalytic/structural cores (e.g., beta-helix cores of depolymerases) and concentrates on surface-exposed or inter-subunit interface coils/hinges or short helical patches.

Exemplars:
- Phage long tail fiber (e.g., T4): activation on an early flexible coil segment, not across the central helical shaft—consistent with an exposed/interface stretch.
- Capsule-depolymerase tailspike (Klebsiella phages): activation on disordered C-terminal tail and a surface loop outside the structured beta-helix catalytic core—matching glycan-binding/depolymerase tip regions.
- Phage tail sheath protein: activation at a focused site within a long alpha-helix and at an unstructured N-terminal patch—helical/hinge elements at assembly interfaces.
- Flagellar hook/cap proteins (FlgK/FliD-like): activation on short helical/coil connector segments of bacterial extracellular/periplasmic appendages.
- S-layer surface protein: broad activation across a large, intrinsically disordered, glycosylated C-terminal region, including multiple N-linked glycosylation motifs—an exposed, low-complexity surface tail.
- Internal virion proteins (adenovirus pVIII, rotavirus VP6): activation on cementing/intermediate-layer interface segments within the capsid lattice.
- Secreted carbohydrate-active enzymes: activation on low-complexity acidic tails or flexible linkers adjoining the catalytic domains.

Summary: Short, solvent-exposed loop/hinge segments that bridge or flank secondary-structure elements—typically G/S/T/P-rich and often adjacent to disulfide-bonded cysteines or N-glycosylation sequons—serving as lids/entrance loops to ligand-binding pockets or as interaction epitopes, especially in secreted/extracellular and periplasmic proteins, but also occurring as disordered terminal tails or internal loops in diverse folds.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over 15–40-residue patches with residue-level peaks on coils/turns and at helix/strand edges; commonly near the N-terminus of mature secreted proteins but also in internal loops or C-terminal tails; frequent low-pLDDT loops yet also present in well-structured loop–strand/helix modules; often coincident with cysteines forming disulfides or NXS/T glycosylation motifs.
Exemplars: - Avidin/streptavidin family: activation on the loop/adjacent beta-strand bordering the biotin-binding pocket.
- Fatty-acid-binding proteins: activation on the N-terminal helix–turn–helix “cap” that gates the lipid-binding cavity.
- Lipocalins/retinoid-binding proteins: activation on entrance loops of the beta-barrel ligand pocket.
- Ly6/uPAR three-finger proteins (including related toxins/inhibitors): activation on cysteine-rich loop segments within the disulfide-stabilized domain.
- Plant plastid lipid-associated proteins (fibrillins/plastoglobulins): activation on disordered, coil-rich C-terminal segments exposed on lipid particle surfaces.
- Bacterial penicillin-binding proteins and other periplasmic/outer-membrane proteins: activation on flexible, disordered C-terminal tails or exposed loops away from catalytic motifs.
- Receptor ectodomains (e.g., BMP receptor): activation on N-terminal extracellular loops bearing N-linked glycosylation and flanked by disulfide-forming cysteines.
- Chromophore lyases: activation across a helix–loop–strand module forming a surface-exposed interaction/positioning element.

Summary: Extracytosolic secretory-pathway proteins: the mature lumenal/extracellular/periplasmic domains of secreted or surface-exposed proteins (post–signal peptide), including GPI-anchored and lipoprotein exodomains, fungal cell‑wall adhesins, and lumenal glycoprotein regions
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation over long contiguous stretches of the mature exodomain; largely absent on signal peptides, transmembrane helices, and cytosolic tails; occurs in both flexible/disordered and well-structured regions, with occasional peaks at N‑linked glycosylation sequons
Exemplars: V-type proton ATPase subunit S1 (Ac45): strong activation across the N-terminal lumenal ectodomain, including at N‑glycosylation sites; Trypanosome variant surface glycoproteins (VSGs): broad activation over the C‑terminal exodomain preceding the GPI-anchor signal, largely disordered; Vitellogenins: activation across the C‑terminal secreted tail region with low structural confidence; Fungal cell-wall adhesins (Flo11/Rbt1 family): activation within the Flo11 adhesive domain; Borrelia outer surface lipoprotein OspC: activation over the C‑terminal helical surface-exposed region, excluding the signal peptide; Photosystem II extrinsic protein O (PsbO): activation concentrated in the C‑terminal lumenal segment of the secreted extrinsic subunit

Summary: EF-hand–based Ca2+ sensing modules: the feature recognizes EF-hand calcium-binding domains in calmodulin-like proteins (including PEF domains and photoreceptor Ca2+ sensors) and their characteristic structural elements, especially the Ca2+-binding loop, flanking E/F helices, and the short linker between paired EF-hands; in Ca2+-regulated membrane proteins it often extends to cytosolic calmodulin-interacting regions that couple to these sensors.
Activation pattern: Primarily domain-level activation across EF-hand clusters with residue-level peaks in the canonical Ca2+-binding loops and adjacent helices; in some EF-hand proteins, strongest signal lies in the inter-EF-hand linker/hinge rather than the loop itself; in multi-pass membrane proteins, activation occurs as long, charged cytosolic stretches (often C-terminal tails or large loops) rather than within transmembranes.
Exemplars: - Calpains (PEF family): strong activation on the C-terminal PEF-hand domain (Domain IV), peaking in Ca2+-binding loops and flanking helices.
- Calmodulin-like myosin light chains/centrins/troponin C-like proteins: activation in the linker between tandem EF-hands and E/F helices, with reduced signal in some Ca2+-coordinating loops.
- Plant calcium-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs) and plant CMLs: activation across the C-terminal calmodulin-like EF-hand domain.
- Photoreceptor Ca2+ sensors (recoverin/GCAPs): activation over EF-hand arrays that mediate Ca2+-dependent signaling.
- Phosphoinositide signaling enzymes (e.g., phospholipase C): activation on their N-terminal EF-hand domain.
- PEF-family adaptors (sorcin/grancalcin/ALG-2/peflin): activation across EF-hand arrays involved in Ca2+-regulated trafficking.
- Calcium channels/transporters and regulators (voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, TRP channels, Na+/Ca2+ exchangers, MCU regulators like MICU): activation on cytosolic C-terminal tails/loops that bind calmodulin or EF-hand sensors.
- Secreted EF-hand/ECM proteins (S100 family, SPARC/osteonectin): activation centered on EF-hand motifs.
- Cilia/flagella/cytoskeletal Ca2+-sensor systems (centrin-binding complexes, myosin-I assemblies): activation within EF-hand modules that regulate motility and cytoskeletal dynamics.

Summary: An acidic–aromatic (Y/W next to D/E) β-strand–centered patch that typically lies in the early part of the mature, extracytoplasmic/periplasmic domain (post-cleavage) or the analogous N-terminal β-hairpin of soluble folds; frequently includes a Tyr–Asp (YD) dipeptide and marks a short, ordered edge-of-sheet segment sometimes adjacent to dimerization/cofactor-binding regions.
Activation pattern: Predominantly short regional activation (≈10–30 aa) over one or two β-strands and the connecting loop, often beginning 40–120 residues into signal-peptide-bearing precursors; peak(s) commonly align to an acidic–aromatic pair within a strand. In multi-pass membrane proteins, the signal can collapse to isolated residue-level peaks within a transmembrane helix or a juxtamembrane helical linker.
Exemplars: - BRICHOS-domain secreted proteins (e.g., Gastrokine): N-terminal half of BRICHOS, a structured segment that includes the disulfide-bearing region.
- Outer-membrane lipoprotein chaperone/receptor LolB: central β-strand cluster in the mature periplasmic lipoprotein domain.
- AlgU anti-sigma regulatory protein MucB: a short, well-ordered β-strand patch immediately after the signal peptide.
- Frataxin/CyaY: the conserved WYD/YD-containing β-strand region in the N-terminal half of the mature domain.
- IMPase/FBPase-fold phosphatases (IMPase/BPNT/IMPL/TTM): two adjacent β-strands with a Tyr flanked by acidic residue(s).
- Heme oxygenase-like proteins (HugZ/HutZ/HOZ): a helix–strand segment just C-terminal to the heme-binding His, within a dimerization/interface region.
- MHC class I-like glycoproteins: early luminal segment including the N-linked glycosylation sequon on a β-sheet/loop region.
- Tetraspanins: isolated peak within TM3 near the start of the large extracellular loop (membrane-proximal helical context).
- Reticulon family: sparse peaks within the helical linker between the two re-entrant transmembrane segments.

Summary: Acidic, glycine-rich flexible loop segments (GG/GxG with DG/SG/TG contexts) in the mature, extracellular/lumen-exposed portions of secreted and surface-associated proteins (including outer-membrane and virion-exposed proteins), commonly within beta-rich folds
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 15–40+ residue windows enriched in small/polar residues (notably Gly with DG/SG/TG patterns), typically appearing mid-to-late in the sequence after the signal peptide/propeptide; signal concentrates on surface-exposed loops/turns and adjacent short strands/coils rather than whole domains
Exemplars: - IL-1/IL-18 family cytokines (beta-trefoil): activation on acidic glycine-rich surface loops within the mature cytokine core.
- Neurotrophins (e.g., NGF) and leptin: activation on flexible Gly/acidic loop segments in the secreted growth-factor domains.
- RNase A family (secreted ribonucleases): activation on exposed Gly/Ser-rich loops between secondary-structure elements.
- Plant apoplastic proteins (dirigent, pectinesterase inhibitors, Kunitz trypsin-type inhibitors): activation on glycine/acidic surface loops of the secreted inhibitory/structural domains.
- Photosystem II OEE1/PsbO (thylakoid lumen protein): strong activation on its extended acidic, Gly-rich loop region that contacts PSII.
- Gram-negative outer-membrane beta-barrels and adhesins (e.g., PagP, fimbrial/outer-membrane proteins): activation on extracellular loops enriched in GG/GxG and DG/SG/TG patterns.
- Bacterial ice-binding/antifreeze beta-solenoids: activation on glycine-rich turn segments between solenoid repeats.
- Vitellogenins/yolk precursors: activation on long acidic Ser/Gly-rich internal regions (phosvitin-like segments) within the precursor.
- Phage/viral structural proteins: activation on glycine-/acidic-rich loops decorating capsid or tail-fiber surfaces.
