Summary: Compositionally biased low-complexity segments, especially N-terminal hydrophobic helices that form the hydrophobic core of signal peptides or membrane-anchoring amphipathic helices, and serine/threonine-rich intrinsically disordered tracts; the feature reflects sequence-composition bias rather than a specific fold or function and commonly occurs at protein termini across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation over extended contiguous blocks (typically 8–20 residues), frequently at the N-terminus; strong peaks within hydrophobic cores of signal peptide–like helices or within S/T-rich low-complexity patches; minimal activation in structured catalytic/core domains
Exemplars: - Viral nonstructural/accessory proteins: activation on a short, flexible N-terminal hydrophobic helix (amphipathic/membrane-anchoring segment).
- Plant secreted signaling peptides (SCOOP family): activation on the N-terminal signal peptide hydrophobic core, not on the C-terminal functional motif.
- Eukaryotic transcriptional coactivator scaffolds (Mediator subunit 24): activation on multiple S/T- and Q-rich intrinsically disordered, low-complexity regions.

Summary: Short β-strand and β-hairpin “edge-sheet” elements (strand–turn–strand or helix→strand transitions) that flank catalytic/binding loops or mediate β-augmentation at assembly interfaces; sequence-biased toward small/hydrophobic and Gly/Thr residues with frequent Gly–Gly motifs
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous 10–60 aa segments with sharp residue-level peaks; predominantly maps to single β-strands or β-loop-β hairpins (often an edge strand of a sheet), occasionally at helix-to-strand junctions; commonly positioned adjacent to catalytic residues or at inter-subunit/contact interfaces; multiple segments can activate within one protein
Exemplars: - Bacteriophage tail/tube/baseplate and T6SS structural homologs: edge β-strands/hairpins used for inter-subunit β-augmentation during fiber/tube/baseplate assembly
- Viral capsid/scaffolding proteins (e.g., jelly-roll/β-sandwich folds): outer sheet edge strands that form lattice contacts
- ADP-ribosyltransferases (mART family): a β–loop–β hairpin immediately following the catalytic Glu that shapes the active site
- Trigger factor chaperone: helix→β-strand transition forming an edge strand in the N-terminal region linked to client/ribosome interaction
- Lon protease (N-terminal domain): a β-strand within the N-terminal β-sandwich implicated in substrate capture/oligomeric contacts
- Heme oxygenase-like proteins (HugZ family): a β-strand adjacent to an activity-critical residue, contributing to the local active-site sheet
- RNA modification enzymes (tRNA pseudouridine synthases and tRNA/SAM methyltransferases): short β-strands bordering catalytic loops in the core fold
- YTH domain RNA-binding proteins: β-strands of the central sheet flanking the m6A-binding pocket
- Histone H3K9 methyltransferases (SUVH/SET): short β-strands/β-hairpins that border the SET catalytic core (I-SET/post-SET vicinity)
- UHRF-like and RING E3 ubiquitin ligase systems: β-strand elements within auxiliary β-sandwich/recognition modules engaged in DNA/ubiquitin binding
- Cysteine-rich secreted cytokines/growth factors (chemokine/cystine-knot/EGF-like): β-strands forming the disulfide-stabilized β-sheet cores used for receptor interaction

Summary: Short linear motifs at secondary-structure transitions and domain/linker junctions—helix caps and nearby loops/turns at the edges of structured domains or processing/targeting cleavage sites—often enriched for Pro and aromatic residues (especially Trp) and composed of mixed basic and polar/hydrophobic residues; these segments frequently border or contribute to ligand/RNA-binding pockets
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks clustered in short (≈3–10 aa) stretches; localized to coils and helix N- or C-caps or short elements within domains; rarely continuous domain-level activation; often at N-termini or domain boundaries and occasionally exactly at processing/cleavage junctions (e.g., transit peptides) or canonical binding loops (e.g., FAD- or RNA-contacting segments)
Exemplars: - Mitochondrial ribosomal proteins: N-terminal transit peptides with a sharp peak at the cleavage boundary before the mature chain
- YTH domain m6A readers: loop/helix–strand elements forming the RNA-binding pocket, including the Trp of the aromatic cage
- BTB/POZ and Kelch-repeat proteins: short linker between disordered N-terminus and the BTB domain, with minor peaks in BTB helices/Kelch blades
- C2H2 zinc-finger BTB proteins: weak activation in the N-terminal unstructured segment and small coil regions between zinc-finger elements
- Flavin-dependent oxidoreductases: N-terminal helix/strand and the FAD-binding loop/short helix, including turns with Pro
- Flavin-dependent thymidylate synthase (ThyX): coil-to-helix N-cap segment near the active-site region, with weaker peaks on catalytic helices
- Plant MORF/MEF RNA-editing factors: low-confidence loop plus helix C-terminus and inter-strand loop within the core domain

Summary: Extended, beta-strand–rich, solvent‑exposed assembly scaffolds of outer structural proteins (beta‑solenoid/jelly‑roll/beta‑sandwich–type repeats) typical of bacterial/viral surface architectures, driven by long TGDS‑rich stretches; with occasional weaker matches to compositionally similar exposed linkers or surface helices/strands in unrelated proteins
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation over long, contiguous blocks corresponding to repetitive beta‑sheet/turn segments; dense segments in extracellular/virion structural domains, with occasional sparse, residue‑level peaks in noncanonical matches (e.g., acidic linkers or surface helices)
Exemplars: - Bacterial flagellar structural proteins (flagellin and FliD/cap): activation on the outer beta‑rich D2/D3/head regions that form solvent‑exposed assembly surfaces
- Bacteriophage structural proteins (tailspikes/fibers/baseplates/capsids): strong activation across trimeric beta‑helix (beta‑solenoid) shafts and jelly‑roll beta‑barrels, including carbohydrate‑binding/degrading ridges of tailspikes
- Non‑bacteriophage viral capsid/outer‑capsid proteins: activation along jelly‑roll beta‑barrel sheets and exposed lattice segments
- Bacterial S‑layer proteins: activation over contiguous beta‑strand lattice segments (e.g., a 60‑aa beta‑rich block)
- Autotransporter passenger domains: activation along right‑handed beta‑helix repeats forming extracellular scaffolds
- Apicomplexan AMA1 ectodomain: moderate, shorter activation in disulfide‑stabilized extracellular loops/sheets
- CRISPR Cas13a: weaker regional activation in an acidic, predicted helical linker between HEPN‑like domains (compositionally similar exposed segment)
- RqcH (Rqc2/NFACT‑N): isolated peak on a beta‑strand near the tRNA‑binding surface (surface strand match)
- XRCC4‑like factor: sparse activation on residues within a solvent‑exposed helix of the coiled‑coil assembly region

Summary: A glycine-anchored, Pro–Gly–centered beta-turn/N-cap motif (often P–G–Y or P–G–T) that marks the loop-to–beta-strand start of beta-hairpins/edge strands; a generic structural signal recurring across diverse proteins, especially secreted/surface proteins, proteases, CAZymes, and phage structural proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks in short 2–4 aa windows, maximally on Gly at the first residue of a beta-strand or within a tight turn; commonly preceded by Pro and often followed by Tyr/Thr. Signals recur multiple times within large proteins, typically at coil-to–beta-strand transitions or hairpin connectors, and are not tied to catalytic residues.
Exemplars: - Calpains (cysteine proteases; C2-like beta-sandwich domains): activation on SPGY/SVGY segments with a peak at Gly that initiates a beta-strand after a coil.
- Bacterial S-layer/adhesion proteins: activation on Gly/Pro in short coils linking beta-strands (beta-hairpin turns) and at strand starts.
- Neutral ceramidase-like amidases: activation on Q–P–G–I–… segments at the loop-to–beta-strand transition with a sharp peak at Gly.
- AMPK/SNF1 beta subunits (CBM48 glycogen-binding modules): activation at a conserved PG-containing loop capping/starting a beta-strand.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes and polysaccharide lyases (jelly-roll/beta-sandwich folds): activation on PG/GP motifs, often followed by Tyr/Thr, at hairpin turns and beta-strand N-termini.
- Phage tail and receptor-binding proteins: activation on PGY/T-containing turns at edges of beta-sandwich domains that form strand starts.

Summary: A recurrent domain-boundary module in secreted/ectodomain proteins: long C‑terminal α‑helical “capping” segments at the end of an extracellular catalytic/effector domain, often transitioning into an adjacent low‑complexity Ser/Thr/Gly‑rich linker to the next module. This architectural element recurs across extracellular proteases, carbohydrate‑active enzymes, adhesins, and complement MACPF proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over extended contiguous stretches (typically a single long helix of 20–40 residues) located at or just beyond the C‑terminus of a domain; signal often peaks at the last helical turn of the domain and can spill into the immediately adjacent disordered/low‑complexity linker; generally at high residue indices and not tied to a specific catalytic site.
Exemplars: - GH16 β‑agarase: activation rises from the C‑terminal tail of the catalytic domain and peaks in the immediately following low‑complexity/disordered segment.
- GH18 chitinase: strong activation on the terminal α‑helix capping the catalytic domain, with a peak at the last domain residue and into the short trailing coil.
- Chondroitinase/hyaluronidase with EGF‑like module: activation on a long α‑helix directly N‑terminal to the EGF‑like domain; drops upon entering the EGF module.
- Carboxypeptidase (peptidase M14 family): strong activation on the long α‑helix at the C‑terminal end of the peptidase domain; weaker signal continues into the following region.
- Complement MACPF (C7): activation on the long α‑helical segment in the C‑terminal region of the MACPF domain (the final helical bundle at the domain boundary).

Summary: Surface-exposed polar/charged interaction patches—typically flexible loops and helix–coil boundaries that flank catalytic or cofactor-binding motifs—representing a generic electrostatic interface signal rather than a specific catalytic motif.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks dispersed across the sequence; enriched in low-to-medium confidence/disordered segments and at helix–coil transitions, with additional signal on exposed helical faces; often adjacent to (but not centered on) catalytic residues or ligand/cofactor-binding sites; coverage ranges from sparse peaks to diffuse stretches across large proteins.
Exemplars: - CRISPR-Cas13a endoribonuclease (HEPN nuclease): peaks on polar residues across flexible regions within and outside HEPN domains, avoiding the core catalytic residues yet flanking functional areas.
- Bacterial ElaD-like cysteine protease/deubiquitinase: peaks on Gly/Ser/Thr-rich coils and nearby helices away from the Cys/His catalytic dyad, consistent with surface loops used for interactions.
- ERO1-like FAD-dependent thiol oxidase: peaks at helix–coil transitions adjacent to the redox-active Cys motif and near the FAD-binding region, with little signal on the N-terminal signal peptide.

Summary: Hydrophobic alpha-helical context, especially transmembrane and signal-peptide helices, with additional preference for helix boundary/capping positions and short amphipathic segments; activations favor small/hydrophobic residues and are largely structural rather than catalytic
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks concentrated within alpha-helices (most strongly in TM and signal-peptide helices) and at their starts/ends or immediately adjacent loop residues; often near the N-terminus due to signal sequences; occasional weak peaks in flexible loops/linkers flanking helical segments; cysteine is rarely highlighted
Exemplars: - SEDS-family peptidoglycan glycosyltransferase (FtsW): peaks inside multiple transmembrane helices and at an extracellular helix end.
- V/A-type ATPase subunit a/I: peaks within TM helices and in helical residues just preceding TM entry.
- DHHC palmitoyl acyltransferase: residues in the loop before the first TM, at the start of a TM helix, and within another TM helix near the DHHC catalytic region.
- Secreted plant peptide precursors (CEP family): peaks in the mature signaling peptide segment and at the N-terminal signal-peptide helix, including residues near the processing site.
- Subtilisin-like extracellular serine protease: scattered low-level peaks in non-catalytic loops/linkers between domains (structural context rather than active-site chemistry).
- Homing endonuclease (SceI): peaks at the start of an alpha-helix and at the end of another helix (helix-capping/boundary positions).

Summary: Membrane-interface motif at the C-terminal end of an N-terminal transmembrane signal (signal peptide or single-pass signal-anchor) and the first extracytoplasmic/periplasmic/lumenal residues—i.e., the TM-to-solvent exit used by secretory and cell-envelope proteins, typically a short hydrophobic helix enriched in interfacial aromatics.
Activation pattern: Regional activation in short contiguous windows (~15–25 aa) that span the C-terminal half of a transmembrane helix and extend a few residues into the extracytoplasmic loop or post-cleavage N-terminus; strongest at the helix–solvent boundary or signal-peptide cleavage site. Often near the N-terminus, but can occur at internal TM exits in multi-pass proteins. Segments are hydrophobic with frequent W/Y/F and helix-to-coil transitions with lower structural confidence.
Exemplars: - Type II Golgi glycosyltransferases (e.g., alpha-2,3-sialyltransferases): activation over the N-terminal signal-anchor helix and its lumenal entry segment.
- Ceramide synthase complex subunits (Lip1): activation from the signal-anchor TM into the first lumenal loop, peaking at the lumenal boundary.
- Phosphoethanolamine transferase MCR-1: activation at the periplasmic exit of a transmembrane helix.
- Teichoic acid D-alanine hydrolases (Gram-positive cell wall enzymes): activation at the end of the signal peptide and start of the mature secreted enzyme.
- TamB (translocation and assembly module component): activation across the N-terminal signal-anchor and periplasmic transition.
- Periplasmic c-type cytochromes: activation immediately after signal peptide cleavage within the N-terminal helix of the mature chain.
- Sortase B (Gram-positive surface enzyme): activation at the boundary between the N-terminal membrane anchor and the extracellular catalytic domain.

Summary: Structural motif: short coil/turn segments and the first residues of β-strands at sheet “blade” edges, most prominently within β-propeller-like repeats (WD/kelch, Sema, VPS10p/BNR/neuraminidase) and other β‑rich solenoids (parallel β‑helix CAZymes). These loop→β-strand transitions often include aromatic+acidic signatures (e.g., WD) and Gly/Pro turns, and mark blade/rung architecture rather than catalytic sites.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks in many short (5–15 aa) segments distributed across a domain; periodic within repeat blades. Peaks localize to coil→β-strand boundaries and the first/last residues of β-strands; strong across β-propeller/β-helix regions; little or no activation in long helices or disordered tails.
Exemplars: - WD40/kelch β-propeller scaffolds (Mediator subunit 16; cilia/flagella CFAP43): recurrent peaks within WD repeats/blades, including loop connectors and the C‑terminal WD motif region.
- Semaphorin Sema domain (7‑bladed β-propeller): localized peaks on β-sheets and adjacent turns within blades.
- Viral/bacterial neuraminidase/tailspike-like proteins (BNR/Asp‑box propellers): peaks on flexible loops and β‑strand boundaries near sialic‑acid–binding regions between repeats.
- Oligogalacturonate lyase/pectate lyase CAZymes (parallel β‑helix): peaks in coil segments immediately N‑terminal to β‑strands (rungs) across the solenoid.
- Macrocyclase–peptidase: multiple non‑catalytic peaks at β‑strands and their N‑terminal flanking coils.
- Vacuolar tethering complex subunit VPS11 (HOPS/CORVET): discrete peaks at coil↔β‑strand boundaries in the N‑terminal β‑rich region; absent from helical CHCR repeats and Zn‑finger.
- Elongator complex protein 1: numerous short peaks marking β‑strands and N‑terminal turns throughout the β‑rich portions.

Summary: Intrinsic-disorder–associated, low‑complexity terminal segments enriched in Asp/Asn/His/Tyr and depleted of Lys/Arg—typically N‑ or C‑terminal propeptides or regulatory tails, and occasionally N‑terminal amphipathic helices in small viral proteins—rather than structured catalytic cores.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks on D/H/N/Y within low‑pLDDT regions that often coalesce into contiguous activation across long terminal IDRs; minimal activation in folded domains; occasional activation within an N‑terminal helix when the helix presents an acidic/polar face.
Exemplars: - Fibroblast growth factor propeptides: selective peaks in the disordered N‑terminal propeptide (e.g., H/N/D) with no activation in the mature growth factor domain.
- Bacteriophage minor capsid proteins: activation in the N‑terminal amphipathic helix at polar/acidic residues (D/Y/N) near the helix’s N‑end.
- Uncharacterized eukaryotic microproteins/regulatory peptides: scattered D/H/Y peaks across very low‑confidence, disordered regions, often strongest near termini.
- Short‑chain dehydrogenase/reductase family enzymes: activation confined to a disordered, acidic/polar C‑terminal extension, absent from the structured NAD(P)‑binding/catalytic domain.
- DNA‑binding apoptosis regulators (Killin‑like): largely disordered proteins with highest peaks on D/N and additional H/Y, mostly outside the annotated DNA‑binding segment.

Summary: Acidic–histidine catalytic/liganding microenvironments: the feature highlights His together with nearby Asp/Glu (often flanked by Pro and aliphatic residues), marking general acid/base residues and metal/proton‑binding sites that underlie catalysis in soluble enzymes and proton‑coupling/ion coordination in membrane transporters
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks centered on His and adjacent Asp/Glu; peaks cluster into short motifs or short stretches (loops, active‑site walls, periplasmic/TM proton-relay residues). In some proteins this expands into longer acidic/histidine‑rich regions; location varies from catalytic pockets in soluble domains to conserved TM/loop positions in transporters
Exemplars: - Adenylate-forming/acyl‑CoA synthetases and NRPS adenylation domains (ANL superfamily): activation on His-containing loops and proximal acidic residues that help position Mg2+/ATP and the acylate substrate
- NRPS/assembly-line enzymes: activation on A‑domain His–Asp/Glu submotifs within the adenylation active site
- RND/cation efflux transporters and mycobacterial MmpL: activation on conserved Asp/Glu/His in transmembrane helices/periplasmic loops that form the proton-antiport relay/ion-binding network
- Secreted subtilisin-like serine proteases and related peptidases: activation on the catalytic His–Asp pair and neighboring loop residues shaping the active site
- Sulfotransferases (tyrosyl-protein and carbohydrate sulfotransferases): activation on the catalytic His and adjacent Asp/Glu in the PAPS-binding/catalytic site
- Methionine sulfoxide reductases (MsrA/MsrB): activation on the His–Asp acid/base partners adjacent to the catalytic Cys/SeCys
- RNA polymerase small subunits (archaeal Rpo11; eukaryotic RPAC2): activation on acidic/histidine patches that ligate metals or mediate subunit-interface contacts near the catalytic core
- LrpA-family regulators and MORF/ORRM RNA-editing factors: activation on acidic/hydrophobic–His patches used for nucleic-acid/protein interactions
- Cell-division membrane proteins (FtsX/FtsQ/DivIB): activation on conserved D/E/H residues in periplasmic/TM regions implicated in proton coupling or partner binding
- Metal homeostasis/transport and diverse oxidoreductases/dehydrogenases: activation on metal‑ligating Asp/Glu/His and general acid/base residues at catalytic or ion‑binding sites

Summary: N-terminal helix-cap/turn-to-beta initiation motif at the start of protein domains (often beta-rich), frequently in secreted/periplasmic/extracellular proteins and especially the calycin superfamily (lipocalins and avidin/streptavidin-like barrels); the segment seeds the first beta-strand (or an early beta element) and often lies at oligomerization interfaces rather than ligand-binding sites, with a sequence bias toward small/polar and acidic residues (Gly, Asp, Pro) and simple dipeptides (TG, DG/GD, PP).
Activation pattern: Short contiguous windows (~8–20 aa) with sharp residue-level peaks; usually within the first ~40 residues of the mature chain; centered on the C-terminus of a short alpha-helix and the adjacent coil that feeds into an ensuing beta-strand (helix→turn/coil→beta junction).
Exemplars: - Lipocalins (e.g., heme/NO-binding nitrophorins): activation on the N-terminal coil/short helix immediately preceding the first beta-strand of the lipocalin barrel.
- Avidin/streptavidin-like biotin binders: activation on the N-terminal alpha-helix/turn at the beginning of the avidin-like domain, just before beta 1.
- Plant plastid lipid-associated proteins (fibrillins/plastoglobulins; plant lipocalins): activation on the early helix/turn leading into the beta-barrel.
- CD-NTase-associated beta-barrel/pore-forming proteins: activation at the helix-to-coil connector feeding a beta-strand critical for barrel oligomerization.
- Bacterial Ser/Thr receptor kinases with extracellular domains: activation on a short coil immediately before a beta-strand near dimerization-sensitive positions.
- Outer-membrane/periplasmic beta-barrel or beta-rich surface proteins: activation at the N-terminal helix and subsequent beta-strand start.
- Secreted/periplasmic enzymes (proteases; class 4 penicillin-binding proteins): activation on the early helix/turn-to-beta segment at the start of the mature domain.
- Also observed at the N-terminus of some cytosolic alpha/beta scaffolds (e.g., F-box proteins), where a short helix-cap/turn precedes an early beta element or interface region.

Summary: Extracellular attachment fibers and their assembly/anchoring modules in secreted or virion‑surface proteins—encompassing phage tail fiber/spike receptor‑binding and capsule‑depolymerase β‑solenoids (often with intramolecular chaperone/autoprotease tails), Gram‑negative autotransporter translocator β‑barrels (Type Va/Vc), trimeric viral fiber/capsid attachment proteins, bacterial Type IV pilins, and analogous attachment/glycan‑interacting segments in viral envelopes and extracellular matrix proteins. These modules are often β‑rich (β‑solenoids, jelly‑rolls) or fibrous helical (pilins).

Activation pattern: Domain‑level activation as long, contiguous blocks across β‑architecture repeats or helical fiber modules; especially strong on terminal assembly/anchor regions (e.g., autotransporter outer‑membrane β‑barrels; tailspike intramolecular chaperone/autoprotease segments; pilin class III signal peptide/assembly helix). Modest secondary peaks at N‑terminal signal/leader peptides; residue preferences skew to short runs of small/polar residues (G/T/S/N). Large proteins often show extended multi‑domain coverage.

Exemplars:
- Classical and trimeric autotransporter adhesins (Type Va/Vc): strong activation on the C‑terminal translocator β‑barrel; weak/modest on N‑terminal signal peptides; little signal across most passenger regions.
- Bacteriophage tailspikes/capsule depolymerases: activation along β‑helix/β‑solenoid carbohydrate‑binding/depolymerase repeats and on the C‑terminal intramolecular chaperone/autoprotease segment.
- Phage long tail fibers and baseplate/structural modules that interface with fibers: activation on β‑solenoid stalks, β‑rich receptor‑binding tips, and contacting baseplate elements.
- Filamentous phage minor coat protein pIII: activation on receptor‑binding domains and adjacent low‑complexity, small/polar–rich segments.
- Bacterial Type IV pilins: activation on the conserved N‑terminal class III signal peptide/assembly helix and β‑sheet head/adhesive loops.
- Retroviral envelope glycoproteins: activation on attachment regions and mucin‑like Ser/Thr/Asn‑rich loops.
- Extracellular matrix collagens and EMILIN/Multimerin: activation on Gly‑X‑Y–type repeats and C‑terminal C1q‑like β‑sandwich/trimerization domains.
- Bacillus thuringiensis Cry toxins: activation on β‑sheet‑rich receptor‑binding domains (II/III) and their receptor‑contacting loops.

Summary: Terminal export signals: the model feature recognizes secretion/translocation targeting sequences at protein termini—primarily classical N‑terminal Sec signal peptides (hydrophobic helical H‑regions with cleavage) and also short, low-complexity export signals of type III secretion systems, with occasional recognition of C‑terminal translocation tails used by type IV effectors—common to secreted, surface, and host‑interacting proteins across pathogens.
Activation pattern: Regional activation confined to extreme termini. Strong, contiguous activation over the first ~5–30 residues of the N‑terminus (peaking in the hydrophobic H‑region of signal peptides or across the unstructured T3S signal), dropping sharply at the signal peptide cleavage or immediately after the export signal; rarely, activation occurs over the final ~10–20 residues at the C‑terminus for T4SS translocation tails. Activated segments are often predicted helical for Sec signals or disordered/low‑complexity for T3/T4 signals; mature domains show little to no activation.
Exemplars: - Apicomplexan adhesins/surface proteins (e.g., RH5, PIMMS43): activation on the N‑terminal Sec signal peptide helix directing secretion.
- Secreted chemokine-binding immunomodulators: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide preceding the mature secreted domain.
- Type III–secreted bacterial effectors (e.g., Salmonella SteC): activation on the first 1–10 residues forming the T3S export signal.
- Chlamydia inclusion membrane proteins (IncA): activation on the disordered N‑terminal T3S signal before the transmembrane region.
- Type IV–secreted Legionella effectors (e.g., AnkX): activation on the disordered C‑terminal Dot/Icm translocation signal.
- Venom peptide toxins (e.g., κ‑scoloptoxin): activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide of short secreted peptides.

Summary: Helix N-cap / β→α transition motif: short loop-to-helix initiation sites at the start of α-helices, typically at β–α or coil–helix junctions, enriched in Pro and polar/charged residues (S, T, D, E, K, R) that act as capping/helix-initiating residues; often coincides with functionally important entry points into helices (e.g., nucleotide-binding loops, coiled-coil starts, and DNA-binding helix entries).
Activation pattern: Predominantly short regional activation spanning ~5–10 residues that straddle the loop/β to α-helix transition, with sharp residue-level peaks on the N-cap or the preceding residue (often Pro or Ser/Thr). Occurs repeatedly in large multi-helical proteins and can appear as single-residue spikes at a Pro immediately before long coiled-coil helices.
Exemplars: - P4-ATPase flippases: activation on the ATP-binding β→α junction in the cytosolic N-domain, peaking at an N-cap Thr within the annotated ATP-binding site.
- Plant B3/ARF transcription factors: activation at a loop-to-helix junction inside the B3 DNA-binding domain, peaking on a Pro immediately before the helix.
- Rab-effector coiled-coil proteins: single sharp peak on a Pro that precedes the start of a long coiled-coil α-helix.
- Deubiquitinases (USP) and calpains: conserved loop-to-helix capping motifs adjacent to catalytic or substrate-recognition segments.
- Microtubule-binding CAP-Gly/dynactin and translation scaffolds (eIF4G/4E-BPs): repeated coiled-coil helix starts with N-cap polar/Pro residues.
- Nucleic acid-binding/processing proteins (e.g., helicases, ligases, RPA/SSB): β→α phosphate- or ligand-binding loops at helix entries (including Walker/Rossmann-like helix starts where present).
- Bacterial DNA sliding clamp: short β→α junctions leading into clamp helices.
- Viral scaffolding/protease precursors (e.g., herpesvirus): helix starts within long coiled-coil segments.
- Membrane transporters (Na+/H+ exchangers, CNNM, P-type ATPases): cytosolic loop-to-helix starts near regulatory or binding regions.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes (e.g., TIM-barrel families, CBMs): recurring β–α units with helix N-cap residues.
- Toxin–antitoxin antitoxins: short S/N-rich N-terminal helix-initiation segments.

Summary: Extended soluble regions of mature proteins—primarily extracellular/lumenal domains and secreted peptides, but also analogous C‑terminal soluble tails in cytosolic/nuclear proteins—characterized by long hydrophilic stretches that often include acidic/histidine residues, disulfide/glycan motifs, or low‑complexity segments
Activation pattern: Broad domain- or regional-level activation over long contiguous stretches of the mature polypeptide (typically starting just after a signal peptide or structured N‑terminal module and often extending into C‑terminal tails), with occasional residue‑level peaks at catalytic/structural motifs (e.g., His clusters, beta‑strands). Signal peptides and transmembrane segments are not activated; both well‑ordered domains and intrinsically disordered tails can show sustained activation.
Exemplars: - Alpha-carbonic anhydrases: strong activation across the catalytic alpha‑CA core (including His/active‑site regions) but not the signal peptide or unstructured tail.
- BRICHOS-domain secreted chaperones (e.g., Gastrokine): activation begins at the BRICHOS domain start and stays high across the domain and into the C‑terminal tail, including disulfide-bonded segments.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors (e.g., crotalicidin): strong activation over the disordered, compositionally biased region and the mature C‑terminal AMP.
- Plant dirigent proteins: activation focused on the structured, beta‑rich C‑terminal half corresponding to the extracellular domain; low‑complexity N‑terminal region is inactive.
- Ankyrin repeat proteins with long tails: minimal activation on the ANK repeats but strong activation over the low‑complexity, phosphorylated C‑terminal tail.
- Tyrosyl-DNA phosphodiesterase (TDP1): activation on the distal C‑terminal portion of the catalytic/lid region and the flexible tail near DNA‑interaction sites, not on the core catalytic histidines.

Summary: Generic marker of residues within folded, mature protein domains, with mild enrichment for extracellular disulfide-stabilized folds; it largely avoids signal peptides and highly disordered segments and can also highlight residues near domain boundaries or proteolytic processing sites
Activation pattern: Sparse, low-magnitude, residue-level peaks scattered across secondary-structure elements (beta-strands and helices) and adjacent loops/turns within well-structured regions of the mature chain; little/no signal in N-terminal signal peptides or highly disordered stretches; occasional peaks in propeptides just upstream of cleavage and at domain starts
Exemplars: - Cystine-knot/CTCK secreted antagonists (DAN/NBL1 family): peaks on beta-strands within the CTCK core, including disulfide-forming cysteines.
- Wnt morphogens: scattered peaks across the structured C‑terminal half of the Wnt domain (helices/strands), often in regions containing disulfide bonds; absent from the signal peptide and disordered N-terminus.
- Chemokine-like TAFA/FAM19A proteins: weak peaks confined to the mature secreted chain (loops/helix/strand), with no activation in the signal peptide.
- Proteasome beta catalytic subunits: a prominent peak in the N‑terminal propeptide just upstream of the autocatalytic cleavage site, plus minor peaks in loops connecting secondary structures; the catalytic Thr is not highlighted.
- BTB/POZ domain proteins: a main peak at residues immediately N‑terminal to and within the BTB domain, with additional minor peaks in downstream sheets/loops.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered and other compositionally biased segments—often enriched in Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly and/or basic (Lys/Arg) patches—typical of flexible linkers, propeptides, and embedded bioactive peptides; also includes targeting/signal regions (signal/transit peptides) and short membrane microproteins with biased composition.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks and short runs concentrated in low-pLDDT segments; bias toward coils/IDRs but can occur in predicted helices/strands when those segments are low-confidence or compositionally biased (e.g., signal/transit peptides, short transmembrane helices).
Exemplars: - Kininogen/kinin precursors: activation on bradykinin and flanking unstructured coils
- Disordered regulatory proteins (e.g., ST20 family): diffuse activation across IDRs with short sustained segments
- Testis-specific basic proteins (e.g., TSPY family): widespread peaks across low-confidence, basic low-complexity regions
- Secreted defensins with mucin-like glycosylated tails (e.g., DEFB126): activation on Ser/Thr-rich low-complexity segments
- Transit-peptide-containing enzymes (mitochondrial/chloroplastic): activation on N-terminal targeting peptides
- Small membrane proteins (e.g., ATP synthase subunit 8): activation at termini/loops and signal-like helices within compositionally biased regions

Summary: Stable alpha-helical structural segments in soluble proteins, enriched in small hydrophobic residues, typically serving as scaffold/packing helices; often positioned immediately C-terminal to or adjacent to conserved ligand/ATP-binding loops in kinases, or within regulatory/architectural helical domains of enzymes and RNA-processing factors.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 10–20-residue blocks that align with high-confidence alpha-helices; smooth helical runs with internal peaks at Ala/Leu/Val/Ile/Gly/Ser; occasional weaker secondary blocks on other helices; rarely isolated residues or loop-only regions.
Exemplars: - Enolase-superfamily enzyme (mitochondrial dehydratase/cycloisomerase): strong activation on a core alpha-helix not bearing annotated catalytic residues.
- 2‑Isopropylmalate synthase (leucine biosynthesis): two strongly activated helices within the C‑terminal regulatory domain.
- Mevalonate kinase (GHMP kinase): helix immediately C‑terminal to the ATP‑binding segment shows peak activation.
- Shikimate kinase: helix directly C‑terminal to the ATP‑binding site is strongly activated, with minor activation on another helix.
- Exosome complex subunit Rrp45: primary activation on a central alpha‑helix and weaker activation along a long C‑terminal helix in the RNase PH‑like core.

Summary: Charge-enriched, low-complexity helical/IDR scaffolding segments—often coiled-coil or amphipathic/basic helices in cytosolic regions—that mediate non-catalytic interactions with membranes (notably phosphoinositides) and assembly of cytoskeletal/ciliary/endocytic complexes; the feature is generally low in catalytic globular cores but can also highlight long continuous, charge-enriched helices even within otherwise folded proteins.

Activation pattern:
- Long, contiguous activation bands over low-complexity or coiled-coil segments, enriched in charged/polar residues (E/D/K/R/Q/S/T; often Ser/Pro-rich).
- Typically low in catalytic active-site–containing globular cores, but can mark extended amphipathic/basic helices embedded in folded proteins (e.g., small helical chaperones).
- Frequently located at N- or C-termini or cytosolic tails flanking transmembrane helices; includes polybasic/amphipathic lipid-binding helices.
- In membrane proteins, concentrates on cytosolic low-complexity tails; in soluble scaffolds, follows extended coiled-coil tracts.

Exemplars:
- Bacterial TIR-domain virulence proteins (e.g., TcpB/TirS family): activation on the N-terminal phosphoinositide-binding amphipathic/basic helix; no activation on the TIR domain.
- Store-operated Ca2+ sensor STIM1: activation across the cytosolic coiled-coil/IDR tail (SOAR/CAD and adjacent splice-variable, low-complexity region) used for Orai coupling/PM targeting; silent in luminal EF-hand/SAM.
- Ciliary/axonemal coiled-coil scaffolds (CCDC proteins, dynein assembly factors): activation along long charge-rich coiled-coils that organize axonemal assemblies.
- Endocytic/actin adaptors (epsins/AP180/EPS15/amphiphysin): activation on acidic/serine- and proline-rich low-complexity segments and PIP-binding amphipathic helices outside folded domains.
- THO/TREX complex subunits: activation over extended low-complexity scaffolding regions mediating nuclear mRNP assembly/export.
- Viral structural scaffolds and bacterial toxins/effectors: activation on extended charged tails/repeats rather than catalytic cores.
- Small helical chaperones (e.g., Tubulin-specific chaperone A) and bacterial conjugation/secretion proteins (e.g., relaxases) when they contain continuous charge-enriched helical tracts.

Summary: Signature of exported/secreted (non‑cytosolic) proteins, with a strong preference for well‑structured beta‑strand regions of their mature extracellular/lumenal domains and, in many precursors, the N‑terminal signal peptide; in unrelated intracellular proteins the feature typically reduces to isolated peaks at conserved residues within structured motifs
Activation pattern: Mixed: long regional/domain-level activation across beta-strands in mature secreted/lumenal domains; frequent broad activation on N‑terminal signal peptides of secreted precursors; sparse residue-level peaks at single conserved residues in intracellular proteins
Exemplars: - Photosystem II extrinsic OEE1 (thylakoid lumen): activation across beta-strands of the mature luminal domain, absent on the transit peptide
- Phycobilin chromophore lyase: broad activation over the beta-strand–rich catalytic domain
- Cystatin-family protease inhibitors: strong N‑terminal signal peptide activation plus a segment of the structured cystatin fold
- Cathelicidin precursors (cathelin domain): activation over C‑terminal beta-strands including a disulfide-forming cysteine
- Rhamnogalacturonate/pectate lyases (secreted enzymes): clusters on beta-strands and adjacent loops within a disulfide-bounded region of the fold
- Nitrobindin/peroxynitrite isomerase (lipocalin-like/calycin fold): multiple clusters on beta-strands of the nitrobindin domain
- Nuclear hormone receptors: single-residue peak at a conserved glycine within the C4 zinc-finger DNA-binding motif
- Poly(ADP-ribose) glycohydrolase: isolated peak at a valine in a beta-strand within a well-structured region

Summary: Short proline/glycine–enriched turn/loop motifs at strand–loop junctions of beta-rich domains (especially Ig-like C2/I-set modules), most commonly on cell-surface and secreted proteins but also in periplasmic enzymes and intracellular beta-sandwich DNA-binding proteins; the feature captures exposed GP/PG/PP- and S/T–P–containing coils that flank β-strands, often near disulfide bonds (when present extracellularly) and occasional N‑glycosylation sites, and recurs as multiple short patches along long multidomain proteins.
Activation pattern:
- Residue-level peaks in 3–7 aa coils at β-strand boundaries within beta-rich domains
- Strong preference for GP/PG/PP-rich segments with nearby Ser/Thr (e.g., EPETQ-like loops), sometimes adjacent to disulfide-forming cysteines and N-glycosylation when extracellular
- Multiple short activated clusters across domains; minimal/absent in transmembranes, catalytic kinase cores, and typically not in long low-complexity repeats
Exemplars:
- Immunoglobulin superfamily cell-adhesion proteins (e.g., CEACAMs, NCAM/L1): activation on short Ig-domain loops (includes the conserved CEACAM EPETQ loop)
- Axon guidance proteins with Ig-like modules (receptors and ligands; e.g., ROBO/DCC/Neogenin/Sidekick, Semaphorin-4D): exposed Ig loops between β-strands
- Receptor tyrosine kinases with Ig-like ectodomains (e.g., FGFR/VEGFR-like): loop/turns at strand–loop junctions in Ig C2 domains; no activation in TM or kinase domains
- Periplasmic/extracytoplasmic bacterial enzymes (e.g., penicillin-binding proteins TGase/TPase; secreted carbohydrate-active enzymes and proteases): P/G-rich surface loops and short linkers on secreted or periplasmic catalytic/accessory domains
- Bacterial/archaeal surface-layer and outer cell wall proteins: short proline/glycine turn motifs in exposed β-sandwich/Ig-like repeat modules
- Viral structural/immunomodulatory Ig-like proteins: solvent-exposed loops in Ig-like folds
- Intracellular beta-sandwich DNA-binding proteins (e.g., RBPJ/CSL): short solvent-exposed loops at β-strand junctions

Summary: Extracellular ectodomain segments of secreted/surface proteins—most strongly the short stretch immediately following signal peptide cleavage and other Ser/Thr‑rich, glycosylation‑prone low‑complexity loops (often containing N‑X‑S/T sequons and occasional Cys clusters)—common across glycoproteins such as immune receptors, fusogens, adhesins/tailspikes, and large luminal domains.
Activation pattern: Regional activation in contiguous stretches of ectodomains, with pronounced peaks at the signal peptide–mature chain junction and early ectodomain residues; additional moderate peaks within extracellular/luminal low‑complexity or repeat‑rich regions (enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly and N‑glycosylation sequons), sometimes including short β/coil segments; largely absent from transmembrane helices and cytosolic regions.
Exemplars: - Bacteriophage tailspike/depolymerase proteins: activation confined to the first 10–15 residues of the mature chain immediately after the signal peptide; not on catalytic/chaperone domains.
- Alpha‑2‑macroglobulin–like secreted protease inhibitors: rising through the signal peptide and peaking just past the cleavage site at the N‑terminus of the ectodomain, with smaller luminal peaks.
- T‑cell receptor CD3 epsilon (immunoglobulin‑like receptor subunit): narrow peak in the few residues immediately after signal peptide cleavage at the start of the extracellular Ig‑like domain.
- Metazoan cell–cell fusogens (AFF family): broad activation over a glycosylated ectodomain patch containing multiple N‑linked N‑X‑S/T sites.
- Nuclear pore membrane glycoprotein gp210: strong peak at the signal peptide–ectodomain junction and scattered peaks across the perinuclear luminal domain; none in the transmembrane helix or cytosolic tail.

Summary: Alpha-helical interaction segments—typically coiled-coil or single-α-helix (SAH)-like heptad regions enriched in acidic/basic residues—that mediate protein–protein assembly across many complexes
Activation pattern: Primarily regional activation over α-helical stretches (often predicted/observed coiled-coils), with superimposed residue-level peaks at interface positions (e/g salt-bridge pairs such as E/D with K/R and occasional hydrophobics). Can span long helical rods or appear as short helical patches that may lie within or adjacent to acidic low-complexity segments; little activation in unrelated disordered regions.
Exemplars: - Clathrin coat: clathrin light chain heavy-chain–binding helix (focused peaks within the binding helix).
- Centrosomal/ciliary scaffolds: extended coiled-coil rods used for organelle scaffolding and docking.
- Anaphase-promoting complex (APC) subunits: TPR/coiled-coil helices at subunit–subunit interfaces.
- Proteasome assembly factors (e.g., UMP1): helical segments engaged in assembly contacts.
- SMN complex and spliceosome-associated factors: oligomerization helices and acidic helical tracts connecting modules.
- Histone/RNA methyltransferases: dimerization/oligomerization helices outside the catalytic core.
- Meiotic recombination cofactors (Swi5/SAE3/Mei5 family): coiled-coil helices that bind and organize recombinases.
- BED-type zinc finger/transposase proteins: coiled-coil dimerization helices.
- Bacterial transcription regulators and stress/toxin systems: N/C-terminal coiled-coils or leucine-zipper–like helices mediating dimerization adjacent to DNA-binding or toxin cores.

Summary: Residue-level signal for mature regions of secreted extracellular proteins and peptides—including ligands, cytokines, toxins, antimicrobial peptides, and matrix/matrix-associated modulators—with emphasis on disulfide-stabilized/cysteine-rich domains; captures functional/bioactive regions rather than signal peptides or prosegments.
Activation pattern: Predominantly sparse residue-level peaks concentrated within the mature secreted chain or other folded extracellular domains (e.g., cystine‑knot, CSαβ, chemokine-like, or non-repetitive globular domains); minimal activation in signal peptides and low-complexity prosegments; peaks occur on beta-strands and loops/turns and may lie near processing boundaries or adjacent to N‑glycosylation motifs.
Exemplars:
- Glycoprotein hormones (common alpha subunit): peaks near N‑glycosylation motifs and at the signal peptide cleavage boundary within the hormone domain.
- DAN family BMP/Wnt antagonists (e.g., Cerberus/Gremlin) and Chordin: activation on beta‑strands of cysteine-rich domains; little/no signal in the signal peptide.
- Neurotrophins (NGF/BDNF/NT‑4/5): activation confined to the mature growth‑factor chain across beta‑strands and loops; absent from the propeptide.
- IL‑17 family cytokines: sparse peaks in core strands and flexible loops of the secreted cytokine domain.
- Venom toxins (e.g., scorpion κ‑toxins; snake BPP‑CNP precursors): peaks in loop/turn segments of disulfide‑stabilized cores and/or in the proline‑rich BPP/CNP mature segments; minimal in signal peptides.
- Chemokine‑like GPR15 ligand: activation within disordered segments of the mature secreted peptide.
- Antimicrobial peptides (LEAP‑2): peaks on the disulfide‑stabilized core of the mature peptide.
- Extracellular matrix proteins (e.g., Collagen IV chains): sparse peaks within non‑repetitive folded extracellular domains (e.g., NC1 domain or triple‑helix interruptions), not in signal peptides.

Summary: Short strand-connecting beta-turns/loops that link adjacent beta-strands (beta-hairpin or inter-strand connectors), typically enriched in acidic/polar/small residues, often positioned adjacent to ligand/cofactor/catalytic sites across diverse folds
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks in 1–4 residue segments; short local clusters confined to coil/turn regions that connect beta-strands; sparse elsewhere in the domain; frequently adjacent to (but not always coincident with) annotated binding or catalytic motifs; generally absent from long disordered termini or signal peptides
Exemplars: - EGF-like repeat proteins: loop within the EGF domain between beta-strands (e.g., D63–I64 in an EGF-like ligand)
- FHA-domain proteins: inter-strand loop inside the FHA beta-sandwich (peak around Q66 linking two strands)
- START-domain lipid-transfer proteins: loop linking beta-strands within the START fold (e.g., P178/T176/K179 connector)
- TA-system RNase toxins (RelG family): tight beta-hairpin turn connecting strands (D68–T71 with strongest at E69)
- NADPH oxidase FR-type FAD-binding domains: loop immediately C-terminal to the FAD-binding motif and a strand-to-loop junction (e.g., L858–E859; K813–E815)
- Serine hydrolases (alpha/beta-hydrolase fold): short acidic loop connecting beta-strands at the domain edge (E58–D60)
- Glycoside hydrolases (endo-alpha-L-arabinanase): multiple turns between beta-strands, including near substrate-binding residues (e.g., D233, D109, D179; Y189–S190 region)

Summary: Solvent-exposed loop/turn segments connecting transmembrane beta-strands in outer-membrane beta-barrel proteins, especially the C-terminal translocator barrels of Type V autotransporters; also present in porins, TonB-dependent receptors, and Omp85/TpsB family proteins across Gram-negative bacteria and organellar outer envelopes.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks confined to short coils/beta-turns between beta-strands; repeated across multiple loops to form regional clusters within beta-barrel domains. Minimal activation in the membrane-embedded strands, plug domains, periplasmic POTRA repeats, or soluble passenger regions. Often strongest toward the C-terminus of autotransporters. Activated residues are enriched for polar/acidic and glycine residues, frequently with nearby aromatics; loops can be flexible (low pLDDT) or well-ordered.
Exemplars: - General porins (e.g., NanC-like): activation on extracellular loops linking barrel strands; strands and periplasmic regions largely inactive.
- TonB-dependent receptors: activation on specific interstrand loops of the beta-barrel; plug domains not activated.
- Type V secretion system autotransporters (Pmp family, EibA; intimin/invasin family): activation in the C-terminal translocator beta-barrel loops/turns; little to none in passenger or receptor-binding regions.
- Omp85/TpsB/BamA-like outer-membrane transport/assembly proteins: activation in flexible loop/linker regions around the barrel, outside periplasmic POTRA domains.
- Chloroplast outer-envelope porins (OEP): activation on loops connecting transmembrane beta-strands on both sides of the membrane.

Summary: N-terminal targeting and processing segments—including signal peptides, signal-anchors or other non-cleavable targeting elements (e.g., import signals for outer-membrane porins/translocases), and propeptides (including leaderless cytokine prodomains)—together with adjacent low-complexity, disordered tracts enriched in Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly and/or basic Lys/Arg (often harboring processing/convertase sites). These regions precede extracellular domains or outer-membrane beta barrels and commonly include O-glycosylated Ser/Thr-rich repeats; in cytosolic/membrane-associated proteins they often correspond to basic NLS-like or palmitoylation-adjacent LCRs.

Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation concentrated at N termini: continuous high activation across signal/transit or other targeting segments and propeptides, often extending into long low-complexity repeat regions; occasionally spans other long basic or Ser/Thr-rich LCRs; little motif-level peaking.

Exemplars:
- Fibroblast growth factors (FGFs): activation on the N-terminal signal peptide and propeptide (including basic convertase sites) preceding the growth factor domain.
- Interleukin-1 family cytokines: activation on N-terminal propeptide/processing regions that are cleaved to release the mature cytokine (leaderless secretion allowed).
- Lectins and lectin-like proteins (e.g., C-type lectins; plant/fungal lectins): activation on signal peptides and Ser/Thr-rich linkers/stalks.
- Fungal/yeast cell wall adhesins and mannoproteins: activation on the signal peptide plus long Ser/Thr-rich, O-glycosylated low-complexity repeats.
- Bacterial and cnidarian toxins/venom components: activation on secretory signal peptides and propeptides with Lys/Arg-rich convertase or activation sites.
- Secreted protease inhibitors (Kunitz-type, cystatins): activation on N-terminal signal peptides and propeptides preceding the inhibitor domain.
- Mitochondrial/chloroplast outer-membrane porins and translocases: activation on N-terminal targeting or signal-anchor–like segments or basic/unstructured import signals, even when lacking a cleavable transit peptide.
- Axonemal/cytoskeletal-associated proteins: activation on basic Lys/Arg-rich and/or Pro/Ser/Thr-rich low-complexity tails or N-terminal targeting stretches.
- Cytosolic and membrane-associated proteins with basic LCRs (e.g., phospholipid scramblases, tubby-like proteins): activation on N-terminal basic/NLS-like or palmitoylation-adjacent low-complexity segments.

Summary: Glycine-centered loop/turn motifs (often with adjacent Pro; GP/PG) located at beta-strand edges and loop–beta transitions, serving as short flexible “hinge” segments frequently used in surface/binding-site loops across diverse proteins.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on glycine within compact 3–8 residue segments that form loops/turns immediately before or after a beta-strand; activations appear as short local clusters (sometimes multiple loops per protein) rather than broad domains.
Exemplars: - Glutathione hydrolase (gamma-glutamyltransferase): extracellular-domain loop transitioning into a beta-strand with a peak at glycine; additional peak in a distal loop of the light chain.
- Uridine phosphorylase: short loop feeding into the N-terminus of a beta-strand adjacent to phosphate/uridine-binding sites, peaking at glycine.
- JmjC histone demethylase (FYR domain): coil adjacent to a beta-sheet centered on a glycine in a short loop.
- Argonaute (PIWI/PAZ domains): localized coil in the PIWI domain with a strong glycine peak and a weaker loop peak in PAZ.
- Queuosine-tRNA galactosyltransferase: C-terminal coil immediately following a short beta-strand, peaking at glycine.

Summary: Surface-exposed β‑strand/loop patches in extracellular or lumenal glycoproteins—most commonly carbohydrate‑active enzymes (hydrolases, transferases, lyases) but also other secreted/ecto enzymes—frequently encompassing or adjacent to N‑linked glycosylation sequons (N‑X‑[S/T]) and not coincident with catalytic motifs
Activation pattern: Regional activation in short-to-moderate contiguous segments (≈10–40 residues), typically in mid‑to‑C‑terminal regions; sharp residue‑level peaks centered on single β‑strands that spill into flanking loops; multiple such patches can occur per protein; generally away from annotated catalytic/metal‑binding sites
Exemplars: - Alpha-amylase: a C‑terminal loop/β‑strand patch that includes a predicted N‑glycosylation sequon (N‑X‑[S/T])
- Alpha-galactosidase: an isolated C‑terminal β‑strand with adjacent coil in a well‑ordered region
- Glucuronoxylanase (xylanase): a short C‑terminal β‑strand within a stable β‑sheet; no overlap with active‑site annotations
- Endoglycoceramidase (glycosphingolipid hydrolase): paired C‑terminal β‑strands and adjoining coil in a high‑confidence region
- Aminopeptidase N (M1 family): multiple non‑catalytic β‑strand segments (one near the N‑region and additional mid/C‑terminal patches), distinct from Zn‑binding and substrate‑binding residues

Summary: A structural micro-motif: residues in short coil/turn segments immediately N-terminal to β-strands (α→β linkers/β-strand N-caps), sometimes extending into the first residue(s) of the strand; broadly conserved across α/β enzyme folds and not tied to specific catalytic residues.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks, sparse and dispersed along sequences. Peaks occur in high-confidence coils that precede β-strands or at the β-strand start; often at hydrophobic or glycine residues, occasionally charged. Frequently near—but not on—annotated active or binding sites; sometimes includes the initiator Met when the first structured element is a β-strand.
Exemplars: - Nonribosomal peptide synthetase modules (including thioesterase domain): peaks at glycine/aliphatic residues in loops immediately before β-strands; occasional peak within a β-strand of the thioesterase (α/β-hydrolase) domain.
- PLP-dependent threonine dehydratase-like enzymes: isolated peaks in short helix-to-strand connector loops (α→β linkers), away from PLP-binding residues.
- Dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (fumarate-dependent): distinct peaks in loops directly preceding β-strands, including near but not at FMN/substrate-binding positions.
- Indole-3-glycerol phosphate synthase (TIM-barrel): multiple peaks at loop residues just before successive barrel β-strands.
- N-acetylneuraminate lyase (class I aldolase/TIM-barrel): peaks at coil residues immediately before β-strands, adjacent to strands bearing catalytic residues downstream.
- UDP-hexuronate transferase/glycosyltransferase: activations in coil segments connecting α-helices to β-sheets, marking α→β transitions.
- AMP-forming acyl-CoA ligase (ANL family): peaks in unstructured loops within the substrate-binding domain that connect helices to β-strands; minor signal on a short helix within the linker region.

Summary: Extended, non‑transmembrane interaction/recognition domains—typically entire ectodomains or analogous exposed regions—used for membrane fusion/adhesion or assembly of large complexes; favored in secretory‑pathway and membrane‑associated proteins (glycosylated, cysteine/Ser/Thr‑rich, mixed secondary structure), but also appearing as long PPI/ligand‑binding segments in soluble proteins (including dimer/cofactor/substrate‑binding portions), while avoiding signal peptides and transmembrane helices
Activation pattern: Primarily domain‑level, long continuous stretches (often 200–400+ aa); starts after signal peptides when present and terminates at proteolytic or domain boundaries; excludes transmembrane segments; peaks often align with glycosylation motifs, cysteine motifs, or known binding/interaction sites; frequently overlaps low‑to‑moderate pLDDT regions with mixed secondary structure, but can also cover well‑structured ligand/dimer interfaces
Exemplars: - Retroviral envelope surface subunits (SU) and other viral entry/fusion ectodomains: activation spans the entire receptor‑binding ectodomain and stops at the SU–TM cleavage site, highlighting glycosylation and Cys motifs (Env SU).
- ER/Golgi lumenal glycoprotein subunits: strong activation across the glycosylated lumenal region and not in TM/cytosolic catalytic tails (DSC E3 ligase lumenal subunit).
- TRAPP (transport protein particle) complex subunits: broad activation over central, lower‑confidence regions implicated in complex assembly, avoiding other structured segments.
- UFM1 protease regulatory segment: activation on the long non‑catalytic insert N‑terminal to the peptidase core, consistent with interaction/regulatory roles; no activation on the compact catalytic domain (UFSP2).
- Polycomb PRC2 component SUZ12: activation on the mid‑region mediating interactions with AEBP2/PHF19 and dimerization; no activation on the folded VEFS‑box.
- Secreted lipid/ligand carriers: activation in the C‑terminal portion of the vitellogenin domain containing an N‑glycosylation site and stopping at the VWFD boundary (Vitellogenin).
- ESCRT‑associated membrane‑trafficking proteins: activation on the CHMP7 central region involved in partner/membrane interactions, not on the C‑terminal ESCRT‑III helical module.
- Large soluble enzymes with exposed binding interfaces: activation over the NOS oxygenase domain and into the calmodulin‑binding region, highlighting substrate/cofactor and dimer‑interface residues while excluding distal reductase domains (inducible nitric‑oxide synthase).

Summary: Terminal accessory regions that mediate trafficking to/through membranes and regulate activation—signal/transit peptides, secretion/translocation segments, and cleavable pro- or autoinhibitory domains—typically low-complexity and/or amphipathic/hydrophobic helical, often bounded by a proteolytic cleavage site.
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation over long contiguous stretches, usually confined to one terminus. Frequently starts at the initiator methionine (N‑terminal leaders) or immediately after an annotated cleavage site, and can cover an entire inhibitory/pro-domain (often C‑terminal). Peaks are not residue-specific but span extended, coil-rich or helix-rich segments; internal globular cores are typically less activated.
Exemplars: - Bacillus thuringiensis Cry toxins: activation on the C‑terminal accessory/pro-domain that supports crystallization and is removed upon activation.
- S‑type bacteriocins (pyocins/colicins): activation on the N‑terminal disordered translocation/TonB‑interacting region used for import across the outer membrane.
- Gasdermin family: activation across the C‑terminal autoinhibitory domain downstream of the activation cleavage site that releases the pore‑forming N‑terminus.
- Type III secretion system translocon components: activation on N‑terminal secretion signals and chaperone‑binding, low‑complexity segments required for export.
- Viral fusion/entry glycoproteins: activation on signal peptides/fusion peptides and adjacent low‑complexity regions that initiate membrane engagement.
- Secreted bacterial toxins/hemolysins: activation on cleavable leader/pro‑peptides that target proteins to secretion pathways and regulate maturation.
- Apolipoproteins and lipid‑associated host proteins: activation on amphipathic helix clusters and signal peptides that mediate lipid binding and secretion.
- Mitochondrial and chloroplast preproteins: activation on N‑terminal transit peptides that direct organelle import across envelope/thylakoid membranes.
- RNA bacteriophage maturation/assembly proteins: activation on membrane‑associating/targeting segments that facilitate assembly or host interaction.

Summary: Long, compositionally biased, charged low‑complexity segments (polyampholyte IDRs) enriched in Glu/Asp and Lys/Arg with frequent Gln—used as Q/acidic‑rich activation domains, flexible linkers, E/K‑rich helical/coiled‑coil assembly rods, or basic nucleic‑acid–binding tails across diverse proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended low‑complexity tracts (often tens to hundreds of residues), typically outside conserved catalytic cores and spanning N‑ or C‑terminal tails or internal linkers
Exemplars: - Transcription factors and chromatin regulators: Q/E/K‑rich acidic activation domains and low‑complexity linkers that mediate coactivator/histone interactions
- Ser/Thr protein kinases: disordered, charge‑biased N‑ or C‑terminal regulatory extensions and linker regions
- Viral capsid/nucleocapsid proteins: Lys/Arg‑rich basic N/C‑terminal tails that bind genomes and drive assembly
- Ciliary/axonemal scaffold proteins (e.g., tektins, radial spoke/axonemal assembly factors): long E/K‑rich coiled‑coil stalks and low‑complexity rods
- Bacterial SSB and other DNA‑maintenance factors: acidic, disordered C‑terminal tails that recruit partner proteins
- Ribosomal and other small RNA‑binding subunits: highly basic low‑complexity N/C‑terminal extensions contacting rRNA
- Secreted/precursor proteins: low‑complexity propeptides and acidic/basic stalk regions outside signal peptides
- Dictyostelium discoideum regulatory/adaptor and coiled‑coil proteins: extensive Q/E/K‑rich repetitive regions serving as flexible linkers or assembly scaffolds

Summary: Hydrophobic H-region at the start of alpha-helical membrane spans—i.e., the core of signal peptides and the N-terminal half of signal-anchor/transmembrane helices used for membrane targeting/insertion; typically a short, aromatic-enriched hydrophobic run often preceded by Lys/Arg and frequently near the protein N-terminus
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short (≈8–15 aa) contiguous hydrophobic alpha-helical stretches with sharp residue-level peaks; most common at positions ~1–30 (beginning of the first TM or signal peptide) but can recur for additional helices; enriched for Leu/Ile/Val/Phe and flanked by basic residues
Exemplars: - Multidrug efflux membrane fusion protein (periplasmic adaptor, MdtA family): activation on the hydrophobic core of the N-terminal signal peptide/signal-anchor.
- Cell shape–determining protein MreC (single-pass membrane anchor): activation on the N-terminal portion of its lone transmembrane helix.
- Amyloid-beta precursor–like single-pass membrane protein: activation on the N-terminal half of its transmembrane helix.

Summary: Membrane-proximal interfacial segments on either side of biological membranes (periplasmic/extracellular/lumenal or cytosolic leaflet-facing), often flanking or preceding a membrane-embedding element (outer-membrane β-barrel, single-pass transmembrane helix, or peripheral anchor), that mediate bilayer engagement, lipid handling/transfer/assembly, adhesion, or organelle contact/sensing; typically acidic/polar and Gly/Ser/Thr-rich with intermittent aliphatic hydrophobics, and few cysteines
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation across long stretches of interfacial domains; strong peaks in flexible coils or short β/α segments near membrane anchors; cytosolic catalytic cores are largely inactive; weaker, sporadic residue-level peaks can occur elsewhere (occasionally incidental in soluble enzymes)
Exemplars: - Gram-negative autotransporter adhesins/proteases (Type V secretion): activation over C-terminal passenger/translocator stretches comprising β-strands/coils associated with OM assembly/adhesion surfaces
- LPS-assembly protein LptD (OM β-barrel): activation on a structured periplasmic coil and at the extreme C-terminus consistent with the outer-membrane β-signal; minor peaks in nearby loops
- Secreted surfactant protein (latherin/PLUNC-like): activation on a flexible, amphipathic C-terminal helical segment immediately following a disulfide-bonded core, consistent with lipid/water-interface activity
- ER stress sensors (PERK/IRE1): activation across the ER-lumenal sensing domain, absent from the cytosolic kinase/RNase domains
- ERMES SMP-domain tethers (Mdm12, Mdm34): activation on cytosolic membrane-contact surfaces bridging ER and mitochondrial outer membrane for lipid transfer
- Cytosolic/organellar RNase E: isolated single-residue peaks in internal helices (likely incidental relative to the membrane-interface concept)

Summary: Short, solvent‑exposed aromatic–acidic interface loops (short linear motifs) that act as binding/gating segments—often centered on Trp/Tyr next to Asp/Glu (frequent WD/YD/YDS variants)—used to anchor at membranes or to form partner/ligand‑recognition and active‑site “gate” loops across diverse proteins (secreted, membrane‑associated, and enzymes).
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks clustered in short segments (~8–20 aa), typically multiple per protein; peaks map to surface loops at pocket entrances, gate/lid regions, inter‑subunit interfaces, or membrane‑interfacial loops with mixed charged and hydrophobic composition and frequent Trp hotspots.
Exemplars: - Lipid transfer/contact‑site proteins (START/OSBP/ORP/PITP/VPS13/Lam/Atg2): activation on membrane‑interfacial loops or pocket lids containing aromatic–acidic residues (Trp with D/E) that gate/anchor lipid binding.
- Vitellogenins/lipovitellins: activation on amphipathic surface loops at the lipid‑cargo binding interface.
- RNase A/angiogenin family: activation on short substrate‑binding/catalytic cleft loops enriched in charged/aromatic residues that position bases and phosphates.
- mRNA export machinery (e.g., Rae1/Gle2 WD‑propellers, NXF/TAP partners): activation on WD/YD blade loops that contact FG‑nucleoporins or partner surfaces.
- Aromatic ring‑hydroxylating dioxygenase/oxygenase small subunits (Rieske‑type systems): activation on inter‑subunit and active‑site entrance loops guiding substrate access.
- Fungal secondary‑metabolism enzymes (cyclases, dehydratases, terpenoid/polyketide biosynthesis): activation on substrate‑channel/gating loops with aromatic–acidic residues.
- Na+‑translocating NQR and RNF complex components: activation on periplasmic/cytosolic membrane‑adjacent loops with Trp‑anchored, mixed‑charge segments mediating cofactor/subunit contacts.
- Cysteine proteases (deneddylases/UBL proteases and pathogen effectors): activation on short Y–D–S–containing loops near the catalytic Cys/His/Asp that help position substrate.
- Plant ABA receptors (PYR/PYL/RCAR) and chloroplast division/Chl b synthesis proteins: activation on latch/gate loops over ligand pockets or membrane‑contact loops with aromatic–acidic composition.

Summary: Transmembrane beta-barrel domains of bacterial outer-membrane proteins (and organellar homologs)—the beta-stranded pore architecture found in porins, Type V autotransporter translocator barrels, Omp85/LptD-like barrels, and pilus ushers; occasional local matches in unrelated proteins due to short beta-strand patterns.
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation across long, contiguous stretches of the beta-barrel, peaking on beta-strands and strand–loop transitions; minimal on N-terminal signal peptides and soluble/periplasmic regions. In autotransporters (including Chlamydia Pmps), activation is concentrated in the C-terminal translocator barrel; in porins and ushers, it spans the barrel-forming C-terminal portion. Rare, isolated residue-level peaks can occur in unrelated cytosolic enzymes.
Exemplars: - Classical outer-membrane porins: activation across the mature beta-barrel after the signal peptide.
- Type V secretion autotransporters (including Chlamydial polymorphic membrane proteins): activation on the C-terminal translocator beta-barrel.
- Omp85 superfamily/LptD: broad activation over the C-terminal beta-barrel (not the N-terminal periplasmic/POTRA or signal peptide).
- Chaperone–usher pathway ushers (e.g., FimD): strong activation across the C-terminal barrel that forms the secretion pore.
- Nonribosomal peptide synthetase megasynthase: a single-residue, likely spurious activation within a helical carrier region (illustrating occasional local pattern matches).

Summary: Short, basic, low‑complexity termini and linkers enriched in Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro that act as targeting/leader peptides or RNA‑binding tails (e.g., chloroplast transit peptides, Sec/Tat N‑regions, and basic IDR tracts on RNA/DNA processing enzymes)
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous stretches (often 10–40 aa) with residue‑level peaks at Lys/Arg interspersed within G/P/S/T‑rich runs; typically at the extreme N‑terminus, occasionally multiple such clusters per protein and sometimes on internal low‑complexity linkers
Exemplars: - Plastid/chloroplast RNA polymerase subunits (nuclear‑encoded): activation on the N‑terminal chloroplast transit peptide (Ser/Thr/Gly/Pro‑rich, low complexity, mildly basic).
- Bacterial tRNA/rRNA modification enzymes (e.g., Trm methyltransferases, pseudouridine synthases, RNase P proteins): activation on short basic, low‑complexity tails that mediate RNA binding.
- Proteins with Sec/Tat signal peptides (periplasmic/secreted and thylakoid lumenal proteins): activation on the positively charged N‑region (including twin‑arginine RR leaders) and adjacent G/S/T‑rich low‑complexity segment.
- Lipoyl metabolism components (lipoate ligase LplA, octanoyltransferase LipB, lipoyl synthase LipA; and lipoyl‑carrier/E2/H‑protein families): activation on flexible low‑complexity N‑termini and short linkers/loops surrounding the lipoyl‑lysine region.
- DNA/RNA replication and processing factors (primases, ligases, helicases, RNA polymerase‑associated proteins): activation on Lys/Arg‑dotted low‑complexity termini used for nucleic‑acid binding or localization.
- Small secreted peptides/bacteriocin precursors (double‑glycine‑type leaders): activation on the N‑terminal leader peptide immediately preceding the GG processing site.
- Membrane proteins obeying the positive‑inside rule: activation on short cytosolic, Lys/Arg‑rich N‑tails or loops adjacent to the first transmembrane helix.
- Viral basic nucleic acid‑binding proteins: activation across short, low‑complexity, Arg/Lys‑containing regions spanning much of the small protein.

Summary: Short A/G/S/P-biased low-complexity tracts (~7–10 aa) in intrinsically disordered tails or loops; activation is contingent on the presence of such tracts and is not a family-level hallmark. Segments that are highly cysteine-dense (metallothioneins), strongly polybasic (protamines), or dominated by hydrophobic amphipathic character (many AMPs/lasso peptides) typically do not activate unless they also contain an A/G/S/P-rich stretch.
Activation pattern: Optional, subset-specific short regional activation with a single peak, often near termini and in low-pLDDT regions; may coincide with short, low-confidence helices. Many homologs are inactive when the requisite tract is absent.
Exemplars: Observed in some homeobox proteins (e.g., DLX members with proline-rich disordered tails); some RiPP precursors where the propeptide includes an A/G/S/P-biased short helix; select ESX/ESAT-6 family members with flexible C-termini (e.g., ESAT-6, but not all paralogs such as EsxG); subsets of Cas2 and GatC proteins that carry short disordered C-terminal tails. Generally absent in metallothioneins, protamines, and strongly hydrophobic AMPs; membrane proteins only when short cytosolic/luminal loops meet the composition.

Summary: Extracellular, modular β‑sheet/disulfide‑rich ectodomains of secreted and cell‑surface proteins—especially lectin/SRCR/kringle/CCP(Z)/ZP‑type ligand‑binding modules used in adhesion, complement/coagulation, and glycan recognition
Activation pattern: Domain‑level, long activation across the mature ectodomain beginning after the signal peptide; weak on signal peptides, transmembranes, and flexible/helical linkers. Residue‑level peaks align with well‑structured β‑strands within small disulfide‑stabilized modules and repeat units, yielding periodic hotspots across domain arrays; loops and helices are de‑emphasized. Cys/Gly/aromatic‑rich positions typical of these extracellular modules are often included, with occasional dips at specific cysteines or modification/catalytic sites.
Exemplars: - SUEL‑type rhamnose‑binding lectins: strong, repeated peaks on the β‑strands of each lectin repeat; helices and loops suppressed.
- Complement classical‑pathway serine proteases (e.g., C1s/C1r/MASP): activation over the CUB, EGF, and CCP/Sushi ectodomains (and associated zymogen regions), consistent with β‑rich, disulfide‑stabilized secreted modules.
- Adhesion GPCRs (latrophilin‑like): activation concentrated on the large N‑terminal ectodomain (rhamnose‑binding lectin, olfactomedin, HRM, GAIN) with low signal on the 7TM bundle.
- Kringle‑containing coagulation/fibrinolysis proteins (e.g., plasminogen/prothrombin/apolipoprotein(a)): activation across kringle repeats and other β‑sheet ligand‑binding modules.
- Scavenger receptor cysteine‑rich (SRCR) proteins: activation spanning SRCR domain arrays of secreted/soluble receptors.
- Zona pellucida and related extracellular matrix/adhesion glycoproteins (e.g., uromodulin/ZP proteins): activation over the ZP β‑sandwich module and associated extracellular repeats.

Summary: N-terminal coiled-coil initiation/transition segments in long coiled-coil scaffolds: the charged, flexible “head/neck” that transitions from disorder into, and often includes, the first helical heptads (e.g., IF Coil 1A), rather than the stable coiled-coil core
Activation pattern: Strong, localized regional activation at protein N-termini (typically ~15–70 aa); begins in disordered/coil, peaks at the disorder-to-coiled-coil boundary, and may extend into the first helical turn; negligible across the downstream coiled-coil rod, tandem helical repeats, or catalytic domains; can recur at starts of additional rod segments in multi-coiled-coil proteins
Exemplars: - Ciliary rootlet/striated fiber coiled-coils (SF-assemblin): activation at the nonhelical-to-rod boundary at the N-terminus.
- Synaptonemal complex structural proteins (e.g., SCP3): activation on short N-terminal helices preceding the axial coiled-coil.
- Plant nuclear lamina-like scaffolds (CRWN/NMCP; CROWDED NUCLEI): activation on the N-terminal flexible region just before the long coiled-coil rod.
- Vesicle tethers/Rab-effectors (taxilin family): activation on the loop/coil immediately before and overlapping the start of the coiled-coil.
- Intermediate filament proteins (e.g., nestin): activation across the head plus Coil 1A at the rod N-terminus, stopping at Linker 1.
- Actin-associated coiled-coils (tropomyosin): activation confined to the extreme N-terminus (N-cap/neck), absent from the long rod.
- RING E3 ligase BRE1 family: activation on the N-terminal helical segment immediately preceding the N-terminal coiled-coil dimerization region.
- Bacterial gas vesicle scaffold GvpC: activation on the flexible N-terminus before the series of helical repeat rods, absent from the repeats.

Summary: PEST-like, low-complexity acidic/proline-rich intrinsically disordered segments, predominantly at protein N-termini, that serve as regulatory tails enriched for degrons and phosphorylation/SLiM sites in intracellular eukaryotic proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation with a strong peak at the extreme N-terminus (first tens of residues), favoring low-complexity runs enriched in S/P/G/A and acidic D/E; secondary activation on compositionally similar internal or C-terminal stretches; little activation within folded domains or transmembrane regions
Exemplars: - Ubiquitin-system components (RING/U-box/HECT E3 ligases; F-box/BTB/SOCS adaptors): activation on N-terminal PEST-like disordered segments harboring degrons and phospho-sites controlling turnover.
- Membrane trafficking tethers/complexes (exocyst subunits, COG complex, Golgins, VPS proteins): activation on acidic, proline-rich N-terminal linkers preceding long coiled-coils.
- Nuclear pore complex proteins (nucleoporins): activation on low-complexity acidic/serine-rich N-terminal stretches (including regions flanking FG repeats) used as flexible regulatory tails.
- Protein kinases and phosphatase regulators: activation on unstructured N-terminal tails rich in S/E/P that carry multiple phosphorylation sites and docking motifs impacting stability/localization.
- Chromosome/centromere and mitotic regulators (kinetochore/cohesin/condensin-associated factors): activation on PEST-like N-terminal IDRs used as degrons and phospho-switch regions.
- Coiled-coil scaffolds/structural tethers: activation on N-terminal acidic/proline-rich disordered linkers that connect to coiled-coil scaffolding cores.
- Viral regulatory proteins: activation on N-terminal acidic/serine-rich PEST-like segments that interface with host ubiquitin-mediated degradation pathways.

Summary: A short, local hydrophobic–aromatic micro‑motif (often including Tyr together with a charged residue) that marks interaction/catalytic hotspots across many folds—commonly the signature segments of active sites or nucleic‑acid/protein interfaces (e.g., kinase DFG/HRD/APE segments, RRM RNP1/2 aromatic motifs, SDR YxxxK)—rather than a family‑specific pattern
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks on compact 3–6‑residue stretches; typically multiple small hotspots per protein; enriched for bulky hydrophobics with frequent Tyr and occasional charged residues; rarely involves Cys; located in loops/turns, β‑strand edges, or juxtamembrane/interface regions
Exemplars: - Protein kinases (ser/thr and tyr kinases): activation on catalytic‑core signature segments such as DFG, HRD, and APE motifs and adjacent aromatic/charged residues in the activation loop.
- RRM‑containing RNA‑binding proteins (poly(A)‑binding proteins, cap‑binding proteins, splicing factors): activation on RNP1/RNP2 aromatic motifs on β‑strands that stack with RNA bases (Phe/Tyr‑rich with a basic residue).
- Ribosomal protein uL23 (bacterial/archaeal/mitochondrial/chloroplast): activation on the conserved hydrophobic/basic patch at the peptide‑exit tunnel interface that contacts rRNA and nascent chains.
- SPFH/band 7 family (stomatin/prohibitin/flotillin scaffolds): activation on short aromatic/hydrophobic segments in the cytosolic loop adjacent to the membrane hairpin that mediate complex assembly.
