- Type IV pilus/secretion assembly factors and secretion chaperones: activation on short periplasmic/membrane‑proximal aromatic/hydrophobic motifs used for subunit docking or sorting.
- Oxidoreductases/dehydrogenases (e.g., SDR/ADH‑like): activation on the catalytic YxxxK motif or neighboring hydrophobic/charged residues of the active site.
- Heme oxygenases (bacterial HmuO/IsdG‑type and related): activation on the His‑centered heme‑ligating segment flanked by hydrophobic/aromatic residues in the active‑site pocket.
- Ribosome biogenesis/maturation factors: activation on aromatic/basic patches in RNA‑contacting loops that guide rRNA processing/assembly.
- Plant stress‑related α/β‑barrel and cupin‑like proteins: activation on hydrophobic/tyrosine‑rich micro‑motifs at cavity mouths or interface loops involved in ligand binding or oligomer contacts.

Summary: Hydrophobic, aliphatic-enriched repeat segments that assemble into extended interaction scaffolds in large eukaryotic adaptor/scaffold proteins—primarily alpha‑solenoids (HEAT/ARM/TPR) but also beta‑propeller WD40/PROPPIN repeats; the feature can also fire on structurally analogous short motifs embedded in other folds (e.g., the kinase N‑lobe).
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation over contiguous repeat blocks (helical turns or propeller blades), with peaks on individual repeats and their loop/connectors; de‑emphasized in low‑complexity tails, though it can extend into low‑confidence helical/linker segments; occasionally a single localized peak within a structured domain (helix–loop–strand motif in a kinase).
Exemplars: - TELO2–TTI co‑chaperone HEAT‑repeat scaffold (TTI1): activation across multiple helical repeat blocks, strongest toward the C‑terminal solenoid
- CCR4–NOT complex subunit CNOT10 (helical solenoid): strong activation on core alpha‑helices, minimal on disordered termini
- Condensin/Cohesin HEAT‑repeat subunits: extended activation along long alpha‑helical solenoid segments; little in fully disordered tails
- Karyopherin‑β/Transportin‑1: widespread activation along HEAT repeats of the nuclear import solenoid
- Autophagy PROPPIN ATG18 (WD40 beta‑propeller): activation across propeller blades/loops forming the lipid‑binding scaffold
- eIF2α‑family protein kinase: a localized peak on the N‑lobe helix–loop–strand motif within the kinase domain

Summary: Short coil/turn segments at the loop-to–beta-strand junctions that recur within blades of beta‑propeller repeat folds (WD40, Kelch, NHL, BNR/VPS10/YWTD), i.e., the surface blade loops that connect the strands and often form ligand/substrate‑interacting sites; occasionally extends to analogous coil-to‑strand turns in adjacent beta‑rich repeat modules (e.g., EGF-like repeats of LDLR family)
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks in 4–8 aa coil regions immediately preceding or following a beta‑strand, repeated periodically across successive repeats/blades within a propeller domain; dispersed multi‑peak activation across the domain rather than a single motif; favored in Gly/Pro‑rich, acidic/hydroxyl‑containing loops often near aromatics (e.g., WD)
Exemplars: - VPS10/sortilin receptors: repeated activation on blade loops in the beta‑propeller and on adjacent coil segments in LDLR class B (EGF‑like) repeats
- Phage tailspike neuraminidases (BNR/sialidases): strong activation on BNR blade loops on the propeller top surface, including near the catalytic/binding Asp
- WD40 beta‑propeller adapters (e.g., APC/C co‑activator Cdh1) and generic WD‑repeat proteins: periodic activation on the inter‑strand loops within WD repeats across multiple blades
- BTB–Kelch substrate adaptors: activation in the C‑terminal loop portions of successive Kelch repeats, not in the BTB or sheet cores
- NHL‑repeat beta‑propellers (amidating lyase/PAM PAL domain): activation within NHL repeat loops and adjacent short loop/turn segments
- Predicted seven‑bladed beta‑propellers: regular activation at coil→strand junctions repeated across blades

Summary: Glycine-rich, flexible loop segments associated with nucleotide phosphate handling—primarily the glycine-rich loop of protein kinases and analogous glycine/P-loop-like motifs in NTP-binding folds—plus compositionally similar Gly/Pro/charged loops in repeat scaffolds and membrane proteins (including non-ATP transporters/translocon subunits) and dinucleotide-binding Rossmann-like motifs.
Activation pattern: Regional activation with sharp peaks over glycine-rich phosphate-binding motifs (e.g., ePK N-lobe GxGxxG, histidine-kinase ATP lid/G-boxes, Walker A GxxxxGKT; Rossmann TGxGGxxG/A) and over Gly/Pro/charged solvent-exposed loops; multiple dispersed segments per protein, typically tens of residues.
Exemplars:
- Eukaryotic Ser/Thr and dual-specificity protein kinases (including ULK/Atg1 and receptor kinases): activation on the N-lobe glycine-rich loop (GxGxxG) and adjacent flexible loops.
- Bacterial/archaeal sensor histidine kinases: activation on the CA-domain glycine boxes/ATP lid.
- Fungal SSK1/sskA-type response regulators: activation on Gly/Pro/charged linker and receiver-domain loops that interface with partner kinases.
- Ankyrin, armadillo, WD40, and TPR repeat scaffolds: activation on solvent-exposed inter-repeat loops enriched in Gly/Pro/charged residues.
- Membrane transporters: activation on ABC/NBD Walker A P-loops (GxxxxGKT) and, in secondary transporters and ER translocon subunits, on Gly/Pro/charged luminal/cytosolic loops lacking NTP-binding.
- Rossmann-fold NAD(P)-dependent enzymes: activation on the N-terminal TGxGGxxG/A phosphate-binding loop and adjacent flexible segments.
- Plant glycine-rich/RGG-box RNA-binding proteins and repeat RBPs: activation on low-complexity glycine-rich segments (RGG/GGXG motifs).

Summary: Terminal connector regions (predominantly C‑terminal)—low‑complexity or marginally structured beta/coil segments of variable length (often Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly‑rich with scattered Trp) that act as linkers, stalks, propeptides, short terminal tails, or appendage subdomains at protein ends; commonly just before a final module (e.g., a transmembrane helix or CBM) or as appendages in large cytosolic complexes, and often bear post‑translational modifications.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over broad contiguous stretches or compact terminal tails, usually in the C‑terminal half/tail but also at N‑termini when functioning as propeptides; absent from catalytic motifs; tolerates both intrinsically disordered and weakly structured beta/coil character and frequently overlaps low‑complexity and glyco/phospho‑modified segments.
Exemplars (add): Urease and other small enzyme subunits: activation on short C‑terminal tails/appendages distal from catalytic residues.

Summary: Disulfide-stabilized cysteine-rich extracellular repeat microdomains—principally EGF-like repeats, thrombospondin type-1 repeats (TSR), and disintegrin folds—used for adhesion and ligand–receptor interactions; with spillover to related small Cys-rich repeats such as LDL receptor class-A (LA) and CCP/Sushi modules.
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation concentrated within compact Cys-rich repeats; minimal signal in catalytic peptidase cores, transmembranes, or cytosolic tails. Residue-level peaks center on conserved cysteines and nearby glycine/acidic/polar/proline residues in loop/beta contexts, producing long contiguous activation across tandem ectodomain repeats and near-complete coverage in isolated disintegrin peptides.
Exemplars: - ADAM/ADAMTS proteases and snake-venom metalloproteinases/disintegrins: strong activation on the disintegrin domain and adjacent EGF-like repeat; not on the M12B catalytic domain, TM helix, or cytosolic tail.
- Notch receptors and ligands (Delta/Jagged): activation across tandem EGF-like repeats that mediate ligand binding and modulation.
- Thrombospondins and ADAMTS-like proteins (including R-spondins): activation on thrombospondin type-1 repeats.
- Complement and coagulation systems: activation on EGF-like repeats of coagulation factors and on CCP/Sushi modules of complement regulators.
- LDL receptor family (LDLR/LRP/VLDLR): activation on LA repeats and EGF-like modules in the ectodomain.
- Extracellular matrix/matricellular proteins (e.g., fibrillins, tenascins, laminins, periostin): activation on arrays of EGF/TSR repeats.
- Wnt/Hedgehog/Slit–Robo pathway modulators (e.g., sFRPs/Frizzled CRD, HHIP, Slit): activation on cysteine-rich CRDs and EGF/TSR-containing segments.
- Occasional off-target activation in intracellular CCCH-type zinc fingers or RCC1-like proteins likely reflects generic sensitivity to clustered cysteines.

Summary: Terminal export/targeting leaders at protein ends: chiefly N-terminal signals for membrane entry or secretion (Sec-type signal peptides/signal anchors), but also non-Sec N-terminal export signals (e.g., bacteriocin double‑glycine leaders, Type III/VI secretion N-termini) and amphipathic mitochondrial presequences; occasionally C‑terminal signals (GPI‑attachment segments and some tail‑anchor targeting peptides).
Activation pattern: Regional activation concentrated in a contiguous block at an extreme terminus—most often the first 5–30 residues at the N-terminus (starting at Met1), and sometimes at the extreme C-terminus (GPI/tail‑anchor propeptides)—with activation dropping sharply after the leader/cleavage/targeting motif; little to no activation across internal transmembrane helices; N‑terminal blocks need not be strongly hydrophobic (e.g., bacteriocin/T3SS leaders, mitochondrial presequences).
Exemplars: 
- Antimicrobial/venom peptide precursors (big defensins, moricins): activation on N‑terminal signal peptides; minimal on mature peptides.
- Viral envelope/fusion glycoproteins: activation on N‑terminal ER signal peptides.
- Bacterial pore-forming toxins/secreted components and T3SS/T6SS cargos (e.g., translocators, ADP‑ribosyltransferase effectors): activation on short N‑terminal export/secretion leaders.
- Bacteriocins/circular bacteriocins: activation on N‑terminal double‑glycine leaders used for secretion/processing.
- Magnetosome membrane proteins (e.g., Mms6/MamG): activation on very short, basic N‑terminal cytosolic stretches; not on internal TM helices.
- GPI‑anchored proteins (e.g., prion proteins): activation on N‑terminal signal peptides and weaker at C‑terminal GPI signals.
- Mitochondrial proteins (e.g., IFI27, Fis1): activation on N‑terminal mitochondrial presequences or at extreme C‑terminal tail‑anchor targeting segments.

Summary: Short, solvent-exposed linear patches (≈6–12 residues) enriched in glycine and acidic/polar residues that recur across modular repeats; these occur in loop regions of beta-rich extracellular domains or at the edges of amphipathic IQ helices and often coincide with partner-binding/adhesion SLiMs (e.g., RGD-like loops, calmodulin-binding IQ segments).
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks confined to short stretches; periodic across tandem repeats (one patch per Sushi/CCP module; two small patches within each IQ repeat; many regularly spaced loop peaks across large extracellular repeat arrays); strongest in coils/loops linking beta-strands or at helical cap/edge segments; little or no activation in signal peptides, transmembranes, or well-packed core/catalytic regions.
Exemplars: IQ-domain proteins and myosins: two short hotspots within each IQ helix that engage calmodulin, including the N-terminal segment of the IQ repeat; Complement control protein (Sushi/CCP) receptors/regulators and viral CCP mimics: one 8–10 aa patch per CCP module in the C-terminal half of the domain; Single-pass extracellular proteins with cysteine-rich, beta-strand loop architectures: repeated peaks on Asp-rich, disulfide-flanked loops connecting beta-strands; Mycobacterial PE–PGRS family proteins: multiple glycine-rich, low-complexity coil segments; Disintegrins/ADAM metalloproteases: exposed integrin-binding loops (e.g., RGD) within disulfide-bonded segments.

Summary: Short structural boundary motif marking the start of a folded domain: the coil-to-β transition that nucleates the first β-strand (β1) at a domain’s N-terminus, enriched in hydrophobic residues and often flanked by Lys/Pro; overrepresented in ubiquitin-like/UBX β-grasp folds but general across β-rich domains (e.g., C2, ferredoxin)
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short 4–10 aa windows with sharp residue-level peaks on hydrophobic residues; typically located at the extreme N-terminus or annotated domain start and coinciding with a disorder-to-ordered transition; multiple discrete peaks may occur in multi-domain/repeat proteins, with sparse activation in long disordered regions
Exemplars: - Ubiquitin-like modifiers (SUMO/UBL): activation at the transition from disordered N-terminus into the first β-strand of the UBL fold
- UBX-domain p97 cofactors: short peaks at early β-strands, including the N-terminal boundary of the UBX domain
- BAG family cochaperones (UBL domain): activation marking the N-terminus and first β-strand of the internal UBL domain
- 2Fe-2S ferredoxin/adrenodoxin family: activation at the N-terminal boundary of the ferredoxin domain spanning the first β-strand
- Molybdopterin synthase sulfur carrier (MoaD/ThiS-like): activation at the transition from unstructured leader to the initial β-strand of the fold
- C2-domain proteins: activation at the beginning of the first β-strand of the β-sandwich

Summary: A general, composition-driven signal for non-globular sequence regions: it prefers low-complexity, compositionally biased tracts and repetitive helical polymers, emphasizing charged/polar (E, D, K, R, S, Q) or Gly/Pro-rich content, and residues at helix–coil transitions; it is largely muted in compact, well-packed helical cores.
Activation pattern: Broad regional activation across long low-complexity or repeat segments (coiled-coil stalks, collagenous repeats, disordered regulatory regions), with residue-level peaks at helix N/C caps and adjacent coils; minimal within stable helix cores; can span extensive stretches rather than a single short motif.
Exemplars: - bHLH transcription factors: activation on disordered, charged/polar flanks and at the disordered boundary of the bHLH domain; little signal inside the structured helical core.
- Helical antitoxin (VapB-like) proteins: peaks at helix–loop interfaces (N- and C-caps and adjacent coils) with generally low signal in the interior helices.
- Golgin/centrosomal/cytoskeletal coiled-coil scaffolds: sustained activation along long acidic/basic, low-complexity coiled-coil stalks.
- Extracellular-matrix collagens: activation across Gly–X–Y (often Gly–Pro–Hyp) repetitive triple-helix regions.
- Muscle long coiled-coil motors/partners (e.g., myosin/tropomyosin/titin segments): activation along extended coiled-coil helical repeats.
- Neuronal/presynaptic scaffolds: activation in coiled-coil/disordered linker regions that form extended scaffolds.
- Prokaryotic regulators (ECF sigma factors, toxin–antitoxin antitoxins, two-component histidine kinases): activation on acidic/basic low-complexity segments, helix–loop caps, and helical linkers/coiled-coils.

Summary: Residue-level signature of outer-membrane beta-barrel architecture: prefers transmembrane beta-strands and membrane-interface “aromatic belt”/C‑terminal beta-signal positions in OM beta-barrels across Gram‑negative bacteria and organellar homologs (e.g., TOM40), spanning porins, TonB-dependent receptors, autotransporter translocators, and OM enzymes/channels
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks distributed across the beta-barrel domain (DSSP E), enriched on aromatic (Tyr/Phe/Trp) and other hydrophobic/small residues; strongest in transmembrane strands and near strand boundaries at the periplasmic/extracellular interfaces, often including the C-terminal assembly beta-signal. Signal peptides and non-barrel passenger/coiled regions remain inactive; in autotransporters, activation is confined to the C‑terminal translocator barrel.
Exemplars: - TonB-dependent receptor/transporter (iron/copper TBDT): sharp peaks on C-terminal beta-barrel strands, including residues near the barrel’s C-terminal assembly signal.
- Long-chain fatty acid transporter FadL: multiple high peaks on tyrosines within beta-strands of the OM barrel.
- Autotransporter OmpB (Rickettsia): activation restricted to the C-terminal translocator beta-barrel; N-terminal passenger is inactive.
- Neisseria adhesin autotransporter: localized peaks in the C-terminal translocator’s transmembrane beta-strands.
- Functional amyloid transporter FapF: peaks in transmembrane strands and periplasmic boundary; includes a residue known to be critical for outer-membrane insertion.
- Mitochondrial TOM40: sparse peaks on beta-strand residues within the barrel core; disordered N-terminus is inactive.
- Lipid A deacylase PagL: peaks on beta-strands across different topological regions of the barrel, not on catalytic residues.
- Alginate exporter AlgE: high peaks on beta-strands, occasionally in adjacent coil immediately at strand termini.
- Opacity/adhesin Opa: strong activation on aromatic residues within barrel strands with minor signals in adjacent coil.

Summary: Surface-exposed loop/turn motifs in large extracellular/passenger domains—specifically the short coil-to-β-strand initiator turns and adjacent linker loops at repeat edges of parallel β-helix/β-solenoid (PbH1/pectate-lyase–like) architectures common in adhesins and polysaccharide-acting proteins, and analogous glycan-proximal loops in eukaryotic receptor ectodomains
Activation pattern: Multiple short (∼5–10 aa) peaks distributed across extended extracellular regions; concentrated at coil/loop segments just before β-strands and at repeat junctions, enriched for small/polar residues (G/S/T/N/D) and frequently adjacent to NXS/T sequons; absent from signal peptides, transmembrane helices, cytosolic tails, and autotransporter β-barrels; peaks occur in both well-structured turns and flexible low-pLDDT linkers
Exemplars: - Type V autotransporter adhesins/proteases: repeated coil→β turns throughout the passenger domain; no activation in the N-terminal signal peptide or C-terminal β-barrel.
- Bacterial mannuronan C5-epimerases (AlgE/AlgG with PbH1 repeats): flexible loop segments at PbH1 repeat boundaries and disordered tails.
- Fungal cell-surface adhesins (AWP family): N-terminal extracellular patches across β/coil segments, with peaks adjacent to N-linked glycosylation sequons.
- Receptor tyrosine kinases (EGFR family): structured ectodomain loops/short helices near multiple N-linked glycosylation sites; no activation in TM/cytosolic regions.
- Class C GPCRs (metabotropic glutamate receptor-like): N-terminal ectodomain peaks near annotated PbH1-like repeats and very low-pLDDT linkers preceding the first TM, often close to N-glycan sequons.

Summary: Interface elements of modular peptide-recognition networks comprising either (i) the C-terminal specificity substructure of SH2 domains (alphaB helix with adjacent beta-strands and BG/EF loops that read residues C-terminal to pTyr) or (ii) cognate glycine/proline- and aromatic-enriched linear segments (including PxxP, PPxY, NPxY, YxxΦ) that engage SH2/SH3/WW/PTB/EVH1 and related peptide-binding modules across diverse proteins and kingdoms.
Activation pattern: Two modes. Mode A—regional activation within the back half of SH2 domains: a moderately long, contiguous, well-structured stretch spanning terminal beta-strands and the C-terminal helix, with peaks near the start of alphaB; little signal in the N-terminal half. Mode B—moderately long, contiguous, low-to-medium complexity segments enriched in Pro/Gly and aromatics, often bearing multiple PP/PxxP and tyrosine- or hydrophobic-flanked motifs (NPxY, PPxY, YxxΦ); typically found in linkers, termini, or cytosolic tails that serve as docking/sorting ligands for modular domains.
Exemplars: SH2 adaptors and nonreceptor tyrosine kinases (Fes/Fer)—Mode A on the SH2 alphaB/terminal strands; STATs—Mode A on the STAT SH2 fold; PI3K regulatory subunits and PLCγ—Mode A across C-terminal halves of their SH2 domains; CBL/SOCS (SH2/TKB)—Mode A on the SH2/TKB C-terminal segment. PARP family (e.g., PARP3)—Mode B on Pro/Gly-rich linkers; Kinetochore factors (KNL-2)—Mode B on proline-rich low-complexity regions; Transcription/chromatin regulators (SPT6)—Mode B on acidic/proline-rich segments; ER lectins (ERLEC1/XTP3-B)—Mode B on short cytosolic tails bearing sorting/docking motifs (e.g., YxxΦ/di-lysine context); Actin regulators (gelsolin)—Mode B on proline-rich linkers; Ras/Rab interactor (RIN1)—Mode B on proline-rich SH3-binding regions; SHIP2—both modes (N-terminal SH2 C-terminal region and adjacent proline-rich segments).

Summary: Residue-level detector for short loop/turn positions at the edges of beta-strands in beta-sheet–rich folds (beta-sandwich and beta-barrel), often repeated once per domain module; common in secreted/extracellular and outer‑membrane proteins but also present in soluble beta‑rich cores (Sm/LSm/Hfq, frataxin); favors small/acidic/polar residues at these strand‑boundary turns
Activation pattern: Sparse, single‑residue peaks in high‑confidence structured regions; one or a few peaks per domain, frequently in loops connecting beta-strands or at strand termini; recurrent at equivalent positions across tandem repeats (e.g., CUB domains); avoids signal peptides/disordered segments
Exemplars: - TonB-dependent outer membrane receptors (heme/iron/corrinoid transporters): peaks in plug-domain loops and scattered loops of the beta-barrel.
- Secreted metalloproteases with CUB modules (e.g., BMP1): conserved loop/turn site repeated in each CUB domain.
- Cupredoxin-like copper-binding proteins (cupredoxins/multicopper oxidases): loops between beta-strands, often adjacent to metal-binding His/Cys.
- Frataxin family: turns linking beta-strands within the acidic beta-sheet core.
- Sm/LSm/Hfq RNA-binding proteins: loop and strand-boundary positions within the Sm domain ring.
- p24/TMED cargo receptors (GOLD domain): isolated coil/loop site within the GOLD beta-sandwich lumenal domain.

Summary: Signal that preferentially marks extracellular ectodomain short β-strand elements of β-sandwich modules (Ig-like, fibronectin type III, and cytokine-receptor homology regions) together with adjacent S/T/P/E/D/G-rich, low-complexity “stalk” linkers of secreted and single-pass surface proteins; it also occurs on compositionally similar low-complexity tracts in some intracellular proteins (e.g., Host Cell Factor); it ignores transmembrane helices and occurs across taxa.
Activation pattern: Regional activation predominantly in extracellular/luminal regions; residue-level peaks on short β-strands within Ig/FNIII-type folds with spillover to their coil flanks; extended, high activation on flexible, low-confidence, low-complexity ectodomain segments immediately N-terminal to the transmembrane helix; little to no signal on signal peptides, transmembrane segments, or intracellular catalytic/signaling catalytic cores; additionally, activation can occur on acidic/S/T-rich low-complexity tracts irrespective of localization (e.g., HCF).
Exemplars: - Receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatases: Ig/FNIII β-strand cores plus the extracellular juxtamembrane “stalk”; no activation in phosphatase domains.
- Type I/II cytokine and related hormone receptors: CHR/FNIII β-sandwich strands and ectodomain segments; absent on TM and cytosolic tails.
- Receptor tyrosine kinases (insulin/IGF, Eph, torso): extracellular Ig/FNIII repeats and proximal ectodomain linkers; not the kinase domain.
- Neuronal adhesion/Ig superfamily proteins: repeated activation on Ig-like/FNIII module β-strands across long ectodomains.
- Secreted and lysosomal carbohydrate-active enzymes/PUL proteins: appended FN3/CBM β-sandwiches and S/T-rich secretion/luminal linkers.
- Uroplakins/tetraspanins: large luminal loops of multipass tetraspanins.
- Lysyl oxidase family: secreted low-complexity/glycosylated segments outside the catalytic core.
- Viral structural and immune-modulatory proteins: Ig-like ectodomains or low-complex luminal stretches.
- Host Cell Factor family: acidic/S/T-rich low-complexity tracts consistent with the feature’s compositional preference.

Summary: Recognition of eukaryotic beta-sheet cores, primarily in C2 and C2-like/PH beta-sandwich modules, and also in structurally similar beta-sheet cores of some kinases and scaffolds (e.g., AGC kinase N-lobe, certain centrosomal proteins).
Activation pattern: Domain-level, multi-segment activation across internal beta-strands of compact, well-structured domains; minimal in disordered linkers and transmembranes; repeated peaks for multiple repeats in multi-domain proteins.
Exemplars: Tandem C2 scaffolds (synaptotagmins, ferlins, Munc13, extended synaptotagmins); Lipid/phosphoinositide enzymes with C2 (PLC, cPLA2, PTEN, PI3K-C2); Small GTPase regulators with tandem C2s (CAPRI/RASA); HECT E3 ligases (NEDD4/HECW1) via N-terminal C2; PH-domain scaffolds (e.g., anillin); Notch ligands via MNNL (C2-like) domain; AGC/PKC kinases via beta-sheet cores (PKC via C2; AKT/PKB via PH; some AGC kinases lacking these, e.g., Sck2, via N-lobe beta-sheet); Centrosomal/cilium proteins with compact beta-sheet modules (e.g., C2CD2/C2CD3; CEP76 via an internal beta-sheet scaffold).

Summary: N-terminal short leaders/motifs: classical Sec-type signal peptides plus other short N-terminal export/targeting/assembly signals (signal anchors, organellar transit peptides, type III/flagellar export signals, and amphipathic/basic N-termini used for macromolecular binding).
Activation pattern: Short, contiguous N-terminal segments (~15–40 aa) enriched in hydrophobic and/or small residues (often helical). Signal peaks over the hydrophobic h-region when a signal peptide is present and drops after cleavage; in non-cleavable contexts (T3S/flagellar signals, amphipathic/basic N-termini of cytosolic/organellar proteins) the activation remains confined to the initial helix/low-complexity stretch without a cleavage motif. “Precursor” annotations are frequent but not required.
Exemplars:
- Chemokines and viral mimics: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide before the cysteine-rich mature core.
- Bacterial exported/periplasmic proteins (T2SS pseudopilins, lipoproteins) and outer-membrane biogenesis factors: activation on Sec/lipoprotein signal peptides.
- Flagellar/type III export substrates (e.g., hook/rod proteins): activation on the non-cleavable N-terminal export signal.
- Organelle-targeted proteins (mitochondrial/chloroplast): activation on transit peptides or signal anchors.
- Ribosomal proteins (and organellar homologs) and diverse cytosolic/phage enzyme subunits: activation on short N-terminal amphipathic/basic helices or small-residue stretches mediating assembly or nucleic-acid binding.

Summary: Residue-level recognition of β-strand microenvironments—typically hydrophobic (Val/Ile/Leu) or small residues embedded in or immediately adjacent to β-strands, often at strand termini/edge strands—spanning many β-rich domains across diverse proteins rather than a function-specific signal.
Activation pattern: Sparse, single–residue peaks concentrated in DSSP E regions and the immediately following connecting coils; frequent preference for C-terminal positions of β-strands or edge strands; little to no activation in α-helices, transmembrane helices, or disordered regions; mild bias toward hydrophobic/small side chains.
Exemplars: - FMN reductase (RutF family): peaks on isolated residues within β-sheets; no signal in helical or unstructured regions.
- Co-chaperonin GroES: strongest at ends of β-strands with minor peaks in the adjacent loops.
- Transcription factor NusG/SPT5: β-strand residues in both the N-terminal NGN and C-terminal KOW β-domains.
- Cell shape protein MreC: discrete β-strand positions within the periplasmic β-sandwich; absent from TM and low-complexity segments.
- Flagellar L-ring (FlgH): localized peaks on β-strand residues in the periplasmic ring domain.
- Sortase D: single-residue peak within a β-strand of the catalytic domain, away from active-site residues.
- Ribosomal protein uS17 (including mitochondrial uS17m): activation on N-terminal β-strands; no activation in the helical C-terminal domain.
- MCE/MlaD family lipid transport component: β-strand residues in the periplasmic MCE domain; no activation in TM or disordered tails.
- Type I secretion periplasmic adaptor protein (HlyD family): β-strand termini and adjacent coils in the periplasmic domain; absent from cytosolic and TM segments.

Summary: Short, structural β-strand-to-α-helix junction motif (often centered on Ser/Thr) in well-ordered domains—most prominently within ubiquitin-like β-grasp folds (UBL/UBX) but also recurring in other folds—capturing conserved β-sheet segments rather than catalytic sites
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks forming short, disjoint patches; maxima typically on Ser/Thr (but can include other residues) located in β-strands at or just before β→α transitions; confined to well-structured regions (high confidence), often two hotspots per UBL fold (near N-terminus and a central segment); generally avoids active-site residues
Exemplars: - SUMO-activating enzyme (E1/UBA2 subunit): peaks on β-strand residues at strand–helix boundaries within the adenylation/catalytic core, with a minor site adjacent to the ATP-binding lysine.
- USP-family deubiquitinases: multiple discrete peaks on threonines within β-sheets across the USP domain; no activation on the catalytic Cys/His.
- UBX-domain p97/CDC48 cofactors: activation within the UBX ubiquitin-like fold on β-strands that transition into α-helices.
- UBL-domain proteins (e.g., BAG-family co-chaperones, UBL–UBA scaffold proteins, tubulin-specific chaperone cofactor E-like): activation confined to β-strands of the UBL domain; non-UBL domains (e.g., BAG, UBA) remain largely inactive.
- Small ubiquitin-like modifiers (ubiquitin, SUMO, NEDD8, ISG15, ATG8/Ubl): peaks align to conserved N‑terminal and central β-strand motifs of the β-grasp fold surface.
- FAD-dependent oxidoreductases (e.g., L-gulonolactone oxidase; PCMH-type FAD-binding domain): peaks at β-strand residues immediately preceding α-helices within the FAD-binding core.
- Aromatic monooxygenase components (toluene-4-monooxygenase γ subunit): isolated peaks on β-strands directly before short α-helices.

Summary: Proline-anchored loop/turn motifs at beta-strand termini and strand–loop–strand connectors (often in P/Ser/Thr/Gly-rich segments), marking boundaries between ordered beta structure and coil/disorder and recurring in beta-rich/repeat architectures (e.g., LRR, beta-propeller) as well as soluble beta-grasp–like folds
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short loop segments (typically 8–20 aa) with sharp residue-level peaks centered on prolines; multiple peaks recur across repeat units; strongest at strand ends, beta-turns, and structured-to-unstructured boundaries; occasionally peaks on S/T/G when they occupy the turn apex; rare inside helices
Exemplars: - Integrin alpha subunits (extracellular beta-propeller): activation on loops connecting beta-strands, peaking at prolines at strand termini or at transitions into flexible regions.
- Alpha-2-macroglobulin/thioester proteins: activation on a proline-centered unstructured loop between a beta-strand and a coiled-coil near the C-terminus.
- Photosystem II PsbP/OEE2 family: activation on the loop connecting adjacent beta-strands, with a peak at a proline at the end of the first strand.
- Secretory lumenal glycoprotein Pbn1: activation on a Pro-Pro coil that links two beta-strands within a well-ordered hairpin.
- ESCRT-I UEV-domain proteins (e.g., Vps23/Stp22): activation on a proline-centered strand–loop segment in the UEV fold near the ubiquitin-interaction surface.
- Ubiquitin-conjugating E2 enzymes (UBC fold): activation on the short loop immediately following a beta-strand (peak on loop apex residue, here Ser).
- LRR proteins/receptors (e.g., plant NLR RPM1): activation on recurrent prolines in coil/turn segments of LRR repeats; mutating one such proline disrupts function.

Summary: Surface-exposed, short loops/turns at beta‑strand junctions within beta‑sandwich domains—especially Fibronectin type III (FN3) and Immunoglobulin-like modules—common in single-pass receptors and IgCAMs, but also present in secreted enzymes, viral structural proteins, and some cytosolic scaffolds; these PGTS/acidic‑rich segments often host N‑glycosylation sequons (when lumenal/extracellular) and serve as ligand/regulatory interaction loops.
Activation pattern: Multiple residue-level peaks per protein, recurring across successive FN3/Ig domains; peaks localize to coil or strand–loop transition segments (e.g., BC/DE/FG loops and occasional short connector helices) and are absent from signal peptides and transmembranes; present on solvent-exposed loops of FN3/Ig-like domains irrespective of cellular location.
Exemplars: - Type I/II cytokine receptor subunits (e.g., gp130/IL‑6Rβ, IL‑20 receptor β): strong peaks on loops between β‑strands within Ig-like and consecutive FN3 domains; includes segments whose deletion/isoform loss alters signaling.
- Ig-superfamily adhesion molecules (e.g., Contactin family): peaks on short connectors in Ig-like domains and stronger activations in FN3-domain loops, frequently starting at N‑linked glycosylation sites.
- Receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatases and IL‑17 receptor-like ECDs: repeated peaks on analogous FN3/Ig loop regions across their multi‑domain extracellular repeats.
- Cytosolic FN3/Ig-domain scaffolds (e.g., RIM-BP family): peaks on loops within FN3 repeats.
- Viral/baseplate and secreted enzyme beta-sandwich folds: peaks on exposed loop segments consistent with interaction surfaces.

Summary: A broad “ordered helical/assembly scaffold” signature: long, structured segments—often alpha-helical (TM helices, coiled-coils, helical hairpins) and stable cores of ligand/effector-binding domains—that mark architectural elements used for signal transfer and assembly across diverse molecular machines (signaling, secretion, transport, nucleotide/quinone metabolism, and viral replication), rather than specific catalytic micro-motifs.
Activation pattern: Domain-level, long contiguous activation along helical bundles and adjacent linkers/loops; frequently includes N‑terminal transmembrane segments but also long ordered helices in soluble proteins; activation is moderate, widespread, and residue-type agnostic, with small peaks at helix boundaries and some flexible coils.
Exemplars:
- Two-component sensor histidine kinases: activation on TM helices, HAMP linkers, and helical regions of the kinase core.
- Class A GPCRs: activation across the TM bundle and loop boundaries in well-structured segments.
- Secretion/competence systems: minor pilins (e.g., ComG) and T3SS chaperones (e.g., YscG) with long alpha-helical/coiled-coil scaffolds.
- Second-messenger effectors: PilZ c-di-GMP-binding domains showing activation over their stable cores.
- Transport ATPases: ABC-type ATP-binding subunits (e.g., CcmA) with activated helical subdomains/dimerization surfaces.
- Metabolic/viral enzymes: MenE (quinone biosynthesis) and viral replication proteins (helicase/RdRp) where activation tracks long ordered helices or domain-spanning segments.

Summary: Cleavable Sec-type N-terminal signal peptides—specifically the short, hydrophobic, helical h‑region (flanked by a basic n‑region) that targets proteins to the secretory pathway/periplasm/extracellular space
Activation pattern: Regional activation over a contiguous N‑terminal stretch (~residues 2–25), strongest on hydrophobic/aromatic residues (L/I/V/F/W) within a predicted α-helix, with few acidic residues; often preceded by basic residues at the extreme N terminus; activation drops sharply at or just before the signal peptidase cleavage site; generally low pLDDT in the activated segment; occasionally also fires on internal signal‑anchor/transmembrane helices that mimic a signal peptide h‑region
Exemplars: Secreted glycosidase (exo‑α‑L‑arabinofuranosidase): activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide; Secreted hydrolase (polyglycine hydrolase): activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide; Periplasmic/secreted phosphatase (phosphatidylinositol‑3‑phosphatase): activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide; Periplasmic redox/membrane complex component (DsbD): activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide; Secreted toxin (saporin ribosome‑inactivating protein): activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide; Type IV secretion system component (VirB9): activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide; Secreted cysteine protease: activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide; Secreted signaling protein (Counting factor 50): activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide; Secreted peptide hormone (yeast mating factor α): activation on the N‑terminal signal peptide

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity Ser/Thr–rich segments densely containing proline‑directed motifs (SP/TP repeats) that act as multisite phosphorylation hotspots, especially in cytoskeletal/cell‑cycle scaffolds, membrane‑trafficking adaptors, small‑GTPase regulators, and viral matrix/tegument proteins; often acidic (D/E‑enriched) and found in flexible linkers or cytosolic tails.
Activation pattern: Strong regional activation across long IDRs enriched in S/T (with frequent P nearby), D/E and occasional Q/N tracts; peaks track stretches with many SP/TP sites rather than isolated residues. Little or no activation within structured domains or transmembrane cores; strongest in cytosolic N‑ or C‑terminal tails and flexible linkers of large scaffolds/adaptors.
Exemplars: - Kinetochore/centrosome and spindle pole scaffolds: disordered S/T‑P–rich N‑termini or linkers bearing clustered CDK/MAPK sites for mitotic control.
- Microtubule‑associated and coiled‑coil adaptors (MAPs, CLASPs, dynactin/p150): S/T‑rich linkers with SP/TP motifs modulating microtubule binding and dynamics.
- Small GTPase regulators (Ras/Rho/Arf GEFs/GAPs): low‑complexity regulatory regions with dense SP/TP sites controlling activation cycles and membrane recruitment.
- Endocytic and vesicle‑trafficking adaptors (clathrin/epsin/AP‑associated scaffolds): acidic Ser/Thr‑rich disordered segments harboring proline‑directed multisite phosphorylation.
- Large multi‑domain scaffolds with SAM/SH3 or coiled‑coil modules: long S/T‑rich insertions used as phospho‑switches and docking platforms.
- Cytosolic tails of single‑pass membrane proteins: acidic Ser/Thr‑rich C‑terminal regions carrying SP/TP clusters for regulation.
- Viral matrix/tegument proteins (large DNA/RNA viruses): hyperphosphorylated Ser/Thr‑rich low‑complexity stretches with SP/TP motifs targeted by host CDKs/MAPKs.
- Fungal cell‑cycle/mitotic regulators: extended SP/TP‑dense IDRs coordinating timing via CDK‑driven multisite phosphorylation.

Summary: Proline/serine–rich, low-complexity intrinsically disordered regions with clustered short linear motifs (PxxP/GP plus SxIP, PPxY, and phospho-Ser sites) that recruit SH3/EVH1/WW/14-3-3 and related peptide-binding modules in large scaffolds spanning cytoskeletal/centrosomal, membrane/junctional/ciliary, and select nuclear chromatin-assembly proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long Pro/Ser/Gly-rich IDRs with peaks over dense motif clusters (PxxP/GP, SxIP, PPxY, and 14-3-3 phospho-sites); little to no activation in adjacent structured modules (coiled-coils, DH/PH, GAP, DENN, kinase or catalytic domains).
Exemplars:
- Rho GEFs (VAV/TIAM/ARHGEF, DOCK): activation on PRDs with multiple PxxP motifs docking SH3 adaptors.
- Rho GAPs (SRGAP/ARHGAP): activation on proline-rich linkers mediating SH3-dependent cortical targeting.
- AKAP scaffolds (AKAP9/AKAP6/AKAP13, testis AKAPs such as AKAP2/3): activation on extended Ser/Pro-rich regions assembling PKA–cytoskeletal complexes via SH3/14-3-3 partners.
- PP1 regulatory scaffolds (spinophilin/neurabin, MYPT/PPP1R12, GADD34/PPP1R15A): activation on P/S-rich PRDs adjacent to PP1-binding motifs organizing signaling hubs.
- Actin regulators/scaffolds (WASP/N-WASP, zyxin/LPP/LASP, cortactin-binding proteins): activation on PRDs with clustered PxxP/FPPPP for SH3/EVH1 interactions.
- Microtubule plus-end adaptors (SLAINs, CLASPs): activation on SxIP-rich low-complexity regions that bind EB1/EB3.
- Centrosomal/centriolar scaffolds (PCM1, CEP/pericentrin-like, CP110): activation on Pro/Gly-rich tracts connecting coiled-coil blocks for hub assembly.
- Membrane/cell-junction scaffolds (afadin, SHANKs, spectrin/ankyrin-associated adaptors, LMO7): activation on large PRDs recruiting SH3/WW-domain proteins at junctions.
- Cilium/flagellum/testis-enriched coiled-coil proteins (CCDC/SPATA and related): activation on Pro/Ser/Gly-rich low-complexity segments linking structural repeats.
- Membrane trafficking GEFs/adaptors (DENN/Rab GEFs such as DENND2B): activation on P/S-rich linkers that scaffold trafficking complexes.
- Nuclear chromatin assembly factors (HJURP): activation on P/S-rich IDRs harboring 14-3-3–binding phospho-motifs for adaptor/chaperone recruitment.

Summary: Active-site nucleophilic cysteine motif: a short loop→helix segment that positions the catalytic Cys of a Cys–His (±Asp/Asn) dyad/triad, often in a local Cys–Gly/glycine-rich context, shared across cysteine-dependent enzymes including cysteine proteases/deubiquitinases (OTU/ULP/USP/UCH/Josephin), NlpC/P60 peptidoglycan amidases/endolysins, viral cysteine proteases, and YopJ-family acyltransferases.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks centered on the catalytic cysteine within a compact 10–30 aa cluster spanning the preceding loop and the N-terminus of an alpha-helix; frequent secondary peaks on the catalytic histidine and occasionally nearby substrate-binding or processing residues (e.g., Gly-Gly sites); typically high structural confidence; rare weaker activation on structurally analogous helix/coil patches in non-catalytic binding domains.
Exemplars: - OTU deubiquitinases: peak on the Cys-loop catalytic Cys with spread into the adjacent helix; minor signal on nearby acidic/variable-loop residues.
- SUMO/ULP proteases (including viral ULP-like proteases): peak at the nucleophilic Cys at a helix N-terminus; secondary peak at the catalytic His; extension to a substrate-binding residue.
- Legionella SdeA deubiquitinase: sharp peak at the catalytic Cys in the N-terminal DUB domain; minor activation near the His of the active site.
- NlpC/P60-type peptidoglycan amidases (e.g., Tse1): strong peak at the nucleophilic Cys in a short helix; His typically not highlighted.
- Viral cysteine proteases (e.g., adenovirus protease): peak at the catalytic Cys in a helix; minor peaks at the catalytic His and an autolysis Gly-Gly site.
- YopJ-family Nε‑fatty acyltransferases (e.g., IcsB): peak at the catalytic Cys at a loop→helix junction; minor activation adjacent to the active-site His.
- Calponin-homology binding domain (MICAL): weak activation on a conserved helix/coil segment that mimics the geometry of the targeted motif despite lacking a catalytic cysteine.

Summary: Long, intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity tracts enriched in Ser/Thr with interspersed Pro and often acidic residues (E/D)—i.e., S/T‑P‑rich IDRs—capturing mucin‑like O‑glycosylation‑prone repeats in secreted proteins and acidic/proline‑rich activation/interaction regions in nuclear/viral regulators.
Activation pattern: Strong regional activation across extended low‑complexity/disordered segments; highest over S/T runs with P and acidic residues but tolerant of other small/polar residues (A/Q/G/V); depleted in structured elements (signal peptides, helices/folded domains, transmembranes) and C‑terminal GPI‑anchor/propeptides; does not target specific short motifs or N‑glycosylation sequons.
Exemplars: - Herpesviral nuclear antigens/transactivators (e.g., EBNA family): activation on long central proline‑/acidic‑rich disordered blocks that serve as activation/interaction regions; low signal over adjacent structured helical islands.
- Fungal GPI‑anchored cell‑surface adhesins (e.g., Fig2p/Flo/Als families): activation on extracellular Ser/Thr‑rich mucin‑like repeats immediately after the signal peptide; absent on the signal peptide and on the C‑terminal GPI‑anchor/propeptide; no specific boost at N‑glycosylation sequons.
- Broadly across eukaryotic regulatory proteins and viral regulatory/accessory proteins: activation on Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich, acidic low‑complexity IDRs used for flexible interactions and post‑translational modification.

Summary: Negatively charged, low-complexity tracts enriched in Asp/Glu with abundant Ser/Thr (often glycine-rich) that form intrinsically disordered acidic tails or weakly helical/coiled-coil segments; these acidic segments act as flexible regulatory/linker regions and interaction surfaces (frequently N‑terminal) and the feature also extends to extended acidic surface patches on compact acidic proteins such as frataxin/CyaY
Activation pattern: Regional activation on a single contiguous stretch (tens to low hundreds of residues); frequently near N-termini but not position-specific; recognizes long D/E- and S/T-enriched, low-hydrophobicity segments (including acidic coiled-coil-like regions or extended acidic surface patches)
Exemplars: - Frataxin/CyaY family: activation on the extended acidic ridge/loops that present clustered D/E for metal/protein binding
- Signal recognition particle small subunits/components: activation on acidic/low-complexity tails or linkers involved in SRP RNA–protein assembly
- Kinetochore Ndc80-complex subunits SPC24/SPC25: activation on acidic, coiled-coil dimerization segments and flanking acidic stretches
- PARP family ADP-ribosyltransferases: activation on long acidic, serine/threonine-rich N-terminal regulatory IDRs
- Protein kinases (WNK; eIF2α/GCN2-related): activation on acidic, S/T-rich low-complexity N-termini and regulatory coiled-coil segments (autoinhibitory/scaffold-binding)
- Ubiquitination machinery (E3 ligases/E2s; RWD-domain proteins): activation on acidic low-complexity linkers and D/E-rich regions adjacent to catalytic or RWD/UBC-like folds
- Viral proteins (including RNA phage coat proteins): activation on acidic/glycine-rich N- or C-terminal arms and low-complexity acidic stretches used for assembly/host interactions
- Translation/ribosome/SRP and transcription coactivator factors: activation on acidic activation domains and acidic IDR linkers that mediate protein/RNA-binding and phospho-regulation

Summary: Short coil/loop linkers at secondary-structure junctions (alpha–beta and helix–helix connectors), typically surface-exposed and enriched in small/charged/polar residues; often adjacent to functional sites but rarely on catalytic residues themselves
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks confined to brief coil/turn segments that connect secondary-structure elements within folded domains (e.g., just before a beta-strand or between helices); occurs across many protein families; generally favors D/E/K/R/S/T/G/P and depletes aromatics/Cys
Exemplars: - 3′–5′ exonuclease domain: peaks on short loops within the exonuclease core, including a glycine-rich loop immediately preceding the catalytic histidine
- Glutamate–tRNA ligase: activations on well-structured coil loops linking helices and beta-sheets near the active-site cleft but not on annotated sites
- Phospholysine/phosphohistidine inorganic pyrophosphate phosphatase (LHPP/PHP family): strong peak on a short helix–helix loop and weaker peaks on helix–strand linkers
- Peroxiredoxin (thioredoxin-like fold): loop connecting an alpha-helix to a beta-strand and at the start of a beta-strand, away from the catalytic cysteine
- Transcription factor TFIID subunit (TAF10; histone-fold protein): helix–helix connector loop and a C-terminal coil segment

Summary: Transmembrane–cytosolic junction motif: the C-terminal end of a membrane-spanning helix together with the immediately following juxtamembrane segment on the cytosolic/nucleoplasmic side. The recognized pattern combines a hydrophobic TM tail with interface aromatics (W/Y/F) and nearby basic residues (Lys/Arg), consistent with the positive-inside rule and short amphipathic “cap” helices that anchor/orient diverse membrane proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous stretches (~15–30 aa) that start in the last third of a TM helix and extend 5–15 residues into the subsequent cytosolic/nucleoplasmic helix or loop; peaks typically occur at or just beyond the TM exit, with occasional secondary weaker peaks at additional TM–loop junctions in multipass proteins.
Exemplars: - Plant cytochrome P450 monooxygenases (e.g., secologanin synthase): N-terminal signal-anchor helix into the first cytosolic residues, peaking at the initial cytosolic aromatic/charged position.
- Inner nuclear membrane LEM-domain proteins: C-terminus of TM2 and the following nucleoplasmic helix.
- ER signal recognition particle receptor beta subunit: end of the N-terminal TM anchor and the adjacent flexible cytosolic helical/strand segment.
- Hyaluronan synthases (polysaccharide synthases): TM-helix exit into a short cytosolic loop; weaker secondary activation at another TM boundary.
- Type VII secretion system EccC membrane ATPase: TM terminus into a cytosolic helix that leads into a coiled-coil.
- CD-NTase–associated small membrane proteins: N-terminal TM exit into a cytosolic segment centered on an interface aromatic.
- ER sphingolipid enzyme 3-ketodihydrosphingosine reductase (Tsc10/KDSR): N-terminal TM exit into a cytosolic loop preceding the NAD(P)H-binding/catalytic domain.
- GPI-anchor biosynthesis complex subunit (PIGH): membrane-proximal helix→coil→β transition consistent with a juxtamembrane segment immediately after a membrane-associated helix.

Summary: Short, flexible coil/linker segments at or flanking structured domains—especially domain boundaries, inter‑domain linkers, and proteolytic processing junctions (signal peptides/propeptides)—with occasional peaks in loops within the domains themselves; not broadly marking long intrinsically disordered regions.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks or very short stretches; sparse and low-intensity; enriched in coils/loops at domain starts/ends and between domains, and sometimes at processing segments (signal peptides/propeptides). Secondary structure context is mixed (can occur in coil, helix, or strand) but favors loop-like regions. Large, low-confidence disordered tails are typically inactive. The number of peaks scales loosely with protein length.
Exemplars: - Secreted phospholipase A2 precursor: strongest activation on the N‑terminal propeptide; weaker, scattered peaks in loops of the mature enzyme.
- PH/SEC7 ARF GEFs: minimal overall but a peak in the short linker between SEC7 and PH domains.
- RhoGAP with PH domain: peaks at the end of a long disordered region abutting the PH domain, within PH-domain loop(s) including a lipid-binding loop, and scattered in loops of the GAP domain.
- YTH-domain RNA-binding protein: short activated coil immediately preceding the YTH domain; minor peaks in domain loops adjacent to the RNA-binding site.
- WRKY transcription factor: activation localized to the structured WRKY DNA-binding domain (beta/coil), absent in the disordered N-terminus.
- Homeobox transcription factor: peak in the short disordered stretch just before the homeobox domain; minor activation within a domain helix.
- Secreted growth factor (placenta growth factor): sparse peaks within the structured mature domain; none in the signal peptide or disordered tail.
- Periplasmic nitrate reductase electron-transfer subunit: sparse peaks in surface loops and a small cluster in the N‑terminal signal peptide.

Summary: First exposed extracellular module after export/assembly in secreted or surface-exposed proteins—especially Bacteroidetes—used for adhesion or substrate attack; also observed in some viral/eukaryotic extracellular structural proteins. Most often corresponds to an Ig-like BIG2/PKD β-sandwich or a catalytic/binding module of carbohydrate-active enzymes and extracellular proteases involved in host/environmental glycan/protein processing.
Activation pattern: Domain-level, long contiguous activation that starts at the onset of the first exposed extracellular module (typically immediately after the signal peptide, but C-terminal in autotransporter adhesins like intimin); often includes the adjacent linker. Preference for β-rich Ig-like/adhesion modules or catalytic CAZyme/protease domains; enriched in S/T and S/T–P stretches; later tandem repeats of the same module frequently show little/no activation.
Exemplars:
- Bacterial Ig-like (BIG2/PKD) adhesion modules in ice-binding and other surface adhesins: strong activation across the first exposed BIG2 domain.
- Secreted endo-β-N-acetylglucosaminidases (ENGases; GH18/GH85): activation over the N-terminal catalytic domain that cleaves N-glycans.
- Marine polysaccharide lyases (e.g., alginate/pectate lyases): activation on the initial catalytic or CBM-like β-sandwich module following export.
- Extracellular virulence proteases from oral/gut bacteria (Gram-positive and Bacteroidetes): activation across the exported N-terminal adhesin/catalytic region.
- Modular surface CAZymes with S/T- and Pro-rich repeat stalks: activation on the first repeat-rich/linker segment and adjacent Ig-like/CBM module.
- Autotransporter adhesins (e.g., intimin): activation across the first exposed C-terminal passenger subdomain.
- Occasional viral capsid/extracellular structural proteins: activation over the first externally exposed module.

Summary: Surface-exposed loop/turn elements that mediate protein–protein interactions on large endomembrane-trafficking and regulatory scaffolds, including beta-propellers (WD40/kelch/BNR/PROPPIN, CNH-like) and also inter-repeat linkers of HEAT/ARM α-solenoids and coiled-coil tethers.
Activation pattern: Predominantly domain-level/regional activation across propeller-like regions with repeated residue-level peaks at beta-strand→loop/turn junctions; additionally, peaks concentrate in short coil/linker segments between repeats within α-solenoids/coiled-coils; strong in lumenal/stem or non-catalytic scaffolding domains; little activation in transmembranes or catalytic kinase cores, and minimal within continuous helices themselves.
Exemplars: - BLOC-2 subunits (HPS3/HPS6): multiple signals on surface loops proximal to adaptor-binding regions.
- Sortilin/VPS10 family: periodic activation across N-terminal BNR beta-propeller blades; absent in LDLR/EGF/FN3 modules.
- PERK/IRE1 ER stress sensors: activation confined to lumenal beta-sheet/loop domains; absent in TM and cytosolic kinase/RNase cores.
- Nup170/Nup214 nucleoporins: peaks on loops linking beta-strands within N-terminal beta-propellers; low in extended helical regions.
- MON1–CCZ1 regulators: activation on beta-strand→loop/turn motifs in the non-Mic1 portions.
- Rho1 GEFs: broad activation across C-terminal CNH-like scaffolds rather than DH/PH catalytic cores.
- HOPS/CORVET tether subunits (e.g., VPS11): activation in inter-helical linker/loop segments within the α-solenoid/coiled-coil scaffold.
- Ric1 (Rab6/Ypt6 GEF subunit): activation on loop/turn linkers within the α-solenoid scaffold.
- DDB1–CUL4 adaptors (e.g., DCAF1): activation on WD40 beta-propeller surfaces.
- Rho-effector kinases (e.g., MRCK-1): activation in non-catalytic C-terminal regulatory scaffolds (PH/CRD/linker loops), not in the kinase core.

Summary: A eukaryote‑biased signal for long, often C‑terminal accessory regions—acidic/serine/proline‑rich low‑complexity tails or structured C‑terminal lobes—that mediate complex assembly, adaptor/cargo interactions, or catalysis. Common in Mediator, kinetochore/CCAN, vesicle coat/adaptors, BBSome, OSBP/ORP, and ER lectin OS‑9; also seen in the C‑terminal catalytic halves of certain enzymes (prenyltransferases, lipoxygenases).
Activation pattern: Predominantly domain‑level activation across extended C‑terminal segments in long contiguous blocks; enriched for S/T/P/E/D/K and P/G; active in both disordered tails and structured C‑terminal domains; occasional residue‑level peaks at metal/substrate‑binding sites.
Exemplars: 
- Mediator complex subunits (MED14/MED1/MED17/MED27): long acidic regulatory regions.
- OS‑9/ER lectins: inactive MRH domain; active disordered C‑terminus including ER‑retention tail.
- BBSome (BBS7/BBS9): strongly active C‑termini, including alternatively spliced exons.
- Vesicle coat/adaptors (AP‑3 delta, COPI gamma): activated C‑terminal appendage/ear domains.
- Kinetochore/CCAN (fta2, CENP‑N): activated C‑terminal third implicated in assembly.
- OSBP/ORP family: active low‑complexity linkers and C‑terminal lipid‑binding/FFAT‑adjacent regions.
- Lipoxygenases: active, well‑structured C‑terminal catalytic lobe encompassing Fe‑binding residues.
- Indole prenyltransferases/dimethylallyltransferases (e.g., TdiB/EasL): activated C‑terminal catalytic subdomain with substrate‑binding Tyr residues.
- Also observed in RNA transcription/export cofactors, plant repeat‑rich chloroplast proteins, secreted proteins with acidic repeats, and E2‑like Atg3 flexible acidic/proline‑rich segments.

Summary: Sequence/structural signature of β‑propeller modules and their immediately flanking N‑terminal secretory/stalk segments, spanning repeat-based propellers (WD/kelch/tectonin/YWTD, VPS10, Sema) and catalytic propellers (PQQ‑dehydrogenases, GH68 fructosyltransferases, carotenoid/retinoid oxygenases), with occasional detection of coiled‑coil/helix stalks preceding propellers (e.g., olfactomedins) and β‑propeller nucleoporin scaffolds.
Activation pattern: Primarily domain-level activation over long stretches. Strong across blade-repeat arrays and adjacent low-complexity/linker regions; enriched for Gly/Ser/Thr with acidic/aromatic residues typical of propeller repeats. In many secreted/periplasmic proteins, activation begins at the signal peptide and coiled‑coil/stalk immediately N‑terminal to the propeller and may taper within very well-ordered β‑sheet cores (as observed for an olfactomedin), while remaining low on unrelated domains in the same proteins.
Exemplars: - Olfactomedin glycoproteins: high on signal peptide and long N‑terminal coiled‑coil/helical stalk preceding the OLF β‑propeller; weak/absent over the ordered OLF core.
- Semaphorin guidance proteins: Sema-domain β‑propeller (and adjacent PSI/secretory segments) highlighted.
- LDL receptor family: ectodomain YWTD β‑propeller and connecting repeats in secreted/cell-surface receptors.
- VPS10-domain sorting receptors: N‑terminal luminal β‑propeller module.
- WD‑repeat/kelch/BTB adaptors: activation across WD/kelch blade arrays and N‑terminal BTB/coiled‑coil dimerization regions.
- Nucleoporin scaffolds: Sec13/Seh1-like β‑propeller subunits of the nuclear pore Y‑complex.
- Carotenoid/retinoid oxygenases (RPE65/BCO family): catalytic seven-bladed β‑propeller cores.
- PQQ‑dependent dehydrogenases: periplasmic 8‑bladed β‑propeller enzymes (often including signal peptides).
- GH68 fructosyltransferases/invertases: secreted enzymes with 5‑bladed β‑propeller catalytic domains.
- Tectonin-repeat lectins and other propeller-bearing extracellular proteins: repeat-based propeller modules and their flanking regions.

Summary: C-terminal assembly and membrane-engagement modules of membrane-active proteins—pre-stem β-strands, coiled-coil oligomerization helices, and flexible/disordered tails that enable pore formation, partner recruitment, membrane penetration, or membrane remodeling
Activation pattern: Long, contiguous segments that are predominantly C-terminal; often low-confidence/disordered or coiled-coil, enriched in polar residues, but can also be well-ordered β-strand blocks; aligns with pre-stem “transmembrane β-strand” regions in β-pore formers; little activation over N-terminal signal peptides or compact core domains
Exemplars: - Aerolysin-like pore-formers (Monalysin): activation on a flexible C-terminal tail beyond the core pore-forming domain
- Bacillus BinAB toxins (BinB subunit): activation on a C-terminal segment required for toxicity and partner (BinA) internalization
- Cholesterol-dependent cytolysins (Streptolysin O): activation on C-terminal pre-stem β-hairpins annotated as transmembrane β-strands that insert into membranes
- Type III secretion translocon proteins (SctE/EspD/EspB family): activation on the C-terminal coiled-coil assembly/oligomerization region
- Mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU family): activation on the disordered, acidic/basic-rich C-terminal regulatory tail
- Bacterial dynamin-like proteins: activation on the C-terminal GTPase effector domain (coiled-coil) that drives self-assembly and membrane remodeling
- Staphylococcal bicomponent leukocidins/gamma-hemolysin: activation on a C-terminal β-strand domain essential for pore assembly (mutations here abolish hemolysis)

Summary: Hydrophobic alpha-helical segments and their boundary regions (helix starts/ends), with strongest responses in transmembrane helices of membrane proteins but also detectable in hydrophobic helices of soluble proteins and N-terminal signal peptides.
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks within alpha-helices enriched for hydrophobic/aromatic residues; concentrated in TM helices and at helix–membrane interfaces, with additional weaker peaks in compact hydrophobic helices of soluble proteins and in signal peptides.
Exemplars:
- SEDS peptidoglycan glycosyltransferases (RodA/FtsW): multiple peaks across TM helices, including the first TM and C-terminal bundle
- ClC chloride channels: scattered low peaks within several TM helices and just before helix entry points
- Formate/nitrite transporters (FNT/FocA): strongest at initial residues of TM helices (helix boundaries) and within helices
- V-/A-type ATPase a-subunit (subunit I): peaks immediately preceding and within TM segments
- Archaeal Agl glycosyltransferases (AglJ/Agl6): peaks contained within membrane-spanning helices
- Ribosomal proteins (e.g., uL15): low-level peaks in hydrophobic helical cores of soluble proteins
- Homing endonucleases (e.g., I-DmoI): sparse peaks in hydrophobic helices
- Soluble/periplasmic oxidases (e.g., paromamine 6'-oxidase): peaks in signal peptides or hydrophobic helical segments
- Neurensin-1: peaks within its vesicular membrane TM helices
- Gemin-1: occasional peaks in predicted hydrophobic helical regions

Summary: Non-cytosolic beta-sheet module surface loops—predominantly in secreted/periplasmic and organellar (e.g., chloroplast/vacuolar) proteins—especially the conserved N‑terminal cysteine-starting segment of Ig‑like domains and analogous loop regions in cupredoxin (blue‑copper), carbohydrate‑binding/adhesion modules, and other beta‑rich accessory domains appended to enzymes, receptors, and toxins; occasional intracellular beta‑sandwich loops are also captured.
Activation pattern: Regional, multi‑patch activation on short solvent‑exposed loops enriched for S/G/T/A and Pro; often anchored by a conserved Cys in oxidizing compartments (extracellular/periplasmic) but not required in reducing organelles (e.g., plastids). Activates both near the N‑terminus (after signal/transit peptides) and in distal domains, recurring across multi‑domain proteins.
Exemplars: - Ig‑like immune receptors and cell‑adhesion molecules (IgCAMs, Fc receptors, Siglecs): first Ig V/I/C2‑set domain starting at the N‑terminal Cys and adjoining beta‑loop.
- Carbohydrate‑active enzymes (glycoside hydrolases, carbohydrate esterases, polysaccharide lyases, including GAG lyases): appended CBMs and flexible beta‑loop linkers in secreted/periplasmic enzymes; plastidial debranching enzymes (pullulanase/limit dextrinase) show activation on exposed beta‑loops of the catalytic barrel.
- Blue copper proteins and multicopper oxidases (laccases/ceruloplasmin): cupredoxin beta‑sandwich loops near metal‑binding regions.
- Secreted proteases (aspartic, serine, metalloproteases, cysteine proteases): accessory beta‑rich domains (Ig‑like/FnIII/CUB/hemopexin) and nearby exposed loops.
- Bacillus thuringiensis Cry toxins: beta‑prism/sandwich receptor‑binding loop regions (domains II/III).
- Accessory Sec system components (e.g., Asp3): periplasm/extracellular‑facing loop segments; extracellular matrix/adhesion proteins: Ig‑like/FnIII modules and Ser/Thr/Pro‑rich linkers.

Summary: Generic detector of solvent‑exposed, compositionally biased contiguous segments—often acidic and Ser/Pro/Gly‑rich—that occur as N‑terminal ectodomain/pro‑region stretches in secreted or lumenal proteins and, analogously, as flexible linkers/connector helices or surface loops within cytosolic domains; it highlights interface/processing regions rather than tightly conserved catalytic cores (though it can include catalytic phosphorylation loops).
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long contiguous stretches (tens of residues), forming broad peaks that span mixed secondary structure (short helices, beta‑strands, and connecting coils). Activation frequently begins just after signal peptides or at TM–lumen junctions in secretory/membrane proteins, and in cytosolic proteins targets exposed loops or connector helices; typically low‑to‑moderate pLDDT/disordered segments but also structured surface subdomains. Rarely single‑residue spikes, with occasional inclusion of catalytic histidines in PTS EIIA loops.
Exemplars: - GH81 1,3‑beta‑glucanases (laminarinases): activation on a beta‑sandwich subdomain (beta‑strands and loops) away from catalytic/substrate sites.
- Renin/prorenin receptor (V‑ATPase accessory/ATP6AP2): strong activation immediately after the signal peptide within the N‑terminal ectodomain (coil/short beta), with a secondary luminal patch.
- GPI‑anchor transamidase subunit (PIGS): primary activation in a low‑confidence lumenal segment (mixed short helices/coil) and minor activation at the first TM–lumen transition.
- TetR‑family transcriptional repressors: activation on a long C‑terminal helix that connects the HTH DNA‑binding domain to the ligand‑binding helical bundle.
- Yeast transcription factor WAR1: activation on a disordered regulatory region containing transient helix/short beta elements.
- Nonsense‑mediated mRNA decay factor EBS1: activation across alpha‑helical segments in central/C‑terminal regions with modest structural confidence.
- PTS EIIA‑type phosphotransfer proteins: activation over a loop/β segment that includes the phosphorylatable histidine and adjacent beta‑strand (protein–protein interaction/phosphotransfer surface).
- SLC4 anion exchangers (AE2): activation within the cytosolic N‑terminal domain just proximal to the transmembrane region (short helix, β‑strands, and connecting coils).

Summary: Short beta-strand segments and strand–loop junctions that repeat across beta-rich extracellular domains—especially beta‑propeller blades and related repeat scaffolds—common to secreted carbohydrate-active enzymes and adhesion/ECM receptors; the same structural element is also detected in analogous beta-strand→coil sites of soluble enzymes
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks (typically 5–8 residues) repeated many times within a domain; peaks coincide with beta-strands and their transitions into loops, often centered on Ser/Thr/Gly and enriched for acidic/aromatic residues; strong domain-level restriction to lumenal/extracellular regions (little to none in signal peptides, transmembranes, or cytosolic tails)
Exemplars: - VPS10/sortilin receptors: repeated peaks on the beta-strands of BNR propeller repeats across the luminal domain; absent in TM and cytosolic tail
- Sialidases/endosialidases (neuraminidases): peaks on propeller blade strands and adjacent loops that form glycan-binding/active-site rims
- Kelch/WD/tectonin repeat proteins and F‑box/kelch adaptors: repeated activation on edge strands of propeller blades
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes (e.g., beta-xylosidases, CBMs, sulfatases, polysaccharide lyases): peaks at beta-strand→coil junctions within beta-rich catalytic or binding modules
- Secreted serine/cysteine proteases: activation on beta-sheet elements of their extracellular catalytic domains
- Extracellular adhesion/ECM proteins (netrins, UNC5, contactins, laminins): activation on beta-strands within beta-rich extracellular scaffolds; not in TM/cytosolic segments
- Cation channel auxiliary subunits (CatSper beta-like): widespread activation across the large N-terminal extracellular domain; none in TM/cytosolic regions
- Soluble metabolic enzymes (e.g., nitrate reductase): isolated peak at a well-structured beta-strand followed by a coil

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity repeat tracts enriched in Gly/Pro/Ser/Thr and acidic residues, frequently punctuated by aromatic positions (Phe/Tyr) in short motifs such as FG or GY. These segments serve as flexible linkers/scaffolds or assembly interfaces in large macromolecular complexes and as glycine‑rich structural repeats in secreted proteins; occasional sparse hits mark analogous aromatic/low‑complexity motifs in secreted proteases.
Activation pattern: Predominantly regional activation across extended IDRs with P/G/E/D/S/T bias; strongest at Pro/Gly and acidic/Ser clusters and at aromatic residues within FG/GY‑like repeats; minimal signal in well‑folded β/α cores; in compact enzymes, often restricted to one or a few residues within low‑complexity or aromatic motifs.
Exemplars: - Nuclear pore complex nucleoporins: activation on FG/GLFG/FxFG repeat domains.
- Arthropod cuticle structural proteins (CPR/CPG): activation on glycine‑rich, tyrosine‑punctuated repeats (GY/GG‑rich regions).
- COPII coat assembly proteins (Sec16/Sec31): activation on long proline/serine/threonine‑rich, acidic low‑complexity linkers.
- Ciliary/flagellar and testis-associated scaffolds (radial spoke head, MORN‑repeat proteins): activation on acidic/P/S‑rich tails and aromatic positions within repeats.
- RNA/telomere-associated factors (e.g., H/ACA RNP assembly factor NAF1) and NMD components: activation on N‑ or C‑terminal disordered Pro/Gly and acidic/Ser clusters.
- Secreted subtilisin-like serine proteases and proprotein convertases: sparse activation on isolated aromatic or glycine/tyrosine residues in low‑complexity propeptides or exposed loops.
- Plant trafficking/chloroplast-associated factors: activation on serine/threonine‑rich low‑complexity linker regions.

Summary: Beta-strand–rich structural segments (e.g., Ig-like/jelly-roll/beta‑solenoid/beta‑sandwich/propeller) across diverse proteins; common in secreted or cell‑surface and viral/bacterial structural proteins, and also frequent in cytosolic/nuclear beta‑rich domains.
Activation pattern: Multi‑segment regional activation with numerous 8–15 aa peaks across large domains; enriched for hydrophobic residues interleaved with Gly/Pro/Ser/Thr; frequently adjacent to N‑glycosylation sequons in secretory proteins; little/no activation on signal peptides or transmembrane helices; observed across taxa.
Exemplars: - Nuclear pore membrane glycoprotein GP210/Nup210: discrete peaks throughout the luminal N‑terminal domain, absent on the TM helix and cytosolic tail
- Alpha‑2‑macroglobulin/complement/thioester proteins (C3/C4/C5/A2M): beta‑rich macroglobulin and thioester‑containing domains
- ER oligosaccharyltransferase subunits (ribophorin-like): luminal beta‑rich domains
- Bacterial outer‑surface adhesins/autotransporters and OM ushers/transporters: beta‑helix passenger domains and beta‑barrel/periplasmic beta‑domains
- Bacteriophage structural proteins (capsid/tail/tailspike): jelly‑roll and parallel beta‑helix regions
- Carbohydrate‑active enzymes (CAZymes): beta‑solenoid enzymes and beta‑sandwich carbohydrate‑binding modules
- Transthyretin/transthyretin‑like proteins: beta‑sandwich cores
- Arrestin/ART family: beta‑sandwich folds
- TRIM E3 ubiquitin ligases: PRY/SPRY beta‑sandwich or NHL beta‑propeller domains
- STAT transcription factors: SH2 and DNA‑binding beta‑rich domains
- Fungal velvet regulators: NF‑κB‑like beta‑sandwich domains
- Archaeal/bacterial S‑layer proteins: beta‑solenoid/tiling beta‑repeat regions
- Multi‑pass receptors (e.g., mGluR-like): large extracellular beta‑rich domains with no activation on TM segments

Summary: Short coil-to-beta transition motif at edge beta-strands of beta-rich domains, including small beta-barrels (e.g., SH3, OB, Tudor/MBT) and beta-sandwich readers (e.g., BAH), and also peripheral edge beta-strands within larger alpha/beta enzymes or scaffolds (e.g., kinesin motor cores, RNase II S1/KH accessories).
Activation pattern: Highly localized peaks in 6–20 aa coil→beta transitions at conserved edge strands; often one peak per repeat; strongest at domain boundaries or peripheral edge strands; generally avoids active-site loops even within catalytic domains; minimal signal in long disordered regions or purely helical repeats.
Exemplars:
- Tudor/MBT readers: repeating peaks at the N-terminal edge strand of each repeat; no activation in OTU catalytic cores.
- Retroviral integrase: strong peak at the end of the catalytic core entering the SH3-like CTD; minor peaks in other short coil/beta segments.
- Plant ARFs: short, well-structured beta-strand peaks in the central region; absent from B3 and PB1.
- Chromatin regulators with BAH domains (e.g., CMT1, PBRM1): peaks on BAH edge strands; no signal in helical bromodomains.
- Ubiquitin pathway proteins: peaks on beta-sandwich or small beta-barrel accessory modules (e.g., CAP-Gly in CYLD) rather than in RING/USP catalytic cores; E3s like MIB2 show peaks in short beta-strands of accessory regions.
- Nucleic acid/metabolic enzymes: RNase II family and P-loop NTPase motors (e.g., KIF2C) show peripheral edge-strand peaks away from active-site motifs.

Summary: Membrane-active amphipathic alpha-helices—often long heptad-repeat/coiled-coil segments—that mediate oligomerization and membrane apposition/fusion, translocon/pore assembly, or lipid binding in secreted/extracellular and virulence-associated proteins; distinct from fully hydrophobic transmembrane helices and characterized by long, low‑cysteine stretches intermixing charged and small hydrophobic residues
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation across long, continuous non-transmembrane helices (strongest in coiled-coil/heptad-repeat regions); minimal or absent signal in hydrophobic transmembrane spans; weaker in poorly structured/low-confidence segments; prefers sequences with alternating charged (E/D/K/R) and small hydrophobics (A/L/I/V) and low cysteine content
Exemplars: - Type III secretion translocon components (SctE/YopB family): strong activation on extended coiled-coil stalks flanking/between TMs; TM helices are not activated.
- Viral class I fusion glycoproteins (e.g., HA, F, coronavirus S): activation on HR1/HR2 heptad repeats and fusion-proximal amphipathic helices; little/no activation in TM/signal peptides.
- Bacteriophage entry/structural proteins (tail fibers, baseplate/coiled-coil shafts): activation on long coiled-coil rods used for assembly and host engagement.
- Antimicrobial peptides and bacteriocins (alpha-helical AMPs): activation along amphipathic helical stretches with mixed cationic and hydrophobic residues that insert into membranes.
- Chlamydial inclusion membrane proteins (IncA/Inc family): activation on cytosolic SNARE-like/coiled-coil helices; hydrophobic hairpin TMs do not activate.
- Fungal secreted toxin-like or CAZy-associated proteins: activation on exposed amphipathic/coiled helical segments implicated in host interaction.
- Autophagy-related protein 2 (ATG2) homologs: activation at C-terminal amphipathic membrane-binding helices involved in lipid transfer/tethering.
- Human apolipoproteins: activation on amphipathic lipid-binding helix repeats (11/22-mer type), consistent with peripheral membrane/lipid association.

Summary: A general structural motif: well-ordered loop/turn residues that cap or precede beta-strands (coil-to–beta-strand junctions; beta-strand N-caps) at secondary-structure boundaries, often proximal to catalytic or metal/cofactor-binding sites but not the catalytic residues themselves.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks in short local runs concentrated at loop-to–beta-strand transitions and starts of beta-strands (and occasionally helix termini entering loops); high-confidence regions; moderate number of sites per protein; enriched for turn-prone residues (glycine/proline) and occasional basic clusters.
Exemplars: - CDC25-like dual-specificity phosphatases (Rhodanese domain): loops immediately preceding beta-strands within the catalytic domain.
- Mn-dependent ADP-ribose/CDP-alcohol diphosphatase: coil residues at N-termini of beta-strands (e.g., Q220–R222), near zinc-binding histidines.
- Ornithine racemase: loop segment transitioning into a beta-strand (N113–S117), with minor signal on the adjacent strand.
- RNase H2 subunit A: start of a beta-strand (136–142) adjacent to a metal-binding aspartate.
- tRNA(Ile)-lysidine synthase (TilS): loop connecting an alpha-helix to a beta-strand near the ATP-binding region.
- 4-hydroxy-3-methylbut-2-enyl diphosphate reductase (IspH): loops linking helices and sheets; minor activation at a helix terminus entering a coil.

Summary: Low-complexity “stalk/linker” and mucin-like segments enriched in Ser/Thr/Pro/Ala/Gly (with some Val/Leu), typically in secreted or surface proteins (adhesins, ECM, viral envelopes, protease(-inhibitory) megaglycoproteins) and in analogous low-complexity interdomain linkers of large modular enzymes, including some intracellular bacterial CAZymes.
Activation pattern: Regional activation in long contiguous bands across luminal/extracellular regions and low-complexity linkers; strongest over Pro/Ser/Thr–rich stretches with small/aliphatic residues (S/T/G/A/V/L/P) and depleted charged/aromatics; often flanking but not centered on N-glycosylation sites; minimal/absent in signal peptides, transmembrane helices, and many compact globular domains, but can also appear within low-complexity insertions/linkers of otherwise cytosolic enzymes.
Exemplars:
- Nuclear pore membrane glycoprotein Nup210: multiple activated patches across the luminal domain while the BIG2 segment, TM helix, and cytosolic tail are silent.
- Cadherin/protocadherin family: activation on extracellular low-complexity insertions and inter-repeat linkers adjoining cadherin repeats.
- Bacterial adhesins (including serine-rich repeat adhesins and other surface interaction proteins): strong activation on long S/T/P-rich repeat tracts and glycosylated stalks.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes (glycoside hydrolases/lyases): activation on Pro/Ser/Thr-rich interdomain linkers connecting catalytic and carbohydrate-binding modules in secreted or intracellular multimodular enzymes (e.g., Bifidobacterium glycosidases; some bacterial beta-galactosidases).
- Viral envelope glycoproteins and phage structural/tailspike proteins: activation on mucin-like regions and glycosylated/low-complexity stalks.
- Secreted proteases and protease inhibitors (complement/alpha-2-macroglobulin systems): activation on flexible bait/linker segments and other low-complexity luminal regions within large secreted glycoproteins.
