The marked segments typically center on a long alpha‑helix with adjacent glycine/proline‑rich coils, and are often near conserved cysteines (disulfide or catalytic), but can include short motif‑like peaks.
Activation pattern: Regional activation: single contiguous stretches (tens to >100 residues) with one or two residue‑level peaks, usually centered on an alpha‑helix and spilling into neighboring coils/loops. In secreted proteins the region commonly lies in the N‑terminal extracellular/lumenal portion; in cytosolic families it often occurs in C‑terminal subdomains or helices abutting active sites.
Exemplars: - Vitellogenin/large lipid‑transfer proteins: activation across the N‑terminal vitellogenin (LPD_N) domain (~100–260), with peaks near glycosylation/disordered segments, consistent with a lipid‑binding surface patch.
- BRICHOS‑containing secreted proteins (e.g., gastrokines): activation over the C‑terminal half of the BRICHOS module including the conserved disulfide cysteine and adjacent helices/loops.
- CD36/SNMP1 lipid receptors: activation in a flexible extracellular loop immediately adjacent to a disulfide‑bonded cysteine pair, consistent with a ligand‑entry/gating surface.
- CRISPR Cas6 endoribonucleases: a single well‑structured central alpha‑helix on the RNA‑binding/catalytic face.
- Aminopyrimidine aminohydrolase/TenA (thiamine salvage): a short alpha‑helix bearing the catalytic cysteine and bordering the substrate‑binding residues.
- Ciliogenesis‑associated TTC17‑interacting proteins: a structured mid‑region with a prominent helix embedded in beta‑strands, likely a protein–protein interaction surface.
- Frequently observed in the broader set: tubby/tubby‑like proteins (conserved C‑terminal segment of the tubby domain), photosystem II PsbO (lumenal surface loops), thrombospondin‑repeat extracellular glycoproteins, and periplasmic/outer‑membrane secretion components—all showing N‑terminal extracellular stretches consistent with exposed functional surface patches.

Summary: Structural motif marking the loop-to-transmembrane transition: the N-terminal boundary/start of alpha-helical transmembrane segments (including short amphipathic helices that immediately precede a TM helix and the first few residues within the TM). The feature captures interfacial “anchor” chemistry (Trp/Tyr/Phe, Leu/Ile/Val, Gly/Pro) at membrane-entry points across multi-pass membrane transporters, channels, and intramembrane enzymes.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks clustered at the N-termini of TM helices and in the helical segment immediately preceding a TM; often includes the very N-terminus of the protein and the first 3–5 residues inside the helix. Activation is almost entirely within alpha-helices with a strong bias for hydrophobic/aromatic residues (frequent Trp/Tyr/Phe; also Leu/Ile/Val) and helix-boundary residues (Gly/Pro). Weaker, secondary peaks can occur in adjacent periplasmic/cytosolic helices flanking TM segments; minimal emphasis on catalytic or ion-binding residues per se.
Exemplars: - ECF transporter S-component (ThiT): peaks at the start of the first TM and in helical segments immediately preceding subsequent TMs, marking repeat boundaries and loop-to-TM junctions.
- Fluoride channel (FluC): strongest at Pro/Trp/Tyr residues marking the N-termini of each TM helix.
- ClC-type chloride channel: activation at the start of multiple TM helices and in short periplasmic/cytosolic helices abutting TM segments (membrane-interface anchors).
- Mitochondrial carrier (SLC25 tricarboxylate carrier): periodic peaks at the beginnings of Solcar repeats that immediately precede specific TM helices.
- Intramembrane metalloprotease (MmpA): N-terminal helix and residues just before/at the starts of each TM segment.
- CAAX prenyl protease (ER intramembrane protease): loop-to-TM junctions across several helices, highlighting interfacial segments before entering TMs.
- Bactoprenol-linked sugar translocase (phage-encoded): first residues of consecutive TM helices defining membrane entry points.
- Vacuolar iron transporter (CCC1/VIT family): short cytosolic/vacuolar helices and residues immediately before and into multiple TM helices.

Summary: Short coil/turn motifs at secondary-structure junctions—especially beta-strand termini, beta-hairpin turns, and strand–helix linkers—often enriched in Pro/Gly with acidic/polar residues (E/D/S/T). The feature marks structurally defined loop/hinge segments within diverse domains (Ig-like, FKBP PPIase, T-box, Velvet, lysyl-oxidase-like, enzyme cores) and frequently lies adjacent to binding or active-site regions rather than in signal peptides, transmembranes, or long disordered tails.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks forming very short contiguous stretches (typically 1–3 residues) within well-structured domains; concentrated at loop/turn regions and at the ends of beta-strands or at beta↔helix boundaries; occasional weak spillover to neighboring strand residues; minimal to no activation in signal peptides, propeptides, transmembranes, or extended disordered regions.
Exemplars: - Lysyl oxidase family (lysyl-oxidase-like catalytic domain): short coil patch within the catalytic domain (not in the signal peptide/propeptide), centered on a turn segment.
- Voltage-gated sodium channel beta subunit (Ig-like C2 domain): a short beta-strand edge and bordering loops in the extracellular Ig-like domain, adjacent to a disease-relevant residue.
- Matrix remodeling-associated adhesion receptor (Ig-like V-type domains): histidines at the starts of turns within Ig-like domains (coil/turn beginnings).
- Fungal Velvet-domain regulators: beta-to-coil junction within the Velvet domain; no activation in flanking disordered regions.
- FKBP-type peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase: loop connecting beta-strands and a nearby strand residue within the PPIase fold.
- T-box transcription factors: coil linker between beta-sheets and the end of a beta-strand within the T-box DNA-binding domain.
- Mitochondrial intermembrane proteins: residues at beta-to-helix transitions and strand termini in the folded C-terminal domain.
- Dihydroneopterin aldolase (folate-pathway enzyme): loop bridging a beta-strand to an alpha-helix near the catalytic lysine; additional coil near the active site and at the onset of a disordered tail.

Summary: Hydrophobic “anchor” residues—most often a Thr–Leu pair—at the C‑terminal flank of conserved catalytic loops that feed into a beta‑strand or short helix, immediately adjacent to active‑site motifs (especially phosphoryl‑transfer and hydrolase motifs); the feature generalizes to equivalent hydrophobic beta‑strand positions in structurally similar nonenzymes
Activation pattern: Highly localized residue‑level peaks (typically 1–3 residues per protein); frequently a two‑residue peak on Thr–Leu or hydrophobic–hydrophobic pairs; located in structured segments (beta‑strands > short helices; loop‑to‑strand junctions), usually immediately C‑terminal to catalytic Asp/Ser/His motifs; occasional weaker peaks elsewhere; rarely in disordered regions
Exemplars: - P‑type ATPases (metal‑transporting): activation on the TL immediately following the DKTG… catalytic aspartyl‑phosphate motif (e.g., T–L next to the active‑site Asp).
- HAD‑superfamily phosphatases: phosphoserine phosphatase (SerB) activates on the T of the DxDxT motif and the following L (T–L) beside the nucleophile/general acid; trehalose‑phosphate phosphatase shows a Leu just downstream of the catalytic Asp; phosphatidylglycerophosphate phosphatase activates on T at the motif end and the following L (+1).
- Serine proteases and PBPs: DegS (HtrA) shows hydrophobic beta‑strand residues flanking the catalytic triad (I near His, L near Ser); FtsI (class B PBP) activates on a beta‑strand Val near the SxxK catalytic motif.
- N‑terminal nucleophile hydrolases (gamma‑glutamyltransferase): activation on a beta‑strand residue downstream of the nucleophilic Thr in the processed small chain.
- Peroxiredoxin/thioredoxin‑like enzymes: activation on a beta‑strand Ile within the thioredoxin fold adjacent to the active‑site region (minor additional hydrophobic hit in the same fold).
- Radical SAM heme synthase: activation on a single Val in a well‑structured beta‑sheet of the C‑terminal region, consistent with a hydrophobic strand anchor near the functional core.
- Ribosomal protein L35: activation on a Val within a short beta‑strand, representing a nonenzymatic instance of the same hydrophobic strand‑flanking position.

Summary: Feature detects tandemly repeated or modular, low-complexity segments in exposed regions of proteins across compartments—often extracellular/cell-surface but also intracellular regulatory tails—typically intrinsically disordered and enriched in Ser/Thr/Pro and/or Gln/acidic residues, plus recurrent short motifs within those repeats. It highlights mucin-like extracellular stalks, phosphorylation-prone acidic tails, arrays of cleavable peptide modules within secreted precursors, and also marks the same loop-like subsegment repeated across structured repeat domains or compact cysteine-rich repeat modules.

Activation pattern: Predominantly long regional activation across arrays of repeats, often as periodic blocks; within each repeat, consistent residue-level peaks on specific motif positions (commonly S/T/Y or Q). Activation is typically absent on N-terminal signal peptides, transmembrane helices, and nonrepetitive globular regions, but recurs in the same subregion of successive repeat modules.

Exemplars: Mucin-like secreted glycoproteins: strong activation across S/T-rich, glycosylated extracellular domains immediately after the signal peptide; Peptide toxin/defense and protease-inhibitor precursors (e.g., hyalomin, bracovirus Egf-like inhibitors): activation over modular/disulfide-rich multi-peptide regions and their linkers; Secreted bacterial proteases/adhesins/autotransporters: activation on S/T/P-rich, low-complexity passenger/tail regions; Type III–secreted pathogen effectors (e.g., Tarp): periodic activation over central disordered repeats with Ser/Tyr phosphorylation hotspots; Yeast cell-wall GPI proteins (AWA1/Flo family): activation across Q-/S/T-rich low-complexity extracellular blocks; Tandem-repeat lectins (including compact cysteine-rich repeats): repeat-wise activation on conserved loop subsegments; Cellulosome scaffoldins: reproducible activation in the same C-terminal subsegment of successive cohesin domains; Plant nuclear/organellar regulators (e.g., Toc159 A-domain, RPA32): activation on acidic, Ser-rich disordered regulatory tails.

Summary: Hydrophobic beta-strand core residues of beta-sandwich domains—most prominently immunoglobulin-like modules (V-set/C2-set) and FN3 repeats—capturing interior aliphatic packing in IgSF cell-surface/secreted proteins and also in intracellular Ig/FN3 scaffolds; includes similar beta-sheet cores in macroglobulin/complement proteins
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks, typically single residues or short clusters of V/L/I/A (with occasional G/P/T/E) within beta-strands; strongest in the N-terminal Ig/FN3 module when present in ectodomains (≈25–60 after the signal peptide) and repeated across tandem Ig/FN3 repeats; minimal in signal peptides, transmembrane helices, and non–beta-sandwich regions; low, scattered peaks also appear in beta-strands of large secreted macroglobulin proteins
Exemplars:
- IgSF immune co-signaling receptors (B7/PD family): peaks on beta-strands of IgV/IgC ectodomains
- T-cell antigen CD7: beta-strand peak in its single extracellular Ig-like domain, near the intradomain disulfide
- Voltage-gated sodium channel beta subunits: peaks within the C2-type Ig-like domain; absent from TM/cytosolic regions
- V-set and transmembrane domain–containing proteins: strong peaks on beta-strands in the N-terminal Ig-like domain
- Receptor tyrosine kinases and axon-guidance receptors with Ig/FN3 ectodomains (e.g., Robo/DCC-like): multiple small peaks across Ig/FN3 modules
- Immunoglobulin and T-cell receptor variable domains: interior aliphatic residues in V-set beta-strands
- Thioester/macroglobulin (alpha-2-macroglobulin/TEP, complement-like): sparse peaks on hydrophobic residues within beta-strands of MG domains
- IgSF adhesion/ECM proteins with many Ig repeats (e.g., L1CAM/NCAM/PECAM-like): numerous peaks distributed across Ig ectodomains
- Proteins combining LRR with Ig/FN3 modules: activation localizes to the Ig/FN3 module rather than the LRR
- Intracellular sarcomeric/cytoskeletal Ig/FN3 arrays (e.g., myosin-binding protein C): peaks across Ig/FN3 domains

Summary: Residue-level signal for short segments within beta-strands and strand–turn junctions of well-structured beta-sheet folds—most prominently the beta-sandwich modules of extracellular receptors (fibronectin type-III, immunoglobulin-like, MAM)—but also occurring in beta-strands of diverse soluble enzymes; enriched for polar/hydroxylated residues with frequent tryptophan in receptor FN3/Ig contexts.
Activation pattern: - Residue-level peaks (single residues or 2–3 residue clusters) within beta-strands or immediately adjacent turns.
- In multi-pass receptors, activation is confined to extracellular beta-sheet domains (FN3/Ig/MAM) and avoids signal peptides, transmembrane helices, and cytoplasmic catalytic regions.
- Appears structural rather than catalytic: peaks sit on well-modeled, ordered segments, not specifically at annotated active sites.
- Amino-acid bias toward S/T/Y/N/D/E/K/R and occasional W, consistent with solvent-exposed beta-strand surfaces in these folds.
Exemplars: - Class I cytokine receptors (e.g., interleukin-12 receptor beta chain): peaks on beta-strands within successive fibronectin type-III domains, often including tryptophan-containing positions.
- Receptor-type protein tyrosine phosphatases: scattered peaks on beta-strands across extracellular MAM, Ig-like C2, and multiple FN3 repeats; minimal/no activation in the transmembrane segment or cytoplasmic phosphatase domains.
- 5-hydroxyisourate hydrolase: discrete peaks on core beta-strands of the enzyme, away from the annotated substrate-binding residue.
- Purple acid phosphatase (metallo-phosphatase): a focused peak at the end of a beta-strand and into the following turn within the catalytic domain, plus minor peaks on other beta-strands.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, compositionally biased low‑complexity regions (often Gly/Pro/Ser/Thr‑rich) that serve as non‑catalytic linkers, flexible tails, and targeting/translocation or interaction segments flanking or connecting structured domains in diverse proteins, especially secreted toxins/effectors and eukaryotic scaffold/regulatory proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long IDRs with low pLDDT and coil-dominated secondary structure; strong, continuous activation over hundreds of residues with sharp drop at the start of folded catalytic or binding domains; typically excludes signal peptides and transmembrane helices; occurs at N‑termini, C‑termini, or central linkers, with occasional residue‑level peaks within turns in these disordered segments
Exemplars: Botulinum neurotoxin light chain: N‑terminal low‑complexity segment preceding the catalytic metalloprotease core; Mono(ADP‑ribosyl)transferase SpvB: long N‑terminal non‑catalytic region before the mART core; Secreted effectors (e.g., fungal/bacterial): disordered C‑terminal effector tails after the signal peptide; Inactive tyrosine‑protein kinase PRAG1: extended proline/polar‑rich disordered central region, not the kinase domain; Polymorphic toxins (Rhs/CdiA): secretion‑associated low‑complexity linkers flanking toxic C‑termini; Arthropod cuticle proteins: Gly/Pro/Ser/Thr‑rich low‑complexity repeats; Phosphoinositide and inositol polyphosphate kinases: disordered regulatory tails or insertions outside the catalytic core; Cytoskeletal scaffolds/actin‑binding proteins: proline‑rich IDRs with interaction motifs (e.g., SH3/WW‑binding); Plant HD‑ZIP transcription factors: low‑complexity activation/linker segments; Gram‑negative bacterial toxins and interbacterial effectors: disordered regions implicated in secretion/translocation rather than folded catalytic domains

Summary: Homeobox/homeodomain signature, with strongest preference for the immediate N‑terminal flank (the homeodomain’s N‑terminal “arm”) and selective positions within the three‑helix HTH core; when present in LIM–homeodomain proteins, the feature also weakly marks cysteine/histidine sites of LIM zinc‑binding repeats upstream of the homeodomain.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks concentrated:
- just N‑terminal to the annotated homeobox start (often the strongest signal),
- at select residues within high‑confidence homeodomain helices (H1–H3),
- largely absent across long disordered/low‑complexity tails;
- in LIM–homeodomain proteins, additional low‑amplitude peaks on cysteine/histidine/polar residues in coil segments of LIM repeats.
Enriched residue types among peaks include Lys/Arg and small/polar residues (Gly/Ser/Thr/Ala) and Leu; LIM‑associated peaks are cysteine‑rich.
Exemplars: - Goosecoid homeobox transcription factor: peaks at the helical extension immediately N‑terminal to the homeobox and scattered sites in helices within the domain.
- Engrailed (pair‑rule/homeotic TF): strongest peak just upstream of the homeobox, plus sparse sites within the homeodomain core.
- Abdominal‑A (HOX homeotic TF): low but focused activation at the N‑terminal edge and within helical segments of the homeobox; silent in disordered C‑terminus.
- DBX1 (developmental homeobox TF): maximal activation at the N‑terminal boundary of the homeodomain and selective helical residues inside.
- Aristaless‑like 3/ALX3 (PRD‑class homeobox TF): pre‑homeobox basic residues and multiple sites across homeodomain helices.
- LIM‑4 (LIM–homeodomain TF): scattered peaks across cysteine‑rich LIM repeats and a strong pre‑homeobox signal; homeodomain helices mostly quiet.

Summary: Hydrophobic alpha-helical transmembrane segments of polytopic (multi-pass) membrane proteins—the bilayer-embedded helical cores shared by GPCRs, transporters, channels, and membrane enzymes—independent of specific function and across all taxa.
Activation pattern: Regional activation concentrated in contiguous runs within alpha-helical, membrane-spanning segments, with residue-level peaks on hydrophobic and small residues (Leu, Ile, Val, Phe, Ala, Gly) and occasional signals on aromatics, Cys, or Pro; minimal to absent in periplasmic/cytosolic loops, beta strands, and disordered tails. Multiple activated stretches per protein, corresponding to successive transmembrane helices.
Exemplars: - Cytochrome c biogenesis protein CcmF: activation restricted to its numerous transmembrane helices; periplasmic/cytosolic loops are silent.
- GPI-anchor remodeling enzyme PGAP3 (ER multi-pass enzyme): strong clusters within annotated transmembrane helices; lumenal and cytosolic regions show little to no activation.
- Respiratory complex I antiporter-like subunits (ND5/NuoL/M/N family): sparse-to-moderate peaks along transmembrane helices; beta strands and low-confidence coils remain off.
- 7-transmembrane GPCRs: activation along the seven membrane-spanning helices, with little signal in intra-/extracellular loops.
- Ion channels and gap-junction-like proteins: signal concentrated on pore-forming/transmembrane helices rather than loop regions.
- Membrane lipid–metabolizing enzymes (e.g., desaturases, acyltransferases): activation on their membrane-embedded helical segments.

Summary: Residue-level marker of positions within ordered structural domains that often coincide with functionally constrained or ligand/cofactor-interacting sites (notably heme‑ligating histidines), with no strict secondary-structure preference and generally reduced activation in extended intrinsically disordered regions.
Activation pattern: Multiple sparse residue-level peaks scattered across the length of proteins, concentrated in well-structured regions; occasional short adjacent clusters in some proteins; little to no activation across long low-pLDDT/disordered segments.
Exemplars: - Type IV pilus tip adhesin (PilY1 homologs): many discrete peaks across the folded domain; depleted in the disordered C-terminal tail.
- Hydroxylamine oxidoreductase–nitrite reductase fusion enzymes: peaks directly on and immediately adjacent to heme axial histidines within the oxidoreductase domain, plus additional scattered peaks elsewhere.
- Mitochondrial ribosomal proteins: short adjacent clusters within structured segments.
- Viral capsid/maturation proteins: dispersed residue-level peaks across folded capsid domains.
- CRISPR system components (nucleases/effectors): scattered peaks over structured nuclease and binding domains.
- Ion channels and gap junction proteins: dispersed peaks across transmembrane and cytoplasmic structured regions, often including positions at helix kinks or boundaries.
- Carbohydrate/glycan-active enzymes: peaks around structured catalytic or carbohydrate-binding regions.
- Cilia/flagella and microtubule-associated proteins: scattered peaks within folded domains and coiled-coil regions.

Summary: Short loop/turn motifs at secondary-structure junctions—especially helix–strand (alpha–beta or beta–alpha) connectors and occasional strand–strand loops—often centered on glycine or other small/polar residues, typically within catalytic domains. These positions commonly flank (but rarely coincide with) catalytic or substrate-binding sites, making them particularly prominent in glycoside hydrolases and other carbohydrate-active enzymes, yet they also appear in unrelated enzymes.
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks (one to a few sites per protein) focused on structured coils/turns that bridge alpha-helices and beta-strands or link beta-strands; moderate-to-high structural confidence with occasional activation in flexible/disordered loops. Bias toward glycine and nearby small/acidic residues. Frequently inside the catalytic domain and adjacent to active-site/substrate-binding regions rather than on the catalytic residue itself.
Exemplars: - Alpha-agarase: peaks at individual residues in loops linking helices and beta-strands (including one in a disordered loop); no direct overlap with annotated active-site residues.
- Endo-β-N-acetylglucosaminidase (GH18): strong activations at glycine residues in loops within the GH18 catalytic domain, plus sites at a helix C-terminus and a helix–strand connector; distinct from the catalytic glutamate.
- Alpha-galactosidase: major peak in a helix-to-strand loop immediately upstream of substrate-binding residues and another at an annotated turn adjacent to the catalytic nucleophile; minor peaks on nearby beta-strands.
- Tissue alpha-L-fucosidase (lysosomal glycosidase): isolated peaks in high-confidence coils that connect an alpha-helix to a beta-strand.
- tRNA (guanine-N7)-methyltransferase: sparse peaks in coils linking beta-strands and other secondary-structure elements; not on SAM- or substrate-binding residues.

Summary: Short, charged/polar, Gly/Pro-enriched secondary-structure boundary elements—helix/strand capping segments and β–α/α–β linkers—often marking domain edges or flexible hinges rather than catalytic sites.
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks clustered in short 8–12 aa patches; multiple discrete patches per protein. Preference for coils and helix↔coil transitions (pre-β loops, helix N/C-caps), but can also occur within short helices adjacent to flexible regions. Frequently just upstream of domain starts or between repeats. Composition enriched for K, R, E, D, S, T, G, P, with frequent Gly-Gly motifs.
Exemplars: - Enolpyruvyl transferases (EPSPS/MurA): loops immediately preceding β-strands in the core fold.
- Secretin/TpsB/Omp85 outer-membrane proteins: N0-domain helix→coil transition and minor caps in N1–N3 and the secretin barrel.
- Type VI secretion VgrG spikes: coil segments abutting short helices in the spike stem.
- DNA translocase FtsK/SftA: short β–α linker just before the AAA+ FtsK domain.
- Translation initiation factor IF-3: short helical starts/caps within α-helical segments.
- Nudix hydrolases: N-terminal coil directly preceding the Nudix domain and small internal loops.
- PRD-domain transcriptional regulators: α-helices adjacent to low-confidence tails N-terminal to the PRD module.
- ETS and Forkhead (FOX) transcription factors: wing/loop and helix-capping segments flanking the DNA-recognition helix.
- Histone H1 and other lysine-rich chromatin proteins: short Lys-rich linkers and helix caps within otherwise flexible regions.
- Plant PPR/CRM RNA-processing factors: inter-repeat linkers and capping turns between modular repeats.

Summary: Short linear elements at protein peripheries—juxtamembrane linkers, terminal tails and propeptides—characterized by low-complexity/charge-biased composition (Ser/Gly/Pro and acidic/basic clusters) and embedded SLiMs for ligand/protein binding; the feature also fires on glycine-rich phosphate-binding Walker A (P-loop) segments within otherwise folded enzymes. Activation is generally absent from core catalytic folds and metal-chelating sites but concentrates on flexible loops/tails or short peripheral helices (sometimes centered on Trp or Sec).
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous windows of tens of residues, most often spanning disordered or flexible segments that flank transmembrane helices or domain boundaries, with sharp residue-level peaks at embedded motifs (e.g., CRIB SLiM) or glycine-rich Walker A P-loops. Minimal signal across globular cores; when present in enzymes it is confined to the phosphate-binding loop.
Exemplars: - Plant RING-H2 E3 ubiquitin ligases: serine-rich juxtamembrane linker between a transmembrane helix and the RING finger.
- Respiratory complex I 4Fe-4S subunit: flexible loop preceding the ferredoxin-type domain; no activation on the cysteine metal ligands.
- Lipid A 4'-kinase (LpxK): ATP-binding Walker A/P-loop within the kinase domain.
- Phosphatidylglycerophosphatase C: periplasmic alpha-helical segment immediately after the single transmembrane helix (Trp-centered peak).
- Short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase sphingolipid reductase (Tsc10): C-terminal helix/coil tail following a transmembrane helix, outside the Rossmann core.
- CRIB-motif Cdc42/Rac effectors (RIC proteins): the CRIB short linear motif within a low-confidence stretch.
- Antimicrobial peptide precursors: the disordered, low-complexity C-terminal propeptide (not the signal peptide or the mature antimicrobial peptide).
- Autophagy-related membrane protein Atg27: flexible cytosolic C-terminal tail.
- Bacterial RNase E: acidic/basic compositionally biased region within the C-terminal scaffold.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity proline‑rich regions (PRRs)—especially long poly‑proline and P‑Xn‑P tracts often interleaved with Gly/Ser—encompassing FH1 domains and generic SH3/EVH1/profilin‑binding linkers, as well as secreted proline‑rich peptides and other proline‑rich flexible linkers
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered, coil segments with dense proline content; sharp residue‑level peaks on prolines and occasional peaks on adjacent hydrophobics within P‑rich motifs; little/no activation in folded domains or in non‑proline low‑complexity (e.g., acidic) tracts; frequently spans extended tails or regions following signal peptides
Exemplars: - Formins (FH1 domains): strong activation across multiple poly‑P runs in the FH1 linker that binds profilin
- WASH complex subunit 3: activation on the disordered, proline‑rich C‑terminal tail; absent in the structured N‑terminal helical region and acidic runs
- Verprolin/WIP family: multiple disordered PRRs throughout; no activation in WH2 actin‑binding helices
- Actin‑regulatory RA/PH adaptors (e.g., RIAM/lamellipodin‑like): activation in the C‑terminal proline‑rich disordered regions, not in RA/PH domains
- Salivary proline‑rich proteins: activation across the mature secreted proline‑rich chain, not the signal peptide
- Plant SCOOP/proline-/hydroxyproline‑rich secreted peptides: activation on the P/S‑rich region immediately C‑terminal to the signal peptide
- Bacterial TonB: activation on the central periplasmic proline‑rich linker with a long poly‑P tract
- Bro1/ALIX family: activation in the C‑terminal disordered tail containing short P‑rich motifs, with occasional peaks on neighboring L/I/V within those motifs

Summary: Hydrophobic membrane/lipid-contacting segments: the signal-peptide H-region and analogous transmembrane or juxtamembrane helices; also amphipathic helical or β-strand hydrophobic patches that mediate membrane binding in soluble lipid-transfer/tethering proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation of long, hydrophobic blocks with residue-level peaks; strongest at N-terminal signal-peptide H/C boundary and the first helix of the mature chain; also on selected internal TM helices and their juxtamembrane helices (often a subset of TMs; includes single-pass scaffolds); basic residues frequently precede N-terminal activated blocks; activation can recur multiple times within a protein; in soluble lipid-transfer/tether proteins, amphipathic helical or β-rich hydrophobic patches are highlighted; occasional weak activation occurs on peripheral ER coiled-coil tethers at amphipathic helical faces
Exemplars:
- Secreted lipid-transfer families (BPI/PLUNC, vitellogenins, secretoglobins): activation on the hydrophobic H-region of the signal peptide and the immediately following N-terminal helix of the mature chain
- ER-shaping/membrane contact site proteins (reticulon/DP1/Yop1): activation on a non-TM helix just after the first hairpin element and on the entry/N-terminal half of the next TM hairpin segment
- Multi-pass membrane proteins (transporters/receptors, tweety/Ttyh): strong activation on specific TM helices (e.g., TM2–TM4) and adjacent extracellular/luminal helical segments; little/no signal on other TMs or large soluble loops
- Plastid lipid-associated/fibrillin proteins: activation on a defined hydrophobic patch (often β-strand–dominated) in the mature core that forms a lipid-facing surface; no signal on the transit peptide or unrelated helices
- Autophagy membrane tethers/lipid-transfer proteins (ATG2): activation on amphipathic helical lipid-contact motifs
- Single-pass membrane scaffolds (prohibitins): activation on their TM and juxtamembrane helices
- Peripheral ER tethering complexes (e.g., Tip20/Dsl1): occasional weak activation on amphipathic/helical faces despite lacking TMs

Summary: Amphipathic, positively biased hydrophobic α-helical segments used for protein targeting and membrane insertion—i.e., N‑terminal signal peptides and organellar transit peptides, as well as transmembrane helices with Lys/Arg‑rich flanks (positive‑inside rule)
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks in short clusters, chiefly on aliphatic hydrophobics (Leu/Ile/Val/Ala) within helical stretches and on adjacent basic residues (Lys/Arg). Enriched at N-termini for precursors (signal peptides, mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides) but repeated throughout multi-pass membrane proteins across the sequence; small-to-moderate coverage per protein, larger in polytopic pumps/transporters; modest dynamic range. Sparse or near-silent on long soluble nuclear proteins lacking targeting/TM motifs (e.g., MBD/PWWP chromatin proteins).
Exemplars: - Mitochondrial and chloroplast ribosomal proteins (mitoribosomal/chlororibosomal): activation on N-terminal transit peptides (Arg/Leu-rich amphipathic helices).
- Multi-pass membrane transporters/pumps (e.g., P-type ATPases, ABC transporters): activation across TM helices and cytosolic Lys/Arg flanks (positive-inside).
- Single-pass membrane proteins and small membrane anchors: activation on the TM helix and basic boundary residues.
- Secreted peptide hormone precursors: activation on the N-terminal signal peptide (positively charged n-region + hydrophobic h-region).
- Viral membrane proteins/viroporins/envelope proteins: activation on signal peptides and TM anchors.
- Nuclear chromatin readers (MBD/PWWP family): largely no activation, consistent with absence of targeting/TM segments (as seen for an MBD5/6 homolog).

Summary: Hydrophobic core segments of alpha‑helical transmembrane domains in multi‑pass membrane proteins (i.e., the lipid‑embedded mid‑helix portions of TM helices), independent of protein family and distinct from catalytic or loop regions.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on 10–25 residue blocks that coincide with the central part of transmembrane alpha‑helices; highest values on hydrophobic residues with bell‑shaped profiles that taper at helix ends; often recurs on multiple helices per protein but selects specific TM cores; minimal/absent in loops, soluble helices, catalytic/metal‑binding positions, and disordered/low‑confidence regions; aromatic residues frequently occur near the edges of activated blocks, with occasional small/kink‑prone residues (e.g., Gly) within the core.
Exemplars: - Intramembrane metalloprotease SpoIVFB (sporulation S2P‑like protease): activation on the hydrophobic core of specific TM helices, avoiding Zn‑binding and catalytic residues.
- Rhomboid intramembrane serine protease: strong activation on a single transmembrane helix within the rhomboid bundle.
- PRA1 family multi‑pass membrane trafficking protein: activation on two short mid‑helix stretches within/adjacent to annotated TM spans.
- Reticulon family ER membrane‑shaping proteins: activation on the cores of the two transmembrane hairpin helices in the reticulon domain.

Summary: Structural motif: alpha-helical segments with a strong preference for helix termini and adjacent coil/turns (helix-capping positions and short helix–loop linkers), largely independent of protein function
Activation pattern: Sparse, residue-level peaks concentrated at C- and N-termini of alpha-helices and the immediately adjoining coil linkers; occasional peaks within helix cores; minimal signal in beta-strands/beta-barrels; generally away from annotated catalytic residues
Exemplars: - GH18 chitinases and di-N-acetylchitobiase: peaks at helix C-termini and the following coil within the catalytic domain, not at the catalytic Glu
- Endo-beta-mannanase: peaks within helices and at helix ends, including a site adjacent to a disulfide-bonded cysteine
- TonB-dependent ferric enterobactin receptor: activation confined to the N-terminal plug domain in short helical linkers and helices; absent from the outer-membrane beta-barrel
- Plant phosphoglucan phosphatase (protein tyrosine phosphatase-like): a single strong peak in an alpha-helix of the catalytic domain
- HTH-type transcriptional regulator: peaks in a central helix and connecting loops, not in the N-terminal DNA-binding HTH motif
- METTL-like methyltransferase: strongest signal in a coil linking two alpha-helices and at helix termini

Summary: N-terminal targeting/secretion presequences (chloroplast/mitochondrial transit peptides and Sec-type signal peptides/signal-anchor helices) and adjacent amphipathic, aliphatic- and Ser/Thr-rich low-complexity stretches that route large envelope- and lipid-handling proteins to membranes
Activation pattern: Primarily strong regional activation at the extreme N-terminus, often dropping at the mature-chain boundary; in very large lipid-transfer/envelope biogenesis proteins (e.g., AsmA/TamB, ATG2-like), activation can extend across long, low-complexity, solenoid-like regions; unrelated enzymes show only sparse residue-level peaks within hydrophobic signal-anchor helices
Exemplars: - AsmA/TamB family (Gram-negative periplasmic/outer-envelope lipid transport/assembly): activation on N-terminal signal-anchor and extending into long periplasmic rods.
- ATG2-like lipid-transfer tethers: activation on N-terminal amphipathic membrane-targeting segment and extended aliphatic/Ser/Thr-rich stretches.
- Plastid-lipid-associated fibrillin/plastoglobulin proteins: activation restricted to the chloroplast transit peptide; absent in the mature domain.
- LPS transport system components (e.g., Lpt pathway proteins): activation on Sec signal peptides/signal-anchors and elongated periplasmic repeats.
- Mitochondrial/outer-envelope morphology proteins: activation on N-terminal mitochondrial targeting presequences.
- Solenoid repeat proteins (LRR/PPR): activation on organellar/secretory N-terminal targeting segments.
- Penicillin-binding proteins (periplasmic enzymes): weak residue-level peaks within the N-terminal signal-anchor helix and early periplasmic region, with no activation at catalytic residues.

Summary: Short Pro–Gly–centered beta-turn/loop motif in secreted/extracellular proteins, typically at beta-strand/coil junctions and often preceded by hydrophobic residues (frequently double leucines) with occasional upstream aromatic–Arg; captures structural turns/hairpin nucleators rather than catalytic sites
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks focused on PG dipeptides and immediately flanking residues; appears as multiple short, dispersed segments, commonly in proline/glycine-rich stretches; enriched at edges of beta strands, in loops, or linkers between domains; frequently located outside core catalytic domains (e.g., C-terminal to peptidase domains or in N-terminal linkers after signal peptides); strongest in secreted/extracellular proteins across taxa
Exemplars: - Metallocarboxypeptidases (Peptidase M14 family): activation on short extracellular coil/loop segments downstream of the catalytic domain, often around variants of an aromatic–Arg–Leu–Leu–(T)–Pro–Gly motif.
- Polysaccharide lyases (rhamnogalacturonate lyase): activation on a strand–turn–strand connector containing PxxPG, with peak at the PG-centered turn.
- TonB-dependent outer-membrane transporters: activation on an N-terminal proline-rich segment (e.g., LPPG) linking the signal-peptide-cleaved region to the plug domain.
- Extracellular matrix proteins (e.g., CILP family): repeated activations on flexible linkers and beta-edge loops with V/LP–PG motifs between structured domains, avoiding the core domain interiors.

Summary: Short, structured motif recognition centered on aromatic/hydrophobic residues (W/Y/F/L/M) often juxtaposed to cysteine/histidine, capturing key residues in zinc‑finger DNA‑binding cores (WRKY, GATA, B‑box), RRM RNP strands, and disulfide/metal‑stabilized cysteine motifs (e.g., Ly6/uPAR), with occasional detection of compact helical hotspots (e.g., cyclins).
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks within short motifs: on aromatics in beta-strands (RRM RNP1/2), on zinc‑coordinating or disulfide‑bonded cysteines in folded domains (WRKY/GATA/Ly6), and across brief, well-formed helices (cyclin substructures); little to no activation in disordered/low-complexity regions.
Exemplars: - WRKY transcription factors: peaks in the WRKY domain on a short beta-strand motif adjacent to the zinc-binding Cys pair and an RSYYK-like aromatic/basic segment.
- GATA-family transcription factors: activation over the C-terminal portion of the GATA-type zinc finger and the immediately following helix, peaking at Tyr and nearby hydrophobics.
- Ly6/uPAR (LU) domain proteins: sharp, selective peaks on disulfide-bonded cysteines positioned on beta-strands within the LU fold.
- RNA-binding proteins with RRMs (e.g., hnRNPs): strong peaks on phenylalanines of the canonical RNP1/RNP2 beta-strand motifs.
- Cyclins/cyclin-like subunits: short, high-confidence alpha-helical segments within the cyclin fold.
- Bacterial enzymes/signaling proteins: short N-terminal beta-strand motifs containing aromatic–Cys/His patterns (e.g., HWYCH) and adjacent hydrophobic residues.

Summary: Alpha-helical transmembrane segments and their juxtamembrane interfaces (including signal-anchor/signal peptide helices), highlighting residues in TM cores and at helix-to-loop transitions across diverse membrane proteins
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated within transmembrane alpha-helices and at TM–loop boundaries; multi-pass proteins show multiple peaks across several helices and connecting loops; single-pass or signal-anchored proteins often show a single peak at the lone TM or immediately adjacent flexible region; occasional peaks occur in disordered tails following the final TM or processed secretory segments; enriched for hydrophobic/aromatic and small polar residues typical of membrane interfaces
Exemplars: - TonB/TolA energy transducers: peak immediately C-terminal to the N-terminal signal-anchor TM at the periplasmic interface (TM-to-disorder transition).
- Photosynthetic light-harvesting antenna alpha chain: peak at the end of the TM helix in the periplasmic loop between helices (helix boundary).
- Neuropeptide GPCRs (and opsin-like photoreceptors): peaks within multiple TM helices (e.g., TM2) plus additional sites in intra- and extracellular loops and the C-terminal tail near TM7.
- Adiponectin receptor/PAQR family: discrete peaks within several transmembrane helices.
- Lysoplasmalogenase and other multi-pass lipid-metabolizing enzymes: peaks at TM–loop interfaces, within TM segments, and immediately after the final TM.
- Plant CLE/CLAVATA peptide precursors: weak peak in the N-terminal signal peptide helix and a stronger peak in a flexible C-terminal region downstream of the mature secreted peptide, consistent with secretory pathway context adjacent to membrane-targeting segments.

Summary: Flexible, glycine/threonine–enriched loop-and-boundary segments that flank and lead into catalytic domains of large polymer‑processing enzymes (nucleic acid and cell‑wall/carbohydrate enzymes), typically in the C‑terminal half; these regions neighbor active/metal‑binding sites but often exclude the exact catalytic residues, marking linker→domain transitions and active‑site–adjacent loops within the catalytic core.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous 20–60+ residue stretches, often beginning in a coil/disordered linker and extending into structured α/β elements of the catalytic domain; strongest near domain starts or active‑site neighborhoods, frequently in late/C‑terminal regions of the protein; peaks commonly flank, and sometimes avoid, the catalytic/metal‑binding residues.
Exemplars: - CRISPR-Cas9 HNH nuclease: activation on the HNH-domain loop/secondary structure surrounding the active site, excluding the Zn-binding Cys and catalytic His.
- Retroviral RNase H (Pol polyprotein): activation from the linker into the N-terminus of the RNase H domain, peaking adjacent to and terminating at the Mg2+-binding acidic site.
- DNA ligase I: broad activation across the catalytic adenylation core, with a peak just N‑terminal to the active‑site Lys and ATP-binding motifs.
- Type IIA topoisomerase/ParE (Toprim-bearing subunit): activation in the disordered segment immediately preceding the Toprim domain, diminishing as the structured domain begins.
- Class B penicillin-binding protein (transpeptidase): activation confined to the C‑terminal transpeptidase domain, on a β–loop–β region proximal to the active site.
- Neutral α-glucosidase: activation in the C‑terminal catalytic region, including a loop containing the catalytic Asp and a prominent downstream segment within the core.
- DNA adenine methyltransferase (PglX): activation in a C‑terminal flexible tail and an internal loop of the MTase region, consistent with TRD/catalytic boundary and active‑site–proximal flexibility.

Summary: Long, low-complexity ectodomains and other extracytoplasmic segments of secretory‑pathway proteins—especially adhesion/fusion and secreted enzyme regions—characterized by Ser/Thr/Pro/Glu/Lys‑rich stretches and clusters of cysteines forming disulfide bonds; the feature also extends to analogous long disordered linkers in cytosolic, membrane‑proximal trafficking/signaling scaffolds (e.g., TRAPP, NPHP/transition‑zone components, autophagy receptors, RNAi helicases) that interface with the secretory/endocytic pathway
Activation pattern: Regional activation over extended luminal/extracellular or periplasmic stretches (often immediately after the signal peptide and across mucin‑like stalks, propeptides, and ectodomains), with broad plateaus rather than sharp catalytic-site peaks; strongest signal on S/T/P/E/K‑rich low‑complexity segments and cysteine‑rich, disulfide‑bonded regions; secondary activation on long acidic/lysine‑rich or S/T‑/Gly‑rich disordered linkers of trafficking/adaptor and membrane‑proximal cytosolic scaffolds (including ciliary TZ, autophagy, and RNA silencing factors)
Exemplars: - Cell adhesion molecules (integrins, cadherins/protocadherins/desmogleins): activation across large extracellular ectodomains, including disulfide‑rich EGF/PSI repeats and S/T‑rich stalks.
- Bacterial chaperone‑usher/fimbrial adhesins and outer‑membrane autotransporters: activation on exported passenger/stalk regions and periplasmic/extracellular low‑complexity segments.
- Secreted proteases (trypsin‑like serine proteases; ADAM/ADAMTS metalloproteases; cathepsins): activation on propeptides, mucin‑like S/T/P‑rich spacers, and disulfide‑bonded loops rather than on catalytic triads.
- Ciliary/flagellar membrane and ciliopathy proteins (e.g., polycystin/fibrocystin‑like receptors): activation on very large extracellular/mucin‑like ectodomains; cytosolic ciliary scaffolds (NPHP family) show activation on long low‑complexity/coiled‑coil linkers.
- Gamete and viral fusogens (HAP2/fusexins and envelope‑like glycoproteins): activation on disulfide‑bonded fusion ectodomains and flexible loops.
- ER/early secretory pathway machinery (TRAP luminal subunits; AP‑adaptins, COPI, TRAPP, VAPs): activation on luminal ectodomains (TRAP) and on long acidic/lysine‑rich disordered hinge/linker regions of cytosolic subunits.
- COX11 copper chaperones: activation on the periplasmic/IMS cysteine‑rich metal‑binding domain.
- Extracellular/periplasmic glycoside hydrolases (beta‑glucosidases/mannosidases/xylosidases): activation on signal peptide‑proximal regions and S/T‑rich linkers between catalytic modules and carbohydrate‑binding modules.
- Cytosolic, membrane‑proximal signaling/quality‑control factors (e.g., inositol polyphosphate 5‑phosphatases, autophagy receptors like Nbr1, RNAi helicases like SDE3): activation on extended low‑complexity, acidic/lysine‑rich or glycine‑rich regions adjacent to membrane trafficking hubs.

Summary: Residue-level preference for beta-strand/loop junctions—especially strand starts/ends and adjacent coils—in beta-rich domains (OB-fold, Ig-like, and outer-membrane beta-barrels) and alpha/beta cores, often marking surface-exposed sites involved in ligand/partner or nucleic-acid contacts rather than catalytic centers
Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks enriched on beta-strands and neighboring coils/turns; frequently at domain boundaries (including near N-termini) or short linear motifs; number of peaks per protein varies widely
Exemplars: - Mitochondrial single-stranded DNA-binding protein (OB-fold): peaks within the ssDNA-binding domain at an N-terminal boundary residue and selected beta-strand/loop positions implicated in DNA binding.
- TonB-dependent outer-membrane transporters (22-stranded beta-barrels): peaks on barrel beta-strands and within the C-terminal TonB box interaction motif.
- Hotdog-fold acyl-CoA thioesterases: peaks at a strand start and intervening coils adjacent to CoA/substrate-binding residues.
- Beta-galactosidase (alpha/beta enzyme): multiple peaks at loop–strand junctions and strand starts, away from the catalytic glutamates.
- Immunoglobulin-like proteins (beta-sandwich): expected peaks on sheet edges and loop bases (e.g., at CDR base regions) within Ig domains.
- Translation factors/ribosomal proteins (e.g., IF‑1, uS17): peaks on OB-/beta-rich surfaces at strand/turn elements contacting rRNA or the A-site.
- Nucleic-acid/replication/telomere proteins more broadly: enrichment on OB-like or sheeted regions that mediate ssDNA/RNA contacts.
- Nudix hydrolases and aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetases: peaks at sheet–loop segments flanking conserved binding motifs and tRNA/ligand interfaces.

Summary: Short, structured patches in soluble enzyme cores that scaffold and shape functional sites—typically beta-strand/loop elements enriched in small/polar/acidic residues—with peaks flanking but rarely coinciding with catalytic or metal-binding residues; this “active‑site–adjacent scaffold” recurs across diverse metabolic, nucleic‑acid, redox, and energy‑transduction proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation in short contiguous clusters within confidently structured domains (beta-strands and neighboring loops); biased toward small/polar/acidic residues with frequent glycine but also tolerating hydrophobics; peaks occur near active/metal-binding pockets or functional interfaces rather than within transmembrane segments, signal/transit peptides, or proteolytic cleavage sites; number and placement of patches vary widely per protein.
Exemplars: - Phosphatidylserine decarboxylase proenzyme (lipid decarboxylase beta chain): short beta-strand/coil immediately upstream of the catalytic histidine and additional low-level patches on core beta-strands; no signal on the N-terminal transmembrane helix, catalytic residues, or the autocatalytic cleavage site.
- Fe(II)/2-oxoglutarate oxygenases/demethylases: beta-strands and adjacent loops that flank the iron/2-OG binding site and Hx(D/E)…H region, emphasizing the surrounding scaffold rather than the coordinating residues.
- Ferrochelatase (heme biosynthesis): alpha/beta core segments lining the porphyrin-binding cavity, highlighting the structural framework around the active site.
- Isomerases/epimerases/racemases (various folds): short beta-strand/loop elements that shape the catalytic cleft adjacent to catalytic bases or acids.
- Arginine/polyamine/urea pathway enzymes: substrate-positioning loops and acidic patches in the catalytic core that support chemistry without marking the catalytic residues themselves.
- Shikimate/tryptophan/phenazine/salicylate pathway enzymes: structured core elements of alpha/beta enzymes that frame substrate/cofactor pockets.
- Nucleic acid repair and processing proteins (e.g., polymerases/nucleases/ligases): acidic patches and hairpins bordering metal-dependent active sites and DNA/RNA-binding grooves.
- Redox and Fe–S proteins: core scaffold near cofactor-binding pockets, typically avoiding direct cysteine ligands but marking adjacent structured supports.
- ATP synthase F1 gamma subunit: helical coiled-coil core segments at the rotor–stator interface, marking the mechanochemical scaffold rather than a catalytic residue.

Summary: Peripheral membrane interaction modules—especially C2/PLAT β-sandwich lipid-binding domains and related β-sandwich recognition folds (e.g., lectin and viral jelly-roll cores)—together with adjacent acidic, serine/proline-rich disordered cytosolic linkers; broadly marking anionic phospholipid/phosphoinositide engagement in signaling and vesicle trafficking.
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation on β-sandwich cores (strong within C2/PLAT regions, often peaking over loop/N-terminal portions) plus broad elevation across acidic, low-complexity Ser/Pro-rich cytosolic segments; minimal in transmembrane helices and luminal/extracellular tails; frequently spans long regions of large multidomain proteins.
Exemplars: Phosphoinositide phospholipase C family: activation on the C-terminal C2 domain and acidic linkers; Ferlins/synaptotagmins/DOC2 (multi-C2 proteins): strong in cytosolic C2 repeats and pre-transmembrane disordered segments; Lipoxygenases: activation on the N-terminal PLAT (C2-like) membrane-targeting domain; Ras GTPase-activating proteins with C2/PH modules: signal over the C2 region and flanking low-complexity linkers; Vesicle coat/adaptor complexes (AP, COPI/COPII, clathrin adaptors): activation on β-sandwich ear/appendage domains and acidic Ser/Pro-rich linkers; Phospholipid transfer proteins (PITP, Sec14-like): signal around lipid-binding surfaces and acidic loops; Lectins (galectins, jacalin-related): activation on β-sandwich carbohydrate-recognition domains that engage glycoconjugate-rich membranes; Viral capsid/structural polyproteins: activation across jelly-roll β-sandwich cores and acidic/disordered termini mediating assembly/membrane contacts.

Summary: Short acidic/histidine-centered micro-motifs embedded in hydrophobic/aromatic stretches that mark compact functional hotspots—most often the metal- and phosphate/diphosphate‑binding elements of active sites (e.g., DDxxD, HD/EAL, HRD/DFG, Walker‑B hhhhDE) and, in small globins, the His‑ligated heme pocket.
Activation pattern: Short regional activation: compact 3–8 residue clusters with sharp peaks on D/E and/or H flanked by hydrophobic/aromatic residues (L/I/V/A/F/Y/W); typically 1–2 clusters per protein.
Exemplars: - Polyprenyl/isoprenoid diphosphate synthases: activation on the Asp‑rich DDxxD Mg2+/diphosphate‑binding motifs.
- IRE1-like Ser/Thr kinases: activation on catalytic-loop HRD and/or DFG segments that chelate Mg2+–ATP.
- Bacterial cyclic dinucleotide phosphodiesterases: activation on EAL-domain EAL motifs and HD‑GYP HD/HHE/HxH metal‑binding segments.
- MutS (MSH) mismatch-repair ATPases: activation on the P‑loop NTPase Walker‑B hhhhDE acidic pair that binds catalytic Mg2+.
- Signal recognition particle GTPases (SRP54/Ffh, FtsY): activation on Walker‑B hhhhDE/adjacent acidic switch segment in the NG domain.
- Truncated/two‑on‑two hemoglobins: activation at the proximal/distal His and surrounding hydrophobic/aromatic residues of the heme pocket.
- Ketopantoate reductase (PanE): activation near the Rossmann NADPH site/catalytic patch where an acidic residue and nearby aromatics contact cofactor/substrate.
- Cyclic nucleotide–gated channels (CNBD proteins): activation in the phosphate‑binding cassette with D/E and adjacent hydrophobic/aromatic residues that engage cAMP/cGMP.
- HTH-type transcriptional regulators: activation on a short acidic–hydrophobic segment within the HTH core/dimerization helix (helix‑capping/interface acidic residues).
- DPY‑30/SDC1 adaptors: activation on an acidic–hydrophobic short segment in the four‑helix bundle interface used for partner binding.

Summary: Extended beta-strand–rich segments in extracellular/periplasmic secretory proteins, especially within noncatalytic precursor modules (propeptides, chaperone/inhibitor domains such as BRICHOS and cystatin) and, more generally, in ectodomain scaffolds of secreted/surface proteins; these stretches are enriched in hydrophobic/aromatic and small residues and are typically N-terminal relative to the mature functional unit.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long, contiguous blocks, with strongest signal on consecutive beta-strands; frequently located in the luminal/extracellular/periplasmic portion of precursors, often N-terminal to the mature domain or cleavage site; avoids signal peptides, transmembranes, and catalytic residues; can spill into adjacent coil/helix or low-pLDDT linker immediately flanking the beta-sheet.
Exemplars: - BRICHOS-domain proproteins (e.g., pro–surfactant protein C/Bri2-like): activation over the C-terminal half of the BRICHOS domain and into the immediately C-terminal linker preceding the mature peptide.
- Thermolysin-like metalloprotease precursors (gelatinase): a defined block within the propeptide composed of two beta-strands; no activation in the signal peptide or mature catalytic domain.
- Cystatin-family cysteine protease inhibitors: the beta-strand hairpin/secondary area of contact within the cystatin fold; not the N-terminal reactive site or signal peptide.
- Alpha-carbonic anhydrase-like enzymes: a short beta-sheet patch within the CA core, away from annotated catalytic residues.
- CD36/SCARB scavenger receptors: beta-strand motifs within the extracellular lipid-binding scaffold of the ectodomain.
- Vitellogenins and other lipid-transfer/binding proteins: beta-sheet elements within the secreted lipid-binding domains.
- Bacterial periplasmic/outer-membrane lipoproteins and envelope factors: beta-sandwich segments in periplasmic domains following the lipidated N-terminus.
- Viral surface glycoproteins/capsid proteins: beta-strand-rich surface segments in the extracellular capsid/envelope domains.

Summary: Von Willebrand factor A (VWA/I) domain–based, metal‑ion–dependent adhesion modules (MIDAS) in secreted/cell‑surface and extracellular‑matrix proteins, with activation extending into the characteristic secreted‑precursor context (cysteine‑rich segments and long Pro/Gly/Ser- and acidic‑rich linkers); the feature also generalizes to VWA‑like folds or extended acidic/disordered regions in some intracellular proteins
Activation pattern: Domain‑level activation over the ∼180–220 aa VWA/I domain (including the MIDAS motif and surrounding β‑sheet/α‑helix core), typically spreading into adjacent cysteine‑rich modules and low‑complexity Pro/Gly/Ser/acidic linkers of secreted precursors; in non‑secreted exceptions, activation maps to VWA‑like structural cores or extended acidic/disordered regions
Exemplars: - Integrins and integrin‑like receptors: activation on the inserted I/VWA domain (and β‑I–like domain) including the MIDAS metal‑binding site.
- Voltage‑gated Ca2+ channel α2/δ subunits: activation on the extracellular VWA domain with MIDAS and flanking glycosylated linkers.
- Anthrax toxin receptors (TEM8/CMG2): activation on the extracellular VWA/MIDAS module mediating ligand binding.
- Bacterial Type IV pilus adhesins (PilY1 and homologs): activation on the VWA‑like adhesion domain with MIDAS.
- VWA‑domain ECM proteins (e.g., collagens with N‑terminal VWA repeats, matrilins, cochlin): activation across VWA repeats and adjoining cysteine‑rich/low‑complexity extracellular segments.
- ADAM/ADAMTS and snake‑venom metalloproteinases: activation on ancillary VWA/GON‑1–like modules where present and on disulfide‑rich/disintegrin‑like regions characteristic of secreted precursors.
- Extracellular matrix glycoproteins lacking obvious enzymes (e.g., periostin): activation across long Pro/Ser/acidic‑rich, cysteine‑containing extracellular regions that accompany adhesion modules.
- COPII coat components (SEC23/SEC24): activation on extended acidic/Ser/Pro‑rich regions and insertions that mimic the physicochemical profile of VWA‑context linkers.
- DNA repair Ku70/Ku80: activation on extended acidic/disordered tails and adjacent α/β cores with VWA‑like features.
- Type II topoisomerases/gyrase B (including viral Topo II): activation on long acidic, Ser‑rich regulatory regions or acidic loop clusters resembling MIDAS‑like metal‑binding environments.
- Bacterial outer‑membrane LpoA: activation on periplasmic low‑complexity, acidic/Ser‑rich stretches adjacent to structured domains.
- Plant RING‑type E3 ubiquitin ligases and transcription/processing factors: activation on long acidic/Pro/Ser/Gly‑rich low‑complexity regions.

Summary: Residue-level detector of alpha-helix boundary/anchor positions—most commonly at the loop-to-transmembrane-helix transition (often just N‑terminal to or within the first turn of a TM helix) and, more generally, analogous helical-register positions immediately upstream of key motifs or processed segments; enrichment for hydrophobic/aromatic residues and membrane-interface contexts
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks (few sites per protein), biased to hydrophobic/aromatic residues. Enriched at N-termini and at helix entry/exit interfaces of multi-pass membrane proteins; additional peaks occur within TM helices near functional motifs, and in soluble helical proteins at a fixed register upstream of catalytic motifs. Rarely, the same “segment-boundary” pattern appears at the start of a processed (mature) peptide.
Exemplars: - Aquaporins/aquaglyceroporins: fires on residues immediately before the first TM helix and at TM ends, with occasional intramembrane aromatics near the NPA motifs.
- TMEM175 proton channels: peaks at cytosolic residues just upstream of the first TM of each repeat (loop-to-helix transition points).
- Class A GPCRs: single residues within multiple TM helices and a cytoplasmic helical segment just before a TM, consistent with membrane-interface/helix-anchor positions.
- PAP2/LPP/dolichyldiphosphatase family membrane enzymes: residues in short loops adjacent to TM helices (often lumenal/cytosolic interfaces, sometimes near glycosylation) and immediately after a TM helix.
- Sphingolipid/ceramide-related synthases: loop residues directly preceding TM helices and hydrophobic residues within TM spans.
- Terpene synthases: hydrophobic residues in long helices at a conserved register (≈9 residues) upstream of the DDxxD and NSE metal-binding motifs, matching an “anchor” position within the helix.
- Secreted peptide precursors (CLE family): the residue immediately before the start of the processed mature peptide in a disordered tail, reflecting a segment-boundary signal.
- Broad membrane classes noted among top activators (purple bacterial light-harvesting α subunits; small respiratory chain TM subunits; TonB/TolA anchors): aromatic/hydrophobic interfacial “belt” residues at TM entry/exit positions.

Summary: Short amphipathic alpha-helix segments (≈10–30 aa): non-transmembrane helices enriched in L/I/V/A with interspersed E/D/K/R, typically at N-termini or as internal packing/interaction helices, sometimes adjacent to metal-binding Cys/His motifs
Activation pattern: Regional activation on single helical stretches (often including the immediate flanking coil), with residue-level peaks centered in the helix core; frequently near N-termini and not tied to catalytic residues
Exemplars: - PARP family mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase (PARP10): multiple short alpha-helical segments, including a prominent C-terminal helix within the catalytic/Myc-binding region
- Procarboxypeptidase B2 zymogen: an alpha-helix within the N-terminal propeptide (activation segment) containing a nearby N-linked glycosylation site
- Polyketide synthase PksE acyltransferase domain: a localized internal alpha-helix within the AT fold
- Copper-exporting P1B-type ATPase HMA (Atx1-like) domain: the N-terminal alpha-helix of the HMA domain
- KEOPS/EKC complex subunit LAGE3: a single alpha-helix (with flanking coil) in the N-terminal half of the protein
- AdoMet-dependent tRNA methyltransferase: a strong N-terminal alpha-helix and a minor internal helical segment

Summary: An exposure/low-complexity boundary signal: the feature activates on solvent-exposed terminal and interdomain boundary segments—most often C‑terminal tails—enriched in charged and Pro/Gly residues. These regions are typically intrinsically disordered or flexible and lie just beyond the last structured helix/strand of a domain, though the signal can extend into short exposed helices adjacent to functional sites (e.g., cofactor-attachment residues).
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous stretches (tens of residues, sometimes longer), with a strong bias toward C-termini and linker/boundary segments; signal often grows toward the chain end. Little or no activation in catalytic cores or transmembrane helices; occasional peaks in exposed helices immediately flanking functional motifs.
Exemplars: - Lipoyl/octanoyl transferases (BPL/LplA family): activation at the C-terminal edge of the catalytic domain (domain-boundary segment).
- Mitochondrial large ribosomal protein mL55: activation confined to a flexible C-terminal tail of the mature protein.
- UXT (prefoldin-like transcriptional cofactor): activation only on the low-confidence C-terminal tail beyond the last helix.
- WNK serine/threonine kinases: activation within the long intrinsically disordered C-terminal region downstream of the kinase domain.
- Cardiolipin synthase (PLD phosphodiesterase family): dominant activation on the C-terminal tail and weaker signal in interdomain linker loops; absent from TM segments and catalytic cores.
- Ion-translocating oxidoreductase subunit G (FMN-binding RnfG): activation over an exposed helix encompassing the FMN-attachment threonine (boundary/adjacent functional segment).
- Frataxin: activation on the unstructured C-terminal tail following the final helix.

Summary: Small disulfide-bonded, cysteine-rich extracellular recognition modules and tandem repeats—especially EGF-like repeats and related CRDs (e.g., TNFR cysteine-rich repeats, disintegrin domains, LDL receptor class A and thrombospondin type-1 repeats)—common to secreted and membrane proteins and many venoms
Activation pattern: Domain-level enrichment within these extracellular modules and at boundaries between tandem repeats; residue-level peaks on conserved cysteines (disulfide pairs), glycines in turns/loops, and acidic residues of Ca2+-binding motifs; signals concentrate in coils/edge β-strands and linkers between modules; little to no activation in catalytic cores (e.g., metalloprotease M12, MACPF), transmembranes, or cytosolic tails
Exemplars: - ADAM/disintegrin metalloproteases: activation on the disintegrin domain loops and adjacent C-terminus; absent from the peptidase M12B catalytic site.
- Notch EGF-repeat proteins: recurrent peaks at starts/ends of EGF-like repeats and within glycine-rich loops; strong signal in calcium-binding EGF repeats.
- TNF receptor superfamily: activation confined to extracellular TNFR cysteine-rich repeats, with peaks on the repeat cysteines; no signal in TM/cytosolic regions.
- Complement MACPF proteins (e.g., C8β): activation in small extracellular modules (LDLR-A Ca2+-binding repeat, EGF-like domain, thrombospondin type-1 repeat) and inter-module linkers; MACPF pore-forming core largely inactive.

Summary: Exposed low‑complexity, polar/acidic, P/S/T/G‑rich flexible segments that act as propeptides, protease‑susceptible bait/activation stretches, or inter‑domain/terminal linkers; typically extracellular/lumenal but also present in cytosolic proteins as accessible N/C‑terminal tails
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long contiguous stretches; strongest in terminal tails and in the C-terminal end of propeptides just before proteolytic cleavage; not residue-specific but spans flexible, low‑complexity segments
Exemplars: - TGF-beta superfamily precursors (e.g., inhibin/BMP/GDF): activation on the C-terminal prodomain segment immediately upstream of the RXXR furin cleavage site
- Secreted polysaccharide lyases/glycosidases and polymerizing glycosyltransferases (e.g., GlfT2): activation on C-terminal tails or P/S/T-rich linker segments near CBMs/domains or termini
- Complement and alpha-2-macroglobulin/thioester proteins: activation on the flexible protease “bait” region preceding the thioester module
- Secreted proteases/zymogens (trypsin-like, subtilisin-like): activation on N-terminal activation peptides/propeptides cleaved for maturation
- Viral major capsid proteins: activation on flexible N-/C-terminal arms and long acidic loops associated with maturation cleavage or exposed exterior surfaces
- MAM-domain and other large ectodomain receptors/ECM proteins (laminins, netrins): activation on Ser/Thr-rich mucin-like linkers between structured domains
- Bacillus Cry-family toxins: activation on propeptide segments removed by host gut proteases
- Structural proteins of bacterial extracellular appendages: activation on exposed terminal tails or low-complexity linker segments
- Cytosolic glycan-processing enzymes and transport/assembly factors (e.g., PNGase/NGLY1, intraflagellar transport protein 25): activation on acidic/polar terminal tails or inter-domain linkers

Summary: Phosphate-ester processing/binding pockets and catalytic centers, typically acidic and metal-coordinating, but also including basic, metal-independent phosphate-recognition sites (e.g., cap-binding) and related nucleotide/cofactor pockets
Activation pattern: Domain-level activation over phosphate-interacting pockets with residue-level peaks at motifs that engage phosphates (Asp/Glu/His for metal-coordinated sites or Lys/Arg/His and aromatic stacking for metal-independent binding); frequent Mg2+/Mn2+ chelation when present; occasional cross-activation on ion-conduction pores
Exemplars: - Argonaute/PIWI and CRISPR Cas9/Cas12 (incl. Cas12f/Cas14): activation on RNase H–like RuvC/PIWI catalytic carboxylates
- RNase HII and related RNase H enzymes: activation at DDE active sites
- Cas2 endoribonucleases: activation at the dimeric metal-dependent RNase pocket
- DEDD-family exoribonucleases such as PARN: activation on the DEDDh catalytic center
- EEP (metal-dependent) and PLD-like (metal-independent) phosphodiesterases such as TDP2/TDP1: activation on their phosphodiesterase cores
- Metal-dependent protein phosphatases (PP2C): activation on the binuclear metal site and surrounding acidic loop
- Phosphopantetheinyl transferases (AcpS): activation at the CoA phosphate-binding/Mg2+-coordinating pocket
- Cap-binding proteins (eIF4E): activation on the metal-independent m7GTP-binding pocket recognizing the phosphate chain via basic residues and aromatic stacking
- Ion channels such as TMEM175: occasional cross-activation on polar cation pores

Summary: Transmembrane beta‑barrel domains of outer membrane proteins (and organellar homologs), with activation concentrated on discrete positions within the C‑terminal beta‑barrel used for transport or secretion (porins/TonB‑dependent receptors, FadL/FapF channels, Type V autotransporter translocator barrels, Omp85/Toc75/BamA‑like barrels, and TolC/OprM‑like efflux barrels).
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks restricted to well‑structured beta‑strands (and strand–loop junctions) of the membrane‑embedded barrel; multiple sparse peaks per protein, typically confined to the C‑terminal barrel region; little/no activation in N‑terminal signal peptides, periplasmic POTRA domains, coiled‑coils, or large passenger regions; peaks often on small/polar residues; high structural confidence.
Exemplars: - TonB‑dependent receptors (e.g., siderophore receptors): activation across beta‑strands within the 22‑strand barrel, including near the TonB C‑terminal box.
- FadL‑like long‑chain fatty acid transporters: sharp peaks on beta‑strand residues within the barrel.
- Type V autotransporters: activation exclusively on the C‑terminal translocator beta‑barrel, absent from the N‑terminal passenger.
- Omp85/Toc75/BamA‑family (e.g., chloroplast OEP80): activation on the C‑terminal barrel, not the N‑terminal POTRA repeats.
- Chloroplast outer envelope porins (e.g., OEP39): discrete sites in beta‑strands and strand boundaries of the barrel.
- Outer membrane efflux channels (TolC/OprM‑like; e.g., BepC): sparse peaks on the beta‑barrel segment, with minimal signal in periplasmic helices.
- FapF amyloid secretion pore: multiple beta‑strand positions in the transmembrane barrel, including residues important for secretion/oligomerization.

Summary: A cross-family detector of function-defining hotspots: single residues and very short segments that form or flank catalytic or cofactor-binding sites in enzymes, or, in zymogens, the inhibitory propeptide that gates the active site; when not enzymatic, it flags short interaction-prone strand/loop elements within folded domains. These hotspots often involve acidic residues or are positioned next to Lys/Arg clusters, and may include aromatic or glycine-rich micro-motifs.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks, with occasional short regional activation (about 10–30 residues) confined to one secondary-structure element and an adjacent loop. Longer continuous activation is mainly seen in N-terminal propeptides of secreted proteases. Peaks commonly coincide with catalytic acids, PLP or pyrophosphate-binding environments, or residues immediately flanking catalytic histidines; in nonenzymes they occur in short interaction loops or β-strands.
Exemplars: - Peptidoglycan lipid I synthase MraY (bacterial envelope biogenesis): single essential Asp in transmembrane helix 8 that is required for catalysis and inhibitor binding.
- Thermolysin-like zinc metalloprotease (aureolysin precursor): activation confined to the inhibitory propeptide, strongest on a β-strand segment that occludes the active site prior to maturation.
- Prenyl-diphosphate synthase (isoprenoid biosynthesis): single helix residue adjacent to IPP-binding Lys/Arg in the active site.
- Ornithine decarboxylase, PLP-dependent enzyme: single Glu that coordinates the PLP cofactor.
- PTS EIIA phosphotransfer domain: Proline immediately adjacent to the catalytic phospho-acceptor histidine.
- Alpha-carbonic anhydrase-like protein: solitary Trp within an α-helix of the CA domain, consistent with a conserved structural packing hotspot rather than the metal-binding site.
- Mediator complex subunit 18: short β-strand-to-loop region near the N-terminus with low structural confidence (interaction-prone), plus a secondary peak in a well-structured β-strand.

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity Ser/Thr‑ and Pro‑rich stretches (often long terminal tails or repeat tracts, including mucin‑like segments) rather than folded domains; common in secreted/extracellular and viral/regulatory proteins but also present as flexible termini of diverse proteins.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long IDRs with coil secondary structure and low pLDDT; minimal or absent in well‑folded, high‑confidence domains; occasional residue‑level peaks at S/T, Pro, or Gly and at coil↔helix boundaries; frequently concentrated at N‑ or C‑terminal tails.
Exemplars: - Viral fusion glycoprotein F: activation on the disordered N‑terminal segment and scattered coil residues across unstructured regions.
- Antimicrobial peptide (ixosin): strongest activation within the low‑confidence helix/coil region of the mature peptide and additional activation in the disordered propeptide.
- ABC transporter ATPase (PotA): activation confined to disordered N‑ and C‑terminal tails; no activation within the structured nucleotide‑binding domain.
- Nucleolar regulatory protein (proapoptotic nucleolar protein 1): widespread activation across IDRs, including the C‑terminal nucleolar‑localization region.

Summary: A short beta-strand micro-motif: the feature marks brief, hydrophobic/aromatic beta-strand segments (≈4–10 residues) enriched in V/L/I/F/Y/W and often adjacent to basic residues (K/R), frequently near the N-terminus and sometimes centered on cysteines. It recurs across small beta-sheet modules (e.g., SH3-, KOW-, GYF-, PWWP-, PHD-like folds) and comparable beta-strands in diverse proteins and taxa.
Activation pattern: Sharp, residue-level peaks on short contiguous stretches that align with beta-strands; multiple peaks in proteins containing repeated beta-sheet domains (e.g., serial KOW motifs); little/no signal in long disordered regions or helical repeats; many sites near N-termini and some centered on cysteine residues.
Exemplars: - RNase H1: activation on an N-terminal beta-strand just before the catalytic RNase H domain.
- Inactive rhomboid (iRhom/RHBDF): lumenal beta-strand hairpins centered on cysteines.
- Transcription elongation factor SPT5/DSIF (NusG family): repeated activation on beta-strands across multiple KOW domains.
- Myosin heavy chain: a beta-strand within the N-terminal SH3-like domain.
- GYF-domain adaptors: core beta-sheet strands of the GYF fold.
- Chromatin readers/writers (e.g., PWWP, PHD, ZMYND/MORC/SET-associated): short beta-strands or hairpins within reader modules.
- Small large-subunit ribosomal proteins L20/eL20 and L30/L33: compact beta-strand segments in basic ribosomal proteins.
- DNA replication/repair factors (PriA helicase; GINS subunits PSF1/SLD5): short beta-strands within mixed alpha/beta subdomains.
- Viral proteins and cyanobacterial light-harvesting/photosystem components: short beta-strand/hairpin segments in diverse contexts.

Summary: Basic, low‑complexity terminal or inter‑domain segments flanking catalytic cores—typically the C‑terminal tails of large DNA/RNA‑processing enzymes and, by extension, analogous N‑terminal targeting helices (signal peptide/lipobox regions). These stretches are often flexible/disordered, enriched in Lys/Arg and Gly/Pro, and positioned at structured–unstructured boundaries where they mediate nucleic‑acid or partner interactions and regulation.
Activation pattern: Extended regional activation over contiguous blocks (tens to >100 residues), most often in later sequence positions (C‑termini) of large nucleic‑acid enzymes, and occasionally at N‑terminal signal peptides. Activation commonly coincides with drops in structural confidence (low pLDDT), spans mixed secondary structure (helix/strand/coil), and shows local peaks around loop/turn residues (e.g., Pro or Tyr) adjacent to catalytic modules.
Exemplars: - Type IA topoisomerase (e.g., Topoisomerase III‑beta): activation begins just C‑terminal to the catalytic Tyr and extends through the C‑terminal half of the core into the long, unstructured/basic C‑terminal tail.
- SF1 UvrD/Rep helicase: activation on the flexible C‑terminal extension immediately beyond the annotated helicase C‑terminal domain.
- MCM AAA+ helicase subunit (replication licensing factor): activation on the intrinsically disordered, compositionally biased C‑terminal tail enriched for basic/polar tracts and regulatory phosphosites.
- CRISPR Cas9 nuclease: activation across the RuvC‑II to HNH boundary, covering helix–strand–helix elements and a coil at a structured–to–flexible transition that abuts catalytic residues.
- YidC membrane protein insertase: activation on the N‑terminal signal/anchor segment including the lipobox cysteine—an amphipathic, low‑confidence helical region analogous in charge/low‑complexity to basic targeting tails.

Summary: Compositionally biased, intrinsically disordered low‑complexity regions (LCRs), especially repetitive S/T/P/G‑ and cysteine‑rich segments in coils and unstructured tails, rather than structured/catalytic domains.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long disordered/repeat blocks (often N‑ or C‑terminal), with multiple modest peaks within these LCRs; minimal activation in well‑structured, higher‑confidence domains. Peaks can occur regardless of local helix/coil predictions if the region is compositionally biased.
Exemplars: - Keratin-associated proteins (KRTAP/KAP family): strongest on repetitive, cysteine/serine‑rich low‑complexity arrays and disordered regions.
- Viral accessory proteins (e.g., herpesvirus ICP47): highlights disordered C‑terminal tails; weak on more structured, functional N‑terminal domains.
- Human microproteins/small ORFs (e.g., ST20 microprotein class): broad activation across the largely unstructured, low‑complexity peptide with scattered peaks.

Summary: Processing junctions and N-termini across compartments, with strongest signal at the P1′ residue immediately after proteolytic cleavages (e.g., proprotein convertase KR/RR, RXXR/furin-like) and at signal or transit peptide cleavage sites that define mature chains; the same signature also marks processed N-termini in non-secreted proteins (initiator Met excision/acetylation, calpain/caspase-like or other endoprotease cleavages) and flexible linker/domain-boundary junctions. Strongest in small cysteine-rich secreted peptides, toxins, and extracellular signaling factors, but common as well in nuclear/cytosolic regulators.
