Exemplars: mucins and mucin‑like glycoproteins — PTS O‑glycosylation repeats; secreted neuropeptide/hormone/toxin precursors — acidic/Pro/Ser/Thr‑rich prosegments; lectins — low‑complexity signal–propeptide/linkers; bacterial surface/secreted factors — PE/EP‑rich or cysteine‑repeat flexible segments (e.g., H. pylori Hcp proteins); polyubiquitin — conserved N‑terminal stretch; RNA‑binding/splicing factors — SP/TP‑rich prion‑like regions and RGG/RG‑rich low‑complexity tails (e.g., hnRNPs); fibrous repeat proteins — simple Gly/Ala‑rich tracts; oomycete RxLR effectors — RxLR/EER‑adjacent low‑complexity; viral proteins — flexible S/E/P/T‑rich stretches; bacterial protoxins/enzymes (e.g., Cry toxins, modular glycosidases) — low‑complexity insertions and Pro/Thr‑rich linkers; reproductive/sperm‑associated proteins — Pro/acidic‑rich low‑complexity segments.

Summary: Short polybasic linear motifs: Arg/Lys‑rich, low‑complexity, intrinsically disordered segments (RG/RGG/ARM/NLS‑like), often at N‑termini and sometimes adjacent to transmembrane helices, that mediate binding to polyanionic targets (DNA/RNA or acidic membranes) and nuclear import; characteristically enriched in R/K with frequent P/G and occasional Trp
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short cationic stretches (typically 5–30 residues) with clustered R/K and flanking G/P, often beginning at the extreme N‑terminus or on the cytosolic side of a transmembrane segment; residue‑level peaks on basic residues (and sometimes W); variable span and copy number per protein
Exemplars: - Herpesvirus nuclear egress complex proteins (UL31/UL34): activation on their N‑terminal/cytosolic basic patches used for inner nuclear membrane association and capsid envelopment
- Viral envelope and small ORF proteins: activation on short Arg/Lys‑rich cytosolic tails or cell‑penetrating ARM‑like segments, often with interfacial Trp
- Human nuclear/chromatin proteins (e.g., HMG/H1 variants, chromatin remodeler subunits): activation on classical K/R‑rich NLSs and nucleic acid‑binding basic patches
- Tumor suppressor/apoptosis regulators (e.g., p53 family, BAX/TP53BP1): activation on basic NLS/DNA‑binding regions within disordered termini
- Testis/spermatogenesis chromatin proteins (protamines/transition proteins; Tudor‑associated RGG proteins): activation on arginine‑rich DNA‑condensing or RGG motifs
- Aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetases and tRNA‑modifying enzymes: activation on basic RNA‑contact surfaces or N‑terminal basic extensions that engage tRNA
- Secretory pathway/membrane proteins: activation on N‑regions of signal peptides and cytosolic juxtamembrane polybasic clusters (positive‑inside rule), sometimes with Trp at membrane interfaces
- Short cationic micropeptides/AMP‑like peptides: activation on Arg/Lys‑ and Trp‑containing, disordered, membrane/nucleic‑acid‑binding stretches

Summary: Ser/Thr/Pro–rich, intrinsically disordered low‑complexity segments (often acidic and/or Q/N‑biased), typically bearing clustered SP/TP or generic S/T phosphorylation motifs—ubiquitous IDRs used as phosphorylation hot‑spots, Q/N‑rich activation/prion‑like regions, mucin‑like S/T‑rich repeats, or flexible linkers/terminal tails in enzymes and structural proteins across diverse taxa (including viruses).
Activation pattern: Broad regional activation across long, contiguous low‑complexity stretches (frequently N‑ or C‑terminal), rather than sharp residue‑level peaks.
Exemplars:
- Transcription factors and co‑activators: acidic or Q/N‑rich activation domains and neighboring low‑complexity linkers enriched for S/T/P (often SP/TP) motifs.
- Serine/threonine kinases: disordered regulatory N/C‑terminal tails containing clustered proline‑directed or generic S/T phosphorylation sites.
- RING‑type ubiquitin E3 ligases: flexible, acidic S/T/P‑rich regions harboring PEST‑like degrons and phospho‑regulatory clusters.
- Chromatin modifiers/remodelers: extended low‑complexity acidic/QN‑biased regions used for regulatory interactions.
- Viral proteins: regulatory and structural components (e.g., transactivators and capsid/scaffold proteins) with repetitive P/E/S/T/Q low‑complexity arms for host binding or assembly.
- Secreted/membrane proteins: PTS‑rich O‑glycosylation‑prone stalks, and proteases/CAZymes with low‑complexity propeptides or inter‑domain linkers enriched in S/T/E/D/P; ion channels/transporters with long disordered cytosolic loops rich in S/T/P and phosphorylation sites.
- Bacterial/archaeal proteins with compositionally biased repeats: long S/T/E/D‑ or K/E‑rich low‑complexity segments (tails/linkers) lacking defined folds.
- Autophagy/UPS adaptors and cofactors (e.g., UBX‑domain p97 cofactors): acidic and S/T/P‑rich regulatory IDRs.

Summary: Ampipathic, surface-exposed secondary-structure segments—typically 30–60-residue stretches enriched in alternating hydrophobic (L/I/V/A) and charged (E/D/K/R) residues and often containing aromatic anchors (Y/W/F)—that occur at membrane interfaces (β-barrel loop/edge regions and peripheral/coiled-coil helices) and, more generally, on solvent-exposed helices of diverse proteins across taxa
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous mid-length segments (~30–60 aa), frequently with multiple discrete segments per protein; strongest on sequences showing coiled-coil heptad patterns or β-strand/loop alternating polarity and interfacial aromatics; not confined to termini
Exemplars: - Gram-negative outer membrane porins and other β-barrel proteins: activation on surface loops and aromatic “girdle”/edge regions at the membrane interface
- Lipid A acylation/deacylation outer membrane enzymes (e.g., PagL/LpxR-type β-barrels): activation on extracellular loops/β-edge segments
- F1Fo ATP synthase peripheral stalk subunits b/b′: activation on long amphipathic coiled-coil helices
- Type IV pilus/competence/secretin assembly proteins: activation on periplasmic coiled-coil segments and/or secretin β-barrel loops
- Plant U-box E3 ubiquitin ligases (PUB family): activation on amphipathic helical surfaces/coiled-coil regions adjacent to the U-box involved in E2 engagement
- Photosystem II lumenal/assembly lipoproteins and related thylakoid factors: activation on lumenal amphipathic helices or coiled-coil-like stretches near membrane/lipid anchors
- Algal carotenoid ketolases (β-carotene ketolase/BKT/CrtW): activation on amphipathic loops/helices between transmembrane segments at stromal/lumenal interfaces
- 7-carboxy-7-deazaguanine synthase (QueE; radical SAM): activation on exposed amphipathic helices/loops around the catalytic core rather than the active-site motif itself

Summary: Extracellular/luminal ectodomains of secreted and membrane glycoproteins with large N-terminal domains—predominantly type I single-pass receptors (plant RLKs; animal adhesion/immune and growth factor receptors), but also GPI-anchored receptor-like proteins and multi-pass proteins with substantial ectodomains (e.g., adhesion GPCRs, DOMON–cytochrome b561 fusions)—characterized by modular repeat domains (LRR, lectin/LysM, EGF, Ig/FNIII, cadherin) interspersed with long low-complexity Ser/Thr/Pro-rich, glycosylation-prone and cysteine-rich segments
Activation pattern: Regional/domain-level activation spanning long N-terminal luminal/ectodomain regions (from signal peptide-proximal segments up to the transmembrane region), with broad coverage across repeats and glycosylated linkers; little to no activation on short cytosolic tails
Exemplars:
- Plant LRR receptor-like serine/threonine kinases (e.g., FLS2/BRI1/EFR families): activation across the extracellular LRR array, N/C caps, and adjacent Ser/Thr/Pro-rich, glycosylated linkers.
- Plant lectin and LysM receptor kinases and receptor-like proteins (LecRKs; CERK1/LYK family; GPI-anchored CEBiP): activation on lectin/LysM carbohydrate-binding modules and flanking low-complexity glycosylated segments.
- Animal receptor tyrosine kinases (insulin/IGF1 receptor family): activation over the disulfide- and N-glycan–rich ectodomain (CR region, L domains, FNIII modules).
- Animal adhesion/immune receptors (TLRs, Notch/EGF-repeat proteins, Ig/FNIII CAMs): activation across LRR or EGF/Ig/FNIII repeat ectodomains and cysteine-rich motifs.
- Adhesion GPCRs (e.g., ADGRF/GPR113): activation along the long N-terminal ectodomain (lectin/EGF/GAIN modules) up to the GPCR proteolysis site.
- Multi-pass oxidoreductases with large luminal domains (DOMON–cytochrome b561): activation on the N-terminal DOMON domain and luminal loops.
- Secreted mucin-like and Pro/Ser/Thr-rich glycoproteins (including plant arabinogalactan proteins/extensins): activation over long O-glycosylated low-complexity stretches.
- Viral envelope glycoproteins: activation along luminal, heavily glycosylated ectodomains.

Summary: Short cationic amphipathic helices and targeting signals: Lys/Arg‑flanked, glycine/hydrophobic‑rich segments that function as N‑terminal Sec/Tat signal peptides or mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides, and similar internal amphipathic helices at transmembrane boundaries or assembly interfaces (for anchoring to membranes or binding large RNA/protein assemblies).
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks on short windows (≈8–25 aa), frequently at extreme N-termini (signal/transit peptides) but also internally at amphipathic helices adjacent to or within TM segments or protein–protein/RNA interfaces; peaks enriched for hydrophobics and Gly, with interspersed/flanking Lys/Arg; number and positions vary widely across proteins and taxa.
Exemplars: - V-/A-type ATPase subunit a/I family (multi-pass membrane proteins): activation on short basic–hydrophobic segments that act as signal anchors or amphipathic helices at TM edges (positive-inside rule).
- DyP-type peroxidases: activation on N-terminal Sec/Tat signal peptides (basic N-region + hydrophobic h-region; small residues like Gly/Ala near cleavage).
- Ribosomal proteins and ribosome biogenesis factors: activation on short cationic amphipathic helices/patches that contact rRNA.
- RNase P/MRP protein subunits: activation on arginine-rich/amphipathic helices used for RNA binding.
- Bacterial microcompartment/carboxysome shell proteins: activation on short N-terminal amphipathic helices or interface helices involved in shell assembly/cargo targeting.
- Gas vesicle proteins: activation on short hydrophobic/amphipathic helices required for vesicle assembly and membrane association.
- Nucleoside diphosphate kinase/NME proteins (often organellar): activation on N-terminal mitochondrial/chloroplast transit peptides or membrane-associating amphipathic helices.
- Archaeal/plant mevalonate-pathway enzymes (novel archaeal route): activation on N-terminal amphipathic helices; in plants, plastid transit peptides.
- Thiamine metabolism enzymes (TMP kinase, ThiDN): activation on N-terminal targeting peptides in organellar isoforms.
- Transcription elongation factor SPT5/SPT5-like: activation on short basic amphipathic helices within NGN/KOW-adjacent regions that mediate nucleic-acid/protein interactions.
- Viral membrane/secreted proteins: activation on N-terminal signal peptides or short amphipathic helices mediating membrane insertion/association.

Summary: Short N‑terminal leader segment in a subset of presequences, especially plant chloroplast and some mitochondrial transit peptides, defined by a Ser/Thr/Ala/Pro–rich, low‑acidic stretch with a required Proline within positions 11–15 and without dense Arg/Lys clusters; also present on compositionally similar leaders of some small precursor proteins (e.g., cyanobactin‑type RiPPs), and absent from the mature chain. This feature does not generally mark all transit peptides or all RiPP leaders.
Activation pattern: A single narrow window at residues ~8–16, usually disordered coil or marginal helix with low pLDDT; requires SP/TP/AP enrichment and a Pro within the window; avoids strongly amphipathic, highly basic helices and Arg/Lys‑rich stretches; negligible activation elsewhere.
Exemplars: 
- Chloroplast transit peptides with SP/TP/AP‑rich, Pro‑centered cores (e.g., plastid ribosomal proteins, PSII small subunits, CP12, NDH assembly factors) — activation on the cTP window ~8–16.
- Mitochondrial presequences of soluble proteins with weak helicity and SP/AP/TP clusters (e.g., ferredoxin/adrenodoxin, some complex I subunits) — activation on the mTP window ~8–16.
- RiPP precursors of the cyanobactin class — activation on the N‑terminal leader preceding the core peptide.
Exclusions (non‑activating despite being “precursors” or targeted): lantibiotic nisin‑type RiPP leaders, arginine‑rich protamine P1‑type N‑termini, short metazoan COX8‑like presequences, and unrelated cysteine‑rich keratin‑associated proteins.

Summary: Feature marks extracellular polysaccharide‑active and adherence modules, with a primary preference for right‑handed parallel β‑helix (PbH1‑type) solenoids, but it also activates on non‑β‑helix glycan‑processing domains (e.g., hyaluronidases, β‑glucanases) and, secondarily, on β‑strand–rich polar surface patches in diverse proteins.
Activation pattern: Strong, often contiguous activation across β‑strand–rich catalytic/adherence cores of secreted proteins—classically the β‑helix rungs (PbH1 repeats) in depolymerases/epimerases/pectate lyases and β‑solenoid autotransporter passengers—with little signal on translocator barrels, long helices, RTX/Ca‑binding repeats, or disordered tails. Additional (usually weaker/sparser) activation can occur in other folds that present clustered polar/charged residues on β‑sheets (e.g., hyaluronidase ectodomains, some β‑jellyroll/β‑sandwich enzymes, RTK ectodomains, TBCC), explaining non‑PbH1 activations.
Exemplars: Phage capsular depolymerases/tail spikes (β‑helix core), alginate C5‑epimerases (PbH1 repeats), pectin/pectate lyases (β‑helix catalytic domain), autotransporter passengers (β‑solenoids), large β‑solenoid surface/OM repeat proteins; plus non‑β‑helix extracellular glycan enzymes such as cell‑surface hyaluronidases and fungal 1,3‑β‑glucanases; occasional secondary hits in RTKs, F‑box proteins, and TBCC due to polar β‑sheet patches.

Summary: Catalytic DNA-binding helix–loop module of base-excision-repair DNA glycosylases/AP lyases—the terminal helix of an HhH (or analogous helix-turn) motif and the adjoining loop/helix that engage DNA and include key catalytic residues (typically the G(P/P)D Asp and nearby nucleophile such as Lys), i.e., the lesion-recognition/catalytic core.
Activation pattern: Regional activation of one or a few contiguous alpha-helical blocks (~20–60 residues) within well-structured catalytic cores; peaks on the DNA-binding helix and immediately adjacent loop housing active-site residues (e.g., Lys and Asp of the G(P/P)D motif); little to no activation on Fe–S cluster ligands or disordered termini; sometimes appears as multiple neighboring blocks in the same core region.
Exemplars: - Endonuclease III (Nth family): activation over the C-terminal HhH segment encompassing the Lys nucleophile and GPD Asp; Fe–S-binding cysteines are not activated.
- 8-oxoguanine DNA glycosylase (OGG family): helix with the active Lys and adjacent loop containing the catalytic Asp.
- 3-methyladenine DNA glycosylase (AlkA/Tag family): helix–loop region around a substrate-recognition Trp and the active-site Asp proton acceptor.
- Plant DEMETER/ROS1 glycosylases: strong C-terminal activation between the annotated DEMETER domain and the Fe–S cluster, covering helices of the catalytic HhH–G(P/P)D module.
- MBD4/TDG-like glycosylase domain: C-terminal catalytic helix/loop including the essential Asp and surrounding residues.
- Adenine DNA glycosylase (including Nudix-fused proteins): helical stretch centered on the transition-state–stabilizing Asp; the auxiliary Nudix domain is not activated.
- NEIL/Endonuclease VIII-like proteins: DNA-binding alpha-helix within the catalytic core (H2TH region) annotated for DNA contact.

Summary: A short, structured loop/turn motif at β‑sheet edges—typically the connector between two β‑strands (β‑hairpin/β‑arch junctions) and sometimes a β→α junction—enriched in glycine and acidic residues (often GxG or D/E). The feature captures this generic, solvent‑exposed, well‑ordered loop segment found across many β‑rich folds (e.g., START/Bet v 1, PRELI, TNF homology, cystatin, LPMO, FlgH, Rieske oxygenase subunits) rather than a specific catalytic site or function.
Activation pattern: Regional activation with sharp residue‑level peaks in short contiguous blocks (~8–20 aa) that span the C‑terminus of one β‑strand, the intervening coil/turn, and often the N‑terminus of the next secondary element; occasional peaks at β→α junctions. Multiple blocks can occur in large precursors. Peaks favor Gly and Asp/Glu. Little or no activation in signal peptides, long disordered tails, α‑helical cores, or metal/ligand catalytic motifs.
Exemplars: - Bet v 1‑like/PR‑10 enzymes (e.g., thebaine synthase): activation on loops linking adjacent β‑strands within the helix‑grip fold.
- ABA receptors (PYL/RCAR; START‑like) and START domain lipid‑transfer proteins: activation on β‑strand–connecting loops inside the START/Bet v 1 fold; absent in N‑terminal disordered tails.
- PRELI/MSF1 lipid‑transfer proteins: multiple proline‑/glycine‑containing coil/turns that connect β‑strands in the PRELI domain.
- AA9 lytic polysaccharide monooxygenases: structured loops at β‑sheet edges, including segments adjacent to N‑glycosylation motifs.
- Rieske/ring‑hydroxylating monooxygenase small (β) subunits: β‑to‑α transition loops and β–β connectors within the oxygenase fold.
- Cystatin‑like cysteine protease inhibitors: short turns/loops that connect or terminate β‑strands (distinct from the canonical inhibitory loops).
- Flagellar L‑ring proteins (FlgH): short loop immediately following a β‑strand within the periplasmic β‑rich domain.
- TNF ligand superfamily (THD): extracellular β‑sandwich loops connecting β‑strands.

Summary: Long, highly charged alpha‑helical interaction/scaffolding segments—predominantly coiled‑coils or alpha‑solenoid/helical tails (often low‑complexity, acidic/basic, S/T‑rich)—used for oligomerization and macromolecular assembly, typically located in mid‑to‑C‑terminal regions of large proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation over long contiguous blocks (~100–300 aa), frequently in mid/C‑terminal portions; often low‑to‑moderate confidence (flexible, helix‑prone IDR→helix segments) spanning mixed helix/coil; multiple separate blocks can occur within the same protein
Exemplars: - Ku complex subunits (DNA end‑binding/NHEJ): strong activation on the C‑terminal charged/disordered tail downstream of the Ku domain (e.g., the Ku‑domain protein’s C‑tail in ATP‑dependent DNA repair factor).
- CRISPR‑associated effectors (e.g., Cas3 and large type I/III subunits): extended charged helical stalks/coiled‑coil linkers appended to catalytic cores.
- Dynamin‑like large GTPases (SEY1/DLP/Mx/OPA1): acidic C‑terminal GED/stalk coiled‑coils that mediate self‑assembly and partner binding.
- Nuclear pore and kinetochore scaffolds (HEAT/TPR/coiled‑coil nucleoporins; Ndc80/CCAN components): long alpha‑solenoid/coiled‑coil scaffolds.
- Chloroplast protein import GTPases (Toc159/Toc34 family): acidic low‑complexity A‑domains or helical tails involved in receptor/assembly functions.
- Augmin and Integrator complex subunits: elongated coiled‑coil arms that scaffold complex assembly.
- Nucleic‑acid enzymes (polymerases, helicases): charged helical accessory regions or regulatory C‑terminal tails appended to catalytic domains.
- Lipoxygenases (multiple lineages): lineage‑specific charged helical insertions/tails used for partner/membrane interactions.

Summary: Positively charged, lysine/arginine‑rich intrinsically disordered segments (often at the N‑terminus) that serve as generic nucleic‑acid/chromatin‑binding patches and/or classical nuclear localization signals, frequently flanked by serine/threonine sites for phosphoregulation; prevalent in nuclear and DNA/RNA‑associated proteins, including many nuclear DNA viruses.
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks centered on Lys/Arg (with secondary peaks on nearby Ser/Thr) within low‑pLDDT/disordered regions; often concentrated at very N‑terminal positions; patchy across long nuclear proteins; little to no activation in folded catalytic domains.
Exemplars: - Epstein–Barr virus nuclear antigen (EBNA3): sharp activation on a KRKR motif in the disordered N‑terminus; minor activation in another disordered segment.
- Herpesvirus capsid‑associated protein VP80: peaks on K/R clusters within disordered C‑terminal tail consistent with genome/transport interaction patches.
- Multi‑domain enzyme with a structured Mg‑binding catalytic C‑terminus: activation confined to disordered, basic N‑terminal segments (putative NLS/nucleic‑acid‑binding tail), absent over the catalytic domain.
- U3 small nucleolar RNP factor: N‑terminal disordered basic residues (R/K) adjacent to multiple S/T phosphosites in a nucleolar RNA‑processing protein.
- Yeast chromatin regulator Spt21: isolated peaks on R/K within low‑confidence helices/coils, consistent with basic IDRs used for chromatin association.
- RNA chaperones (e.g., La/SSB): activation on basic low‑complexity regions that mediate RNA binding and nuclear localization.

Summary: Short hydrophobic–acidic sequence motifs that mark active‑site Asp/Glu residues, typically in beta‑strand or adjacent loop contexts, that chelate Mg2+/Mn2+ or serve as catalytic acids in phosphoryl‑transfer and phosphodiester‑cleaving enzymes (kinases and nucleases).
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks in short 4–8 residue windows that almost always end in D/E and are flanked by hydrophobics (I, V, L, F); strongest signals often sit on the hydrophobic residue immediately N‑terminal to the acidic residue or on the acidic residue itself; enriched in well‑ordered beta‑strands near catalytic metal‑binding motifs; multiple discrete windows per protein; weak in helices and at cysteine‑based metal sites.
Exemplars: CRISPR Cas4 exonucleases: highlights a central beta‑sheet containing the Mn2+‑binding Glu and neighboring hydrophobics; Holliday junction resolvases (RuvC‑like) and DEDD/DEEDh exonucleases: selects the acidic metal‑binding cluster; PD‑(D/E)XK restriction endonucleases: activates on the acidic pair of the PD‑(D/E)XK motif and its hydrophobic flank; viral alkaline DNases: marks the catalytic acidic residue in the active site; DNA2 and FAN1 nucleases: activates on nuclease‑site acidic ligands; eukaryotic‑like serine/threonine and atypical protein kinases (including Dictyostelium and viral UL13): peaks around HRD/DFG/APE region, especially the hydrophobic‑acidic segment terminating in Glu/Asp; small‑molecule kinases (choline/ethanolamine and aminoglycoside kinases): highlights the conserved acidic residue that coordinates catalytic Mg2+ within a hydrophobic context near the catalytic loop/P‑loop.

Summary: Non-cytosolic coordination micro-motifs: the feature targets solvent-exposed acidic/asparagine/cysteine/histidine positions that act as ligands for extracellular/periplasmic cofactors or metal ions (e.g., Ca2+ in LDLR class A repeats, heme-Fe ligated by His) and short disordered segments flanking small extracellular domains; it also sporadically fires on isolated conserved residues in unrelated enzyme cores.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks at specific conserved positions (often one per repeat/module), with short regional clusters at domain boundaries or termini in low-confidence coil; occasional single-residue peaks within well-ordered secondary structure of soluble enzymes.
Exemplars: - LDL receptor/LRP family repeats: one Asp/Asn per LDLR class A module in the conserved acidic, Ca2+-binding loop.
- OS-9/MRH-domain lectins: the MRH C-terminal disulfide Cys and the immediately following low-confidence, Cys/His-rich segment.
- Outer-membrane assembly factor BamE: flexible periplasmic C-terminal tail, peaking at the terminal Asn.
- Cytochrome b (bc1 complex): axial heme-ligating histidine within a transmembrane helix.
- Kinesin motor proteins: isolated leucine peak within an internal alpha helix of the motor domain.
- Thiamine-biosynthesis hydroxymethylpyrimidine kinase: isolated alanine within a well-ordered helical segment.
- Enoyl-CoA hydratase: isolated phenylalanine within a beta strand in the enzyme core.

Summary: β-strand repeat scaffolds of extracellular/surface proteins, with a strong emphasis on right‑handed β‑helix/β‑solenoid–like architectures built from gly/ser/thr/asn/asp‑rich turn→β motifs; the feature also highlights the C‑terminal autochaperone/cleavage interface of Gram‑negative autotransporter passengers.
Activation pattern: Primarily domain‑level activation across long β‑repeat tracts, with residue‑level peaks on small/polar residues (G, S, T, N, D) in glycine‑anchored turns and at β‑strand starts that recur each repeat; contiguous blocks often appear around autotransporter passenger→translocator junctions, while signal peptides, disordered Ser/Thr‑rich stalks/glycodomains, propeptides, and translocator β‑barrels are largely inactive.
Exemplars: - Type V autotransporter adhesins: activation across β‑solenoid passengers and a strong block at the passenger–translocator auto‑cleavage/autochaperone region; little/no signal in the β‑barrel translocator.
- Bacteriophage tailspikes/long tail fibers/depolymerases: extended β‑helix shafts with repeating G/S/T/N/D motifs along rungs.
- Polysaccharide‑active enzymes (pectate/pectin lyases, polygalacturonases, rhamnogalacturonases, alginate epimerases, some hyaluronidases/glucanases): right‑handed β‑helix catalytic/binding domains with repeated turn→β signatures.
- Type VI secretion spikes (VgrG/gp27–gp5‑like): β‑helix spike regions marked along the repeat rungs.
- Psychrophilic ice‑binding adhesins: β‑solenoid ice‑binding repeats (e.g., Thr/Ser ladders) activated over long stretches.
- S‑layer and surface lattice proteins: β‑repeat/solenoid segments highlighted.
- Fungal GPI‑anchored cell‑wall adhesins: strong signal in the structured β‑rich N‑terminal adhesive domain; minimal in low‑complexity Ser/Thr‑rich stalks, GPI signal, and propeptides.
- Archaeal repeat proteins (e.g., short 13‑aa repeats in enzyme subunits): recurrent glycine‑anchored coil→β transitions within the repeat array.

Summary: Aromatic/pi-system hotspot detector in well-structured domains: the feature targets Tyr/Phe/Trp (and often His, occasionally Arg) that line hydrophobic/ligand-binding pockets or stabilize packing at helices/strands and short inter-helical turns, especially within repeat scaffolds (MBT, ARM/coiled-coil, PFTB) and enzyme active/binding sites (e.g., prenyl- and inositol‑phosphate–processing enzymes).
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks confined to compact, high‑confidence secondary structure (alpha‑helices, beta‑strands, and the short coil turns linking helical repeats); little to no signal in disordered regions, signal peptides, transmembranes, or unrelated domains. Activations often occur as multiple nearby peaks across a repeat array or around substrate/metal-binding neighborhoods; occasional sharp peaks on basic residues at equivalent coiled‑coil interface positions.
Exemplars: - MBT/Scm chromatin regulators (MBT repeat domains): strong peaks on Trp/Tyr confined to the MBT repeats, absent from disordered tails and unrelated zinc‑finger segments.
- Armadillo/HEAT‑repeat scaffolds: localized peaks in the short inter‑helical loops/turns of the repeat solenoid, enriched for His/Tyr/Phe.
- ZYG‑11 family substrate receptors (helical repeat proteins): sparse peaks on Tyr/His/Phe in coil turns connecting alpha‑helices in the C‑terminal repeat-rich region.
- Inositol polyphosphate 5‑phosphatases: clusters on Trp/Phe in beta‑strands of the structured C‑terminal domain.
- OST subunit 2 (Ribophorin II): multiple peaks on Tyr/Phe (and occasional small residues in the same segments) within the lumenal alpha‑helical domain; no activation in signal peptide, TMs, or cytosolic tails.
- Prenyltransferase beta subunits (FTase/GGTase PFTB repeats): repeated peaks on aromatic residues in alpha‑helices of PFTB repeats, including known substrate‑binding positions and near Zn‑binding histidines.
- Aromatic small‑molecule prenyltransferases (AsqH‑like): peaks centered on annotated substrate‑binding tyrosines in beta‑strands/loops, with additional sites across beta‑strands in the catalytic core.
- Coiled‑coil scaffolds (Angiomotin‑like): sharp, isolated peaks on arginines at positions within the coiled‑coil region consistent with interface/heptad hotspots.

Summary: All‑beta strand scaffolds that present successive hydrophobic residues in beta‑strands, with emphasis on beta‑solenoids (right‑handed parallel beta‑helix/PbH1) and inclusion of other beta‑rich architectures (jelly‑roll/beta‑sandwich, beta‑propellers, some LRR‑type solenoids); common in secreted CAZymes, phage tailspikes/depolymerases, alginate C5‑epimerases, autotransporter passengers, and also in certain intracellular beta‑rich domains (including some F‑box proteins).
Activation pattern: Residue‑level peaks on hydrophobic/small‑polar residues within beta‑strands (DSSP ‘E’), producing extended coverage across the beta‑core; little/no preference for catalytic or Ca2+‑binding residues; occurs in both secreted and non‑secreted beta‑rich proteins.
Exemplars:
- Pectin/pectate lyases (PL1/PL3): activation on core beta‑strand residues within PbH1 repeats.
- Bacteriophage tailspike/depolymerase and pre‑neck/appendage proteins: activation along beta‑helix rungs.
- Alginate mannuronan C5‑epimerases (AlgE): activation across the beta‑solenoid ladder.
- Gram‑negative autotransporter adhesins (pertactin‑like passengers): activation on passenger beta‑helix repeats.
- Polygalacturonases (GH28) and related pectin hydrolases: activation across parallel beta‑helix/jelly‑roll strand cores.
- 1,3‑beta‑glucanases (e.g., GH16/GH17) with jelly‑roll/beta‑sandwich folds: activation on sandwich beta‑strand cores.
- F‑box proteins, including FBXO proteins with FBA‑like beta‑sandwich or other beta‑rich C‑terminal domains: activation along beta‑strand cores even without canonical Kelch/WD/LRR repeats.

Summary: Charged, low‑complexity interaction regions: intrinsically disordered acidic/Ser/Thr‑rich stretches and adjacent helix–coil interfaces (including coiled‑coil oligomerization helices) that serve as flexible linkers or assembly surfaces across diverse proteins
Activation pattern: Mixed regional activation with multiple residue‑level peaks: strong peaks at helix↔coil junctions and within/next to coiled‑coil segments; broader activation across low‑complexity acidic/S/T‑rich or Gly/Pro‑rich stretches; often multiple activated patches distributed along long proteins, but can also appear as compact peaks in short proteins
Exemplars: - CRISPR‑Cas13a RNases: flexible loops at HEPN domain boundaries and a coiled‑coil segment
- Anti‑restriction (DarA‑like) proteins: coil‑to‑helix transition sites and adjacent coiled‑coil regions
- Viral structural proteins (capsid/matrix/nucleoprotein/tegument): disordered acidic/basic tails and coiled‑coil oligomerization helices
- Bacteriophage structural/anti‑host proteins: coiled‑coil stalks and low‑complexity linker regions
- Gram‑positive surface adhesins and heme/iron acquisition proteins: long S/T‑rich, Gly/Pro‑rich low‑complexity stalks and coiled‑coil spacers
- Eukaryotic cytoskeletal/mitotic coiled‑coil proteins: coiled‑coil stalks and helix–coil junctions
- Secreted precursors and apicomplexan invasion/surface proteins: low‑complexity Ser/Thr‑rich or acidic repeats near structured segments
- Viral nucleic acid‑binding/processing factors: charged disordered regions and coiled‑coil interfaces used for assembly and RNA/DNA association

Summary: Intrinsically disordered, low‑complexity, serine/threonine- and charge‑rich segments (flexible linkers, targeting regions, and cytosolic/luminal tails), often containing P/G and K/R/E/D, and frequently forming transient/low‑confidence helices; largely absent from well‑folded domain cores and transmembrane helices
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended IDRs with many residue‑level peaks on S/T and adjacent polar/charged residues; sparse or absent over structured globular domains, coiled‑coils of high confidence, and transmembrane spans; occasional activation on low‑pLDDT helical segments embedded within disordered regions and juxtamembrane basic clusters
Exemplars: - Eisosome/cortical membrane protein (yeast Sle1 family): activation on disordered, polar eisosome‑targeting region and other low‑complexity coils, with strongest peaks in long IDRs.
- 12‑TM solute carrier–type sodium transporter: activation confined to disordered N‑terminal tail and large extramembranous loops; silent across all transmembrane helices.
- ArfGAP regulator with PH and ankyrin repeats (AGAP family): activation on long disordered linkers between domains and basic low‑complexity blocks after the PH domain; off in GLD/PH cores, C4 zinc‑finger catalytic region, and ankyrin repeats.
- TORC1 scaffold subunit (Tco89‑like): strong hotspots in low‑complexity, disordered basic/acidic segments with sporadic peaks at helix edges; does not uniformly track annotated phosphosites.
- Inner nuclear membrane SUN‑domain protein: activation on low‑confidence helical stretches and basic clusters in the post‑TM luminal tail and juxtamembrane region; absent in the coiled‑coil, transmembrane helix, and structured SUN domain.

Summary: Residue-level detector of functional hotspots within protein domains—peaking near catalytic or ligand/cofactor-binding sites (often adjacent to catalytic or covalently modified cysteines), disulfide bonds, and short helices that mediate gating, dimerization, or protein–protein interactions—across both soluble enzymes and membrane/channel proteins.
Activation pattern: Sparse residue-level peaks, sometimes clustered within a single functional domain; peaks occur in loops adjacent to active/attachment sites, within nearby beta-strands or helices, and at the starts of transmembrane or short interaction helices; intensity and spacing vary widely across proteins.
Exemplars: - Cys-loop ligand-gated ion channels (GABA-A receptor beta subunits): peaks in extracellular beta-strands/loops and at the starts of transmembrane helices involved in gating.
- Proton-gated ion channel subunits (nematode pH-gated channels): peaks in extracellular loops/strands including disulfide-bond cysteines, with additional weaker peaks in transmembrane segments and a cytoplasmic helix.
- Bacteriophytochrome photoreceptors: strongest peak adjacent to the biliverdin-attachment cysteine in the N-terminal PAS/GAF region, with additional peaks on PHY/PAS2 helices including a dimerization helix.
- Lipoyl/octanoyl transferases (LipM; BPL/LPL-fold enzymes): peaks in the catalytic domain near the active-site cysteine and nearby residues that tune catalytic chemistry, spanning loop, beta-strand, and helix elements.
- Ripply family transcriptional repressors: peaks concentrated in the Ripply homology helical segment implicated in partner binding, with little activation on the WRPW repression motif.
- BBSome-interacting proteins: weak, isolated peaks within an N-terminal predicted helix consistent with a short interaction region subject to isoform variation.

Summary: Proline/serine/threonine–rich low‑complexity linkers at boundaries of modular β‑sandwich domains (especially Ig‑like and fibronectin type III repeats) in metazoan proteins—including secreted/cell‑surface receptors and intracellular scaffolds; often enriched immediately after signal‑peptide cleavage in precursors—and avoided within structured domain cores and transmembranes.
Activation pattern:
- Regional, multi‑site activation across long multi‑domain chains, concentrated in coil/low‑pLDDT segments that flank structured modules.
- Frequent band just downstream of signal‑peptide cleavage in precursors, sometimes extending from the C‑terminus of the signal helix (optional, not required).
- Recurrent bands immediately N‑terminal to Ig‑like domains and ahead of FN3 (and other ectodomain) modules; may include the first 1–3 residues of an entering β‑strand before dropping to baseline inside the domain.
- Residue‑level peaks on runs of proline interleaved with Ser/Thr and small hydrophobics (A/V/L/G); charged residues contribute less.
- Suppressed within stable β‑sheet cores, disulfide motifs, and transmembrane helices; in membrane proteins, cytosolic tails are typically silent, but purely cytosolic multidomain scaffolds show the same boundary‑linker activation.
Exemplars:
- IgSF cell‑adhesion molecules (neurofascin/L1CAM‑like, ROBO): activation on splice‑variable, disordered linkers bracketing Ig and FN3 domains; silent in domain interiors and TM/cytosolic regions.
- Leucine‑rich repeat + Ig domain receptors (LRIG): activation at LRR–Ig junctions and adjacent linkers.
- Ig‑domain receptor ectodomains (IL‑1R/PDGFR/FGFR): peaks in coil segments immediately N‑terminal to each Ig‑like domain and at β‑strand onset, with rapid decay inside domains.
- LDL receptor‑related proteins: activation at ectodomain linkers between LA/EGF/propeller modules.
- Secreted regulatory proteins (IMP‑L2/IGFBP‑like, PIP): focused peak at the mature N‑terminus after signal‑peptide removal and other ectodomain linkers; absent across structured cores.
- Sarcomeric cytoskeletal scaffolds (myomesin/titin‑associated): activation across inter‑repeat linkers between Ig/FN3 modules; quiescent within the β‑sandwich cores.

Summary: Methionine-biased hydrophobic packing positions in alpha-helices, especially within tandem helical repeat solenoids (notably plant PPR repeats), and more generally in helical bundles of membrane-associated signaling and redox proteins (e.g., two-component histidine kinases/response regulators, SDR-type dehydrogenases, ABC transporters, and enzymes of lipid/isoprenoid/quinone metabolism)
Activation pattern: Regional activation across long helical repeat arrays (many sites per PPR protein), with scattered residue-level peaks on internal M/L/I/V/F in helix cores of globular enzymes; in signaling/transport proteins, enrichment along transmembrane helices, HAMP/coiled-coil linkers, and coupling helices
Exemplars: - Plant PPR RNA-binding proteins (organelle-targeted): activation spans the repeated PPR helix pairs, highlighting methionine/other hydrophobics at helix–helix packing positions across the solenoid.
- Two-component histidine kinases: activation on transmembrane sensor helices and on long helical HAMP/dimerization coiled-coils leading into the catalytic core.
- Response regulators: activation on helical regions of the receiver/output domains (dimerization/HTH helices) at buried hydrophobic sites.
- Short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) and related dehydrogenases: activation on buried hydrophobic residues within Rossmann-fold alpha-helices.
- ABC-type transport systems: activation on transmembrane helices of permeases and on helical “coupling helices” adjacent to the ATP-binding domain.
- Membrane-associated enzymes in lipid/isoprenoid/quinone metabolism (e.g., quinone oxidoreductases, prenyl/lipid pathway dehydrogenases): activation on TM helices and adjacent helical bundles around cofactors.
- Specialized metabolite reductive enzymes (e.g., ketoreductases/enoyl reductases in bacterial/fungal pathways): activation on hydrophobic helices near NAD(P)-binding cores.
- Giant virus and other large helical proteins: activation on predicted coiled-coils or membrane-spanning helices enriched in Met/Leu/Ile.

Summary: Gly/Pro-enriched, hydrophobic low‑complexity segments that function as extracytoplasmic propeptides/linkers (in secreted/periplasmic and outer‑membrane proteins) and, by extension, analogous flexible linkers/mobile loops in certain soluble enzyme systems; in eukaryotic secreted proteins these regions often include paired cysteines forming disulfide‑stabilized loops.
Activation pattern: Regional activation on contiguous mid‑sequence stretches (typically tens of residues) enriched in hydrophobics with frequent Gly and Pro and recurrent short motifs; local peaks often center on short consensus motifs or Cys‑pair segments in disulfide‑rich extracellular proteins.
Exemplars: - Secreted metalloproteases (e.g., MMPs, serralysin-like proteases): activation on the prodomain/inhibitory segment preceding the catalytic domain (cysteine‑switch or analogous hydrophobic, GP‑rich propeptide).
- Gram‑negative flagellar L‑ring proteins (FlgH): activation on the long glycine/proline‑rich, hydrophobic periplasmic belt that wraps the rod, just downstream of the signal peptide.
- Outer‑membrane/periplasmic assembly and stress factors (e.g., Pal/OmpA‑like, SurA/Skp/DegP systems): activation on periplasmic low‑complexity linkers adjacent to the signal peptide or between domains.
- Eukaryotic extracellular lipid‑binding proteins (lipocalins, non‑specific lipid‑transfer proteins): activation on hydrophobic loops/prosegment‑like regions that often contain paired cysteines forming disulfides.
- Plant secreted cysteine‑rich proteins (defensins, nsLTPs): activation on the 8‑Cys/disulfide loop region and nearby hydrophobic segments.
- Lipoate system enzymes (LipA/LipB/LplA and E2 lipoyl‑bearing components): activation on flexible GP‑rich linkers or the mobile loop surrounding the lipoyl‑lysine motif connecting lipoyl domains to catalytic cores.
- Redox/electron‑transport membrane complexes (periplasmic/extracytoplasmic subunits): activation on amphipathic helices or GP‑rich periplasmic loops near membrane interfaces.
- Shikimate/chorismate‑pathway enzymes: activation on interdomain flexible segments/insertions enriched in hydrophobic residues with Gly/Pro repeats.

Summary: Short, exposed coil/turn segments at beta‑strand boundaries within extracellular/luminal domains—especially in repeat-rich beta‑sandwich modules (Ig‑like, FN3, cadherin) and luminal S-layer–like repeats—enriched in small/polar residues (G, S, T, often N), frequently encompassing N‑linked glycosylation sequons (N‑X‑S/T) or glycan‑associated motifs; these loops recur once per domain and are typical of adhesion/recognition receptors and other secreted surface proteins.
Activation pattern: Multiple short (≈5–15 aa) residue-level peaks per protein, predominantly in the extracellular/luminal region; each peak localizes to a loop/turn adjoining a beta‑strand (often loop→strand boundaries), with one recurring peak per repeat domain. Sequence bias toward G/S/T (±N) with GP/PG context; relative depletion of Cys. No activation in signal peptides, transmembranes, or cytosolic tails. Periodic patterns across tandem repeats (Ig/FN3/cadherin/luminal repeats), sometimes overlapping family motifs (e.g., WSXWS) or N‑glycosylation sequons.
Exemplars: - Class I cytokine receptors (gp130/IL‑6 receptor family): discrete loop activations in the N‑terminal Ig‑like C2 domain and in each FN3 domain; one peak overlaps the family WSXWS motif within an FN3 loop.
- Immunoglobulin superfamily cell‑adhesion receptors: short peaks in strand‑connecting loops within each Ig‑like domain and adjacent FN3 modules.
- Classical cadherins/protocadherins: a single short activation near the C‑terminal end of each cadherin repeat, consistent with inter‑repeat loop/strand boundary segments.
- Nuclear pore membrane glycoprotein family (Nup210/GP210; yeast POM152): regularly spaced activations across the luminal repeat region, marking flexible coil/strand mixed loops.
- Gram‑positive serine‑rich repeat adhesins (SRRPs): loop→beta‑strand boundary segments in the non‑repeat region centered on Asn within N‑X‑S/T sequons (e.g., NKT/NKS), consistent with glycan‑decorated extracellular loops.

Summary: N-terminal segments of secreted, surface-exposed, or virion structural proteins that, immediately after any signal/transit peptide (when present) or at the start of the mature chain (when absent), are enriched in small/polar residues and form extended beta/coil-rich or flexible low-complexity regions; these segments often act as glycan-decorated linkers or constitute the N-terminal portion of beta-rich extracellular scaffolds (jellyroll/Ig-like/beta-helix), but can also flank compact helical cores in small cytokines and occur in viral matrix/capsid proteins.
Activation pattern: Long, contiguous regional activation near the N-terminus, typically absent from the signal peptide itself; spans mixed beta-strands and coils or low-complexity loops with loop-centered peaks; in non-secreted virion proteins (e.g., matrix) activation begins at the mature protein N-terminus.
Exemplars: - PsbO/OEE1 luminal factors: activation across the structured beta-rich portion of the mature domain.
- Secreted fungal LysM effectors: activation immediately after the signal peptide, including N-glycosylation sequons, preceding LysM domains.
- Yeast cell-wall adhesins (Flo11/flocculins): activation within the N-terminal part of the adhesion domain, flexible/beta–coil-rich.
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes (GH11 xylanases, pectin lyases, CBMs): activation on N-terminal jellyroll/beta-helix regions or glycosylated linkers.
- Pore-forming toxins/hemolysins (RTX/aerolysin-like): activation on Gly/Asp-rich repeats or other N-terminal beta-rich segments after the prodomain.
- Viral structural proteins: activation across N-terminal exposed strands/loops of capsid/surface proteins and low-complexity N-termini of matrix proteins.
- Small secreted cytokines: activation in the short flexible N-terminal segment following the signal peptide, preceding the helical core.

Summary: Charge-rich, low-complexity alpha‑helical spacer/rod segments (SAH‑like helices) in large eukaryotic scaffolding and trafficking proteins; prefers long, continuous helices enriched in Lys/Glu/Asp (with Q/N/S/T) that serve as tethers, and de-emphasizes compact globular domains and hydrophobic/leucine‑rich coiled‑coils.
Activation pattern: - Domain-level: broad, continuous activation across central helical rods; typically weak at extreme termini and drops within folded domains.
- Structural bias: tracks alpha-helix and remains high through brief coil interruptions; strongest where helices are long, isolated, and charge-rich; suppressed in globular domains (e.g., CH, GRIP) and in later, more hydrophobic coiled-coils.
- Sequence bias: strong enrichment for K/E/D (often with Q/N/S/T) and tolerance of runs of like-charged residues; not tied to short motifs or phosphosites.
- Regional dynamics: often peaks in mid-rod segments and tapers toward boundaries or upon transition to different domain architecture.
Exemplars: - Septation/cytokinesis scaffold (yeast “up‑regulated during septation” protein): high activation on a long central helical body; low on an extensive disordered C‑terminal tail and N‑terminal segment.
- Cytoskeletal adaptor with CH domain (Cytospin‑A family): strong activation on the early, charge‑biased helical rod (sometimes annotated as coiled‑coil); off across the C‑terminal CH domain and distal segments.
- Golgin/GRIP-domain organelle tether (quick‑to‑court): peak on a central SAH‑like helix and adjacent basic/acidic low‑complexity region; suppressed over the C‑terminal coiled‑coil and GRIP domain.

Summary: Low-complexity basic/metal-binding stretches: contiguous Arg/Gly/Pro-rich repeats (RG/RGG/GAR and similar) often interleaved with Cys/His clusters (C2H2-like or HExxH), typically in disordered linkers or tails of secreted, viral, and nucleic-acid–binding proteins; Trp residues embedded in these regions are frequently included. In addition, conserved catalytic/metal-ligand His/Cys/Gly motifs within structured enzymes (e.g., heme-Cys in P450s, HRD/HxD in kinases, glycine-rich P-loop/Walker motifs in helicases) can show peaks even without surrounding low complexity.
Activation pattern: Regional activation over contiguous low-complexity segments, with pronounced peaks on Cys/His in zinc-binding or catalytic motifs and on embedded Trp; peaks can also occur on conserved His/Cys/Gly motifs within folded catalytic cores; rarely isolated single-residue hits.
Exemplars: • C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factors — activation on the Cys and His positions of the finger motifs and adjacent RG/G-rich linkers.
• RNA-/DNA-binding proteins with RGG/GAR or basic low-complexity tails (hnRNPs, nucleolin, FMRP-like, SF2 helicases including DDX/DEAH families) — activation on RG/RGG repeats, basic tails, and glycine-rich Walker/P-loop regions.
• Viral basic RNA-binding proteins (nucleocapsid, Tat/Rev-like) — activation on arginine-rich stretches and CCHC/Cys/His zinc-knuckle motifs.
• Secreted glycoside hydrolases/lyases with carbohydrate-binding modules — activation on Pro/Gly-rich extracellular linkers and Trp-rich CBM surfaces.
• Bacterial secreted metalloproteases (e.g., M4/M12/M13 families) — activation on HExxH motifs and neighboring His/Gly clusters.
• Papain-like cysteine proteases — activation around the catalytic Cys/His dyad and nearby glycine-rich loops.
• Mycobacterial PE/PPE family proteins — activation on proline-rich low-complexity repeats with interspersed Gly/Arg.
• tRNA/rRNA processing and modification enzymes — activation on basic RG-rich tails or RNA-binding loops.
• Cytochrome P450 monooxygenases — activation on the heme-binding Cys-containing motif and adjacent basic TM-proximal region.
• Protein kinases — activation on the glycine-rich loop and HRD/HxD catalytic motif.
• Multi-pass solute carriers (e.g., MCTs) — activation on cytosolic basic low-complexity loops/tails enriched in Arg/Lys/Gly.

Summary: Generic structural signal for residues positioned in beta-strands (and adjacent well‑ordered loops) of globular domains, with a slight bias toward small polar/charged residues; broadly taxonomic and functional, often near—but not at—ligand/metal/catalytic motifs
Activation pattern: Residue-level peaks concentrated at individual positions within beta-strands in high-confidence structured regions; minimal in disordered segments and transmembrane helices; sometimes enriched in early N‑terminal strands
Exemplars: - Fe(II)/2‑oxoglutarate–dependent dioxygenases (e.g., gibberellin 3β‑dioxygenase): beta‑strand residues adjacent to the Hx(D/E)…H metal/2‑OG binding environment in the DSBH fold
- CRISPR Cas7 (RAMP family): isolated residues within beta‑strands of the core domain
- Inflammatory caspases (caspase‑1): single residues on beta‑strands in the p20/p10 subunits, away from catalytic residues
- Bacteriophage endolysins/peptidoglycan hydrolases: early N‑terminal beta‑strand T/G residues near the catalytic domain
- Diacylglycerol kinase (DAGKc-containing): scattered beta‑strand residues within the catalytic/C‑terminal structured regions
- YTH RNA‑binding domain proteins: beta‑strand residues within the YTH domain, including positions adjacent to the aromatic cage for RNA recognition
- Acid‑sensing ion channels (ENaC/DEG family): multiple peaks on extracellular beta‑strands; absent from transmembrane helices
- C5‑cytosine DNA methyltransferases (SAM‑dependent): residues in beta‑sheets/adjacent structured loops of the MTase domain, excluding the catalytic cysteine
- Legume‑lectin–like F‑box proteins: residues on beta‑strands of the lectin‑like beta‑sandwich
- Type VI secretion VgrG spike proteins: single‑residue peaks on beta‑sheets of the spike body; not in disordered segments or catalytic tail regions

Summary: Polysaccharide-binding surfaces and accessory modules of carbohydrate-active proteins—especially beta/loop-rich carbohydrate-binding modules (CBMs) and analogous substrate-binding cleft segments in glycoside hydrolases, polysaccharide lyases, sugar phosphorylases/glucanotransferases, and epimerases—enriched in acidic/polar and aromatic residues that contact sugars; occasionally matches compositionally similar periplasmic loops in non-CAZymes.
Activation pattern: Regional/domain-level activation over long contiguous stretches (often mid-to C-terminal), with peaks on beta-strands and connecting loops that form or flank the sugar-binding surface; typically away from catalytic residues, and sometimes extending into flexible/disordered tails; sporadic weaker activation on acidic, low-confidence periplasmic loops of non-carbohydrate proteins.
Exemplars: - Cellulosomal scaffoldin CBM3: activation confined to the CBM3 domain (beta-sandwich cellulose-binding surface).
- Acid trehalase (GH-family trehalase): strong activation on a periplasmic beta/loop block within the catalytic region, consistent with a sugar-binding surface.
- 1,2-beta-oligoglucan phosphorylase (glycan phosphorylase/glucanotransferase): activation on extended, flexible loop segments away from the catalytic Asp, consistent with substrate-engaging loops.
- Mannosylglycerate hydrolase (glycoside hydrolase): activation on a structured C-terminal beta-region likely forming part of the substrate-binding face.
- Endo-acting ulvan lyase (polysaccharide lyase): activation across a C-terminal segment comprising structured beta elements and a tail, consistent with a polysaccharide-interaction extension.
- Glucose-6-phosphate 1-epimerase (aldose 1-epimerase/mutarotase): activation on a loop between beta-strands that includes a substrate-binding residue.
- YidC membrane protein insertase: activation on a periplasmic disordered loop, likely a compositional mimic of carbohydrate-binding loops rather than a true functional match.

Summary: Extracellular glycoprotein-like low-complexity segments: long Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly-rich stalks and linkers, often repetitive and enriched for Asn-X-Ser/Thr motifs, found in secreted and cell-surface/luminal proteins (mucin-like regions, S-layer/fimbrial/flagellar surface stretches, and linkers in secreted enzymes and adhesins), typically flexible and surface-exposed; occasionally, analogous low-complexity linkers occur in intracellular scaffolding proteins.

Activation pattern: Regional activation over long contiguous low-complexity coils with proline clusters and NXS/T glycosylation motifs, frequently in the C-terminal halves of large secreted/luminal proteins; occasional shorter peaks at flexible helix-to-coil transitions near domain boundaries. While biased to secreted/luminal proteins, similar long low-complexity coils in cytosolic coiled-coil/IDR segments can also activate.

Exemplars:
- Mucins and mucin-like ECM/adhesion proteins (ADAMTS, von Willebrand–related, zona pellucida): activation across Ser/Thr/Pro-rich glycosylated stalks and repetitive segments
- Lysosomal-associated membrane proteins (LAMP family): activation on the luminal, heavily N-/O-glycosylated low-complexity region
- Carbohydrate-active enzymes (glycoside hydrolases, polysaccharide lyases): activation on Ser/Thr-rich flexible linkers between catalytic modules and CBMs, often toward the C-terminus
- Secreted proteases and secreted toxins/superantigen-like proteins: activation on propeptides or exposed low-complexity stretches (glycosylated where applicable)
- Bacterial/archaeal surface structural proteins (S-layer glycoproteins, flagellins, fimbrial components): activation over repetitive, glycan-decorated Ser/Thr/Pro/Gly-rich surface regions with frequent NXS/T motifs
- TNF receptor superfamily decoy receptors (e.g., osteoprotegerin, DcR3): short activated patches in flexible segments within extracellular domains
- Cytosolic scaffolds and nuclear factors (e.g., SAS-6, NHEJ components): activation on low-complexity linkers adjacent to coiled-coils/IDRs despite lacking secretion and glycosylation

Summary: Generic structural signal for buried aliphatic residues (primarily Val/Ile/Leu, occasionally Phe/Tyr) within beta-strands that pack beta-sheet cores of diverse protein domains; sometimes extends to immediately adjacent coil positions at sheet edges.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue-level peaks (often single residues, sometimes 1–5 residue clusters) localized to beta-strands of well-structured domains; minimal activation in helices/disordered regions; recurring at analogous positions across homologs and taxa.
Exemplars: - SET-domain histone lysine methyltransferases (SET/PRDM/SMYD): activation on V/I/L residues in beta-strands of the SET catalytic core (e.g., I33, I136 in Set5).
- Auxin Response Factor transcription factors (B3 DNA-binding domain): activation on Val/Phe within beta-strands of the B3 domain (e.g., V242).
- Membrane-bound lytic murein transglycosylase A (SLT domain): sharp peaks on Leu residues within a beta-strand of the catalytic domain.
- NAD(P)-dependent dehydrogenases/reductases: V/I/L positions in the central beta-sheet of Rossmann-like cores.
- Amino-acid decarboxylases and racemases: hydrophobic beta-strand residues in the alpha/beta core sheets of PLP-dependent or related folds.
- HtrA/Do-like serine proteases: core beta-sheet hydrophobics within the trypsin-like protease domain.
- Ribosomal proteins (bacterial and organellar): conserved beta-strand hydrophobic residues in small beta-sheet domains.
- RNA polymerase subunit 5/h homologs (archaea/eukaryotes/large DNA viruses): hydrophobic beta-strand residues in the conserved sheet of the core subunit.

Summary: Outer-membrane beta-barrel strand–turn architecture, with emphasis on the short turns at the membrane interfaces (especially periplasmic turns) and the C‑terminal beta-signal (terminal aromatic) of translocator barrels across Gram‑negative bacteria and bacterial-derived organelles; the feature marks residues at strand ends, short loop turns on either face, and helix–beta-barrel junctions, rather than soluble plug or non-barrel domains.
Activation pattern: Domain-restricted, multi-peak activation across the beta-barrel transmembrane domain: highest at periplasmic turns/strand termini and frequently at the final C-terminal aromatic residue; additional peaks can occur in short extracellular turns and at helical-to-barrel transition points; little or no activation in N-terminal signal peptides, periplasmic plug domains, or large soluble/helical regions.
Exemplars: - TonB-dependent receptors (e.g., hemophilin receptor): activation confined to the C-terminal barrel, peaking in the loop/turns connecting strands (here predominantly extracellular), absent from the N-terminal plug.
- Specific/general porins (e.g., NanC): strong activation of short periplasmic turns and strand ends at the barrel base.
- Type V autotransporters (e.g., IgA1 protease, Neisseria adhesin A): activation restricted to the C-terminal translocator beta-barrel, including peaks within strands and at the terminal aromatic beta-signal.
- Functional amyloid secretion channel FapF: concentrated on periplasmic turns; includes a periplasmic loop region known to affect outer-membrane insertion.
- Outer-membrane factor TolC (trimeric channel): peaks at helical–beta-barrel junctions in the periplasmic domain and in periplasmic loop connectors.
- Mitochondrial porin/VDAC: sparse peaks within barrel strands and connecting turns; no activation in the N-terminal amphipathic helix.
- Small 8-stranded OMPs (e.g., OmpX): periplasmic turns and the C-terminal aromatic residue.
- Omptin family outer-membrane protease (e.g., plasminogen activator Pla): recurring activation in periplasmic turns and at the C-terminal aromatic beta-signal.

Summary: Compositionally biased low-complexity segments enriched in polar/charged residues (often Lys/Arg‑rich) — typically intrinsically disordered polybasic patches and repeats, with occasional short basic helices — a general sequence/structural property common in viral proteins and DNA‑associated factors rather than a specific motif.
Activation pattern: Regional activation across extended low‑complexity stretches (frequently at N/C termini or linkers) with broad, distributed signal over many residues; minimal signal in well‑folded globular cores; can reappear on isolated short basic helices adjacent to or outside the disordered regions.
Exemplars: - Viral nucleocapsid/core and protamine-/histone-like proteins: strong activation across Lys/Arg‑rich, low‑complexity RNA/DNA‑binding regions used for genome packaging.
- Viral replication proteins (RNA‑dependent RNA polymerases, helicases, methyltransferases/capping enzymes): activation on basic, compositionally biased N/C‑terminal tails and interdomain linkers.
- Viral ubiquitin-system E3 ligases: activation on flexible, charged low‑complexity segments implicated in adaptor/substrate engagement.
- Viral and eukaryotic serine/threonine kinases (especially from large DNA viruses): activation on disordered, basic terminal extensions and insertions.
- DNA-associated nuclear proteins: activation on polybasic, low‑complexity patches (including NLS‑like regions) and other compositionally biased stretches.
- Holocytochrome c‑type synthase: activation over the disordered, compositionally biased N‑terminus containing heme‑regulatory motif repeats and the N‑myristoylation context, silence across the structured core, and re‑activation on a distal basic C‑terminal helix.

Summary: Short secondary-structure transition/capping segments (helix/strand-to-loop linkers and nearby hinges) that are often flexible or low-confidence and frequently flank or include catalytic, ligand-, or metal-binding residues; typically acidic/glycine-enriched and found broadly across enzymes and nucleic-acid–associated proteins
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short contiguous stretches (~8–20 aa) with bell-shaped peaks; commonly starts at the last residues of a helix or strand and peaks in the following loop; multiple such segments can occur per protein; preference for loops/linkers and disordered tails, with occasional inclusion of the residue(s) coordinating metal ions or contributing to catalysis
Exemplars: - CRISPR-associated endoribonuclease Cas2: C-terminal helix–strand–loop junction with peak in a low-pLDDT loop.
- Zn-dependent nuclease: structured-to-loop transitions surrounding Zn2+-coordinating H/E/D residues, with strongest signal in the loop immediately after the coordinating residue.
- Respiratory complex I subunit ND5: disordered C-terminal loop following a short helix; minor signals at strand/turn transitions.
- S-adenosylmethionine decarboxylase: loop bearing the catalytic cysteine that extends into the adjacent helix.
- Prolyl-tRNA editing protein (ProX): inter-strand and strand-to-helix connecting loops.
- Reverse transcriptase: coil between helices and the segment immediately preceding the catalytic D–D metal-binding motif within the RT domain; additional helix/coil connectors.
- Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase: helix containing an L-aspartate–binding residue, nearby loops with allosteric glucose-6-phosphate–binding arginines, and the disordered C-terminal tail.
- Ribosomal large subunit pseudouridine synthase B: beta-to-coil linker preceding a disordered C-terminal tail and a linker following an S4 RNA-binding domain.

Summary: Recognition of repetitive helical segments and hydrophobic/amphipathic motifs—most prominently the X/Y positions of collagen G–X–Y triple-helical repeats, but also contiguous hydrophobic alpha-helical transmembrane segments and proline/glycine-rich low-complexity stretches; predominant in secreted and membrane proteins but also occurring in soluble proteins that present amphipathic helical patches
Activation pattern: Regional activation over stretches: dense, domain-scale activation across collagenous triple-helix regions with zero or minimal signal on the invariant glycine (G) and peaks at X/Y (especially proline/hydrophobic residues); contiguous activation across single-pass or multi-pass transmembrane alpha-helices and amphipathic helical motifs; sparser peaks within short secreted, low-complexity segments; overall bias toward hydrophobic and helix-favoring residues with enrichment for proline and glycine context
Exemplars:
- Fibrillar collagens: strong activation along the triple-helical G–X–Y domain, peaking at X/Y positions (especially proline/hydroxyproline-like Y), with minimal signal on G.
- Light-harvesting complex alpha subunits (photosynthetic bacteria): activation along their single transmembrane alpha-helix.
- YhhN/TMEM86 lysoplasmalogenases: activation across multiple transmembrane segments.
- Viral accessory proteins (including non-membrane factors like replication enhancers), envelope proteins, and viroporins: activation on short hydrophobic or amphipathic helical motifs (membrane-anchored or not).
- Single-pass receptors and small transporters: activation on the transmembrane helix.
- Plant CLE/CLAVATA/ESR peptide precursors: activation on the conserved proline-rich mature peptide region and adjacent low-complexity stretches.
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: activation in the N-terminal secretion/translocation region and nearby low-complexity repeats.
- Fungal secreted/surface-associated effectors (e.g., hydrophobin-like): activation on hydrophobic, repetitive patches outside core cystine motifs.
- Small cysteine-rich toxins/defensin-like peptides: activation on hydrophobic patches within or adjacent to the disulfide-stabilized core.
- Soluble cytosolic enzymes/regulators: activation on internal amphipathic helices or repetitive helical bundles.

Summary: N-terminal leader/targeting segments and the immediate start of mature chains: the feature recognizes cleavable N-terminal signal peptides (h- and c-regions) and transit peptides—often including the lipoprotein lipobox and +1 cysteine—and, more generally, the first structured element (short amphipathic helix/coil) at the beginning of a protein or domain.
Activation pattern: Typically a long, continuous block at the extreme N-terminus of secreted/lipoprotein precursors that spans the C-terminal part of the signal/leader and the first 10–25 residues of the mature chain; in non-secretory/cytosolic proteins it reduces to short N-terminal segments or isolated residue-level peaks in the first helix/coil; occasional single-site peaks at hydrophobic/aromatic positions within early helices of cytosolic domains.
Exemplars: - Vitellogenins (yolk precursors): strong activation beginning at the signal-peptide cleavage site and across the first helix of the mature chain.
- Gram-negative periplasmic/outer-membrane lipoproteins: activation over the signal peptide c-region/lipobox and the lipidated +1 cysteine of the mature protein.
- Plastid/mitochondrial targeting precursors: activation over the N-terminal amphipathic transit peptide and into the nascent mature N-terminus.
- Checkpoint clamp proteins (RAD1/Rad17 family): activation on the N-terminal 10–35 aa spanning the initial β-strand and α-helix.
- Frataxin (CyaY) family: activation on the N-terminal α-helix, including acidic residues that participate in iron binding.
- Flagellar hook protein (FlgE): activation on the early N-terminal helix-to-coil segment.
- Heme oxygenases: activation on an early α-helix in the N-terminal portion of the domain.
- c-di-GMP phosphodiesterases (EAL-domain proteins): isolated activation on a hydrophobic/aromatic residue within a helical segment of the domain.
- Ran-binding proteins (RanBD1 domain): sparse activation in the N-terminal coil immediately preceding the first β-strand.

Summary: Disorder-to-helix initiation segments—typically at extreme N-termini or domain starts—that seed the first α-helix/coiled-coil used for assembly, membrane engagement, or Type VII secretion (e.g., short amphipathic N-helices and LXG/WXG helix–turn–helix starts).
Activation pattern: Short regional activation (≈15–35 aa) centered on the transition from low-complexity/coil to the first structured helix; often begins at Met1, includes a few preceding coil residues and the first helical turn; strongest peaks at hydrophobic/aromatic residues at or just after helix onset; little to no activation in downstream stable helices; occasionally a second weaker site at another helix-start (e.g., a C‑terminal coiled-coil boundary). In bacterial T7SS substrates, peaks often occur around W in the 40–70 region.
Exemplars: - LXG Type VII secretion toxins: activation at the extreme N-terminus within the LXG domain’s initial helix–turn–helix that seeds export/targeting.
- Syntaxins (t-SNAREs): activation across the N-terminal disordered patch into the first α-helix; no signal in the SNARE coiled-coil or TM.
- FG-nucleoporins (e.g., Nup62): activation at the boundary from FG-repeat IDR into the C-terminal coiled-coil anchor.
- ABI/ABL-interactor family (WAVE/SCAR complex): activation at the N-terminal start of a long helical scaffold following a short IDR.
- BLOC-1 complex subunit 8: activation over the N-terminal coil-to-long-helix transition.
- Dps (DNA protection during starvation): activation at the loop-to-first-helix transition that initiates the ferritin-like core.
- Consistent with broader set: ESCRT-III/CHMP N-terminal amphipathic helices (polymer initiation) and WXG100/ESAT-6/Esp/PE/PPE substrates around WxG/YxxxD/E motifs (≈40–70) for Type VII export.

Summary: Polybasic, Ser/Thr‑rich amphipathic helices (typically at extreme N termini) and adjacent low‑complexity basic tracts that mediate transient peripheral binding to acidic membranes and are often tuned by Ser/Thr (frequently Pro‑proximal) phosphorylation
Activation pattern: Regional activation over short‑to‑extended helical segments of intermediate confidence, most prominently in the first 5–20 residues and other semi‑ordered linkers; signal tracks Lys/Arg clusters interleaved with Ser/Thr/Pro repeats and can occur in multiple clusters per protein; little or no activation within well‑folded enzymatic cores or canonical catalytic sites. In SRP receptor FtsY, for example, the feature peaks on the N‑terminal membrane‑targeting amphipathic helix and is absent across the NG/GTPase core.
Exemplars: - SRP receptor FtsY: N‑terminal amphipathic membrane‑targeting helix
- Rab11 recycling adaptors and endocytic/coat assembly proteins: polybasic membrane‑binding helices/linkers that recruit to vesicle coats
- Rho/Rac/Cdc42 regulators (PAKs, RhoGEFs/GAPs, small effectors): basic autoinhibitory/membrane‑targeting N‑terminal segments with Ser/Thr‑Pro regulatory sites
- Membrane–cytoskeleton adaptors/scaffolds (e.g., MARCKS/ERM‑like): polybasic effector domains whose membrane binding is modulated by multisite Ser/Thr phosphorylation
- Yeast eisosome/cortical proteins: amphipathic helices and basic low‑complexity stretches used for plasma‑membrane recruitment
- Plant dehydrins: Lys‑rich K‑segments (amphipathic helices) and Ser‑rich S‑segments that engage acidic membranes
- Viral matrix/envelope/accessory proteins: basic clusters/amphipathic helices for membrane association
- Secreted complement components: positively charged N‑regions of signal peptides and nearby basic stretches at the extreme N terminus

Summary: Short, composition-biased linear “edge” segments at structural boundaries—especially C‑terminal tails and juxta‑membrane helix ends/hinges—often enriched in Pro and/or charge clusters; the same signal extends to long proline‑rich repeats (e.g., collagen PPII/triple‑helix regions) and short cationic/acidic motifs common in secreted and membrane proteins across taxa.
Activation pattern: Predominantly residue‑level hotspots in short spans (≈3–10 aa) at protein edges: extreme C termini, helix caps/breaks, and immediately cytosolic to a transmembrane exit; suppressed over well‑ordered helical cores and catalytic/metal‑binding sites. In proline‑rich proteins (collagens/collagen‑like), activation expands into long continuous runs. Signals frequently coincide with a local drop in structural confidence or a coil interruption, but can also occur in high‑confidence juxta‑membrane helices.
Exemplars: - Multi‑pass membrane proteins/transporters: hinge or helix‑break motifs preceding disordered C‑tails (short K/R/L hotspots at the first helix interruption).
- Ribosomal P1 acidic stalk proteins: final few residues forming a short, low‑confidence C‑terminal helix within the disordered tail.
- GPI‑anchor remodeling enzyme PGAP3: a cytosolic EDD triad immediately after a transmembrane helix (juxta‑membrane helix cap), including a disease‑linked Asp.
- Collagens and collagen‑like extracellular proteins: long proline‑rich Gly‑X‑Y repeats (PPII/triple‑helix segments).
- Oomycete RxLR effectors: N‑terminal RxLR/EER regions and adjacent basic clusters used for host targeting.
- Short secreted bioactive peptides and venoms: cationic amphipathic segments and Pro/Gly‑mediated kinks in the mature peptide.
- TOM22 (mitochondrial import receptor): cytosolic/juxta‑membrane receptor tail that engages targeting peptides.
- Lipid phosphatases/ceramidases and other membrane lipid enzymes: charged juxta‑membrane cytosolic loops or helix caps adjacent to TM segments.
- Alternative oxidase/cytochrome b559 components: short interfacial/juxta‑membrane segments next to their anchors.
- Coiled‑coil/Golgi/cytoskeletal scaffolds and Ripply family: short conserved, composition‑biased motif regions within otherwise low‑complexity or coiled‑coil contexts.

Summary: Short amphipathic alpha-helical segments with coiled-coil–like heptad repeat character (hydrophobics mixed with charged residues), often including helix–coil junction/capping motifs used in scaffolding/tethering interactions across taxa.
Activation pattern: Regional activation in short 6–15 aa windows; strongest within an alpha-helix and frequently spilling a few residues into adjacent coil; multiple independent windows along long helical/coiled-coil scaffolds; peaks often on helix residues (e.g., Leu/Ala/Val) with neighboring charged positions; moderate pLDDT in helices and lower in flanking coil; position-agnostic along the sequence.
Exemplars: - Ribosomal protein L31 (bacterial/organellar): end of a C‑terminal helix and adjacent flexible tail.
- Intermediate filament rod domain (Coil 2): short heptad-repeat segment within the coiled-coil and the rod–tail junction.
- Anaphase-promoting complex scaffold (APC subunit 2): C‑terminal helical segment and immediate downstream coil.
- Cullin scaffolds (ubiquitin ligase cullins): multiple short helices, including within the C‑terminal neddylation region and at helix–coil transitions.
- rRNA-processing factor RRP17: annotated coiled-coil helix segment.

Summary: Short, hydrophobic/π-rich interface segment—typically an amphipathic α-helix or adjoining β–β–α patch—that serves as a binding hotspot in large macromolecular assemblies and nucleic‑acid enzymes, sometimes incorporating basic clusters for RNA contact or acidic residues for metal coordination.
Activation pattern: Regional activation: a single contiguous block (~20–80 aa), most often in the N‑ to mid‑portion of the protein, with strongest peaks on an α‑helix or a loop bridging β‑strands; generally well‑structured (high pLDDT) but can include flexible/disordered loops in some families; occasionally overlaps catalytic/metal‑binding residues in nucleases.
Exemplars: - TRAPP trafficking complex subunit: C‑terminal interface helix with flanking β elements used for subunit packing.
- Mitochondrial translation initiation factor IF‑3: CTD α‑helix at the 30S/28S binding surface.
- CRISPR Cas6 endoribonuclease: C‑terminal β–β–α element involved in RNA recognition/dimerization.
- RusA crossover endonuclease: active‑site helix harboring Mg2+‑binding acidic residues of the RNase H‑like fold.
- Dynein light chain Tctex‑type: long loop between β‑strands that docks partner chains/cargo.
- Kinetochore protein Spc24: C‑terminal helix/coil patch forming the interface with Spc25/Ndc80.

Summary: A general signal for intrinsically disordered, low-complexity N-terminal leader regions—encompassing signal peptides/propeptides and flexible N-terminal extensions—often enriched in Y/P/G/S and containing short helices/adjacent coils; the feature frequently peaks at or immediately flanking signal peptide cleavage sites and is absent from stable transmembrane segments and well-folded catalytic domains.
Activation pattern: Primarily regional N-terminal activation with sharp residue-level peaks (e.g., at cleavage junctions or isolated Pro/Tyr within coils); strong preference for low-pLDDT segments and short helices/coils; little to no activation across transmembrane helices or structured enzymatic cores; occasional isolated peaks in other low-complexity coils.
Exemplars: - RxLR secreted effectors (oomycete effectors): strong activation across the N-terminal signal peptide; additional isolated peaks at Pro residues in disordered coils and weak signal near the RxLR motif (consistent with low pLDDT).
- Vacuolating cytotoxin (Helicobacter pylori VacA): sharp peak at the signal peptide cleavage site (first residue of the mature chain) with weaker activation in the C-terminal end of the signal peptide; no spread into the folded toxin domain.
- Bacterial DNA ligase: activation confined to a low-confidence, disordered N-terminal extension of unknown function; no activation in the well-structured ligase domain.
- Viral small type I membrane/accessory proteins: activation at the extreme N-terminus preceding the transmembrane helix; absence across the TM helix and subsequent ordered regions.
- Secreted/precursor and microprotein-like entries across taxa: activation on Y/P/G/S-rich low-complexity N-termini or short helical leader segments, consistent with widespread, length-independent detection of flexible N-terminal leaders.

Summary: Hydrophobic, Leu/Ile/Phe/Ala‑enriched alpha‑helical segments that form helix–helix packing faces (often amphipathic and coiled‑coil–like) used for intra-/intermolecular helical interfaces across diverse proteins, rather than catalytic motifs
Activation pattern: Regional activation on short to medium alpha‑helices with contiguous runs of hydrophobic residues; sharp residue‑level peaks at Leu/Ile (often at i and i+3/4 positions of a heptad‑like pattern); multiple such patches per protein in well‑structured regions; occurs in soluble domains and extra-/cytoplasmic portions of membrane proteins, not restricted to transmembranes
Exemplars: - Type VII secretion system component (EccE3): strong activation on two cytosolic helices with Leu peaks spaced four residues apart, consistent with a coiled‑coil/helix‑interface segment.
- Podocalyxin-like type I membrane adhesion/mucin: localized activation on a short helical patch in the ectodomain upstream of the transmembrane region, indicative of a structural/dimerization helix.
- AIG1-type GTPase domain protein (chloroplast translocase–associated): activation on helical elements within the G domain away from P‑loop motifs, matching noncatalytic helix‑packing faces.
- Cyclic dinucleotide synthase (cGAS/DncV‑like enzyme): activation on long core helices in the catalytic fold, not overlapping catalytic residues, consistent with helix–helix packing surfaces.
- Chitin synthase (processive GT2 glycosyltransferase): activation on a well‑structured helix in the catalytic region (including a glycosylation‑adjacent stretch), fitting an amphipathic helix interface.

Summary: Short coil/turn connectors between adjacent alpha-helices in alpha‑solenoid helical repeat scaffolds—especially the inter‑helical loop of TPR/TPR‑like and SEL1‑like repeats, and analogous helix–helix linkers in HEAT/ARM‑type assemblies—used by large adaptor/scaffold proteins in eukaryotic complexes and organelle receptors
